column16: A dashboard that allows users to visualize the information on reported knowledge products and datasets from the MEL platform.
column17: The WorldFish MEL System and its related repositories—WF Dataverse and DSpace—store extensive data, knowledge, and information on aquatic foods. However, they have historically lacked a user-friendly interface that enables researchers, academics, students, policymakers, NGOs, and other CGIAR centers to easily explore, synthesize, and summarize the available data and knowledge products.; To address this gap, an innovative dashboard has been developed, allowing users to visualize the types of datasets and knowledge products stored in WorldFish Dataverse and DSpace, together with their key characteristics and metadata. The dashboard also includes data analytics on user access patterns and interests, helping to identify evolving research priorities and data needs across different stakeholder groups over time.; This tool provides a simple and efficient way to navigate and access aquatic food system data, supporting more informed decision-making, research planning, and evidence uptake. The dashboard is currently available and actively used within WorldFish and through the public DSpace website.; Currently, the dashboard is accessible via FishNet, the WorldFish internal intranet platform, to more than 350 people. Its integration into FishNet ensures that all WorldFish staff are systematically informed about available datasets and knowledge products, strengthening internal knowledge sharing, cross-program collaboration, and the consistent use of institutional evidence across research, MEL, and engagement activities.

column16: Micronutrient contribution modeling integrated with a near real-time fisheries monitoring system (PeskAAS) helps close population-level nutrition gaps through sustainable fisheries.
column17: This work introduces a novel approach to calculating and visualizing the nutrient composition of fisheries catches within an integrated fisheries monitoring and automated analytics workflow in Timor-Leste. The approach provides decision-makers with actionable guidance on the contribution of fisheries to recommended daily intakes of key micronutrients, including zinc, vitamin A, selenium, calcium, iron, protein, and omega-3 fatty acids. By explicitly linking fisheries data to nutritional outcomes, the system shifts the focus from catch volumes to nutrient yields, enabling fisheries management to better address population-level nutrient gaps and contribute more effectively to the reduction of malnutrition.; The nutrition module is currently operational and fully integrated into Timor-Leste’s Peskas digital platform - managing 15,000ha of coastline, with planned scale-up to four additional countries supported through bilateral investments. Beyond its operational relevance, the module has strong scientific value: the underlying concept has been peer-reviewed, with a publication accepted and currently in press at Nature Food.

column16: WorldFish Aquatic Food Ontology enables standardized global data analysis across CGIAR Initiative on Aquatic Foods
column17: The Aquatic Food Ontology (AQFO) is an innovation currently used to enable efficient aggregation and analysis of aquatic food data generated by the CGIAR Initiative on Aquatic Foods and WorldFish. By structuring the meaning and relationships between terms, AQFO provides a common language for data interoperability, facilitating harmonization across datasets. The standardization of aquatic food data labels using controlled vocabularies ensures greater consistency, easier data integration, and improved analytical capabilities.; AQFO is hosted on AgroPortal and is built upon FAO AGROVOC terminology, complemented by terms derived from WorldFish innovations. As the ontology continues to evolve, its application supports seamless data sharing and interpretation across research, policy, and decision-making processes, enhancing the impact and scalability of aquatic food system innovations.; In 2025, AQFO is undergoing further enhancements to improve its AI readiness and interoperability with other data systems and ontologies. These improvements aim to strengthen machine readability, enable more advanced analytics and AI-assisted applications, and ensure compatibility with emerging CGIAR and external semantic frameworks, thereby increasing its long-term usability and integration potential.

column16: Digital data collection system for understanding and comparing small-scale aquaculture systems and their sustainability
column17: WorldFish has developed a digital data collection and analysis system that allows to understand and compare how aquaculture systems operate and perform across countries. The system combines standardized surveys and analytical methods to describe production practices, livelihoods, sustainability outcomes, and risks in a consistent and comparable way.  The innovation addresses a major gap in aquaculture development: although small-scale aquaculture supports millions of households, it is poorly represented in national statistics and global analyses, which are often too general to guide effective policy, investment, or support programs. By generating reliable and fine-grained data, the system enables evidence-based decision-making for research, policy formulation, and sustainable aquaculture planning. The system has been tested and applied in Bangladesh, Egypt, Kenya, Myanmar, Nigeria, and India, and has been adopted by a bilateral project to support baseline assessments and benchmarking of aquaculture systems.

column16: Inclusive Business Models ensuring access and adoption to climate smart solution for fish farmers in Southeast Africa
column17: Inclusive business models are essential for ensuring small-scale fish farmers have access to quality feeds, seeds, extension services, and training. Partnering with the private sector, an accelerator grant program was co-designed to reduce risks and scale climate-smart aquaculture (CSA) innovations. Six small and medium enterprises (SMEs) received these grants to expand CSA adoption among smallholder farmers. Each SME operates within the aquaculture value chain, integrating CSA practices and Climate Information System (CIS) extension services. This approach has accelerated the uptake of innovative solutions, benefiting 45,154 farmers (36% women) who now have access to millions of high-quality fingerlings and premium-priced fish markets. Farmers have adopted modern fishpond designs resilient to flooding and drought and receive timely weather updates from the Zambia Meteorological Department via WhatsApp and radio, enabling better planning of farming activities. This approach demonstrates the impact of public-private collaboration in scaling sustainable aquaculture practices for smallholder farmers.

column16: System-based theory of change is an improved methodology used by evaluators, managers, and other stakeholders to develop practical theories of change for interventions in the aquatic food system space.
column17: A systems-based Theory of Change (ToC) methodology has been applied for the first time to aquatic food systems projects and interventions. This approach advances standard ToC practice by integrating systems mapping, enabling a clearer link between system dynamics and impact pathways. It supports the development of practical, context-aware Theories of Change that explicitly incorporate feedback loops, broader contextual factors, and potential negative or unintended outcomes. The methodology has been adopted across projects in Bangladesh, Kenya, Nigeria, Tanzania, and Zambia and is now being scaled to additional WorldFish initiatives. More recently, it was applied to a case study on digital and data gaps and needs in aquatic food systems to support more structured and context-sensitive analysis. Rather than relying on a linear results chain, the approach used systems mapping to examine interactions among data flows, digital tools, institutions, and stakeholders across aquaculture and fisheries value chains. Insights from this application are feeding into continuous learning processes, allowing the methodology to be refined and adapted to diverse contexts and analytical purposes. This strengthens its relevance and effectiveness for guiding sustainable transformation, evidence-based planning, and innovation design within aquatic food systems.

column16: Contextualized better management practices (BMPs) to support tilapia grow out operations in Timor-Leste
column17: Better Management Practices (BMPs) for grow out production were developed to support the development and scaling of tilapia farming in Timor-Leste. The BMPs manual was published in English and Tetum to provide guidelines for sustainable tilapia production systems in Timor-Leste and to serve as a handbook for aquaculture technicians/practitioners from different stakeholders such as I/NGOs and private sectors. Farmers’ participatory grow-out trials following Better Management Practices (BMPs) were conducted from 2015 to 2023 across ten farmer clusters in four inland municipalities of Timor-Leste. The trials, carried out in two phases, aimed to improve GIFT (Genetically Improved Farmed Tilapia) production by optimizing stocking density, feed quality, and management practices.

column16: 6,000 farmers in Odisha, India, use the ISAT Climate Information Services to enhance productivity and manage climate risks
column17: The ISAT platform, a collaborative effort between ICRISAT, CGIAR, Microsoft, and the India Meteorological Department, with support from the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), has been at the forefront of providing farmers with vital information that can significantly enhance their decision-making processes. More than 6,000 farmers in Odisha, India, use the ISAT Climate Information Services to enhance productivity and manage climate risks. In a continued effort to empower farmers with timely and accurate farming advisories, a team from the ICRISAT recently conducted a field visit to Rayagada and Gajapati districts. This visit enhanced farmers' awareness of region-specific digital climate advisories, while also gathering feedback on the pre-seasonal and in-season guidance delivered via the ISAT platform. The need for village-level training emerged as a top priority for maximizing the benefits of climate information services. ; ; No activities implemented in 2025 due to budget limitation.

column16: Nature Positive Solutions raises awareness about the importance of Neglected and Underutilized Species (NUS) in Burkina Faso
column17: The course "Manuel pratique pour initier les enfants à la connaissance de l’importance des NUS au Burkina Faso" has proven to be an effective tool in raising awareness about the importance of Neglected and Underutilized Species (NUS) in Burkina Faso. Given its success, the initiative will now be expanded, with plans to implement the course in additional countries involved in the project, including Niger, a neighbouring country. This expansion marks a significant step in spreading awareness and promoting the benefits of NUS across the region. Additionally, a detailed report and blog post from the A3.4 Workshop held in July on the NUS platform in Burkina Faso highlight the program’s impact and collaborative momentum. This initiative lays the groundwork for a future continental platform dedicated to NUS, which would not only consolidate regional efforts but also amplify the impact of NUS in sustainable agriculture and food security across Africa.

column16: Sustainable Healthy Diets country coordination unit in Bangladesh supported national partners in implementing the food systems transformation agenda
column17: REVISE. Since the previous CGIAR portfolio (2022-2024) and continuing with Better Diets and Nutrition, the country coordination units (CCUs) in a subset of countries play a central part of the program's strategy to strengthen the connections between CGIAR researchers and national partners in food systems policy processes. In 2024, the CCU in Bangladesh was established and several meetings were held to share updates on research activities and to consult with the two government partners, also known as Strategic Partners, on progress and opportunities relative to food systems transformation in Bangladesh. In 2025, the CCU, coordinated by the Better Diets and Nutrition Country Coordinator, was instrumental in several other results reported in this year's annual report, including the launch of a new training of trainers (ToT) program on food systems for sustainable healthy diets and the participation in the development of the government's new food systems transformation strategy called the Plan of Action...

column16: CGIAR and national research teams globally adopted Enterprise Breeding System for centralized crop breeding data management
column17: The Enterprise Breeding System (EBS) is a digital platform that helps crop breeding teams organize, store, and analyze their research data more effectively. Multiple CGIAR centers including AfricaRice, CIAT, CIMMYT, CIP, ICARDA, IITA, and IRRI, along with National Agricultural Research and Extension Systems teams, integrated EBS into their daily breeding operations. This adoption replaced fragmented data management approaches with a unified system that enables better collaboration between research centers and more informed decision-making in developing improved crop varieties. The system standardizes how breeding data is collected and shared across different crops and locations, ultimately accelerating the development of better-performing varieties for farmers worldwide.

column16: Two National Programs (NARES) that are partners to IRRI onboarded the Enterprise Breeding System ahead of the planned schedule for NARES adoption
column17: The successful early adoption of the Enterprise Breeding System (EBS) by two National Agricultural Research and Extension Systems (NARES) partners, BRRI and PhilRice, represents a significant milestone in modernizing breeding operations across CGIAR-NARES Breeding Networks. These two national programs, both key collaborators with IRRI, integrated EBS into their breeding processes ahead of the scheduled timeline, setting a benchmark for other NARES partners. This early adoption strengthens the EBS's role as the central data management platform for various crops, enhancing the efficiency and scalability of breeding operations. This achievement accelerates the deployment of cutting-edge tools across the broader CGIAR-NARES community, driving better data-driven decision-making and faster crop improvement for food security.

column16: Using automatic speech recognition to transcribe voice messages from African farmers
column17: How do you gather qualitative information from thousands of people, quickly and at scale? That's a question Farm Radio International, a communication for development organization that uses interactive radio as its primary tool to reach and amplify the voices of rural Africans, has an answer to: On Air Dialogues. This on-air polling process uses Interactive Voice Response technology in tandem with Farm Radio's Uliza Interactive suite of services. column16: South Asia Drought Monitoring System (SADMS) remote-data driven monitoring platform is used for drought management in Asia and Africa
column17: The South Asia Drought Monitoring System (SADMS) is an advanced, remote-data-driven platform designed for drought management across Asia and Africa. It empowers farmers, authorities, and extension workers with tools to monitor and mitigate drought impacts effectively. Integrating real-time weather updates with satellite data, SADMS enables (1) district-level drought forecasting and severity monitoring, (2) activation of contingency plans to protect smallholder farmers during droughts, and (3) analysis of satellite and regional data to inform decisions. Originally developed in South Asia, the platform’s success led to its adaptation in Africa, where similar systems were established in Zambia and Pakistan. SADMS exemplifies a scalable and innovative solution that builds resilience in communities facing climatic challenges. By safeguarding vulnerable populations, the platform demonstrates its adaptability and significance in addressing environmental adversity, ensuring proactive drought management at both local and national levels.

column16: Seeds of Change: Transforming School Meals with Biofortified Crops in Malawi
column17: The Seed Equal (SE) initiative is transforming school meals in Malawi by integrating biofortified crops into the Home-Grown School Feeding Program (HGSFP). In collaboration with the Ministry of Education and supported by the European Union (EU) and the World Food Programme (WFP), SE has introduced nutrient-rich crops like high-iron beans, orange-fleshed sweet potatoes (OFSP), and orange maize flour in select schools across Southern Malawi. Training sessions for school feeding committees, lead farmers, and care group promoters have been conducted to enhance the production and utilization of these crops. Awareness meetings have also been held to promote the benefits of biofortified crops, aiming to improve nutrition and food security for school children.

column16: Livestock farmer group model for better innovation uptake in Mai Son District, Son La Province, Vietnam
column17: Since 2023, SAPLING has been assisting eight livestock farmer groups in Mai Son District, Son La Province, Vietnam, as part of efforts to transform the region’s livestock sector. This group model has effectively encouraged smallholder farmers in the area to adopt new technical innovations. By October 2024, membership in these groups grew to 692 households, up from 127 in October 2023. Of the total, 208 households were represented by women, and 484 were represented by men. Each of the 692 households has implemented at least one of SAPLING’s innovations, such as artificial insemination, improved feeds and forages, or animal health practices, impacting around 3,321 individuals based on an average household size of 4.8.

column16: CGIAR breeding centers allocate funding using impact data from Global Market Intelligence Platform across eight research institutes
column17: Multiple CGIAR research centers now systematically use impact opportunity data from the Global Market Intelligence Platform (GloMIP) to guide their breeding program funding decisions. This represents a shift toward evidence-based resource allocation in crop breeding. The platform provides market intelligence through the Harmonised Crop Report and Program Management Platform, both components of the CGIAR Breeding Hub. Eight international agricultural research centers including CIMMYT, IRRI, ICARDA, and others have integrated this data-driven approach into their budget planning processes. This outcome enables more strategic investment in breeding programs by identifying crops and regions with the highest potential impact for addressing climate change, nutrition, and poverty challenges globally.

column16: Scaling Readiness mainstreamed by CGIAR to operationalize its 2030 Research and Innovation Strategy
column17: Scaling Readiness is a component of the new CGIAR performance and results management system (PRMS). Keep overview and track Innovations in an evidence-based way (Innovation Profiling); 2. Agricultural innovation system synergies around packages of innovation (design innovation packages and assess their scaling readiness); 3. Fit-for-purpose partnerships to tackle innovation and scaling bottlenecks (Scaling Strategies); 4. Inform CGIAR innovation portfolio management (prioritization, portfolio diversity, risk management, strategic resource mobilization); ; In 2023, CGIAR Initiatives reported around 900 Innovations under development using key Scaling Readiness metrics. Of the 181 Innovation Use results reported, 47 were reported as innovation Packages that were assessed for their Scaling Readiness. Funders have expressed interest in using the Scaling Readiness approach and learn from the CGIAR mainstreaming journey

column16: VarScout empowers farmers and researchers in Latin America  to conserve crop diversity and adapt to climate challenges
column17: Since 2022, the VarScout mobile app and online interface has supported the documentation and monitoring of varietal diversity – including potato landraces - through citizen science in Peru and Colombia. VarScout is basically the tool that allows for registering varietal observations. ; ; Between 2022 and 2025 in Peru 5,744 observations were made using VarScout covering 3,084 unique potato landraces, contributed by 282 different users and linking 452 farmer households, with data collection concentrated in key highland departments such as Cusco, Pasco, and Puno, reflecting growing level of engagement and varietal richness. The tools is being adopted by a widening community of conservation practitioners, including public institutions (INIA, Ministry of Education), farmers groups and NGOs. In Colombia (2023–2025), the use of VarScout is still at an early stage and 117 observations representing 89 unique landraces were made. All records are concentrated in the Nariño where the Cumbal landscape is located (MFL flagship landscape).  ; ; The use of VarScout plays a vital role in registering varietal observations. In 2025, the tools itself was updated (see: https://www.varscout.org/) and its use expanded to new crops such as peppers, cassava and maize. In terms of use of innovation, the promotion of citizen science contests for agrobiodiversity monitoring have been a major ‘pull factor’.

column16: Underground flood transfer technology adopted by Indian government across hundreds of villages in Uttar Pradesh, India
column17: A novel form of managed aquifer recharge known as underground transfer of floods for irrigation (UTFI) has been piloted in the Ganges Basin, enabling extensive evidence gathering and stakeholder engagment. UTFI has since been recognized as an important part of the solution to two crises facing India: destructive floods and recurring water shortages. The CGIAR Initiative on NEXUS Gains is now supporting the Government of Uttar Pradesh to better implement a national water conservation program. As a result, UTFI ponds and recharge wells have been constructed in hundreds more villages, increasing groundwater availability by up to 8 percent to date and strengthening climate resilience.

column16: Accelerating Zambia’s bean seed systems
column17: The Seed Equal Initiative (SEI) is playing a crucial role in accelerating Zambia's bean seed systems. In collaboration with the Zambia Agricultural Research Institute (ZARI) and supported by the Feed the Future initiative through USAID, SEI focuses on enhancing the production and distribution of biofortified bean varieties like Mbereshi, Kabulangeti, and Lungwebungu. These beans are valued for their nutritional benefits, particularly in combating iron deficiency. The initiative has significantly boosted bean seed production, with Early Generation Seed production increasing by 221.4% and certified seed production growing six-fold between 2021 and 2023. SEI's efforts are complemented by the Accelerated Innovation Delivery Initiative (AID-I), which aims to improve food production and agricultural sustainability across sub-Saharan Africa. Through these integrated efforts, SEI and its partners are transforming bean value chains, promoting greater consumption, and enhancing the livelihoods of smallholder farmers in Zambia

column16: Use of citizen science with youth engagement in the Andes between Peru  and Colombia
column17: The use of citizen science to monitor biodiversity is widely applied for wild diversity such as bees, birds, manta rays and corral reefs. The popularization of applications like e-bird, i-naturalist, PlantNet, QuestaGame, among many others, has added global efforts.  Yet, practitioners working on on-farm or in-situ conservation of crop landraces or ancestral animal breeds, till date, have made less progress innovating the way biodiversity monitoring is conducted.  ; ; The International Potato Center (CIP), in collaboration with partners from the Andean region, has been advancing citizen science as an innovation for landrace monitoring.  In Peru, the National Citizen Science Contest "Guardians of Native Potatoes" – organized together with Peru’s National Science Council (CONCYTEC) and International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) – has promoted landrace monitoring through youth engagement in Peru. ; ; In Peru, participation included 161 participants in the potato landrace observation category (Category 1) and 109 participants in the cultural category (Category 2). Together, these efforts resulted in the documentation of 1,589 unique landraces and more than 2,386 observations, with contributions from approximately 124 farmers across multiple regions of the country. The citizen science initiative successfully connected youth, farming households, and local knowledge through digital tools, linking the ‘student-teacher-parent’ triangle, and cultural expressions, strengthening the systematic monitoring and visibility intraspecific diversity and its conservation. ; ; In Colombia, a much smaller initiative was implemented in Cumbal (Nariño) through the national genebank (AGROSAVIA) in close collaboration with an indigenous school. Institutions in Bolivia and Chile have closely observed the Peru experience, received capacity building, and will implement the same approach in 2026.

column16: Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development in Vietnam pilots mechanized direct seeding in One Million Hectare High Quality and Low Emission Rice Project in Can Tho, Soc Trang, Tra VinhProvince
column17: The one-million-hectare project, where the mechanized direct seeding technology is adopted by the government as key innovation for improved  productivity and rescued greenhouse gas emissions in rice, is implemented in 12 provinces and cities in the Mekong River Delta. Prior to widespread execution, the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD) established model sites in Can Tho City, Tra Vinh, Soc Trang, Kien Giang, and Dong Thap Provinces. The one-million-hectare program, with an emphasis on high quality, low-emission rice production and green growth in the Mekong Delta until 2030, is the first large-scale strategy in the worldwide rice sector. According to the Department of Crop Production (DCP), under MARD's guidance, seven pilot models have been carried out in five localities: Kien Giang, Soc Trang, Tra Vinh, Dong Thap, and Can Tho City, in conjunction with IRRI and private partners.

column16: A robust breeding system (BRIO) for common bean established within the east and central Africa bean research network (ECABREN) component of the Pan Africa Bean
column17: The initial research strategy centered on a pioneering plant breeding method developed by an Australian team, known as BRIO. BRIO stands for accurate breeding values (using genomic and pedigree data), rapid breeding cycles, a selection index for multiple traits, and optimized mating designs via optimal contributions selection (OCS). Early in the project, theoretical results from BRIO applied to crops like canola showed promise. By year four, field trials by the Australian team confirmed superior breeding outcomes, particularly for grain yield and seed quality in commercial canola (Cowling et al., 2023) and improved traits in field peas with lower heritability (Castro-Urrea et al., 2023). This approach has now been adapted for common beans within the East and Central Africa Bean Research Network (ECABREN), under the Pan Africa Bean Research Alliance (PABRA). Breeding is based at the Alliance-CIAT in Uganda, with field trials for selection implemented across six partnering countries.

column16: A survey finds that the ISAT Climate Information Services is the most commonly used source of weather information among farmers in Odisha
column17: This use case focuses on delivering tailored climate information to farmers in two districts of Odisha. The project aims to provide location-specific climate advisories, including weather forecasts and farming recommendations, to help farmers make informed decisions about their agricultural activities. The survey found that the ISAT Climate Information Services is the most commonly used source of weather information among farmers in Odisha (39%). By providing context-specific information, the project supports farmers in optimizing their farming practices, managing climate risks, and improving overall productivity. The study also investigates how farmers use this information in their decision-making processes, highlighting the impact of climate advisories on their choices regarding crop selection, sowing time, and other critical farming operations. Ultimately, this work seeks to understand how digital climate services can empower farmers and enhance the resilience of their farming systems.; ; No activities implemented in 2025.

column16: Impact of CGIAR crop research on global agricultural productivity and poverty reduction: a retrospective analysis (1960–2020)
column17: This study brings together an expanded set of evidence on the diffusion and productivity impact of CGIAR crop research through 2020, and breaks out these impacts by crop, region, and over time. It was developed by two CGIAR-external authors. It is one of the most comprehensive studies on the impact of CGIAR crop innovations. The study found that by 2016–2020, CGIAR-related crop technologies had been adopted on at least 221 million hectares across Asia, Africa and Latin America, generating economic welfare gains of $47 billion annually. In addition to raising farm income, productivity gains in staple crops have lowered food prices, thereby benefitting the whole population. This is a key reason why agricultural productivity growth, and food crop productivity growth in particular, has had greater impacts on poverty reduction in low-income countries than comparable productivity growth in other sectors.

column16: National research institutes in Cambodia and Laos produced  98,157 clean cassava plants using rapid multiplication tunnel technology
column17: National partners in Laos and Cambodia have successfully utilized cassava rapid stem multiplication tunnels, a technology developed by CIAT, to produce an impressive 66,888 basic ‘seed’ cassava plants. This initiative has also focused on introducing elite and disease-resistant varieties for thorough evaluation and experimentation. CIAT introduced cassava rapid stem multiplication technology to national partners in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia to accelerate early generation seed multiplication. To track clean seed production, CIAT is working with the Lao National Agriculture and Forestry Institute (NAFRI), Cambodian Agricultural Research for Development Institute (CARDI) and General Directorate of Agriculture (GDA) under the scope of an ACIAR-funded project. This represents the first improved cassava seed multiplication system to be adopted by the NARES in both countries.

column16: Adoption of feeds & forages and animal health innovations by livestock producers, through co-investment by local partners in Mai Son district, Son La province, Vietnam
column17: This outcome reports on the number of households adopting SAPLING's innovations on Feeds and Forages and Animal Health for cattle and pigs in Vietnam, through strong partnership and co-investment from a local partner - Agricultural Service Center (ASC). With co-investment of approximately $14,000 from the ASC, 34 training sessions with 1,183 farmers, of which 775 were men (65.5%) and 408 (34.5%) were women, were conducted in 9 communes of Mai Son district. Follow up monitoring reported 1,181 households adopted one or more Feeds & Forages or Animal Health innovations following the training. Using an average household size of 4.8 (Hammond et al., 2021), this corresponds to 5,670 beneficiaries.

column16: Nigerian farmers adopt AKILIMO site specific recommendations developed by International Institute of Tropical Agriculture and Partners
column17: Cassava farmers in Nigeria are implementing personalized agricultural recommendations provided by AKILIMO, a decision support tool developed by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture. ; The tool analyzes local soil conditions, weather patterns, market prices, and individual farm characteristics to recommend optimal fertilizer types, application rates, and planting windows and practices. Evidence from farmer surveys demonstrates widespread adoption of these recommendations, with farmers applying suggested fertilizer formulations and implementing improved planting techniques. This uptake represents successful scaling of digital agricultural technology adapted for smallholder farmers, contributing to more productive and profitable cassava farming systems while addressing soil health and sustainable intensification challenges in West Africa.; ; Maize farmers in Kano, Nigeria receive safe planting window recommendations from this innovation. Other recommendations are beeing developped for maize farmers.

column16: Low glycemic index and high protein rice to transform health benefits of rice consumers
column17: The escalating global burden of diabetes underscores the urgent need for rice varieties that are inherently diabetic-friendly while maintaining agronomic performance. Here, we report the development of high-yielding recombinant inbred lines combining ultra-low to low glycemic index (GI) with elevated protein content (14–16%) in milled rice—an achievement not previously realized within a single genetic background. By integrating genomics, metabolomics, and predictive modeling, we moved beyond trait description to mechanistic dissection, identifying OsSBEIIb as a central regulator and uncovering additional candidate loci within the chromosome 2 interval (qGI2.1/qAC2.1; 18.62–19.95 Mb) that jointly modulate amylose content and GI. This integrative systems-level strategy enabled the rational selection of elite lines, including HAHP_101, which combines low GI with enhanced protein quality enriched in essential amino acids such as lysine. This work establishes a genomics-guided breeding framework for simultaneous improvement of glycemic response and protein density in rice without compromising yield potential.

column16: Local institutions in Mai Son district, Vietnam adopt and promote livestock feed innovations developed by CGIAR
column17: Local institutions in Mai Son district, Son La province, Vietnam have strengthened their capacity to promote and sustain livestock feed and forage innovations developed through CGIAR's Sustainable Animal and Aquatic Foods program. The Son La Sub-Department of Animal Husbandry, Agricultural Service Center, Northern Mountainous Agriculture and Forestry Sciences Institute, and four commune People's Committees now actively promote these innovations through enhanced technical expertise and community engagement strategies. This institutional adoption was formalized through Resolution No. 75/2023, which ensures continued government support for forage cultivation and feed innovations in disadvantaged areas. The innovations address seasonal feed shortages during droughts while providing environmental and economic benefits to farming communities in this mountainous region of northern Vietnam.

column16: Harvest warnings based on weather forecasts through interactive voice messaging deployed to mungbean farmers in Bangladesh
column17: The interactive voice response (IVR) system provides automated real-time weather alerts, warning farmers to harvest their mung bean ahead of forecasted heavy rainfall events which could damage their crop. Harvest warnings are voice calls that are based on a 5-day weather forecasts. It is available and accessible to farmers in Bangladesh without smartphones. Currently, the Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) Initiative is allocating resources for the continuous development, improvement, maintenance, and scaling of the system to achieve impacts at scale. In 2024, voice calls were made regarding rain forecasts with harvest warnings to 13,806 Mung bean farmers (12,751 men and 1,055 women) during the mungbean harvesting period (March to May 2024) across fifty-one (51) locations/unions in Patuakhali District and nineteen (19) locations/unions in Barguna District.

column16: Automated water level sensors adopted by farmers in Can Tho, Vietnam to improve management of rice production
column17: As part of the Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) thrust to increase efficiency of rice production and reduce methane emissions, automated water level sensors are co-developed and scaled in Vietnam together with the Department of Crop Production. These sensors are now installed in around 44 farms in Can Tho, Co Do district and are being adopted by farmer-members of 2 cooperatives. column16: Improved access of farmers in Bangladesh to weather forecast-based agro-advisories through the Agvisely for Crops tool
column17: "Agvisely" is an agrometerological advisory tool that was developed and released in 2019 jointly by the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE) and the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD). Currently, it provide advisories to farmers planting crops including rice, maize, and mungbean through an interactive website that can be access by extension agents to provide information to farmers in Bangladesh as a whole. The advisories are based on a automated 5-day weather forecasts using biological threshhold and forecast data. The tool aims to help the farmers to increase fertilizer use efficiency, irrigation management, and pest management leading to increase in yield and income. The Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) Initiative is allocating resources for the continuous development, improvement, maintenance, and scaling of Agvisely tool to achieve impacts at scale. In 2024, Agvisely has reached 15,000 farmers as seen in the evidence provided.

column16: Improved access of farmers in Vietnam to agro-climatic advisories for informed climate adaptive farm practices
column17: The agro-climatic bulletin (ACB) is an agro-advisory system based on a seasonal, monthly, and 10-day weather forecast that aims to provide climate advisory services to local agricultural institutions, officials, and farmers in Vietnam. It is being co-developed and delivered through the public systems in Vietnam where sub-national offices are integrating the tool on their local agricultural development planning and decision-making. ACB is being scaled by the Department of Crop Production (now known as Plant Production and Protection Department - PPPD) to disseminate agro-climatic advisories to farmers (especially women) in Vietnam. In 2025, ACBs were produced and disseminated across five Mekong River Delta (MRD) provinces, corresponding to 13 former provinces prior to Vietnam’s provincial merger in July 2025. Seasonal, monthly, and 10-day bulletins were developed. The five newly consolidated provinces are Can Tho, An Giang, Dong Thap, Vinh Long, and Ca Mau. These efforts directly reached 318,390 farmers in total (with 26,896 additional farmers in 2025) through the Zalo messaging platform, including farmer-to-farmer sharing via Zalo groups. Outreach was further expanded through multiple dissemination channels, like community loudspeakers, printed posters, and meetings organized by government agencies and civil society organizations. An improved version of the ACB, developed using a human-centered design approach, was piloted in selected areas of An Giang and Can Tho provinces (covering the former provinces of An Giang, Hau Giang, and Soc Trang). The enhanced ACB is planned for scale-up across all MRD provinces in 2026. Notably, as of July 2025, Vietnam underwent a major administrative restructuring, involving the merger of communes, provinces, and government departments, with the district level being eliminated. While partners are still adapting to the new institutional arrangements and working mechanisms, the ACB system continues to be maintained and implemented by PPPDs and sub-PPPDs, covering the geographic areas of the former provinces throughout 2025.

column16: Continued use and integration of the agro-climatic bulletins (ACBs) in the workplans and approaches of national and sub-national public institutions and stakeholders to scale climate advisories for farmers in Vietnam
column17: The agro-climatic bulletin (ACB) is an agro-advisory system based on a seasonal, monthly, and 10-day weather forecast that aims to provide climate advisory services to local agricultural insitutions, officials, and farmers in Vietnam. It is being co-developed and delivered through the public systems in Vietnam where both national and sub-national offices are integrating the tool on their local agricultural development planning and decision-making. In 2025, ACB continues to be implemented and scaled by the Plant Production and Protection Department (PPPD) to disseminate agro-climatic advisories to farmers in the Mekong River Delta, Vietnam, with an allocated budget approved by MAE of VND 400 million (approximately USD 17,000). Five provinces (Can Tho, An Giang, Dong Thap, Vinh Long, Ca Mau) in Mekong River Delta, through their sub-PPPDs, have further integrated ACB into their work plans to ensure continued scale-up. In addition, PPPD has incorporated ACB into its national work plan for nationwide expansion during 2026–2028, with dedicated funding of VND 3,916,800,000 (approximately USD 150,000). National implementation has been kick-started through capacity-building activities for technical staff from all other regions in December 2025 (as reported under Capacity building). It is important to note that as of July 2025, Vietnam was gone through a big restructuring process with merging of communes, provinces, and deparmments. District level is disappear. The continuation of ACB implementation and scaling during this period—when numerous priority tasks are competing for attention—demonstrates strong government buy-in and commitment to replicating ACB nationwide in the coming years.

column16: With the provision by CGIAR of chicken, training, and alternative feed solutions, 100 farmers in Murehwa, Zimbabwe adopted Sasso poultry production, increased their income, and enhanced diversity of their diets.
column17: Since 2023, over 100 farmers in Ward 27 and surrounding wards in Murehwa district have embraced small-scale Sasso poultry production, raising an average of 25 birds per household. Three dual-purpose breeds—Sasso Sussex, T-Rainbow, and Sasso C431—have been promoted, with approximately 17,000 birds sold through Hamara Farmer and Trendsetter Pvt Ltd. The adoption of these improved breeds has increased household income through chicken sales and enhanced protein diversity via access to meat and eggs. These breeds are valued for their disease resistance and low feeding costs, maximizing profit margins. Women, comprising 70% of participants, benefit from improved financial autonomy. The initiative, in collaboration with Hamara Farmer, provides chicks, feeds, training, and alternative feed solutions like Azolla. It also supports the Hamara App for connecting farmers, buyers, and experts, enabled by Starlink internet. Complementary efforts by IFAD’s SACP and government training have reinforced productivity, market linkages, and the role of poultry in agroecology

column16: Systematic assessments of national programs' strengths and change ambitions in Africa and South Asia leads to a growing community of breeding teams accelerating genetic gains for major food crops
column17: Continuing with efforts made by the Excellence in Breeding Platform, 128 in-depths assessments of NARES Breeding Programs have been done since 2019. Each partner assessment has been followed by NARES developing a customized improvement plan. So, far 93 NARES have completed them. These plans are the basis for developing individual and regional capacity development plans, increasing NARES engagement in regional collaborative breeding approaches, and modernizing regional breeding strategies, such as through centralized rapid cycle genomic selection and expanded on-farm testing at earlier stages. Network partners are using the improvement plans as a basis for internal and external funding applications, such as to Crops to End Hunger. The overall benefits are: 1. more targeted approaches to capacity development, 2. increased NARES capacity to participate in breeding networks and develop varieties, 3. stronger CGIAR-NARES collaborative efforts, and 4. a growing community of breeding teams accelerating genetic gains for major food crops.

column16: CGIAR breeding pipelines are oriented towards specific market segments, enabling greater focus on farmers’ needs, drivers of adoption, and impact
column17: Accelerated Breeding has developed tools and approaches for taking stock of current breeding pipelines and mapping them to a portfolio of distinct, achievable target product profiles (TPP’s) - each a unique combination of productivity, adaptation, resilience, quality, processing and consumer traits. TPPs should be feasible, impactful, gender-relevant, and in-demand. By 30 November 2024, CGIAR breeding programs have aligned 157 Breeding Pipelines and 418 TPPs 1:1 to sub-regional market segments (418 out of 701 defined) using the Breeding Portal. Each TPP contains trait requirements and targeted scores. The traits are categorized through 14 value propositions that make breeding pipeline orientation toward Impact Areas transparent. Almost all (>95%) of CGIAR breeding programs have systematically oriented breeding pipelines towards farmers’ needs, drivers of adoption, and impact. 55% of all TPPs were informed by gender studies, gender specialists or gender-disaggregated on-farm feedback. Together, the TPPs target close to 400 million hectares grown by smallholders.

column16: A cooperative in Nepal starts commercialising biofermentated rice straw, an technology introduced by SAPLING that also gets support from other organisations
column17: Under the SAPLING initiative, biofermentation technology was used to upgrade the nutritional quality of rice straw, which forms the basal diet of dairy animals. Production of biofermented straw was done in collaboration with Maharanijhoda Small Farmer Agricultural Cooperative Limited (SFACL), which first produced biofermented straw for trial purpose. Later, intrigued by its potential, the cooperative decided to produce more than what was required for the trial so some of their member farmers could test it on their own. Considering the potential of commercializing the biofermentation technology, the Livestock System Innovation Lab (LSIL), supported Maharanijhoda SFAC  to fine tune the technology and develop business plans for production and marketing of “strawlage” on a commercial basis. In November 2024, Heifer Project International placed an order to purchase 20 tons of “strawlage” from Maharanijhoda SFAC to their beneficiary farmers associated with their Milky Way Project.

column16: In the Kiambu Agroecology Living Landscape, more than 20 farmers made more efficient use of their cultivation space increasing their fresh food yields, saving costs of buying groceries, increasing incomes
column17: The initiative has increased farmers' knowledge of farm planning and layout. This allowed the farmers to organize their plots and grow more plants per square meter, enabling them to get more produce from a small land area. They have therefore increased their fresh food yields, saving the cost of buying groceries, and increased their incomes. This has also shown some levels of food security and reduced stress brought about by lack of money and food. We have also seen a lot of creativity among the farmers. They have been using gunny bags, which is a readily available item, to make cone gardens instead of buying conventional polythene. column16: 20 farmers utilize every drop of water using water recycling techniques in the Agroecology Living Landscape in Kiambu county in Kenya
column17: Since 2023, at least 20 farmers have implemented water recycling processes like adding wood ash into the soapy water used in their households. The recycled water is then used to water the crops in their kitchen gardens ensuring continuous production. Farmers have learned and implemented modern water recycling techniques that are less time-consuming and not labor-intensive. This being a dry area, the water recycling practice has helped the farmers to utilize every drop of water. Any used household water is purified then applied to crops in the kitchen gardens and none of it goes to waste. As a result, the farmers grow their food even in dry months ensuring consistent supply of food in the household and sometimes extra for sale. The Agroecology Initiative promoted training on the principle of water recycling techniques since water is an important element in crop production.

column16: Since 2023, 200 dairy farmers of the Agroecology Living Landscape in Burkina Faso have established dairy production units on their farms that integrate several principles of agroecology
column17: Dairy farmers who are members of the Agroecological Living Landscape (ALL) of Burkina Faso (ALL = Dairy Innovations Platform- DIP of Bobo-Dioulasso) have established dairy production units on their farms that integrate several principles of agroecology such as the biodiversification of the fodder system, the strengthening of agriculture-livestock synergies, the recycling of crop and livestock co-products from the dairy production unit, the reduction of industrial inputs (feed concentrates), and therefore several agroecological technologies such as: fodder cultivation, forage seeds production, the recycling of crops and livestock co-products into fodder and manure, the balanced use of the farm's feed resources to feed dairy cows (spontaneous pastures, fodders, and limited use of concentrated livestock feed). 200 dairy farmers members of the DIP established dairy production units. This represents more than 60% of the dairy farmers who deliver milk to the dairy processors units of Bobo-Dioulasso city.

column16: Centenary Bank pilots CGIAR's climate-linked digital risk-scoring system, integrating climate risk analytics and weather forecasts to improve financial access for 600 smallholder livestock farmers in Uganda across 6 branches.
column17: Centenary Bank is piloting climate-linked digital risk-scoring system that integrates climate risk analytics, weather forecasts and adheres to quality standards to improve access to finance for smallholder farmers in Uganda with support from the CGIAR Livestock and Climate Initiative. This innovative system combines weather data, market trends, and farmer profiles to assess and manage risks effectively. By incorporating these factors, the system supports informed lending decisions while promoting resilience among farming communities. Centenary Bank’s approach aligns with the broader objectives of enhancing financial inclusion and addressing climate challenges faced by farmers. The system also prioritizes inclusivity, enabling smallholders to access financial services tailored to their needs and vulnerabilities. It is estimated that this has improved financial access for 600 livestock farmers in Uganda.

column16: Integrated Agriculture-Aquaculture (IAA) system to produce aquatic and terrestrial foods on the same land using resources from one to benefit the other, adopted by farmers in Egypt
column17: Integrated Agriculture-Aquaculture (IAA) systems, which are diversified farming systems where aquatic and terrestrial foods are grown together on the same plot using the resources from one to benefit the other, have to date (2024) been adopted by 200 farmers in the Menia governorate of Egypt, and other parts of the country.  In an IAA system in Egypt, the production of fish such as Nile tilapia, mullet, and African catfish creates nutrient-rich water that can then be used to irrigate crops such as date palm, olives, figs, pomegranates, guava, onions, sugar beets, and tomato. IAA includes a range of technologies and methods that can be put together and adapted to each farming situation as needed. IAA is one of the most promising and fastest-growing food production systems in Egypt since it enhances production diversity, land productivity, water efficiency and nutrient cycling on farms.

column17: The main dairy product consumed by the population of Bobo-Dioulasso is yogurt. The majority of dairy processors make yogurts based on imported milk powder and flavor the yogurts with artificial flavors. The Bobo-Dioulasso dairy processing units that are members of the Agroecology Living Landscape (and who are part of the Dairy Innovation Platform) that process locally produced fresh milk have started to diversify their yogurt production by flavoring them with natural extracts of non-timber forest products and local agricultural products (pineapple, sweet banana (poyo), coconut, date, ginger, horchata (chufa), kinkéliba, mango, mint, moringa, nere, monkey bread (théodo), orange-fleshed sweet potato, tamarind, zeguene (balanites)). And it works. There is an outlet for these yogurts that we can qualify as ''agroecological yogurts'' because they are made from real milk and flavored with local natural flavors.

column16: Bayer Crop Sciences scales up site-specific nutrient management for rice farmers in India by integrating the Rice Crop Manager (RCM) algorithm into the FarmRise application
column17: ; [No activity in 2025] ; ; From 2022 to 2024, Bayer Crop Sciences expanded the reach of Rice Crop Manager (RCM) advisories to farmers in Odisha and Eastern Uttar Pradesh, India, through its FarmRise platform. FarmRise, an Android-based advisory application developed by Bayer, provides farmers with real-time agronomic insights, including best practices for multiple crops, market prices, and government schemes. A key enhancement was the integration of IRRI’s Site-Specific Nutrient Management (SSNM) application programming interface (API) into FarmRise, allowing tailored nutrient management advisories for rice farmers. This integration ensures that farmers receive personalized, data-driven recommendations to optimize fertilizer application, boosting yields, soil health, and resource efficiency. Additionally, timely reminders guide farmers on the optimal timing of fertilizer applications, reducing waste and enhancing productivity.; By leveraging IRRI’s SSNM API, FarmRise delivers a comprehensive, inclusive and technology-driven advisory system, strengthening food security, climate resilience, and sustainable agricultural practices in India’s rice-growing regions.

column16: Genesis Empresarial Foundation pilots and adopts a novel climate-linked scoring system, improving financial access for 17 livestock producers in Guatemala.
column17: In Guatemala, the Livestock and Climate Initiative supported the development of an innovative approach to addressing climate risks by establishing a climate-risk credit score, improving financial access for 17 livestock producers, with the potential to scale to an additional 306 producers. A two-stage pilot was implemented in Quiché, Santa Rosa, and Jutiapa. The first stage focused on designing a financial product for resilient and sustainable livestock practices, including participatory workshops. 31 promoters were trained in digital tools for livestock profiling, climate risk assessment, and client consultations using the YAPU platform. A total of 306 clients were assessed, emphasizing the importance of a climate resilience taxonomy tailored to livestock farmers. The second stage launched the pilot with training sessions for 70 participants, including promoters and office managers. Seventeen loans were granted, with 88% supporting livestock genetic improvement and 12% funding multispecies farming practices, demonstrating the product's potential for scaling and impact.

column16: Smallholder pig keepers in Uganda adopt a SAPLING developed pig weigh-band
column17: A pig weigh band, which is a tape placed around the pig’s heart girth from which a weight is read, was developed; for the smallholder pig sector in Uganda.  The weigh-band was piloted with 171 smallholder pig keepers in; 4 districts of Uganda. The farmers were given the weigh-band and a recording booklet, as well as training on; these. After a 7-month period, weigh-band use was found to be  high with 97% of respondents using the weigh-band for one or more of the intended purposes (supporting pig sale, weigh monitoring, or drug dose determination). In total, 166 households adopted the weigh band, corresponding to 746 people benefiting assuming average household size of 4.5; (DHS, 2024). Based on this successful pilot, further scaling of the weigh-band is planned.

column16: Since 2022, 1000 food system actors in Mbire, Zimbabwe reduce the use of synthetic chemicals as part of their agroecology transition, facilitated by the CGIAR Initiative on Agroecology
column17: Since 2022, farmers in Ward 2, Mbire district, Mashonaland Central, have reduced synthetic chemical use, adopting traditional methods for pest and livestock management. They use Katunguru leaves for crops and grain storage and Mutyora, Gavakava, and Murembe for deworming livestock. Women and youth dominate crop production (75%), while men focus on livestock (45%). This shift reduces dependence on costly chemicals, promotes sustainability, and fosters environmental conservation. Farmers now rely on local resources, enhancing resilience to market and environmental shocks. The Agroecology Initiative has supported this transformation by establishing demonstration plots, organizing organic farming training, and facilitating community dialogues to promote sustainable practices like push-pull techniques. These efforts have empowered women and youth in agriculture and equipped farmers with the knowledge to transition away from chemical inputs. This change reflects growing inclusivity, environmental stewardship, and a shift in market dynamics affecting agrodealers.

column16: With improved access to inputs and technical support provided by CGIAR, farmers in Mbire, Zimbabwe adopt conservation agriculture leading to yield increments, reduced production costs, and greater participation in markets.
column17: Since 2022, farmers in Mbire Ward 2 have increasingly adopted conservation agriculture practices such as mulching, minimum tillage, and sorghum-cowpea intercropping. This shift has expanded land under sorghum cultivation and improved yields while reducing costs, creating more sustainable farming systems. Farmers now access structured markets like the Grain Marketing Board (GMB) and contract farming programs with the private sector company P.H.I. Commodities, enhancing food security and economic stability.  ; Conservation agriculture builds resilience to climate variability, improves soil health, and supports dietary diversification through increased sorghum production. Intercropping with cowpea boosts nutrient cycling and profitability. The Agroecology Initiative has driven this transformation by facilitating contract farming with P.H.I., establishing demonstration plots, and providing training through the Utariri project. Complementary initiatives, such as the Pfumvudza program, promoted sustainable techniques, improved input access, and created stable markets for sorghum. Mechanization support and conservation agriculture extension services further solidified these sustainable practices. By improving access to inputs and technical support, the initiative has encouraged sustainable farming practices, linking smallholder farmers to larger value chains and fostering financial stability.

column16: Since 2022, 150 farmers in Murehwa, Zimbabwe, reduce labor time and production costs in their maize, sorghum, and legumes systems by using mechanization packages, processes and support provided by CGIAR.
column17: Since 2022, 150 farmers in Ward 27, Murehwa district, have integrated mechanization into their maize, sorghum, and legume production systems. Two farmers, supported through the mechanization Service Provider model, received power-intensive equipment such as tillage tools, basin diggers, and threshers, while 22 others (including 10 youths and 12 women) gained access to basin diggers. Mechanization reduced labor costs by 75% for activities such as basin preparation, cutting preparation time from 16–24 hours using hand hoes to 1–2 hours with machines. Multicrop threshers increased efficiency, processing 3–4 tonnes per hour. This allowed farmers to plant more efficiently and focus on other agricultural activities, enhancing agroecological practices. The initiative provided operator training, facilitated farmer access to machinery, and linked them to manufacturers. Collaboration among government, NGOs, and private actors, such as CIMMYT's Feed the Future Mechanization project, improved conservation agriculture adoption and closed gender gaps through inclusive technological innovations.

column16: Community-based climate monitor networks strengthen local resilience in Guatemala and Honduras
column17: "In 2025, CGIAR and partners strengthened community-based climate monitor networks in Guatemala and Honduras, enhancing local capacities to generate, interpret, and use climate information in highly climate-vulnerable rural areas. In Guatemala, the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, in collaboration with the World Food Programme (WFP) and national and local partners, expanded the network across Huehuetenango, Quiché, and Chiquimula. A total of 221 community climate monitors were trained and equipped to collect and share local climate data, with 68% women, reinforcing inclusive leadership and community-level decision-making. Monitors contribute data and insights to Agroclimatic Technical Committees (MTAs), improving the relevance of agroclimatic advisories.; ; In Honduras, CGIAR supported the consolidation of a national community rainfall monitoring network with more than 240 community observers and rain gauges, working alongside COPECO–CENAOS, SAG, academic institutions, and local governments. Data generated by the network feed national forecasting systems and digital platforms, improving early warning, planning, and climate-informed decisions. Together, these advances demonstrate strengthened local ownership, gender-responsive participation, and more effective use of climate information to build rural resilience in 2025.";

column16: Thirty-four organizations across three departments of Guatemala (Izabal, Santa Rosa, Jutiapa) engage in the Technical Agroclimatic Commitee (MTAs) to co-produce and disseminate livestock climate information services, benefiting 7,259 farmers.
column17: With support from the Livestock and Climate Initiative, the Technical Agroclimatic Committees (MTAs) in Guatemala use a participatory approach to deliver gender-sensitive livestock climate information services. This support has included training, new tools for climate data analysis, and strengthened coordination between 34 organizations and scientific institutions. The MTA, across three departments—Izabal, Santa Rosa, and Jutiapa—co-produce agroclimatic advisories tailored to the needs of 7,259 farmers. By integrating scientific forecasts with local knowledge, the MTAs develop actionable information products, such as agroclimatic bulletins and radio programs, that address specific climate risks like extreme weather and seasonal variability. This inclusive process ensures that advisories are accessible, enabling producers to make informed decisions about livestock and pasture management. The MTAs have scaled their efforts to reach over 55,000 rural producers, fostering resilience and adaptive capacity to climate risks across Guatemala.

column16: YAPU Solutions, a FinTech company, uses climate data and livestock management practice knowledge to co-develop a climate-linked credit scoring system to unlock green financing in the Guatemalan livestock sector
column17: YAPU Solutions, FinTech leader, partnered with CGIAR Initiative Livestock and Climate to co-develop an innovative platform addressing climate risks. The initiative began with the identification of indicators for establishing an innovative climate-risk credit score and a holistic assessment of exposure to climate hazards—especially for droughts, storms, floods and frosts. To date, 100,000 people have used the YAPU platform, resulting in 105,000 loans. Leveraging CGIAR’s advanced data and expertise, the YAPU platform evaluates client exposure to these hazards, integrating geo-referenced assessments with analyses of climate sensitivity and adaptive capacity. This empowers microfinance institutions like Fundación Génesis Empresarial to identify client-specific risks and offer tailored financing solutions. Piloted in Jutiapa, Santa Rosa and Quiché, the credit scoring system demonstrated its potential to unlock green financing, addressing a critical gap—fewer than 5% of farmers currently access climate-related financial incentives—this scalable, replicable model bridges financial inclusion and climate resilience of Guatemala’s rural livestock communities.

column16: The Cooperative Climate Cleverness Check of the Asian Mega Delta (AMD) Initiative in collaboration with Agriterra, was used by cooperatives in Vietnam
column17: The Climate Clever Check (CCC) tool was developed by Agriterra and the Alliance, to better integrate climate considerations into cooperative assessments. This tool stands out as an accessible and user-friendly solution for climate impact assessments. Unlike many existing tools that require specialized knowledge, the CCC tool allows users without technical expertise to confidently conduct evaluations, delivering rapid and objective results. Covering the key areas of FAO's climate smart agricultural practices, the tool can be used when climate issues are a high priority topic for the cooperative.  A tool prototype was developed based on previous work of the Alliance and Agritera, in consultation with the feedback survey from Agriterra staff Global team. The tool is currently being used by rice cooperatives in 2 Mekong River Delta provinces (Soc Trang and An Giang) as part of the pilot phase to gather their feedback and assessement.; ;

column16: Agroecological Living Landscape in Kef-Siliana drives forage crop adoption and Public-Private Partnerships in Tunisia
column17: The Agroecological Living Landscape in the Transect of Kef Siliana has become a catalyst for positive change within rural communities and decision makers, focusing on increasing the cultivation, valorization, and use of forage crops and mixtures to enhance livestock feeding and restore Soil health. Co-testing and demonstrating innovations in the region contributed to raising the demand for these crops and to the increasing engagement of private seeds companies to support the scaling of these innovations.  ; In 2024, the outcome evidencing exercise and study revealed  that the Initiative allowed actors to the integrate the co-design methodology into partner's projects, which has made it possible to create seed solutions adapted to new agroecological conditions. Cooperation with partners such as ICARDA has made it possible to increase the area cultivated with vetch and mixture seeds (ID 26 it doubles each year for mixture seeds it has gone from 10T to 30T to 80T), particularly for adaptation to changing climatic conditions. column16: Since 2022, over 100 small-scale farmers of the Agroecology Living Landscape in Tunisia started to grow fodder with olive trees, improved and increased their livestock, becoming more involved in cooperatives
column17: Since 2022, over 100 farmers in Elles, Hamman Biadha, Rhahla, Kesra and Sers have adopted agroecological practices, combining fodder cultivation with olive trees to improve their livestock. These farmers, who are aged between 35 and 60 and are organised into cooperatives, have received continuous training and support. They have benefited from networks, technical knowledge and material assistance for innovation. This shift was initiated by the Agroecology Initiative and was further supported by the MFL Science Programme, especially in terms of the evidence-based feedback provided to farmers. This has enhanced their livelihoods and business opportunities. The Science Programme has also organised information sessions on agronomic practices and olive tree care, such as pruning, irrigation and fertilisation. Additionally, the MFL Science Programme supported the creation of an origin certificate for Elles olive oil, documenting local good agroecological practices and promoting traditional knowledge. These efforts have supported diversification and resilience among farmers, particularly in remote areas, by enhancing access to resources and fostering sustainable agricultural practices.

column16: Since 2022, 298 pioneering farmers in Tunisia have improved fertilizer quality by using composted crop residues (by-products of olive oil production) and oil mill wastewater (combined or not) with manure.
column17: Pioneering farmers in Hammam Biadha, Essers, and Chouarnia in Tunisia have been composting olive oil by-products and manure since 2022. Previously, they seldom used manure or applied it incorrectly, causing weeds and pests. This new approach, still in its testing phase, enhances fertilizer quality, reduces costs, and improves soil low in organic matter. It also combats pollution from oil mill effluents and mitigates climate change effects. The Agroecology Initiative supports this change with trials, demonstration plots, and composting units. Other projects, like GIZ-Prosol and IFAD-PROFITS, expand the practice to neighboring areas and mixed farming systems. These projects provide small-scale composting equipment and train farmers, extension agents, and administrative staff to institutionalize and scale up the method. Through MFL support, MFL team in Tunisia raised additional funding from GIZ to further support the development of a scalable business model fir further up and outscaling of this innovation. Together, these efforts promote sustainable farming, improve productivity, and address environmental challenges in vulnerable agricultural communities.

It supports a shared commitment to advancing innovative, sustainable, and climate-resilient agricultural methods for a better future.

column16: Researchers at the Olive Tree Institute in Tunisia adopt the  co-design approach of the Agroecology Initiative, installing more experimental trials and field-level demonstration plots on farmers' plots.
column17: Researchers at the Olive Tree Institute traditionally focused on station-based studies to track environmental impacts on plants and soil. Through a co-design approach, they shifted to establishing experimental trials and demonstration plots on farmers' land. This led to co-designed technologies like biochar (to enhance soil water retention), compost (to reduce erosion and boost yields), and improved olive pruning techniques. Farmers were actively involved in decisions regarding technologies, plots, and trees. Researchers are now more and more advocating for broader adoption of these participatory methods within the Institute and the Ministry of Agriculture.  IO researchers are now also being involved in additional national and international projects, funded by various donors such as GIZ, IFAD, etc. Thus, they are adopting and using this innovation in broader projects with expected higher scaling. This approach proved more effective as farmers gained trust and adopted new practices through hands-on experience rather than passive training.  Contributions from past projects like CLCA (Use of Conservation Agriculture in Crop-Livestock Systems) and initiatives such GIZ-PROSOL fostered organizational innovation, sustaining participatory efforts at the community and landscape level.

column16: Over 230 farmers in Siliana and El Kef in Tunisia have been working with the Agroecology Initiative and now produce their own forage seeds, improving soil fertility, and fodder quality.

column16: Collaborative action research of the Agroecology Initiative with OEP (Office des Elevage et des Pâturages) in Tunisia leads OEP to integrate biofertilization technology in its new strategy
column17: OEP (Office des Elevages et des Pâturages) has integrated biofertilization technology into its activities, making Rhizobium inoculation for forage legumes a key part of its strategy. This shift has been supported by participatory trials with farmers, leading to a voluntary increase in the adoption of sulla. OEP is now seeking additional funding from GIZ and other donors to establish a rhizobium unit to scale up specific forage crops in Tunisia. The initiative initiated a rhizobia experiment in Rhahla in 2022 to address soil fertility and climate change. This, alongside ongoing demonstrations with PROSOL-ICARDA, has influenced OEP's decision-makers, prompting them to request GIZ’s support for the investment. The experiment was supported by GIZ, with changes driven by partnerships with ICARDA under various initiatives, including IFAD-CLCA and GIZ-ICARDA-ProSol. The creation of a rhizobium inoculation unit is essential for OEP's goal to diversify local forage resources.

column16: Integration of Conservation Agriculture: Excellence in Agronomy Morocco's Use Case Enhancing Adoption, Research, and Digital Monitoring in Agricultural Ecosystems
column17: The Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) Morocco Use Case is propelling the advancement of Conservation Agriculture (CA) through focused initiatives. This involves a thorough update on CA research, concentrating on crop diversification and weed control, adapted to Morocco's diverse soil and climate. Emphasis is placed on data collection and analysis to uncover key factors influencing CA adoption, including an in-depth look at farmers' practices and barriers to CA adoption by 2030. A significant development is the pilot digital platform for CA monitoring, designed to track vital elements like soil health, crop rotation, and yield. This platform integrates CA suitability maps, identifying priority areas for effective scaling interventions. These concerted efforts aim to boost CA adoption, promoting sustainable agricultural productivity and environmental conservation in Morocco.

column16: A harmonized advisory system providing locally tailored fertilizer and agronomy recommendations and bundles multiple soil, land, and water management practices into a single tool accessible to farmers and extension services
column17: This innovation combines multiple types of agricultural advice: fertilizer guidance, soil and crop management practices, and land and water recommendations, into a unified system designed to help farmers, extension workers, and development partners. Instead of relying on separate tools developed by different organizations, national research institutions, and global partners, national research institutions and global partners worked together to merge their efforts into a single, practical advisory system that responds to real field conditions. ; ; A key part of this effort involved using system analysis tools provided by the Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning, and Impact team. These tools helped identify how farmers, extension agents, and partners were using existing advisory tools, where gaps existed, and what changes were needed to make sure the harmonized system was practical, accessible, and widely adopted. The system analysis also guided decisions on combining innovations, understanding the enabling environment, and assessing readiness for scaling up. The unified advisory system offers locally tailored recommendations by using data on soils, landscapes, climate, and farm practices. It provides fertilizer advice suited for specific fields, guidance on soil and crop management, and instructions on land and water practices that support higher yields and healthier soils. ; ; The information is delivered through digital channels and direct extension support, ensuring it reaches farmers with varying levels of connectivity and literacy. National research institutions lead the coordination and validation of the system, working closely with government agencies, extension services, and international partners. Donor support has been strong because the system improves the consistency, quality, and usefulness of agricultural guidance nationwide. Since its launch, the advisory system has attracted interest from extension agents, farmers, and development organizations. The combined digital and field-based approach, strengthened through MELIA’s system analysis, has made the innovation more effective, relevant, and better suited for wider scaling across Ethiopia’s agricultural sector.

column16: India Meteorological Department adopts CGIAR-developed Meghdoot Dashboard to monitor agricultural weather advisory app usage across India
column17: The India Meteorological Department integrated a CGIAR-developed dashboard to strengthen its Agrometeorological Advisory Service capabilities. The dashboard provides real-time analytics on mobile app usage patterns at district and state levels, enabling staff to track how farmers access weather information for agricultural decision-making. This adoption allows the department to better understand user engagement, optimize service delivery, and allocate resources more effectively to support climate-informed farming practices. The tool represents a significant advancement in how meteorological services can monitor and improve their digital outreach to agricultural communities across India.

column16: Since 2022, more than 11,000 Food systems actors engaged in the cocreation of agroecological innovations in eight countries
column17: The CGIAR initiative on Agroecology is actively engaging with food system actors (FSA) in eight countries (Burkina Faso, India, Kenya, Lao PDR, Peru, Senegal, Tunisia, and Zimbabwe), particularly to codesign, test, ; and adapt agroecological innovations, both technological and institutional, from food production to consumption. ; The engagement takes place in Agroecological Living Landscapes (ALLs) that are formed in selected territories of each country with diverse stakeholders, including farmer associations or communities, ; researchers from multiple disciplines, extensionists, private companies, international and national non-governmental organizations as well as local, regional, and national policymakers. ; The engagement of food system actors is addressed in the monitoring, evaluation, learning and impact assessment (MELIA) component of the initiative.; This summary analyzes the data from 2022 to 2024, collected by each country team, quarterly.
