column16: Carob: A framework to standardize legacy agricultural data
column17: Carob is an open-source community project that standardizes and aggregates agricultural research data. The Carob project cleans and transforms agricultural research data from experiments and surveys into a standard format and aggregates individual data sets into larger databases that can be used in further research. This tool addresses the critical challenge of incompatible data formats that previously limited agricultural research potential.; The framework has gained adoption across the agricultural research community, with growing numbers of researchers and organizations using it to standardize their datasets. This widespread adoption enables more comprehensive analyses for predictive agronomy, supporting evidence-based decisions that can improve farming practices and food security worldwide. ; ; ; ;

column16: Dairy farmers in Nepal adopt SAPLING supported innovations on impoved feed, better reproductive performance and genetic gain.
column17: Considering the yield gap existing in the dairy sector, the SAPLING initiative generated several livestock solutions that resulted in enhanced buffalo productivity. The innovations developed and promoted using a ‘technology bundling’ approach include genetic interventions, nutritional improvement and management of reproductive health. The genetic intervention consists of an ICT based platform to record and analyse dairy animal performance systematically to aid selection of superior genetics. The feed-based intervention is a unique integrated nutrition package supported by a mobile based nutrient balancing application that helps local extension agents (Village Livestock Promoters) to advise farmers for formulating least cost ration for feeding their dairy animals. The reproductive health innovation also uses an integrated approach consisting of managing infertility in buffalo. All these innovations are being adopted by more than 4000 buffalo farmers in Nepal.

column16: Human-centered co-design advances and prepares scaling of the Rice Crop Manager Advisory Service cluster-based nutrient recommendation module in the Philippines
column17: In 2025, partners in the Philippines continued the human-centered design (HCD) process to strengthen and scale the Rice Crop Manager Advisory Service (RCMAS) cluster-based nutrient recommendation module (CLeveR). Building on earlier co-design work, the Philippine Rice Research Institute and the International Rice Research Institute convened priority-setting and technical discussions to ensure the module’s features, workflows, and outputs remain usable and relevant for extension delivery and decision-making. This included refining and updating recommendation algorithms, strengthening operational monitoring through a Power BI–based dashboard, and clarifying responsibilities for maintenance and upgrades as the service transitions toward sustained implementation.; In parallel, the 2025 work applied an innovation package and scaling readiness approach to translate the co-designed module into a scalable offer for farmer clusters. Government and local partners—working with Department of Agriculture units, the Agricultural Training Institute, local government units, and the National Irrigation Administration—defined a shared scaling ambition, identified key adoption and implementation bottlenecks, and agreed practical solutions to enable wider use. Together, these activities represent a 2025 innovation use outcome because they moved the CLeveR module from development into institutional preparation for use at scale, grounded in continued HCD and partner-led implementation planning.

column16: Ministry-led training strengthened Indonesia’s extension workforce to deliver field-specific rice fertilizer advice using the Layanan Konsultasi Padi 2.0 digital service.
column17: Indonesia’s Ministry of Agriculture strengthened the use of the Layanan Konsultasi Padi 2.0 digital advisory by embedding it in its own training and extension system. From 6–8 August 2025, the Indonesian Center for Agricultural Extension (Pusat Penyuluhan Pertanian) hosted a three-day Training of Masters in Jakarta with the Agency for Agricultural Extension and Agricultural Human Resources Development (Badan Penyuluhan dan Pengembangan Sumber Daya Manusia Pertanian) and the Center for Food Crops Engineering and Modernization (Pusat Perakitan dan Modernisasi Pertanian Tanaman Pangan), with technical support from the International Rice Research Institute. Seventeen master trainers—extension staff, government trainers, and polytechnic lecturers—were trained on field-specific nutrient management, conducting farmer interviews, generating field-specific fertilizer recommendations, and measuring fields using a global positioning system. The Training of Masters explicitly prepared these participants to train additional extension workers, creating a cascade model for routine dissemination through ministry channels. Follow-on ministry-led socialization sessions in provinces (for example, Bali, with nine districts represented) are reinforcing uptake among local extension officers so they can disseminate recommendations to farmers. Ministry partners also reported that earlier testing across irrigated, rainfed, and swamp rice systems reduced urea use while increasing yields, supporting scale-out through the national extension network.

column16: Integration of breeding under One CGIAR highlights the value of partnerships; 33 countries release 145 crop varieties that help in climate change adaptation and lowering malnutrition among women and children
column17: In 2025, 60 scaling partners in 33 countries registered a total of 145 crop varieties deriving from CGIAR breeding pipelines. They were improved in collaboration with over 600 partner organizations in Africa, Asia and Latin America. ; ; By analyzing the Breeding Strategy affiliated with the variety releases, the breeding goals can be established for 136 out of 145 varieties. Among these 136 varieties, 81% were improved for climate resilience. 14% were biofortified with iron, zinc or provitamin A and directed to lower malnutrition among women and children. 4% were aimed at reducing cooking time which also has a gender differential impact. ; ; By analyzing the Market Segments affiliated with the variety releases, the benefit arising from these variety releases can be projected for 117 out of 145 varieties. The varieties are adapted to 111 million hectares, where: (i) 16.5 million people with incomes below $2.15 live; (ii) 5.9 and 8.7 million disability adjusted live years (DALYs) are lost due to chronic and hidden hunger, respectively; (iii) 114 million, 138 million, 148 million, 74 million 34 million people are exposed form down-side risks due to changed rainfall, drought, flooding, high growing season temperatures and salinity.   ;

column16: An international community of research and development actors engaged with the Agroecology Initiative has enhanced its capacity for action-research, codesign and multistakeholder approaches to promote agroecological transitions
column17: Through methodological development and support, hands-on learning and regular virtual and face-to-face exchanges among country teams, the Initiative implementation has fostered a diverse and highly motivated international community of research and development actors.  Its primary members include international and national researchers, development partners, national and local governments, farmer organizations and individual farmers directly involved in codesigning diverse innovations. The community is developing a deeper understanding of agroecology and agroecological transition,  along with a deep appreciation for the value of multistakeholder partnerships as a means to transform existing food systems. They also share increasing skills and experiences related to Agroecology Living Landscape (ALL) emergence and functioning, visioning, action-research, codesign approaches, assessment of agroecology performance, value chain development, policy lobbying and formulation, among others. They understand the need to tailor generic concepts and approaches to the unique context in which Agroecological Transition is being promoted. The community aims to expand efforts nationally and internationally and intensify activities supporting Agroecological Transition.

column16: Based on an initiative study and knowledge exchange with Youth in Mandla, Madhya Pradesh, India, local stakeholders commit to include youth in agroecological transitions, recognizing their role in driving change
column17: To drive change, the Agroecology Initiative team organized two key events: a local engagement in Mandla and a national workshop in Bhopal. These events provided young women and men with a platform to share their views with key stakeholders. At both events, youth participants presented insights from the Photovoice activity, giving them the opportunity to amplify their voices. As a result, two key outcomes emerged:; 1.	Amplified Youth Voices: Initially, reluctant youth participants shared their stories and perspectives confidently during the national workshop.; 2.	Securing Stakeholder Commitment: The study secured commitments from stakeholders to include youth in agroecological transitions, recognizing their role in driving change. Local stakeholders in Mandla expressed support for organizing youth into collectives to ensure they receive training and access to information.;

column16: Rice farmers in Indonesia use field-specific fertilizer advice delivered through the Layanan Konsultasi Padi digital advisory service
column17: In 2025, the International Rice Research Institute and Indonesia’s Ministry of Agriculture partners assessed how rice farmers used fertilizer advice from the Layanan Konsultasi Padi digital advisory service. The study followed 216 farmers in eight provinces who received field-specific recommendations via extension workers and compared their previous-season practices with the season when they implemented the recommendations. After adoption, 86–92% of users applied fertilizer three times per season (vs. 26–35% previously) and application timing became more structured. Average nitrogen use declined by about 18 kilograms per hectare, while yields increased by about 600 kilograms per hectare (11%) on average, with the largest gains in rainfed areas (15–24%). Net income rose by around 3–5 million Indonesian rupiah per hectare in irrigated and rainfed areas. Farmer feedback was largely positive: 78% were willing to continue using the service and 76% would recommend it. These findings provide 2025 evidence of farmer uptake of the digital nutrient-management recommendations and associated productivity and income benefits.

column16: Public-private partnerships in Guatemala leverage climate data management support to improve response times, enhancing the delivery of timely and effective agro-climatic services
column17: Guatemala has significantly improved its climate data management systems, enhancing efficiency and data quality. INSIVUMEH (Instituto Nacional de Sismología, Vulcanologia, Meteorologia e Hidrología in Spanish), with CIAT`s support, implemented an innovative data capture system using Kobotoolbox, reducing data collection time by 83% while ensuring accuracy. Over 90 observers were trained in the field with financial and technical backing from CIAT. Additionally, a new ETL (Extraction, Transformation, and Loading) system was developed to streamline daily climate data processing, reducing validation times by 89% and guaranteeing data integrity. The Instituto Privado de Investigación sobre Cambio Climático (ICC) also adopted an effective ETL (Extract, Transform, Load ) process for climate station data and initiated a national catalog for integrating climate and agronomic data. These advancements position Guatemala to manage better and utilize climate data for sustainable agricultural and environmental decision-making.

column16: One private institution use CGIAR's human-centered design (HCD) approach to co-design agroclimatic information products, enhancing digital agricultural advisory services for farmers across three departments of Guatemala
column17: By applying Human-Centered Design (HCD), Guatemala has co-designed innovative agroclimatic bulletins tailored to the needs of farmers in the Altiplano and Santa Rosa. This process identified user profiles through producer focus groups, enabling prototyping and refinement of bulletins in accessible, contextualized language. Disseminated in Chimaltenango and Santa Rosa, these bulletins have shown strong adoption, supporting farmers in planting, managing, and harvesting crops. The Climate Change Institute  (ICC) embraced the HCD approach, integrating it into its processes to bridge dissemination gaps and better address the needs of both traditional users (e.g., large-scale producers) and small-scale farmers. This approach has strengthened inter-institutional collaboration, ensuring timely access to actionable agroclimatic information and fostering a user-focused perspective among researchers and institutions.

column16: Last-mile participatory climate services strengthen farmer decision-making and resilience in 116 communities in western Guatemala
column17: In 2025, CGIAR and partners advanced the implementation of last-mile climate services in Guatemala by operationalizing the Participatory Integrated Climate Services for Agriculture (PICSA) methodology in Huehuetenango and Quiché (116 communities), translating prior investments into measurable use and outcomes. Through PICSA workshops implemented under WFP-led projects, farmers strengthened their capacity to interpret historical climate data and seasonal forecasts and to apply this information to key decisions such as planting dates, soil preparation, crop selection, and risk management. Monitoring and evaluation conducted in 2025 covered 553 participating farmers, with results showing that over 90% understood and used climate information to guide agricultural decisions, and that learning was actively replicated within households and communities, reaching an additional 2,765 people through farmer-to-farmer sharing, more than half of whom were women. The approach demonstrated strong inclusion outcomes, with 68% of participants identifying as Indigenous and a high proportion of women engaged.

column16: Since 2024, the farmers associated to the cooperatives Colpa de Loros and Banaqui Curimana who participated in the Initiative are more motivated to adopt sustainable practices.
column17: Farmers participating in the Initiative reported significant changes in agricultural practices, focusing on cacao plot and home garden management. Eight out of ten farmers identified improvements in disease management, prioritizing moniliasis. Six adopted new agronomic treatments, while five integrated home gardens into their activities. Participants gained knowledge in organic cacao practices, including composting, pruning, and disease control using solutions like boiled lime and trichoderma. Home garden training, provided by AgroSalud, introduced practices such as seed germination, organic pest control, and vegetable cultivation.  Farmers highlighted increased production, improved cacao quality, reduced disease, and soil recovery, though some noted higher workloads. Experimental plots, established collaboratively since 2023, provided inputs and technical support. Monitoring by Initiative agronomists revealed enhanced yields and quality in most cases. Overall, the Initiative fostered sustainable agricultural practices, benefiting farmers and their families through technical training and improved productivity.

column16: Farmers participating in the Agroecology Living Landscape and the co-design and implementation of innovative agroecological practice in Makueni, Kenya reduced their input expenditure through the use of locally available inputs.
column17: Farmers in the Makueni Living Landscape observed that agroecological practices improved yields and reduced pest and disease pressure, enabling them to rely less on synthetic inputs. Over two seasons (Oct 23–March 24; May 24–Sept 24), maize grain yield increased significantly under manure, with predicted yields of 4.7 t/ha compared to 4.0 t/ha in the control. Bean yields also rose across treatments: 0.6 vs. 0.5 t/ha for IPM, 0.5 vs. 0.4 t/ha for manure, and 0.5 vs. 0.4 t/ha for terraces. Pest pressure dropped significantly, particularly under IPM, with incidences for maize at 2.9% vs. 8.1% (control) and beans at 17% vs. 39%. Beans treated with manure showed pest incidences of 13% vs. 34% in the control. These improvements reduced the need for external inputs, lowering farm input costs and enhancing sustainability.; This increase in yields positively contributed to food security, both by increasing available produce for consumption, and by allowing surplus to be sold in the market. While the MELIA study evidenced the outcome with 30 farmers, the Agroecology team observed the results with approximately 75 farmers. Training curricula of the host centers of the Agroecology Living Landscapes in Makueni included approximately 750 farmers in Makueni.

column16: The Kenya Meteorological Department delivers gender-sensitive livestock climate information services across 9 counties through its engagement in the participatory scenario planning approach.
column17: The Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD), with support from Livestock and Climate initiative collaborated with key stakeholders to co-develop and integrate gender-sensitive climate information services and climate risk management strategies tailored for livestock producers. Using the Participatory Scenario Planning approach, KMD engaged in nine counties to produce localized, actionable advisories blending scientific forecasts with regional and community-specific insights to manage farm risks. These advisories include practical guidance on livestock management strategies, addressing challenges such as climate risks and disease outbreaks. Special emphasis is placed on incorporating gender considerations, ensuring that women livestock producers were actively involved and that their specific needs were addressed.

column16: Cambodian rice farmers accessed and used agro-climatic bulletins developed and provided through the Local Technical Agro-Climatic Committee (LTAC)
column17: The agro-climatic bulletin (ACB) is an agro-advisory system based on a seasonal, monthly, and 10-day weather forecast that aims to provide climate advisory services to local agricultural insitutions, officials, and farmers in Vietnam. It is being co-developed and delivered through the public systems in Vietnam where sub-national offices are integrating the tool on their local agricultural development planning and decision-making. In Cambodia, ACB is being scaled by the Provincial Department of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries (PDAFF) through Local Technical Agro-Climatic Committee (LTAC) to disseminate agro-climatic advisories to farmers (especially women). In 2024, ACBs are being accessed by and provided to 23 agricultural cooperatives in 2 provinces (Takeo, Prey Veng) in Cambodia. A signifant number of women is being targeted to receive advisories.

column16: Improved access of farmers and fisherfolk to electronic training and education materials on climate risks adaptation through private sector digital platforms in Myanmar
column17: Within the context of Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) Initiative Work Package 1 and building on-going work on climate information services in Myanmar, the project team from the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT in collaboration with Village Link Company Limited focused on the development of e-training materials to promote Smart Aquaculture and Smart Agriculture using short video format to provide more in-depth information which can complement the current agro-advisories developed by Village Link in the Irrawaddy Delta, Myanmar. This is an opportunity to support farmers with more specific, qualified and user-friendly information so that farmers can implement agricultural practices in more appropriate ways. In 2024, these materials have reached around 122,000 farmers and fisherfolk in the region. In 2025, with support from S4I through collaboration between the Alliance and Village Link, the videos continued to be shared through Village Link’s digital platforms, reaching over 1.7 million views.

column16: Tanzanian farmers adopt AKILIMO cassava management recommendations through digital and paper-based decision support tools
column17: AKILIMO is a comprehensive decision support system developed by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture that provides cassava farmers with site-specific recommendations for optimal crop management. The tool combines digital soil and weather data with market insights to deliver personalized advice through mobile apps, simplified paper formats, and educational materials. In Tanzania, smallholder farmers are increasingly adopting AKILIMO recommendations, which help them make informed decisions about fertilizer use, variety selection, and farming practices. The system addresses the challenge of providing tailored agricultural advice to resource-constrained farmers by offering multiple access formats. Early evidence shows that farmers implementing AKILIMO recommendations experience improved yields and increased net revenue, demonstrating the practical value of data-driven agricultural decision-making tools for enhancing cassava production sustainability.

column16: Farmer adoption of the Africa Asia Dairy Genetic Gains (AADGG) platform in Tanzania, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda and Nepal: an update for 2024
column17: Smallholder dairy farms productivity is constrained by  the need for access to appropriate seedstock, due to the absence of sustainable breeding programs, certification systems, access to related information and effective farmer extension. Artificial insemination has not been supported by proper national animal identification, pedigree, and performance recording, all of which would enable local evaluation and certification of seed stock. The Africa Asia Dairy Genetic Gains (AADGG) project  address these problems through the innovative application of Information Communication technology and breeding, including genomic. technologies. Here we report  4282 new adopters (3060 male and 1222 female) of the AADGG platform in the SAPLING countries of Tanzania, Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda and Nepal for the year 2024 .

column16: Business incubation and mentorship program improves pig agripreneurs business practices in Uganda
column17: The agripreneur business incubation/acceleration program was started in 2023 in Uganda to address challenges associated with market inefficiencies, poor business practices and limited networks to enable optimal business operations. The program  focused on both supply side (agripreneur focused) and demand side (farmer focused). For the supply side, the pig agripreneurs specifically AI service providers and pig aggregators were empowered through business skilling and mentorship.  On the demand side, the demand for inputs and services delivered by the agripreneurs was catalysed by sensitizing pig farmer groups on the necessary inputs and services required to run the pig enterprise as a business, and how to bargain for better terms through collective action. The results show improved customer care and business practices by the agripreneurs.

column16: Application of the COAXIM (COconut AXIllary Meristems) method for good quality planting production by laboratories in the Phillipines, Vietnam, India, Sri Lanka, and Indonesia
column17: Scientists at the Alliance and KU Leuven have developed a method to multiply seedlings faster and conserve coconut genetic resources for the long term. The method was developed based on the expertise that was gained with banana tissue culture at the  International Transit Centre (ITC) and more specifically on the influence of the plant growth regulator, TDZ, on multiplication of shoots. This will help to preserve coconut tree biodiversity and meet the increasing demand for coconuts and derived products. This protocol has successfully applied to a wide diversity of coconut cultivars and is been protected by a patent in 2021. Because coconut production is often in the hands of small scale farmers, a special clause included in the patent license: whoever applies the technique will have to ensure that small farmers can purchase the plant material at a reasonable price. The COAXIM methodology for the production of good quality planting materials has been further optimized with a focus on regeneration of rooted plants. Hundred COAXIM developed plants are now available to be planted in the greenhouse/field for final proof of concept. The method has been successfully applied in Vietnam.  The method is now being adopted at an Indonesian in vitro laboratory.

By enabling users to quickly find large amounts of publications and data, GARDIAN helps data scientists and analysts accelerate research and innovation.

column16: Bridging the Gap: Digital Agronomic Advisory Platform for Smallholder Farmers and farmer facing organisations
column17: This innovation bridges the gap between validated agronomic research and smallholder farmers by creating a digital advisory platform. With limited extension services (1 officer per 2,000 farmers), the initiative delivers site-specific agronomic recommendations through Farmer Facing Organizations (FFOs) via SMS, IVR, WhatsApp, and chatbots. Focused on soil health, climate-smart practices, and precision cropping, the platform tailors content to Nigeria’s agroecological zones, translating it into local languages.; ; Piloted with 17,000 users, it achieved remarkable results, doubling yields from 2000–2500 kg/ha to 4000 kg/ha. A Human-Centered Design study enhanced usability, emphasizing simplified language, time-stamped content, and geotagged weather advisories. Future plans include expanding services to Kenya and integrating digital crop calendars to address climate risks.; ; This demand-driven, open-data initiative fosters collaboration with farmer facing organisations (FFOs) to monitor and assess impact, providing actionable solutions to smallholder farmers while advancing productivity, resilience, and sustainability in agriculture.

column17: The innovation is an integrated package of agronomic solutions tailored to Northern Ghana's soybean production challenges. It bridges knowledge gaps, ensures access to certified seeds, legume fertilizers, and inoculants, and delivers timely market, price, and weather advisories. Leveraging the ESOKO digital platform and scalable methods like video sessions, demonstration field days, and community sensitization, the initiative has reached over 60,000 smallholder farmers.; ; The solution empowers farmers and extension agents to adopt sustainable practices, increasing yields and profitability. For broader CGIAR impact, the initiative also introduces a gender-sensitive mechanization service platform, reducing labor-intensive tasks and promoting inclusivity. Robust technical infrastructure is essential to scale the effort and ensure its transformative impact across regions and initiatives.

column16: The National Meteorological Agency of Senegal uses multi-disciplinary working groups to deliver gender-sensitive livestock climate information services, benefiting estimated 4,322 pastoralists in eight regions of Senegal.
column17: The National Meteorological Agency of Senegal (ANACIM),  supported by the Livestock and Climate Initiative, has significantly enhanced the co-production and delivery of gender-sensitive livestock climate information services through multidisciplinary working group (MWGs). Through participatory processes, MWGs bring together diverse stakeholders, including meteorologists, local governments, extension agents, and community representatives, to tailor climate advisories to the needs of agro-pastoralists. The integration of scientific forecasts with indigenous knowledge ensures the relevance and accuracy of advisories, addressing key concerns such as rainfall patterns, dry spells, and extreme weather events. Dissemination via trusted channels, including local radio and community forums, has increased accessibility for women and marginalized farmers through MWGs. In 2024 climate information services had reached estimated 4,322 pastoralists in four departments. By institutionalizing MWGs, ANACIM is ensuring sustainable and inclusive climate services that support the livelihoods of Senegal's livestock-dependent communities.

column16: Scientists of the Agroecology Initiative in Zimbabwe take up research results on farmer agency and drivers of change facilitating the shifting of gender norms related to mechanization of post-harvest activities.
column17: The introduction of machinery has increased men’s participation in post-harvesting activities like threshing, which were traditionally labeled as women's roles. Initiative research on the experiences and agency of diverse farmers provided insights into the potential for mechanization to mitigate gaps in men’s resources and opportunities as well as their tendency to experience a decline in agency as they aged, while also revealing to community participants the shared benefits of a mechanized and collaborative approach to post-harvest activities. Mechanization has also fostered collaborations between NGOs and farmers with 2 operators in Mbire supplying hay bales for other projects in the district. The operators are receiving coupons from the Environmental Management Agency (EMA) to collect grass as a way of reducing veld fires and promoting environmental conservation.

column16: Scientists, local government, and practitioners of the Agroecology Initiative in Zimbabwe take up research results on farmer agency and drivers of change engaging elders as knowledge holders for agroecological innovations.
column17: The findings from the WP5 studies about which actors had (and which lacked) agency in decision-making and opportunities for agroecological innovation was taken up to design the activities and/or inclusion effort for specific actors. This research revealed that elder farmers in Zimbabwe, particularly men, face reduced agency and opportunities compared to younger counterparts. However, traditional knowledge offers valuable insights for sustainable agroecological practices. Since 2024, the Initiative has taken action and engaged 179 elderly community members in Mbire and Murehwa districts through the Community Dialogue of Elders (CDE). ; ; The CDE serves as a platform to integrate Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS) with modern agroecological techniques, addressing topics like traditional farming, resource governance, cultural ceremonies, gender inclusion, intergenerational knowledge transfer, and human-wildlife conflict. ; ; The initiative yielded three key benefits: 1) cultural and ecological integration by emphasizing rituals (e.g., seed sanctification, rainmaking) and traditional governance for sustainability; 2) inclusivity by engaging diverse stakeholders, including women and youth, fostering gender equity and knowledge sharing; 3) community ownership, building trust and ensuring agroecological practices align with local traditions. These efforts reduce external dependency, address barriers, and build resilience.

column16: In Tunisia, an upgraded business model integrates agroecological principles in olive oil production
column17: The olive oil value chain in the Elles community of Northwest Tunisia is a vital, yet underdeveloped, part of the national economy in Tunisia. Farmers face challenges including limited access to markets, reliance on conventional practices, and inadequate infrastructure. The potential for high-quality olive oil production is significant, driven by the area's unique climate, indigenous olive varieties, and rich cultural heritage. However, achieving this potential requires a business model that promotes sustainable practices, increases local value addition, enhances product marketability, and secures better returns for producers. Therefore, an upgraded business model, rooted in agroecological principles, is contributing to transform the existing system, supporting economic growth and environmental stewardship. This new business model enhances productivity, promotes a strong product identity and engage the community in the transformation of their local economy. The creation of a farm organization was a key element in this transformation in order to enhance collaboration and social inclusion, create a unified voice and enable access to needed financial and technical support.

column16: In Zimbabwe, investors, the private sector, NGOs, and farmers participate equitably in partnerships to co-develop poultry and sorghum business models, linking agroecological innovations to markets and investment.
column17: The activity began with a value chain analysis of 11 agroecology-aligned chains in Zimbabwe's Mbire and Murehwa districts, identifying business models for upgrading and support. Detailed business model canvases, cost-benefit analysis, and SWOT analyses were conducted for four promising value chains, narrowing to two supported models. In Mbire, Agrowth/PHI implemented a sorghum contract farming model to pre-finance production and mitigate drought risks. Sorghum, suited to Mbire’s harsh conditions, gains market access via offtakers like Buffalo Breweries. In Murehwa, a Sasso poultry model promoted dual-purpose poultry for nutrition and income, linking farmers to local and urban markets with growing organic demand. Innovations like mechanized feed processing, threshers, and conservation agriculture practices supported these transitions. These efforts, informed by WP1 innovations and WP2 contextual analysis, facilitated improved resilience and market integration for farmers.

column17: The assessment of use of Climate Information Services (CIS) was done in four regions in Senegal to retrieve feedback from users to improve the delivery system. The survey revealed its significant impact on improving decision-making, reducing risks, and enhancing resilience among agro-pastoralists. Jokalante disseminated timely, actionable climate and agropastoral information through channels such as SMS, IVR, and community radio broadcasts. The services were widely adopted, with 90% of beneficiaries utilizing the information to optimize agricultural and livestock activities, safeguard resources, and mitigate losses. A notable 81% of respondents credited the information with preventing losses, while 99% expressed strong interest in continued access to these services, reflecting their perceived value. In total, 906,005 (451,661 males and 454,344 females) producesr got access to CIS. However, challenges such as message comprehension and financial sustainability were identified, underscoring the need for refinements in delivery methods and engagement strategies.; ;

The biomass derived from these processes will be used for producing compost aimed at improving cacao fertilization.; ; With Banaqui Curimaná, we supported the reactivation of a cacao collection center, benefiting over 100 farmers. column16: In Zimbabwe, food system actors co-design or adapt financial mechanisms that support agroecological innovations: Tailored microfinance options, digital financing models, contract farming agreements for sorghum farming.
column17: We identified and co-developed financial solutions to address the main barriers faced by smallholder farmers, such as high interest rates and lack of collateral. Key mechanisms proposed include tailored microfinance options via partnerships with institutions like Zambuko Trust, enhanced community-based financing by upgrading Internal Savings and Lending Schemes (ISALs) to Savings and Credit Cooperative Organizations (SACCOs), and digital financing models using platforms like EcoCash. Additional strategies involve contract farming agreements to ensure stable market access, credit guarantees to mitigate lending risks, and insurance options to manage climate and production risks. These financial tools create a more accessible and resilient financial ecosystem, supporting the long-term sustainability of agroecological business models in sorghum farming. By facilitating affordable and secure funding pathways, the support provided recommendations to empower smallholder farmers to continue their operations sustainably and with reduced financial risk

column16: FishBase and SeaLifeBase: Global Information Systems on aquatic species for specialist researchers and hobbyists to support fisheries management and conservation
column17: FishBase and SeaLifeBase are online, publicly accessible information systems on aquatic species. They are used globally by researchers, practitioners, students, and hobbyists as authoritative sources of data, illustrations, and bibliographic references covering more than 40,000 aquatic species. Species information can be queried by common name, genus, species, geographic distribution, family, ecosystem, literature reference, analytical tools, and other attributes, and is available in multiple languages. As of 2025, the FishBase initiative is coordinated by an international consortium of 17 organizations, including WorldFish, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, and the University of British Columbia, together with other leading universities, research institutes, and natural history museums. The initiative is supported by a global network of over 2,570 registered collaborators, who contribute to data curation, validation, and thematic updates. FishBase currently records approximately 700,000 unique users per month, reflecting its broad and sustained use across disciplines, including fisheries management, marine and freshwater ecology, biodiversity conservation, parasitology, education, and policy-relevant research. Its role as a global digital public knowledge infrastructure continues to expand, supporting both scientific inquiry and evidence-informed decision-making worldwide.

column16: Farmers in Burkina Faso and Tunisia who included fodder crops in the Agroecological Living Landscapes boost their livestock productivity
column17: The inclusion of fodder crops, including cereals and legumes, in Sahelian mixed crop-livestock systems has generated remarkable benefits. In Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso, the availability of cattle feed increased fivefold through fodder crop production compared to traditional foraging. Research by CIRAD, CIRDES, and INERA came up with balanced diets based on these crops to enhance milk production. Additionally, in Tunisia’s El Kef-Siliana transect, ewes grazing a mix of vetch, oat, and triticale led to a 20% increase in flock fertility. Moreover, although not directly linked with livestock productivity, the Tunisia experience, led by ICARDA, OEP, INRAT, and ISA-CM, also doubled soil microbial activity in soils under this sort of grazing, supporting the soil health improvement under mixed systems. These findings underscore the advantages of diversifying crop components in mixed farming systems.

column16: Animal manure applied by farmers in Agroecological Living Landscapes  in Kenya, Burkina Faso and Senegal plays crucial role in agroecological systems, serving as organic fertilizer, soil conditioner, input for bio-inputs
column17: An agronomic assessment undertaken by the Initiative reveals that animal manure plays a crucial role in agroecological systems, serving as organic fertilizer, soil conditioner, and input for bio-inputs. In Kenya (research conducted by IITA, Alliance Bioversity & CIAT, CIFOR-ICRAF, DNRC, and CSHEP), maize yields increased by 18%, and bean yields by 25%, when fertilized with 10 tons/ha of manure. However, applying 4 tons/ha of manure did not significantly increase spinach yields. Furthermore, cattle manure in Burkina Faso and horse manure in Senegal effectively boosted groundnut and millet production. For example, in Senegal, manure increased groundnut and cowpea yields as sole crops by 23% and 36%, respectively. These findings highlight the importance of manure as a strategic resource. However, achieving sustainable impacts requires a thorough understanding of its nutrient composition, availability, and optimal application rates for specific crops and contexts.

column16: Farmers who apply biopesticides in Agroecological Living Landscapes in Kenya, Zimbabwe and India keep pests in check
column17: An agronomic assessment undertaken by the Initiative reveals that plant-based biopesticides derived from neem and chili extracts have proved effective in reducing pests’ incidence. In Kenya, neem-based biopesticides reduced fall armyworm incidence in maize by 5.2% and aphid incidence in beans by 22%. Similarly, chili-based biopesticides lowered brassica aphid incidence in cabbage by 5%. These trials, conducted by IITA, the Alliance of Bioversity & CIAT, CIFOR-ICRAF, DNRC, and CSHEP, revealed promising trends, though pest pressures were lower than typical conditions. Further testing under diverse climatic conditions and pest pressures is needed to confirm their efficacy in supporting integrated pest management (IPM) in diverse environments. Additionally, neem and chili biopesticides are being trialed in Zimbabwe and India, but results are still pending. Comprehensive data collection and analysis are crucial to validate the effectiveness of these biopesticides and ensure their optimal use in IPM across diverse agroecological systems.

column16: Adoption of pig artificial insemination by women and men pig keepers in Uganda through SAPLING supported artificial insemination service providers
column17: Within Uganda, the Sustainable Animal Productivity (SAPLING) initiative is working to strengthen the pig value-chain within four target districts.  As part of this work, a focus has been on strengthening the pig-genetics sub-value-chain, through support to professional pig artificial insemination (AI) service provision and promotion of pig AI adoption.  21 (12 female and 9 male) animal health-care workers have received technical training and other  support from SAPLING in pig artificial insemination and are now offering pig AI services as part of their business activities.  These providers performed pig AI in 242 households, corresponding to 1064 people reached (using an average household size of 4.4 according to the Uganda Bureau of Statistics 2024).

column16: Circular Bioeconomy Innovation Hub in Ghana is used by 17 co-owners for scaling circular economy innovations
column17: The Circular Bioeconomy Innovation Hub in Ghana is a multistakeholder platform initiated by IWMI as one-stop-shop for training, research, advisory support, collaboration and knowledge sharing. The hub unites now 17 stakeholders from the public and private sectors, research institutions, non-governmental organizations, and education to promote circular bioeconomy initiatives. Operating in the organic waste-to-resource value chain, a co-ownership model that ensures shared goals and resources for co-design and co-implementation is used for maximum collective impact. The hub aims to showcase, optimize, and promote existing circular bioeconomy innovations while fostering the development of new, accessible innovations. In 2024, the co-owners of the hub agreed to formalize their collaboration under a Memorandum of Understanding.

column16: Ghanaian cassava farmers adopt AKILIMO digital recommendations for improved crop management and soil health developed International Institute of Tropical Agriculture and Partners
column17: AKILIMO is a digital decision support system developed by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture that delivers personalized cassava farming recommendations through mobile apps and paper formats. The system combines soil and weather data with market information to provide location-specific advice on fertilizer use, planting methods, and soil management. In Ghana, smallholder cassava farmers accessed these recommendations through extension services and began implementing the suggested practices. This adoption addresses the challenge of providing tailored agricultural guidance across diverse local conditions. Farmers reported improved decision-making capabilities in crop management, leading to more sustainable and productive cassava systems that enhance food security and rural livelihoods while promoting better soil health practices.

column16: In Ucayali, Peru, cacao farmers engaged in the Agroecological Living Landscape, who apply traditional, simple and low-cost practices in managing cacao fruit diseases reduce disease pressure on their cacao orchards.
column17: The agronomic assessment done by the Agroecology Initiative revealed: Trials in organic cacao orchards at the Pucallpa ALL in Peru, co-designed by the Alliance Bioversity & CIAT with the Colpa de Loros and Banaqui-Curimana cooperatives, highlighted the vital role of cultural practices in managing cacao fruit diseases. Regularly harvesting diseased fruits proved the most effective strategy, keeping moniliasis incidences below 5% in well-managed orchards, compared to nearly five times higher in orchards neglecting this practice, regardless of biofungicide use. These findings underscore the agroecological value of reducing disease pressure through simple, low-cost practices rather than relying solely on external inputs. Although unusually warm and dry conditions during the 2023–2024 season contributed to low disease levels, the trials demonstrated that cultural practices could safeguard production even in favorable conditions for disease suppression. This evidence underscores the need to prioritize cultural practices as key components of sustainable and agroecological disease management in cacao production systems.

column16: Climate+ reach 3709 new females and 5908 new males with climate resilience agro-advisories in the Philippines in 2025
column17: In 2024, Climate+ was created as an API link between Rice Crop Management Advisory Service (RCMAS), which gives farm-level crop and nutrient advice, and Agro-Climatic Advisory Portal (ACAP), which provides seasonal and 10-day weather forecasts sourced from the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA). In 2025, Climate+ was upgraded to connect directly with PAGASA through dedicated APIs. Using forecast data, Climate+ adjusts RCMAS recommendations when flood or drought risks are detected. Updated, weather-based advisories are sent to registered farmers via SMS. Climate+ was pilot tested during the 2024 wet season in Libmanan, Camarines Sur, and again in the 2025 wet season in Camarines Sur and Isabela. Farmers may receive several SMS alerts in one season when climate risks coincide with critical rice growth stages. Results from the 2024 pilot show that Climate+ is operationally feasible and valuable, helping farmers make timely, practical decisions during extreme weather by translating forecasts into crop- and growth stage-specific guidance.

column16: 522325 farmers reached with climate forecasts and agroclimatic advisories through radio in Guatemala
column17: CGIAR and partners sustained and expanded the dissemination of climate forecasts and agroclimatic advisories through radio as an inclusive “last-mile” channel. Evidence letters from partner radio stations confirm regular broadcasts of agroclimatic spots linked to Local Technical Agroclimatic Committees (LTACs) during key agricultural seasons (MJJ, ASO). In 2025, radio dissemination reached an estimated 597,180 rural listeners, including farmers in Chiquimula/Zacapa (360,000, as reported in station confirmation letters), Petén (168,000), Jutiapa (42,750), Zacapa (12,180), and Izabal (14,250). These broadcasts complemented digital and face-to-face channels, strengthening access to climate information for farmers in low-connectivity contexts and reinforcing radio as a scalable and equitable dissemination mechanism.

column16: Farmers engaged in the Agroecological Living Landscapes in the semi-arid El Kef-Siliana transect, Tunisia, revitalized soils through rhizobium inoculation and treatment with biochar.
column17: In Tunisia, ICARDA and INRAT led research to improve soil health and plant productivity in the semi-arid El Kef-Siliana transect. as revealed by an agronomic assessment of the Initiative, Rhizobium inoculation significantly enhanced biomass production in both durum wheat and the melliferous fodder sulla plant. In sulla, inoculation doubled plant height and boosted biomass to over 7.5 tons/ha, compared to 3.8 tons/ha for non-inoculated plants. Similarly, inoculation in durum wheat doubled biomass, which is used as a high-protein fodder crop under semi-arid conditions. Additionally, combining biochar with chemical fertilizers nearly doubled durum wheat grain yield compared to treatments without biochar, highlighting biochar’s role in optimizing fertilizer efficiency. ;  In Tunisia, the national partner responsible for testing and promoting biochar technologies—the Olive Institute—has recently acquired a biochar pyrolyzer through donor support to further advance this innovation. Field trials conducted in 2023 demonstrated that biochar, when combined with compost, has a strong positive effect on crop productivity in semi-arid areas.; Building on these results, a public–private partnership is being established in the Kef Governorate involving a large-scale compost-producing olive oil processing company and local farmers, who will have access to biochar produced by the Olive Institute. This partnership is expected to support the agroecological and sustainable production of olives and forage crops, while strengthening circular economy approaches in semi-arid farming systems

column16: Community-operated Black Soldier Fly plant transforms organic waste into livestock feed and fertilizer for 83 farmers in Western Kenya
column17: A community-driven Black Soldier Fly plant in Western Kenya has successfully converted organic waste into valuable livestock feed and fertilizer, addressing the challenge of expensive conventional animal feed. The International Water Management Institute supported the establishment of this facility, which is operated by community-selected members and has been running for over a year. The plant has processed 24.73 metric tons of organic waste, producing 1.94 metric tons of protein-rich larvae for animal feed and 3.29 metric tons of organic fertilizer. Beyond production, it serves as a training center where 46 farmers have learned to replicate this sustainable farming model. This innovation improves soil health, increases farm productivity, creates additional income opportunities, and demonstrates strong potential for waste management with projected annual revenue of 1.65 million Kenyan Shillings.

column16: In India and Laos, farmers participating in Agroecological Living Landscapes increase their income by diversifying traditional paddy rice crops.
column17: An agronomic assessment undertaken by the Initiative assessed agroecological innovations in India and Laos, co-designed by IWMI, partners, and local communities, aimed at diversifying traditional paddy rice monocropping systems. In India, 46% of households adopting multilayer crop systems on small plots (approximately 1000 m²) experienced increased income compared to rice cultivation on the same area. These systems, integrating up to 15 crops, were implemented by women self-help groups from tribal communities with support from PRADAN, targeting enhanced income and improved nutrition. In Laos, as part of an integrated wetland management approach, rice-fish culture is being promoted to further diversify paddy rice systems. These efforts collectively seek to strengthen food security, provide year-round income, and reduce reliance on rice monoculture while fostering agroecological practices.

column16: Advancing institutional use of climate information services through Africa-led capacity strengthening to enhance early warning, preparedness, and climate-informed planning and decision-making across public and regional organizations
column17: Through an Africa-led, co-designed advanced course on climate information services, professionals from over 30 countries strengthened their ability to interpret and apply CIS for climate risk management. Evidence from outcome reporting and independent partnership survey results confirms strong uptake and use: the majority of participants reported applying CIS within months in real-world contexts, including early warning systems, seasonal forecasting, participatory scenario planning, advisory services, and institutional planning processes. Survey data further shows substantial peer-to-peer diffusion, with over half of respondents cascading CIS knowledge within their organizations and networks. Together, these changes demonstrate sustained institutional use of CIS, contributing to improved preparedness, early warning, and climate-informed decision-making aligned with Area of Work 2 outcomes

column16: Farmers testing crop associations in Agroecological Living Landscapes in Senegal, Zimbabwe, India and Lao PDR increase crop productivity, resilience, and sustainability.
column17: An agronomic assessment by the Initiative reveals that crop associations have proven highly beneficial across various countries. A trial in Fatick, Senegal, conducted by ISRA, CIRAD, and ENDA, demonstrated that millet grain productivity increased 30-times and the biomass four times when grown after groundnut and cowpea rotation, compared to millet grown without the legume’s rotation. Similarly, CIMMYT, government agencies, and development partners, in collaboration with local communities, implemented push-pull intercropping systems of maize or sorghum with beans or cowpea, reducing fall armyworm damage by 22%. In India, multilayer cropping systems boosted income and food security, while rice-legume rotations in Lao PDR are looking to enhance soil fertility. These examples underscore the versatile roles crop associations play in improving productivity, resilience, and sustainability. By using synergies among crops, agroecological systems can address critical challenges such as pest management, soil health, and food security, making them vital for sustainable agricultural landscapes.

column16: Farmers who apply soil-water conservation practices in Agroecological Living Landscapes in Kenya and Zimbabwe increase bean productivity and reduce severity of fall armyworm damage.
column17: In Kenya, the use of vegetated terraces (i.e., planted with Napier grass) led to an increase in bean productivity of 25%. On these fragile tropical soils, these terraces are also likely to sustain productivity on the long term, though this could not be measure over few seasons. However, a reduction of 22% in the severity of fall armyworm damage on cereals thanks to conservation agriculture was recorded, due to increased abundance of natural enemies.

column16: Empowering Farmers and Facilitators with Digital Agricultural Innovations: Piloting the GeoAgro-MiSR App for Sustainable Farming in Egypt
column17: The GeoAgro-MiSR app, developed by ICARDA in collaboration with the Egyptian government and key partners, is a transformative digital tool designed to enhance agronomic decision-making for smallholder farmers. By integrating real-time data on climate conditions, soil health, and market trends, the app provides targeted recommendations to optimize resource use, improve yields, and enhance sustainability.; ; The app was introduced to 120 farmer groups across 14 governorates in Egypt, covering diverse agroecological zones. Through comprehensive training sessions and real-time feedback collection, ICARDA has refined the app’s usability, ensuring it meets the practical needs of farmers and extension agents. Key features include production planning tools, climate prediction models, and financial analysis resources.; ; With over 3,000 participants engaged, the initiative is driving digital transformation in agriculture, fostering resilience, and improving food security. Future improvements will focus on expanding access, integrating expert consultation features, and enhancing usability to maximize farmer adoption.

column16: Farmers in Bangladesh adopted the potato zero tillage and straw mulch technology
column17: After the introduction of Potato Zero Tillage and Straw Mulch (PTZM) in 2021 and 2022, a survey was conducted in June 2023 in one of the communities with all 428 households who previously participated to understand farmers’ willingness to adopt PZTM. Another follow-up survey was then carried out in February 2024 at the beginning of potato growing season to assess the actual adoption rate. The results confirm that farmers strongly support the PZTM technology as a way to utilize the fallow plots for food production during the dry winter season. The minimum requirement for input of labor, water and fertilizer appears to be contributing to farmers’ adoption.

column16: 1,000 South African youth address environmental challenges through citizen science and digital innovation
column17: Around 1,000 South African youth are tackling environmental challenges through the Enviro-Champs initiative, combining citizen science and digital innovation to drive sustainable change. Originating in Mpophomeni township, KwaZulu-Natal, the program, supported by the Duzi-uMngeni Conservation Trust (DUCT), has expanded with government investment to address water leaks, waste management, and flood preparedness. Through a partnership with the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), the Digital Innovation Initiative empowers young people through UNICEF Impact Youth Market (YOMA) platform with green "learning to earning" opportunities, enhancing their skills in environmental monitoring. The partnership integrates digital tools like Open Data Kit (ODK) to improve data collection and decision-making for water management in the Limpopo Basin. By valuing indigenous knowledge, action-learning, and capacity building, Enviro-Champs not only contribute to ecological restoration but also gain vital skills, employment, and economic empowerment, bridging the digital divide while promoting sustainable development.

column16: In Kiambu, Kenya, the adoption by local small holder vegetable farmers participating in the Agroecological Living Landscape of new agroecological business models and increased production of vermicompost increases sales volumes.
column17: Prior to 2022, smallholder farmers in Kiambu relied heavily on inorganic fertilizers and pesticides, believing organic alternatives were ineffective and unavailable. The Agroecology Initiative WP3 introduced farmer training through a Training of Trainers (ToT) model, training 45 ToTs on agroecological pest control and organic fertilizer production, particularly vermicompost using red worms. Partnering with Comfort Worms and Insects Ltd, the Initiative developed an outgrower scheme, training 10 farmers to produce vermicompost and sell it to the company. Additionally, farmers with access to animal manure supplied it for processing, receiving 30% of the finished product in return. These approaches increased vermicompost production from one to four tonnes per week. Initially, less than 10% of vermicompost was used locally, but with increased production and training, over 25% is now adopted by smallholder farmers, improving soil health and sustainability in Kiambu ALL.

column16: National government (5), national agricultural research systems and universities (3) and CGIAR Centers (10) application of biophysical and socioeconomic modeling tools to explore strategic policy options relevant for developing countries
column17: Food, land and water (FLW) systems face challenges from a host of interacting megatrends as well as local and regional drivers such as changes in population, urbanization, income, inequality, migration, diets, technology, biodiversity, and climate. Many of these trends are themselves influenced by changes in FLW systems, interacting in complex ways that have important impacts on nutrition, poverty, equity, climate, and  environment.  To capture these complexities we need among other things quantitative tools that help us understand how, where and at what cost these complex  interactions are manifest across the food system at global and regional scales.  This innovation draws on CGIAR’s biophysical and socioeconomic expertise to enhance the IMPACT model by developing and enhancing specific modules to better understand FLW system outcomes under plausible future scenarios. Testing of scenarios in IMPACT was done through engagement with researchers from CG Centers, national agricultural research systems and national government in LMICs.

column16: In Fatick, Senegal, in an innovative agroecology business model applied in the Agroecology Living Landscape, millet is now processed locally, contributing to wealth creation and job generation in local communities.
column17: The Senegalese Institute of Agricultural Research (ISRA) has developed short-cycle millet varieties, adapted to climate change and producing large grains, ideal for flour production, thus meeting the needs of millers and bakers. It is in this context that one association of Niakhar (in the department of Fatick) GIE (Economic interest group) JAMM BUGUM is developing compound bread in his bakery, with an incorporation rate of 30% millet, making it possible to reduce wheat imports by the same proportion. In the past, millet was mainly sold raw in markets, without adding value. column17: The Demand-Led Seed Systems model developed by the Pan-Africa Bean Research Alliance (PABRA | The Pan-Africa Bean Research Alliance (pabra-africa.org), and adopted by the CGIAR Seed Equal Initiative, is improving varietal turnover, seed production and bean production. This boosted varietal turnover, increased bean grain production by 10%, and expanded harvest areas by 11% in 2023. The Model has since been expanded and adapted for other commodities including Sorghum, Ground nuts, cowpea, Soybean, Millet, Faba beans, lentils, and Chickpeas.

column16: Uptake of the Prioritizing Agronomy in a Changing Environment (PAiCE) tool for climate change impact analysis and adaptation strategies prioritization
column17: Prioritization of adaptation strategies to enable the smallholder farmers become more resilient  to climate change impacts are not given much attention. Through stakeholder consultations, PAiCE provides a structured approach to characterize and explore potential adaption solutions for specific crop production regions. First, characterization data for production constraints and climate challenges as well as system characteristics are aggregated to ensure that discussions are focused on topics that require the wisdom of groups. Second, experimental evidence of the value of different technologies and management approaches to respond to the current and future challenges are aggregated.  Third, the areas of uncertainty and evidence gaps  are addressed to enhance initial results. A provisional set of priorities is shared with more stakeholders to cross-validate results. Results from the PAiCE tool will provide a strong foundation for agronomy adaptation by steering investment and helping to coordinate the efforts of partners through action roadmap development

column16: Adoption of good manufacturing practices by small scale feed producers in Uganda through SAPLING supported trainings
column17: The livestock feed sector in Uganda is mostly controlled by small-scale companies who offer costly, inadequate feeds, leaving farmers with few choices. The rise of small-scale feed producers has transformed concentrate feed production, offering opportunities while simultaneously presenting challenges such as insufficient technical expertise in feed formulation and mixing, resulting in the manufacture of costly and substandard feeds.; ; An intervention was implemented by SAPLING with 40 feed producers in two phases across the project districts. In the first phase, the feed producers were trained in principles of feed formulation. In the second phase, the trained feed producers were mentored on good feed manufacturing practices (GMP) for feed production for 8 months. They were assessed for their adherence to the procedures they had learned. The results indicate that in addition to those who were already following certain GMPs, a larger number of feed producers are now compliant with most of the practices.

column17: Developed by the CGIAR Research Initiative on Livestock and Climate together with partners as an approach to social learning and scaling, Pioneer Positive Deviance identifies and learns from community members who overcome common challenges using unique solutions without additional resources or external inputs. Note that support to Urochloa hybrid distribution has been provided by SAPLING over these years.

column16: Community-based goat breeding program adopted by 183 households in Mali improves indigenous breeds and livestock productivity
column17: Mali's first community-based breeding program for goats was launched in 2023 to address low livestock productivity among smallholder farmers. The program targets indigenous breeds including Djallonké, Bali-Bali, and Peulh goats that are well-adapted to local conditions but needed genetic improvement. Developed through collaboration between ICARDA, ILRI, and national partners, the systematic breeding framework has been adopted by 183 households representing 1,870 people. The program has registered 1,237 goats and established breeding protocols that enable farmers to improve their livestock while preserving valuable local genetic resources. This community-driven approach empowers farmers to make informed breeding decisions, contributing to enhanced food security and improved livelihoods in rural Mali.

column16: CGIAR co-developed livestock feed technology scaling methodology made accessible to Tunisian farmers through private-public partnership
column17: In Tunisia ICARDA developed a technology and scaling methodology for a more resilient, low-emission livestock feed system to alleviate pressure on grazing lands with the support from Livestock and Climate and the Initiative on Agroecology. The system uses a small-scale compressor that produces pellets from nutritious agricultural byproducts. After refining the formula with farmers using locally available inputs, scaling focused on farmer cooperatives in the south of Tunisia, where there is high demand for supplementary feeds. A private-public partnership was established with the national government Office de l’Elevage et des Pâturages and private sector partner Juhaina to facilitate this scaling. Trainings and demonstrations were co-organised to show farmers the advantages and how to use the pelleting machine. Over 60 machines have now been sold with 100s of livestock keepers benefiting whilst alleviating pressure on grazing areas. The system is now being shared in other countries to encourage uptake.; Other private machine manufacturing companies, like Prmat and EMP have now started manufacturing the small scale pelletizer to satisfy the Tunisian market with locally produced pelletizers. They got inspired from Juhainas imported model.

column16: Empowering students to transform organic waste with innovation in Colombia
column17: An innovation challenge and hackathon was organized to tackle two critical issues: inefficient organic waste management in the agri-food sector and the lack of technological innovation in waste utilization processes. The initiative aimed to foster innovative solutions from students, focusing on optimizing organic waste use through black soldier fly larvae (Hermetia illucens). A total of 70 students—64 from SENA's CDTI and 6 from the Universidad Autónoma de Occidente—participated in the challenge, which unfolded in three phases. Their mission was to design and develop an automated production unit for converting organic waste into valuable resources using black soldier fly larvae. Students worked in multidisciplinary teams to design and prototype the production units during the three phases of the challenge. This initiative empowered students to apply technology and sustainability principles, driving forward a more efficient and eco-friendly approach to waste management. In 2025, partners who participated in the development of the application of the black soldier fly production unit, continue to explore the optimization of the prototypes.

column17: ; [No activities implemented in 2025.]; ; Farmerline, a social enterprise operating in Ghana, utilizes the Multi-Dimensional Inclusivity Index (MDII) to assess and enhance the inclusivity of its Business-to-Farmer (B2F) services. Additionally, the assessment informed strategies to mitigate risks such as digital exclusion and environmental impacts.

column16: Uptake of CGIAR Livestock and Climate innovation 'opportunistic grazing' by Government of Tunisia
column17: Through collaborative research and action, ICARDA and the Tunisian government have co-pioneered opportunistic grazing as an innovative approach to sustainable rangeland management and included in the co-published IUCN-ICARDA Sustainable Rangeland Management toolkit, guided by scientific principles and enriched by local knowledge. Opportunistic grazing involves allowing livestock to graze on available forage during favorable conditions, ensuring optimal resource utilization. By adopting this approach, rangeland managers can maximize forage use, enhance ecosystem health, and achieve livestock production goals. This strategy has proven particularly effective in restoring rangelands and strengthening ecosystem resilience in Tunisia’s semi-arid regions. Recognizing its transformative potential, the Tunisian government has integrated opportunistic grazing into its rangeland management policies, updating regulations to formalize this sustainable practice. To date, this innovation has positively impacted 180,000 hectares, directly benefiting 6,212 individuals and contributing to long-term rangeland restoration and sustainability.

column17: The Integrated Renewable Energy and Sustainable Agriculture (IRESA) biogas model transforms agricultural waste into clean cooking fuel and organic fertilizer.  Developed through CGIAR's Nature-Positive Solutions initiative with local partners, this circular bioeconomy approach addresses rural energy poverty and environmental degradation in India. Ten households and one school in Maharashtra's Akole cluster now use the system, reducing dependence on firewood and LPG while improving air quality and soil fertility. The model generates gas equivalent to 12 LPG cylinders annually . School staff and local youth received training to ensure sustainable operation, while 313 students learn about circular economy principles through hands-on experience with the technology.

column16: Foresight Community of Practice: Interactive platform to enhance information and knowledge on food, land and water systems
column17: The Foresight Community of Practice (CoP) aims to bring together foresight researchers and practitioners interested in transforming food, land, and water systems, with a focus on low and lower-middle-income countries. This is our community. The practices we are interested in discussing include models and tools, data and metrics, and practical foresight analysis for enhanced priority setting, policy, and investment decision-making. Note that these practices range from back-end model development and data analytics to generate actionable metrics, to the use of this knowledge for decision-making support. The Foresight CoP has a discussion forum for its members to exchange information and knowledge and to engage in meaningful discussions on a wide variety of foresight-related topics.

column16: Living Labs for People in China: Introducing low-carbon food systems concept in Qingshan Village
column17: This report summarizes a qualitative evaluation by the MELIA team on China’s Living Labs for People (LL4P), implemented in Qingshan Village by the Mitigate+ Initiative. column16: Systematic mapping of food security and nutrition projects in Guatemala, innovation use
column17: The MICI-SAN platform is an interactive mapping tool that tracks food security and nutrition programs across Guatemala at the municipal level. Developed by CGIAR's International Food Policy Research Institute in collaboration with USAID Guatemala, the platform addresses the challenge of fragmented donor coordination by consolidating project data that was previously scattered across different sources and often outdated. The tool provides detailed information about each intervention including budgets, timelines, and implementing organizations, while integrating socioeconomic and climate vulnerability data to identify gaps in coverage. USAID Guatemala has adopted this platform to enhance strategic decision-making and improve coordination among international donors, leading to more efficient resource allocation and complementary programming in food security and nutrition efforts across the country.

column16: Livestock farmers in Kenya and Ethiopia have access to Pioneer Positive Deviance approach for supporting social inclusive development and scaling of climate-smart livestock practices
column17: Developed by the CGIAR Research Initiative on Livestock and Climate together with partners as an approach to social learning and scaling, Pioneer Positive Deviance identifies innovative farmer-led solutions developed by pioneer households in response to climate-related challenges in livestock management. The solutions are shared through farmer2farmer networks and field days for scaling within and beyond  communities. In Kenya it has enabled 45 pioneer households in Bomet and Nandi counties to share innovations and is being adopted by the county extension systems. In Ethiopia, it was piloted in Amhara region with 40 pioneer households invested in sheep fattening. Though security issues prevented full implementation 13,752 co-designed booklets on sheep fattening were distributed in 36 villages. Stakeholder workshops led three universities to incorporate Pioneer Positive Deviance, with plans to expand its use in the national extension system. These efforts showcase its potential to drive farmer-led innovation and inclusive scaling across diverse contexts.

column16: Pioneer Positive Deviance approach enables 15,424 Kenyan households to access locally-developed climate-smart livestock practices
column17: Developed by the CGIAR Research Initiative on Livestock and Climate together with partners as an approach to social learning and scaling, Pioneer Positive Deviance enables more than 15,424 pioneer households in livestock management in Kenya to access climate-smart livestock practices through farmer2farmer networks. 39 pioneer households have engaged 4,400 participants across 37 field days. Additionally, 23,000 booklets on feed management for dairy, co-designed with these pioneer households, have been distributed in collaboration with 16 network partners. An assessment of the approach at site level highlights the effectiveness of this approach, showing high adoption rates of climate-smart livestock practices e.g. improved forage and feed. Respondents reported significant improvements in livestock productivity after adopting the pioneer-developed practices, including increased milk production (75.8%), better livestock health (52.5%), and enhanced cost efficiency (29.9%). Furthermore, 80% of survey participants actively share knowledge with other, primarily with neighbors and friends, leveraging social networks to expand impact.

column16: Colombia, Ecuador and Peru take up CGIAR innovation CLEANED for use  by multiple stakeholders
column17: CLEANED (Comprehensive livestock environmental assessment for improved nutrition, a secured environment and sustainable development along livestock value chains), is a multi-dimensional modelling tool designed to produce rapid environmental impact assessments in mixed crop-livestock farming systems in developing countries. Improved over the last three years it can be used at the livestock production level as well as guiding policy decisions and public and private sector investments towards more sustainable livestock production. With support from the Livestock and Climate Initiative in collaboration with the Sustainable Animal Productivity Initiative, CLEANED is now being used in three new countries (Colombia, Ecuador and Peru) with further training and assessments carried out in Tunisia, Colombia and Peru. A user survey confirms user benefits.

column16: The Government of Tunisia uptakes CGIAR innovation CLEANED as a contribution to better reporting and meeting its climate targets
column17: The government Office de l'Elevage et du Paturage (OEP), Tunisia has uptaken CGIAR innovation CLEANED to promote sustainable livestock practices in the country. With support from the Livestock and Climate Initiative and GIZ the tool has been integrated into projects aimed at reducing the environmental footprint of livestock systems (particularly dairy) while improving productivity and livelihoods. The tool has been used to assess the impact of livestock on water, land and greenhouse gas emissions, raising awareness of policymakers to the climate impacts of their livestock sector and options for mitigation. On-demand trainings on CLEANED were provided enabling OEP to use CLEANED for scenario analysis and decision-making. The OEP and others undertook a national survey of dairy farms using the CLEANED concrete assessment. This contributes to Tunisia's national objectives and efforts to meet its Paris Agreement climate commitments by improving data collection, availability and assessment through tools such as CLEANED.

column16: Bridging Science and Action: Early Warning, Early Response, and Financial Readiness for Strengthened Disaster Preparedness
column17: The CGIAR AWARE Platform, in collaboration with World Vision, is strengthening community resilience and disaster preparedness in Sri Lanka through Early Warning, Early Action, and Early Finance initiatives. By leveraging advanced forecasting tools and data-driven insights, the platform enables timely interventions that reduce climate-induced risks. A successful anticipatory action (AA) simulation in Nuwara Eliya. The platform has also helped disaster management organizations improve coordination and collaboration, supporting World Vision Lanka in scaling and digitalizing its Anticipatory Action Protocol. A joint training program for disaster management officers marked a milestone in institutionalizing AA in Sri Lanka. Additionally, the establishment of a National Technical Working Group and the development of a national AA framework have paved the way for influencing policies and shaping future programs, ensuring a more proactive and coordinated disaster risk management approach.;
