column16: Kenya Agricultural Observatory Platform and Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization use CGIAR-supported KAZNET platform to monitor rangeland conditions in nine counties
column17: The Kenya Agricultural Observatory Platform, supported by the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization, leverages the KAZNET platform, developed by ILRI and supported by the CGIAR Research Initiative on Livestock and Climate, to enhance its capacity for monitoring rangeland conditions, livestock markets, and household coping strategies across five arid and semi-arid counties: Marsabit, Samburu, Isiolo, Garissa, and Wajir. By integrating data from 'citizen contributors' and 'super contributors' trained to gather and validate market and environmental information, Kenya Agricultural Observatory Platform provides real-time, geo-referenced insights essential for decision-making in drought-prone areas. The platform empowers public institutions to deliver timely, data-driven interventions, addressing critical gaps in livestock market intelligence and rangeland management. This collaboration ensures actionable climate and livestock information reaches policymakers, pastoralists, and other stakeholders, fostering resilience in Kenya’s drylands. KAZNET's integration within the Kenya Agricultural Observatory Platform underscores the importance of participatory and digital solutions in transforming livestock production systems.

column16: Zep-Re insurance company increases reach of CGIAR innovation Index-based Livestock Insurance to predicted 250,000 pastoralists in Kenya, Ethiopia and Somalia in five years
column17: The CGIAR-supported innovation Index-Based Livestock Insurance is a risk-mitigating tool that encourages livestock keepers to insure their livestock against loss in times of drought or other crises. Facilitated by private sector insurance companies, this insurance provides payouts triggered by satellite-monitored vegetation data, reducing the financial burden of livestock losses caused by forage scarcity. Since 2012 ILRI has been developing IBLI with insurance companies gradually extending its reach. Since 2022-3 its accessibility has been significantly increased to pastoralists Ethiopia, Kenya and Somalia with support from a new World Bank project - De-risking, Inclusion and Value Enhancement- and uptake through Zep-Re Insurance company predicting reach to 250,000 pastoralists in five years. As of 2025, DRIVE is estimated to provide  financial coverage to over 3.2 million pastoralists (https://www.financialprotectionforum.org/blog/pilot-scale-how-research-powers-pastoralists-progress)

column16: Living Labs for People in Kenya: Outcomes of Participatory Action Research in Nandi County
column17: This report summarizes a qualitative evaluation by the MELIA team on Kenya’s Living Labs for People (LL4P), implemented in Nandi County by the Mitigate+ Initiative. LL4P provides a space for stakeholders to co-design, test, and advance socio-technical innovations for sustainable food systems with mitigation benefits. Key users include farmers, organizations, and local governments. The evaluation found that LL4P successfully established an inclusive, co-owned, and autonomous framework. Researchers identified the Kaimosi Agricultural Training Center (KATC) as a local host and secured stakeholder commitment. While the Initiative facilitated the process, stakeholders have taken the lead. LL4P now operates independently with a diverse nine-member board, including four women, one youth, and six farmers.;

column16: 43,897 hectares of shared grazing land benefiting 6,638  pastoralists in Parakuyo, Twatwatwa and Ngaite villages, Kilosa District, Morogoro region, Tanzania secured through facilitation by the CGIAR Livestock and Climate Initiative
column17: Joint village land use planning was developed to address the challenges of protecting and facilitating the sharing of natural resources across village administrative boundaries. Supported by enabling policy and legislation it enables villages sharing a grazing land, water point, forest or conservation area to develop a joint village land use agreement. This agreement protects the use of the land (no village can change the use without approval of all villages and is the foundation of secure collective resource rights through the issuing of certificates of customary rights of occupancy. Piloted, implemented and being scaled by the Livestock and Climate Initiative working closely with the Government of Tanzania, in 2024 it facilitated the securing of 43,897 hectares of shared grazing lands for 6,638  livestock keepers (3,445 male and 3,193 female) from three villages - Parakuyo, Twatwatwa and Ngaite in Kilosa District, Morogoro region.

column16: Opportunistic grazing implemented over 50,000 hectares of rangeland benefiting 1,250 livestock keepers
column17: Through collaborative research and action, ICARDA and the Tunisian government have pioneered opportunistic grazing as an innovative approach to sustainable rangeland management within the Sustainable Rangeland Management toolkit, guided by scientific principles and enriched by local knowledge. Opportunistic grazing involves allowing livestock to graze on available forage during favorable conditions, ensuring optimal resource utilization. By adopting this approach, rangeland managers can maximize forage use, enhance ecosystem health, and achieve livestock production goals. Pastoralists in the Al Mustakbal "Future" Agricultural Development group located in Douz, south Tunisia have optaken opportunistic grazing across 50,000 hectares of rangelands benefiting 1,250 pastoralists.

column16: Government of Ethiopia uptakes participatory rangeland management principles in second phase of Lowlands Livelihoods Resilience Project
column17: The Government of Ethiopia, namely the Ministry of Irrigation and Lowlands has committed to investing US$52.5 million of a US$340 million World Bank soft loan Lowlands Livelihoods Resilience Project (Phase II) to the updating of the 28 existing rangeland management investment plans prepared under the first phase and the formulation of new rangeland management plans through participatory rangeland management principles to identify additional climate-smart mitigation and nature-based solutions, validate their feasibility based on indicative land-use planning and characterization and formulate rangeland management bylaws (page 9 in World Bank Project Appraisal Document). Their point of reference is the Introductory Guidelines on Participatory Rangeland Management produced by ILRI Senior Scientist Fiona Flintan. Participatory rangeland management is a community-led process facilitated by practitioners to build community capacities to better manage, govern and restore their lands. column16: CGIAR Livestock and Climate Initiative facilitates the securing of 2,365 hectares of shared grazing land benefiting 10,167 pastoralists in Kimange, Miono, Mkwajuni and Kweikonje villages, Chalinze District, Coastal region, Tanzania
column17: Joint village land use planning was developed to address the challenges of protecting and facilitating the sharing of natural resources across village administrative boundaries. Supported by enabling policy and legislation it enables villages sharing a grazing land, water point, forest or conservation area to develop a joint village land use agreement. This agreement protects the use of the land (no village can change the use without approval of all villages and is the foundation of secure collective resource rights through the issuing of certificates of customary rights of occupancy. Piloted, implemented and being scaled by the Livestock and Climate Initiative working closely with the Government of Tanzania, in 2024 it facilitated the securing of 2,365 hectares of shared grazing lands for 10,167 (5,527 female and 4,640 male) livestock keepers from four villages - Kimange, Miono, Mkwajuni and Kweikonje villages, Chalinze District, Coastal region, Tanzania

column16: Buffer zones developed by the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT are being used by Hacienda San Jose, Colombia
column17: Hacienda San José (HSJ) demonstrates the remarkable ecological benefits of maintaining buffer zones around riparian forests and connectivity corridors in the Orinoquia region of Colombia. These buffer zones, spanning 200 meters and preserved from cattle grazing and annual burning for over seven years, provide critical habitat for bird biodiversity, offering refuge and resources for diverse avian species. The undisturbed native savanna vegetation within the 200-meter-wide and 3–4-kilometer-long connectivity areas enhances carbon sequestration, contributing significantly to carbon stocks by maintaining soil health and vegetation cover. Additionally, these zones promote natural connectivity, enabling the movement of wildlife and the regeneration of native flora, which are vital for ecosystem resilience. By integrating these conservation practices, HSJ fosters sustainable land management, contrasting sharply with the degradation caused by uncontrolled grazing and burning in the region. This approach highlights the multifaceted benefits of buffer zones for biodiversity, carbon storage, and long-term environmental sustainability.

column16: Formal adoptatin of the TRICOT method by the Nigerian Variety release commitee as an official way to carry out on farm testing for variety release
column17: This document demonstrates a concrete policy outcome of sustained efforts to promote the TRICOT approach in Nigeria’s seed system. In the revised Guidelines for Registration and Release of New Crop Varieties in Nigeria (adopted April 2025), TRICOT is formally recognised as an approved alternative method for on-farm testing. The guidelines explicitly allow applicants to use data from participatory TRICOT trials to obtain exemption from conventional on-farm trials during variety release, provided minimum quality and documentation standards are met (Section B, Exemption D). This institutional change reflects the acceptance of TRICOT as a scientifically credible, farmer-centred testing methodology by the National Variety Release Committee. It therefore is not only positioned as an alternative to do on farm testing for variety release but also a method that allows more varieties to be tested earlier in the breeding program and having the on farm testing nested within that. Its inclusion marks a shift toward more inclusive, evidence-based, and scalable on-farm evaluation processes, and represents a clear uptake of TRICOT advocacy and piloting efforts into national regulatory practice.; ; The sections on tricot are on page 8 (Definitions section) where tricot is formally defined as “Triadic comparison of technologies; this is an alternative method of conducting on-farm trials” and on page 18, Section 15.0 – Exemption D: No on-farm trials when providing data from tricot testing of candidate varieties.

column16: Big data technology and system (Peskas) to improve small-scale fisheries management across six countries
column17: Peskas, a digital catch documentation and fisheries monitoring system, combines tamper-proof, solar-powered trackers developed by Pelagic Data Systems with an open-source decision dashboard to provide real-time data on small-scale fisheries production and effort. Since its adoption as Timor-Leste’s national fisheries monitoring system in 2019, Peskas has received continuous investment from the Government of Timor-Leste (GOTL), with a second installment in 2021. By 2020, the system covered 15,690 km² of coastline in Timor-Leste, enabling evidence-based fisheries management.; By 2024, Peskas has expanded through bilateral investments and is now implemented in six countries: Timor-Leste, Malaysia, Malawi, Tanzania, Mozambique, and Kenya. The publicly available dashboard has gained global recognition, receiving >4,800 visits from 2,400 unique visitors across 65 countries in 2024. This scaling demonstrates the increasing international adoption of digital tools for sustainable and transparent fisheries governance.; ; ; ; ;

column16: Kenya Integrated Agricultural Management Information System integrates CGIAR-supported KAZNET platform delivering livestock market intelligence directly to 1,010 pastoralists and  and indirectly to another 2,979
column17: Kenya Integrated Agricultural Management Information System (KIAMIS) leverages the KAZNET platform, developed by ILRI and supported by the Livestock and Climate Initiative to deliver real-time livestock market intelligence, to enhance decision-making and resilience among Kenya’s pastoralists. Through KAZNET, data on market prices, traded volumes, livestock quality, and household coping strategies are collected by 51 citizen contributors across Kenya's arid and semi-arid lands. This information is disseminated directly to 1,010 pastoralists through pastoralist groups and indirectly reaches another 2,979 pastoralists belonging to 270 pastoralist groups in Kenya. This information is crucial for empowering pastoralists with actionable insights to optimize livestock trade and resource management. KIAMIS’s integration of KAZNET represents a significant step in institutionalizing market intelligence within public systems, ensuring accessibility and transparency for both pastoralists and policymakers. The geo-referenced data collection system and innovative use of photo validation enhance the accuracy and reliability of market data.

column16: Success Story Vegetable varieties in Benin
column17: Access to adapted and market-preferred vegetable varieties is critical to increase production and supply. Before the FRESH interventions in Benin started, only 10 locally released tomato, pepper, onion, and African eggplant were registered in the national seed catalog. Many of them did not match the needs of farmers and consumers and were susceptible to diseases. For example, available tomato varieties were susceptible to bacterial wilt, which can cause 100% yield loss and has led farmers in the Valley of Ouémé, a major vegetable production area, to abandon tomato production totally. Overall the  limited variety choice for farmers was a great obstacle for vegetable production. The FRESH Initiative has introduced WorldVeg vegetable breeding lines to Benin that match major market segments and target product profiles.

column16: Scaling territorial innovation networks as coordination mechanisms for climate-smart agriculture in Guatemala
column17: In 2025, CGIAR and its partners consolidated territorial innovation networks as coordination mechanisms to scale climate-smart agriculture in eastern and western Guatemala, building on institutional and community processes established in previous years, with financial support from NORAD. These networks functioned as learning and knowledge exchange platforms that enabled the integration of local organizations and institutions through field days, workshops, and webinar series. A total of 714 cumulative participations reflected sustained engagement of farmers, technicians, and other stakeholders across iterative learning cycles. In collaboration with partner organizations, capacity-building processes supported 695 farmers, contributing to the adoption of climate-smart innovations by 1,029 farmers. Diversification of staple grain systems using climate-adapted seeds and intercropping, improved post-harvest management, soil and water conservation measures, and the use of agroclimatic information for production planning generated evidence, through participatory research platforms and extension areas, of increased agrobiodiversity and yield gains of up to 44% in maize and 0.85 t/ha in beans, strengthening resilience under climate variability.

column16: Issuing of Livestock and Climate Initiative developed group Certificate of Customary Rights of Occupancy secures 50,589 hectares of shared grazing lands in Kiteto District, Tanzania benefiting 15,407 pastoralists
column17: In Tanzania policy and legislation provides for the provision of certificates of customary rights of occupancy (CCROs). However commonly these are issued on an individual basis and challenges arise when trying to secure tenure for a group that shares resources. The Livestock and Climate Initiative has been working with the Government of Tanzania to pilot the provision of group CCROs to livestock keeper associations. In late 2024 a group CCRO was issued to the Amei village livestock keepers association to secure 50,588 hectares of shared grazing land benefiting 15,407 livestock keepers predominantly pastoralists. Amei is part of the four village cluster of villages making up the ALOLLE shared grazing land.

column16: CGIAR innovation community conversations transforms harmful norms and practices and bolsters knowledge capacities and equitable adapation
column17: Community conversations can support locally led adaptation and, when part of a sociotechnical bundling approach,  are a method of engaging communities to address development and social issues based on their identification of priorities and actions. Community conversations were implemented in two villages in Baringo County, Kenya to support locally led equitable adaptation, whereby local people identified key activities to increase adaptation capacities of women, men and youth. Baseline findings showed that adaptation capacities were relatively low and that norms restricted women’s participation in decision-making, time use and movement. A total of 4 conversations involving 1,325 farmers and agropastoralists were held over one year. Interactive and participatory methods included drama, a radio show, and technical training to enhance livestock production. Analysis of midline quantitative and qualitative data showed significant changes in women’s and men’s beliefs in both communities around livestock ownership, selling and, among other areas, women’s mobility.

column16: PlaSA Colombia: A Collaborative Platform Transforming Food System Monitoring and Policy Influence in Colombia
column17: NPS, in collaboration with local actors—including universities, research centers, public and private entities, and NGOs—co-designed PlaSA Colombia, the first platform in Colombia dedicated to monitoring food systems. This initiative prioritizes inclusivity and innovation by ensuring accessibility for local stakeholders and fostering cross-sector collaboration in the agrifood system.; PlaSA Colombia serves as a tool for education, research, and outreach, integrating interactive games, virtual courses, and academic programs. It has been cited in academic articles, theses, and research projects, reinforcing its role in knowledge generation. Additionally, it has gained visibility in major media outlets and has been shared with key stakeholders across sectors. The platform has enabled critical analysis during crises, supporting evidence-based decision-making and food security discussions.; By empowering diverse actors to understand, analyze, and influence food systems, PlaSA Colombia has become a national reference for food system information and a transformative force for inclusive and sustainable food system innovation in Colombia.; ;

column16: Improved governance, management and restoration through strengthened joint village land use planning, participatory rangeland management and restoration across 165,326 hectares of grazing land in Tanzania
column17: The Livestock and Climate Initiative has strengthened governance, management and restoration of 165,326 hectares of shared grazing lands in four clusters of villages in Kiteto district, Manyara region, Tanzania through joint village land use planning and participatory rangeland management. This has resulted in reduced land use conflicts for the four livestock keeper associations and the residents in the area, who are better placed to protect their lands from encroachment. Land tenure security had incentivized communities to improve livestock production through buying improved breeds and mobilising their own resources to undertake rangeland restoration on 162 hectares of land. Women’s involvement in decision making processes has increased aided by building women’s confidence through women’s leadership forums. These successes have been recognized by national government, including the uptaking of joint village land use planning into national guidelines.

column16: Groundwater Management Information System adopted by government agencies in Pakistan to guide sustainable water resource policies
column17: Pakistan faces critical groundwater depletion threatening agricultural sustainability and water security. The International Water Management Institute developed the Groundwater Management Information System (GMIS), a decision support tool that helps government agencies make informed decisions about groundwater regulation and management. The system is now operationally used by four major Pakistani institutions: Punjab Irrigation Department, Pakistan Council of Research in Water Resources, Living Indus Initiative, National Disaster Risk Management Fund, and Sindh Irrigation Department. Both male and female officers utilize GMIS to develop evidence-based policies addressing long-term groundwater challenges. The system's adoption represents a significant step toward sustainable water resource management in Pakistan's water-stressed regions.

column16: Use of criteria for identification of seed product market segments
column17: The Market Intelligence Brief No. 1 defines a set of eight harmonized criteria used to segment markets for crop varieties, which was adapted for crops mandated by non-CGIAR partners. The eight criteria comprise: crop type, material type (such as hybrid or open-pollinated seed), subregion where cultivation occurs, end-use (fresh market, processing, etc.), color, production environment (climate and elevation), production system, and maturity/harvest traits. Each criterion captures attributes that influence farmers’ varietal needs and market opportunities. For example, “production environment” accounts for differences in altitude and climate that necessitate specific disease resistance packages, while “end-use” reflects how consumers or processors demand particular traits.; ; WorldVeg applied these criteria in stakeholder workshops and research across East and West Africa to develop validated market segments for tomatoes and peppers. Using the criteria, researchers identified multiple distinct segments within each crop that reflect real-world variation in production conditions and market demands—such as lowland versus highland tomato production zones or diverse pepper uses (fresh, dry, or dual-purpose).; ; The segmentation exercise helps WorldVeg tailor its breeding priorities and target product profiles (TPPs) to meet specific market needs. By linking segmentation data to spatial and stakeholder insights, WorldVeg enhances its capacity to develop varieties that are not only agronomically improved but also aligned with farmer preferences, consumer traits, and market realities. This demand-driven approach aims to increase adoption of improved varieties and ultimately improve livelihoods, nutrition, and food systems resilience.

column16: Municipal Food System Profiles, concise snapshots decisionmakers in Honduras are using to steer food systems transformation processes
column17: In 2023, the Honduran Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (SAG), as the designated Country Convenor for the United Nations Food Systems Summit (UNFSS) with support from the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) and researchers from the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Healthy Diets, co-developed municipal level food system profiles for two municipalities. The process was based on guidelines developed by CGIAR for national Sustainable Food System Profiles. The profiles and the overall process support decisionmakers to prioritize transformative actions in food systems and demonstrate that sustainable healthy diets can be an outcome of food systems transformation. In 2024, the two profiles plus easy-to-use guidelines on how to develop the profiles were published in Spanish. In 2025, SAG took the lead and made an investment to develop 20 more municipal food system profiles based on this published methodology. Their work started in 2025 and will be finalized in 2026. Researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition provided training for SAG staff and their consultants on the methodology and will provide in-kind mentoring and technical backstopping into 2026.

column16: CGIAR teams and partners use File Manager platform to manage and share research FAIR datasets and metadata securely
column17: File Manager is a free, open-source file management platform designed to enhance data management and security. It enables seamless sharing of data files and related documentation (e.g. trial protocols, scripts, ODK forms, and analysis reports) with relevant teams and individuals, regardless of the data collection tools used. ; ; The platform is currently used by 51 users. Among them, the Sustainable Farming Program teams store datasets from field trials together with protocols and data collection forms. It is also used by the AgVACS project team that inclues CGIAR and Rothamsted Research staff. File Manager allows teams to securely store and share datasets and related documents hence avoiding the transmission of sensitive data via email.

column16: terminag is used by the carob framework to standardize legacy datasets and is also used in data collection form to collect born-FAIR data
column17: terminag is a controlled vocabulary used to organize and standardize agricultural research data. It is used by carob curators to harmonize legacy datasets by updating column headers with terminag variables, ensuring consistent naming across datasets. terminag also enforces standardized units for variables, allowing the same measurements to be compared reliably across different datasets.; ; Implemented through the carob framework, terminag has enabled the creation of a harmonized database of 2,296 original datasets, containing a total of 2,029,049 records that can be directly compared and analyzed together.; ; terminag variables are also used by CGIAR centers and partners to design data collection forms for agronomic trials, enabling the collection of born-FAIR data. For example, BioSSA project and the Hub for Fertilizer and Soil Health in West Africa and the Sahel have integrated terminag variables into their data collection tools. This ensures that newly collected data are immediately comparable with the existing pool of datasets already standardized using terminag, thereby continuously expanding a high-quality, interoperable agronomic database suitable for large-scale analytics and modeling.

column16: George Washington University uses Toolkit for conceptualizing and measuring effective voice and agency of women in climate-related governance at the individual and group levels
column17: George Washington University, through the graduate student capstone program at the Elliott School of International Affairs, took up this innovation—a toolkit for conceptualizing and measuring women’s effective voice and agency in climate-related governance at both individual and collective levels. The toolkit was introduced and shared across the graduate capstone cohort and applied by a student research team in a peer-reviewed study (attached as evidence, with authorship listed therein), which serves as documented evidence of uptake by a university.;  ; Within this use, the toolkit informed the design of qualitative interview instruments and guided analytical frameworks to examine gender-responsive anticipatory action programming. Specifically, it supported analysis of whether, how, and under what conditions such programming can meaningfully empower women and contribute to transformative shifts in gender relations. The uptake demonstrates the toolkit’s utility as a teaching-embedded analytical resource and as a practical research tool for applied policy analysis by non-CGIAR graduate researchers.

column16: Overcoming Scarcity: How Local Innovations Are Shaping Water Management in Western Kenya
column17: In western Kenya within the Lake Victoria Basin, communities in Agoro village face a familiar cycle  of intense rains causing flooding and soil erosion, followed by long dry spells that left farms water-stressed and livelihoods vulnerable. Responding to community concerns, IWMI through the CGIAR Nature-Based Solutions (Nature+) and the Multifunctional Landscape Science Program collaborated with local and international partners to co-design practical water management solutions at the Agro-West aggregated farm in Kisumu County. Detailed field investigations, combining community knowledge with surveys, GIS mapping, and geophysical assessments, identified priority flow paths, storage zones, and aquifer recharge areas. Based on these assessments and continuous discussion with communities, a climate-resilient infrastructure was in place on a 76 hectares land. The infrastructure put in place includes concrete-lined drainage channels, water storage facilities, and a solar-powered irrigation system. Additionally, a 1.25-hectare vegetable and spice farm with drip irrigation was developed as a community-managed demonstration and income-generating site. Beyond technical gains, the initiative strengthened social cohesion through dialogue, knowledge exchange, and joint management, embedding resilience and sustainability within the community. The interventions reduced flooding and soil loss during heavy rains, secured water availability in the dry season and improved water-use efficiency.

column16: Conflict-sensitive Nature-based Solutions strengthen resilience for 7,000 households in northern Mozambique
column17: Cabo Delgado, in northern Mozambique, faces overlapping crises of conflict and environmental degradation. Since 2017, an insurgency has displaced thousands and disrupted livelihoods in communities exposed to climate extremes. As WFP expanded recovery and resilience work, it recognised the need to avoid interventions that could worsen tensions.; ; CGIAR Climate Security researchers at the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT partnered with WFP Mozambique to build an integrated evidence base for Mocímboa de Praia and Palma districts. The work combined an assessment of ecosystem functionality and services with a participatory analysis of local conflict dynamics, to inform conflict-sensitive Nature-based Solutions (NbS) within WFP recovery and stabilisation programmes.; ; CGIAR mapped how households depend on inland and coastal ecosystems for food, energy, and income, using surveys across 10 communities and spatial analysis of land and water systems. In parallel, the team examined how drivers such as youth unemployment, weakened customary governance, and low trust between groups interact with resource competition to shape stability.; ; As WFP’s Christian Grassini noted, “The ecosystem services study gave us a holistic overview of the landscape and how communities interact with natural resources.” Findings showed heavy reliance on wood and charcoal, fisheries, and wild foods. These strategies are essential, but they can also degrade ecosystems and create potential flashpoints. Scenario analysis helped identify interventions that could restore ecosystem services while reducing conflict risk.; ; CGIAR provided operational recommendations, including mangrove and coastal restoration, agroforestry, more sustainable charcoal production, beekeeping for income diversification, and improved water catchment and treatment. WFP is integrating these recommendations into its programming in Palma and Mocímboa de Praia, expected to benefit about 7,000 households.; ; To support delivery, CGIAR and WFP briefed staff and partners and ran a conflict-sensitivity training in September 2025, training 42 staff on practical tools to assess risks and adapt activities.

column16: CGIAR’s Climate Security Observatory (CSO) framework and measurement tools being embedded into Honduras' Permanent Household Survey (EPHPM)
column17: Honduras is among the most climate-vulnerable countries in Latin America. Recurrent droughts, hurricanes, and floods interact with economic insecurity and violence to drive displacement, with consequences for displaced households, host communities, and national response systems. Yet until recently, national statistics have not systematically captured the links between climate change, mobility, and human security.; To address this gap, Honduras’s National Institute of Statistics (INE) formally adopted and began using a CGIAR climate security innovation in 2024, signing a Memorandum of Understanding with CGIAR Climate Security at the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT. CGIAR’s Climate Security Observatory  (CSO) framework and measurement tools are being embedded into the country’s Permanent Household Survey (EPHPM), integrating climate and displacement dimensions into the national statistics system. A first milestone in this innovation use was the 2025 analysis of the 2024 EPHPM displacement module, led by INE and UNHCR with CGIAR analytical support. The analysis generated nationally representative evidence on internal displacement and demonstrated how floods, storms, and droughts interact with poverty and insecurity to shape mobility decisions—validating the CSO approach and underscoring the value of tracking climate drivers systematically. Building on this uptake, CGIAR supported INE in redesigning the displacement module for the 2025 EPHPM. The revised instrument operationalizes CGIAR’s climate-security innovation by introducing new questions on climate-related displacement triggers, vulnerability in both displacement and host settings (including services, livelihoods, and emerging risks), and pathways through which climate shocks may heighten social tensions and conflict.

column16: Retail-level strategies to make fruits and vegetables more affordable and accessible to consumers in urban areas of Nigeria
column17: In 2025, a team led by the University of Ibadan, were awarded funding to refine and expand a bundled retail-level innovation that will address barriers in the affordability and acceptability of fruits and vegetables among low-income consumers in Nigeria. The innovation was originally designed and tested by members of Better Diets and Nutrition with the University of Ibadan and other partners under the CGIAR Research Program on Agriculture for Nutrition and Health (from January 2020 to December 2021). Results from the initial evaluation were promising enough that two bilateral donors wanted to further invest in the innovation to address issues that impeded sustainability. The new project builds on the proven aspects in the original bundled intervention, such as vendor innovation and co-created consumer behavior change strategies, and makes significant changes related to gender-transformative activities and policy integration, that will support scalability. The overall goal remains to improve the access of fruit and vegetables and the overall diets of low-income populations in Nigeria.

column16: Uptake and continuation of price data collection and dissemination for selected neglected and underutilized species (NUS) crops in Niger following project collaboration with a national public platform
column17: One of the key barriers hampering the commercialization of Neglected and Underutilized Species (NUS) is the asymmetry of market information—particularly regarding prices. Because NUS are often traded in small volumes, sold in informal markets, and available only seasonally or irregularly, they are rarely included in national market information systems. Producers and traders therefore operate with little to no data on prevailing prices, demand patterns, or seasonal fluctuations. This lack of information weakens producers’ bargaining power, as they often sell at the first price offered without knowing the value of their product elsewhere. It also reduces incentives for traders to invest in NUS value chains, since they cannot easily anticipate profitability or market trends. Ultimately, this limits the scaling potential of NUS within local and regional food systems.; Within the SUSTLIVES project, one activity specifically addressed this challenge by establishing a system for collecting and disseminating NUS price information through digital platforms and community-based communication tools.; In Niger, he Alliance partnered with RECA (Réseau National des Chambres d’Agriculture du Niger), a national institution with long-standing experience in agricultural advisory services, market information systems, and public communication. RECA ensured rigorous data collection and implemented a diversified communication strategy—including WhatsApp groups, community radio broadcasts, and a dedicated hotline for producers to inquire directly about market trends.; This approach proved highly effective. Radio programs focusing on NUS prices attracted a growing number of listeners, and even after the formal collaboration ended, RECA reinforced this momentum by signing agreements with community radios to secure regular agricultural broadcasts.

column16: Provincial authorities in Son La and Dien Bien, Vietnam adopt International Livestock Research Institute food safety innovations to transform local food systems
column17: Food safety innovations developed by the International Livestock Research Institute and partners were successfully adopted by provincial authorities in Son La and Dien Bien provinces, Vietnam. These innovations addressed critical food safety challenges in traditional markets through risk-based approaches tailored for local authorities. The interventions improved knowledge and practices among food system actors, including vendors, consumers, and regulators. Provincial leaders confirmed the usefulness of these innovations during official meetings, noting significant improvements in food safety awareness and implementation. This adoption represents a meaningful step toward transforming regional food systems by strengthening local capacity to ensure safer food for communities while supporting sustainable livestock value chains.

column16: Scaling Nutrition-Sensitive Bean Innovations: Lessons from Rwanda’s Market Activation of Biofortified Porridge and Uganda’s Consumer Acceptability Assessments of Precooked Beans and Composite Flour
column17: CIAT/PABRA, in partnership with Rainbow Health Food Ltd, conducted a market activation across Rwanda’s four western districts promoting Monti 7‑in‑1 biofortified porridge. The campaign (market activation) reached over 8,000 people and sold 635 kg of product worth 1,438,600 RWF. Despite challenges such as low rural purchasing power, limited nutrition awareness, and packaging concerns, the initiative strengthened partnerships and boosted product visibility. In Uganda, CIAT/PABRA, NARO‑NARL, Harvguard, and YellowStar assessed consumer and trader acceptability of precooked dehydrated beans and composite bean flour in two districts. Direct engagement reached 243 consumers (65% women) and 13 traders, while indirect outreach created awareness among 5,000 more. Masavu beans and composite porridge scored highly on taste, yet awareness was extremely low. Respondents highlighted barriers of access, affordability, and promotion, recommending targeted campaigns, wider distribution, and fair pricing to support scaling.

column17: The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) developed the Women in Business innovation to help young women veterinarians, paraveterinarians, and farmers start successful chicken businesses while challenging gender norms that typically restrict women's participation in agricultural enterprises. This innovation was integrated into 13 episodes of the Maisha Makutano TV series, broadcast on Kenya's Citizen TV and YouTube in 2025. Each episode reached 3.7 million viewers, providing practical business guidance and promoting positive images of women entrepreneurs and supportive male partners. Based on adoption rates from similar educational entertainment programs, an estimated 85,100 young women adopted the Women in Business practices after watching the series, demonstrating the power of television to scale agricultural innovations and promote gender-equitable participation in livestock value chains.

column16: Quezon City in the Philippines adopts vendor business school ordinance developed with CGIAR support for informal market vendors
column17: Quezon City has officially implemented an ordinance establishing a vendor business school program that provides ongoing training for small-scale informal market vendors. This policy innovation was co-developed with three CGIAR centers: the International Potato Center, International Livestock Research Institute, and International Rice Research Institute. The ordinance addresses the lack of business skills training among urban informal food vendors who typically have limited access to formal education and business development resources. The program helps vendors improve business practices, food safety standards, and market access. By integrating this training framework into city governance, the ordinance ensures sustained support for vulnerable urban food system participants, contributing to poverty reduction and enhanced livelihoods.

column16: Pig artificial insemination services adopted by 326 smallholder households in Uganda
column17: Smallholder pig farmers in Uganda traditionally faced challenges accessing quality breeding services, often unable to afford keeping boars while facing disease risks and high costs. The International Livestock Research Institute, through CGIAR's Sustainable Animal and Aquatic Foods Science Program and prior to that the Sustainable Animal Productivity initiative, addressed this by training 19 animal health workers to provide pig artificial insemination services. These trained providers successfully delivered services to 326 smallholder pig-keeping households, inseminating 391 pigs and benefiting approximately 1,434 people. This innovation use demonstrates how artificial insemination technology can improve pig breeding by providing access to superior genetics while reducing costs and disease risks, creating sustainable livelihoods for service providers while enhancing productivity for previously underserved farming communities.

column16: Animal health care workers in Uganda adopt pig artificial insemination as part of their livelihod activities, with support from the Sustainable Animal and Aquatics Food Science Program
column17: Women and men animal health-care workers in Uganda were trained and back-stop supported as pig artificial insemination (AI) service providers, under the One CGIAR Sustainable Animal and Aquatic Foods Science Program (SAAF) and previously the Sustainable Animal Productivity (SAPLING) initiative. Given an average household size of 4.4 (Uganda Bureau of Statistics 2024) this translates to 1,434 people benefitting.

column16: The Moroccan government declares 160,000 ha of land under 'semis direct' (direct seeding, i.e., no tillage) conservation agriculture in 2025, achieved with the support of CGIAR
column17: The Moroccan government aims to implement direct seeding ('semis direct') conservation agriculture on 1 million hectares of the total 4 million hectares of rainfed areas used for cereal and legume production by 2030, as stated in its "Generation Green 2030" strategy, produced by the Ministry of Agriculture (MAPMDREF) in 2021. Direct seeding conservation agricultural practices help to conserve the dryland soil structure and its soil water and organic carbon content. CGIAR is involved in achieving this aim through its work on no-till seeders, bundled agronomic solutions for CA systems, the development of improved varieties, hydroponic forage production, the Zar3Direct online dashboard, as well as numerous stakeholder engagement and farmer capacity-building events. The area under direct seeding for these agricultural seasons has been officially declared by the Minister of Agriculture (MAPMDREF) as follows: 160,000 ha in 2024/2025; 118,000 ha in 2023/2024; 85,000 ha in 2022/2023; and 15,000 ha in 2019/2020.

column16: Community vaccination platforms supported by CGIAR reach farmers with peste des petits ruminants vaccine in Mali
column17: Peste des petits ruminants is a deadly viral disease that devastates sheep and goat populations across Africa, threatening the livelihoods of vulnerable farmers who depend on these animals for income and food security. CGIAR's International Livestock Research Institute, through the Sustainable Animal and Aquatic Foods program, partnered with Technologies for African Agricultural Transformation to establish 26 community-led Innovation Platforms across three regions in Mali. These platforms successfully coordinated vaccination campaigns using thermotolerant vaccines, benefiting 10,000 people in farming houesholds and demonstrating how community engagement can significantly improve livestock health interventions in rural areas where traditional veterinary services are limited.

column16: Livestock champions in Mali integrate herd management training into their services, reaching 18000 small ruminant farmers
column17: Small ruminant farmers in Mali struggled with animal health, nutrition, and reproduction management challenges that reduced their productivity and income. The Sustainable Animal and Aquatic Foods program developed an integrated herd management package using behavior change communication approaches to address these issues. Forty private livestock service providers, known as livestock champions, were trained to deliver this package to farmers. These champions successfully integrated the training activities into their regular business operations, reaching 18,000 farmers across 87 villages in 13 municipalities throughout central Mali in 2025. This integration demonstrates how private sector actors can effectively scale livestock management innovations while maintaining their commercial viability.

column16: Adoption of Urochloa hybrid improved forage grasses by farmers within Cambodia, Colombia, Kenya, Malawi, Malaysia, Uganda, Vietnam, and Zambia
column17: Here we report on the adoption of Urochloa hybrids—an improved forage grass—by farmers in the SAAF focal countries of Cambodia, Colombia, Kenya, Malawi, Malaysia, Uganda, Vietnam, and Zambia in 2024. The number of adopters was estimated based on the area sown, average farm size, and household size. The total number of people living in newly adopting households in 2024 is estimated at 106,561, comprising 4,319 in Cambodia, 5,503 in Colombia, 9,287 in Kenya, 2,464 in Malawi, 27,607 in Malaysia, 54,712 in Uganda, 1,135 in Vietnam, and 1,534 in Zambia. ; Consistent with previous years, we are using the year before the reporting year as we receive seed sale data from our private partners with a 1-year lag.

column16: Open traceability framework provides guidance for the European Deforestation-free Regulation (EUDR) compliance decisions in Honduras’ coffee value chain
column17: TraceFoodChain.org is an open-access traceability tool for EUDR compliance, developed by Permarobotics based on a digital infrastructure blueprint co-created with stakeholders of the Honduran coffee value chain. Facilitated by the Alliance, the three-month prototyping process defined key elements for interoperability, data ownership, and confidentiality. With a potential adoption by Honduran Coffee Institute (IHCAFE) and Forest Conservation Institute (ICF) as a national standard, this blueprint could benefit up to 120,000 farmers and foster pre-competitive collaboration, enabling transparent and verifiable compliance with EUDR through integrated digital solutions.; ; The core innovation of the traceability tool lies in treating EUDR compliance not as a proprietary, buyer-specific solution but as open digital public infrastructure: it is interoperable by design, co-governed with public institutions and producers, and centered on producer data rights. By separating data generation, data ownership, and data use, the tool lowers compliance costs, avoids vendor lock-in, and allows multiple traceability and monitoring systems to plug into a shared, trusted backbone—making deforestation-free compliance scalable, auditable, and inclusive for smallholders rather than exclusionary.

column16: Vietnamese pig slaughterhouses and pork vendors sustain food safety hygiene practices
column17: Food safety practices developed by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) continued to be used by Vietnamese meat processors and vendors after initial training ended. Twenty-one slaughterhouses across six provinces maintained the use of stainless-steel grids and hygiene protocols, while expanding these practices to new locations. Sixty pork vendors in Dien Bien and Son La provinces adopted the same food safety package. This sustained adoption led to significant reductions in harmful Salmonella bacteria contamination: from 60% to 47% in Dien Bien markets and from 83% to 60% in Son La markets. The results demonstrate that food safety interventions can be successfully transferred and maintained across different locations, strengthening routine food safety management in Vietnam's pork supply chain.

column16: Government Adoption of an IWMI-Developed Irrigation Water Monitoring System in Nepal for Improved Water Allocation Decisions
column17: The National Irrigation Policy of 2023 emphasizes the importance of volumetric water allocation for enhancing agricultural productivity in Nepal. A key part of this is enhancing the availability and use of flow data from canals to fields. Currently, Nepal lacks a consistent system for monitoring and managing irrigation water, resulting in inefficiencies and inequities in water distribution. Many systems suffer from poor infrastructure and ad hoc management, leading to serious head–tail disparities in which tail-end farmers receive little or no water, particularly during dry periodsTo support the policy’s goals, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), in partnership with the Department of Water Resources and Irrigation (DWRI), initiated a pilot intervention in the eastern canal system (21,000 ha) of Babai Irrigation Project in western Nepal. The project involves the installation of basic instruments that monitor real-time water flow, soil moisture, and weather conditions. These tools help irrigation managers to distribute water more efficiently and inform water allocation and planning. ; Following the successful installation in 2024, the Department of Water Resources and Irrigation (DWRI) initiated and invested in replicating the system within the western canal network (15,000 ha), thereby extending coverage to the entire irrigation scheme (36,000 ha). In parallel, the Babai Irrigation Information System (BIIS) dashboard has been fully integrated into the Nepal Irrigation Management Information System (NIMIS) hosted on DWRI’s website. This adoption of innovation enables DWRI to replicate a similar integrated irrigation monitoring system across other irrigation schemes in Nepal and directly supports the operationalization of the irrigation policy.

column16: Uganda’s pig value chain partners adopt PigSmart platform training materials
column17: PigSmart is an extension platform developed by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) that delivers practical pig farming knowledge through audio content in local languages. The platform covers feeding, health management, breeding, genetics, and heat stress mitigation to improve pig productivity and farmer incomes. Uganda's Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Industry (MAAIF) recognized PigSmart's value for livestock extension and trained 12 veterinary officers through its Oil Palm Project to support 510 households in Kalangala District with alternative livelihoods. Simultaneously, All Across Africa, a social enterprise supporting over 3,200 rural artisans, used PigSmart materials to train approximately 1,500 farmers across three days in Mukono District. This adoption demonstrates how research-based extension tools can be scaled through government and private sector partnerships to reach smallholder farmers across East Africa.

column16: Research and Development Actors Build Capacity and Adopt Gender-Transformative Practice in Ethiopia
column17: This result captures the extent to which research and development actors engaged in, reflected on, and adopted gender-transformative approaches in their work. Through a structured reflecting and co-planning workshop linked to the implementation and evaluation of the SASA Gender-Transformative Approach (GTA), 15 R&D and development actors (10 men and 5 women) actively participated in implementation, evidence review, collective reflection, and forward planning.; ; Pre- and post-workshop assessments demonstrate increased knowledge, confidence, and commitment among participants to apply gender-responsive and gender-transformative strategies. While familiarity with GTA was uneven prior to engagement, the process led to substantial learning gains, stronger recognition of community-led mechanisms for norm change, and broad agreement on the effectiveness of GTA-informed approaches. As a result, participating actors strengthened their capacity to integrate gender-transformative principles into ongoing and future research, extension, and development interventions, contributing to more inclusive and equitable agri-food system outcomes.

column16: Experiential learning games adopted across Indian states improve groundwater governance and increase women's participation in decision-making
column17: CGIAR and partner institutions developed and scaled experiential groundwater and surface water management games to strengthen collective action and governance in water-scarce farming systems. The games simulate crop choice and water-use decisions, enabling farmers to observe system-level impacts of individual actions and to co-design cooperative management rules. Implemented at scale through trained local facilitators, the approach led to measurable behavioral and institutional changes, including improved maintenance of water infrastructure, adoption of local water-use rules, reduced pressure on aquifers, and increased participation of women in decision-making. The innovation has been widely adopted across multiple Indian states and piloted internationally as a cost-effective tool for sustainable groundwater governance.;

column16: Community Conversations approach adopted by partners in Ethiopia, Kenya and Somalia to address One Health hazards
column17: Pastoralist communities in the Horn of Africa face significant health risks from zoonoses, antimicrobial resistance, and food safety issues that affect both humans and animals. The Community Conversations approach, a participatory social innovation developed by CGIAR researchers and partners, enables communities to recognize, analyze, and act on these interconnected health challenges. This method brings together women, men, local leaders, and frontline service providers to co-develop locally relevant solutions. Implementation across pastoralist communities in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Somalia demonstrated improved knowledge, attitudes, and practices related to One Health hazards. The approach proved particularly effective in low-resource settings, empowering communities to take collective action on priority health risks affecting their livestock and livelihoods.

column16: Vietnamese provincial authorities independently implement ILRI-developed food safety interventions across six provinces' slaughterhouses and markets
column17: Food safety challenges in Vietnamese slaughterhouses and markets prompted the development of a comprehensive intervention package under the One Health Initiative. column16: Scaling Fund Outcome
column17: The CGIAR Scaling Fund is a strategic financing and technical support mechanism designed to bridge the gap between innovation development and impact at scale by combining flexible funding with tailored, hands-on scaling support. Anchored in CGIAR’s commitment to responsible and demand-driven scaling, the Fund supports innovation teams to translate research outputs into context-specific solutions with measurable benefits, while anticipating and mitigating social and environmental risks. In 2025, the Fund supported eight innovation teams across six CGIAR science programs, five CGIAR centers, and 11 countries through a dual structure comprising the competitive Scaling Challenge and the flexible Needs-Driven Support window, complemented by a strategic partnership with ENABEL. Now in its third year, the Scaling Fund continues to embed scaling science into practice, strengthen partnerships, and advance equitable, sustainable impact at scale.

column16: Digital Water Body Inventory System Adopted by Pakistan Government Agencies to Map Nationwide Water Infrastructure
column17: Water Body Inventory of Pakistan is an interactive digital platform designed to provide comprehensive data on water storage infrastructure across Pakistan. It includes detailed information on large and small dams, retention dams, ponds, flood protection structures, rivers, lakes, canals, and other surface water resources. Built with high-resolution satellite imagery and verified by national and provincial agencies, the portal ensures data accuracy and offers insights into both seasonal and non-seasonal water bodies. Users can explore this data through interactive maps, tables, and downloadable reports, with filtering options by region, administrative boundaries, or type of structure. ; ; It is an interactive digital platform adopted by multiple government agencies, including the Pakistan Council of Water Resources (PCRWR), the National Disaster Risk Management Fund (NDRMF), and provincial irrigation departments, to map and manage nationwide water infrastructure. It is accessible via these multiple official channels, including the Living Indus site, PCRWR and NDRMF portals, IWMI dashboards, and direct links ensuring that stakeholders can use it for water resource planning, monitoring irrigation systems, flood risk assessment, and infrastructure development. A collaboration proposal letter from the Irrigation Department to IWMI confirms the government’s institutional engagement and support for the platform. By integrating verified spatial data with user-friendly tools, It enables government agencies to make informed, timely decisions on water allocation, management, and development planning across Pakistan.

column16: One Health Units deliver integrated human-animal-environment services to pastoralists across Horn of Africa communities
column17: One Health Units provide integrated services for people, livestock and the environment in remote pastoral areas of the Horn of Africa, addressing the challenge of limited service access in these communities. Before these units were introduced, pastoralists faced poorly coordinated healthcare, long travel distances, and frequent self-treatment. In this reporting period, the CGIAR Sustainable Animal and Aquatic Foods program supported research exploring how communities understood and valued the OHU services in northern Kenya. Communities now report increased use of preventive and curative human and animal services , and greater awareness of hygiene and diseases shared between animals and people. One Health education and care for pregnant women emerged as top priorities. Despite challenges related to mobility and limited resources, communities expressed strong support and willingness to contribute fees, demonstrating potential for sustainable service delivery in pastoralist areas.

column16: The Lower Kafue Basin Multi-Stakeholder Platform (MSP) addresses pollution incident in a coordinated manner
column17: Since 2023, the Lower Kafue Basin Multi-Stakeholder Platform has brought together diverse voices from traditional leaders, private sector representatives, and policymakers, to farmers, fisherfolk, and researchers. The platform co-creates sustainable food and climate solutions by turning scientific knowledge into locally relevant tools that farmers can use and scale. ; The platform has proven its value in addressing pressing issues, such as the mining pollution incident in the Kafue River on February 18, 2025. When the incident was reported, the platform’s stakeholders — who previously operated in silos — came together to discuss the impacts on the basin. The platform worked with local leaders to channel information to communities, coordinated a joint statement to policymakers, and reached consensus on actions to address pollution and its potential impacts on livelihoods and ecosystems.

column16: Fifty youth adopt cage fish farming in small reservoirs across four communities in Ghana's Northeast Region
column17: Young people in northern Ghana now have new livelihood opportunities through aquaculture after CGIAR's International Water Management Institute and Sustainable Animal and Aquatic Foods Program demonstrated that cage fish farming works in small reservoirs. The program trained 50 youth (one-third women) in tilapia production techniques across four communities in Ghana's Northeast Region. Participants received capital, inputs, and technical support to complete full production cycles while ensuring existing water uses remained unaffected. This adoption of cage fish culture increased local fish availability and improved dietary diversity in participating communities. The success demonstrates aquaculture's potential for youth employment and food security in similar reservoir systems across the region.

column16: Farmers and food system actors in Kenya adopt low-emission agricultural solutions through community-driven Living Lab
column17: The Living Lab for People (LL4P) in Kenya has successfully transitioned from design to implementation, creating a citizen-centered space where farmers and food system actors collaborate to develop locally relevant agricultural solutions. This innovative approach addresses the need for sustainable, low-emission farming practices while ensuring community ownership of the solutions. The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) and partners established this collaborative platform at Kaimosi Agricultural Training Centre, where practical demonstrations and field activities showcase climate-smart innovations. Local farmers are organically adopting these solutions based on their practical relevance to their farming contexts. The Living Lab strengthens partnerships across multiple stakeholders and serves as a replicable model for community-driven agricultural innovation that supports both climate action and food system transformation in sub-national contexts.

column16: CGIAR partners and funders use Innovation Portfolio Management principles, anaytics and tools
column17: Innovation portfolio management is an emerging topic in the public sector and has gained traction in the agrifood innovation sector. Most organizations do not just manage one, but multiple innovations. Innovation portfolio management refers to managing a portfolio of innovations, innovation projects or interventions aimed at delivering (positive) societal impact. The main objective is to ensure that the innovation portfolio of a project, program, country or entire organization is healthy and delivers against outcomes and impact. It can support portfolio managers in strategic decision-making, prioritization (e.g. as part of stage-gating), risk management and resource mobilization around gaps in the portfolio. It can also support strategic communication about the innovation portfolio with external audiences such as funders. CGIAR has been at the forefront of advancing science and practice of innovation portfolio management. Other organizations have started to adopt key principles and tools that CGIAR developed

column16: Food vendors in Philippines and Kenya improve business practices after completing CGIAR Vendor Business School training program
column17: Small food vendors in urban markets face daily challenges including poor food safety practices and limited business skills that affect their livelihoods. The CGIAR Resilient Cities Initiative developed and piloted the Vendor Business School program in Quezon City, Philippines and Nairobi, Kenya to address these challenges. The program provides practical training on business operations, food safety measures, and essential skills for market vendors and street food sellers. Vendor testimonials collected after program completion demonstrate measurable improvements in their business practices and personal development. These success stories were presented at the Urban Food System Policy Forum in Quezon City, showing how targeted capacity building can transform the lives of informal food sector workers and strengthen urban food systems.

column16: Adoption of cattle artificial insemination (AI) by livestock keepers in Northwest Vietnam (2025), through an AI service provider co-operative supported by the Sustainable Animal and Aquatics Foods Science Program.

column16: Agronomic gain key performance indicators (KPIs) framework used to monitor, evaluate and measure the impact of changes in agronomic practices
column17: There is a strong need to systematically measure the impact of improved agronomic practices across diverse geographies, farming systems, and stages of research in order to better understand agronomic gain. The Key Performance Indicator (KPI) framework provides a standardized and transparent approach for assessing agronomic gain across the full Research and Development continuum. It has been developed for all Sustainable Farming Program focus areas (e.g., water, perennials, regenerative agriculture). The KPI framework has been applied through designated “use cases” within the Excellence in Agronomy Initiative and the Sustainable Farming Program to assess agronomic gain and the multi-dimensional inclusivity index, as reflected in the Impact Dashboard (https://eia.cgiar.org/impact-dashboard).

column16: Forage evaluation protocol developed by Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT adopted by Zambia's Seed Control and Certification Institute for multi-site trials
column17: The Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT developed a standardized protocol for evaluating forage grass performance across different environments. This protocol enables systematic data collection and analysis for forage variety trials. Zambia's Seed Control and Certification Institute adopted this protocol after receiving training from Alliance researchers in April 2025. The institute is now using the protocol to evaluate 10 forage grasses and 1 forage legume across six contrasting environments in Zambia, with the goal of identifying varieties suitable for release. Five researchers from the institute were trained and will cascade the training to other technical staff to ensure uniform data collection. This adoption strengthens Zambia's capacity to conduct robust forage evaluations and supports the development of improved livestock feed options for farmers.

column16: Fish-keeping households in Bangladesh adopt  the genetically improved Rohu generation 3
column17: Initiated in 2012, the WorldFish Carp Genetic Improvement and Dissemination Program (CGIDP) in Bangladesh aims to enhance the productivity and profitability of carp aquaculture by improving growth rates of key carp species.  Genetic gains of greater than 10% per generation in growth rate have been achieved in rohu (https://doi.org/10.3389/faquc.2022.1060335). Furthermore, evidence from Bangladesh shows that adoption of genetically improved Generation 3 (G3) rohu has resulted in significant improvements in farm-level productivity and profitability, highlighting the program’s long-term potential to strengthen carp aquaculture systems (https://doi.org/10.1155/are/9986779).  Dissemination of genetically improved Generation 3 (G3) rohu in Bangladesh began with the first commercial seed sales reported by partner hatcheries in 2022. Since then, production and sales of G3 rohu seed have increased steadily.  An estimated, 295,655 farmers were reached through G3 rohu seed produced and sold during the 2025 spawning season . This corresponds to an estimated 1,478,276 people living in aquatic food-producing households reached through G3 rohu dissemination in 2025. Of these, 41,533 farmers are estimated to have been newly reached in 2025, while the remainder adopted G3 rohu in earlier years and continued its use into 2025. This translates into an estimated 207,667 people living in producer households newly reached in 2025.

column16: Improved rice varieties adopted across 8,900 hectares in South Asia through national institutes and women's groups
column17: Enhanced rice varieties developed through CGIAR's Breeding for Tomorrow initiative are being adopted across India, Bangladesh, and Nepal, covering an estimated 8,900 hectares. National research and extension institutes validate these varieties and manage seed supply chains, while self-help groups and women's federations handle local seed production and distribution. This collaborative approach ensures smallholder farmers, particularly women, have access to high-performing varieties that meet market demands. The strong field performance and farmer preference for these varieties drive their continued adoption, contributing to improved agricultural productivity and food security in the region.

column16: Ethiopian government extension services adopt farmer-to-farmer learning methods using locally-developed sheep fattening handbook in North Shewa Zone
column17: Government extension offices in three districts of North Shewa Zone, Ethiopia, along with Debre Birhan University, have integrated a farmer handbook on sheep fattening into their regular extension activities. The handbook was co-developed by the International Livestock Research Institute and local pioneer farming families, capturing proven feed management practices that improve sheep fattening outcomes. Extension workers now use this resource during farm visits, training sessions, and group learning activities to promote knowledge exchange between farmers. This approach validates farmers as sources of innovation and makes extension services more relevant by anchoring advice in locally-tested practices. The integration represents a shift toward more participatory extension methods that strengthen community-based learning and institutionalize successful local innovations within public agricultural systems, particularly benefiting climate adaptation efforts.

column16: Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) method for detection of seedborne diseases by Burkholderia glumae in the early stages of adoption by partner institution in the Philippines.
column17: IRRI’s Seed Health and Logistics Unit (SHU) developed a rapid and simple diagnostic test for bacterial panicle blight using the Loop-mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) method. LAMP is a technique that rapidly amplifies specific DNA sequences, allowing for the quick and accurate detection of Burkholderia glumae. This method is performed at a constant temperature without the need for complex laboratory equipment, making it ideal for use in the field. As part of scaling out this method, IRRI-SHU introduced it to the Bureau of Plant Industry-National Seed Quality Control Services (BPI-NSQCS) through a Capacity Development Workshop on the Rapid Detection of Bacterial Panicle Blight of Rice. The workshop aimed to enhance the seed health diagnostic skills of BPI seed analysts and facilitate the adoption of LAMP technology to strengthen seed quality management and plant quarantine efforts. Following the workshop, the partner institution had taken the lead in the adoption process by developing and initiating their own internal training program to capacitate their target users; as well as securing equipment and consumables with the aim of incorporating the method into their routine diagnostic procedures.

column16: CGIAR climate-peace-security training module adopted by African Group of Negotiators Expert Support reaches over 1,000 participants across 30+ African countries
column17: Climate change increasingly threatens peace and security across Africa, yet policymakers often lack tools to address these interconnected challenges. CGIAR Climate Security partnered with the African Group of Negotiators Expert Support (AGNES) to develop training modules that help African leaders integrate climate, peace, and security considerations into their work. Between 2022 and 2025, these modules were embedded in AGNES's existing leadership programs and delivered through a new eight-week specialized course. The training translated complex climate-security research into practical frameworks for assessing risks, ensuring conflict sensitivity, and promoting inclusive climate action. Over 1,000 participants from more than 30 African countries—including policymakers, researchers, and practitioners—gained skills to design climate policies and programs that strengthen resilience, stability, and peacebuilding in their communities.

column16: Co-developed Integrated Mycotoxin Management training materials strengthen capacities of farmers, extension agents, policymakers, and private sector actors to adopt climate-smart food safety practices.
column17: This result delivers a comprehensive set of co-developed Integrated Mycotoxin Management (IMM) training materials tailored to farmers, extension agents, NGOs, private sector actors, and policymakers. Building on Aflasafe and broader aflatoxin mitigation experience, materials include farmer-friendly manuals, extension guides, interactive e-learning modules, and policy briefs available in digital and print formats. The result strengthens stakeholder knowledge on climate-smart mycotoxin prevention, integrating pre-harvest biocontrol, post-harvest handling, storage, and food safety practices. By enhancing awareness and practical skills, this outcome supports wider adoption of IMM approaches and contributes to sustained reductions in aflatoxin exposure and food safety risks.

column16: Colombian dairy companies adopt VISIPRAST digital platform supported by the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT to verify zero deforestation compliance in supply chains
column17: Colombian dairy companies that signed Zero Deforestation Agreements lacked tools to verify supplier compliance, risking reputational damage and market access. VISIPRAST, a geospatial monitoring platform developed by Proyección Eco-Social with technical support from the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, addresses this challenge by integrating government deforestation data with supplier mapping. The platform enables real-time visualization of supply chains and identifies properties in protected areas or deforestation zones. By August 2025, 23 of 26 companies adopted VISIPRAST as their monitoring tool, with 14 submitting compliance reports and many introducing zero-deforestation policies. The platform became the official sector evaluation tool, creating transparency and accountability. Compliant companies now access tax benefits and green financing, while Congress advances nationwide legislation for forest protection.

column16: Solar-powered borehole for drought management co-developed and scaled by IWMI used by households in Zambia to improve access to clean water for drinking and domestic use
column17: The Hanzila community in Zambia successfully implemented a solar-powered borehole system to address water scarcity during droughts, with support from the International Water Management Institute and government partners at district and national levels. This locally-led initiative overcame traditional government decision-making barriers by fostering collaboration across different administrative levels. The solar-powered water system provides year-round access to clean water for drinking, household needs, livestock, and crop irrigation. Community assessments show that 86% of residents now rely less on contaminated water sources and travel shorter distances to access water. The reliable water supply also enabled more families to grow home gardens, with participation increasing from 23% to 69% of households, significantly improving local food security and nutrition outcomes.

column16: CIP institutionalizes FAIR data and responsible AI policies through an organization-wide digital transformation strategy.
column17: CIP’s Digital Transformation Strategy outlines a roadmap to become a digitally native, AI-enabled science-for-development organization by 2030. It is anchored in five strategic goals: accelerating scientific breakthroughs, optimizing operational excellence, enhancing stakeholder engagement, scaling impact through open science, and fostering an inclusive and secure digital culture. Delivery is enabled through three capability pillars—Digital & Data Backbone, AI-Driven Decision Intelligence, and Stakeholder Platforms & Services—supported by strong people, culture, governance, and cybersecurity enablers. With clear KPIs, governance cadences, and ethical safeguards, the strategy aligns with CGIAR’s Digital Transformation Agenda and strengthens CIP’s ability to deliver faster, fairer, and more inclusive impact across Africa, Asia, and Latin America.

column16: Solar-powered water lift system developed by IWMI adopted by 55 marginalized households in Nepal's Sindhupalchowk hills
column17: The International Water Management Institute (IWMI) developed and installed a solar-powered water lift system to address severe water scarcity faced by the Majhi people, a highly marginalized indigenous community in Nepal's Sindhupalchowk district. The community previously relied solely on rainfall for their upland fields, limiting cultivation to six months annually, while seasonal floods destroyed fertile lowlands. The innovative system pumps water uphill from the river to reach both agricultural fields and households that were previously inaccessible due to lack of infrastructure. Since implementation, 55 Majhi households have gained reliable water access, significantly reducing women's daily water collection burdens and enabling year-round cultivation. Early adopters report improved livelihoods and living conditions, demonstrating the system's potential for transforming water-scarce mountainous communities.

column16: Adoption of the Africa Asia Diary Genetics Gain (AADGG) platform by smallholder dairy farmers in East Africa and Nepal
column17: The AADGG Data Platform (Africa Asia Dairy Genetic Gains) is a digital repository and analytics system that collects, stores and organizes dairy farm and animal performance data from participating countries in Africa and Asia. The data is also used to identify genetically superior animals for use as breeders.; ; In 2025, there were 1121 smallholder dairy households newly registered, across East Africa (Tanzania, Kenya, Ethiopia) and Nepal.
