column16: Improved Agricultural and Livestock Practices Applied by 90% of Project Beneficiaries
column17: From the study conducted at the end of the project’s first year of implementation, it was observed that approximately 90% of beneficiaries are applying various practices and technologies aimed at improving agricultural production, poultry and livestock management, as well as good nutritional practices. column16: CGIAR research assessment of climate adaptation and mitigation co-benefits, unlocking US$300 million for climate-smart agriculture in Togo
column17: Utilizing an impact pathway-based approach, CGIAR researchers assessed the potential adaptation and mitigation co-benefits of large-scale climate-smart agriculture interventions.This assessment was instrumental in unlocking US$300 million in climate finance for Togo’s agricultural sector. By quantifying how specific practices—such as soil health management and resilient cropping—simultaneously build climate resilience and reduce emissions, CGIAR enabled the Togolese government to meet the rigorous technical requirements of the World Bank. This engagement demonstrates the direct application of CGIAR-informed tools in national policy design and the successful mobilization of high-level climate investment.

column16: CGIAR research informs IPCC's Technical Guidelines on Impacts and Adaptation
column17: During its 60th plenary session, the IPCC decided to update the 1994 Technical Guidelines on climate impacts and adaptation. This distinct product, which will incorporate indicators, metrics, and methodologies for measuring adaptation and will be developed alongside the Working Group II Report. The revision addresses the urgent demand for tools to assess climate impacts and track progress in adaptation, including the Global Goal on Adaptation. Following standard IPCC procedures, parties first agreed on a formal outline to guide the development of the guidelines. The Alliance and the African Group of Negotiators Expert Support Group (AGNES) supported African countries in drafting a proposal that significantly informed the final IPCC-approved outline of the technical guidelines. A notable idea was to organize the guidelines around the iterative adaptation cycle.

column16: CGIAR evidence synthesis protocols and methods used to assess global adaptation implementation
column17: CGIAR has successfully scaled the use of a research protocol, originally developed under AICCRA, to synthesize evidence within national adaptation plans and reports. This protocol was instrumental in assessing adaptation progress reported in Biennial Transparency Reports (BTRs) submitted to the UNFCCC through August 2025. By applying this methodology to the 2025 UNEP Adaptation Gap Report (AGR), CGIAR enable a systematic, global comparison of how countries are translating their NDCs and NAPs into tangible action. This pathway bridges the gap between raw national reporting and high-level policy synthesis, providing a standardized lens to evaluate the effectiveness of climate resilience-building efforts worldwide.

column16: CGIAR science informs the development of a resilience measurement method of the World Bank in Ethiopia.
column17: Measuring resilience is challenging, as it requires tracking the ability of human and natural systems to maintain well-being despite climate shocks, data that traditional metrics often fail to capture. To address this, CGIAR supported the integration of key indicators and contributed to the design of baseline methodology for Ethiopia’s Lowlands Livelihood Resilience Project (LLRP II). LLRP II is a five-year World Bank–financed initiative implemented by the Government of Ethiopia through the Ministry of Irrigation and Lowlands. It targets pastoral and agro-pastoral communities across eight lowland regions and 120 woredas, aiming to strengthen livelihoods and resilience to climate shocks. Insights from CGIAR research, including the use of an impact pathways-based approach to assessing resilience enhanced the robustness of the baseline methodology, supporting the collection of key data that can show the contribution of the project to resilience building.

column16: Strengthening On-Farm Performance Testing and Market-Driven Variety Advancement Through TRICOT-Based Evaluation
column17: The TRICOT (Triadic Comparison of Technologies) approach was successfully implemented across three East African countries to strengthen on-farm performance testing and accelerate variety development. This participatory evaluation method allows farmers to compare crop varieties under real farming conditions, providing crucial data for breeding programs. In Tanzania, 450 trials across three agroecological zones identified three high-performing lines for release. Uganda conducted 65 trials covering four market segments, identifying three promising varieties, while Ethiopia focused on verification trials for small red and white bean profiles. The approach used digital data collection tools and centralized platforms to ensure efficient data management. Strong participation from men, women, and youth farmers enhanced the inclusivity of variety selection. During the implementation period, nine improved varieties were officially released across the participating countries, demonstrating measurable yield advantages and enhanced disease resistance. This initiative, supported by the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT through the AVISA program, established systematic on-farm testing as a core mechanism for improving cultivar targeting and adoption in regional breeding programs.

column16: Operational regional trialing network developed for testing early generation common bean breeding materials in East African PABRA countries
column17: Six East African countries now systematically use an enhanced regional testing network to evaluate early-generation common bean varieties developed by the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT with collaboration of researchers for University of Western Australia (UAW). The early generation testing network operates across six PABRA countries, namely Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Rwanda, and Burundi, focusing on nutritious, rapid cooking and climate-resilient bean varieties that meet specific country needs. Countries receive breeding materials from the central program and select promising lines based on their agricultural priorities and environmental conditions. The Alliance, together with UAW strengthened the network by improving data management systems, enhancing trial coordination, and establishing regular regional meetings for joint evaluation of results. This coordinated approach enables countries to make evidence-based decisions about which bean varieties to advance toward release, ultimately supporting food security and farmer livelihoods across the region.

column16: Water-saving rice technique (alternate wetting and drying) developed by IRRI adopted by 1.73 million farming households in Bangladesh
column17: Rice production traditionally requires continuous flooding, consuming vast amounts of water and contributing to greenhouse gas emissions. The International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) developed alternate wetting and drying (AWD), a water management technique that periodically dries rice fields for at least 5 days during the growing season. This approach reduces water use by up to 30% while maintaining yields and decreasing methane emissions. During Bangladesh's 2024 boro season, a comprehensive study documented that 1.73 million rice-growing households practiced AWD on at least one of their irrigated plots. This widespread adoption demonstrates how IRRI's water-efficient innovation addresses critical challenges of water scarcity and climate change while supporting the livelihoods of millions of smallholder farmers across Bangladesh's rice-growing regions.

column16: Axial flow pump (AFP) promoted by CIMMYT is adopted by farmers in Bangladesh
column17: Axial flow pumps, irrigation technology promoted by CIMMYT, have been widely adopted by agricultural households in Bangladesh to enhance farm productivity through improved water management. This technology addresses critical water access challenges faced by smallholder farmers, enabling them to maintain consistent crop production and increase agricultural yields. The widespread adoption demonstrates the effectiveness of CIMMYT's technology transfer efforts and represents a significant scaling achievement that directly benefits rural farming communities across Bangladesh by providing reliable irrigation solutions for enhanced food security and income generation.

The mechanical reapers provide an accessible mechanization option for farmers cultivating these staple crops, contributing to enhanced efficiency in agricultural operations across Bangladesh's farming communities.

column16: Adoption of carp–Small Indigenous Species (SIS) polyculture systems
column17: Small indigenous fish species like Mola, Dhela, Kachki, and Chapila, traditionally harvested from open waters, are now being cultivated alongside carp in integrated polyculture systems. CGIAR research through WorldFish demonstrated the nutritional benefits of these small fish species and developed sustainable cultivation methods to enhance their availability. This approach addresses food security and nutrition challenges while preserving biodiversity. The polyculture system allows farmers to diversify their production and income sources while providing communities with access to highly nutritious small fish that are rich in essential micronutrients. column16: Principal Component Analysis methodology used by governments to identify critical locations for sustainable groundwater monitoring
column17: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) approach is an that helps in identifying and prioritizing critical locations for groundwater monitoring. This method applies advanced statistical techniques to integrate multiple environmental parameters including land use, hydrology, climate, and soil characteristics to assess the susceptibility of regions to groundwater quantity and quality risks.; ; The International Water Management Institute (IWMI) piloted this innovation in collaboration with the Government of Punjab, Pakistan, where it has empowered stakeholders to make evidence-based and collaborative decisions for prioritizing areas requiring targeted groundwater interventions. Through the application of this approach, the Punjab Irrigation Department (PID) has not only strengthened the existing groundwater monitoring network but also expanded it beyond canal command areas, significantly improving spatial coverage and representativeness across Punjab.; ; Building on its success in Punjab, the PCA-based methodology has been upscaled and applied in the pilot districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) Province, Pakistan. In KP, the approach is guiding decisions on optimal locations for installing groundwater monitoring devices, ensuring efficient allocation of resources and improved groundwater governance.

column16: Groundwater management information system supporting sustainable water resource decisions and policies to address long-term groundwater challenges
column17: This innovation is a web-based data-driven tool that will help policy makers and implementers to manage, analyze, and report on groundwater data. It will be further upscaled to the country level in order to support implementation of National and provincial water policies. Initially pilot for the districts of Rahim Yar Khan and Okara in Punjab province. Later on upscaled to whole Punjab province. column16: Designing Evidence-Based Models for Central Highlands Ecoregion Foodscape, Enhancing Soil and Water Efficiency, and Localizing Seed Varieties
column17: The Nature Conservancy and CGIAR Excellence in Agronomy Initiative are collaborating to develop a strategic use case for the Central Highlands Ecoregion Foodscape, focusing on scientific research and evidence-based solutions. The innovation comprises three Minimum Viable Products (MVPs):; ; MVP 1 - Scenarios and monitoring systems to ensure water availability in source areas (water towers) and its sustainable use in neighboring ecologies.; MVP 2 - Integrated regenerative portfolios targeting efficient and sustainable land, soil, and water (including river) management.; MVP 3 - Regenerative solutions to improve water use efficiency, resilience, and climate adaptation in semi-arid agricultural landscapes.; ; These MVPs aim to enhance sustainable resource management, bolster ecological resilience, and address climate challenges across diverse ecosystems within the Central Highlands. This partnership underscores the importance of integrating scientific innovation with practical strategies to promote sustainability and resilience in foodscapes and beyond

column16: High-yielding, disease-resistant white and water yam varieties developed by IITA and partners for West African farmers
column17: In collaboration with national yam breeding programs in Nigeria, Cote d’Ivoire, Ghana and Benin, IITA yam breeding seeks to develop and deploy end-user preferred White Yam and Water Yam varieties with higher yield, greater resistance to pests and diseases and improved quality, targeted at West Africa. Together these collaborators seek to address common yam breeding challenges: reducing lengthy crop cycles to 3-4 years, poor seed multiplication ratio, poor understanding of genetic diversity, limited breeding enabling technologies, and limited current capacity in West Africa. Significant strides were made in enhancing the efficiency of breeding programs, including defining the yam market segmentation, refining the yam product profile, deploying marker assisted selection, and use of quantitative genetics methods to optimize breeding approaches. Yam consumers participated in elite clone selection. Between 2022 and 2024, the National Root Crops Research Institute registered five white yam varieties in NIgeria, one of them in 2024.; ; ;

column16: Climate-resilient, zinc-biofortified wheat varieties developed by CIMMYT and ICARDA with 200+ partners registered for smallholder farmers globally
column17: CIMMYT's Global Wheat Program, working with ICARDA and over 200 research institutions, has developed wheat varieties that help farmers adapt to climate change while improving nutrition. These varieties tolerate drought and heat stress, resist diseases and pests, and contain higher levels of zinc and iron to reduce malnutrition, particularly benefiting women and children. Using advanced molecular breeding tools and speed breeding techniques, the program reduced development time to three years. Between 2022 and 2025, partners registered 149 varieties across Africa, Asia, and Latin America. These varieties are currently grown on more than 60 million hectares worldwide, providing smallholder farmers with seeds that produce higher yields under challenging climate conditions while delivering better nutrition to farming communities.

column16: Heat and drought tolerant bread wheat varieties developed by ICARDA and partners for farmers in Africa and Asia drylands
column17: Growing wheat demand across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia faces challenges from climate change, pests, and diseases that limit local production. ICARDA developed two breeding programs targeting different regional needs: rainfed spring wheat for Central and West Asia and African drylands, and heat-tolerant spring wheat for broader regions. Working with public and private partners and farmers, these programs create varieties with high yields, stress resistance, and good quality traits. The breeding process takes three years per cycle. Partners across four countries have released eight new varieties from these programs, all selected for heat and drought tolerance. Additional work includes developing zinc and iron-enriched varieties to improve nutrition. This collaborative approach helps farmers access wheat varieties better suited to challenging growing conditions.

column16: Durum wheat breeding network accelerates genetic gains for more productive, resilient varieties that meet end-user requirements for farmers in Africa, the Middle East, and Asia
column17: Growing demand for pasta and semolina products across Africa, the Middle East, and Asia faces challenges from climate stress, pests, and diseases that limit local durum wheat production. ICARDA, working with CIMMYT and partners, developed six specialized breeding pipelines targeting different dryland environments: South Asia with limited irrigation, rainfed systems in West/Central Asia, North Africa, East Africa, and high-cold regions, plus irrigated West Africa savannas. Using advanced techniques like speed breeding and genomic selection, the breeding cycle was reduced to 2.5 years. The resulting varieties offer drought and heat tolerance, stable yields, disease resistance, and meet end-user quality requirements. Thirteen scaling partners across nine countries have released 17 improved varieties, providing farmers with more resilient and productive options suited to their specific growing conditions.

column16: Climate-resilient and nutrient-enriched maize varieties developed by IITA and CIMMYT breeding network for West and Central African farmers
column17: A collaborative maize breeding network led by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center has developed improved maize varieties for West and Central African farmers. The network operates four breeding pipelines targeting different maturity periods and grain colors to meet diverse market needs: fresh consumption, processing, poultry feed, and home use. Orange and yellow varieties are biofortified with Provitamin A to address malnutrition. The breeding program has reduced development time from traditional cycles through functional markers and genomic selection techniques. Working with public and private partners across the region, 13 scaling partners in 10 countries have released 48 varieties that offer improved yields, drought tolerance, and resistance to Striga weed and pests, addressing climate challenges while meeting growing food and feed demands.

column16: Drought-tolerant, disease-resistant maize varieties with enhanced nutrition developed through advanced breeding networks for smallholder farmers in Latin America
column17: CIMMYT and the International Maize Improvement Consortium for Latin America, comprising over 30 public and private organizations, developed high-yielding maize varieties specifically designed for smallholder farmers and local markets across Latin America and the Caribbean. These varieties address critical agricultural challenges by combining drought tolerance, resistance to tar spot complex and other locally important diseases, plus enhanced nutritional quality including Provitamin A. The breeding program uses cutting-edge technologies such as doubled haploids and genomics-assisted breeding to reduce development time to 4-5 years. In 2025, scaling partners successfully released 14 varieties that demonstrate improved productivity while maintaining stress tolerance traits essential for climate-resilient agriculture in the region.

column16: Climate-resilient maize varieties with disease resistance developed through advanced breeding networks for smallholder farmers in Eastern Africa
column17: Smallholder farmers in Eastern Africa face significant challenges from climate change, diseases, and pests that reduce maize yields and threaten food security. CIMMYT and IITA collaborated with public and private partners across Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda to develop improved maize varieties addressing these challenges. The breeding programs created three pipelines targeting early-, intermediate-, and late-maturing white maize varieties with drought tolerance, nitrogen efficiency, and resistance to major diseases including Maize Lethal Necrosis, Gray Leaf Spot, and Fall Army Worm. Advanced technologies like genomic selection and molecular markers reduced breeding time to 3-5 years. Large-scale testing on over 450 farms incorporated farmer preferences into variety development. This collaborative effort resulted in 21 scaling partners releasing 40 climate-resilient maize hybrids across six countries, covering 8.3 million hectares and enabling reduced pesticide use.

column16: Climate-resilient and biofortified white maize varieties developed and released by CIMMYT and IITA with partners for smallholder farmers in Southern Africa
column17: Smallholder farmers in Southern Africa face significant challenges from climate change, pests, diseases, and malnutrition. To address these issues, CIMMYT and IITA collaborated with public and private partners across Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia, and Zimbabwe to develop improved white maize varieties. Using advanced breeding techniques including doubled haploids and genomics-assisted breeding, researchers created varieties with drought tolerance, nitrogen use efficiency, disease resistance, and enhanced provitamin A content. Large-scale testing on over 700 farms captured feedback from both men and women farmers to ensure varieties met their needs. This collaborative effort resulted in 69 varieties being released by 27 scaling partners, with eight specifically selected for higher provitamin A content and fall armyworm resistance that reduces pesticide dependency.

column16: Climate-resilient maize hybrids developed through collaborative breeding networks with 60+ partners registered for smallholder farmers across South Asia
column17: CIMMYT and the International Maize Improvement Consortium in South Asia brought together over 60 public and private organizations to develop climate-resilient maize hybrids for smallholder farmers. These hybrids withstand drought, heat, and excessive moisture while resisting key diseases - critical traits for farmers cultivating 8.85 million hectares of stress-prone rainfed environments across the region. Using advanced breeding techniques including doubled haploids and genomics-assisted selection, the consortium reduced breeding cycles to just over four years. On-farm testing with more than 75 farmers in India, Bangladesh, and Nepal validated performance under real farming conditions. This collaborative effort resulted in 19 registered climate-resilient maize hybrids now available through scaling partners in Bangladesh, India, Nepal, and Sri Lanka, providing smallholder farmers with improved varieties suited to their challenging growing conditions.

column16: Biofortified bean varieties with enhanced zinc and iron developed and registered by African partners for improved nutrition and farmer income
column17: Common beans provide essential nutrition and income for over 200 million Africans but often lack sufficient micronutrients. The Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT collaborated with the Pan Africa Bean Research Alliance and national breeding programs to develop improved bean varieties addressing farmer and consumer needs. Building on previous disease resistance and drought tolerance work, researchers focused on biofortification with zinc and iron, reduced cooking time, and gender-responsive traits. Through systematic breeding cycles and farmer feedback, 19 scaling partners successfully tested and registered 53 new bean varieties across Africa. These varieties combine nutritional enhancement with practical benefits like shorter cooking times, supporting both food security and women's time management while providing income opportunities for farming communities.

column16: Soybean breeding network for Africa accelerates genetic gains for more productive, rust-resistant varieties that are adapted to poor soil conditions, to provide smallholders with diversification opportunities
column17: In collaboration with public and private sector partners and farmers, IITA soybean improvement targets increased and stable yields, resistance to soybean rust that can cause up to 60% yield loss, reduced pod shattering and tolerance to soil nutrient and pH deficiencies. Breeding pipelines are pursued: 1. Early and 2. Medium-to-late maturing soybean for the lowland savanna in West Africa, 3. Early and 4. Medium-to-late maturing soybean for the mid-altitude savanna in southern Africa. Breeding cycle time was reduced to 2.5 years. Collaboration with public and private sector partners improves the pace, scale, and output of varietal development and widens the genetic diversity available to African countries. Joint advancement meetings with female and male value chain stakeholders identify candidate varieties for on-farm testing. Six scaling partners in five countries released 7 varieties.

column16: Productive and resilient rice varieties developed through Latin American breeding network for farmers in Latin America and Africa
column17: Rice production in Latin America faces challenges from diseases, climate stress, and the need for direct-seeded varieties that are more competitive and nutritious. The Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT works with the Latin American Fund for Irrigated Rice, a network of 36 public and private partners across 17 countries covering two-thirds of Latin America's 5.7 million hectares of rice. This collaborative breeding program develops rice varieties that are more productive, resilient to climate stress, and resistant to major diseases. The breeding process takes 32-62 months and uses targeted selection in disease hotspots to accelerate development. Partners have successfully registered 28 new varieties, with breeding materials routinely shared with African partners to expand impact beyond Latin America.

column16: Climate-resilient rice varieties developed by AfricaRice and partners using indigenous germplasm and modern breeding for African farmers
column17: Many African farmers still grow low-yielding rice varieties that cannot withstand climate change impacts, limiting their productivity and income. AfricaRice, working with national research systems and international partners, has developed a comprehensive breeding program that combines Africa's rich indigenous rice genetic resources with modern breeding techniques to create superior varieties. The program operates eight breeding pipelines targeting sixteen market segments across 12.6 million hectares of rice-growing areas. In 2023, target product profiles were validated with stakeholders in 10 countries, and 20 African countries now routinely assess candidate varieties. This collaborative approach has resulted in 52 varieties being registered by 21 scaling partners across 17 countries, many selected specifically for climate resilience traits, providing farmers with improved options adapted to local growing conditions and market demands.

column16: Climate-resilient rice varieties developed through collaborative breeding network by IRRI and AfricaRice for Eastern and Southern Africa
column17: Eastern and Southern Africa relies heavily on rice imports, creating food security challenges for the region. To address this gap, the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and AfricaRice established a collaborative breeding network with national partners to develop climate-resilient, market-demanded rice varieties suited to local growing conditions. The network uses modern breeding approaches to accelerate variety development, reducing cycle time to 36 months. The program leverages IRRI's Asian breeding investments to create early and medium-maturing, stress-tolerant varieties for direct seeding and various water systems. Through on-farm trials in Mozambique, Kenya, and Tanzania, followed by late-stage testing across multiple countries, the network ensures varieties meet farmer and end-user demands. Five scaling partners have successfully registered 23 varieties, many enhanced for climate resilience traits, contributing to increased domestic rice production capacity.

column16: Climate-resilient rice varieties developed through breeding networks in Southeast Asia reduce emissions and labor requirements
column17: Rice production in Southeast Asia accounts for nearly 30% of global rice harvest but generates significant greenhouse gas emissions while facing challenges from floods, droughts, and labor shortages due to urbanization. The International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) leads multi-sectoral breeding consortia including public and private partners to develop climate-resilient rice varieties suitable for direct seeding. These improved varieties help farmers save water, reduce labor requirements through better mechanization compatibility, and lower greenhouse gas emissions. The breeding program incorporates genomic selection techniques and considers gender-specific trait preferences when defining target characteristics. Through partnerships in Myanmar and the Philippines, 11 varieties with climate resilience traits have been registered for farmer use, demonstrating the maturity and readiness of these innovations for broader scaling across the region.

column16: Climate-resilient rice varieties developed by IRRI and partners through accelerated breeding networks for diverse farming systems in South Asia
column17: Rice production in South Asia faces mounting challenges from climate change, pests, diseases, and evolving farmer and consumer demands. IRRI collaborated with public and private partners and farmers to develop improved rice varieties through nine specialized breeding pipelines. These pipelines focus on early-maturing, stress-tolerant varieties for direct seeding and medium to late-maturing varieties for irrigated, deep-water, semi-deep-water, and saline environments. Advanced techniques including genomic selection and rapid generation advancement reduced breeding cycles to three years, with a new SpeedFlower protocol promising further reductions. Large-scale on-farm evaluations in Bangladesh and India incorporated gender-disaggregated farmer feedback to identify varieties suited for different market segments. Twenty scaling partners have registered 71 climate-resilient varieties, demonstrating the maturity and readiness of these innovations for widespread adoption across diverse South Asian farming systems.

column16: Sweetpotato breeding networks in Asia & Latin America accelerate genetic gains for diverse market segments; shorter season varieties, varieties with low sweetness or purple flesh are in demand
column17: The CIP sweetpotato breeding program in Peru is serving mostly Asia and Latin America with breeding pipelines for  1. “orange flesh sweet potato (OFSP) for wide adaptation and earliness” suitable for 90 days crop seasons which are in demand in wheat/rice rotation systems, 2. “OFSP with no/low sweetness after cooking” suitable for 120 days crop seasons, and 3. purple-flesh sweetpotatoes for 120 days crop seasons. Genomic tools accelerate the development of more productive, biofortified, consumer-preferred varieties with higher foliage yield. Breeding cycle time is 30 months. Dissemination to local partners is through true seed from elite-crosses, and via in-vitro plantlets of advanced clones. On-farm testing in Peru has been completed, identifying two clones for release. Close to 93,000 true seeds, each a unique genotype, were distributed to partners in Bangladesh, Vietnam, China, with further requests from Mozambique, India, Uganda and Vietnam. Ethiopia released a biofortified variety from the Peru-based program.;

column16: Sweetpotato breeding network in Southern Africa accelerates genetic gains for market-demanded, resilient, high provitamin A varieties, generating new income opportunities for women farmers
column17: The Southern Africa collaborative sweetpotato breeding network accelerates and enhances the breeding of orange-flesh and white sweetpotato varieties for improved yield, virus and weevil resistance, and end use traits, to reduce malnutrition and raise incomes. Since 2022, demand- and gender- responsive target product profiles (TPPs) draw on the input of user studies (Malawi, Mozambique), and product design and advancement meetings. As a result, TPPs were updated for sensorial traits that lead to greater adoption and consider gender-differentiated perspectives. Market Segments were better defined and now target 660,000 hectares. Modified breeding schemes, novel designs, larger-scale testing and genotype-by-environment analyses have increased selection intensity and genetic gains. On-farm trialing has grown to 64 sites across Mozambique, Malawi and Zambia, assessing farmers ranking and preferences and, in some instances, cooking qualities. Mozambique registered three biofortified varieties in 2022; Zambia promotes eight clones in 2024.

column16: Sweetpotato breeding network in Eastern Africa accelerates genetic gains for market-demanded, resilient, high provitamin A varieties, generating new income opportunities for women farmers
column17: Sweetpotato is a vital crop for 15 million resource-poor households in Africa and Asia, providing essential nutrition and income. The International Potato Center and partners established a collaborative breeding network across Eastern and Southern Africa to accelerate development of improved sweetpotato varieties. The network uses demand-driven breeding approaches, incorporating farmer preferences through participatory trials and gender-responsive target product profiles based on user studies in Ethiopia, Uganda, and Tanzania. Advanced breeding methods including larger-scale testing and genetic analysis have increased selection efficiency. The network focuses on developing orange-flesh varieties rich in vitamin A and white-flesh varieties with improved yield, virus and weevil resistance, and earlier maturity. Between 2022-2024, partners registered four new white-fleshed varieties in Burundi and Uganda. Large-scale farmer trials using innovative comparison methods evaluated seven promising varieties across 17 traits, with yield identified as the key driver of farmer preference, supporting evidence-based variety advancement decisions.

column17: Potato is a smallholder cash crop in East and Central African highlands. In many of the drier potato-growing regions, more frequent water and heat stress are leading to declining yields. The East Africa Potato Breeding Network was formalized in May 2023.  In 2024, newer candidate varieties are to include resilience traits such as heat tolerance, earliness-to-ripen, virus and late blight resistance, good water-use efficiency. Breeding cycle time is 3-4 years. The resulting varieties are being tested in multilocation trials with public and private partner organizations, and through citizen science approaches with farmers. Even though varieties have been released in the past, recent insights point to yield, taste, marketability, and tuber quality as being most important to farmers. These insights help to adjust target product profiles. Their development is being accelerated through genomic selection, faster cycle times, spatial and GxE analyses that optimize variety testing, and more accurate consumer trait assessments. ; ;

column16: Early-maturing, stress-resilient potato varieties delivered to Asian farmers through accelerated public–private partnership breeding.
column17: Potato cultivation in the tropical and subtropical regions of Asia faces major constraints from biotic stresses such as late blight, viral diseases, bacterial wilt, and nematodes, as well as abiotic stresses including heat, drought, and salinity driven by climate change. Despite these challenges, the potato area in Asia has expanded from 4.1 million ha to 10.3 million ha since 1981, growing at an annual rate of 2.45%, while potato area in Europe declined significantly during the same period. However, varietal turnover in Asia remains very low, with decades-old, long-day–adapted varieties still dominating production due to a lack of locally adapted varieties and weak seed systems. To address these constraints, CIP and HZPC Holland B.V. established a public–private partnership in 2016 through the TAP5 project, aimed at developing tropically adapted, early-maturing, and climate-resilient potato varieties for diverse Asian agro-ecologies and market segments. The program focuses on improving productivity, profitability, and food security for smallholder farmers, while ensuring access to quality seed through strong private-sector engagement. The breeding pipeline BP00123 (Asia Fresh and Processing) supported by the public-private partnership R&D progressed systematically across stages, six advanced clones from stage 5 & 6 were discussed in the PAM meeting in detail, resulting in the rejection of HCIP317111.40 and HCIP317230.28 due to consistent scab sensitivity and skin cracking, while four clones were advanced, with HCIP316040.7 emerging as a lead candidate identified for registration trials in Vietnam and further testing in additional target countries. In addition, the advancement decisions were made across the stages in the pipeline i.e. 242 clones selected from 3,633 in Stage 1 and genotyped for late blight and PVY, of which 84 clones advanced to Stage 2 for multi-environment testing in lowlands and highlands during 2025–26. At Stage 4, three clones are advanced to Stage 5 (HCIP320031.21, HCIP320590.41 for the red-skin segment, and HCIP320603.10), while in the processing segment 14 clones were evaluated across the Red River Delta and Central Highlands, with four clones selected for advancement (HCIP317111.121, HCIP317126.80, HCIP320094.24, and HCIP320390.10). In parallel, 13 clones were screened for bacterial wilt under natural disease pressure, with six selected and recycled into the pipeline to strengthen resistance in commercial backgrounds

column16: Cowpea breeding network in Africa accelerates genetic gains for more productive, resilient cowpea varieties, based on an improved understanding of gender-specific end-user requirements, to benefit smallholders in Africa
column17: Globally, cowpea is cultivated on about 14.5 million hectares. In Africa, cowpea is more of a woman's crop. The overall productivity is very low, with average yields ranging from 100 to 400 kg/ha. This is due to several biotic and abiotic constraints. The CGIAR-NARES collaborative cowpea breeding program seeks to develop higher-yielding, disease- and pest-resistant varieties that meet the requirements of local markets. Breeding pipelines differ by maturity to fit different season lengths and cropping systems. They consider that cowpea can be used for both grain and fodder, and for both boiling as grain and making home-made flour. Consequently, in 2025 four clear breeding pipelines were defined: i) Short duration boiled grain and dual-purpose cowpea, ii)Short duration home-made flour cowpea, iii)Medium duration boiled grain and dual-purpose white & brown cowpea and iv)Medium duration home-made flour cowpea.  Breeding is a cyclical process, with new, further-improved varieties forthcoming regularly, building on feedback from farmers and markets. Large-scale farmer feedback is received using the Triadic-comparison-of-technologies (TRICOT) methodology. Current breeding cycle time is 4 years. Between 2022-2025, partners registered 29+9 (38)  varieties for use.

column16: Disease-resistant cassava varieties with enhanced processing traits developed through collaborative breeding networks for African smallholders
column17: Cassava is a vital food crop for millions of African smallholders, but devastating diseases like cassava mosaic and brown streak viruses threaten productivity and food security. The International Institute of Tropical Agriculture and the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT collaborated with national research partners across 13 African countries to develop improved cassava varieties. These breeding networks focused on creating varieties that resist major diseases while meeting specific market demands for fresh consumption, drying, granulation, and industrial processing. The collaborative approach incorporated farmer preferences and market requirements into breeding programs, resulting in 33 new varieties released by scaling partners. Advanced infrastructure improvements enabled efficient root-quality testing and streamlined breeding processes. On-farm trials using both classical and participatory methodologies validated variety performance, ensuring the innovations meet real-world conditions and farmer needs across diverse African farming systems.

column16: Enhanced forage breeding partnerships between Africa and Latin America accelerate development of productive and climate-resilient livestock feed varieties
column17: Smallholder livestock farmers in Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America struggle with poor-quality forage that limits animal productivity and farm sustainability. To address this challenge, the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT developed an enhanced forage breeding system that accelerates genetic improvements through strategic partnerships between regions. This innovation combines advanced breeding techniques including genomic selection and improved evaluation methods to develop productive and climate-resilient Urochloa and Megathyrsus varieties. The system incorporates participatory approaches to ensure varieties meet specific farmer needs. Between 2022-2024, this breeding innovation enabled training of national research partners in advanced evaluation techniques, strengthened public and private sector involvement in testing, and resulted in 10 new forage varieties being registered by scaling partners for farmer use across multiple regions.

column16: Disease-resistant banana and plantain varieties developed through accelerated breeding networks by IITA for African smallholder farmers
column17: The International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) developed improved banana and plantain varieties through three specialized breeding pipelines targeting different African regions and preferences. Working with public and private partners and farmers, IITA created cooking matooke and mchare banana varieties for East Africa, and plantain varieties for Central and West Africa. These varieties resist major diseases like Fusarium wilt and pests while maintaining high yields and fruit quality that meets local market demands. The breeding program uses advanced genomic tools and digital phenotyping to reduce development time to 9 years. Extensive on-farm trials and farmer taste-testing ensure varieties meet local preferences. By 2025, scaling partners released 10 varieties, demonstrating the program's success in delivering practical solutions for smallholder farmers across Africa.

column16: High-yielding disease-resistant cassava varieties developed through accelerated breeding networks and released by partners in Colombia and Vietnam
column17: Cassava demand is rapidly growing for large-scale processing into starch, animal feed, and ethanol, requiring varieties with specific traits. The Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT, working with IITA and global partners, developed accelerated breeding approaches that reduced breeding cycles from traditional timelines to just three years. The program created four specialized breeding pipelines targeting different market needs: good cooking quality, high dry matter content, biofortified varieties with provitamin A, and waxy starch types. These innovations address smallholder farmers' income needs while meeting industrial processing requirements. The breeding networks incorporate rapid cycling techniques, genome-wide predictions, and flowering induction to speed genetic gains. Partners in Colombia and Vietnam have already released varieties from these programs, demonstrating the maturity and real-world application of these breeding innovations for improving farmer livelihoods.

column16: Enhanced biophysical and socioeconomic modeling tools to explore food, land and water system impacts and strategic policy options relevant for low- and middle- income countries
column17: Food, land and water (FLW) systems face challenges from a host of interacting megatrends as well as local and regional drivers. These include changes in population, urbanization, income, inequality, migration, diets, technology, biodiversity, and climate. Many of these trends are themselves influenced by changes in FLW systems, interacting in complex ways that have important impacts on nutrition, poverty, equity, climate, and the environment.  To capture these complexities we need  among other things quantitative  tools that help us understand how, where and at what cost these complex  interactions are manifest across the food system at global and regional scales.  This innovation draws on CGIAR’s biophysical and socioeconomic expertise to enhance the IMPACT model by developing and enhancing specific modules to better understand FLW system outcomes under plausible future scenarios.;

column16: A disaggregated water-energy-food systems model to study the economywide effects of water and energy interventions in the face of climate change.
column17: This innovation contributes to the discussion on water-energy-food nexus that has remained at the forefront of development policymaking. Understanding the nexus between water, energy, and food security requires a well-customized model that traces the supply and use of water, energy, and land resources and their spatial allocation. The two-stage production nesting structure in the standard IFPRI Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model is extended to a seven-stage nesting structure where various types of water (surface and groundwater) and various types of energy (hydro and non-hydro) are explicitly combined with irrigated land such that the close substitutability and complementarity between water, energy, and land are well captured. A disaggregated Social Accounting Matrix (SAM) that represents the agro-ecological specificity of agriculture and resource distribution (irrigation) is generated. The model and data are used to analyze the economywide effects of water and energy interventions in the face of climate change-induced weather variability. The model was used to assess how agri-food system investments priorities in Ethiopia could change under climatic and world price risks. To analyze this, additional outcome indicators - including changes in poverty and diet quality – were introduced. In 2025, The analytical product titled “Modeling the economy-wide effects of water and energy interventions in the face of climate shocks in Ethiopia” was published in a peer-reviewed journal.

column16: Circular Bioeconomy Innovation Hub in Ghana: A Multistakeholder Platform for scaling circular economy innovations to minimize urban environmental pollution
column17: The CBE Hub is one-stop-shop for training, research, advisory support, collaboration, and knowledge sharing. The hub unites 16 stakeholders from the public and private sectors, research institutions, non-governmental organizations, and education to promote circular bioeconomy initiatives. Operating in the organic waste-to-resource value chain, a co-ownership model that shared goals and resources for co-design and co-implementation was used for collective impact. It aims to showcase, optimize, and promote existing circular bioeconomy innovations while fostering the development of new, accessible innovations. This is accomplished through five strategic operational areas: demand-driven capacity building; research for innovation and scaling; advisory support for policy development and implementation; monitoring, evaluation, and learning; and information sharing, collaboration, and partnerships.  In 2024, the hub successfully organized and co-organized several multi-stakeholder workshops on waste valorization.; In 2025, the Circular Bioeconomy Innovation Hub advanced from piloting to coordination and scale through the following key actions:; Formalized partner commitment to the hub through the signing of a multi-partner Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) led by IWMI bringing together 16 public, private, research, and development partners to jointly advance and scale circular bioeconomy solutions in Ghana.; Scaled the RRR Schools & Youth Program to 23 basic schools, reaching 15,612 students, supported by 47 trained teachers, 42 EWB-KNUST volunteers, and 1,185 student leaders driving daily waste segregation, composting, and school gardening activities.; Convened the CE4 Ghana Consultation Workshop, engaging 100+ stakeholders from government, finance, research, development partners, and the private sector to identify priority circular markets, investment readiness gaps, and enabling conditions for scale; insights from this are directly informing the design of the upcoming CE4Ghana Innovation Challenge.; Strengthened policy dialogue and public awareness through national and international platforms, including a GBC WASH Hour panel discussion, a UNOSD–Ghana waste management workshop, and a Ghana Institution of Engineers technical talk on advancing Ghana’s circular bioeconomy through the IWMI-led Innovation Hub.

column16: Tools and approaches to help breeders to optimize breeding schemes aligned with the desirable characteristics of farmer and market demanded crop varieties
column17: As breeding teams refine Target Product Profiles (TPPs), breeding schemes must be continuously reviewed to ensure appropriate emphasis on priority traits while maintaining competitiveness. Under this result area, two complementary innovations were delivered to support breeding scheme optimization and decision-making across CGIAR.; 1. Breeding Scheme Manager (BSM).; The Breeding Scheme Manager is a decision-support tool that enables breeders to document, review, and optimize their breeding schemes in alignment with defined breeding targets. It captures crossing, evaluation, and selection decisions, facilitating continuous improvement of breeding strategies and responsiveness to market and product profile requirements. In 2025, training and support videos were developed and deployed to assist breeding teams across CGIAR in using the tool. By the end of 2025, 83 users were registered and actively documenting breeding schemes at varying stages of completion.; 2. Repeatability Explorer.; The Repeatability Explorer supports optimization of multi-environment trial (MET) designs by visualizing how entry-mean repeatability (H²), selection accuracy, and Fisher’s LSD respond to changes in trial network size, including numbers of locations, replicates, and years. Deployed in 2025, the tool enables breeders to explore trade-offs in testing resource allocation and translates results into expected repeatability and selection accuracy in the target population of environments (TPE), incorporating user-defined genetic correlations.;

column16: Climate-Smart Risk Maps and Adaptation Plans (CS-MAP) for Rice Production in Bangladesh, Cambodia and Vietnam
column17: The climate-smart risk maps and adaptation plans (CS-MAP) is a participatory approach involving experts from various local and national offices for (1) identifying climate-related risks; (2) delineating affected areas and risk levels; (3) proposing corresponding adaptive plans; (4) fine-tuning and verifying propose measures; and (5) developing integrated provincial and regional adaptation plans. Risk maps were developed for normal and El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) years by using technical data, infrastructures, and local observations. ; ; The CS Maps are designed to be used by policymakers and planners from regional and local offices to inform annual crop planning at province and district levels for scaling of adaptation solutions in rice production. The CS-MAP approach has been expanded to Cambodia and Bangladesh with numerous consultations, evaluations and validation with local stakeholders and farmers to develop and scale the CS-MAP approach for local planning.

column16: Video-based Product Concept Testing (VPCT) tool for market segmentation of maize and sorghum seeds in East Africa
column17: The video-based product concept testing tool (VPCT) is an innovative market-intelligence methodology that helps agricultural researchers and breeders understand farmers’ preferences for future crop products before those products exist in physical form. At its core, VPCT translates hypothetical seed or crop product ideas into short, structured videos that communicate the concept’s key traits, potential benefits, and trade-offs in a consistent, visual, and local-language format, making them accessible to smallholder farmers regardless of literacy level.; ; The process begins with ideation: breeders, socio-economists, seed system actors, and farmers co-develop a set of product concepts—for example, hybrid seed with improved stress tolerance or varieties tailored for specific end uses. These conceptual profiles are then recorded as professionally produced presentations, often with an actor or voiceover explaining the product in context. During field surveys, each farmer views a subset of these videos (often three at a time in a randomized incomplete-block design) and is asked to rank or select the concept they would most prefer. This generates revealed preference data on latent demand that is far richer and more consistent than text-only descriptions.; In East Africa, this tool was first applied to next-generation maize seed concepts with thousands of farmers in Kenya and Uganda, showing clear interest in resilience-focused and context-specific traits. More recently, VPCT was deployed with 1,100 sorghum farmers in Tanzania’s Dodoma and Shinyanga regions, where seven sorghum seed product concepts—including home use, forage, industrial malting, intercropping, and hybrid varieties—were translated into videos. Farmers overwhelmingly favored the hybrid seed concept, followed by home-use oriented products, supporting revisions to sorghum seed market segments and target product profiles for breeding strategies in Tanzania.; ; By leveraging visual storytelling and systematic choice data, VPCT provides actionable insights into what smallholder farmers truly value, enabling demand-led breeding, targeted product development, and evidence-based investment decisions across diverse crops and regions.

column16: Market Intelligence Briefs: Evidence-Based Insights Linking Crop Breeding and Seed Systems Investments to CGIAR Impact Areas Through Multidisciplinary, Peer-Reviewed Collaboration Informing Strategic Decisions Across CGIAR, NARS, Private Sector and NGOs
column17: n 2025, the Market Intelligence Brief (MIB) Series continued to serve as a key evidence-based platform for informing strategic investments in crop breeding and seed systems development across CGIAR and partner organizations. More importantly, the innovation strengthened its core purpose: to provide a structured and systematic mechanism for generating, synthesizing, and sharing market intelligence with stakeholders—particularly to inform Product Design Team meetings and Product Advancement Meetings. The MIB Series supports evidence-based decision-making at critical stage-gates in breeding pipelines.; ; The series offers rigorously peer-reviewed insights into the potential for increased impact across CGIAR Impact Areas, reinforcing demand-led research and innovation. By bringing together perspectives from marketing and agribusiness, gender analysis, plant sciences, and climate change, the MIBs equip breeding teams, NARS partners, private sector actors, and NGOs with clear intelligence on market segments, trait preferences, regional demand patterns, and investment priorities. This ensures that product profiles and advancement decisions are better aligned with farmer and market needs.; ; In 2025, the series operated under a new Editorial Team led by Dr. Melanie Connor (IRRI) as Editor-in-Chief and supported by Ms. Ruvicyn Bayot (IRRI) as Managing Editor. The Editorial Committee included experts from CIMMYT, CIP, IFPRI, IITA, and IRRI, ensuring cross-crop and cross-regional relevance. Design and layout, led by Mr. Neale Marvin Paguirigan (IRRI), enhanced clarity and accessibility for decision-makers.; ; By year’s end, 13 Market Intelligence Briefs had been published on CGSpace under the Breeding for Tomorrow collection and made available through a dedicated GloMIP webpage. Expanded collaboration with CIRAD and WorldVeg strengthened coverage in West Africa and broadened crop scope. An enlarged reviewer pool and coordinated communications campaign further enhanced quality, reach, and institutional uptake—positioning the MIB Series as a practical decision-support tool embedded within breeding governance processes.

column16: Seed Product Market Segment Database for CGIAR and NARES breeding programs
column17: CGIAR developed a comprehensive database containing over 650 seed product market segments across crops and regions where CGIAR and national agricultural research systems invest in breeding and seed development. Each segment uses eight standardized criteria and consistent descriptors including production area, crop value, population data, and poverty indicators. This systematic framework enables breeders, researchers, seed companies, and funders to compare market opportunities using key agricultural, demographic, and economic data. The database supports evidence-based priority setting for breeding investments and provides a common framework for designing crop varieties that meet specific market needs. It facilitates strategic dialogue between CGIAR centers, national partners, and the private sector on where to focus breeding efforts for maximum development impact.

column16: Eight-criteria framework developed by CGIAR centers to systematically identify seed product market segments globally
column17: CGIAR centers developed a comprehensive framework with eight criteria to help agricultural researchers and seed companies systematically identify and define seed product market segments. The framework addresses the challenge of targeting appropriate markets for new crop varieties by providing clear segmentation guidelines. The first three criteria (crop type, material characteristics, and geographic subregion) form the foundation, covering 25 crops including specialized varieties like spring and durum wheat, and distinguishing hybrid crops such as maize, sorghum, and rice. Ten subregions derived from CGIAR's seven recognized regions complete the geographic framework. This tool enables more strategic seed product development and market targeting, supporting improved agricultural outcomes across diverse farming systems worldwide.

column16: Potato breeding network in Latin America accelerates genetic gains for biofortified, disease- and heat-tolerant varieties, also creating income and nutrition benefits for farmers in Africa and Asia
column17: CIP potato breeding harnesses the latest scientific knowledge and tools to develop better varieties. Even though targeted and first tested regionally, the Latin American potato breeding pipelines have significant benefits globally as they pursue: 1. Late blight, heat tolerant potato varieties to enable farmers to cope with climate change. 2. Biofortified potatoes with elevated levels of iron and zinc, and disease and heat resilience traits to reduce malnutrition. Breeding cycle time is 3 years. Selection is for marketable tuber yield and late blight resistance. Biofortified potatoes crosses were made in 2012 between a Peruvian landrace and elite lines with high yield and resistance to prevalent diseases. Twelve clones were selected in collaboration with Peruvian partners and 1600 farmers. Between 2022-2024, partners in China, NIgeria and Peru released 11 varieties, two of them with 37% more iron and 35% more Zinc, contributing to reducing malnutrition.

column16: Global network of regional scaling hubs developed by CGIAR to accelerate agricultural innovation adoption worldwide
column17: Agricultural innovations often fail to reach farmers due to fragmented scaling efforts and poor coordination between researchers, partners, and end users. CGIAR developed a global network of interconnected regional scaling hubs to address these challenges. Starting with the Eastern and Southern Africa Scaling Hub as a pilot, the network has expanded to include operational hubs in Kenya and Nepal, with preparations underway in Latin America. Each hub serves as a neutral platform that brokers partnerships, builds local capacities, and shares practical knowledge to support responsible scaling of agricultural innovations. The hubs strengthen coordination across CGIAR centers, provide trusted interfaces for governments and development partners, and enable cross-regional learning. This network positions CGIAR to deliver coordinated, impact-oriented scaling of agricultural innovations that can transform food systems globally.

column16: A Program Management Platform allows to align a programmatic agenda across initiatives and non-pooled projects, enabling Program-wide learning and reducing transaction costs for staff and research leaders
column17: Genetic Innovation is a large endeavor, involving 21 crops, a large number of staff, partners, funders and projects. In collaboration with Breeding Resources and Scriptoria Ltd UK, Accelerated Breeding implemented a Project Management Center (PMC), to make workplans transparent across the two initiatives and several non-pooled projects. It became obvious that uploading workplans by project attracts high transaction costs and does not facilitate cross-initiative/project learning, mostly because interventions are framed and clustered differently.  Therefore, a Program Management Platform (PMP) was developed and tested with 20 non-related workplans of a wide range of bilateral projects. It enabled alignment of all (100%) projects to a common results framework that e.g. could be applied to one or several Program or Accelerator Theory(-ies) of Change. The PMP received positive feedback because it makes the agenda transparent, enables cross-project/initiative learning, and reduces transaction costs. It could facilitate Program and Accelerator implementation effective 2025. ;

column16: Advanced breeding methods developed by CGIAR centers reduce crop development time to 39 months for farmers globally
column17: Innovations under this result include implementing genome-assisted rapid-cycle recurrent selection schemes, more accurate and earlier selection of crossing parents, and rapid advancement approaches, to accelerate the rate of genetic gain in major food crops.  As per 2025, cycle time across crops has further reduced from 41 months in 2024 to 39 months in 2025. In 2024, end-of-initiative deep-dive sessions with CGIAR breeding teams captured 2022-2024 progress. Fifty-eight percent of programs use rapid-cycle genomic selection in at least one pipeline, while 32% are establishing genomic selection approaches. This represents significant progress from 2022 and 2023 when only 35% and 45% implemented genomic selection, and cycle times were longer. Use of genomic selection implies and drives that programs also adopt more sophisticated and capable data management systems. Successful models need to be scaled across more breeding pipelines and parameters for estimating breeding value need continuous improvement.

column16: The Breeding Portal helps CGIAR crops to optimize pipeline structure and leverage breeding gains within a particular crop, complementing diversity studies and quantitative genetics analytics
column17: Having adequate genetic variance is necessary to make genetic gain. Making genetic gain also means depleting genetic variance. Strategies are needed to augment trait variance in the elite germplasm pool. This variance can come from trait discovery and deployment (TD&D) pipelines, other crop breeding pipelines, or less-related genetic resources. An effective germplasm use strategy aligns breeding pipelines with target product profiles (TPP), understands trait availability viz priorities, and strategically leverages investments across pipelines and organizations. Since 2023, all CGIAR programs use the Breeding Portal to document the Breeding Pipeline - TPP relationships and define the essential traits that need to be improved. During deep-dive sessions in 2024, 74% of programs stated that they introgress between 1 to 11 critical traits into the main breeding pipelines (see Result 1241). There is need to better document and rationalize the TD&D - Breeding Pipeline relationships in the Breeding Portal. ;

column17: CGIAR breeding programs have developed improved approaches to test and identify crop varieties that better represent real farming conditions and market requirements. These enhanced testing methods help breeders select varieties earlier in the development process by measuring essential traits under conditions that mirror where farmers actually grow crops. The approaches include refined target product profiles, multi-environment trials across diverse locations, and on-farm verification testing. Between 2022 and 2024, breeding teams made significant progress in aligning their strategies with farmer and market needs, with 58% of programs now able to measure about 75% of essential traits during early testing phases. This enables faster identification of promising varieties and accelerated development of crops that perform well in farmers' fields, ultimately supporting food security and climate resilience.

column16: Crop-specific approaches for innovative and collaborative on-farm trialing approaches systematically use simpler, yet larger-scale evaluations, and capture gender-disaggregated data, for a more farmer- and market-relevant selection of new crop varieties
column17: In recent years, there has been a concerted effort by regional Breeding networks to validate the performance of new candidate crop varieties under farmer conditions to ensure they meet the needs of farmers. However, this process is challenging due to the logistics involved in mass producing seed/clones, distribution and the need to sample a representative set of farmers in the target environment across multiple countries with different implementing partners with different capacities. In recent years, new approaches to scalable on farm verification such as Triadic Comparison of Technologies (TRICOT) have been developed and piloted for both seed and clonal crops. Other methods employing non-replicated, sparse testing models have also been piloted across a range of crops and pipelines. This result assesses the organizational change across crops. In 2025, 95% of breeding programs conducted on-farm verification in at least one pipeline utilizing a methodology that met minimum standards. In 2026, best practices will be harvested from across these efforts to develop a standard, scalable and cost effective strategy for all regional breeding networks.

column16: Standardized genetic gain assessment tool developed by CGIAR centers to monitor breeding pipeline performance across crops globally
column17: CGIAR centers developed a standardized approach to assess genetic gains in crop breeding programs, addressing the previous lack of consistent methods for measuring breeding progress across different crops and traits. The innovation uses a Bioflow module integrated with the Breeding Portal to provide annual updates on genetic gains across CGIAR breeding pipelines. In 2025, ten CGIAR centers reported genetic gains for 61 breeding pipelines covering 71 market segments, with 61% showing statistically significant positive gains for yield. Nearly half of the market segments achieved the target of over 1% annual genetic gain for yield, an improvement from 40% in 2024. The tool also successfully assessed nutritional improvements, with all bean breeding pipelines showing significant iron gains and rice pipelines demonstrating zinc improvements, supporting efforts to develop more nutritious crops for food security.

column16: Definition of the portfolio of distinct, achievable Target Product Profiles, by all CGIAR breeding programs, provides the basis for collaboratively assessing and agreeing on the most impactful CGIAR breeding targets
column17: The organizational innovation develops tools and approaches for taking stock of current CGIAR breeding pipelines and mapping them to impactful, gender-relevant and gender-intentional, in-demand, feasible target product profiles (TPP’s) - each a unique combination of productivity, adaptation, resilience, quality, processing and consumer traits, that is aligned to a sub-regional market segment, since 2023 using the Breeding Portal. Each TPP contains the traits required and targeted scores. As per November 2024, CGIAR and NARES defined a total of 607 TPPs aligned to Breeding Pipelines and Market Segments. Traits were aligned with 14 distinct value propositions that drive Impact Area tagging of TPPs. Market Intelligence uses the information to develop pipeline investment cases that describe benefits to the five Impact Areas by breeding pipeline. The innovation makes transparent and optimizes the focus of current and new CGIAR breeding pipelines. Through the 2024 review, the quality of TPPs has improved.

column16: Digital platform developed by CGIAR centers to track and share crop breeding strategies and performance data globally
column17: The Breeding Portal is a comprehensive digital platform that captures collaborative breeding strategies between CGIAR centers and national agricultural research systems. Developed by multiple CGIAR centers led by CIMMYT, the platform tracks key breeding information including target traits, breeding pipelines, variety releases, market segments, and partnerships. The system makes selected data publicly available through the Global Market Intelligence Platform while maintaining secure access controls for detailed information. In 2025, the platform launched the Harmonized Crop Report, which provides quantitative analysis of breeding portfolio performance across all CGIAR centers. This innovation addresses the critical need for transparent, evidence-based tracking of crop improvement efforts, enabling better coordination and impact assessment across the global agricultural research community. The platform serves 12 organizations with 92 active users, demonstrating its value for breeding program management and strategic decision-making.

column16: Partnership strategy and tracking tool developed by CGIAR Breeding for Tomorrow to prioritize collaboration in global crop improvement networks
column17: The partnership strategy assesses historically grown partnership models and creates transparency on partner inclusion. In 2023, 55 regional crop improvement networks were defined based on discussions with CGIAR breeding programs. 26 of these networks are based in Africa. A country prioritization tool developed in 2022 that incorporates crop acreage, world bank income status and existing partnerships was deployed in 2023 with 22 crop x region breeding networks in Africa and 11 crop x region breeding networks outside of Africa. Network members were prioritized according to a four-tier system: Level 1, Level 2, Level 3 and self-funded partner countries. A Level 1 Country: indicates that CG centers provide support to strengthen local breeding and testing capacities. A Level 2 Country: indicates that CG centers provide support to strengthen local testing and variety release capacities. A Level 3 Country: Countries where spillover is expected.; By 2025, all (20) crops had updated the level of engagement with partner countries, accordingly. Current breeding networks include 412 partner organizations that are involved as either Level 1 (136), Level 2 (103), Level 3 partners (107) or self-supported (66) partners. The partnership strategy provides an objective approach for networks to prioritize their focus and investments in Level 1 and 2 countries, where the impact is likely to be greatest, whilst ensuring other countries have access to international public technologies.

column16: Standardized partnership agreements developed by CGIAR centers to enhance equitable collaboration in African crop breeding networks
column17: Regional crop improvement networks in Africa previously lacked formal agreements defining partnership terms, leading to inconsistent collaboration approaches across different networks. CGIAR centers developed standardized network membership agreements that clearly outline benefits, commitments, and obligations for partners in breeding collaborations. These agreements establish transparent frameworks for germplasm sharing, data exchange, decision-making participation, and contribution acknowledgment. The innovation emerged from extensive stakeholder consultations with national agricultural research systems and CGIAR leadership across Africa during 2021-2022. The standardized template was first implemented by the Africa Root and Tuber network, involving the International Potato Center, International Institute of Tropical Agriculture, and 16 national partners in 2024. Subsequently, the Africa Dryland Crop Network, coordinated by the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center and International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics with 20 national partners, adopted the agreement in 2025, demonstrating its applicability across different crop networks.

column16: Standardized Product Design Team approach developed by CGIAR to help national partners define crop breeding priorities across Africa, Asia and Latin America
column17: National agricultural research systems often struggle to systematically identify and document breeding priorities that align with farmer needs and market demands. CGIAR's Breeding for Tomorrow initiative developed Product Design Teams as a collaborative approach where national partners lead meetings to define market segments and create Target Product Profiles that guide breeding decisions. Since 2022, this innovation has been scaled to 120 meetings across 25 countries covering 15 crops, resulting in approximately 400 national breeding priority profiles. The approach strengthens national capacity to modernize breeding programs by effectively identifying priorities and allocating resources, while ensuring CGIAR regional efforts align with country-specific needs and incorporate gender perspectives into breeding objectives.

column16: Partner assessment framework developed by CGIAR to evaluate national breeding programs and create customized improvement plans across Africa, Asia, and Latin America
column17: National agricultural research systems often lack systematic approaches to assess their breeding program strengths and identify improvement priorities. CGIAR's Breeding for Tomorrow initiative developed a standardized framework that evaluates partner capabilities, identifies capacity gaps, and creates tailored development plans. The innovation includes assessment tools and methodologies that help national programs define their roles in regional breeding networks based on their comparative advantages. Since 2019, this framework has been applied to 132 breeding programs across multiple crops including rice, maize, and sweet potato. In 2025, nine additional programs were assessed, expanding for the first time to Southeast Asia with evaluations in the Philippines and Vietnam. The assessments enable evidence-based allocation of responsibilities within regional breeding networks and support national programs in developing strategic improvement roadmaps.

column16: Aligning CGIAR breeding processes to a common, high level organizational structure create clarity of roles and contributions among the individual initiatives and teams to the overall breeding success
column17: Modern breeding organizations drive efficiency gain, opportunity identification, and operational effectiveness through the coordinated engagement of specialized teams and processes. In interaction with the other Genetic Innovation initiatives, this innovation builds upon the extended stage plan established and validated in 2022 and 2023. It comprises ten distinct stages from product concept and market segmentation to product launch. It includes an extended suppliers-inputs-process-outputs-customers (SIPOC) model that provides a high-level overview of the processes, defines the inputs needed, the supplier(s) of each input, the key processes at each stage, the outputs of the processes, and the customers of each output. The approach was socialized and promoted across CGIAR breeding teams and partners. Deep-dive sessions in 2024 show that 53% fully and 41% partially implemented harmonized stage gate terminology. The terminology is also used in interactions with partners. This development entails a significant step change for consistently aligning CGIAR breeding processes.

column16: Aligning standardized breeding pipeline processes and stage gates in Genetic Innovation with skill-sets of diverse teams required to execute vanguard breeding programs
column17: In 2022, common stage gates spanning the whole breeding pipeline and sub-pipeline segments of collaborative breeding networks were defined. They provide a framework to define the connection between teams along the germplasm development process in a systematic manner for more effective handover between breeding teams, including those in partner organizations. The stage gating is the basis for more clearly communicating individual team focus, success, and defining professional development strategies. During 2024 high-level skill sets were defined that drive the product development process in different stages. Insights help in identifying potential gaps, duplications, and reorganization opportunities, given that similar skill sets are repeated across centers, crops and locations. Participants in a crop lead meeting highlighted the need and intent to better leverage capabilities across centers, based on such understanding. Skill sets may also drive gender-differential preferences for professional roles. The approach supports the design of more inclusive career pathways.

column16: A methodology for assessing the anticipated return on investment and likelihood of success of CGIAR Trait Discovery & Deployment Projects, as a mechanism to orient upstream investments towards high-impact activities
column17: This innovation underpins investment case standardization, implementing a dynamic pipeline developed in 2023 to establish pilot estimates of trait valuation. The approach looks at trait mapping across market segments, leveraging trait experts’ estimation of ultimate benefit of their work to yield benefit and stability. Based on productivity impacts across market segments, additional yield and resulting monetary value are calculated. The framework was applied to 2023 mapped Trait Discovery & Deployment (TD&D) project activities in eleven crops. The analysis highlights the value of investment case standardization and provides valuable input on the need to benchmark estimates in productivity gain, ranging for the same trait from 1% to 15% and 30% to 80% across some programs working on the same TD&D opportunity in the same crop. Leveraging information on investments and understanding the likelihood of success as we advance provides a robust foundation to estimate the relative merit of different TD&D opportunities.
