column16: Stata command file that simplifies the calculation of all versions of the Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index (WEAI)
column17: The WEAI ado file is a Stata user-written program that can calculate all versions of the Women's Empowerment in Agricultural Index (WEAI) depending on the options specified by the user. WEAI is a standardized, survey-based tool that has been widely used to track gender equality and measure empowerment, agency, and women's inclusion in the agricultural sector (Alkire et al. 2013). Since the WEAI's release in 2012, an abbreviated version of the WEAI (referred to as A-WEAI) and a project-level version of the WEAI (referred to as pro-WEAI) have been developed (Malapit et al. 2017; Malapit et al. 2019). The tool allows users to specify the binary adequacy indicators, empowerment cutoff, and indicator weights. WEAI provides a decomposition by indicator and, when specified, by sub-groups. Note that because the WEAI requires data from women and men, users are required to specify a variable (and values) identifying the sex of respondents.

column16: Improved community-led water governance approach through strategic sluice gate operation for sustainable ropping in the coastal polder zones of Bangladesh
column17: Engaging with communities to employ more pragmatic land-use planning and scheduling of sluice gate operations has shown the potential to intensify and diversify cropping systems, and increasing production by 2-3 fold. Several trainings are also being provided to ensure synchronized operation of sluice gates of intended users such as water management groups and rice farmers for improved productivity and intensified production systems in the polders.

column16: Decision-support system to help researchers, development actors, donors and governments assess trade-offs between social, economic, and environmental outcomes at different scales, for evidence-based planning of investments in sustainable livestock production.
column17: Failure to address constraints to livestock productivity and the growing risks from climate change and other shocks can limit productivity gains while putting sustainability at risk. Increasing yields through climate-smart interventions can, but may not always, contribute to lowering emissions intensities while enhancing livelihoods. It is therefore important to provide information to stakeholders about trade-offs and synergies between productivity, economics, gender & social equity, and environmental factors. So that they can be considered when developing and scaling livestock innovations and during policy making at national or regional level. In response to this challenge, we are developing a toolbox for scenario assessment that describes trade-offs and synergies associated with those scenarios at different scales. This decision-support system (integrating ex-ante modelling tools) helps researchers, development actors, donors, and governments to consider trade-offs between social, economic, and environmental outcomes at different scales during evidence-based planning of investments in livestock production.

column16: Co-operative for women and men beef-cattle artificial inseminators, for improved artificial insemination sevice provision and increased income generation by the service providers.
column17: CGIAR researchers developed an innovative cooperative business model to address the challenge of limited access to artificial insemination services for beef cattle farmers in Vietnam. The model focuses on creating sustainable income opportunities for both women and men service providers while improving breeding services for smallholder farmers. Through participatory studies, researchers identified lack of access to liquid nitrogen as a key barrier and designed a cooperative structure that enables shared access to essential resources. The Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT and the International Livestock Research Institute collaborated with local partners to create this gender-sensitive approach that enhances economic performance and social responsibility. This innovation supports the expansion of quality artificial insemination services using farmer-preferred breeds, ultimately contributing to improved beef cattle productivity and profitability for smallholder enterprises in Southeast Asia.

column16: An innovative genetic improvement strategy for sheep and goat that involves the end users, farmers, in the design and implementation of the scheme
column17: Breeding programs that are community-based cover a range of situations. Typically, they target low input systems with farmers within a limited geographical area who have a common interest to work together for the improvement of the genetic resources of their animals. Community-based breeding programs (CBBPs) focus on indigenous stock and consider farmers’ needs, views, decisions and active participation, from inception through to implementation. Most importantly, they provide a participatory and bottom-up approach. CBBP combines farmer training to improve selection methods, consisting of pooling community flocks to create a larger gene pool from which breeding animals can be selected, scientific support to provide farmers with information on different breeding options and data collection to monitor how well individual animals perform. The entire community flock is treated as one. Livestock keepers who choose to participate in the program are organized into sheep/goat breeding associations, many of which later evolve into formal cooperatives.

column17: The assessment of an experimental vaccine for the control of East Coast fever (ECF). Thelieria parva, the causative agent of ECF, is a killer parasite infecting cattle. The experimental vaccine is based on the use of nanoparticles to present and deliver p67C antigen. In future the vaccine will be developed by an animal health company and used by livestock keepers to significantly reduce morbidity and mortality in their cattle herds, with a focus on cattpe type parasites. The new technology will also validate the nanoparticle platform for the delivery of subunit vaccines for livestock.

column16: Reproductive platform delivering services, such as fixed-time artificial insemination and sires’ certification, in sheep and goat Community-Based Breeding Program sites leading to genetic gain in small and medium-scale livestock systems.
column17: This innovation revolves around the development of artificial insemination (AI) protocols that are adapted to low-input systems where central AI labs do not exist and where basic commodities are lacking. It aims at democratizing access to improved genetics for small ruminant farmers. The platform is a network of labs supporting the breeding programs in Ethiopia. The innovation resorts to co-investment with partners in low-infrastructure, mobile labs that are operational under remote, rural conditions. AI relies on the use of fully certified sires that are genetically superior. Vaccination against infectious diseases mitigates the risk for these sires to transmit diseases. Inseminated females are synchronized with prostaglandin-based protocols that yield clean estrus, are easy to use, cheaper and are adapted to breeds under inter- tropical and equatorial African condition. The fixed time AI protocol relies on the use of fresh, non-cooled semen that is collected, assessed, processed and subsequently packed and used.

column16: Foresight and Rapid Response Modeling System (FARRMS) is an on-demand modeling tool to analyze impact of global crises to advise donor government in responses.
column17: Governments and donors often request modeling analysis to help understand the immediate consequences of, for example, global crises or local shocks, such as droughts/floods, and inform the design of policy and investment responses. The Foresight and Rapid Response Modeling System (FARRMS) streamlines our global and national data and modeling systems so that we can more rapidly respond to these requests and increase the likelihood that policy actions are evidence-based. FARRMS was conceived of during our response to COVID and was substantially developed in response to the fallout from the Russia-Ukraine War. FARRMS was used in mid-2022 to analyze impacts of the global crises on a large number of developing countries, and to advise donor governments in their responses. The country studies were conducted together with local partners, including country-based CGIAR researchers. The country studies were updated/extended in late-2022 to analyze a global economic slowdown during 2023.

column16: Novel Indicators for an Agri-Food System Dashboard Empowering Evidence-Based Policy for Sustainable Growth
column17: As agricultural growth accelerates and food systems gain focus, the need for robust indicators to quantify the scale and composition of agri-food systems has become critical. Addressing this gap, we developed two pioneering indicators: AgGDP+ measures total value added within key agri-food system segments, while AgEMP+ tracks total employment, including informal and self-employment, with gender disaggregation. Utilizing data and statistical imputation, we provide consistent estimates at national, regional, and global levels for 2010–2019.; ; To continually improve, we plan to gather the most recent Input-Output Tables (IOTs), Supply Use Tables (SUTs), and other essential data to update and expand measurements to additional years. With new Social Accounting Matrices (SAMs), we aim to extend coverage to more countries. Complemented by an online dashboard offering open access, these indicators provide the foundation for evidence-based policy and analysis of agri-food systems.

column16: Food Security, Environments and Nutrition Framework: A decision support framework to identify and prioritise barriers and solutions for improved food security for use by decision makers at lower jurisdictional levels.
column17: Achieving food security and good nutrition requires coordinated action between multiple sectors, including agricultural production, food processing and marketing, health and hygiene, and cultural work to improve equity and knowledge. Food systems research, and the food environment concept, aim to make sense of this. It can be difficult to develop a comprehensive picture of a food system, and to identify the most influential leverage points. The framework, first is for the structuring of information regarding a local food system; second a participatory process in which stakeholders to develop a shared understanding and prioritisation of challenges within the food system; and third a searchable database of potential food security interventions which may be matched to the needs of a specific food system. The objective of the framework is to help sub-national decision makers operationalise food systems concepts, in order to tackle inadequate nutrition and food insecurity.

column16: The sub-setting tool provides Genebank managers and users (breeders, scientists, students, NGOs) a web-tool to subset (select) genebank accessions available from genebanks based on environmental parameters
column17: Breeders are forced to seek the variation they require from genetic resource collections conserved in genebanks. The challenge when searching specific traits from genebanks is that resources to search for a given trait are often such that only a relatively small subset of the available genebank can be evaluated. Thus, to be effective, a strategy is required to identify the smallest possible subset of germplasm to evaluate whilst increasing the chances of capturing the sought-after variation. Genesys currently holds more than 4 million genebank accessions from 462 institutes and is accessed by users to order germplasm. From these, around 768,576 accessions are held at CGIAR genebanks. Identifying the correct set of accessions to respond to these requests adequately can be time-consuming.The subsetting tool allows to develop and implement data mining techniques for subsetting germplasm accessions, thus helping address germplasm requests more effectively and efficiently. The sub-setting is based on indicators for historical climate information, soil information and specific per crop regarding stresses. This web tool allows users to compose the needed subsets and order them directly from genebanks in Genesys. In the tool, a user identifies a series of potential subsets using data and analytics and then selects the subset of accessions that best suits their interest. For example, amongst four potential subsets, they may select the subset with accessions grown in the driest places.

column16: Innovative Software Tools for Estimating Environmental Flow Requirements Based on Monthly River Flow Time Series
column17: The Environmental Flow Estimation Tools are a set of user-friendly (online and offline) software tools enabling desktop estimation of quick,  coarse-scale environmental flow requirements of rivers. The input data required are time series data of monthly “natural” river flows, either measured or estimated. The tools are meant to be used by water planners and managers in making initial planning-level estimates of environmental flows, which may then be followed by more comprehensive assessments using further data related to aquatic ecology, moving beyond river flow data. Five tools are currently available, two covering major rivers of the world and the other three specifically for estimating environmental flow requirements in the Ganges Basin, Sri Lanka and Nepal. The tools are also useful for building capacity on environmental flow estimation, including for students and practitioners seeking to gain an initial understanding of the concept of environmental flows.

column16: Agrobiodiversity Solution Hotspot Tool for local stakeholders to address water, energy, food and environment (WEFE) challenges
column17: The agrobiodiversity solution hotspot tool is improving understanding of relationships across the food system in India and helping identify priority interventions to restore and enhance ecosystem functions and services for sustainable social and economic benefits. Location-specific threat datasets have been combined with diversity datasets from the Agrobiodiversity Index to create a threat hotspot and agrobiodiversity solution tool for local stakeholders to address water, energy, food and environment (WEFE) challenges. Initially focusing on the Ganges Basin in India, the project has utilized a collaborative approach, co-developing and co-creating with local stakeholders and government partners to develop and refine the tool. This has led to a practical downscaled Agrobiodiversity Index approach that can be used by local stakeholders to address WEFE challenges. Using a locally relevant methodology, the project has prioritized locations to enhance agrobiodiversity, improving agricultural system sustainability and resilience in India. Intensive collaboration took place in India with local and national research and government partners. Due to its methodology, this innovation can be transferred to other geographies.

column16: Multistakeholder Platforms are networks designed to implement program interventions by bringing together critical actors to improve business ecosystems and incentivise actors in bean corridors
column17: Multistakeholder platforms were established organized around lead firms as major buyers of beans, linked to bean producers, and supported by other service providers such as finance, credit, information, research and extension, and policy support. PABRA and NARS provided initial facilitation for the establishment of the platforms. An assessment was conducted based on 227 women and 53 youth who actively participated in the bean business platforms across Rwanda, Cameroon, Madagascar, Tanzania, and Burundi between 2017 and 2023. Among the women and youth who participated, an average of 81% indicated that they were satisfied with the business platform indicator. The satisfaction levels were measured by the sampled individuals using a scale of one to five, with five being the highest, and were then converted to a percentage. In 2024, demonstration of the role of multistakeholder platforms in accelerating new variety dissemination and demonstrated the use of improved and certified seeds in Malawi.

column16: Gliricidia intercropping into maize cropping combines trees and crops to increase diversity, productivity, profitability, and environmental management. This is relevant for resource constrained smallholder farmers
column17: The sustainable intensification initiatives of Southern Africa use Gliricidia sepium, a leguminous tree species which is well adapted to the environment for their sustainable intensification practices. The importance of this system is to grow the trees in hedge rows or as dispersed trees so that leaves can be utilized in a “chop and drop” fashion with limited labour needed for transporting the biomass from one plot to the other. The spatial arrangement also aims at keeping the competition as low as possible while reaping the benefits of the agro-forestry species. Maize-Gliricidia hedge-row and Maize-Gliricidia disbursed shading are the two main systems. In the first one, maize-legume rotations are planted at normal plant population, in addition, hedgerows of Gliricidia trees are planted in rows spaced 5 m apart with an in-row spacing of 1 m. In the second, the disbursed shading system aims at developing larger Gliricidia trees that provide shade, less competition and in addition some green leaves that can be applied to the soil after pruning every year. One tree is usually planted every 10 m in rows 5 m apart.

column16: Creating cost-effective home-mixed livestock fattening rations using hay, grain or pod shells of Mucuna pruriens and other legume hays to substitute expensive commercial supplements
column17: This innovation involves incorporation of coarsely-ground Mucuna pruriens grain as a unique, cost-effective ingredient and energy-protein dense substitute in maintenance or fattening rations of ruminant livestock, where standard commercial supplements would usually contain a combination of cereal grains (e.g. maize) and legume oil cakes (e.g Soyabean, cotton seed etc), which are themselves generally expensive.  These expensive ingredients make the commercial concentrates out of reach for most farmers.  In contrast, Mucuna is cheaper and provides both energy and protein in one grain.  Once ground, the Mucuna meal will be constituted together with home-made tropical forage legumes (e.g. Lablab purpureus) hay to make a complete diet which smallholder farmers can brand and trade among themselves. Incorporation of legume hay reduces the amount of poor quality grass hay and cereal crop residues that will be included as basal forage in the complete diet and will simultaneously improve the digestibility of the poor quality residues, leading to improved animal growth.

column16: Conservation agriculture system integrating annual maize-legume rotations developed by CIMMYT for smallholder farmers in Eastern Africa
column17: This conservation agriculture system combines annual rotation of maize with leguminous crops like cowpea, groundnuts, soybeans, and common beans to address persistent challenges of pest buildup, disease pressure, and declining soil fertility faced by smallholder farmers. CIMMYT developed this integrated approach as an alternative to continuous maize monoculture, particularly targeting areas with high pest pressure and nutrient-poor soils. The system enhances soil fertility through nitrogen fixation by legumes while breaking pest and disease cycles that typically accumulate in monoculture systems. This innovation builds on traditional rotation practices but integrates them systematically within conservation agriculture principles, offering farmers a sustainable method to maintain productivity while improving soil health and crop nutrition across multiple growing seasons.

column16: Mbili Mbili is an innovative cropping system to ensure crop diversification and resilience in smallholder farming systems
column17: Mbili Mbili intercropping system has been promoted as a crop diversification and intensification approach. Mbili-Mbili exploits plant spatial configurations to increase light penetration to the legumes, otherwise often shaded by cereals. The main aim is to increase legume productivity, while maintaining the same productivity of the cereal and taking advantage and complementarity of the different growth habits and durations of the combined crops. Mbili Mbili enables a farmer to grow both legumes and cereals on the same land and thus harvest at different times. In event of a loss, one crop serves as an insurance. This makes the system climate smart. Mbili Mbili system has been reported to have a higher returns (upto 37% more) compared to the standard farmer intercropping practices. The technology has been tested, and widely promoted in maize growing areas in Kenya and other countries in east and southern Africa.

column16: Guidance for conducting randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of complex interventions published to improve RCT design and the interpretation of results
column17: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are increasingly used as one of the tools to build the evidence base on the effectiveness of complex interventions to address food systems. Researchers conducting RCTs of complex interventions face design and analytic challenges that are not fully addressed in existing guidelines. This leads to questions and confusion about how to conduct these trials and interpret their findings. Guidelines, co-authored by a Sustainable Healthy Diets researcher, were published in 2022 to address key topics of confusion including the number of outcomes that can be assessed, the definition and meaning of primary and secondary outcomes and whether to control for multiplicity. The guidance ensures that trials are conducted to the highest scientific standards while maximizing the evidence that can be extracted. In 2025, the teamed continued efforts to disseminate this innovation and build capacity for use by researchers, funders, policymakers and others. A Learning Lab was provided at the 2025 Agriculture, Nutrition, and Healthy Academy conference and according to Altmetric, the 2022 publication has been cited 34 times, 73% of which have been received in the past two years, suggesting that it is currently receiving a lot of interest. Compared to other publications in the same field, it has received approximately 9.95 times more citations than average.

column16: Mechanization starter pack for smallholder farmers in Southern Africa
column17: Smallholder agricultural mechanization is the call of the day for Africa to improve land and labour productivity, reduce production cost and drudgery, and make agriculture attractive to youth. Successful mechanization in most of African countries relies on selection, validation, piloting, and scaling of appropriate inexpensive machinery solutions adapted to farm size and financial ability of smallholder farmers. Over the past decade, CIMMYT has tested, validated, and piloted small scale machinery and business models suitable for southern African farmers. Based on the experiences and successful piloting, a ‘mechanization starter pack’ has been developed and is recommended for scaling through a business model called the ‘Service Provider Model’. The ‘mechanization starter pack’ includes a two-wheel tractor (2WT), a 2WT operated ripper, a 2WT operated trailer, an engine operated multi-crop thresher, peanut sheller, peanut roaster, peanut butter machine and chopper grinder depending on the farming context of the country. As per the model, a service provider (SP) owns and maintains the machines and operate them on a fee-for-service basis throughout the year benefiting many farmers. The service fee is usually much cheaper for end users (farmers) compared to the cost of traditional practices and creates a win-win situation that makes the business viable for both SP and farmers. The machines chosen for the starter pack allows the SP to generate income throughout the year by providing ploughing, ripping, and threshing/shelling (depending on time of the year), and transportation (year-round) services. Currently there are more than 300 SPs are operating their businesses in Zimbabwe, Malawi and Zambia benefiting thousands of farmers.

column16: Conservation agriculture practices refined by CIMMYT for maize-legume farming systems in Eastern and Southern Africa
column17: Conservation Agriculture (CA) is based on three key principles: minimum soil disturbance, provision of permanent soil cover and the use of rotations or associations amongst other good agriculture practices. These CA principles are applicable to a wide range of crop production systems from low-yielding, rainfed conditions to high-yielding, irrigated conditions. However, the techniques used may vary from place to place depending on farm power, system management conditions and farmer circumstances. Recent work conducted in Zambia showed that CA-based systems are capable of increasing economic and nutritional returns. The social and economic benefits gained from combining production and protecting the environment under CA are greater than those from production alone. CA in maize-legume systems addresses major production challenges in farming areas of Eastern and Southern Africa where both cereals and legumes are commonly grown.

column16: Regional and national policy dialogues to scale support to the enabling environment for sustainable crop diversification and trade in East and Southern Africa (ESA)
column17: The policy support program provides governments in East and Southern Africa (ESA) with context-specific recommendations to help improve their enabling environment for climate-resilient agricultural transformation. Specific interests are in sustainable crop intensification and diversification and agribusiness and value chain development, with attention to gender and youth empowerment. The program comprises two pillars: 1) national policy dialogues, which bring together governments, agribusinesses, donors, researchers, and civil society organizations to explore feasible policy and investment interventions, and 2) the ESA Policy Hub, which scales the key takeaways from dialogues to the regional level to tap opportunities arising from trade and regional integration of national economies. Moreover, the program consists of two main innovation bundles: One, the main bundle, is “long-term technical assistance to governments,” garnering results from crosscutting scientific research and national policy dialogues and taking into account climate shocks and stresses to inform policy-making. Two, a “demand-driven technical facility” is available to national actors (government agencies, farmers, and small- and medium-scale enterprises) and connects strategically selected enterprises with a high-impact potential to agribusiness accelerator programs. The program fosters strategic alliances between various innovation partners and works closely with governments to ensure mainstreaming of recommendations into policymaking and implementation.

column16: Development and Scaling of Bean-Based Composite Flour Formulations for Enhanced Community Nutrition and Small-Scale Industries: Nutrition, Gender and Climate-smart Technologies to Enhance Income Generation and Social Impact
column17: This innovation converts beans and other nutrient-dense foods into composite flours, addressing major challenges in Africa's food systems. Protein deficiencies affect 26% of African's population, while micronutrient deficiencies like iron and zinc are widespread, with sub-Saharan Africa having the highest rates of anaemia (46%-71%) and vitamin A deficiency (48%) in children under-five. These deficiencies contribute to stunted growth, weakened immunity, and poverty. Traditional bean processing is also labour-intensive and inefficient, limiting the appeal of beans. This innovation improves nutrient absorption by reducing anti-nutritional factors like phytic acid and lectins through techniques such as soaking, malting, roasting and pressure cooking. Instant and regular bean composite flour products also offer extended shelf life, reducing food waste and improving food security. The technology supports small and medium enterprises, fosters economic growth, and strengthens supply chains while improving nutrition across families and communities.

column17: The science-driven accelerator program for climate-smart agribusinesses focuses on scaling climate-smart agricultural innovations and strengthening the commercial capacity of private sector entities in the agricultural ecosystem. Operating in Zambia, it aims to expand the reach of climate-smart innovations and enhance the business capabilities of participating agribusinesses.;  ; The program concludes with a demo day, connecting agribusinesses to public, concessional, and private investors, as well as potential market partners, facilitating access to finance and market linkages. After two accelerator cohorts and a large-scale bootcamp, the importance of expanding the scientific network across underrepresented countries like Zambia, Zimbabwe, Uganda, and Malawi became clear. Additionally, fostering ongoing networking among founders with complementary value propositions has become a priority, enabling sustained collaboration and shared growth across programs.

column16: Strip cropping is an improved intercropping strategy for smallholder farmers that capitalize better plant arrangement. Two types of strip cropping are common: Double-row strip cropping and four row strip cropping.
column17: Intercropping is a system based on producing two or more crops within the same space. However, such a system is characterized by competition between crops. To curb competition, strip cropping, an innovative way of growing crops using spatial arrangements that reduce competition can be used. Two forms of this system (two-row and four-row) are based on the reduction in the spacing of maize rows to open space for legumes to grow. Under two-row strip cropping, maize is planted into rip-lines opened in double rows (50cm apart) and a gap of 130cm is left in between the maize double rows where legumes will be planted. For four-row strip cropping four rows of maize alternate with four rows of a legume but the inter-row spacing of maize is reduced from the usual 90 cm to 45 cm. This narrowing and reduction in size increases the growing space for four rows of legumes.

column16: Traditional maize/legume intercropping to reduce the risk of total crop failure and improves nutritional yields.
column17: Maize monocropping usually leads to soil nutrient mining, the prevalence of pests and diseases, and undiversified household nutrition. Diversification through either intercropping or crop rotation is a method that can be used to reverse these negatives. However, crop rotations are usually not feasible for farmers with small landholding sizes. For such farmers, intercropping is a viable solution. Intercropping is the practice of growing two or more crops in the same area, at the same time. In general, intercropping is better suited to farmers with small landholdings whereas crop rotation is more suitable for farmers with larger landholdings. However, other factors such as household needs and farm economics determine the choice of these two practices. The land equivalent ratio (LER) is often used to measure the benefits of intercropping compared to planting a single crop (sole cropping).

column16: Conjunctive use of groundwater and surface water with solar irrigation pumping to enhance irrigation water availability and productivity, food and water security for smallholder farmers in dry areas
column17: The innovation uses the site suitability mapping for implementing the Aquifer Storage and Recovery (ASR) method called Bhungroo Irrigation Technology (BIT) and solar irrigation pumping to smallholder irrigation schemes that use groundwater and surface water in the Inkomanti-Usuthu Catchment Management Area in South Africa. The ASR /BIT uses one borehole to recharge the aquifer during the wet season and abstract water from the same borehole during the dry season. This resulted in increased irrigation water availability and reduced energy use from grid electricity and fuel pumps, thereby increasing farm profit. Energy use for irrigation contributed 50-70% of the total farming expenses. Successful implementation of the BIT and solar irrigation pumping at a site requires the delineation of suitable areas based on scientific, natural parameters and expert judgment.

column16: User interface of e-Agrology directed to farmers as a one stop shop where farmers can consult localized decision support for the management of their fields
column17: AGROTUTOR, a decision-making framework for smallholder farmers in Mexico, Peru and Colombia, prioritizes practicality and actionable information. Unlike offering unique recommendations per plot, it provides scenarios, benchmarks, and tools empowering farmers to make informed, tailored choices. Operating on a circular knowledge approach, it collects farmer data and feedback, enhancing advisory services. ; AGROTUTOR's flexible architecture integrates information from diverse sources, allowing farmers to compare results from different models and data sources. Its strength lies in geo-localized data, using AI models for crop-specific optimization, weather updates, pest identification, and agronomic recommendations. Historical training data spanning a decade helps to identify limiting factors, provide insightful comparisons among soil and climate clusters. The data wallet feature and digital identity ensure farmers' data rights and introduce a compensation model, treating their data as an asset. column16: A Bundled Digital Agro-Advisory, Weather Insurance, and Credit Package to Support Risk-Informed Decision-Making by Smallholder Farmers
column17: The innovation is a bundled digital agro-advisory and financial services package that integrates localized agronomic advice with weather-index insurance and access to credit to support risk-informed decision-making by smallholder farmers. The package combines tailored crop management recommendations with complementary financial instruments that reduce production risk and enable timely input investment. By linking advisory services with insurance coverage and credit access, the innovation addresses key constraints faced by smallholders—information gaps, climate risk, and limited liquidity—within a single, coordinated solution. Designed for deployment through digital channels and partner delivery systems, the package enables farmers to make better production decisions under uncertainty while providing service providers and financial partners with a structured mechanism to align advisory, risk management, and finance. When applied at scale, the innovation supports improved productivity, resilience, and inclusion in smallholder farming systems

column16: The Herd Dynamics Model (HDM) component of the Linked Economic and Animal Systems (LEAS) model, a tool for or policy analysis on livestock management in Ethiopia
column17: Animal systems often receive less attention or are treated separately from crops in national agricultural strategies and investment plans. To address this, the Foresight Initiative developed a standardized Herd Dynamics Model (HDM) to analyze trends and investments in animal systems. Supported by a global livestock database with reconciled historical data and demographic parameters, the HDM enables integrated analysis of crop and animal system priorities when embedded in agrifood system models. Piloted in an Ethiopia case study, and in early second-phase testing in Rwanda, Tanzania and Nigeria, this system reduces the cost of modeling animal systems in national planning.; ; Building on this foundation, the Linked Economic and Animal Systems (LEAS) model now includes sheep and goats alongside cattle. Work on crop-livestock interactions in semi-subsistence economies was presented at ICAE 2024. The model has expanded to Rwanda to analyze livestock interventions, with IFPRI collaborating with ILRI to advance and align livestock modeling efforts.

column16: GeoAgro-MiSR: A comprehensive digital solution that enables Egyptian small holder farmers achieve climate smartness, sustainable intensification and economic optimization under climate change and economic volatility
column17: The GeoAgro-MiSR system represents a powerful digital transformation that serves the national extension system, farmers, youth, and women, providing them with site-specific agronomic recommendations generated from farm analytics. EiA envisions a bottom-up and top-down synergy approach to agricultural transformation by leveraging digital tools and engaging stakeholders at different scales. At the grassroots level, the GeoAgro-MiSR smartphone application offers tailor-made agronomic advisories and services to smallholder farmers. It also facilitates citizen science by allowing users to contribute data to a centralized database. The GeoAgro-MiSR system comprises a centralized server hosted at ICARDA and two user interfaces: the GeoAgro-MiSR app and the GeoAgro-MiSR administrative dashboard. Communication between users and experts is via real-time interaction, including the "ask an expert" module and P2P chatting. The system also provides weather forecasts, remote sensing analytics for biophysical variability, and crop-specific agronomic practices. ;

column16: WikiPapa Platform: a decision support tool for monitoring the conservation status of potato landraces in space and time in diversity hotspots
column17: WikiPapa is an online, real-time, and integrated data & decision-support platform created in 2021 to support the in situ and on-farm conservation of Andean potato landraces. It functions as a conservation-centered digital Information & Decision Support System that systematically documents data underlying the occurrence of potato intraspecific diversity or landraces, combining citizen science knowledge and basic conservation statistics.; The platform connects a diverse network of conservation practitioners, including researchers, decision-makers, custodian farmer associations, and citizen scientists. Through mobile tools—most notably the VarScout app—citizen scientists and farmers report field-level observations on the presence, distribution, and status of specific potato landraces. These observations are temporally and spatially tagged and centrally recorded, enabling the tracking of conservation dynamics and the detection of potential genetic erosion over time.; The central objective of WikiPapa is to strengthen conservation intelligence for Andean potato biodiversity by integrating real-time observational data with culturally grounded knowledge systems and citizen participation. Currently, the platform documents over 960 potato landraces from Peru, Chile, Bolivia, and Colombia. It has accumulated approximately 5,744 field observations contributed by 946 farmers, representing 3,084 unique vernacular registers.; By bridging modern digital technologies with traditional agricultural knowledge, WikiPapa plays a crucial role in supporting evidence-based decision-making, empowering farming communities and on-farm conservation practitioners, and ensuring the long-term conservation in one of the world’s most important centers of crop diversity. The innovation model can be expanded to other crops in their centers of origin. ;

column16: Satellite-based regional scale climate data extractor for Central and West Asia and North Africa (CWANA) web-based innovation to ease the weather data acquisition process for NARES, scientists and policymakers
column17: This web-app has been developed to ease the weather data acquisition process. This web-app allows the user to extract long-term monthly scale temperature and precipitation data for selected countries in the CWANA region. Users are required to indicate the country of interest and the desired time period. Consequently, the web-app presents annual weather information and time-series precipitation and temperature data as well as meteorological drought indices such as Standard Precipitation Index (SPI) and Standard Temperature Index (STI). Additionally, the platform allows users to generate spatial maps for weather parameters and to export data in the form of maps, tables and figures. This web-app automatically retrieves up-to-date weather data from the ERA5-Land archive. This tool has strong interest in the region. Local private organizations and research institutes are still very interested in using it. Recently, we started new discussions with Uzsanoatqurilishbank JSCB to further improve the tool by adding more indicators. This shows that interest in the tool is growing and remains strong.

column16: Incorporation of organic growth additives to enhance in vitro propagation of selected shrub/tree species for large scale restoration and for supporting local communities dependent on agrosilvopastoral systems in building resilience.
column17: Climate change and anthropogenic activities have negatively impacted agro-silvo-pastoral ecosystems across the planet. The global agenda to achieve ecosystem restoration targets has resulted in an increased demand for plant materials that current production systems are unable to satisfy. Under open field cultivation, several species show a low rate of seed germination or need special climatic conditions to germinate or take a long time to establish. Consequently, there is an urgency to preserve and propagate selected genotypes by improving efficient mass propagation techniques. It is necessary to resort to innovation tools, such as in vitro tissue culture technology. Plant tissue culture is used for producing high-quality, disease-free, and true-to-type plants at a fast rate. In vitro propagation can help meet the increasing demand for planting materials aimed at large scale restoration and afforestation programs. Incorporating organic growth additives can stimulate tissue growth and increase the number of shoots, leaves, and roots. ;

column16: Scaling Readiness: an evidence-based approach to co-design, implement and monitor scaling strategies for innovation teams and innovation portfolio managers.
column17: Scaling Readiness is an innovation management framework that helps agricultural research and development teams strategically plan how to scale their innovations for maximum impact. Developed by CGIAR researchers, this approach combines innovation systems thinking with rigorous evidence synthesis methods originally created by NASA and the European Commission. The framework enables research managers to assess which innovations, investments, and partnerships should be prioritized to achieve impact at scale. It provides practical tools and metrics to evaluate the readiness of innovations for scaling and guides teams in designing targeted strategies for different contexts. The framework has been adopted across CGIAR centers and beyond, helping bridge the gap between agricultural research outputs and real-world impact for farmers and food systems globally.

column16: Online Economics Modeling Course for Policy Analysts
column17: This effort seeks to leverage significant advances in distance learning technologies and techniques to deliver a step change in the capabilities of countries to utilize simulation models in pursuit of their development goals, notably food security in a context of climate change. It has been designed with a focus on scaling economic simulation modeling capacities for meeting the climate challenge in low- and middle-income countries, targeting four sets of key institutions: central decision-making units within governments; research institutes with formal linkages to policymaking; central banks; and large research networks. Central to this innovation is an online economic modeling program. Alongside in-person trainings, communities of practices, and a website portal, the program targets different audiences: people who i) want to know what insights can be gained and generated using economic modeling tools b) run the models for decision making, and iii)  design scenarios or models of their own.

column16: Epidemiology and Control of Peste des Petits Ruminants Study Design and Toolbox: A suite of tools for stakeholders toward understanding epidemiology and socio-economic impact of peste des petits ruminants (PPR)
column17: To fully understand the epidemiology and socio-economic impact of Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR) to overcome the challenges faced by stakeholders in the control of the disease, an interdisciplinary approach that brings together social and biosciences should be followed. A collaborative effort was made to harmonize data collection across countries and partners. As a result, a study design and toolkit consisting of different methods and types of data collection tools was developed. Each tool addresses a specific set of data needs and when combined they will provide in-depth understanding of the PPR situation of the country under research, which will help to identify entry points for evidence-based control of PPR.

column16: Genomic selection-based breeding programs for dairy cattle, based on performance records provided by farmers, linked to natural sire and artificial insemination-based delivery systems
column17: Milk production in developing countries is dominated by smallholder dairy farmers, each keeping 1-3 dairy cows. Majority of these farmers are not extracting optimum benefits, because herd and cow production and productivity levels are low. Small holder dairy farming is constrained by lack of sustainable breeding program that delivers adaptable high yielding dairy animals that suits the different production system, inadequate access to various services and inputs, and limited access to information or farmer education. The problem was addressed through innovative application of ICT and genomic technology.  The data generated is used to define more robust breeding objectives, develop realistic selection indices, and the information is ultimately used to select top ranking bulls and cows for breeding under local production conditions. The African Dairy Genetic Gains project has established a pipeline that harness performance data captured that incorporates genomic data for genomic prediction for milk yield and efficiency.

column16: The Women's Empowerment in Livestock Index (WELI) for measuring women's empowerment in systems where livestock is important for livelihood
column17: The WELI facilitates assessments of the impact of livestock interventions on the empowerment of women involved in the sector. By getting better at understanding what interventions work best at providing empowering opportunities, we can refine these interventions and in the long term, provide better empowering opportunities for women involved in livestock. Providing women farmers with opportunities for empowerment through livestock is important to both enhance household livelihoods and nutrition while also promoting progress on gender equity. In 2015, the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), in collaboration with Emory University developed the WELI tool based on the Women’s Empowerment in Agriculture Index (WEAI) developed earlier by IFPRI. The WELI measures women’s empowerment in livestock and crop agriculture and focuses specifically on key areas of livestock production, such as animal health, breeding and feeding; and on use of livestock products, such as animal-source-food processing and marketing.

column16: Dashboard of ex post impact assessment studies relevant for informing foresight modelers conducting parameterization of foresight modeling tools.
column17: The Initiative has been developing a pioneering innovation: a cutting-edge Ex Post Impact Assessment Dashboard. This tool showcases its innovation by providing a dynamic platform for foresight modelers, researchers, and policymakers. It enables the seamless integration of ex-post impact assessment studies into foresight modeling, setting a new standard in informed decision-making. This innovation is undergoing a rigorous process of ideation, proof of concept, pilot testing, and controlled and uncontrolled testing before roll out.. This transformative dashboard leverages rich metadata tagging to ensure FAIRness, enhancing its utility and accessibility. Its potential extends beyond modeling to serve as a valuable resource for analyzing the adoption and impact of past innovations, solidifying its position as a game-changing innovation in the field

column16: High level engagement for co-creation of collaborative breeding networks: building more equitable partnerships that more effectively address regional priorities, and collectively increase genetic gain and farmer variety adoption
column17: Since 2022, ABI-Transform has organized an annual leadership consultations between Genetic Innovation and NARES in Sub-Saharan Africa to assess partnership health and identify priority areas to further improve collaboration. Key decisions and outputs from these meetings have been captured in Aide Memoires which have been endorsed by leaders from CGIAR, NARES and SROs. Resolutions and actions are tracked and pursued by the Core Technical Team that meets quarterly and is composed of representatives from the CGIAR, NARES and SROs. These meetings have highlighted 8 key areas: 1. need for co-creation and increased alignment with national and regional priorities; 2. Increased role for partners in regional breeding networks; 3. Better attribution; 4. Increased funding transparency; 5. Joint ownership and decision making; 6. Need for an annual partnership health check through a representative survey; 7. Need to incorporate Universities and SMEs in regional breeding networks; 8. Need to institutionalize human capacity development.

column17: Empowering Smallholder Producers for Perennials in West Africa for Climate Resilience. This innovation integrates three tools—Aclimatar, Cacao Diversity, and Croppie—to address challenges faced by smallholder farmers in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire.; ; Aclimatar and Cacao Diversity provide site-specific climate risk assessments and tailored adaptation strategies. Through an intuitive map interface, users access critical climate data, crop-specific impacts, and prioritized measures to promote resilience. The Cacao Diversity Tool supports cacao farm sustainability by predicting climate change impacts, recommending propagation materials, and assessing cadmium levels in soils and cacao beans.; ; Croppie is an AI-assisted yield estimation tool that simplifies certification by replacing costly, time-consuming manual methods. It reduces costs by 50% and prevents uncertified produce leakage during onboarding without harvest records, enhancing efficiency and inclusion of smallholders.; ; Together, these tools equip farmers with actionable insights, strengthen local projects, and foster sustainable practices, ensuring resilience and climate adaptation in smallholder communities.

column16: Fertilizer recommendation tool for six priority crops plugged in the Smart Nkunganire System (SNS) in Rwanda to deliver site-specific fertilizer recommendations to extension agents and smallholder farmers
column17: The Smart Nkunganire System (SNS) was created in response to the Rwandan Ministry of Agriculture's (MINAGRI) request for enhanced digital extension services and precise, site-specific fertilizer recommendations for essential crops. The project aims to develop a digital advisory tool integrated within the existing SNS platform, managed by BKTechouse. This tool is designed to provide customized fertilizer recommendations for six priority crops in Rwanda: cassava, maize, wheat, potato, rice, and beans, making these recommendations accessible to both extension agents and farmers through the SNS platform.; ; This initiative is further supported by making these tools and methodologies available to the Rwanda Agriculture and Animal Resources Development Board (RAB), aiming to enhance the innovation's development. This strategic approach ensures that the digital advisory tool effectively meets the specific needs of Rwanda's agriculture sector, providing tailored support to improve productivity and sustainability.

column16: Integrating Water Storage Diagnostic to diversify and expand water storage options to enhance Water Energy Food Environment Benefits for water planners and basin managers.
column17: The water storage diagnostic is an approach to integrating assessments of different storage types, such as aquifers, soil moisture, and dams. The diagnostic framework supports planning and management decisions across these water storage types by identifying and comparing their relative opportunities and risks. Methods for evaluating individual storage options include recession flow analysis and hydrogeological modelling (for aquifers); analysis of earth observation data (for dams); and analysis of in-situ and remotely sensed or modelled data (for soil moisture). Planning and management across (rather than within) storage types enable the identification of complementary roles for alternative storage options and the design of a diversified path to storage development, which brings a suite of benefits including greater WEFE benefits to water-using communities. The results of diagnostics have now been used by River Basin Organizations and basin managers

column16: Water Productivity Atlas that enables planners and managers to identify solutions to improve water productivity
column17: Water productivity constitutes one of the key ways to expand Water Energy Food Ecosystems (WEFE) benefits in water scarce contexts, yet water productivity is variable and in cases low. This innovation is focused on development of a Decision Support System (DSS) that enables planners and managers to identify solutions (e.g., resources allocations or crop mixes) that improve productivity. The DSS is a computer-based platform reveals the productivity associated with alternative investment choices, which can support investment decisions that optimize water productivity and WEFE benefits in different geographies. Key users of the DSS platform are water planners and managers, as well as those in related sectors (i.e. Energy, Food and Ecosystems).

column16: Climate-credit risk scoring system for farming systems to guide adaptation finance
column17: A novel data-driven, climate-credit risk scoring tool has been developed for dairy farmers, integrating a climate module into the traditional credit assessment. This tool empowers lenders to assess climate- related risks accurately, making more informed, precise, and fair lending decisions. Climate-credit risk scoring allows farmers to secure loans and establish credit histories. It also helps in identifying climate risk drivers, and adaptation pathways for risk-prone farming systems, promoting financial inclusion for vulnerable communities. The tool combines data and science and has been developed based on the inputs of diverse livestock, crop and climate scientists, enabling a holistic and comprehensive tool development.

column16: Cactus pear a drought-tolerant crop, provides food and livestock feed and thereby improves the livelihood of poor farmers in the dry areas
column17: In collaboration with the FAO-ICARDA cactus network and NARS partners to promote and scale up cactus pear as a crop well-adapted to agricultural farming in the dry areas, that can be utilized by millions of poor farmers for important nutritional and income-creating purposes. Being a versatile crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM) with an extraordinary water use efficiency makes it a viable resilient important agricultural resource that enable farmers getting valuable products, including fruits for human consumption and fodder for livestock while helping to reduce the need for watering livestock due to its high-water content. This collaboration led to a substantial increase in demand for planting materials, resulting in providing improved planting materials, that can serve different agro-ecological zones. ICARDA alongside its NARS partners, has also carried out extensive awareness campaigns and capacity development activities to train farmers on promoting cactus pear as a multi-functional crop.

column16: Participatory rangeland management: an inclusive approach for improving governance, tenure security and productivity of rangelands
column17: Participatory Rangeland Management (PRM) is a defined step-by-step process for improving local level rangeland management by local pastoralist communities. It follows three stages of investigation (including participatory mapping), negotiation and implementation. It supports establishment and/or strengthening of rangelands management institutions, and supports the production of a rangeland management plan and an agreement with local government to improve access of communities to natural resources and land. M&E and capacity building are also important steps.

column16: An improved framework for cost benefit analysis of land use change investment decisions in pastoral areas for land use planners and investment decision makers
column17: A framework(s) for improving large-scale land use change decision making processes in pastoral areas, particularly those related to commercial sector agricultural investments. Currently the frameworks used for such decision making do not take into account the full costs and benefits of the land use change from rangeland to e.g., crop farming including the full value of rangelands and their contribution to such as ecosystem services. This framework will endeavor to do this ensure a broader range of costs and benefits are included. The framework will be developed through a consultative process, tested with beneficiaries, decision makers, researchers and investors, to support the development of short- and long-term scenarios, the prioritization of interventions, and the design of supporting strategies, and policies. It is anticipated that the framework will be used by governments and other decision-makers concerned with land use planning and land investment decisions.

column16: A global platform for multiple users including the UN and other development agencies for sourcing, consolidating, and sharing information on rangelands status, change, influencing forces, and restoration opportunities.
column17: The global rangelands data platform is being established in response to a gap in rangelands data identified by the UN Environment Assembly through Resolution L17 Innovations in Sustainable Rangelands and Pastoralism 2019 and the complimentary report: A Case of Benign Neglect. Knowledge Gaps About Sustainability in Pastoralism and Rangelands. With funding from the CGIAR Big Data Platform and through a consultative process the outline of the platform was conceptualised. A global rangelands atlas was launched as a first step. It is anticipated that the global rangelands data platform will be launched in 2026. It will bring together big data on rangelands, source data including exploring crowd-sourcing and be an interactive platform for producing reports and trends for multiple users including UN Agencies monitoring rangeland and development agencies and actors developing interventions for rangelands, researchers and academics, and ultimately pastoralists themselves.

column16: Participatory land use planning across administrative borders in pastoral areas for protecting shared grazing lands and other resources.
column17: Participatory land use planning (PLUP) for pastoral areas overcomes many of the challenges of conventional land use planning including creating hard boundaries around villages or other administrative units, breaking up and limiting or preventing access to shared grazing lands and water points. PLUP for pastoral areas aims to keep rangelands and particularly grazing lands intact working across administrative boundaries through joint PLUP agreements strengthening reciprocal relations, collective tenure and good governance and resolving and preventing conflicts between land users. Pastoral communities traditionally marginalized from village PLUP process benefit particularly from the approach due to it being more inclusive of all land users in the planning and decision-making processes. The PLUP process includes the collection of data for assessing land potential most relevant for pastoral systems.

column16: The new user-friendly environmental impact assessment tool, CLEANED, with additional functionalities
column17: CLEANED is a rapid environmental impact assessment tool that allows users to explore impacts of developing livestock value chains using forecasting methods. It models the foreseen impact of changes in the livestock production systems and value chains in terms of: land use, productivity, economics, water impacts, greenhouse gas emissions, and soil health. It helps decision-makers understand the environmental impacts of intensification and develop sustainable livestock intensification plans that mitigate negative impacts and enhance positive ones. The tool generates fast results and has potential in policymaking, proposal development and extension service to farmers.; ; CLEANED-eXtRA is a new version of an already freely accessible and widely implemented excel-version of the CLEANED tool. It is programmed in R and comes with a user-friendly graphical user interface.  The expansion of functionality includes: regional aggregation of results, comparison of different scenarios, refinement of the water module.

column16: Integrated-approach with Public Private Partnerships and community-based engagement through stakeholder platforms for vaccine delivery, monitoring and evaluation, and improved biosecurity for control of diseases in smallholder livestock systems
column17: In Mali, vaccination campaigns against major endemic livestock diseases are conducted every year by the Direction Nationale des Services Vétérinaires (DNSV). Some of these diseases include contagious bovine pleuropneumoniae (CBPP), peste des petits ruminants (PPR) and bovine and ovine pasteurellosis. However, adequate vaccination coverage that will lead to sufficient herd immunity is often hard to achieve. Some of the challenges to vaccination are logistical, socio-economical, institutional and organisational. To address the various vaccination challenges, a multi-stakeholder approach through Innovation Platforms (IPs) was applied to create a sphere of learning, information sharing and interaction among vaccine supply chain stakeholders. The IP approach focused on three pillars: Communication and collaboration, Knowledge sharing through collective action and Capacity building. This IP approach has been successful in increasing uptake of vaccines by farmers and raising the health of livestock, which makes the livestock more productive."

column16: Multidsciplinary working group (MWG) as a dedicated approach for building farmers' resilience through improved local climate information production, dissemination and update in Senegal
column17: The multidisciplinary working group (MWG) serves as a pivotal and inclusive platform dedicated to advancing the production of climate services, their interpretation into actionable decisions, and widespread dissemination. This is an innovative approach to establsihing multi-stakeholder platforms to enhance the uptake of weather and climate information services. The national MWG comprises key departments and institutions, fostering collaboration and comprehensive representation. At the local level, 32 MWGs, led by district Prefects, address region-specific challenges through decentralized structures to ensure that MWGs are well-connected with local realities and can effectively address region-specific challenges. Regular collaboration is maintained through tri-monthly meetings where members from both national and local MWGs convene. These meetings cover a spectrum of pertinent topics, including meteorology, hydrology, agriculture, livestock, environment, and market dynamics. The collective insights garnered from these discussions are distilled into recommendations, consolidated in a bulletin. To ensure widespread awareness, these recommendations are disseminated through community radios.

column16: Financial tool targeted to help pastoralists cope with drought related risks in the drylands of Africa
column17: Index-based drought risk financing and insurance (IBDRFI) instruments have been designed to protect pastoralists in the face of drought. In all Index-based livestock insurance (IBLI) products,Normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) time series are elaborated to obtain an area-aggregated index of relative seasonal forage availability. When the index falls below a pre-defined threshold, payouts are triggered and increase proportionally to the severity of estimated forage scarcity. This assumes that, when forage is scarce, grazing resources are depleted quickly, leading to deteriorating livestock conditions and increased livestock mortality. Pastoralists could use the payouts to make production decisions that reduce their herd losses during the drought including, purchasing animal fodder, water or veterinary services. IBDRFI initiatives have been so far implemented in Africa with different modalities, including retail microinsurance products, macrolevel insurance schemes for social livelihood protection, or scalability mechanisms of social safety net programs.

column16: A digital decision support tool to help livestock farmers to produce improved animal diet on farm by balancing nutrients, processing roughages and mixing feed ingredients in proper proportion in Nepal.
column17: The tool is a mobile based application that can be used by extension agents and farmers to balance their animals’ diet by matching nutrients required by the animal (for body mainetance, production and reproduction) and their availability in the feed offered. The application selects the cheapest locally available feeds to bridge the nutritional gap.  The suggestions are given in the form of an advice memo, which includes guidelines for efficient use of different feeds. Additional information such as the nutrient gap, cost of purchased feeds and additional income before and after balancing the diet are also given.

column16: Farmer-to-Farmer Scaling Networks for scaling climate adaptation technologies
column17: The Farmer-to-Farmer Scaling Networks is a farmer-led innovation connecting farmers to each other for information exchange and capacity building, and ultimately the scaling of climate adaptation technologies and innovations that have been developed by the farmers themselves. The pioneers of adaptation are farmers who have developed their adaptation practices with their own endogenous innovations beyond piloting stage. We support them in developing a farm-level adapted scaling approach complementary to existing institutions, involving pioneers themselves as the main actors in the scaling process. Together with the pioneers we study their practices, and then progressively include more farmers, farmer groups, cooperatives in a knowledge exchange through participatory field days where pioneers share and discuss the findings of this data collection on their practices. Gradually, we develop a Farmer2Farmer knowledge network that connects pioneers and their learning groups with research, extension, development organisations, and private sector actors.

column16: The Climate Security Observatory (CSO) online dashboard for livestock production systems
column17: The Climate Security Observatory (CSO) is an online dashboard targeting policy and decision makers, development and humanitarian practitioners and advisors to help them with targeting, programming and prioritization of investments particularly in areas under climate stress. The CSO uses a mixed method approach to give answers to four lead questions: Where are the most vulnerable areas to climate-related insecurities and risks? Who are the groups vulnerable to climate and security risks that should be targeted? How does climate exacerbate the causes of conflict? What needs to be done to break the vicious cycle between climate and conflict? The CSO brings together robust, localized and contextualized and policy-relevant evidence on the climate-security nexus. It includes a dashboard on climate security programming for climate finance, the climate security sensitivity tool, climate security mapping and an interactive dashboard for climate security dialogues.

column16: Feed pellet production using a small-scale pelletizer and available agricultural products and agroindustrial by-products for agro-pastoralists, farmers and farmer organizations.
column17: Compressing local agro-industrial by products into nutrient dense livestock feed pellets is a worthwhile innovation to compete with expensive and imported feed pellets or concentrates. Use of such pellets also alleviates pressure on rangelands or grasslands.  This innovation consists of a small scale compressor 'pelletizer' and formulas to create qualitatively suﬃcient feed pellets with locally available inputs. In Tunisia, there are many agro-pastoralists that are dependent on expensive and imported livestock feed pellets to improve livestock quality and to supplement feed shortages. Risks of relative feed shortages are likely to increase due to climate change. Also there are many discarded by-products from local agro-food supply chains such as olive cakes, date kernels, and downgraded dates, which still contain nutrients. Feed pellet production with this small scale pelletizer producing 500 kg pellets / hour is also an interesting income generating activity for farmer organizations and creates employment. ; This technology has been first introduced in Tunisia, and as it has proven it's potential it was scaled to Mali and Ethiopia. Now there are two farmer organizations in Mali who are producing feed pellets using different locally available materiel like maize bran and cotton cake. In Tunisia the feed pellet production is still ongoing. A new farmer organization in the south (oasis production system) are using downgraded dates, luzerme and barley to produce quality pellets, mainly for sheep, goats and camels. ; A mechanization workshop was organized in Tunisia and brought together farmer organizations using the pelletizer machines and local machine importers and manufacturers discussing the issue of pelletizers and other small scale machinery

column16: National food systems greenhouse gas emission profiles to help decision makers plan for food systems emissions reduction strategies
column17: There is a lack of data on food systems greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions at the food system level. The country profiles, which will take the form of reports and briefs, will synthesize GHG emission-  and climate change-related data at the national level, provide an analysis of key drivers of and contributors to GHG emissions in food systems and explore the potential of alternative mitigation actions and associated trade-offs, taking into account environmental boundaries and transformational needs. Iterative versions of these profiles will include new data on emissions generated by the Initiative and deepen the food systems approach in order to break down entrenched sectoral categories and existing adaptation and mitigation silos while providing a means to integrate and assess emissions from multiple sources along the food value chain from production to consumption. In 2022 progress was made on draft profiles for Bangladesh, China, Colombia, Kenya and Vietnam.

column16: Supporting diversification and climate resilience in coffee systems through improved agronomy and advisory services for smallholder farmers.
column17: The innovation is an App-based digital tool, which agronomists from the demand partner organization and farmer leadres can use to identify and to guide climate-smart and best agricultural practices in coffee farms. A stepwise approach will be used to set increaing packages of the agricultural practices (package 1= basic, package 2 = package 1 + other agricultural practices).  Packages of the agricultural practices will be developped based on the identified farmer groups and coffee farms. The digital tool will be able to assist in identifying the typology along which the household belong, based on some basic socio-economic conditions of the household. The second part of the digital tool will assist in idenfiying the package of agricultural practices that the household can accomodate and the types of the needs for him/her to move to the second level of agricultural practice. Biological coffee is targeted, excluding mineral fertilizers and pesticides.

column16: Sustainable intensification of cocoa production through the development and dissemination of Integrated Soil Fertility Management option (CocoaSoils Use Case)
column17: The Cocoa Soils project aims to enhance cocoa productivity sustainably by developing and sharing Integrated Soil Fertility Management (ISFM) strategies, aiming to prevent deforestation. Targeted at cocoa farmers, this innovation is in the development phase, utilizing the Stepwise Investment Pathway to guide the adoption of Best Management Practices (BMPs). This approach ensures each investment maximizes returns at minimal risk, facilitating a transition to climate-smart cocoa production. The project's app will assist farmers in identifying and prioritizing management practices based on carefully designed criteria, enabling informed, low-risk investment decisions.

column16: RiceAdvice Lite - Digital Agronomy Advisory Tool for Site-Specific Fertilizer and Crop Management in Economic Community Of West African States countries
column17: RiceAdvice Lite is a decision support tool designed to provide smallholder farmers, Atafi lead farmers, and extension agents with expert guidance on fertilizer and weed management, specifically tailored to enhance rice cultivation. Another component of the innovation is the development of a digital data collection tool to support the Sustainable Rice Platform (SRP) Standard and Performance Indicators. This aspect of the project aims to automate the assessment of farmer compliance with SRP standards, streamlining data processing, analytics (incorporating machine learning and yield decomposition analysis among other Key Performance Indicators), and visualization for external stakeholders. The innovation is  focusing on delivering these sophisticated advisory and analytical services to directly benefit rice producers and contribute to sustainable agriculture practices.

column16: Supporting sustainable soybean production in Northern Ghana (SSPiNG) through improved agronomic advisory services (GHANA-SOY/ESOKO Use Case)
column17: The innovation targeting soybean production in Northern Ghana introduces four key MVPs: site-specific fertilizer recommendations, varietal suitability maps, location-specific maize-soy intercropping systems, and a mechanization platform. These components complement existing digital agronomic, weather, and market advisories, reaching over sixty thousand smallholder farmers. Addressing challenges like limited mechanization, insufficient access to input credit, and low yields, this initiative offers a holistic solution. Features include customized agronomic advice, a digital credit system for inputs, direct linkages to certified input suppliers, and real-time market insights, all delivered through the ESOKO, the demand partner. ESOKO is pivotal in this transformation, providing a user-friendly interface on basic mobile phones, serving as a vital information hub and bridging the gap between farmers and agricultural services. This strategy not only addresses immediate agricultural challenges but also promotes a sustainable, technology-driven ecosystem, enhancing productivity and profitability in Northern Ghana's soybean sector.

column16: Strengthening CGIAR crop breeding impact through prioritized trait discovery and deployment efforts aligned with clear target product profiles
column17: CGIAR centers maintain a broad and active portfolio of Trait Discovery and Deployment (TD&D) innovations that underpin crop improvement for resilience, climate change adaptation, nutrition, and end-use quality. In 2022 and 2023, 350 and 325 distinct TD&D activities, respectively, were documented across CGIAR programs. A 2024 deep-dive with breeding teams confirmed that this portfolio contributes predominantly to disease resistance (42%), abiotic stress tolerance (21%), production traits (16%), end-use quality (13%), and yield (7%) within active breeding populations.; Despite the scale and diversity of these efforts, TD&D investments have historically lacked sufficient prioritization and alignment with product development pipelines. Key gaps included the absence of a systematic mechanism to identify priority trait targets, assess their frequency and variance in breeding pipelines, define required target levels in elite germplasm, and determine the critical haplotypes needed to deliver intended value propositions.; To address these challenges, the TD&D module was developed and deployed within the CGIAR breeding portal in 2025. This module provides a structured, transparent approach for identifying and prioritizing high-value TD&D targets aligned with target product profiles. During this reporting period, 58 priority TD&D target entries were documented across CGIAR centers. This innovation strengthens strategic decision-making by ensuring that TD&D investments are highly focused, closely aligned with breeding strategies, and deployed into product development pipelines using clear best-practice guidelines – thereby maximizing impact and efficiency across CGIAR breeding programs.;

column16: Availing digital advisory content through an easily searchable content hub for farmer support organizations (Nigeria)
column17: Mercy Corps is collaborating with the Excellence in Agronomy initiative to develop agronomic advisory solutions aimed at benefiting over 300,000 smallholder farmers. This initiative focuses on creating gender- and youth-responsive agronomic solutions, covering soil health, crop productivity, climate change adaptation, and precision cropping system management. The collaboration involves digitizing specific value chain agronomic content for Nigeria, which will be disseminated through the MercyCorps Sprout platform. This digital content is designed to reach farmers via organizations and various communication channels. The first year of the project was dedicated to establishing partnerships, developing the Minimum Viable Product (MVP) tool, and outlining data and tool requirements along with prototype development. The second year focuses on validating and piloting the MVP to ensure its effectiveness and impact. This innovative approach seeks to sustain agricultural productivity and ecosystem services, adapt to climate change, and refine cropping system management solutions for smallholder farmers.
