column16: South Asia Drought Monitoring System (SADMS) platform supports national and local authorities for drought monitoring and management.
column17: South Asia Drought Monitoring System (SADMS) is a powerful platform that helps farmers, authorities, and extension workers to monitor and effectively manage droughts. It combines real-time weather updates and satellite data to provide (1) forecast droughts and monitor their severity at district-level, (2) trigger contingency plans when drought strikes, protecting smallholder farmers, and (3) analyze national and regional data from satellites and other sources. SADMS was developed successfully in South Asia and was now transferred to Africa. It inspired similar platforms in Zambia and Pakistan, proving its adaptability and effectiveness. SADMS is a data-driven approach empowers communities, safeguards vulnerable populations, and builds regional resilience against a shared climatic challenge. SADMS stands as a testament to innovation in the face of environmental adversity.

column16: Improved soybean digitally mediated agronomic advisory to improve yields, soil health and incomes in the Chinyanja Triangle(Malawi/Mozambique/Zambia)
column17: The innovation, a digital Agronomy Advisory tool in its prototype phase, delivers site-specific guidance on soybean farming to smallholder farmers. It advises on the best planting times, varieties, fertilization strategies, and crop establishment methods. Integrated with Solidaridad's digital advisories, this tool targets yield optimization, increased profitability, and sustainable farming in the Chinyanja Triangle (Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia).; ; Smallholder soybean farmers are the main users, with Solidaridad overseeing the tool's implementation. The content, developed by agronomists and agricultural experts, is research-based and customized for the region's specific needs. This digital solution aims to overcome soybean production hurdles, offering farmers practical, technology-driven support to enhance their agricultural productivity.

column16: The GANSO (GANaderia SOtenible or Sustainable Livestock) guarantee is a voluntary evaluation tool for livestock producers to improve livestock production systems to sustainable landscapes.
column17: The 'GANSO Guarantee' is a voluntary evaluation tool for livestock producers. It was developed by the GANSO (GANadería SOstenible / Sustainable Livestock) organization, co-founded by the Alliance BI-CIAT, created to improve the livestock production systems in the Colombian Eastern Plains, from extensive degraded pastures and soils to productive and sustainable landscapes.  The guarantee has grown and developed as a set of 5 pillars (environment, people, animal welfare, management & meat quality) and 52 practices are independently assessed and categorized in order of their compliance level. This gives the farmers incentives to sell beef at a premium price, supported by the consumers' willingness to pay for environmental-friendly products. These products are currently available in one the largest retail store in Colombia, with 182 stores in 6 cities. Starting in Meta department, now the tool is being implemented in other departments of the Orinoquia region.

column16: e-Agrology: A High-Frequency Monitoring System Enhancing Sustainable Agriculture and Livestock Production for Farmers in the Global South
column17: e-Agrology is a high-frequency monitoring system for agricultural production in the global South. This open-source solution for web and mobile includes a data collection module adapted for any crop and production system (perennials, seasonal, intercrops); a transformation module for automated data cleaning and standardization; and a visualization module for dashboard creation and data download. It allows monitoring of production systems, including detailed data on planting dates, pest and disease management, agronomic practices, costs, yield, input prices, commercialization, and post-harvest. The system has supported CGIAR private sector partners in measuring their sustainability within agri-food systems; also, we have generated site-specific recommendations for farmers based on optimal planting dates, nutrient management, best practices, and yield limiting factors per agroecology. By December 2022, more than 250,000 farmers are registered with 350,000 agronomic seasonal logbooks. Sustainability indicators have been measured for including water-use efficiency, nutrient-use efficiency, CO2 emissions, profitability, yield, and others.

column16: User-focused design approach developed by CGIAR researchers to create more inclusive digital agricultural innovations
column17: This innovation systematically integrates human-centered design principles into digital innovation development across CGIAR and partner organizations. Traditional digital agricultural solutions often face challenges including high development costs, limited farmer adoption, and insufficient consideration of women's and marginalized groups' needs. This approach addresses these issues through two pathways: building institutional capacity through training programs and practical guidance materials adapted for agricultural research contexts, and providing hands-on support for research teams in problem identification, user research, prototyping, and testing. The Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, along with other CGIAR centers, developed tools and methods that help researchers prioritize user needs, integrate gender considerations, and ensure solutions are technically feasible and financially viable. Applied across multiple countries including Kenya, Rwanda, Guatemala, and Colombia, this innovation enables agricultural researchers to create digital solutions that better serve diverse farming communities, particularly women and marginalized groups.

column16: Crowdsourced digital platform developed by CGIAR to monitor diet quality and food systems in Rwanda and Guatemala
column17: The innovation is end-to-end integrated system that combines citizen engagement for data curation with modern agile analytics to provide real-time and actionable insights about dietary patterns and food system dynamics. The system is made up of three components: citizen-powered high-frequency data collection, user-centered dashboard analytics, and demand-driven reflexive modeling of intervention options. The innovation stands out by leveraging crowdsourced data collection methods that are both cost-efficient and easily deployable, enabling more frequent and accurate insights compared to traditional in-person methods on diets, markets, and transport infrastructure. It aims to serve as scalable platform to engage, inform, and empower individuals and decision-makers; support data-driven and informed decision-making; and provide robust data to inform policies and interventions, direct capital investments to improve food system resilience, and increase preparedness/planning for potential and direct risk. It is already under development with diet quality, food flows, and transport network being mapped in Rwanda and Kenya.

column59: The evidence provided shows that the innovation has been implemented and tested under real-world, uncontrolled conditions. Since the first pilot in 2023, the diet quality monitoring system has been deployed in five of the 22 departments of Guatemala, reaching more than 500 individuals who have participated consistently in the monitoring process. Based on a human-centered design approach, iterative adjustments were made to both the DQQ tool and the implementation methodology. To date, 20 survey deployment cycles have been completed, generating a database with more than 6,000 individual observations. These data are visualized through a near–real-time dashboard hosted on the Sistema de Información Territorial Trinacional (SIINTET) platform, managed by the local partner CUNORI, where aggregated diet quality results are publicly accessible. This evidence demonstrates the innovation’s capacity to generate reliable and actionable information at scale under uncontrolled conditions.

column16: Gender-inclusive protocol developed by CGIAR centers guides crop breeders in creating target product profiles
column17: Crop breeding programs often develop varieties that fail to meet the diverse needs of different farmer groups, particularly women farmers who may have different preferences for traits like processing quality, storage, or cooking characteristics. CGIAR centers developed this comprehensive protocol to address this gap by providing step-by-step guidance for creating Target Product Profiles that intentionally consider gender differences in crop variety preferences. The protocol defines key terms, outlines the multi-disciplinary team structure needed, and describes how to identify distinct market segments at regional and national levels. It enables breeding programs to systematically incorporate farmer preferences from the beginning of variety development, leading to improved varieties with higher adoption rates across different user groups.

column16: Tracking Adaptation in Livestock Systems (TAiLS): tool designed to enable governments to track and report on climate change adaptation in the livestock sector
column17: The Paris Agreement encourages countries to track and report on their progress in adapting to climate change. But there are no suitable frameworks and tools are not suited for tracking adaptation for international reporting, more so for the livestock sector. TAiLS tool is designed to enable governments to track if adaptation is taking place across space and time and its outcomes. The tool has been co-produced in consultation with livestock keepers and government officials in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Uganda. It integrates a set of indicators related to three dimensions, i.e., climatic hazards, impacts, and adaptive capacity and actions. The tool is also customized to leverage on the existing dataflows at national and subnational levels of government.

column16: Improved dual-purpose adaptive chicken strains for smallholder farmers in Ethiopia
column17: The innovations aim to develop improved chicken that grows fast and produces more eggs compared to the existing smallholder poultry production system. Imported commercial chicken lines lack adaptation characteristics when managed under smallholder systems. As a result the performance is usually low. They also do not meet the farmer preferences such as plumage and skin colour, mothering ability among others. This innovation entails developing various crossbred combinations that meets the needs and aspirations of smallholder farmers using improved inbred lines. It will also include evaluating the performances of the crossbreds on station and on-farm to identify best combinations using reciprocal crossing. The names of the four inbred lines are: LIL20: BIL20 Local ILRI 2020: Barred NHIL20: ILRI 2020 Brown ILRI 2020 WIL20: White ILRI 2020 The naming is subjected to change.

column16: Modeling Service Center (MSC): providing long-term training to researchers across the Agricultural Policy Research Institutes in Africa (ANAPRI) network, on economywide analysis, including food policy modeling and shock analysis.
column17: In 2022, IFPRI and ANAPRI (formerly ReNAPRI) collaborated to establish the Modeling Service Center (MSC) at ANAPRI's Secretariat in Lusaka, Zambia. IFPRI conceptualized the modeling community of practice (MODCOP), which evolved into the MSC, and shaped the Policy Prioritization through Value Chain (PPVC) Analysis II proposal funded by BMGF. The MSC focuses on training researchers in economywide analysis, including food policy modeling and climate impact assessments. In 2023, it conducted four training events for ANAPRI partners, offering tiered programs for ambassadors, affiliates, and fellows. By 2024, the MSC became independently operational and self-funded, with ANAPRI fully embracing the model. IFPRI continues to provide advisory support and capacity building to strengthen MSC activities.

column16: Groundwater governance toolbox: Guidance on how to identify, adapt, and combine tools to improve groundwater governance in a participatory and locally-appropriate manner for government agencies and communities
column17: Groundwater is especially challenging resources to govern, because it is mobile and difficult to observe. Externally imposed rules often fail to work, but examples of community governance of groundwater are also scarce. This toolbox offers examples of innovative procedures, policy instruments, and institutional tools. Stakeholders engaged in enhancing groundwater governance can utilize these examples to comprehend their issues and opportunities. Additionally, they can deliberate on and potentially reach consensus on norms or rules aimed at preventing aquifer depletion. Furthermore, the toolbox facilitates the creation of shared gains that enhance water productivity. Institutional tools for groundwater governance could help deal with complex nexus linkages such as transitions to solar-powered pumping, aquifer recharge and storage to buffer against drought, and regenerating ecosystems. This groundwater governance toolbox offers government agencies and communities resources for thinking about the variety of instruments available and how they might be chosen, combined, and adapted to create customized toolkits to solve problems and achieve gains in specific contexts.

column16: A unified data and research portal where researchers, public and private sectors, and policy and decision-makers can access data, evidence, and stories of impact and change on aquatic foods
column17: The lack of coherent, accessible, and reusable data remains a major barrier to informed decision-making in aquatic food systems. Data are often dispersed across projects and institutions, stored in incompatible formats, or difficult to interpret by non-specialist users, limiting their uptake in policy, investment, and planning processes. This result presents a unified data and research portal designed to improve access to data, evidence, and knowledge on aquatic food systems for researchers, public and private sector actors, and policy and decision-makers. The portal brings together datasets, analytical outputs, and documented evidence in a single digital environment, supporting transparency, reuse, and cross-country learning. The portal enables users to explore and compare information through interactive visual tools, making complex data easier to interpret and apply. It supports the integration of multiple types of evidence, including quantitative indicators, contextual information, and documented stories of impact and change, helping bridge the gap between research and decision-making. As part of its functionality, the portal implements and hosts analytical tools such as the AquaIndex, allowing users to interact with sustainability indicators and country-level profiles within a broader data and evidence ecosystem. The portal is designed to clearly signal data limitations and gaps, ensuring responsible use of evidence. By providing a shared digital space for accessing, visualizing, and contributing data, the portal strengthens knowledge exchange across institutions and geographies. It supports more informed policy dialogue, research prioritization, and investment discussions, while offering a scalable foundation that can evolve as new data, tools, and analytical frameworks become available.

column16: An innovative model for collaborating across CGIAR centers to facilitate a meta-analysis of research on how to increase adoption of new varieties
column17: Market Intelligence Area of Work on social and behavioral Intelligence has developed an innovation in research practice, which is a model of collaborative research coordination and data collection between multiple CGIAR centers around a shared learning agenda. Partners align on intervention design, harmonize core survey instruments, and jointly define analytical frameworks. This enables pooling of data across countries and centers and supports rigorous meta-analysis to generate more externally valid insights. We pilot this model by applying it to a learning agenda around testing interventions that accelerate farmer uptake of new crop varieties. The research is implemented through coordinated, parallel experiments across Ethiopia, India, Kenya, Nigeria, and Uganda, enabling CGIAR centers to jointly generate evidence that is both locally grounded and globally relevant. This multi-country design allows the program to distinguish between common behavioral constraints affecting adoption across contexts and location-specific barriers or opportunities faced by farmers. The evidence of this innovation features a portfolio of registered trials and a shared meta-analysis research design, demonstrating how cross-center collaboration can generate scalable insights. By combining standardized methods with contextual experimentation, this collaborative model strengthens CGIAR’s ability to inform breeding, seed systems, and delivery strategies with robust social and behavioral intelligence that is applicable across regions while remaining sensitive to local realities.

column16: Supporting smallholder farmers’ access to diversified seed systems for food and nutrition security and climate change adaptation
column17: Nature+ aims at achieving its impact through support for crop and variety diversification and agroforestry (trees on farm), including the use of minor crops and farmer varieties. All of this diversity requires to be available to farmers through well-functioning seed systems. Seeds need to be of good quality and have the traits women and men farmers are interested in. Given that private sector and formal seed systems focus on only a few crops, this innovation is about developing strong and functioning farmers’ led seed systems that will allow farmers to access the required diversity to ensure success in achieving the impact of the initiative, including improving nutrition, biodiversity conservation, and resilience. Key activities include agro-ecological farming, participatory crop selection and improvement, community ; seed banking, value chain development, and seed policy development. In 2025, we continued to strengthen the community seed banks and framer seed enterprises through expansion of their collections, improvement of their equipment, and value addition activities related to seeds and products.

column16: Longa artificial intelligence tool developed by IFPRI to analyze farmers' voice messages for targeted extension services in East and West Africa
column17: Agricultural extension organizations in Africa face challenges in efficiently analyzing farmers' voice messages to understand their needs and deliver appropriate services. IFPRI developed Longa, an artificial intelligence-powered audio analytics tool that automatically translates and analyzes voice message data collected through rural radio programs. The tool uses advanced machine learning techniques to process multiple African languages and generate insights about farmers' requirements. Developed as a proof-of-concept for Farm Radio International's work in Tanzania, Uganda, Kenya, and Nigeria, Longa enables extension organizations to quickly understand farmers' needs and provide targeted support. The innovation includes automatic speech recognition models for Chichewa, Luganda, and Bambara languages, expanding accessibility for diverse farming communities across the region.

column16: Actionable drought forecasts for the transboundary natural resource management authorities in Southern Africa using satellite-based climate information
column17: Based on information and services currently available in the region and the requirements expressed by stakeholders such as LIMCOM, we are developing a seasonal forecast of droughts for the Limpopo River basin in Southern Africa. This system is based on state-of-the-art data processing and machine learning tools currently developed by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) for the generation of seasonal temperature and precipitation forecasts at global scales. The innovation seeks to adapt this system for the forecasting of drought events and intensity over the Limpopo River basin using indices selected according to their suitability to describe droughts locally, which is carried out using satellite and climate information. The forecast system will be embedded in the Digital Twin platform developed by CGIAR Research Initiative on Digital Innovation to assess the potential impacts of seasonal climate anomalies on agricultural and hydrological systems.

column16: Digital Traceability: A biofortified rice traceability system for seed businesses in Indonesia
column17: Seed, grain, and food businesses in Indonesia rarely use any form of traceability, with some limited use of paper-based records or digitized business management systems. This makes protecting the value of biofortified zinc rice difficult to protect throughout the supply chain. This innovation aims to bring together private-sector businesses that offer digital traceability systems to seed businesses that supply zinc-fortified rice in Indonesia. In 2023, we collaborated with a local innovation partner to design and develop a digital tool to monitor full supply chain activities of zinc wheat in two regions: Jakarta and Yogyakarta. In 2024, users will also participate in the research pilot. The final tool will be presented to users in 10 districts with proportion of the users selected for questionnaires on likeability and usability of the tool.

column16: Protocol for exploring production, business conditions, and demand for rice in the Colombian Caribbean region
column17: The methodological steps proposed in this guide seek to support the Producers' Association of Leticia and the Canal del Dique in market research. The tool uses a value chain approach to evaluate their current situation or position at the production and business level in the rice chain, their relationships or potential commercial alliances in the primary grains market, and the market or demand for rice in the region of interest for green paddy, dry paddy, white rice, and other by-products. This methodology proposes to approach these issues through qualitative research that combines the collection of secondary information, semi-structured interviews with key actors in the sector, chain mapping exercises, and observation and inquiries at key locations where the product is sold. The methodology aims to strengthen capacities and generate tools that allow access to markets, and has already been applied in the departmentof Bolivar.

column16: Results from survey experiments published to improve the quality of household food consumption data collected in Ethiopia
column17: CGIAR researchers from Sustainable Healthy Diets with other academic partners developed a series of experiments to improve the quality of household food consumption data collected through surveys. The first experiment studied telescoping. Telescoping errors occur when respondents recall an event but their memory of the date of the event is inaccurate. In food consumption surveys, this means a respondent may report that their family ate eggs last week, but it might have been that they last ate eggs nine days ago (outside of the seven-day reference period). A second experiment studied whether food consumption data can be reliably collected over the phone. The experiments found that (1) telescoping leads to substantial overstatement of the consumption of high-nutrient foods and (2) survey data collection via phone leads to understatement of consumption. This innovation can be a valuable resource for researchers and policymakers keen to accurately measure sustainable healthy diets.

column16: Integrated stock assessment modelling in digital fisheries monitoring for targeted species in Timor-Leste
column17: Many small-scale fisheries lack the data needed to understand fish stock health, limiting effective management and recognition as sustainable. This work integrates length-based fish stock assessment into a digital fisheries monitoring system, using routinely collected catch data to assess stock condition across key fishing areas. The results provide clear, science-based guidance for fisheries managers, showing that assessed stocks are in good condition and have potential to sustainably increase production while supporting long-term food security and livelihoods.; In 2025, digitally collected fisheries data were used to conduct multi-year assessments of key fish stocks across major fishing areas in Timor-Leste. The assessments provide clear information on stock condition and fishing pressure, supporting evidence-based fisheries management. Results indicate that assessed stocks are generally in good condition and have the potential to sustainably increase production, strengthening the contribution of fisheries to food security and livelihoods.

column16: Decision Support Tool for Right Sizing of Solar-powered Irrigation Pumps in Africa and South Asia
column17: Improvements in technology, reduction in costs and significant policy support has driven expansion of solar irrigation in Asia and Africa. In India - which is the early leader in solar irrigation adoption, the number of solar pumps is estimated to have grown from a handful in 2010 to more than 350,000 by 2020. The Government of India has announced an ambitious campaign to support the deployment of more than 3.5 million solar pumps over the coming years. Given the significant public and private investments in solar pumps, it is critical that these pumps be 'right-sized' - over-sizing can lead to wasteful expenditure and poor utilization while under-sizing can seriously limit the pumps' benefits. With support from GIZ, IWMI partnered with ICAR and BISA to develop the Beta version of the SIP Sizing Tool for MNRE, Government of India. The tool estimates irrigation and pumping requirement, analyzes future scenarios and recommends the right size for installation of a solar pump. ; In 2023, IWMI and GIZ expanded their collaboration in promoting this innovation in Nepal. An Innovation Package and Scaling Readiness (IPSR) workshops was conducted in Kathmandu to identify challenges towards solar irrigation in Nepal and co-create solutions for promoting the Decision Support Tool for Right Sizing of Solar-powered Irrigation Pumps. In 2024, the project team has developed a Beta version of an excel based ‘Solar Water Pump Planning Tool for Nepal’.  The tool is officially launched for use by the AEPC and Provincial governments in Nepal. The simple and user-friendly tool will help local government and other stakeholders to quickly estimate the system costs for budget planning. The team will continue its work with further engagement for scaling the tool in India, Nepal and elsewhere.

column16: Towards a One CGIAR germplasm licensing strategy to foster wide and equitable use of CGIAR-center germplasm by public and private entities
column17: The innovation develops common germplasm licensing approaches for use by CGIAR centers under One CGIAR. It is being developed by an inter-initiative work group – including Seed Equal, Genebanks and Accelerated Breeding - for review, discussion and endorsement by Centers and the System Management Board.  ; ; At this stage, few centers have systematic germplasm licensing approaches in place, approaches differ between centers, and there is a lack of awareness among public and private sector entities how to access CGIAR Center germplasm for research, breeding or commercial use. The innovation seeks to implement more streamlined approaches and conditions to foster wide and equitable use of Center germplasm by public and private entities under One CGIAR. column16: A standardised quantitative methodology to locate data gaps in FishBase databases to prioritise Aquatic Foods Systems transformation
column17: In aquatic food systems, decision-making is often constrained not only by limited data, but by a lack of clarity on where the most important data gaps are. This innovation provides a standardized, quantitative method to systematically assess data coverage within the FishBase database, allowing users to identify critical gaps in knowledge across countries and species. The method analyses data availability across four dimensions: thematic areas (such as conservation, ecology, and human use), time, taxonomy, and geographic coverage. It has been applied to eleven priority countries and is operationalised through an interactive dashboard that enables comparison across regions and data categories. By revealing where information is missing or unevenly distributed, the approach supports more efficient allocation of research effort, improved prioritisation of biodiversity and conservation actions, and stronger evidence bases for sustainable fisheries and aquaculture planning.

column16: Methodology for analyzing data gaps and needs was developed to identify and remove limitations in data and information that hinder the development of aquatic food systems.
column17: Stakeholders in aquatic food systems often make suboptimal decisions due to limited, fragmented, or inaccessible data. Data needs vary across stakeholder groups, countries, and development stages, making it difficult to define shared priorities or design coherent data strategies. This innovation provides a standardized, participatory methodology to identify and compare data gaps and information needs across aquatic food systems. It combines multi-stakeholder consultations with a structured review of existing data sources to clarify what data are most needed, by whom, and for what purpose. The approach allows country-level findings to be compared while remaining sensitive to local contexts.

column16: Metadata mining methodology to facilitate integration of databases for aquaculture and fisheries
column17: Research and policy decisions on aquatic food systems depend on large volumes of data produced by multiple projects and organisations. However, these data are often described inconsistently, making it difficult to locate, compare, or reuse information across countries and themes. This is an innovative approach to data and data analytics that introduces a standardised, automated method for analysing and organising dataset descriptions from aquatic research repositories. The innovation works by systematically reading dataset titles, keywords, and descriptions and assigning them to clearly defined thematic areas and geographic contexts. This allows datasets that were previously disconnected to be grouped, compared, and analysed together. The method produces structured outputs that show what types of data exist, where they are concentrated, how recent they are, and where important gaps remain. These outputs support cross-country comparisons, quality checks of data documentation, and more efficient use of existing research investments. In addition, the approach includes a complementary tool that summarises research documents into accessible narratives, enabling non-specialist users to quickly understand key findings and potential impacts without reading full technical reports. By turning fragmented dataset descriptions and research texts into a connected and interpretable knowledge layer, this innovation improves access to aquatic resource evidence and strengthens its use for research prioritisation, policy analysis, and strategic decision-making.

column16: Fish cage production in small reservoirs in Ghana to support the livelihoods and empowerment of empowerment of youth, women, and small-scale farmers
column17: In Ghana’s North-East Region, an innovative aquaculture pilot initiative is transforming local communities by creating new livelihood opportunities. The completion of the first cycle of the aquaculture pilot marks a significant milestone for the participating communities.  2024 saw the completion of the harvest for the first cycle of production of fish in the reservoirs of four communities in Northern Ghana(Langbinsi, Nalerigu, Nansoni, and Tombu). The second cycle of production is now on-going and was partly financed from the earnings from the first round.; The success of the pilot has caught the attention of various stakeholders, including the Ministry of Fisheries and Aquaculture Development, which is now planning to expand the initiative across all 5 regions of Northern Ghana. ; The introduction of aquaculture is turning local dams into sources of growth and development. By utilizing aquaculture, the initiative not only boosts economic prospects but also fosters community resilience and pride.

column16: Community Based Resource Management (CBRM) Training Package for coastal fisheries in the Solomon Islands for providing technical support and inclusive planning to communities
column17: The Community-Based Resource Management (CBRM) Training Package for coastal fisheries in the Solomon Islands was developed to provide technical support and inclusive planning for communities managing their coastal resources. Over four years, a CBRM program was implemented in partnership with the Ministry of Fisheries and Marine Resources (MFMR), Malaita Provincial Government, and WorldFish.; The program engaged 96 communities, raising awareness about CBRM and assessing existing practices. Until now, 32 communities had developed eight management plans, and 72 community facilitators from 51 communities were trained using a CBRM monitoring and evaluation tool. Recognizing the importance of customary land tenure, the Solomon Islands Government has designated CBRM as the primary coastal resource management strategy. This training package strengthens the role of Provincial Fisheries Officers (PFOs), equipping them with the knowledge and capacity to support community-led fisheries management, ensuring sustainable resource use and guiding future CBRM scaling across other provinces.; In 2025, this work and tool was integrated in the development of a 2026-2031 Provincial Fisheries Division Development Strategy by MFMR, indicating uptake and end use. ; ;

column16: DataScribe - a tool for creating standards-compliant, shareable agronomic survey questionnaires
column17: DataScribe enables users to collaboratively create agronomic surveys or upload ODK questionnaires (as xls forms), share them (or particular questions within them), and easily specify variables aligned with data standards (via the tool's semantic engine). Users upload their forms to ODK to collect data. The tool also standardizes surveys by enabling questionnaires to draw from the same global choice lists (over 50 currently available, for such topics as "inorganic N fertilizer"; "weeding" and more). Questionnaire blocks can be saved and shared or reused, saving time and enabling further standardization across surveys. The tool was developed in 2022 but has been improved in 2023 and used by several EiA Use Cases.

column16: Successful protocol to break dormancy of Oryza glaberrima seeds incorporated into standard procedure after testing on 300 accessions.
column17: AfricaRice developed a protocol under the guidance of Aarhus University to break the dormancy of Oryza glaberrima seeds. In 2022, the protocol was tested among alternative methods and validated using seeds from 300 accessions constituting the core collection. The protocol involves heat treatment of intact seeds at 50 °C for 28 days and resulted in consistently high germination rates (average 97%). The protocol has been formally adopted as a standard operating procedure (AfricaRice-SOP-DORMANCY-v1.0) and is now routinely applied in genebank workflows for viability testing, regeneration, and utilization of O. glaberrima accessions. It has been shared with partners including IRRI and contributes to improved efficiency in conservation and use of African rice genetic resources.

column8: User testing conducted in 2025 provided critical insights that informed this decision.  Summary of user testing findings: 1. Users appreciate having standardized data consolidated in one location as provided by DataLake; however, they see limited value in DataLake if it merely replicates what is already available on Carob website. 2. All users reported that DataLake’s search functionality was difficult and unintuitive. 3.The concept of a single platform providing access to all CGIAR and partners data was described as “a dream no one dares to dream,” largely because most users doubt it is achievable. Nevertheless, all users acknowledged that they currently rely on multiple platforms—and often colleagues—to locate the data they need.  Based on these insights, we decided to discontinue funding for DataLake as a standalone product. Instead, its most valuable functionalities will be integrated into an existing tool, GARDIAN, ensuring continued progress toward more unified and accessible CGIAR data services.
column16: Global agronomy database v. alpha to enable search of standardized data and retrieval of aggregated datasets by researchers
column17: A data-to-analytics infrastructure roadmap was developed for EiA in 2022. A critical part of this infrastructure is a global datapool or database that allows search within standardized datasets largely collected across ; CGIAR (i.e., beyond traditional metadata search) to return aggregated datasets for analyses. A proof-of-concept was developed in Q4 of 2022, built on state-of-the-art graph database technology. Further development in 2023 has generated an alpha version, populated by a public, legacy datasets (about 200) standardized using the Carob (R script) workflow. Users can search the database for gender-disaggregated data, to assess gender-based differences in crop yields or fertilizer application. Aggregated data from such searches is pre-formatted for easier use in analytics (aligned with R scripts used in ML and the Carob model) and for commonly-used AgMIP crop simulation models (as a first step toward data-to-model capability). Users can also upload data directly to private data pools.

column16: Online experimental tools developed by CGIAR researchers to assess how market intelligence influences breeding investment decisions across Africa and Asia
column17: The innovation provides experimental tools to examine how access to market intelligence (MI) information impacts breeding investment decisions and potential heterogeneities in decision making by various characteristics (e.g., breeder and institutional characteristics). The tool also allows to examine breeders’ willingness to pay for market intelligence. The tool can be implemented by means of an online lab-in-the-field experiment. This method will allow to analyze the impacts of different types of market intelligence, investigate underlying behavioral mechanisms, and elicit demand for market intelligence in a more controlled setting, allowing us to estimate causal effects of market intelligence and variations in the way the intelligence is presented.

column16: Mechanized direct-seeding for sustainable, economically-viable and climate resilient rice production in the Mekong sub-region
column17: Mechanized direct seeded rice (DSR) introduces innovations in both the design and sourcing of specialized seeding machines, as well as in developing business models to facilitate access to these machines. This method involves sowing rice seeds directly into the soil using mechanical seeders that precisely plant seeds in rows, covering them efficiently, whether in dry or wet conditions. The innovation lies in the mechanization process, which incorporates advanced seeding machinery designed or sourced specifically to optimize seed placement and soil contact, leading to reduced seed rates and decreased water requirements.; ; Additionally, this approach not only addresses the challenges of labor and cost reduction but also promotes water conservation and faster planting times. By integrating these technological and entrepreneurial innovations, mechanized DSR aims to overcome the limitations of traditional and broadcast seeding methods, such as low yields and high operational costs, while also contributing to environmental sustainability by reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

column16: Contextualized better management practices (BMPs) for Genetically Improved Farmed Tilapia (GIFT) to support tilapia seed production and grow out operations in Nigeria
column17: Most smallholder aquaculture producers rely on traditional production practices, which often result in low productivity and limited profitability. In addition, weak market linkages, insufficient value addition, and capacity gaps across the aquaculture value chain further restrict sector growth. These challenges collectively hinder the ability of aquaculture to contribute meaningfully to income generation, employment, and food security in the state. To address this, Better Management Practices (BMPs) for farming genetically improved farmed tilapia (GIFT) were developed to support the development and scaling of tilapia farming in Nigeria.  An additional BMPs manual was published in 2024, to provide guidelines for sustainable tilapia production systems in Nigeria and to serve as a handbook for aquaculture technicians/practitioners from different stakeholders such as I/NGOs and private sectors. In 2025, to improve Bayelsa State’s aquaculture potential, WorldFish, through the CGIAR Scaling for Impact Program, has implemented targeted capacity-building interventions aimed at strengthening farmers’ technical, business, and better management practices (BMPs). The initiative prioritizes small-scale producers, with particular attention to women and youth, to support the adoption of improved aquaculture technologies and best management practices (BMPs)that enhance productivity, profitability, and environmental sustainability. By fostering innovation, strengthening industry partnerships, and promoting evidence-based practices, the project supports Bayelsa State’s transition from small-scale, subsistence-oriented fish farming to a more commercially viable, inclusive, and resilient aquaculture sector.; ;

column16: Demand-side innovations to accelerate varietal turnover (such as seed trial packs, cooking demonstrations, consumer trial packs, crop insurance, agricultural advisories, leveraging endowment effects, nudging, social distance)
column17: The Market Intelligence Area of Work (Foster motivation) tests and scales demand-side innovations designed to accelerate varietal turnover by reducing behavioral barriers that slow the replacement of older varieties with improved ones. Across six coordinated experiments, this work generates actionable evidence on how targeted interventions can shorten the time it takes for farmers to try, adopt, and ultimately replace existing varieties with higher-performing alternatives.; ; Two core innovations are tested across multiple contexts. The first is the provision of free trial seed packs, which directly addresses farmers’ aversion to risk when experimenting with unfamiliar varieties. Trial packs are intentionally sized to cover only a portion of a farmer’s land—small enough to limit downside risk, yet large enough to allow meaningful learning about agronomic performance, management requirements, and yield outcomes. By lowering the cost of initial experimentation, this innovation facilitates faster learning cycles and earlier decisions to scale up adoption.; ; The second innovation focuses on end-use experience through cooking demonstrations and free samples of the final product (e.g., flour). This intervention targets misperceptions around taste, cooking quality, and consumer acceptance—key factors that often delay varietal replacement even when agronomic benefits are clear. By allowing farmers and household members to directly experience product quality, the intervention reduces uncertainty and increases confidence in switching to improved varieties.; In addition, the Market Intelligence Area of Work tests site-specific complementary interventions that further accelerate varietal turnover. These include crop insurance to reduce downside risk (Kenya and Ethiopia), tailored agricultural advisories (Nigeria and Kenya), behavioral nudges and endowment effects (Uganda), and the use of champion farmers and social distance mechanisms to influence peer learning (India). Together, these innovations provide a scalable evidence base for demand-driven strategies that speed the replacement of outdated varieties with improved ones across diverse contexts.

column17: This innovation enhances smallholder farmers’ access to farm machinery services for new machinery types by strengthening affordable fee-for-service markets in rural Bangladesh. This model improved access to finance, strengthened enterprise capacity, and enhanced readiness for scaling mechanization services through market-led financial solutions.

column16: Dynamic evolutionary populations of productivity of mixtures of different cereals in Ethiopian Highlands
column17: Maintaining inter-varietal crop diversity, created through evolutionary plant breeding (EPB), on farms is proven to improve farmers productivity, resilience to climate change and enhance dietary diversity. We have tested evolutionary populations created through Evolutionary Plant Breeding in Ethiopia, Bhutan, Iran, Jordan, Nepal and Uganda for four crops: Barley, beans, wheat and rice and identified superior performing populations under different farming systems. Integration of evolutionary plant breeding to Sustainable Intensification of Mixed farming System (SI-MFS) in target countries is important to sustain crop production sector of target farming systems. At least one composite or mixture population is developed for each country targeted by the SI-MFS initiative.

column16: Seed policies and laws in Nature-Positive Solutions' countries: understanding legal and policy context for strengthening farmer-managed seed systems
column17: In order to improve farmer-managed seed systems in NATURE+ five countries, it's essential to understand the current existing seed (related) policies and laws in the implementing countries to address and remove potential obstacles for effective support to farmer-managed seed systems. In several countries, right now seed policies and laws are hindering or preventing farmers from fully benefiting from minor crops and local varieties. This report highlights the policy and legal elements required to fully promote farmer-managed based seed systems as a critical innovation to develop a NATURE+ production system. The Initiative already developed a number of innovations related to seed system development, which can only be implemented at scale when a supportive policy and legal context exists.  ; In 2025, a study was undertaken in Vietnam, in Kenya and Colombia, MFL SP has been heavily involved in the policy process (approved in Kenya and the Treaty in Colombia)

column16: Farmer participatory validation and adaptation trials for selected biopesticides against the diamondback moth on cabbage
column17: The diamondback moth, Plutella xylostella (Lepidoptera: Plutellidae) is the major insect pest attacking cabbage crops in West Africa. As commonly practiced control measures, farmers very often resort to spray chemical insecticides at high dose and application frequency. Over the years, this indiscriminate use of chemical pesticides has led to the resurgence of pesticide resistance in the pest, hence demanding more frequent applications with all the unintended harmful effects of human and environmental health. In the attempt to break the vicious circle of pesticide resistance, bio-pesticides such as the entomopathogenic fungus Beauveria bassiana have been identified as very efficient alternative control options in managing the pest and hence are the target of our intervention.

column16: Integrated management options against parasitic weeds and gall disease on faba bean for smallholder farmers in highlands of Ethiopia
column17: Parasitic weeds are major biotic constraints on food legumes and causing a decline in area and productivity in North and East Africa. May efforts have been made to develop  partially  resistant faba bean cultivars from ICARDA breeding lines.  The level of resistance in released varieties is low and requires additional management options to effectively reduce the economic impacts parasitic weeds. Demonstration and scaling of integrated management of parasitic weeds was implemented in five districts in Amhara region. Male and female farmers selected partially resistant cv. Hashengie + two sprays of sublethal doses of glyphosate at early flowering stages of the crop. The innovation reduced parasitic weeds population and doubled crop productivity. Three field days were organized in 2022 with participation of 103 (10 female) farmers, extension agents and experts. Early generation seeds (0.8 t breeder and 1.5 t C2) of cv. Hashengie  will be used next season. ;

column16: Tools for estimating Demand and Supply of Vegetatively Propagated Crops Seed among Smallholder Farmers
column17: Two complementary digital tools were developed to strengthen seed systems for root, tuber and banana crops like sweetpotato, cassava, and yam. The Seed Requirement Estimation Tool helps national research institutes, seed producers, policymakers, and development organizations estimate seed demand at national and enterprise levels using adjustable parameters for adoption rates, area projections, and replacement intervals. The Business Investment Decision Tool enables seed enterprises to develop financially sound business plans by connecting operational and financial decisions across different seed production stages. Both tools incorporate gender-responsive features and were validated across Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, and Nigeria. The International Potato Center and International Institute of Tropical Agriculture developed these tools with partners, making them available through the Technologies for African Agricultural Transformation platform to support data-driven seed production planning and sustainable seed business models.

column16: Conservation methods developed for rare wild bean species
column17: The rare bean species Phaseolus hygrophilus, collected in the Costa Rican rainforest and preserved in CIAT’s gene bank, has proven difficult to conserve due to its inability to produce seeds. To address this, a tissue culture method has been optimized, and the species is now maintained both in tissue culture and as a living collection in specialized growth chambers. These plants are propagated using grafting techniques and cuttings. For Phaseolus albicarminus, a separate grafting and layering protocol has been developed for vegetative propagation. However, this species has not been successfully preserved through tissue culture and is instead maintained as a living collection in growth chambers.; The conservation methods are being used to conserve and produce seeds of wild bean species in the field by genebank staff working on the regeneration of the bean collection.

column16: Multiplication of mucuna seed to support initial on-farm validation and subsequent of scaling of innovative mucuna cover cropping within perennial crops in eastern DR Congo
column17: On-station studies conducted in eastern DR Congo, have shown cover crops including Mucuna to offer multiple services such as erosion control, soil health regeneration, weed management, soil moisture and temperature moderation within banana and coffee fields. These practices improve overall biomass production and crop yields and offer opportunities for livestock integration. These innovations have been tested and are currently being scaled. Access to seed is limiting and is an important complementary innovation crucial for furthering the uptake of Mucuna and other cover crops.  Thus, efforts to demonstrate and multiply Mucuna seed is ongoing at the Mulungu INERA station. This will identify the best way to multiply the seed and is supporting validation trials and ongoing scaling efforts. Strategies will be explored for a more sustainable production of seed to support farmers.

column17: In Ethiopia, we analyzed seed potato stakeholders' perceptions, characterizing interaction networks of potato value chain actors, focusing on stakeholders engaged in seed potato quality assurance. We collected data regarding Ethiopia's potato seed systems using expert knowledge elicitation and analyzed the risk of national spread of the  Ralstonia solanacearum species complex (RSSC) and other pathogens. Network metrics were used to characterize the informal seed system in Ethiopia, along with simulations of pathogen spread across an epidemic network in social-ecological scenario analyses. Ware potato farmers and traders were reported to have weak communication with other stakeholders in the potato value chain. In network analyses and simulated epidemics, locations in Agew Awi, Gamo, Gofa, Kembata and Tembaro zones were identified as candidate priorities for national surveillance of pathogen invasion and important for management interventions and formal seed system development. This analysis provides a baseline for prioritization for implementing surveillance systems and management programs targeting the locations identified, which can be built on as more data and model components become available.;

column16: On-farm validation of velvet bean (Mucuna pruriens) as a cover crop in banana and coffee systems in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo
column17: On-station trials at INERA of shade- and drought-tolerant fast-growing nitrogen-fixing cover crops like Mucuna pruriens and first growing grasses have resulted in increased farm productivity, restoration of degraded lands and soils through improving soil physical, chemical, and biological properties and in banana and coffee systems. Mucuna can also reduce weed burden, improving the quality of life for women and children who provide most of the labor for weeding. Validation trials have also been conducted on farms aligned to large cooperatives/companies. These demonstrations over the year attracted over 800 farmers and partners to learn the soil health enhancement practices and are important demo and learning sites. Lessons from the on-farm testing are informing the innovation finetuning process and on-going scaling process. Studies to capture the agronomic and socio-economic aspects of the innovation, farmers perceptions, innovation uptake and diffusion levels/ process and dis-adoption levels are ongoing to inform the ongoing scaling process.

column16: Vitamin A rich banana adoption in Cibitoke and Gitega provinces of Burundi
column17: A positive perception was observed among farmers growing vitamin A-rich bananas (pVABs) due to their early maturity, high provitamin A content, and long storage life. Adoption rates among initial beneficiaries were 45% in Gitega and 12% in Cibitoke. These rates were influenced by COVID-19 outbreak that hampered complementary innovations. Nevertheless, the willingness to adopt the pVABs was high (86-90%) across the sites. The adopters had expanded their areas under the pVABs. Diffusion from them to other farmers was also high e.g., two farmers reported sharing over 200 suckers with over 70 farmers in Gitega. Alternative uses including beer making had been invented by farmers. Scaling efforts have focused on establishing a robust seed system, engaging local leaders as influencers, and enhancing community awareness of the pVABs for reducing the high prevalence of vitamin A deficiency. Partnerships are being explored to leverage additional support for the promotion of adoption and use.

column16: Customizing Digital AgroClimate Advisory Mobile Application in Ghana to support agricultural value chain actors
column17: The Digital AgroClimate Advisory (HingaSmart) is designed to support agricultural value chain actors with bundled agro-climate advisory services. HingaSmart has been customized to generate context-specific agro-climate advisories for Ghana and other countries. To contextualize the HingaSmart app for Ghana, key crops from the three major Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZs) were mapped using the Ghana land use map. The highest-ranked major crops per AEZ were then subjected to a detailed analysis to determine key descriptors, including region, district, altitude, maximum and minimum temperature, fertilizer recommendations, crop water requirements, crop coefficient (KC) per crop stage, and the seasonal average KC for each crop. In the second year, additional location-specific data on crops and fertilizer recommendations were collected. This information was integrated with climate data to digitally deliver context-specific, location-based, and actionable recommendations along agricultural value chains in Ghana.

column16: A seed potato production planning and business decision tool: streamlining production and business decisions for seed potato entrepreneurs in Kenya and Uganda
column17: Private (small- and medium-scale) seed potato businesses in Sub-Sahara Africa have challenges in the planning of their production and its related factors (screenhouse capacity, labor, land, cash flow, storage capacity, …) leading to premature sales of seed potato due to lack of suitable land available for further multiplication or unsold stock of starter material, among others. Therefore, this seed potato production planning and business decision tool aims to support them to improve their production planning and its related factors while showing the profitability of their planned production schemes.  The development of a user-friendly online and smartphone application is foreseen. Moreover, this tool shows the business opportunities for small- and medium-scale seed businesses in Uganda and Kenya, but it can be used in other countries as well because the identified challenges cut across many countries. ;

column16: Amending the CG Climate Information Services for Rwanda using a downstream service for predicting fall armyworm and Striga infestation areas
column17: The digital advisory is an online and SMS service system that effectively delivers early warning and real time information on production stressors and advises small-scale farmers accordingly. Spatially explicit and multi-scale satellite data and climate and pests/weeds data are uniquely combined in a digital platform, and accurate advisory information is then channeled to end users. For instance, farmers could be advised to plant less cereal crops this season because of anticipated Fall Armyworm infestation for a specific location. Reliable information about abiotic/biotic production constraints will prove critical in managing sustainable cropland productivity. In due time, cropping systems information such as fields are under mono- or mixed-cropping or if fields are irrigated/rainfed will be added in order to improve pest and climate risk forecasting. The production constraints information over time can also be used to guide the scale out of climate and pest-smart agriculture, such conservation agriculture or the “push-pull” system.

column16: Green Pass Protocol to facilitate the exchange of phytosanitary clean germplasm from CGIAR centers.
column17: The CGIAR Greenpass Phytosanitary Protocol (CGPP) represents the systems approach to managing the phytosanitary health of CGIAR genetic resources by the Germplasm Health Units (GHUs). In 2024, an expert consultation on enhancing phytosanitary procedures for germplasm exchange in Africa was organized. The workshop brought together Heads of Quarantine Agencies from nine African nations (Benin, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda, and Zimbabwe), representatives from the Food and Agriculture Organization Regional Office for Africa, CABI, and the African Union Inter-African Phytosanitary Council (AU-IAPSC). The discussions converged on the pressing need for a harmonized framework to facilitate safe germplasm exchange in Africa. Expert recommendations included identifying priority crops for harmonization, capacity building for officials in plant quarantine agencies, raising awareness about CGPP, and establishing a protocol for accrediting germplasm health facilities as per the ISPM-45. The workshop underscored the critical importance of regional collaboration in improving germplasm exchange systems.

column16: Surveillance and monitoring the cereal rust diseases in Lebanon, Morocco, and Tunisia in 2022
column17: Tracking the movement of the wheat rust pathogens and monitoring their pathogenic variabilities are the main pillars in successful breeding for durable rust resistance and disease management programs. Despite the severe drought conditions in wheat growing areas in CWANA in 2022, the rust surveillance was coordinated by the Regional Cereal Rust Research Center-Turkey in Lebanon, Morocco, and Tunisia, following the BGRI rust surveillance protocols. The national rust surveillance teams at the Lebanese Agricultural Research Institute, Institut National de la Recherche Agronomique (Morocco), and INSTITUT NATIONAL DES GRANDES CULTURES-TUNISIA (Tunisia) conducted the rust surveys in target countries. The GPS coordinates of survey sites, the status of rust diseases, and crop phenology were collected and shared with the online Global Cereal Rust Surveillance and Monitoring System (https://rusttracker.cimmyt.org) following the BGRI standard rust surveillance protocol (https://rusttracker.cimmyt.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/11/2013-Updated-BGRI-protocols-v2-web.pdf).

column16: Characterizing rural food environments to identify factors influencing access to and purchase of nutritious food for consumers living in poverty
column17: The innovation aims to identify which factors in the rural food environment or food markets influence access to and purchase of nutritious food for consumers living in poverty. The innovation revolves around the idea of spatial mapping and market surveys of the food environment. It involves geospatial mapping of different types of markets and retail food shops, conducting a market census and survey of the market and retail food environment, and finding the food availability and price of food in local markets. Building on the evidence, we explore if an improvement in the food environment (e.g. diversity of food, placement of food etc.) leads to improved access to nutritious food by consumers living in poverty.

column16: Enhancing Early Generation Root Tubers and Banana Seed Production Planning and Business: Introducing a Seed Requirement Estimation (SRE) Tool for Public Sector
column17: National Agricultural Research Institutes (NARIs) face challenges in correctly estimating the required amount of sweetpotato early generation seed (EGS) every season due to lack of information on adoption of improved seed and varieties by farmers and the negative effect of farmers’ use of planting materials of unknown health status. This makes it difficult for NARIs to fully sustain their EGS business. Therefore, a user-friendly tool to estimate the requirements for EGS was developed and automated using Excel & web based. We also introduced the tool with other roots, tubers and banana crop experts. Each crop owner has developed basic version of seed requirement tool.  We have identified minimum viability of the product by interacting with potential users/clients by segmenting them across RTB crops. This will enable us to increase the adoption of the tool among potential clients/users.  3 customer segments were identified - seed producers, public sector and NGOs etc ;

column16: Validation and feasibility of AI-assisted dietary assessment mobile app (FRANI) for nutrient intake and personalized nudging to improve diets in female youth in Urban Ghana
column17: We previously developed and assessed the validity and feasibility of using innovative AI mobile technology that provides offline real-time diagnostics and tailored "nudging" on dietary intake as a strategy to improve diets and nutrition of adolescents living in urban settings in Ghana and Viet Nam. The innovative AI app FRANI (Food Recognition and Nudging Insights) was developed and tested in younger female adolescent girls aged 15-17 years with promising results. This study aims at further developing the app and evaluating it’s use in older adolescent females aged 18-24 years. Our hypothesis is that by addressing knowledge-related barriers to healthy food choices using information tailored to existing circumstances, adolescents will improve behaviors related to food consumption and diets, and potentially improving behaviors of their peers.

column17: Achieving impact at scale is one of the greatest challenges facing the research and development community, and ‘scaling of innovation’ is increasingly popular in the world of public research and development. However, innovation and scaling often mean different things for stakeholders representing research, development organizations, private sector and government organizations. To support organizations, project teams and their partners in developing a common understanding of innovation and scaling in the context of international development, an online course was developed. ; ; The course covers 6 Modules that answer questions such as:; 1.	What do we mean with innovation?; 2.	How do innovations scale as part of packages?; 3.	How do we ensure (gender-)responsible scaling?; 4.	How do we measure the Scaling Readiness of innovations?; 5.	How to develop evidence-based scaling strategies with partners?; 6.	Why invest in innovation portfolio management?; ; The course is available in English, French and Spanish and can be accessed through: https://innovationandscaling.thinkific.com/.

column17: Most projects, programs or organizations do not just manage one, but multiple innovations. Innovation portfolio management refers to managing a portfolio of innovations, innovation projects or interventions aimed at delivering (positive) societal impact. The main objective is to ensure that the innovation portfolio of a project, program, country or entire organization is healthy and delivers against outcomes and impact. It can support portfolio managers in strategic decision-making, prioritization (e.g. as part of stage-gating), risk management and resource mobilization around gaps in the portfolio. It can also support strategic communication about the innovation portfolio with external audiences such as funders.

column16: FISHTRAC: Real-time monitoring of water quality dynamics using fish-attached sensors
column17: Understanding how fish respond to stressors, such as water pollution and altered flows, is important to monitor aquatic ecosystem health. Fish’s behavioral responses are shown to be up to 100 times more sensitive to environmental stressors than any other established line of evidence, and they are used in various environmental monitoring, conservation, and research programs. Recent advancements in sensor-based telemetry studies showed fish behavior could be observed remotely in real-time, providing prospects for enhanced natural resource management activities. In the Limpopo River Basin, we support the University of Mpumalanga in developing FISHTRAC, a real-time water quality monitoring system using fish-attached sensors, and testing its functionality. In 2022, based on FISHTRAC’s prototype, we improved the system’s real-time monitoring capabilities. The improved FISHTRAC was deployed to a school of Tigerfish in the Crocodile River. In 2023, we collected more data to establish relationships between fish behaviors and environmental variables.

column16: Towards the establishment of Multifunctional Living Landscapes (MLLs): Considerations for stakeholder engagement for sustainable agroecological transitions
column17: Key activities implemented towards the establishment of Agroecological Living Landscapes included stakeholder (STH) mapping, the assessment of existing multistakeholder initiatives, and, in some cases, implementation of the early phases of a visioning exercise.  National and local multi-stakeholder events, review of existing documentation, semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions were used to varying degrees by each country. Agreements are now being negotiated with key national or local stakeholders in some countries (e.g. Tunisia, Kenya) to foster and clarify their active participation in the Initiative and in the decision-making regarding MLL identification and establishment. A rather large number of stakeholders were identified in each country during stakeholder mapping and a total of 1.346 individual Food System Actors (FSA) have been engaged by end of 2024 across the 7 countries. In 2025, a transition year towards the Multifunctional Science Program, most countries teams re-engaged with communities, refreshed the Vision-to-Action exercise and / or included new stakeholders. New countries (Colombia, new sites in Kenya and India) started the  Vision-to-Action process.

column16: Scoring of market smart varieties: A methodology to determine how well the varieties match with market intelligence and determine its impacts to farmers and consumers
column17: The Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning, and Impact Assessment component of the Market Intelligence Initiative is developing a methodology for rating varieties in terms of how well they match the market intelligence developed through the initiative; as a proxy for how impactful they might be for farmers and consumers, if adopted. column16: Rooted Apical Cuttings - cost-effective method for potato seed production in Sub Saharan Africa
column17: Work on rooted apical cuttings (RAC) has been featured in the poverty section of the CGIAR Flagship Report 2025, responding to the decision-maker question: “How can we stimulate rural job opportunities within agrifood systems for young people and women?”; ; RACs provide a low-cost, high-multiplication alternative for early-generation seed production, addressing several critical challenges, including high seed costs and low multiplication rates, weak early-generation seed systems, and limited rural employment opportunities.; ; Public-sector stakeholders—such as national ministries and local governments—are increasingly interested in embedding RACs into seed systems. For example, Ministries of Finance view RACs as a pathway to economic growth, job creation, and poverty reduction driven by local agricultural production, while Ministries of Agriculture emphasize their role in improving seed quality, boosting agricultural productivity, and reducing dependence on imported seed. These outcomes are central to national food security and rural development goals.; ; Similarly, the private sector sees RACs as a high-return investment opportunity within scalable and sustainable agricultural models that offer long-term growth and profitability. Seed producers and agri-tech companies can increase production efficiency by adopting cost-effective, locally sourced RACs, expand market reach, and integrate innovative technologies to further enhance productivity.

column16: Development of a non-invasive seed health testing protocols: standardization of Videometer multispectral Imaging for cowpea seed characterization for virus detection
column17: Seed quality is traditionally assessed using physical, biochemical, and molecular methods, which are often destructive, labor-intensive, time-consuming, and costly. In contrast, multispectral imaging with a videometer enables rapid, non-destructive seed characterization. This study used the VideometerLab4 to differentiate cowpea genotypes, healthy seed lots, and seed lots infected with bean common mosaic virus (BCMV) at different growth stages. Nine genotypes were mechanically inoculated at 7, 21, and 40 days after planting (DAP), with uninoculated plants as controls. The experiment was conducted in an insect-proof screenhouse at IITA, Ibadan, using a 4 × 9 factorial completely randomized design with six replicates. Harvested seeds were analyzed for morphometric traits (size, shape, color, volume, and orientation). ANOVA showed significant genotype effects and strong impacts of infection timing. Early infection (7 and 21 DAP) significantly reduced seed size (area, length, and width), increased deformation, and altered color (CIE Lab A and L), especially in susceptible genotypes. Protecting cowpea from early infection is critical to preserving both seed yield and quality. These findings demonstrate that multispectral imaging enables rapid, non-destructive detection of changes in seed quality. The results highlight the importance of early disease protection and support integrating imaging tools into seed health screening, breeding, and quality assurance systems.

column16: Effective biopesticides for the management of aphids and pod borers on food legumes for smallholder farmers
column17: Aphids and pod borers are key yield limiting factors on temperate food legumes like faba bean, lentil and chickpea. Besides direct economic damage, aphids are vectors of devastating plant viruses. Not much progress has been made to develop aphid-resistant crop varieties due to low levels of resistance available in the gene pools. Farmers in North Africa, South Asia and East Africa use synthetic insecticides to mange aphids and pod borers. This increases cost of production to smallholder farmers and also health risk during applications. Laboratory and field trials of essential oils extracted from indigenous plants and entomopathogenic fungi strains showed promising results to control aphids and pod borers. The innovation will be used to develop biorational pest management innovations that will significantly reduce pesticide applications.;

column16: System dynamics model developed to improve coordination between climate action and peacebuilding in support of social cohesion and sustainable natural resource management
column17: Combining systems thinking with co-benefits theory, a multi-scalar coordination model was developed to map potential synergies among actors implementing programs on various identified entry points along multiple dimensions of the humanitarian aid, development and peacebuilding nexus for preventing and recovering from environmental crises and conflict. Entry points for collaboration between the climate and peacebuilding sectors include climate and conflict risk assessments, the management of land and water resources, ecosystem restoration, nature-based climate adaptation, climate and conflict smart agriculture, natural resources governance, sustainable market development, and policy coherence between climate action and economic development models. Such coordination has the potential to bring social, economic, and environmental co-benefits, such as social cohesion and livelihood creation, while contributing to broader resilience and peace.

column16: AgIncentives policy indicators of Agri-Food Market and Policy Analysis Models (AMPAM) to assess potential trade-offs associated with scaling interventions and innovations along food value chains.
column17: An integrated framework of global and country Agri-Food Market and Policy Analysis Models (AMPAM) is implemented to assess the potential for and trade-offs associated with scaling interventions and innovations that create jobs, boost incomes, and reduce environmental footprints along food value chains. A key component of AMPAM is the consistent and comparable set of indicators of degrees of policy support to agriculture and food sectors by type of support, food commodities, and countries. This set of policy indicators has been prepared in collaboration with the AgIncentives Consortium (FAO-IFPRI-IDB-OECD-World Bank). Together with the agrifood market database and the AMPAM modeling framework, the policy indicator dataset will be a critical ingredient for the scenario analysis the Initiative will undertake to support decision-makers in assessing the full potential, scalability, market opportunities, priorities for, and trade-offs associated with incentive schemes, and investments and innovations.

column16: MiniSASS v2: An Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based water quality monitoring system
column17: The miniSASS (Stream Assessment Scoring System) was developed as a citizen science tool for monitoring the health of river systems and reflecting the water quality by assessing macroinvertebrates communities. The miniSASS samples the macroinvertebrate community in a river reach and compares the community present to the expected community under ideal natural conditions. The information garnered during a survey relies heavily on the accurate identification of macroinvertebrates by low-skilled citizen scientists. This leaves a potential for errors in identification which may impact the accuracy of results and, ultimately, of the river health assessment. In response, we initiated the development of the new version of miniSASS, the MiniSASS v2, a smartphone application with built-in artificial intelligence and machine-learning algorithms for the automatic, real-time identification of macroinvertebrates.

column16: Improving food safety through informed demand: System to catalyze consumer demand for safer food through broad-based testing and provision of information on the relative food safety risk of alternative products.
column17: The informed demand-led approach for the improvement of food safety comprises three key activities. First, reliable data on the level of food safety hazards or relevant production processes is collected across a set of foods within a category (for example, the level of aflatoxin in different types of grain or whole meal vs. refined flour; the hygiene practices of different vendors of fresh foods; the level of lead in different types of cookware). Second, this information is provided to consumers, who are expected to utilize the information to make safer choices. Third, additional rounds of information are collected at regular intervals (and again provided to consumers) to allow producers or markets with significant problems to benefit from corrective action. This approach aims to harness consumer demand for safer food to be translated into action, thus steering markets to provide safer food.;

column17: A production hub is a system comprised by different actors in an agri-food chain of an agro-ecological region who work together to promote sustainable agriculture. The FRESH initiative will implement the hub model for testing, validating, and scaling-out proven technologies for a greater impact in each of its focus countries, in more than one geographic location (production zone) in each country. FRESH researchers will develop and cater research products and services to promote efficient use of resources and adoption of safe and sustainable vegetable production practices. Hub implementation involves three stages: (i) establishing physical components (platforms, demonstration and extension areas); (ii) training extension agents, private sector, and farmers; and (iii) creating, promoting and strengthening local innovation systems. Actors contributing to the success operationalization of these hubs include NARES, members of relevant government ministries, farmer cooperatives and small holder farmers, the private sector, and FRESH researchers and research partners.
