column16: Good Agronomic Practices (GAP) package for smallholder vegetable farmers in Benin
column17: The good agronomic practices (GAP) package in Benin includes mulching, yellow and blue sticky traps, neem-based biopesticides, plant staking, and efficient application of chemical fertilizers specifically for two vegetables, chili pepper and gboma (African eggplant). The GAP packages were developed by World Vegetable Center as part of their work in FRESH during the previous CGIAR portfolio (2022-2024) and continue to be trialed and refined as part of their work in Better Diets and Nutrition. In 2025, the team established demonstration trials on the GAP packages in six locations in Lalo, Klouekanme, and Toviklin in South West Benin. The GAP packages are part of Better Diets and Nutrition’s end-to-end approach, an innovation which combines demand, food environment, and supply interventions to increase desirability, affordability, accessibility, and availability of vegetables and sustainable healthy diets more broadly.

column16: Introduction of legume vegetables in cereal production areas to increase availability of legume vegetables in Benin
column17: Crop diversification has many potential benefits, including but not limited to improving soil health, yields, and farmer income. Starting during FRESH in the previous CGIAR portfolio (2022-2024) and continuing in Better Diets and Nutrition, the World Vegetable Center is working with local partners to diversify maize-based production systems by intercropping with vegetables. This strategy was tested in Allada muncipality in Benin with legume vegetables (yard long bean and mung bean). In 2025, the team tested two more intercropping combinations, chili pepper with mung bean, and mung bean with maize, in demonstration plots. . Researchers are monitoring how this strategy can increase the availability of legume vegetables for consumers, among other outcomes. This innovation complements other supply-side innovations that are being co-developed and piloted in Benin by Better Diets and Nutrition.

column16: PROBFLO v2: A user-friendly environmental flow assessment tool for evaluating socio-ecological consequences of basin-level water management scenarios for transboundary natural resource management authorities
column17: The original PROBFLO was developed as a holistic environmental flow (e-flow) assessment tool. PROBFLO evaluates the socio-ecological consequences of various water resource scenarios and generates e-flow requirements on a regional spatial scale. It follows the ecological risk assessment exposure and effects approach, with multiple stressors, habitats, and ranked ecological impact relationships. Due to the complexity, PROBFLO is currently only used by skilled scientists. As a response to the demand partner in the Limpopo River basin, we are developing a new version of PROBFLO in collaboration with the World Modeler program. The new version will be equipped with a user-friendly interface and streamlined workflow to make the tool more accessible to stakeholders.

column16: Market-driven validation protocols for rice varieties tested across South Asia and Africa by IRRI and partners
column17: Rice breeding programs often struggle to develop varieties that meet diverse market demands and farmer preferences across different regions. To address this challenge, the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and partners developed systematic validation protocols that test new rice products against popular local varieties in real farming conditions. These protocols were applied across seven priority market segments in India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Kenya, Tanzania, and Mozambique, validating 21 new rice products through on-farm trials and farmer participation methods. The approach compares new varieties directly with existing market-dominant options, generating reliable evidence about performance and farmer preferences. In Kenya, this validation process contributed to the official release of three IRRI rice varieties by the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization. The protocols provide agricultural agencies and policymakers with evidence-based methods to accelerate adoption of improved rice varieties that better match market needs and farming conditions.

column16: SEED BRIDGE partnership model developed by IRRI to accelerate rice variety adoption through improved seed systems in Asia and Africa
column17: Rice farmers often lack access to improved varieties due to weak seed supply chains and limited partnerships between breeding programs, seed producers, and markets. IRRI developed the SEED BRIDGE partnership model to address this challenge by creating multi-stakeholder platforms that connect breeding organizations, national partners, private seed companies, seed millers, traders, and regulators. The model was tested through 18 strategic partnerships in India, Bangladesh, and Nepal, resulting in the production and distribution of 7,400 kg of high-quality breeder and foundation seeds. These partnerships strengthened early-generation seed production systems and supported small-scale seed enterprises, including farmer-producer companies and cooperatives, to become self-reliant. The SEED BRIDGE model facilitates germplasm access, creates market linkages, and accelerates the commercialization of newly validated rice varieties, ultimately improving farmers' access to better seeds and promoting faster varietal turnover.

column16: Using business analytical approaches to conceptualize the entire CGIAR portfolio along the two pathways of impact creation and development effectiveness leads to identifying organizational key performance indicators
column17: Searching for a simple road map to explain Genetic Innovation initiative linkages resulted in the creation of a two-dimensional process-based Theory of Change (2D-ToC). The 2D-ToC distinguishes between the main trust of a program or project, and capabilities that need to be developed or improved to achieve the main trust. In the case of Genetic Innovation, the ontological analysis has become the foundation for practically aligning initiatives and bilateral projects through a Program Management Platform. During 2024, the approach was expanded using business analytical approaches to conceptualize the entire CGIAR portfolio along the two pathways of value creation, impact or benefit generation and development or organizational effectiveness. This was done for both the 2022-2024 portfolio and the 2025-2030 portfolio. It was shown that portfolio analytics can be used to conceptualize the total CGIAR research agenda and identify Key Performance Indicators, that could be utilized across a hugely diverse research agenda.

column16: A data migration strategy for future Enterprise Breeding System users is formalised and allows for quick, efficient adoption of EBS
column17: Modern breeding is a data rich process, and requires data management software designed for the task of generating, tracking, storing and using the information produced by breeding programs for breeding decisions.  Many programs are currently not using a formal data management system; others are using older legacy systems.  With the Enterprise Breeding System becoming available, these programs can now adopt the new software.  Data migration into a new database is a complex process with many idiosyncrasies depending on how a breeding programs has been managing its data before adopting a new system, hence a clear and transparent strategy was needed.  Scope, process, and timelines will be defined so new adopters can quickly get value of the system. An important point of agreement for scope was the definition of a minimal set of operational data that would allow breeders to use the system within a year of beginning adoption.

column16: ECOSat: A satellite remote sensing-based carbon offset estimation system to help smallholder farmers estimate carbon offset potentials using freely available datasets
column17: Carbon credits can potentially be used in various ways to improve the livelihoods of smallholder farmers. They may incentivize farmers to switch to crop management practices that reduce the carbon footprint and improve soil health and productivity in the long run. The compensation could be disbursed directly to farmers or be used to improve advisory or community services and cover the cost of inputs. Since their parcels and total land area are relatively small, the monetary value of carbon credits for a farm household is also small. Hence, it is essential for the Measurement, Reporting, and Verification tools to be cost-effective. To address the challenge, we designed a satellite remote sensing-based carbon offset estimation system to help smallholder farmers estimate carbon offsets from conservation agriculture practices using freely available datasets. We tested the proof-of-concept system in Bajío, Mexico. This report describes the data and approaches developed as an early-stage innovation.

column16: End-to-end approach for increasing fruit and vegetable consumption to improve diet quality, nutrition, and health outcomes; whilst improving livelihoods, empowering women and youth and mitigating negative environmental impacts in Tanzania
column17: The end-to-end approach describes a combination of interventions at various points of the food system, namely supply interventions, demand creation interventions, and food environment interventions. Through a participatory process of co-development, which started during FRESH in the previous CGIAR portfolio (2022-2024), CGIAR researchers and local partners conducted extensive research that informed the development of this innovation. Now continuing under Better Diets and Nutrition, a longitudinal evaluation will assess the impact of the end-to-end approach on household vegetable production and fruit and vegetable (F&V) intake among women of reproductive age in Tanzania. The evaluation is being conducted among 2,611 households living in 33 villages in five districts in the Arusha and Kilimanjaro regions. In 2025, the supply interventions continued to be implemented and recent progress and results can be found in this year's report. The team published more baseline findings, focusing on the production of vegetables, fruit, and staple crops and the inputs used in production among different types of farming households in the study area. column16: Efficacy of soft chemistry pesticides, botanical oils and entomopathogens evaluated against cassava whiteflies
column17: Cutting dipping in Mandiplus and application of neem oils significantly reduced adult whitefly numbers 45 – 74% compared to control. Mandiplus alone was the most effective at 74% followed by Mandiplus + neem oil (61%), TopNeem Ultra oil (50%) and crude neem oil in ethanol (45%). Nymphs were also significantly reduced by 49 – 70% in treatments compared to control. Mandiplus + neem had (70%), Mandiplus alone (68%), TopNeem Ultra (56%) and crude neem in ethanol (49%). The root yield in kg/plant was significantly higher in Mandiplus and Mandiplus + neem treatments by 78 – 86% compared to control. TopNeem Ultra and neem in ethanol had yield increases of 18 – 19% though these were not significantly different from the control.

column16: integrated Future Estimator for Emissions and Diets (iFEED) inclusive assessment framework to inform policies for climate-resilient and nutrition secure futures
column17: The integrated Future Estimator for Emissions and Diets (iFEED) is an inclusive integrated assessment framework that combines climate-food-emissions modelling with land use dynamics, trade and nutrition analysis as well as expert judgement to develop policy recommendations towards a climate-resilient and nutrition-secure future. iFEED assesses both climate-smart agriculture and food and nutrient supplies under different climate change and policy scenarios. iFEED has been used in Malawi, South Africa, Tanzania, and Zambia. Through ClimBeR, iFEED is continuing to be developed in Zambia and is expanding to Kenya. iFEED is led by the University of Leeds (lead of ClimBeR Work Package 3) in collaboration with several partners, including the Food, Agriculture, and Natural Resources Policy Analysis Network, UK Met Office and other partners. A technical working group consisting of policymakers, researchers, and other stakeholders is engaged at every stage of the development process to ensure results are policy relevant.

column16: Fall Armyworm Innovation Platform for validating Integrated Pest Management packages through participatory engagement of researchers, extension personnel and farming communities in Kenya
column17: A Fall Armyworm (FAW) Innovation Platform was established by CIMMYT in 2022 at Kiboko, Kenya, in partnership with Kenya Agriculture & Livestock Research Organization (KALRO), International Center for Insect Physiology & Ecology (icipe), and Centre for Agriculture and Bioscience International (CABI). FAW management technologies from partner institutions were integrated into 16 different integrated pest management (IPM) packages (including native genetic resistance, biological control, biopesticides, intercropping, push-pull, and synthetic pesticides). All the blocks were artificially infested with egg masses of FAW. A field day was organized on November 8, 2022, where 89 farmers (20 female) and extension personnel from six counties in Kenya individually evaluated the IPM packages and provided their ratings/observations. Another round of evaluation will be done at the harvest stage by the same group on February 8, 2023, and the results will be used for identification and scaling of highly effective IPM packages against FAW.

column16: Digital Identities: Enabling farming data traceability using open data sharing protocols with self-sovereign identity in Mexico to allow individuals' control on their identity and shared information
column17: Self-sovereign identity (SSI) is a digital identity that is fully controlled and owned by the individual it represents. Unlike traditional centralized identity systems, SSI allows individuals to have autonomy over their own identity, what information is shared, with whom, and for what purposes. SSI is a relatively new concept, but we argue it has the potential to revolutionize how we manage identity and privacy in digital ecosystems. To explore the potential of SSI in smallholder farmers' data sharing and management, we partnered with Bluenumber Foundation to develop a data traceability pilot in Mexico for small-scale maize producers to manage their farm management data. We expect SSI can also help producers securely access financial and other services more easily through the certified digital identity.

column16: Risk-contingent credit product, aimed at increasing farmers access to production credit and protecting financial institutions against the risks of credit default
column17: Risk-contingent credit (RCC) is a linked financial product that embeds within its structure an insurance protection which, when triggered, offsets loan payments due to the lender. RCC mitigates drought-related agricultural risks and provides access to credit for smallholder farmers, requiring minimal collateral. Building on existing partnerships and field collaboration, the current project intends to (1) improve the RCC product to minimize basis risk in product design by incorporating key environmental variables from state-of-the-art remote sensors, along with measurements from weather stations; (2) integrate a gender dimension into RCC analysis by including intra-household and cluster-level randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to reach, benefit, and empower women farmers; (3) develop formal relations with an increasing number of RCC service providers for piloting RCC in Kenya, Zambia, and Ethiopia; and (4) build capacity on risk management through finance and agronomy trainings for farmers in Kenya and Ethiopia, and development of outreach and guidance materials.

column16: Meghdoot v2: An enhanced agrometeorological advisory app for Indian farmers
column17: Meghdoot is an Android mobile application that provides India's official agrometeorological advisories to farmers. Meghdoot was initally developed by International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics (ICRISAT) to support the weather data dissemination effort by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) and later transitioned to IMD. Since the last few years, International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) has been singificantly enhanced in collaboration with IMD to incorporate newer features based on feedback from farmers. Since its release in 2021, Meghdoot has been downloaded more than 400,000 times. The enhancements were initially developed under CGIAR Research Initiative on Digital Innovation to improve user interfaces and the overall user experience of the Meghdoot app by applying human-centered design approaches and improved hyper-local weather source data from IMD. In 2024, new features are added to provide more user-friendly, actionably advisories using AI and the Large Language Model approaches.

column16: Climate Security Observatory (CSO) for providing science-based, site-specific and actionable climate security risk information to policymakers to design and implement interventions for reducing conflict and climate vulnerability of rural communities
column17: The Climate Security Observatory (CSO) is an online decision-making support tool providing robust, localized, and policy-relevant evidence on how exactly climate security risks may emerge across different geographic contexts. It aims to answer several research questions on how the climate security nexus operates at the subnational level. To achieve this, the CSO performs a series of mixed-methods analyses (data-driven literature review, pathway analysis, social media issue mapping, governance coherence analysis, network analysis, spatial analysis, econometric analysis), before synthesizing outputs into an open-access online dashboard.

column16: Climate Security Index for policy makers and international governmental organizations to compare climate security in different areas and prioritize climate investments that will yield maximum benefits for conflict vulnerable people
column17: Climate variability and its impacts on natural and human systems are increasingly visible across the globe. Despite international attention towards this so-called climate security nexus, understanding of how climate, conflict, and resilience interact is sparse. This is partly due to a lack of sources that combine relevant data. The aim of this concept is to develop a Climate Security Index (CSI) that will allow academics and policymakers to conduct evidence-based research into an imperative global challenge. The CSI would be able to produce an aggregate, comparable, subnational dataset that provides relevant information for academics and policymakers to analyze indicators across the nexus.

column16: Early Warning to Early Action and Early Finance (AWARE) Platform for government, humanitarian organizations, and funders to anticipate and reduce the impact of disasters or crises before their occurrence.
column17: AWARE, an anticipatory action mechanism in disaster mitigation and response, helps reduce the impact of disasters or crises before they occur. AWARE integrates technology from space-based information for disaster risk management and local knowledge drawn from key actors and breaks silos across governing entities through the availability of such tools for early warning to early action. The platform uses an open-source large repository of earth observation for monitoring and early warning of floods, drought and landslides, and other data that helps to inform the climate, markets, health, nutrition, and population displacement indicators for timely early action and finance to save lives and build disaster resilience. The platform is the first of its kind globally that supports the use by government departments and agencies, humanitarian organizations, and funders. ClimBeR science contributes to climate resilient solutions that are just, equitable, and sustainable and that build resilience locally to save lives and livelihoods.

column16: Climate Smart Governance Dashboard for environmental policy makers to design and implement multi-sectoral, mid- to -long-term adaptation plans benefiting climate vulnerable rural communities
column17: The Climate Smart Governance (CSG) Dashboard provides accurate data on climate-related hazards, population vulnerability, forecast climate scenarios, sector-relevant data (water, health, agriculture, ecosystem), infrastructure and climate-related projects to support coordinated mid- to long-term adaptation planning aligned to global development goals. Specifically, it can help nations undertake the National Adaptation Planning (NAP) process. The CSG Dashboard has been designed with the NAP process in mind to provide a space in which public- and private sector entities can obtain and use up-to-date data to develop effective, well-coordinated adaptation policies; monitor and evaluate progress towards meeting adaptation goals; collaborate for effective use of resources; and share information on best practices and investment opportunities.

column16: Zambia Drought Management System for environmental and agricultural policy makers to design and implement science-based, integrated, and practical drought interventions benefiting climate vulnerable rural communities
column17: The Zambia Drought Management System (ZADMS), developed by IWMI with the Ministry of Agriculture under CGIAR’s ClimBeR and AICCRA initiatives, is a satellite-based platform providing real-time drought monitoring, seasonal forecasts, and district-level early warning bulletins. column16: An ODK-based tool for real-time surveillance and reporting of banana bunchy top disease by surveyors, quarantine and extension service agents
column17: The ODK-based surveillance tool was developed for the banana bunchy top virus (BBTV) surveillance to enable early detection, map the geographic spread of the virus, and deploy control measures. The tool also streamlines the minimum data set necessary for decision support and provides real-time access to data for the users and decision-makers. The tool was used to delimit surveys in Tanzania from 2022 to 23. The same was scaled in 2024 for use in Uganda and Zambia, and its use is continued in Tanzania and Nigeria to assess the BBTV status in over 300 locations in these four countries. Separate models were developed in Uganda and Zambia, and partners (Zambian Agricultural Research Institute - ZARI in Zambia and the Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries - MAIFF in Uganda) were trained in the application. The tool is now being used independently by partners after one training session with users.

column16: Real-time artificial intelligence driven diagnostic app that can be used to assess diets and nudge app users to make better-informed choices about healthy diets
column17: FRANI is an artificial-intelligence (AI) app for mobile devices that diagnoses diet-related problems for adolescents. The tool provides tailored nutritional advice tailored, allowing users to make decisions to improve their diets. Moreover, the AI tool could provide governments and development partners with real-tie diagnostics to strengthen surveillance systems in health and nutrition. ; ; In Sri Lanka, recent surveys have shown that adolescents may face nutrition-related health problems such as anemia. There is also a growing prevalence of obesity. This research proposal describes the preliminary acceptability, usability, and possible likability of a novel AI-based mobile phone app prototype to be developed for image recognition of food, provide feedback and motivate users to make healthier food choices and improve the lives of millions of adolescents. The proposal was co-authored with IFPRI FRESH researchers and staff from the University of Wayamba, Sri Lanka - who will carry out the research study in-country.

column16: Uber H3 level 6 hexagons Database for characterization of sub national units for key countries
column17: We develop a novel approach for spatial analysis based on databases characterizing sub-national units in various countries using Uber H3 level-6 hexagons—a spatial grid system. Uber's H3 system optimizes spatial data exploration, enhancing geographic information analysis across various data types: crops, livestock, population, and climate. Unique identifiers in H3 hexagons aid data aggregation, outperforming square pixels for broad spatial coverage. Note: Hexagon size may differ from actual pixels like SPAM; values vary by location and underlying pixels. Interpret as important indicators, not absolute values. Our database serves researchers, policymakers, and organizations keen on foresight analysis. We actively promote H3 system integration into existing models, offering documentation, tutorials, and support. Preliminary appraisals ensure system accuracy and reliability. This innovation provides invaluable insights using efficient spatial data analysis for foresight purposes, benefiting stakeholders.

column16: Standard Operating Procedures for field area measurement in field trials for agronomic gain key performance indicators assessment developed for researchers and extensionists
column17: Accurate measurement of crop cultivated area is essential for assessing various agronomic gain key performance indicators (KPIs) including yield, profitability, and resource use efficiency. Previous household surveys heavily relied on farmer-reported plot area. However, it has been reported frequently that farmer-reported plot area is often biased due to various reasons. Here, we describe procedure for a GPS-based field area measurement. Module 1 introduces the use of GPS devices as first option, whereas module 2 describes the use of application software on smartphones and tablets as second option. Here, we describe UTM Area Measure, an android application downloadable for free from Google Play Store, as an example. This module describes the procedures for downloading and performing the measurements with this application. There are many other applications, that have functions similar to those of UTM Area Measure. They can also be used to measure field/plot area

column16: Rikuy-Agrobio: a toolbox for in-situ agrobiodiversity monitoring
column17: Rikuy-Agrobio is a toolbox-based website that contains different methodologies to monitor agrobiodiversity. The tools contained in Rikuy-Agrobio allow agrobiodiversity monitoring from genes to landscape. This toolbox is widely promoted and in 2025 a Community of Practice was launched in Latin America to promote and expand its use. Furthermore, the toolbox was presented at several events, such as the ITPGRFA agrobiodiversity knowledge laboratory (https://www.fao.org/plant-treaty/news/news-detail/Agrobiodiversity-Knowledge-Lab-Connects-Regional-Innovators/es). The following protocols have been updated in 2025: Rapid Agrobiodiversity assessment, Quantitative red listing, Genotyping, Baseline catalogues and Participatory mapping – pGIS (see evidence).

column16: Farmer Interface Application (FIA) validated and operational for Fall Armyworm and cowpea pod borers and pod sucking bugs
column17: The Farmer Interface App FIA (FIA–niébé) developed to scout for Fall Armyworm (FAW) and cowpea pod bug (Clavigralla tomentosicollis). The FIA–niébé was demonstrated to farmers, extension agents, and researchers during several training sessions in Benin and Mali. Scouting for FAW eggs and neonates is difficult and time consuming. To optimize scouting intervals, it was hypothesizing that the optimum timeframe for the FAW female arriving to lay eggs in sown maize fields could be predicted. This was done by back-calculating from interval censored data of egg and neonates collected in emerging maize seedlings. Early time of ovipositing FAW after sowing was recorded in field experiments. Using temperature based phenological models it was estimated that about 210 accumulated degree days is needed for early detection of neonate larvae in the field. This work is meant to provide new insights on timely pest detection and to guide precise timing of control measures.

column16: Standard Operating Procedures and users guide for developing gender and youth responsive agronomic solutions for Use Cases in Excellence in Agronomy Initiative
column17: This Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) is designed for Excellence in Agronomy (EiA) Use Case teams with an interest in developing gender- and youth-responsive agronomic solutions. The SOP is a guide to help Use Case teams move from each step in their workflows when designing, validating, and piloting their Minimum Viable Products (MVPs) to ensure they can develop gender- and youth-responsive agronomic solutions by the end of their Use Case. This stepwise procedure first entails carrying out a diagnostic assessment of gender and generational differences in agricultural management practices and technology adoption and the factors contributing to these differences. These steps (6 total) to developing gender- and youth-responsive agronomic solutions are described with some detail in this SOP. The SOP has been used during the implementation of the integrated survey to ground the Use Cases. Reports from 3 Use cases are shown in the evidence.

column16: Validation trials for a hand-held decision support system for late blight management in Kenya
column17: This report presents the findings from the validation of a Decision Support Tool (DST) developed to optimize late blight management in potato farming. The DST, available as physical discs or an interactive mobile application, integrates host resistance, environmental conditions, and management practices to provide fungicide spray recommendations. Color-coded discs (red, yellow, and green) display spray guidelines that adjust based on potato variety and weather conditions, as informed by research or expert input. The objective of this study was to evaluate the technical efficiency of the tool, assess its efficacy in reducing chemical inputs, and identify potential areas for improvement. The evaluation was conducted on a sample of 61 farms from Kenya's mid- and high-altitude agroecologies, which represent the primary potato-growing regions in the country.

column16: Bundled financial and insurance product targeted towards female smallholder cattle farmers in Bangladesh
column17: This product provides finance for cattle fattening through a profit-sharing model. Eligible smallholder farmers receive cows purchased by the company and then sell them back to the company at a guaranteed price or at a higher price they find in the market. Farmers keep 2/3 of the difference between the purchase and sale price, and the company keeps 1/3. This intervention is bundled with insurance to protect the farmer against cow death. Other possible services include subsidized high-quality feed and growth monitoring to increase the value of the cow. Women will be specifically targeted for contracts to increase their empowerment in a sphere where they are responsible for physical labor. Better Diets and Nutrition are identifying and testing innovations, like this one, that have potential of increasing the access food market actors have to finance. Researchers are conducting a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 1,517 households across 105 villages in Bangladesh, which was started under the CGIAR Initiative on Rethinking Markets (2022-2024). Working closely with WeGro, an "agri fintech" based in Bangladesh, the team offered cattle financing through conventional loans or profit-sharing contracts that spread risk between the farmer and the financial partner and measured the risk preferences of the participating households. By the end of 2025, the results were not yet published but the data indicate that farmers preferred to take-up the livestock sharecropping model (39% of them) than a straight loan (30%). ;

column16: Outsourcing Innovation and Scaling Capacity Development in the Agricultural Research and Development Sector
column17: CGIAR and Wageningen University developed a series of approaches, tools and products aimed at strengthening scaling performance in the Research for Development (R4D) sector, including Scaling Readiness and GenderUp for Scaling. For these and other tools to be used widely in the CGIAR system and broader R4D sector, developing individual and team capacity at scale is essential. Several capacity development products have been developed and are being delivered. Examples include the online course on innovation and scaling, Scaling Readiness Training of Facilitators workshops, GenderUp facilitator training, and a course for innovating and scaling for social transformation in international food systems. However, CGIAR developers of these capacity development products have limited bandwidth to deliver these trainings at the required scale R4D organizations. We want to explore modalities where other organizations that could deliver these trainings cheaper, at the required scale, and in a sustainable way.

column16: Social behaviour change communication (SBCC) campaign on best practices in beef and pig production and marketing, targeting women and men livestock keepers in North-west Vietnam.
column17: Many livestock farmers in Son La province, northwest Vietnam, lack access to information about best practices for cattle and pig production and marketing, limiting their productivity and income. Under the Sustainable Animal and Aquatics Foods Science Program, and prior to that under the Sustainable Animal Productivity Initiative, ILRI, ABC and partners developed a social behavior change communication campaign to address this gap. The campaign delivers targeted messages on animal health, breeding, nutrition, and marketing practices through culturally appropriate channels. It specifically targets both women and men farmers from different ethnic groups, including Thai and H'mong communities. The campaign strategy was co-designed with behavior change specialists and local stakeholders to ensure messages are relevant and accessible to diverse farming communities in the region.

column16: Pig weigh band for use by pig farmers and aggregators in Uganda, to enhance productivity and transparency in trade
column17: In Uganda smallholder pig systems, the pig keepers usually do not have access to weigh-scale to obtain accurate pig weights. Knowledge of weight is important for both pig management decisions (such as determining drug dosage) and for determining sale price (which is based on estimated liveweight or carcass weight derived from this). To overcome this, a pig weigh-band was developed. A weigh-band is similar to a tape-measure, however it shows weight estimates of the pigs based on their heart-girth. The equation to predict weight from heart-girth was developed from  764 pigs of different ages, sex, and breed types, from 157 smallholder pig keeping households in Central and Western Uganda (see Marshall et al., 2023). The weigh-bands and an associated training manual have now been produced, and have been piloted with women and men pig keepers, animal-health care workers and aggregators.

column16: App for use by smallholder pig keepers in Uganda to determine the profit or loss of their household pig enteprises (Pig Profit $ app)
column17: Many smallholder pig farmers in Uganda keep pigs primarily for income but lack tools to monitor their enterprise's financial performance. The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) - under the Sustainable Animal and Aquatics Foods science program and prior to that the Sustainable Animal Productivity initiative -  developed this user-friendly mobile application to fill this gap. Farmers can input all pig-related revenues and costs, and the app calculates profit or loss over their chosen time period. Available in both Luganda and English, the app enables farmers to make more informed decisions about their pig enterprises by providing clear insights into economic performance. This digital tool addresses a critical need for financial tracking among smallholder livestock producers who previously had no systematic way to assess their business profitability.

column16: Processed (shredded) rice straw for improved dairy buffalo milk productivity, for use by buffalo farmers in Nepal
column17: Processed enriched straw is a new processing technique to improve low quality rice straw, which forms 70% of the daily diet of large ruminants in Nepal. In this process the straw is shredded using a shredding machine and fortified with 8% molasses, 1% urea and 1% mineral mixture. It is then compressed and bagged as mash or block. Feed industries procure rice straw from farmers in the harvest season, which will then be processed and sold to dairy keepers through their cooperatives in the lean season when there is acute nutrient stress for dairy animals.

column16: Improved Brachiaria and Guinea grass cultivars, suited to multiple locations in Nepal, for improved agronomic performance, animal nutrition and dairy buffalo performance
column17: Seven improved cultivars of Brachiaria and Guinea grasses along with local forages are being evaluated in multiple locations in Nepal involving farmers and other stakeholders, and best bet cultivars will be scaled for commercial fodder production. Evaluation of the forage cultivars is ongoing on station and performance of forage species/cultivars will be assessed by the farmers and other stakeholders visiting the experimental plots at different stages. The preferred cultivars will be identified for on-farm evaluation as outreach research activities. Use of the improved cultivars will lead to improved diets for dairy buffalo leading to improved productivity.

column16: A guide to developing quantitative tools for measuring gender norms in agrifood systems
column17: This Guide is intended for researchers and practitioners who wish to better understand and transform gender norms as the root cause of gender inequalities and women’s disempowerment in agrifood systems (AFSs). Understanding the impact of gender transformative interventions, as well as the links between gender norms and other AFS outcomes, requires high-quality data and measurement tools designed to measure changes in gender norms. Yet, prior to the development of this Guide, there was no existing, ready-to-use tool to measure and track gender norms specific to AFSs. To address this gap, the CGIAR Gender Equality Initiative developed this Guide, which contains step-by-step guidelines and templates to aid users in the participatory development of measures of gender norms in AFS and, where applicable, draws on empirical examples based on piloting of the Guide in Nigeria and Tanzania.

column16: Forage seed business models through policy influence and forage registration to enhance adoption of elite forages by forage seed businesses and livestock producers.
column17: Quality forages increase livestock productivity while taking care of the environment. Elite forages from selection and breeding require registration in countries to allow private sector uptake for business while improving access to the seeds by livestock producers. Fast tracking forage registration with the regulation entities in the respective countries including sharing policy briefs that highlight areas that require to be addressed is needed in order to support forage seed businesses and use. In addition, we must facilitate use through raising awareness with the livestock producers. We plan to scale across Sustainable Animal Productivity (SAPLING) and other countries registration and highlighting policy issues, where appropriate.

column16: Multi-stakeholders Innovation platform to support the scaling of small ruminant production technologies including vaccines and marketing in Mali.
column17: Multistakeholder platforms are used as a mechanism to harness collective action to address low involvement of grassroots stakeholders and empower livestock value chain actors to scale up innovations to increase livestock productivity. The main stakeholders of the livestock value chain delivery included small ruminant producers, private veterinarians, vaccine producers, feed and forage producers and sellers, traders of live animals, extension, public veterinary services, amongst others. Actors directly supporting farmers such as financial institutions and community leaders were also included. Multistakeholder platforms facilitate the delivery of livestock vaccines and the creation of business models for Brachiaria seed and fodder production and sale, and the market linkage between producers and traders of live animals. Multistakeholder platforms  serve as a mechanism for scaling all the innovation under Sustainable Animal Productivity (SAPLING) in Mali.

column16: High-quality Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR) thermotolerant vaccine to reduce small ruminant mortality
column17: Since 2016, the International Livestock Research Institute has partnered with Hester Biosciences Ltd of India, a private vaccine production company, to support the Central Veterinary Laboratory of Mali in optimizing and producing thermotolerant vaccine called “ILRI thermotolerant Peste des Petits Ruminants vaccine produced by the Thermovac process” developed by Internationa Livestock Research Institute and referred here as “ILRI protocol”. The proposed vaccine has proved considerably stable at ambient temperatures up to seven days, which has tremendous advantage in hot countries and in remote areas. The project has gone beyond technology development to identify and test components of new institutional model for delivering effective Peste des Petits Ruminants control services to small ruminant producers in Mali

column16: Capacity building of animal healthcare workers on pig herd health management
column17: Selected animal health care workers from Mukono and Wakiso districts were identified and trained as herd health champions. The training focused on herd health management concept and how to apply it at farm level. The trained herd health champions will train selected farmer groups on herd health management in two districts. This approach is expected to improve farmers’ skills and technical capacity to raise healthier pigs thereby improving their incomes, profit margins and food safety.

column16: Model farms approach to demonstrate benefits of an integrated herd health package on pig health and productivity in Uganda
column17: Using a farmer field school approach, four model farms were set up by renovating existing housing units through ILRI-farmer co-funding arrangement. The model farms were renovated to showcase integrated technology innovations (herd health package): improved housing, health, welfare, piglet care, biosecurity measures, improved feeds and genetics. The key elements of the herd health package include improved floor drainage, safe water, welfare, reduced piglet deaths & disease burden, improved feeding and breeding. This will be followed by learning visits facilitated by herd health champions. This is expected to spur adoption of the integrated innovation elements, which improve health, survival, growth rates and productivity.

column16: PigSmart digital extension platform for enhancing farmers knowledge in climate smart best practices in herd health, genetics, feeding and manure management.
column17: PigSmart platform delivers digital extension messages to pig farmers. It covers an integrated content that is delivered to pig farmers based on the stage of growth of the pigs. The messages include best practices in feeding, herd health management, breeding and genetics, manure management and heat stress management. The process of integrating and adapting the content followed key steps: (i) curation of research outputs on feeds, health, genetics, and heat stress, (ii) drawing messages from the research outputs, (iii) validating messages from the researchers and government extension  to ensure integrity of content, (iv) integrating messages premised on the different stages of pig growth, and (v) developing audio skits from integrated content in Luganda. A brochure on the integrated content was developed and disseminated to pig farmers in addition to the audio skits. The messages can be used by extension agents to train farmers on best practices in pig production.

VLPs play a critical linkage role between smallholder farmers and inputs/service providers, delivering bundled advisory services and technologies thus enhancing access to and uptake of appropriate technologies/inputs/services by smallholder farmers. VLPs apply entrepreneurial skills to earn sustainable income as they perform their agency roles.

column16: Feeding strategies based on locally available feeds, preferred improved forages and associated farmer-friendly training materials targeting women and men cattle and pig producers
column17: In the Northwest Highlands of Vietnam, cattle and pigs are characterized by low productivity and mainly fed with low quality forages, crop residues and food waste. Feed and forage quality is generally of low quality resulting in low livestock output. Assessments conducted in the region have identified the main feed-related challenges including winter feed shortage, poor diets, and low yield of available forages. Farmers also have limited knowledge on suitable forage types and management, feed processing and preservation, which greatly affects livestock productivity. Gender-responsive feed intervention strategies that can address these context-specific challenges, mainly winter feed shortage, can greatly improve livestock productivity and efficiency. Such interventions include capacity building of women and men farmers, extension & vet staff on utilization of locally available feed resources and purchased feeds, feed conservation, diet formulation, and feeding regimes, and promoting improved forage varieties (establishment, management, and utilization), for cattle and pigs.

column16: Tropical Poultry Platform (TROP) to catalyze a fair share of benefits to all poultry value chain actors in the Tropics
column17: The call for establishing the Tropical Poultry Platform (TROP) has emanated from the need to address the critical bottlenecks constraining the efficient and effective operation of poultry value chains in the tropics. SAPLING will identify key actors and catalyse TROP’s creation. Working alongside national, regional, and private sector partners, we will engage and collaborate with partners, exploiting synergies and complementarities and ensuring alignment and harmonization of actions with like-minded institutions. Key private sector players in the poultry industry, investors, farmers’ groups/associations, civil society organizations and non-governmental organizations. Considering the above, TROP focuses on existing innovation platforms as well as other initiatives. The partnerships to be forged could be crystallized through project implementation/investment proposal agreements, Collaborative Research Agreements, memoranda of understanding and/or simple transactional/contractual arrangements. TROP will be established as a membership-based organization that would mobilize resources both from within its members as well as from potential outside financiers.

column16: School-based model poultry farms for school-feeding programs to increase consumption of animal source foods (eggs) in primary schools.
column17: Malnutrition is one the important cause of morbibity and mortality in the world and highest malnutrion levels are still found in Africa. School-age children are at high risk of nutrition deficiency. Here we develop and test a scalable model for integrating poultry product consumption (eggs) in school feeding programs in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Tanzania. By feeding an egg/day/child through a multi-sectorial collaboration approach we will improve school-age children’s nutrition outcomes. The effect of one egg/child/day will be assessed.  The project will establish a poultry farm in each of the selected schools compounds that will hold about 1200 layers and part of the eggs produced from this farm will be supplied to the existing school feeding program, while the remaining will be sold to the local community to cover production costs.

column16: Tropically adapted and productive chicken breeds (for different flock sizes) that meet the breed and trait preferences of women and men chicken keepers in Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania
column17: Growth, egg production performance and economic feasibility will be evaluated for candidate breeds (strains) across different agroecologies. Brooded and vaccinated chicks (28 to 56 days-of-age depending on the country) will be issued to on-farm households the three agroecologies. The male chickens will be evaluated on body weight until 20 weeks-of-age, while the females will be evaluated on body weight and egg productivity until 72 weeks. The test will be integrated with promotion of access to inputs and support services (feeds, flock health, training, markets).  The strains will be tested at three different flock levels (with a  household receiving 25, 50 or 75 birds of a randomly assigned strain). This arrangement will allow development of viable business models that consider productivity levels, contribution to livelihoods (income, women empowerment, and nutrition), techincal feasibility and sustainability of impact.

column16: Training package on animal health, welfare and biosecurity for cattle and pig livestock keepers and animal health workers in Vietnam, for increased livestock productivity and profitability
column17: Smallholder farmers in Vietnam's Son La province face challenges in maintaining healthy livestock, which affects their productivity and income. CGIAR researchers developed a comprehensive training package that addresses animal health, welfare, and biosecurity for cattle and pig production. The package includes two components: simplified materials for farmers covering biosecurity practices, animal health basics, and welfare standards, and specialized content for veterinary professionals focusing on disease management, vaccines, and outbreak control. Originally created under the Li Chan project and enhanced through the Sustainable Animal Productivity program, this innovation provides practical knowledge to improve livestock management in northwest Vietnam. The training materials are being adapted into a mobile application to increase accessibility and reach more farmers across the region.

column16: Resilient and drought adapted forage cultivars and hybrids to improve productivity, income and livelihoods of households keeping small ruminants in Mali
column17: This innovation will promote up to 10 resilient and drought adapted forage cultivars and hybrids to farmers, technicians and forage seed producers who will be trained on forage (seed) production, processing and utilisation. Nine resilient and drought-adapted cultivars and hybrids of Urochloa (Brachiaria) and Megathyrsus (Panicum) grasses together with one forage legume (Crotalaria) are evaluated along with local forages (as control) at multiple locations in Mali to identify the best options for different regions and livestock systems in the country. Researchers and farmers visiting the experimental plots at different growth stages assess agronomic performance, the impact on animal productivity and environment, and profitability. The Tropical Forages Selection Tool https://www.tropicalforages.info/text/intro/index.html may be used for selection of cultivars and hyrids.

column16: Strengthened agribusinesses through agri-preneur incubation package, including components on gender responsiveness, bundled inputs and services and use of one network ecosystem in Tanzania
column17: Agribusinesses provide important linkages within value chains – linking farmers to product buyers and suppliers of productivity enhancing technologies, inputs, and services. Improving their performance, especially with respect to services they offer to farmers, therefore present significant opportunities. This is more so in a country like Tanzania where the private sector involvement in key commodity value chains remains weak despite the enormous potential of the value chains to improve smallholder access to inputs and services, incomes, food and nutrition security and create jobs. Some of the major current limitations to private sector growth include lack of knowledge and coordination among actors. Successful business training and coordination among actors have been shown to significantly increase the probability of success for both start-ups and established businesses. The “one network ecosystem" proposed here enables both.

column16: Internal Migration Propensity Index (i-MPI) tool to predict domestic migrants for better targeting of policy and development interventions
column17: An internal Migration Propensity Index (i-MPI) was developed in 2023 for Guatemala and Honduras, aimed at predicting permanent domestic migration at the household level, following the methodology of the e-MPI (to predict cross-border migration) and adapting it to challenges specific to internal migration. The index relies on a concise set of simple, non invasive questions that are easy to collect and that combined best predict the probability that at least one individual from a household permanently migrates to a different community within the same country over the next 12-24 months. During 2024 and 2025, the tool was validated completely out of sample (in a new panel household sample) and found to be both predictive of migration and outperform other indicators potentially related to migration. Such a tool can be used for both monitoring and targeting purposes to improve livelihoods at the local level and avoid the need to migrate.

column16: The CGIAR Climate Security Observatory - Displacement module
column17: The Climate Security Observatory (CSO) is an online decision-making support tool providing robust, localized, and policy-relevant evidence on	how	exactly climate security risks	may	emerge across different geographic contexts. It aims to answer several	research	questions on how the  climate security nexus operates at the subnational level. To achieve this , the CSO performs a series of mixed-methods analyses (data-driven literature review, pathway analysis, social media issue mapping, governance coherence analysis, network analysis, spatial analysis, econometric analysis), before synthesizing outputs into an open-access online dashboard. Within the CSO, a module for decision making on displacement-related is being developed.

column16: Pig multistakeholder platforms (MSPs) for enhancing value chain actor and stakeholder interactions for shared learning and enhancing visibility of the pig sector
column17: Pig value chain actors and stakeholders lack platforms to foster interactions and leverage a collective voice to address value chain constraints and influence or contribute to policies that impact the sector. Multistakeholder platforms provide an entry point for various stakeholder groups to engage with pig value chain players e.g. private-public sector partnerships, funding agencies, civil society, policy makers, and development partners. The multistakeholder platforms create networks and avenues for learning, knowledge sharing and empowerment of actors in the pig value chain. The MSPs were formed in 2016 and are still useful avenues for sharing learning on SAPLING innovations and enhancing visibility and voice of pig value chain actors and stakeholders.

column17: The Stability and Peace Accelerator (SAPA) is a joint initiative of the World Food Programme Innovation Accelerator and CGIAR partners that identifies and scales high-potential innovations strengthening food, land and water systems in fragile and conflict-affected settings. SAPA combines venture acceleration, grant funding, and science-based technical assistance to enable locally relevant, market-ready solutions across humanitarian, development and peace contexts. column16: Water security strengthening through disaster risk management in displacement-affected and host communities
column17: Ethiopia hosts over 916,000 refugees and asylum seekers , in addition to over four million IDPs . In many situations, this increases pressure on natural resources due to additional demands for food, water, and other natural resources. IWMI will use its expertise and knowledge assets to address water security challenges of host communities and develop context-specific solutions. The research on the vulnerabilities in this context has informed a package of nature-based solutions options and interventions together with potential areas for implementation. This is coupled with guidance for governance and actions prior to the implementation of identified nature-based solutions.

column16: The gender transformative qualitative field work methodology for fragile contexts to support research on interventions
column17: The gender-responsive and transformative qualitative fieldwork methodology spells out how the Climate Security Team’s research considers gender equity and/ equality to ensure compliance with the Gender Equity and Social Inclusion (GESI) principles. It seeks to promote gender-sensitive, responsive and transformative research that considers and assesses how particular intersections of identities and social positions impact access to rights and opportunities and how policies, programmes, services and laws affect people in different, context-specific or even unexpected ways. Understanding various intersecting systems of inclusion/exclusion and advantage/ disadvantage allows a better appreciation of the lived experiences of different groups of women and men and how all these compound to shape gender inequality embedded in gender norms and power relations within communities.

column17: Private sector engagement in livestock value chains in Tanzania needs strengthening  and therefore, there is need for advocacy to increase investments. This innovation is to enhance collaboration between key government, research and development actors in Tanzania, including the International Livestock Research Institute. It targets private sector investments for scaling of proven innovations involving women and youth. It aims to ensure a more productive, competitive and sustainable livestock sector in Tanzania. Working with relevant government agencies, the Tanzania Ministry of Livestock and Fisheries (MLF) will promote the delivery and use of innovation packages best suited for development of the livestock sector in Tanzania. It will strive to achieve impact through public-private partnerships (PPPs), networks, and complementary institutions across livestock research and development.

column16: Rice Activity Monitoring and Reporing System (RiceMoRe) website to allow multi-level data reporting and access to rice cropping maps for rice stakeholders in Vietnam
column17: The Rice Activity Monitoring and Reporing System (RiceMoRe) is an online interactive monitoring and reporting system that allows multi-level data reporting to produce interactive maps for rice status and coverage of rice production in Vietnam. It is designed to provide site-specific and real-time information on different aspects of rice production such as growth stages, adoption of mechanization, crop establishment and harvesting methods, and other techonologies adopted at farm level and present it in a more structured and visually appealing through maps. It aims to provide comprehensive information on rice production status and coverage to government institutions and staff, researchers, rice value chain stakeholders, and other concerned parties to inform local agricultural planning, decision-making, and other economic activities around rice. ; ; The RiceMore is now turned over to the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD) from continued implementation and scaling in Vietnam.

column16: Web Platform "Targeting Tools": user-friendly geographical information system tools for identifying suitable land areas
column17: Targeting Tools is a web-based Geospatial Information System (GIS) platform that houses a wide range of spatial datasets, both global and country-specific. It provides Land Similarity, Land Suitability, and Land Statistics tools for use on both desktop and web platforms.; The platform not only facilitates the visualization of datasets stored in its geodatabase but also supports user-uploaded raster format datasets. It enables various types of suitability or risk mapping analyses by combining different datasets.; Users are given the flexibility to establish their own criteria and thresholds to identify suitable areas. Moreover, these tools can be used to characterise the identified areas through the calculation of zonal statistics.  ; The tool allows for the integration of multi-dimensional datasets, including bio-physical (e.g. climate, soils, agro-ecology) as well as socio-economic (e.g. poverty, nutritional status, access to markets) data and thus for analyses along the different CGIAR impact areas. In 2025, we changed the whole architecture, and added a user guidance.

column59: The innovation advanced from testing to validation of policy and regulatory frameworks under semi-controlled conditions through demonstrated use, uptake, and forward action by policy actors with limited CGIAR involvement. In India, the WEAGov team convened a national-level policy dialogue in 2025 to translate WEAGov findings into concrete policy discussions on strengthening women’s participation across the agrifood policy cycle. Following short-term training, AWARD policy fellows successfully applied and carried forward the WEAGov tool in their respective home countries without ongoing CGIAR support. This demonstrates that the framework is sufficiently robust, transferable, and policy-relevant to be operationalized by users within real-world policy environments.; Together, these experiences show that WEAGov has moved beyond exploratory testing to validated use in semi-controlled policy settings, where national stakeholders and regional policy actors are able to interpret findings, integrate them into policy dialogue, and apply the framework independently to advance gender-responsive agrifood governance outcomes.

column16: Clustering smallholder shrimp farming for traceability and sustainability certification in Bangladesh
column17: Clustering shrimp farming for traceability and certification strengthens backward linkages with farmers via aggregation, disintermediation, technology transfer, and enabling certification. ; In ACI (Advanced Chemical Industries) Agrolink, clustering shrimp farming organizes groups of 20-25 farmers with contiguous ponds into a cluster with direct shrimp procurement to process by the company. The clustering shrimp farming is bundled with providing Input credit to shrimp farmers who buy ACI Animal Health’s feed, insurance, and formalization of contracts with clusters to support the buyback of shrimp. ; In BSFF (Bangladesh Shrimp and Fish Foundation), shrimp farmers commit to monoculture and are provided SPF-PL (Specific Pathogen Free Post-Larvae), cluster-level credit from designated banks, and a buyback arranged with specific processing firms. Farmers are persuaded to deepen their ponds to reduce water temperature variability that can trigger disease outbreaks, and facilitate increased stocking densities as a precondition to participate.

column16: Scaling up an information clearinghouse to accelerate agricultural technology adoption in Uganda
column17: The innovation described here is a crowd-sourced information clearinghouse, similar to trustpilot.com or yelp.com, to help smallholders secure quality inputs and services such as improved varieties and agronomic recommendations. Farmers use the clearinghouse to rate agro-input dealers as well as the products and services they offer; these ratings are then used to rank the dealers, with the ranking made available to both farmers and dealers in an appealing and marketable manner. A recent randomized trial of a prototype clearinghouse conducted with 350 dealers and 3500 farmers in 11 districts in Uganda found significant positive impacts on input use, enabling farmers to grow more food on less land, and indirect impacts on climate resilience and the environment. Dealers also received more customers, sold more, and earned higher revenues, although there are gender biases observed in the ratings for women dealers that can remedied through a more gender-intentional design at scale-up.

column17: The African Asian Dairy Genetic Gain (AADGG) platform is an International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI)-led investment by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF) that has been developed and tested in Ethiopia and Tanzania and scaled to Kenya, Uganda, Nepal, Nigeria, Zambia, Burundi and Rwanda. The platform uses on-farm performance information and basic genomic data to identify and promote wide use of appropriate superior purebred and cross-bred bulls for artificial insemination (AI) delivery and planned natural mating for smallholder farmers in Africa. The platform has different components: online and offline data capture system, data storage, analytics and genomic evaluation and selection of top ranked bulls and dams. The platform provides summary to enable informed decision and monitoring of progress. The platform has recently been revamped and a new digital application for capturing farm data in both cattle and buffalo developed and launched.

column17: CIAT started an interspecific breeding program with Urochloa brizantha (CIAT-6294 cv. Marandú), Urochloa decumbens (CIAT-0606, cv. Basilisk), and Urochloa ruziziensis (BR4X-44-2) in 1987 (Rao et al. 1998; Miles et al. 1995), and since then delivered numerous Urochloa hybrid lines to the private forage seed sector for further selection and commercialization. This has led to the release of the first Urochloa hybrid ever in 2001 in Mexico by Grupo Papalotla and to several subsequent hybrid releases thereafter. Today, 7 different Urochloa hybrids are being commercialized in around 70 countries globally, mainly among cattle farmers, leading to increased animal productivity, livelihood benefits, and positive environmental externalities.

column16: On-farm bean grain quality testing for smallholders with low-cost, mobile test-kits operated by local technicians from farmer organizations
column17: A novel service for smallholder farmers consisting of quick, on-farm bean grain quality testing with low-cost, mobile test kits operated by local technicians from farmer organizations. Currently, grain testing is done centrally at the association's warehouse or processing facility, and this process needs to be clarified for the farmers. To make the quality-testing process more transparent and create awareness of bean quality and price determination, the Rethinking Markets team in the previous CGIAR portfolio (2022-2024) performed at-farm (on-site, with the farmer) bean grain quality testing focusing on the top three quality parameters typically evaluated later at the processing facility and trained the local technicians from the associations to perform the test on-farm. Farmers registered the test results using an electronic form automatically delivered to the research team and local partners and left with their own printed copy. The innovation was designed to give farmers more knowledge about the quality of beans they sell. In 2025, as part of the work funded by Better Diets and Nutrition, the team published a manual for   trained technicians working with farmer associations, NGOs, traders, and research teams to use this innovation.

column16: Information service, targeting smallholder bean producers with strategic messages on good agricultural practices affecting bean quality from production to postharvest management, as a follow-up to existing training by farmer cooperatives.
column17: The innovation consists of images, voice, and text messages sent by phone on good agricultural practices in postharvest and bean cultivation as a follow-up to existing training by a farmer cooperative. In addition, the producers will be sharing information about crop development (like possible plagues, etc.) with the technical lead to prioritize assistance in specific regions. This innovation will strengthen the capacities of farmers to produce and handle the grains to achieve better quality and income.

column16: Testing Point of Cow, a penside diagnostic test, for treatment decision making in mastitis
column17: Point of Cow is a disposable chip manufactured by Fluimedix (Denmark).  It is a compact and user-friendly diagnostic tool that serves as a crucial component in antibiotic treatment decision making. The chip is engineered to detect both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria within 4-24hrs,  enabling quick decision-making on whether to use antibiotic treatment for mastitis. Point of Cow is primarily designed for dairy farmers, but can also be used by milk processors and quality control professionals in the dairy industry. It is a valuable tool for anyone involved in milk production and processing.

column16: Fish-based (ComFA+Fish) products to tackle malnutrition in Zambia
column17: Various fish-based products have been introduced in communities in several countries in Africa and Asia by WorldFish and partners. In particular, dried fish powder that utilizes nutrient-dense small fish can contribute to making healthy, affordable, and sustainable diets more accessible for vulnerable communities in low- and middle-income countries. In Zambia, nutrient-enhanced complementary foods for Africa and dried fish powder (ComFA+Fish) products and recipes for enhanced nutrition, particularly for mothers and infants in vulnerable households, have been developed and tested with mothers, caregivers, small-scale fishers, fish processors, fish traders, the private sector, and government representatives. These include fortified chibwaba fisashi, kapenta chutney, fortified maize porridge, fortified bean-vegetable soup, fortified cassava bites, and fortified nutri-biscuits. The ComFA+Fish products have been widely accepted in the communities around Lake Kariba in Zambia and were recommended for scaling in communities where malnutrition is high.

column16: Gender-transformative approaches to address inequalities in food, nutrition and economic outcomes in aquatic food systems
column17: Gender transformative approaches (GTAs) represent a powerful tool for addressing the root causes of women's disempowerment and gender inequality. GTAs facilitate critical reflection on gender and social norms, fostering transformative changes in harmful masculinities and societal norms, leading to better lives and livelihoods for women and youths, ownership of assets, and participation in decision-making. To maximize effectiveness, GTAs necessitate integration with technical innovations, offering solutions to both technical and social constraints. GTAs involve the use of experimental learning and capacity building, collective action and multistakeholder dialogue, and a blended learning approach. GTAs-related activities may include conducting comprehensive structural and intersectional gender analyses to comprehend the complex context and the multiple dimensions and layers of inequality and power. They may also involve engaging and enhancing the capacities of various stakeholders, including local actors, men, boys, women, community members, local organizations, traditional leaders, and policymakers, to drive and sustain the change process.

column16: Improved chickens, animal services and markets for women farmers, delivered by women veterinarians in Tanzania
column17: A package combining gender accommodative and transformative approaches to deliver improved chickens, animal services and markets to women farmers by women veterinarians. Gender accommodative approaches were adopted to enhance the business and chicken management skills of the women vets. Gender transformative approaches (in this case social media) were adopted to address gender norms that make women’s involvement in chicken business socially inappropriate. Restrictive gender norms are considered the root cause of gender-based disadvantage; unlike gender accommodative approaches, gender transformative approaches aim to change such restrictive norms for lasting social change.

column16: Women's and Men's Political Participation Training Curriculum
column17: Women’s and Men’s Political Participation Trainings are curricula co-designed by ActionAid Nigeria and CGIAR researchers to strengthen women’s sense of collective efficacy and leadership skills, and to increase men’s support for women’s voice and agency. Women's exclusion from civic spaces often leads to policies that inadequately address issues vital to their well-being, such as provision of public services (e.g., healthcare, education, agricultural extension, etc) and infrastructure. Women's political participation remains low for several reasons, including lack of resources, time and information; social norms that discourage women's involvement in politics; and psychological barriers that make women doubtful of their ability to influence change. The women's curriculum is designed to counteract the psychological and social barriers to women's political participation. Meanwhile, the men's curriculum is designed to enhance the support that women receive from their husbands to participate politically by training men on the benefits of women's political participation for their families and communities, as well as how to operationalize this support for women’s benefit.

column59: The training manuals for a five-month curriculum targeting women and their husbands were initially validated through a large-scale randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted with strong CGIAR support between May 2023 and March 2024, reaching over 5,000 women in Southwest Nigeria. column16: A refrigeration-equipped truck and logistical support system for fruit and vegetable farmers and retailers to transport and preserve their perishable produce stored in standardized plastic crates
column17: Food loss is a significant source of economic inefficiency in value chains. In Nigeria, fruit and vegetable and other nutritious, perishable foods are lost after harvest largely due to inadequate postharvest handling or low adoption of post-harvest management technologies including drying, packaging, storage and cooling technologies such as temperature-controlled transportation and cold storage. One innovation that can overcome this barrier is refrigeration-equipped transportation for vegetables in standardized plastic crates, also known as cool transportation. Cool transportation can preserve the quality of vegetables when transporting them over long distances from production sites to large demand centers. Post-harvest losses in quality and quantity can be reduced to a minimum to benefit producers and consumers. In addition, preserving product quality is expected to increase incentives to enhance product quality. Researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition, previously with the CGIAR Initiative on Rethinking Markets (2022-2024), conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to measure the impacts of cool transportation on outcomes such as income, employment, food security, and nutrition on marketers and producers in three vegetables markets in the northeast region of Nigeria. In 2025, researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition continued their analysis on the economic impacts of the innovation. The results are not yet published, but they conclude that sales price, revenues and profits significantly increased for the marketers who had access to cool transportation. About 66% of the increase comes from cooling; only 34% from transportation. Results also indicated that the market price responds to improved information on the signal of product quality.

column16: Plastic crate rental service for farmers and retailers to circumvent post-harvest losses in the transportation of tomatoes in Nigeria
column17: Postharvest loss remains a critical challenge in sub-Saharan Africa, particularly in Nigeria, where it exacerbates food insecurity and economic vulnerabilities. Postharvest packaging technologies, like reusable plastic crates (RPCs), are a strategy that has shown to drastically reduce food loss of tomatoes during storage and transportation. In Nigeria, the adoption rates of the RPCs remain low because the price is too high for most farmers and retailers and target users do not understand the benefits of using the crates instead of traditional raffia baskets. Researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition are identifying and testing promising innovations, like RPCS, that can reduce food loss and waste of nutritious foods. In 2025, researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition published results from an adoption study on the use of crates offered through a rental service to tomato farmers. The analysis of data from 1,704 farmers indicate that farmers engaged in long-distance sales were more likely to adopt RPCs, motivated by the potential for higher price premiums and reduced losses during transit. High acquisition costs and limited availability in rural areas of the RPCs were two barriers to adoption. The overall study findings also highlighted the importance of irrigation practices, membership in farmers’ associations, and proximity to major output markets as key drivers of the use of RPCs.

column16: Climate+ platform to generate and provide farmers with Agro-advisories to address dynamic weather conditions and potential climate-related risks through printouts and/or SMS in the Philippines
column17: Climate+ is a digital climate intelligence platform that provides rice farmers with timely weather forecasts, early warnings, and tailored farming recommendations through mobile SMS and printed materials. Developed by CGIAR's International Rice Research Institute and Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT, the platform addresses the challenge of unpredictable weather patterns that threaten rice production and farmer livelihoods. The system integrates local weather data with crop management expertise to generate actionable advice on planting dates, irrigation timing, and pest management. Currently deployed across rice-growing regions in the Philippines, India, Vietnam, Indonesia, and Bangladesh, Climate+ helps vulnerable farming communities make informed decisions to reduce climate-related production risks and improve crop resilience.
