column16: Combining improved vegetable seed varieties with extension support and certification of smallholder farmers for greater and more efficient vegetable productivity and marketing.
column17: Two main innovations are improved seed varieties and the extension approach of the East West Seeds - Knowledge Transfer (EWS-KT) . The improved vegetable seed varieties result from advanced breeding techniques by East-West Seed with enhanced traits like yield, disease resistance, and adaptability to diverse conditions. Improved vegetable seed varieties empower smallholder farmers' production capacity, increasing productivity while conserving resources. This ensures that agriculture remains at the forefront of sustainable development and food security. The extension approach provides timely, accessible, and tailored information to smallholder farmers via EWS-KT’s extension agents, enhancing their decision-making and crop management. It also encompasses the innovative approaches of publicly certifying trained farmers – to increase innovation diffusion and product value – and educating smallholder farming households to optimize income use through an inclusive decision-making process. These innovative approaches hope to empower farmers with actionable knowledge for sustainable farming that can better their livelihoods. column16: Simple, quality monitoring devices paired with a data collection application at milk collection centers in Uganda to differentiate quality and incentivize smallholder dairy farmers to supply better quality milk
column17: The proposed innovation involves making quality visible at milk aggregation points by installing simple quality monitoring equipment. Installing milk analyzers at milk collection centers will enable quick and easy testing of milk delivered by smallholder farmers on compositional quality of the milk, such as butter fat and Solid Non-Fat (protein, carbohydrates, and minerals). The milk analyzer will be paired with a custom application that runs on a tablet computer that can be used to keep track of milk samples. This will enable milk collection centers to increase the quality of their aggregate milk and negotiate a quality premium to processors demanding high-quality milk. (Part of) this premium can be passed on to farmers to encourage them to supply better-quality milk.

column16: Extension and sensitization campaign for smallholder dairy farmers that explains various strategies for increasing the compositional quality of milk, such as choice of animal breed, pasture management, and supplementary feeding.
column17: Extension and sensitization campaigns targeting smallholder dairy farmers generally focus on milk sanitation, highlighting the importance of washing udders and using clean and appropriate receptacles such as steel buckets and milk churns. Processors indicate that milk sanitation is fine, but the quality of milk in terms of composition (butter fat content and solid non-fats such as proteins, carbohydrates, and minerals) often needs improvement. We pilot a short, engaging video that explains various strategies that smallholder dairy farmers can use to increase the compositional quality of milk, such as choice of animal breed, pasture management, and supplementary feeding. By better aligning the quality demands of processors with the supply of raw milk, processors can produce more at a lower cost, and these rents can then be redistributed throughout the value chain.

column16: The EzyAgric app, designed by CIAT, provides smallholder farmers with an integrated service platform to support farm management and good agricultural practices, and access to agri-inputs and credit in Uganda.
column17: The EzyAgric is an App accessible on the Google Play Store, bundling various digital services targeting farmers and agri-input merchants. The services include Farm Manager for undertaking a Cost Benefit Analysis, and proper record management is accessed; Agri-shop, where a platform to digitally purchase genuinely affordable price agri-inputs from certified bulk agro-input manufacturers while providing an end-to-end feedback loop and a traceability trail; EzyCredits where farmers receive credits calculated based on the records generated from Farm Manager and Agrishop transactions as collateral, redeemable for purchase exclusively via the Agri-shop; Agri-Extension provides on-demand information and training tailored to specific agronomic needs. The Produce Market links farmers to aggregation centers established around off-takers and payments made directly to the farmer’s phone. A toll-free call and SMS platform is provided where non-smartphone farmers can access the services. The working model integrates women and youth with smartphones as community agents/service providers.

column16: Toolkit for conceptualizing and measuring effective voice and agency of women in climate-related governance at the individual and group levels
column17: This CGIAR innovation provides a comprehensive framework and set of tools for conceptualizing and measuring women's empowerment in governance, focusing on individual and collective agency beyond the household. Grounded in Kabeer’s empowerment framework, it highlights the interplay of resources, agency, and achievements at both individual and group levels. The toolkit operationalizes key concepts such as collective efficacy, action, and achievements, integrating tangible and intangible resources like social capital. Case studies from India, Guatemala, Uganda, and Nigeria illustrate its application, providing nuanced insights into how group dynamics, organizational structures, and decision-making processes shape empowerment outcomes. The innovation bridges gaps in understanding collective agency, offering participatory and mixed-method tools for analyzing women's roles in climate-related governance and other domains. By advancing measurement and application, this toolkit empowers practitioners, researchers, and policymakers to foster gender-equitable governance systems that enhance women's voice, agency, and community impact.

column16: Optimal groundnut plant density for improved grain yield, fodder availability and quality in smallholder farming systems of northern Ghana
column17: This innovation addresses the challenge of low grain yield and fodder availability in groundnut-small ruminant farming system in northern Ghana. Traditionally, smallholder farmers plant groundnut at a density of less than 10 plants/square meter. Planting ground at a density of 22 plants per square meter increases the rate of canopy closure over the soil surface which protects the soil from erosion, improves water infiltration as well as soil moisture retention, increases grain and fodder yields. The plant density of 22 plants per square meter can be achieved by either sowing the groundnut seed at a spacing of 30 cm inter-row × 15 cm intra-row or 40 cm inter-row × 10 cm intra-row. Feeding groundnut fodder generated from the 22 plants per square meter to sheep increases dry matter digestibility, live weight gain and nitrogen concentration of manure relative to feeding those generated from the farmer practice.

column16: Best Management Practices (BMPs) to strengthen the smallholder's aquaculture sector in Zambia and Malawi
column17: A series of Better Management Practices (BMPs) for smallholder fish farming in pond-based systems has been developed, drawing from field experiences and empirical evidence. These BMPs cover biosecurity, sex-reversed fingerlings for uniform growth, pond construction, species selection, stocking, feeding, harvesting, and marketing.; To enhance accessibility, the BMPs have been compiled into a manual, translated into local languages, and tailored to smallholders, particularly women. The manual serves as a guide for sustainable fish production, such as tilapia, benefiting aquaculture technicians, NGOs, and private sector stakeholders.; Adopting BMPs can significantly improve aquaculture in Africa, where smallholder fish farming has high growth potential, contributing to poverty reduction and food security. By supporting small and medium-sized aquaculture enterprises, BMPs help increase fish production, strengthen local economies, and enhance the availability of fish products in the region.

column16: Political Economy and Policy Analysis (PEPA) Sourcebook: A guide to generating evidence for National Policies and Strategies (NPS) for Food, Land, and Water Systems Transformation
column17: Food system transformation require reforms at global, national, and local levels to address prevailing structural weaknesses exacerbated by multiple crisis. As context matters, the question of what works where, why, and how for scaling innovations for achieving impact requires the application of political economy and policy analysis. Evidence-based from political economy analysis are critical to understanding the [dis-]enabling policy, institutional and governance conditions contributing to the success or failure of development interventions and innovations. This Political Economy and Policy Analysis (PEPA) Sourcebook for food systems transformations is a unique collection of frameworks and analytical tools for unraveling the interaction between policies and economic processes to unpack the power relationships, ideas, policy risks and decision making. This spans across food and nutrition; land and water; and climate and ecology systems to design politically feasible and technically sound development programs for achieving greater impact at the national and local levels.

column16: Development and Application of a Quantitative Tool for Measuring Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Among Animal Health Professionals
column17: It is important to understand how and why antibiotics are used. Usage of such can be categorized into three key areas:;     Knowledge: This involves assessing what veterinarians, farmers, and other stakeholders know about antibiotics and how resistance develops.;     Attitudes: Understanding the attitudes of individuals within the target population towards antibiotic use.;     Practices: Examining how antibiotics are prescribed and used in practice.; Collecting this information can be accomplished through Knowledge, Attitude and Practice surveys. While many studies use the Knowledge, Attitude and Practice surveys, they often fail to collect data comprehensively or use unvalidated instruments. To address these shortcomings, we aim to develop a Knowledge Attitude Practice survey, tailored for small-holder dairy farmers and veterinarians in Kenya. The project also explores the application of Item Response Theory (IRT) modeling in evaluating measurement scales.

column16: Novel stress tolerant (abiotic and biotic), highly productive and resource efficient forages to drive livestock production and productivity for market oriented small and medium, size farm operations.
column17: Good quality feed year-round is limiting livestock productivity on-farm and resource use in farms of small to medium size. Feed production can amount to 50 to 70% of livestock production costs. Forages are a means to overcome the feed gap, and resilient forages responding to different abiotic and biotic stresses, including low soil fertility, drought / excess water, pest diseases, are essential, increasing livestock productivity by up to 15%. To scale such technologies, suitable entry points i.e., market-oriented livestock production particularly dairy are required. Enablers are animal genetics and health technologies which capitalize on the improved feeding as well as capacity and dissemination channels such as cooperatives and functional seed supply systems. We are using a diversity of advanced forages which have a good availability of seed and/or planting material and demand pull through livestock production in Kenya; at the same time a pipeline for improved forages is being maintained.

column17: The innovation is a bundle of three technologies for intensification of maize-small ruminants farming system in northern Ghana. The basal NPK fertilizer timing focuses on applying the fertilizer at planting stage of maize to reduce nutrient stress especially during the emergence-vegetative stage, enhance nutrient use efficiency and yield. Intercropping of cowpea at one week after planting of maize as a living mulch provides soil surface cover, increases soil moisture retention, adds nutrients through biological nitrogen fixation, suppresses weeds growth, and increases yield and food diversity. Harvesting of maize leaves below the cob leaf at silking stage (Leaf stripping) offers quality forage for livestock without compromising grain yield. The stripped maize leaf forage has a 40% higher crude protein content than the crude protein content of feed required for the body maintenance of livestock. Feeding strip maize leaf to small ruminants increases live body, slaughter, and carcass weights.

column16: Unlocking indigenous plants as innovative solutions for restoring agro-ecological zones under changing climate in the dry areas
column17: In response to  rangeland degradation, conventional practices involving exotic species like Acacia saligna and Atriplex nummularia have exacerbated ecological imbalances by endangering local flora and fauna and diminishing biodiversity. While developing the Tunisian National Strategy for Advancing Feed and Forage Resources in Tunisia, ICARDA proposed innovative solutions centered on the reintroduction of indigenous species. These were carefully selected to thrive in specific agroecological zones addressing key constraints, and which will be implemented by the Office of Livestock and Pastures and other national institutions. Drivers of loss of indigenous species planting include limited seed availability, lack of awareness, and entrenched institutional behavior. Therefore, our strategies involve genetic source scanning to match indigenous species with environmental conditions, raising awareness about indigenous species' benefits, and efforts to change institutional behavior. Additionally, we are exploring ways to enhance seed collection and multiplication. This approach revitalizes degraded rangelands, contributing significantly to climate change mitigation. ;

column16: Co-development and delivery of agro-climatic bulletin (ACB) through public systems to provide climate advisory to inform local agricultural planning, decision making, and adoption of climate adaptive farm practices in Vietnam
column17: The agro-climatic bulletin (ACB) is an agro-advisory tool and system based on a seasonal, monthly, and 10-day weather forecast that aims to provide climate advisory services to local agricultural insitutions, officials, and farmers in Vietnam. It is being co-developed and delivered through the public systems in Vietnam where sub-national offices are integrating the tool on their local agricultural development planning and decision-making. To date, the ACB has reached 318,390 farmers.It received funding from the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development (MARD), now the Ministry of Agriculture and Environment (MAE), for 2023–2025 to implement and scale operations across 13 provinces in the Mekong River Delta, and for 2026–2028 to expand nationwide.

column16: Digital information system for rice product labeling of carbon-footprints based on yield recovery (DISPLAY)
column17: The carbon footprint calculator tool for the rice value chain embeds product-scale emission information into a Quick Response (QR) code that can be displayed on the rice package for transparent tracking and tracing. ; ; The interface guides users through each step of the field management activities and post-harvest processing that are relevant for measuring the carbon footprint. A selection of default values have been provided based on empirical measurements from scientific experiments or sourced from scientific literature. It allows users the flexibility to enter their own measured values or values from literature that have not been included by default.; The output provides the carbon footprint from the individual stages of the value chain and allows for comparison across different management options for use as a decision tool.

column16: COMPARE Excel tool: A cost-benefit and GHG analysis software (Prototype) developed by IRRI and UNIQUE for automated mitigation project evaluation, originating from CGIAR research for use in Vietnam.
column17: The Cost-Impact Analysis for Emission Reduction Projects (COMPARE) is a tool developed by UNIQUE Forestry and Land Use in conjunction with International Rice Research Institute. This tool is a Microsoft® Excel workbook with built-in formulas and functions that allow automatic calculation of Cost Benefit Analysis indicators and GHG emissions according to the user's defined inputs.; ; This Excel Tool is designed to provide a Cost Benefit Assessment showing the economic and carbon impacts of different rice management practices at a regional level in Vietnam. The tool is designed to cater to different user types and allows full flexibility to adapt the tool for advanced users. It enables the user to estimate the benefits, costs, and greenhouse gas savings in a "Business As Usual" (BAU) scenario (broadly reflecting the current mix of rice production methods) and a “Project” scenario (reflecting a desired mix of rice production methods).

column16: Development and provision of weather forecast-based agro-advisories to farmers in Bangladesh through the Agvisely mobile application
column17: "Agvisely" is an agrometerological advisory tool that was developed and released in 2019 jointly by the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE) and the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD). Currently, it provide advisories to farmers planting crops including rice, maize, and mungbean through an interactive website that can be access by extension agents to provide information to farmers in Bangladesh as a whole. The advisories are based on a automated 5-day weather forecasts using biological threshhold and forecast data. The tool aims to help the farmers to increase fertilizer use efficiency, irrigation management, and pest management leading to increase in yield and income. ; ; Currently, the Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) Initiative is allocating resources for the continuous development, improvement, maintenance, and scaling of Agvisely tool to achieve impacts at scale.

This methodology can be applied to large and small-scale or micro-scale projects or PoAs.

column16: Provision of agro-advisories to mungbean farmers in Bangladesh through interactive voice response (IVR) system
column17: The interactive voice response (IVR) system provides automated real-time weather alerts, warning farmers to harvest their mung bean ahead of forecasted heavy rainfall events which could damage their crop. Harvest warnings are voice calls that are based on a 5-day weather forecasts. It is available and accessible to farmers in Bangladesh without smartphones. ; Currently, the Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) Initiative is allocating resources for the continuous development, improvement, maintenance, and scaling of the system to achieve impacts at scale. Provision of harvest warnings to mungbean farmers were continued and partnerships for sustainably financing the business model around the innovation was secured.

column16: Brachiarea integration into maize-based cropping system for smallholder farmers multi-benefit, resilient and climate smart agriculture
column17: In Ruzizi plain of DRC, research activities on the integration of Brachiarea into maize-based system to mitigate the the major agricultural constrains in the region (animal feed lack, soil fertility depletion and climate change) are ongoing. So far, the most performing Brachiarea varieties were identified, maize and Brachiarea productivity, carbon incorporation into the soil and soil coverage when Brachiarea is integrated into the system were assessed. The feasibility and productivity of maize resowed in Brachiarea plot established during the last cropping season were evaluated. The feasibility and productivity of replicating Brachiarea suckers to overcome the issue of no seed availability and high cost were assessed and farmers’ impression and opinions on Brachiarea-maize intercropping system were received and integrated in next step of the technology development. During last season, we carried out experiment and identified the best and cost-efficient way to control weeds at early growth stage, in the Brachiarea field.;

column16: Restoring rangelands: the art of flexible livestock grazing to restore soil health, ecosystem function and ecosystem services
column17: Nomadic livestock systems have evolved over millennia in response to seasonal rainfall patterns. In Tunisia, where approximately one-third of the land is semi-arid, arid, or desert, degradation poses a significant challenge. The Gdel resting technique, a low-cost intervention, has been part of the national strategy for rangeland improvement since 1990, and is implemented by developing agencies for rangeland improvement. The pastoralists whose animals would normally graze in these areas are supported through the provision of feed supplements for 3 consecutive years. However, the implementation had its shortfalls. In 2018, unexpectedly high rainfall led to abundant vegetation growth, but the rigid implementation of the resting technique hindered pastoralists from capitalizing on the surplus biomass. In response, ICARDA developed flexible or opportunistic grazing criteria and trained partners to adapt to climate variability. This innovative approach allows pastoralists to optimize resource utilization during favorable years and addressing the shortcomings of previous implementations.

column16: From fleece to screens: Revolutionizing sheep and goat marketing in the digital age by linking small ruminants producers to markets
column17: The International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas (ICARDA) and the Ethiopian national research systems have succeeded to work together to introduce community-based breeding programs and improved fattening technologies that are suitable to various production systems. At the same time, significant commercial and market-oriented patterns and practices are now emerging as result of the support. There exists some scientific evidence for the demand for livestock market facilities being developed and make them accessible, sustainable and guide a national effort. Along with these, ICARDA is collaborating with a private livestock marketing enterprise (Yazerber) to organize and launch a trustful and contented market linkages between sheep and goats producers and domestic consumers in and around Addis Ababa city. This activity is expected to increase sales of animals from target areas through increased market access and improves efficiency in well-organized livestock markets. Buyers have the option of buying their animals digitally.

column16: Design innovations in leveraging social protection for women's engagement in sustainable land management practices
column17: This sustainable land management (SLM) innovation draws on qualitative formative research, co-design of an innovation with partners, a quantitative impact evaluation testing the innovation, and resulting guidance for partners on implementing the innovation. This project is delivered as part of a multifaceted graduation model social protection program, SPIR II (Strengthen Productive Safety Net Program Institutions and Resilience II) that seeks to further sustain nutrition security and reduce risks to livelihoods for households participating in the Ethiopia’s national safety program, the Productive Safety Net Program (PSNP), which provides consumption support in the form of cash and food transfers. The goal of the SLM innovation being tested is to leverage social protection to promote women’s engagement in sustainable land management practices. Strengthening women’s involvement in sustainable land management is seen as potentially important given that extreme weather events pose risks for poor households in rural Ethiopia and women may be disproportionately at risk from these shocks. For example, Kato et al (2021) find that plots controlled by women in Ethiopia are more prone to soil erosion and of poorer quality in terms of soil depth, and women’s participation in watershed committees is low. The sustainable land management practices being introduced may help protect women and their families from these shocks over the longer term as well as introduce an additional livelihoods avenue. The innovation tested includes providing training (to either women only or to both men and women from same households) and free inputs (tree seedlings, vegetable seeds and tools for home gardening) among participants of the PSNP public works program, thus helping to address constraints to accessing information and inputs, and assessing whether spousal cooperation is important for successful adoption of these technologies.

column16: Conservation of tropical indigenous pig Suidae genetic resources using the induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) derived from somatic cells
column17: This innovation is a new/adapted technology for conservation of Suidae (pig) genetic resources in-vitro based on a stem cell approach.The technology relies of harvesting of somatic cells (such as from an animal’s body), which are then bought back to undifferentiated stem cells, also called induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), in the laboratory. The iPSCs can be stored in-vitro (under liquid nitrogen) and later used to produce any cell type (undifferentiated stem cells are characterized by their ability to produce any cell type in the body). To date we have successfully demonstrated stable lines of local pig somatic cells in culture. The steps in progress include inducing pluripotency, characterizing and demonstrating their differentiation potential, and later using them in assisted reproductive technologies to revive the pig which cells were stored in liquid nitrogen. This technology will be used to conserve tropical pig genetic resources in Uganda, Vietnam, and potentially elsewhere.

column16: Analytical approach for researchers to conduct mixed-method multi-country assessment of how social protection shapes gendered impacts of climate change
column17: This innovation develops an analytical approach for researchers to pair quantitative and qualitative research in multiple countries, to assess how social protection shapes the gendered impacts of climate change. The quantitative approach entails merging household survey data from randomized controlled trials on social protection interventions with weather data from satellite data or remote sensing. Doing so allows estimating the effects of climate hazards on gendered outcomes, and assessing how those effects change when climate hazards overlap with receipt of social protection. The complementary qualitative approach entails interviewing women and men in the same setting on how they perceive climate change and social protection’s role in helping them adapt, and what changes to social protection could better support them. The combined approach allows researchers to assess what impacts social protection has on gendered impacts of climate change, how and why patterns vary by context, and how to better design social protection.

column16: Evidence-based guidance on effective social protection design for implementers to promote women's resilience to risk
column17: This innovation draws on impact evaluations testing different social protection designs for implementers to promote women’s resilience to risk, in order to provide guidance on which designs are effective in different contexts in the short and longer term. column16: Production of saline tolerant potato variety under zero tillage using rice straws during the fallow winter season for farmers in rice-based ecosystems in Bangladesh
column17: The potato production through zero-tillage with straw mulch (PZTM) is an innovative technique to sustainably intensify agricultural production with potato uses few inputs and residues from the previous crop without disturbing the soil. It has the potential to address issues being exacerbated by climate change like excessive input use leading to detrimental environmental effects, water scarcity, and worsening air quality due to rice straw burning and, as such, significantly contribute to a sustainable agroecological transformation in Bangladesh. Key to this practice is the efficiency principle, by increasing resource-use efficiencies of major inputs. It recycles straw as mulch, creating value for a residue that would have been burned otherwise. As this technique is associated with economic gains as well as women’s empowerment, it improves rural livelihoods and promotes gender equity, and as such adheres to the principle of human and social values.

column16: Decentralized extension model by engaging local service providers (LSPs) for technology dissemination and nutrition messaging for producers in Bangladesh
column17: WorldFish has established a decentralized aquaculture service delivery model that enables effective delivery of quality inputs, technologies, and technical services to small-scale producers through capacitated Local Service Providers (LSPs). The model emerged from earlier CGIAR collaborative initiatives in Bangladesh and Nigeria and demonstrated clear productivity and income outcomes by embedding advisory and delivery functions within local production and market networks, including deltaic contexts. Under this model, local fish farmers, nursery operators, and business owners are trained and supported to provide bundled services, including production advice, improved management practices, and access to quality inputs. Service configurations vary by provider type and local context, enabling flexible and demand-driven delivery.; The innovation is integrated into the CGIAR Scaling for Impact (S4I) program and is implemented across multiple WorldFish initiatives. Government systems are already applying decentralized extension approaches, creating opportunities for joint learning on implementation mechanisms and pathways for institutionalization.;

column16: Business model for the sustainability of the provision of digital climate advisory through interactive voice response to mungbean farmers in Bangladesh
column17: The Mungbean Interactive Voice Response (IVR) is a system that provides harvest alerts to mungbean farmers in Bangladesh. A business model for this digital application is required for sustaining it in longer term. In 2023, new business models for the system is supported. First model explored the Mungbean value chain to check if value chain actors like exporters are interested to cover the costs of their  farmers supplying mungbean to the exporter firm.  The second model is with microfinance that provides loans to farmers and developing a bundled model that provides the harvest warning as an add-on service to the loans for mungbean farmers. In 2024, microfinance institutions and private company agree to integrate the IVR in the provision of loans to farmers.

column16: MDII: A multidimensional index designed to promote ethical and socially inclusive digital innovation processes within food, land, and water systems
column17: Digital innovations are increasingly being utilized in food, land, and water systems. It's crucial that these innovations are inclusive and cause no harm, especially for less developed countries where many people rely on food systems for their livelihoods. However, there is a lack of standard metrics and guidelines for measuring and promoting digital inclusivity. To address this gap, the Multidimensional Digital Inclusivity Index (MDII) has been developed. The MDII offers 22 indicators of digital inclusivity across five dimensions. It can be used to assess and promote the level of digital inclusivity of an innovation, an innovation bundle, an organization, or a country. This index aims to make digital innovations accessible, usable, beneficial, participatory, and safe for socially and economically marginalized groups in food systems.

column16: Guidance for researchers and development agencies working with women farmers to co-design and implement Socio-Technical Innovation Bundles (STIBs) for strengthening resilience of women farmers
column17: This innovation provides guidance for co-designing and implementing context-specific socio-technical innovation bundles (STIBs) that could contribute to women's empowerment and resilience through participatory processes like multi-stakeholder engagements. This step-by-step participatory co-designing process includes developing inclusive tools and procedures for situation analysis, rapid assessment, and stakeholder engagement for identifying, prioritising, and designing different combinations of STIBs that are implemented through current learning labs and can be rolled out in other projects and initiatives. It will also include indicators, tools, and outcome and impact assessment methods.

column16: Socio-technical innovation bundles dashboard developed by CGIAR's Initiative on Gender Equality and designed to inform research on women empowerment and resilience
column17: We have co-developed and co-designed a dashboard with an interactive map that dynamically displays the global distribution of socio-economic datasets, data, and tools that facilitate bundling in different local, regional, and thematic contexts. Gender and socioeconomic studies from the CGIAR Gender Impact Platform were used to compile the existing STIBs, and more data from learning labs in Kenya, Ethiopia, and India will be added subsequently. Additional socio-economic and gender inventory data has been extracted from FAO’s Agricultural Innovation Systems and the World Bank, but not clustered into different bundles. Out of the 5504 datasets currently housed in the dashboard, 450 have been assessed for their alignment with EMPOWER work package definition of STIBs. The remaining 5054 datasets are inventory data. The inventory data contains 151 from the Living Standards Measurement Study (LSMS), 1314 from FAO’s Agricultural Innovation Systems (AIS), and 3589 from the World Bank’s Agriculture Data.

column16: A Gender-responsive digital extension and learning package using short animations and facilitated discussion to support uptake of socio-technical innovations by women farmers
column17: As most agricultural farmers especially women get older, their responsibilities increase and their patience with longs hours of face-to-face meetings and trainings becomes a problem. Farmers are showing interest in receiving information from the value chain through animations and visual presentations. They prefer listening to an animation of three to five minutes and having a discussion to fill any needed gaps. This way they have more time to attend to other productive or household activities. Also using animation has increased the reach of information and technologies to farmers (where to source seed, varieties to plant, preparation of land, post-harvest losses, nutrition and multistakeholder platforms) through social media channels like WhatsApp.

We intend to measure what combinations work where and why and, provide this learning to next users who could scale these bundles.

column16: Socially inclusive approaches with collectives to support equitable scaling of locally led adaptation in Kenya's dairy sector
column17: Climate impacts are uneven and adaptation research typically focuses on technological practices. However, adaptation processes are embedded within and informed by social contexts and relations. Capacities to adapt differ based on wealth and gender for instance. Uptake of certain climate smart technologies can generate uneven inequitable burdens, especially through income and labor pathways. This innovation aims to support women and men through collectives to overcome challenges and barriers to adaptation. GROOTS Kenya supported the creation and capacity building of grassroots women led collectives in Bomet County in Kenya. The purpose of this innovation is to sustain efforts to build capacities in dairy and to address harmful and restrictive norms and practices in households, that is recognized as an incremental process. This innovation is focused around socio-technical bundling and gender transformative approaches, that includes peer learning and engagements with local champions to strengthen leadership capacities and increase potential to benefit.

column16: Community conversations are an approach to engage local communities in setting project priorities and supporting transformative locally led climate adaptation in pastoral communities
column17: Community conversations aim to advance equitable participation and decision‑making in locally-led adaptation processes to strengthen resilience. The approach draws upon concepts from locally led adaptation and practical insights from gender transformative approaches and was adapted to bolster equitable adaptation ; in Baringo County, Kenya. Four community conversations were held and were based upon priorities set by the community. Priorities included building capacities in diversification activities such as drought tolerant crop production, goat and chicken production, and group formation. Behavioral change was communicated through engaging media such as a co-developed drama and radio program, a photo gallery and interactive and participatory sessions. Reach per each conversation ranged from 254-339 individuals and women often comprised the majority. Baseline and a preliminary analysis of a midline show perception changes surrounding women's mobility. Men leaders' discussions and a gender dialogue enhance the potential of social change in household and communities to bolster resilience.

column16: A web-based based decision support tool for managing Rift Valley fever outbreaks in Kenya
column17: Rift Valley fever (RVF) is a zoonotic disease caused by a virus that is transmitted by a wide range of mosquitoes. The disease mainly affects livestock and people. It has been listed by the World Health Organization as one of the nine diseases that has the potential to cause pandemics. Decision makers often face major challenges predicting and responding to outbreaks, and so we have developed this prototype tool for forecasting risk and identifying actions that can be taken to manage the risk. The tool has two components, the first ingests rainfall forecasts from the Global Precipitation Climatology Centre and processes anomalies to identify periods when above normal rainfall is expected. The second component provides actions that need to be taken at various phases of the outbreak ranging from pre-outreak, outbreak, post-outbreak and peacetime periods.

column16: Improve soybean variety and soil amendment for quality grain and  fodder production in northern Ghana
column17: Soybean is an important legume and cash crop in Ghana. The grains are good source of protein  food for household consumption, it  used to make cooking oil as well as feed in the poultry industry. The fodder is also a good source of feed for livestock and it  also improves soil fertility through biological nitrogen fixation. However, low soil fertility is a major constrain for soybean production in Ghana and the lack of consideration of fodder quality in the selection criteria of improve varieties by national breeding program affects its use in crop-livestock farming system. This innovation assess the effect of soil amendment and improve soybean varieties on quality of grain and fodder production in crop-livestock farming systems in northern Ghana.

column16: A system dynamics approach for assessing policies for promoting resilience of maize-cowpea intercropping in Ghana
column17: This study sought to evaluate the resilience of intercropping (cowpea and maize) in northern Ghana, using system dynamics modelling approach. A simulation model was developed to provide insights into how this intercropping enables households to remain food secure, boost their income, and maintain natural resource capital, concurrently. The model enables quantitative evaluation of cause(s) and effect(s) of implementing an agricultural technology or new policy on different sustainable intensification domains i.e. production, economics, environment, human condition and social inclusion. The model is targeted to be used by policy makers, technology scaling experts and researchers. The model is scalable to other geographies provided that the site specific inter-linkages between different sub-systems are defined after stakeholders consultation.

column16: Crop diversification: An analytical framework for understanding the political economy of policymaking
column17: This analytical framework was developed by the author to facilitate an understanding of the political economy of policies for crop diversification in Bangladesh. It seeks to unravel the intricate connections linking economic processes, political policies, and social institutions. The analytical framework presented here is a practical tool by which to analyze the political economy of agricultural policymaking.  It presents the processes, methods, tools, and techniques followed by the various actors in policymaking, to aid the reader’s understanding of, specifically, the political economy of policies pertaining to crop diversification. It will help us understand the relevant policies, programs, projects, resource use, impacts, scale, good practices, and learnings from specific initiatives. The results of such an exercise may help steer the focus of future policy and development in the agriculture sector.

column16: A decision support tool for preventing and controlling Rift Valley Fever (RVF) epizootic
column17: The RVF tool is a collaborative effort between the One Health Initiative and the Digital Innovation Initiative, designed to analyze climate-epidemic interactions and support decision-making for Rift Valley Fever (RVF) outbreak prevention and control in the Greater Horn of Africa. It includes a decision-support system for managing RVF epizootics, enabling timely and effective responses, and integrates a disease information management system for efficient data compilation and dissemination. The tool enhances disease surveillance in high-risk areas by combining trapping systems with community reports and supports cost-effectiveness studies on RVF prevention strategies, informing contingency planning. It provides meteorological data, including rainfall and precipitation at county and sub-county levels, and incorporates RVF modeling for risk assessment. column16: Digital Genetic Data Base for Small Ruminants in Ethiopia (DTREO) - a digital database revolutionizing small ruminant genetics through a digital platform targeting small ruminant producers and breeders
column17: This innovation involves the establishment of the DTREO - Digital Genetic Data Base for Small Ruminants in Ethiopia, which has now expanded to other countries (East Africa and, Middle East and Northern Africa countries). The DTREO database is designed to be flexible and allows for the capture of reproduction details and performance data using smartphones or tablets operated by enumerators. It has the capability to function offline, enabling data to be saved locally and then synchronized with the cloud when connectivity is available. The data stored in the cloud is subsequently analyzed to rank animals based on their Estimated Breeding Value (EBV), and the feedback is shared with the community. Furthermore, the DTREO database serves to generate input data for genetic analysis. Presently, the DTREO database contains information on 134 thousand animals from 69 Community-based Breeding Program villages.

column16: Marker-assisted introgression of fecundity mutation to support community-based breeding programs of sheep in low input systems
column17: Fecundity gene introgression has become an economical method to improve sheep prolificacy in developing countries. The innovation aims to increase the number of effective carriers of the mutation by the introgression of fecundity mutation into non-carrier conventional flocks based on a marker-assisted breeding program. The genotyping was carried out to follow up on the segregation of prolificacy mutation. The conventional, non-prolific ewes, were inseminated by carrier rams and yielded 100% carriers females at heterozygous state. These females were inseminated with conventional rams and produced carriers’ lambs with 66.7% males and 33.3% females. The prolific males are to be kept in breeding centers to disseminate the fecundity mutation in commercial flocks. The innovation was developed and tested in Tunisia and within Sustainable Animal Productivity (SAPLING) countries. It has the potential to be applied in Ethiopia, particularly in Bonga sheep, where a mutation linked to higher prolificacy has already been identified.

column16: WasteWise - Decision Support Tool for Circular bioeconomy Solutions
column17: The Decision support tool, using a multi-criteria decision method, is designed to assist decision-makers in selecting appropriate business models for Nature-Positive solutions in the context of circular bioeconomy. This tool makes a holistic assessment of interconnected objectives and the evaluation of alternatives while explicitly considering the priorities of various decision makers and stakeholders. It enables decision-makers and practitioners involved in the planning, implementing, and advocating circular economy initiatives to select appropriate circular economy business models that result in positive social, economic, and environmental outcomes. It uses a user-friendly interface where users can modify inputs and test scenarios and an interactive data visualization dashboard for result analysis.

column17: his innovation consists of a database schema to integrate findings from multiple high-profile farm household surveys, including the World Bank's LSMS-ISA and the CGIAR's RHoMIS surveys, and others. This innovation akes two significant contributions: first, by providing a common means to integrate data from multiple farm household surveys; and second, by providing an accessible means to conduct farming systems analysis for the planning and prioritisation of research and development activities. column16: Integration of research and innovation processes that facilitate the co-design and testing of context-specific agroecological innovations:  A process for stakeholder engagement in Agroecological Living Landscapes ​
column17: The Agroecology initiative aimed to contribute to achieving agroecological transition through developing and scaling a range of innovations in 8 countries across three continents. It was proposed to do so by using a participatory action-research approach involving the key stakeholders of the Agroecological Living Landscapes (ALLs), multi-stakeholder territorial spaces in each country on which the Initiative targeted its transformation and innovation efforts. A major pillar of such an approach consists in codesigning the required innovations and corresponding processes as well as effecting the required changes in behavior/practices by the concerned actors. At the heart of the initiative’s ambition and approach lies the ability to mobilize and support ALL stakeholders in co-designing and implementing the diverse activities required to develop the innovations needed in each context. Hence, the initiative has designed a tool to support this process. This process will be continued in a different format but using a similar process under MFL SP.

column17: Food Safety Technical Working Group (FSTWG) will fill the existing gap in communication and coordination of food safety activities in Ethiopia. Moreover, it will serve as an advisory group to the government on matters related to food safety policy and practice. Overtime the FSTWG will become a coordination unit to facilitate integration of food safety activities and projects in the country.  FSTWG members will play their role in advocacy within their respective organizations in an effort to foster collaboration, sharing of information and integration of activities. column16: Empowering Informal food Vendors: Enhancing Business Skills, Practices, and Food Safety through Training and Mentoring to empower informal food vendors through the Vendor Business School
column17: The human population is increasing globally and food systems need to be transformed to ensure supply of healthy; and nutritious diets, and to address the challenge of food insecurity. It is estimated that by 2050, more than two-thirds of the world will be living in urban areas. Informal markets, especially those in low- and middle-income; countries are critical for the food supply in cities. CGIAR Resilient Cities initiative is working towards upgrading these; markets, to not only provide safe food, but also ensure that they are better organized, thus increasing their efficiency; and potential to meet the food demand. Entrepreneurs, especially women, need to be supported to thrive in their; businesses, and contribute to the sustainability of these markets. To this end, a mentorship program, specifically; targeting women vendors in the dairy sector in Kenya, but with potential to be adapted to meet the needs of other; business types, has been developed.

column16: On-farm Water, Energy, Food, and Carbon footprint (WEFC) nexus index for the quantitative assessment of on-farm integrated resources management
column17: The on-farm Water, Energy, Food, and Carbon footprint (WEFC) nexus index has been developed to enable the quantitative assessment of on-farm integrated resources management in wheat and faba bean farming systems in Egypt. The WEFC index is computed as the weighted arithmetic average of the four pillars of (1) water: on-farm saved water consumption/national maximum water consumption; (2) energy: on-farm saved energy consumption/national maximum energy consumption; (3) food: on-farm agricultural yield/national maximum yield; and (4) carbon dioxide (CO2): on-farm saved CO2 emissions/national maximum CO2 emissions. The WEFC nexus index values are, therefore, indicative of resource consumption (inputs) and agricultural production and CO2 emissions (outputs). The index can be used to quantitatively assess the nexus performance of site-specific packages of practices under certain conditions and quantify the impact of new interventions on the nexus status to drive transformative actions at the farm level.

column16: Online Water Accounting Dashboard for the Souss Massa Basin, Morocco, to visualise past, current, and predicted future water status parameters such as water availability, water balance, and long-term hydrological changes
column17: The online Water Accounting Dashboard for the Souss Massa River Basin, Morocco, presents past, current, and potential future water status parameters such as water availability, water balance, and long-term changes in hydrology in an easily accessible, visual, and interactive manner for diverse stakeholders such as water management agencies, policy- and decision-makers. The Souss Massa River Basin has been hard hit by drought in recent years, resulting in reservoir water levels at historic lows. This innovation aims to bridge the communication divide between research findings and decision-makers to facilitate the informed, sustainable planning and management of scarce freshwater resources. The dashboard is publicly available and receives views

column16: Nexus Capacity Scorecard: An Assessment Tool to Enhance Institutional Readiness for Sustainable Water-Energy-Food-Environment (WEFE) Nexus Approaches
column17: The Water-Energy-Food-Environment (WEFE) Nexus Capacity Scorecard (NCS) is part of a toolkit developed to support organizations to assess their institutional processes, readiness, and capacities in understanding and implementing integrated approaches across the water, energy, food, and environmental sectors. It helps to identify opportunities, possible gaps, and inform the planning of tailored nexus capacity-building efforts, programs and interventions, and/or their monitoring over time. The tool can be used by any organization (public, non-governmental, civic, private, research, etc.) and in multiple contexts. It is adaptable to different program need and can also serve as a launchpad for discussions, within and across organizations and sectors, for improving WEFE nexus practice and collaboration.

column16: Rice-sweetpotato production systems using short maturity sweetpotato variety in Mekong River Delta in Vietnam
column17: Sweetpotato is saline and heat tolerant in general, and considered as a climate resilient crop. To promote sweetpotato in the region for smallholder farmers, and address challenges in current sweetpotato seed systems and available varieties, the Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) Initiative through the International Potato Center (CIP) proposes to conduct a breeding pilot project with a 95-day short maturity orange fleshed sweetpotato material which comes from the CIP sweetprotato Asia short duration breeding pipeline (BP00052), and purple fleshed with high-yeilding and high dry-matter content clones. The project duration is planned to be 20 months, starting from April 2023 to December 2024. Sweetpotato true seeds from San Ramon, Peru with elite crosses (humid tropics) will be sent from Lima, Peru to Vietnam and germinated in Dalat, Central Highlands of Vietnam where the temperature is stable year around. Currently, on-farm trials in farmers' field conditions are being done in Vietnam.

column16: Development and deployment of the Rice Crop Manager (RCM) for rice farmers in West Bengal, India
column17: Using the principles of Site-Specific Nutrient Management (SSNM), the International Rice Research Institute developed the Rice Crop Manager (RCM), an application that provides farmers with crop management recommendations tailored to their fields and rice growing conditions through the internet and text messages. In addition to nutrients, RCM also addresses other constraints that limit rice yield and farmers’ profit. These constraints can vary across areas, growing conditions, varieties and climate scenarios. ; ; For West Bengal, RCM will be developed for the rice growing farmers using secondary data on soil crop managemen characteristics to generate recommendations. To develop RCM algorithms, a yield-gain approach will be used to calculate nutrient rate to achieve a target yield, as a direct function of the estimated yield gain with added nutrient. The results nutrient omission plot technique (NOPT) trials will be used to customize and develop RCM with special focus on salinity management. ;

column16: Development of a Human Security Index (HSI) for smallholder farmers and households in rural areas
column17: The development of the Human Security Index (HSI) aims to fill in the gaps on empirical research that has clearly defined the concept of human security and rendered it measurable. The Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) Initiative's research aims to create a HSI specifically tailored for rural areas,where communities are often increasingly vulnerable to impacts of climate change. Inspired from the HSI developed by Adger et al. (2020), AMD aims to better capture and assess the unique challenges and security concerns experienced by people living in rural contexts, particularly those exacerbated by climate change. We collected the data for HSI in the Ganges Delta in Bangladesh and Mekong Delta in Vietnam. This initiative seeks to provide a more accurate and context-specific tool for evaluating and understanding human security in rural environments contributing to effective strategies and policies aimed at addressing the needs of vulnerable populations in the face of climate-related challenges.

column16: Mechanizing maize seed and basal NPK fertilizer application to improve grain yield, nutrient use efficiency and biomass availability for livestock feed
column17: This innovation builds on  Africa RISING technology which evaluated the effect of time of NPK fertilizer application for maize production in northern Ghana and reported an increase in grain yield (22-59%), agronomic nitrogen use efficiency (26-80%), return on investment (1-9 Fold), reduction in ammonia flux emission (1-49%) with application of NPK fertilizer to maize at planting relative to the conversional practice of applying NPK fertilizer to maize at 2 weeks after planting (Irmgard 2021; unpublished data). Adoption study of the innovation by farmers showed that about 40-98% of them are not applying the innovation. Inadequate availability of labor was cited as key barrier to scaling of innovation. The objective of this innovation is to address the labor challenges associated with the planting of maize and application of NPK fertilizer on the same day using sample planters. The hand push planter sow’s maize seed and apply fertilizer in two different holes.

column16: The Multi-Stakeholder Agriculture Knowledge Hub (MSAKH) is a sharing platform on Mixed Farming Systems in Mid-hills of Nepal
column17: The Multi-Stakeholder Agriculture Knowledge Hub (MSAKH) is an innovative platform that fosters collaboration among local and municipal stakeholders to address agricultural challenges, share experiences, and promote sustainable mixed farming systems. Its primary goals include empowering farmers—particularly women, Dalits, and marginalized groups—by improving their access to resources and advocating for policy changes. The key objectives of the platform are to enhance inclusive participation, facilitate knowledge sharing, strengthen advocacy, build capacity, support monitoring and coordination, and scale innovative agricultural practices. In March 2024, four MSAKHs were established—one each in Wards 6 and 7 of Halesi Tuwachung Municipality and Wards 12 and 14 of Gurbhakot Municipality. These hubs were formed in the presence of the research team, social mobilizers, municipal staff, and ward chairpersons. Each MSAKH comprises diverse stakeholders, including farmers, agro-entrepreneurs, local elected representatives and officials, financial institutions, community-based organizations (CBOs), and the private sector.; In 2025, the innovation has been expanded to Indrawati Rural Municipality in Sindhupalchowk district.

column16: Co-designing gender responsive circular bioeconomy models targeting informal producers
column17: Tailored capacity building enables women and young people in urban and peri-urban areas to adopt circular bioeconomy models that strengthen livelihoods. In Kisumu’s informal settlements, 30 women who were previously producing biomass briquettes individually improve product quality, governance, and collective organization through hands-on technical training and support on group dynamics and business model co-creation. As a result, the women transition from informal, fragmented production to a coordinated and commercially viable small-scale enterprise. The group formalizes its collaboration by registering as the Tich En Tich Makwangla Women’s Group Cooperative, marking a shift toward a sustainable, women-led circular bioeconomy initiative. The cooperative is operational for more than a year producing and selling briquettes. In 2025, continuous support including additional in-kind support was provided to the women to improve their operational performance.

column16: Creation and expansion of a Local Technical Agro-Climatic Committee (LTAC) for the provision of climate advisory services to rice farmers in Lower Mekong provinces in Cambodia
column17: The Local Technical Advisory Committee (LTAC) is a dialogue process among a diversity of local actors including scientists, technicians, representatives from the public and private sectors, and farmers, which seeks to understand the climate’s possible behavior in a locality, and to generate agro-advisories to reduce risks associated with expected climate variability. This dialogue is  used to create an agroclimatic bulletin that contains the region’s climate prediction, as well as climate smart recommendations around decision-making for each productive sector. In general, climate predictions produced by each country’s meteorological service are provided in the LTAC meeting, and the LTAC members, from various institutions, identify climate-smart agro-advisories to the climate predictions, and then the climate predictions and the agro-advisories are shared with local extension officers and farmers in the form of agroclimatic bulletins.; ; The LTAC was piloted in Battambang and Kampong Speu and is now being expanded to other Lower Mekong provinces in Cambodia.; ;

column16: Vulnerability assessment framework to identify agricultural livelihood hotspots in Asian Mega Deltas region
column17: The vulnerability assessment (VA) framework is an approach used in mapping hotspot agricultural livelihoods of selected crops in the Asian Mega Deltas region. The framework was developed based on existing literature to identify the strengths and limitations of various VA approaches. Based on the developed framework, vulnerability is a function of three components: exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. Each of the three components is represented by a set of diverse indicators which is spatially aggregated into a shapefile to define a location-specific resolution as the unit of analysis. It is now currently being used by CG researchers to conduct their studies in uncontrolled environments and in designing their research projects. The framework is now integrated for adaptive capacity mapping innovation.

column16: Crop Decision Trees (CDTs) to provide agricultural advisories to rice, cassava, and maize farmers in Cambodia
column17: Crop Decision Trees (CDTs) are an important systematic tool for the development of climate risk responses based on sub-seasonal and seasonal forecasts.; CDTs are unique as they combine the need for a harmonized standardized model at the national level with the ability to tailor responses to the local level.; It generate tailored agricultural advisories to farmers to cope with climate risks occurring at sub-seasonal and seasonal time scales, taking location and crop growth stages into account to reduce climate risks on rice and cassava production and better apply agro-advisories to effectively cope with the climate risks.; ; CDTs can be easily integrated in digital tools and platforms for scaling and automating agro-climatic advisory.;

column16: Agronomy Community of Practices (ACoP) for technology transfer and agricultural development in countries within the Central and West Asia and North Africa (CWANA) region
column17: The CGIAR Initiative on Fragility to Resilience in Central and West Asia and North Africa (F2R-CWANA), and now the CGIAR Scaling for Impact Program, has established Agronomy Community of Practices (ACoP) in countries within CWANA. So far, ACoPs have been established in Sudan, Egypt, Uzbekistan, and Morocco. This collaborative network, hosted on WhatsApp, aims to overcome barriers to technology transfer and agricultural development by facilitating knowledge exchange among its members. The ACoP focuses on discussing scientific ideas, innovations, joint publications, local knowledge utilization, and context-specific agronomic solutions to enhance food and nutritional security in the region. Membership is open to individuals actively contributing to agricultural development through relevant practices. Online training sessions have been delivered to familiarize members with the establishment, rules, regulations, and objectives of the ACoP.

column16: Bundle of retail-level strategies to make fruits and vegetables more affordable and accessible to consumers in urban areas of Nigeria and Viet Nam
column17: This retail-level innovation was developed to address barriers in the affordability and acceptability of fruits and vegetables among low-income women in urban and peri-urban areas of Nigeria and Viet Nam. The intervention included a variety of strategies designed to improve: (1) the affordability through a coupon system; (2) the acceptability through a promotional campaign about the importance of eating fruits and vegetables every day; and (3) a combination of both through a loyalty card system and improvements in point of sales, product display, marketing, delivery of nutritional information to consumers, food safety, and customer service practices. The bundled intervention was implemented over twelve months and led to a marginal increase in the proportion of females consuming fruits and vegetables during the intervention period in both countries. This innovation was implemented and tested in both sites from January 2020 to December 2021. In 2025, no further work was done on the innovation itself, but a new journal article describing the results from the evaluations was published.

column16: Diversified and intensified farming through semi-mechanized, resilient rice-maize production systems by efficient utilization of rainfall and residual soil moisture in the coastal zones of Bangladesh
column17: The Initiative on Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) builds on the work of the Sustainable Intensification Innovation Lab (SIIL) Project in Bangladesh through the International Rice Research Institute. Their joint efforts aim to implement a transformative project in the coastal polder zone, targeting the untapped agricultural production potential of the region. Since waterlogging is the main constraint for wide-scale adoption of improved production systems, the project implemented innovative catchment-level water and crop management for sustainable farming in the polders of coastal Bangladesh. Currently, the rice-maize production system is being introduced. The farmers cultivated HYV rice in the wet season with periodic drainage that almost doubled the productivity. While maize cultivated under semi-mechanized practices efficiently utilizing residual soil water in absence of good quality irrigation water (water is saline in dry season), provides improved livelihood for farmers where most fields remain fallow in the dry season. The system productivity of rice-maize (9.3-11.4 t/ha/yr) increased by at least 2 folds over farmers’ practice and has potential for food security and feed sources for the livestock and fish.

column16: Irrigation water measurement: Standard operating procedures for quantifying the irrigation water used and for assessing water use efficiency and  water productivity  in agriculture systems
column17: With declining water availability due to climate change, making the most use of it is crucial in adapting agricultural ; systems to a changing climate. Furthermore, optimal use of water through irrigation scheduling (when and how ; much) can increase the quantity and quality of produce. Aside from the positive effects on reducing water application ; in agricultural systems, positive effects have been found of improved water management on grain filling, size, color ; and shelf-life of produce, and marketable yield — resulting in higher market prices and income of farmers. In rice-based systems, in particular, co-benefits of improved water management on greenhouse gas emission mitigation have been reported.; ; The Standard Operating Procedures, developed for the use of water scientists, agronomists and other researchers, provides the step-by-step procedure to determine the irrigation water use and the total amount of water applied in the field to evaluate water use efficiency and productivity.

column16: No-till seeder adapted in public-private partnership to Moroccan crops and soil types for Moroccan smallholder farmers to practice zero tillage Conservation Agriculture
column17: The no-till seeder machinery has been developed to support Morocco's national plan of having one million hectares of farming land under Conservation Agriculture practices by 2030 (Generation Green 2020-2030). Developed from a local prototype by an ICARDA, INRA and local manufacturer team, using technology imported from dryland farming machinery in Australia, the no-till (zero tillage) seeder allows smallholder farmers in Morocco to sow seeds directly into the soil (direct seed) without causing any mechanical modification of the soil structure. No-till practices are expected to improve the resilience of dryland smallholder farmers by reducing soil erosion and increasing the amount of carbon dioxide, water, and organic matter retained in the soil.

column16: Linking value chain actors to green business opportunities for agroecological, nature-positive, and restoration-oriented products and innovations
column17: The CGIAR Multifunctional Landscapes Science Program (MFL SP) builds on the foundations of the Agroecology and NATURE+ Initiatives by recognizing inclusive and green business models as a key adaptive scaling strategy for landscape-level innovations. These business models go beyond farm-level agroecological practices to include green agribusinesses that integrate agroecological principles, nature-positive production, ecosystem restoration, and conservation outcomes across value chains. The MFL SP departs from the premise that, by incorporating long-term profitability considerations, enterprises can ensure the economic viability and durability of the social and environmental objectives embedded in their business models. Accordingly, value chains with potential for agroecological upgrading, nature-positive transformation, and landscape restoration are prioritized to enhance the ability of small-scale producers, enterprises, and other food system actors to equitably participate in and benefit from emerging green market opportunities. The innovation consists of a methodological approach to assess value chains within multifunctional landscapes and to identify green business models with scaling potential, including those that support restoration, conservation, and sustainable land-use transitions. The approach is accompanied by examples of its application in diverse contexts and by recommendations for strengthening its relevance, scalability, and alignment with landscape-level outcomes.

column16: Development and piloting the conceptual framework "Agency and Behavior Change in Transforming agri-food systems" ACT, dedicated to researchers and practitioners
column17: A systems perspective is crucial to understanding behavior change processes in agri-food systems transformations. Drawing from three existing frameworks, we developed a conceptual framework of agency and behavior change for agri-food system transformations. It is meant to go beyond the “technology transfer” paradigm in agri-food system research for development, to guide researchers and practitioners in a systems approach that improves understanding of what is enabling or impeding individual and group agency and behavior change in agri-food systems. The Agency and Behavior Change in Transforming agri-food systems (ACT) framework also enables a systematic approach to identifying and addressing gender, social inclusion and and power asymmetries. We expect that along with the use of this framework, more formative research will be conducted to understand food system actor experiences, constraints, and opportunity spaces. We expect the impact of this approach to research and action will be to more effectively achieve agency and behavior change targets, and resulting agri-food system transformations.

column16: Using typologies to target private sector investments in gender equality and social inclusion in agrifood supply chains: Methodology and good practices
column17: This innovation aims to support agrifood companies, Voluntary Sustainability Systems (VSS), and other actors involved in downstream nodes or supportive functions of agrifood supply chains and markets (e.g., in trade, research, policy and programming) to enhance gender equality and social inclusion in their supply chains. The innovation is a toolkit designed to help: 1) understand the diversity of actors, with an emphasis on women, involved in upstream nodes of a given supply chain, 2) assess the differentiated benefits, contributions, and barriers these diverse groups of women (and men) experience within their suuply chains, and 3) identify entry points for improved targeting and tailoring of value chain initiatives to improve the terms of participation for different groups of women and promote gender equality within agrifood supply chains. This innovation is a collaborative effort between the CGIAR Initiatives on Gender Equality and Rethinking Food Markets.

column16: Prioritizing agronomy in a Changing Environment (PAiCE) Tool for researchers and national partners  to characterize crop production risks and explore potential adaptation solutions for specific crop production in Global South
column17: Through discussion-based stakeholder consultations, facilitated by trained researchers, the tool provides a structured approach to characterize and explore potential adaption solutions for specific crop production regions. As a first step, characterization data; for climate challenges and production system characteristics should be aggregated; this helps ensure that discussions are focused on topics that require the wisdom of groups. It is also important to aggregate experimental evidence of the value of different technologies and management approaches to respond to the climate challenge. Following the workshop, areas of uncertainty and evidence gaps should be addressed to enhance initial results. Thereafter, a provisional set of priorities should be shared with a broader set of stakeholders to cross-validate results. As a last step, it is envisioned that results from the PAiCE tool will provide a strong foundation for climate change adaptation by steering investment and helping to coordinate the efforts of partners through action roadmap. ; ;

column16: Capacity development innovation on storytelling training about gender-responsive agricultural solutions
column17: Despite women’s significant contributions to agri-food systems, positive stories about women’s roles are scarce in AFS discussions and media coverage. Dominating narratives often cast women as victims and patronize or misrepresent their roles and contributions. In this way, the currently dominant narratives about women’s role in AFS can be perceived as counterproductive, standing in the way of progress towards inclusive, equitable AFS. Therefore, there is a pressing need to collect, produce and share ‘better’ stories about women in AFS and agricultural solutions that work for women. In 2023 and 2024, the CGIAR GENDER Impact Platform organized three training programs, for science communicators from CGIAR and partners (as well as journalists) from around the world on how to prepare and publish stories on agricultural technologies that work for rural women. This training resource guide was developed as part of this series. Several stories are published in mainstream media outlets.

column16: R workflows to manage and analyze data for yield gap decomposition by data scientists and analysts.
column17: The workflow outlines the processes and step-by step guide to manage and analyze data for yield gap decomposition by data scientists and analysts. It also includes concepts and definitions of yield levels, yield gap and yield gap decomposition and describes the analytical models for yield gap decomposition. Three main data-driven methods have been used for yield gap decomposition in agronomy research: (a) boundary line analysis, (b) stochastic frontier analysis, and (c) machine learning methods. The material documents how to implement these three methods in R are provided with reproducible examples. The R workflows have been used in analyzing data from surveys done by Use Cases in the Excellence in Agronomy to understand the factors causing yield gaps and to prioritize the development of agronomy solutions to close the yield gaps.

column16: Improving water use efficiency through micro irrigation practices
column17: Khotang and Surkhet lie in the mid-hills of Nepal and are drought-prone areas. Insufficient water availability in both areas has impacted agricultural productivity. During the participatory innovation selection process for various components of MFS, farmers ranked micro-irrigation as their priority innovation to increase vegetable productivity. Hence, interested farmers were given training on micro-irrigation practices, along with efficient water use practices including conservation agriculture, mulching, and multi-use water systems. 76 drip irrigation kits and 114 sprinkler heads have been distributed to the farmers for the pilot study. Farmers are selected based on inclusive criteria to ensure that women and marginalized farmers are not left behind.

column16: Acid soils dashboard makes available data to researchers and extensionists on lime requirements, yield response to lime, and profitability of lime for the main crop types cultivated in sub-Saharan Africa.
column17: This dashboard provides state of the art data for ex-ante assessment of the profitability of liming on sub-Saharan Africa's croplands. It provides state-of-the-art data and information on acid soil management for the major cereal, legume, root and tuber, and commodity crops in sub-Saharan Africa. It contains information related to soil pH, lime rates, profitability of liming and technical and scientific resources on soil acidity and acid soil management. The dashboard provides information to researchers, extensionists and the public who are interested to learn about acid soils in Sub-Saharan Africa.; ; A new component was added to the dashboard in 2025. This new component comprises summaries of primary data on yield response to lime across East Africa along with a widget for scenario analysis of liming profitability under different, user-defined price assumptions. The data are presented as plots and can be downloaded by the user in tabular format.

column16: A new soil leaching technique of a network of internal canals and drains across levelled fields to reduce soil salinity in newly reclaimed lands in Egypt
column17: A new soil leaching technique for use by farmers was trialled in newly reclaimed agricultural land in the Sinai Peninsula, Egypt, to improve water drainage and salt removal from the soil via leaching. By the end of the 90-day experiment, the creation across levelled fields of a structured network of (i) internal canals connecting from the external canal into the fields and (ii) parallel internal drains connecting from the fields into the external drain resulted in an 84% decrease in soil salinity and a 96% decrease in internal drain water salinity. These results indicate that this innovative soil leaching technique allows the water to infiltrate and flow more evenly through the soil, laterally and vertically, thereby efficiently removing salt deposits that have built up in the soil.
