column17: The Global Market Intelligence Platform (GloMIP) serves as a global public good, enabling the crowdsourcing, sharing, and analysis of market intelligence data. It provides insights on market segments (CGIAR target regions), target product profiles (breeding blueprints), impact opportunities (development indicators), and investor analytics (projected cost-benefit analysis). The platform aims to make this valuable information freely accessible to all key stakeholders— including donors and investors, program and breeding leads, Genetic Innovation management, scientists and researchers—across both CGIAR and non-CGIAR crops and regions. GloMIP is integrated with the Breeding Pipeline, providing a single source of truth via backend tools deployed online. The frontend is continuously refined and includes navigation guides, videos, queryable pages of Market Intelligence publications, and various dashboards.

column16: Diversified and intensified farming through semi-mechanized, resilient rice-sunflower production systems by efficient utilization of rainfall and residual soil moisture in the coastal zones of Bangladesh
column17: The Initiative on Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) builds on the work of the Sustainable Intensification Innovation Lab (SIIL) Project in Bangladesh through the International Rice Research Institute. Their joint efforts aim to implement a transformative project in the polder zone, targeting the untapped agricultural production potential of the region. Since waterlogging is the main constraint for wide-scale adoption of improved production systems, the project implemented innovative catchment-level water and crop management for sustainable farming in the polders of coastal Bangladesh. Currently, the rice-sunflower production system is being introduced. The farmers cultivated HYV rice in the wet season ith improvd drainage that almost doubled the productivity. While sunflower was mostly cultivated under rainfed environment by semi-mechanized practices effectively utilizing residual soil water that provides livelihood and income generating opportunities to farmers where most fields remain fallow in the dry season. The system productivity of rice-sunflower (10.3-14.1 t/ha/yr) increased by 2-3 folds over farmers’ practice and has potential to reduce edible oil import.

column16: Diversified and intensified farming through rice-vegetables (mungbean, okra, chili) production systems in the coastal zones of Bangladesh
column17: The farmers in coastal polder zones of Bangladesh cultivate traditional rice followed by low input-based rabi crops (mungbean, okra, chilli). Due to longer duration of wet season (WS) rice, dry season (DS) crops established late and often damaged by pre-monsoon rains and cyclones at maturity. The project established “Learning Hubs (LHs)”, where water management groups operated the sluice gates to create favorable water environment for high-yielding rice cultivation in WS that provided opportunities for early establishment and safe harvest of DS crops. Within the LHs, farmers worked closely with researchers to develop resilient rice–vegetable/pulse cropping patterns suitable for the polder zone. The farmers harvested 4.5-6.8 t/ha paddy that almost doubled the WS productivity over traditional rice. The mean yield of chilli, mungbean and okra was 457, 687 and 7205 kg/ha, respectively and most farmers used these crops for home consumption that reduced family expenditure and improved household nutrition.

column16: Diversified and intensified farming through rice-fodder production systems in the coastal zones of Bangladesh
column17: The Initiative on Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) pursues establishment of rice-fodder production systems in the coastal zones of Bangladesh to enhance feed availability that is crucial not only for the well-being of livestock but also for improving the nutrition of the coastal communities in Bangladesh through milk and meat production. The performance of six fodder crops was evaluated in fallow lands under rainfed environment during 2022-23 and 2023-24 dry seasons to document productivity in the coastal zone and palatability by the livestock. The crops were: Barley, Proso Millet, Foxtail Millet, Maize, Sorghum, and Triticale. Among them, maize produced the highest green biomass, followed by sorghum and foxtail millet, while barley and triticale produced the lowest biomass. The consumption rate of cross-breed cows was significantly higher than that of local cows. The palatability findings suggest that sorghum, maize, foxtail and proso millets have the most potential as fodder crops in the coastal polder zone.

column16: Facilitating agricultural mechanization options through local service providers (LSP) model to improve the livelihood of resource-poor women and youth in coastal zones of Bangladesh
column17: Recognizing the importance of agricultural mechanization to address shortage in agricultural labor, the International Rice Research Institute partnered stakeholders had developed local service providers (LSP) model involving women and youth in harvesting paddy by using a reaper (wife-husband model) The Initiative on Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) continued mentoring the LSPs through trainings and demonstrations on mechanized harvesting of paddy to attract more women and youth in agriculture and to ease the physical burden on women during manual harvesting and increase their contribution to household earnings. ; ; Training on mechanical harvesting of rice by reapers was organized at 10 water management group areas in polders to create awareness of agricultural mechanization so that women and youth can explore new livelihood opportunities locally. Four pairs’ women and youths (wife-husband) provided mechanical harvesting services to the community harvesting paddy by a reaper. Other mechanization options include fodder chopper, rice huller, and maize sheller.

column16: Cluster Farmer Field School (CFFS) Model for scaling agronomic innovations via strategic operation of sluice gates of polder systems in coastal Bangladesh
column17: Using Farmer Field School (FFS) model, the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE) has successfully disseminated agricultural technologies across Bangladesh. But there is no significant adoption of improved technologies in 1.2 million hectares polder zone mainly because of prevailing hydrology that the FFS did not consider as the determinant in scaling innovations. The project identified water stagnation and waterlogging are the primary agronomic constraints, and that community coordination and cropping system synchronization is needed for wide-scale adoption of improved production systems. The “Cluster Farmer Field School (CFFS)” model was developed integrating water management groups with FFS to scale agronomic innovations managing hydrology of the coastal Bangladesh. This innovation was employed to strategically operate the sluice gates for water intake and drainage, aligning with high and low tides of the peripheral rivers of polder ecosystems during key intercultural operations in wet and dry seasons to 14 Learning Hubs in 2023 and 2024.

column16: Use of the learning alliance as a network approach to support learning and alignment across stakeholder groups in scaling innovations in the Southeast Asian region
column17: Following the network approach established through the Initiative on Asian Mega-Delta (AMD), the Scaling for Impact and RiceEco project sustained the use of the approach to scale innovations in Cambodia and Vietnam.  The AMD aims to improve the deltaic production systems by working with farmers and local governments through identifying, synthesizing, evaluating, and scaling interventions that help adapt or mitigate climate change. The learning alliance is an approach to bring together a multi-stakeholder network to support learning and alignment of practices related to an innovation. It supports the identification of relevant stakeholders, timely learning activities to observe both on-farm and off-farm innovations, then reflection and experimentation on new practices that support the use of the new skill, technique or tool. In 2022, a learning alliance workshop was done and designed to initially establish learning alliances for a network of diverse stakeholders that has an interest to address climate-related issues in Cambodia. At present, the learning alliance has already conducted several learning and knowledge exchange activities to support strengthening the value chains around different production systems in Takeo. In 2025, these have continued at provincial and national levels in both countries, but also had opportunities for exchange between the two.

column16: Stable and growing user engagement with UXtools4ag and launch of HCD online course in 2025
column17: Uxtools4ag is an open online platform that provides practical tools and guidance to support human-centered design in agricultural innovation research. It helps researchers, practitiones and digital solution providers design products and services that better respond to needs, preferences and constraints of farmers and other user groups. The platform offers step-by-step methods, templates, and real world examles that can directly be applied in project planning, field research, prototyping and testing. By translating design approaches into practical, agriculture-specific guidance, the platform lowers the barrier for teams to apply human-centered design methods. In 2025, the innovation continued to attract a stable and growing community of users. Our platform analytics show sustained engagement from returning users and new registrations. This indicates the relevance and visisbility of the tool. In 2025, we added an online Human-Centered Design training. The training provides structured learning content for beginners, and helps to build practical skills. Through this new feature, Uxtools4ag contributes to improving how agricultural solution are developed, making them more responsive to real users needs, which likely will increase their adoption. With a focus on inclusion and gender-sensitive design, the innovation supports also a focus on introducing more inclusive agricultural innovations.;

column16: Enhanced web-based tool by IFPRI enables investors to evaluate solar-powered groundwater irrigation opportunities across Sub-Saharan Africa
column17: Solar irrigation systems offer promising solutions for sustainable agriculture in Sub-Saharan Africa, but investors need reliable data to make informed decisions. The International Food Policy Research Institute developed this enhanced web-based tool to address this gap. The platform calculates optimal solar system sizes for major crops and estimates economic returns from solar-powered irrigation based on local climate conditions, groundwater availability, and crop requirements. This updated version provides more comprehensive data and improved functionality, enabling investors to better evaluate the financial viability of groundwater-sourced solar irrigation projects across the region. The tool supports the transition to low-emission farming systems while helping expand sustainable irrigation access.

column16: Phenotyping breeding clones for quality traits using sensory panel, texture analyzer and a digital imaging system (DigiEye) in Mozambique
column17: The innovation lies in advancing methods to assess sensory traits, particularly mealiness, hardness, brownness and fibrousness in sweetpotato, thereby enhancing the selection and adoption of varieties. Sensory panels, comprising 12 individuals, were employed to evaluate 114 genotypes. Concurrently, a texture analyzer provided objective data on hardness, facilitating high-throughput phenotyping. Additionally, DIGeye photo scans were utilized to develop models for mealiness and brownness. Notably, subjective assessments of hardness correlated strongly with those obtained via the texture analyzer, validating its utility for selection purposes. While this innovation offers promising avenues for sweetpotato breeding and selection, further evidence is required to refine mealiness models developed by DIGeye. This initiative targets breeders, researchers and stakeholders in sweetpotato value chain and aims to optimize variety development by prioritizing sensory traits. Future plans involve refining and validating these methods to streamline the breeding process and meet consumer preferences effectively

column16: Holistic Localized Agroecology Performance Assessment (HOLPA) tool for assessing the performance of fields, farms and landscapes transitioning to agroecology
column17: HOLPA consists of two parts to permit both context specificity and global comparison of results: (1) a set of global performance indicators (2) the Local Indicator Selection Process (LISP), in which food system actors co-design metrics of agroecological performance in a given context. Together, they constitute a framework for holistic localized performance assessment, or HOLPA, which can be applied across diverse farming contexts and agroecological activities. The evidence will enable communities to see the impact of agroecology on things that matter to them, while also giving investors and other decision-makers a clear picture of agroecology’s performance under a wide variety of conditions.; In 2024, Local performance indicators have been selected in 15 communities across eight countries and incorporated into the HOLPA tool. Data has been collected from more than 1,600 households and has been analyzed. Country reports are under production. In 2025, the guidance materials has been finalized and shared on the HOLPA dashboard together with a portal to display results from data collection. In addition, country teams have been analyzing data and are publishing results in journals.

column16: A satellite remote sensing-based near real-time monitoring of irrigated areas in the Limpopo River Basin
column17: This innovation offers near real-time monitoring of irrigated areas across an entire transboundary river basin. The first version of the system utilized high-resolution Sentinel-2 (optical) satellite imagery data to identify these areas on a monthly basis. It makes use of both expert decision trees and machine learning techniques to identify irrigated regions. Until now, most mapping activities have focused on an annual timescale rather than a near real-time one. This represents a substantial improvement in irrigated area metrics, which directly impacts water availability.

column16: The Enviro-Champs: Establishing a framework for a technologically upgraded community environmental monitoring network for water quality monitoring
column17: The Enviro-Champs are the unsung young heroes of South Africa, bridging the crucial gap between nature and communities. Originating from the Mpophomeni township in KwaZulu-Natal, this initiative, under the Duzi-uMngeni Conservation Trust (DUCT), began by empowering local youth to monitor environmental issues like sewage leaks and illegal dumping. Their efforts quickly extended to tackling water leaks, improving waste management, and enhancing flood preparedness, addressing vital needs within the socio-ecological landscape of South Africa. Technological tools such as group text messaging and Excel for data management have bolstered their activities. Today, approximately 1,000 Enviro-Champs contribute significantly to environmental monitoring, ecological restoration, and food security efforts in KwaZulu-Natal. Their success in various regions showcases the initiative's potential for national expansion. Supported by UNICEF's youth upliftment initiative, YOMA, the Enviro-Champs program is poised for broader national and possibly international growth, demonstrating the power of youth engagement in environmental conservation.

column16: Data-driven advisories for farmers to optimize fertilizer and yields for maize in Kenya using the AgWise recommendation framework
column17: The AgWise generalizable decision support framework was used to develop maize fertilizer recommendations for the county governments, extension, and e-voucher system in Kenya. This was in response to a request from the government and partners to increase maize yields by 30% over existing average yields. The workflow was based on machine learning and crop modeling approaches, and generated fertilizer advice that: (1) Accounts for soil nutrient deficiencies using on-farm data and digital soil maps; (2) Considers fertilizer response under smallholder management (survey data); (3) Considers multi-year data and rainfall, but permits refining based on seasonal forecasts; (4) Allows customised yield targets at (sub) county level relative to current production; and (5) Can generate recommendations for different fertilizer formulations. The recommendations will be field-validated in 2024.;

column16: A suite of digital tools to map the morphology of rivers to enable monitoring of changes due to river flow management
column17: Implementation of e-flows or environmental flows is a requirement of water resource managers but is seldom adequately done. The Digital Innovation Initiative is researching application of digital tools to enable better management of rivers and implementation of e-flows. These tools include drone (UAV) mounted Lidar, Sonar, Ground Penetrating Radar and other sensors that deliver high resolution 3D data describing a river channel and allowing calculation of the river hydraulics. Generated data can be used not only to assess the discharge required to implement e-flows, but can also be used to monitor changes in river morphology over time.

column16: Data-driven advisories for farmers to optimize fertilizer and yields for selected crops (potato; beans) in Rwanda using the AgWise recommendation framework
column17: The AgWise generalizable decision support framework was used to develop potato fertilizer recommendations in Rwanda. This was in response to a request from the Rwanda Agriculture Board to optimize fertilizer rates for potato, either by reducing rates and achieving the same yields, or increasing yields by 10-20% over existing average yields obtained applying the blanket recommendation. This framework has been expanded to include beans in 2025. The workflow was based on machine learning and crop modeling approaches, and generated fertilizer advice that: (1) is compatible with the national fertilizer subsidy scheme complexities; (2) avoids major rework of current system for delivery; (3) tailors advice at agroecology level while providing evidence to refine factors that will capture withi-agroecology spatial variation; (4) considers commonly used fertilizer formulations; and (5) supports validation by providing fertilizer packages and treatment structures. The recommendations are being field-validated or analyzed.;

column16: Carob: A framework to standardize legacy agricultural data
column17: Carob is an open-source community project that standardizes and aggregates agricultural research data. The Carob project cleans and transforms agricultural research data from experiments and surveys into a standard format and aggregates individual data sets into larger databases that can be used in further research. It is the Extract, Transform, and Load (ETL) framework supported by the CGIAR Excellence in Agronomy Initiative to support predictive agronomy analytics.; In 2025, Carob has undergone a reorganization to make the data more usable, improving QC/QA, and being implemented in several SFP use cases (Kenya, Zambia, Ethiopia) and other billateral projects (West Africa Fertilizer Hub, iSPARK), supporting the development of analytics and agronomic advisories.

column16: Empowering Women: A Video to promote Inclusion in India's Government Planning
column17: This video was prepared by Travelling Tripod  in collaboration with the International Food Policy Research Institute to inspire rural women in Odisha State, India to publicly share with leaders their ideas for assets that might be constructed under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee (MGNREGA) program. The MGNREGA Act envisions a participatory, bottom-up process of choosing which asset will be built by allowing MGNREGA job card holders to recommend assets that would be useful to them at community meetings. Increasing women’s participation in the program is an important development goal for IFPRI and their partners in Odisha.; ; --; This video was created to inspire women to participate in the Mahatma Ghandi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) program in Odisha, India. MGNREGA is the largest workfare program in the world and is both an employment guarantee scheme and a program by which communities propose and build assets to help improve their livelihoods. This video tells the stories of women who have successfully received assets and encourages women to request assets themselves.; ; The video is unique in that it tells detailed stories of women who have been successful in requesting and receiving assets under the MGNREGA program. It showcases women that are easy to relate to and provides specific advice and encouragement to women. Given the size of the scheme, the video can inspire women to improve their lives and livelihoods.; ; The video will be easy to scale. It is only 15 minutes long, and is accompanied by a discussion guide for implementers on what to discuss with women at various points during the video to spur engagement and discussions. It is inexpensive to show and it can be implemented by almost anyone within a community. Both the government and NGOs may find it useful as a resource. We also developed a 6-min version in 2024 based on feedback from stakeholders.

column59: This innovation meets Readiness Level 5 through rigorous validation of its ability to achieve a specific behavioral impact under fully controlled conditions. The role-model video intervention was developed by International Food Policy Research Institute in collaboration with Travelling Tripod and evaluated through a randomized controlled trial involving more than 8,000 women across over 50 communities in Odisha, India. Under tightly controlled implementation conditions—including standardized video content, facilitated group viewing, and consistent discussion protocols—the intervention generated causal evidence of increased women’s knowledge of MGNREGA asset planning processes, confidence in articulating asset preferences, and willingness to participate in community meetings, though only when viewed in combination with a skill-based training exercise. These outcomes directly align with the innovation’s intended impact of strengthening women’s voice and agency in participatory public decision-making. The scale, experimental design, and high fidelity of delivery provide strong validation that the innovation functions as intended when implemented under controlled conditions, satisfying the criteria for full validation at Readiness Level 5.

column16: Planning for voice: A novel approach to help women develop the skills they need to exercise voice and agency in their communities
column17: IFPRI researchers developed the curriculum, ‘Planning for Voice,’ to equip women with key knowledge and skills to help them navigate the process of demanding assets through the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 (MGNREGA). It addresses both informational and skills gaps, designed to work with women in small groups within their existing social networks, so that each woman receives intensive focus and opportunities for practicing skills during a condensed time period. By the end of the course, participants should be able to: • Understand the basic process for requesting a MGNREGA asset and the key local stakeholders involved • Describe a  MGNREGA asset that could improve their individual lives or livelihoods or improve the community more broadly • Articulate different ways to play a role in influencing what their community decides to build • Develop a strategy to overcome foreseen barriers to exercising their voice and agency.

column16: The Women's Empowerment in Energy Index (WEEI) supports governments and other next users to reduce inequities in rural energy access
column17: Rural women often face barriers accessing clean energy technologies, limiting their economic opportunities and well-being. The Women's Empowerment in Energy Index is a measurement tool developed by CGIAR researchers to help governments, investors, and development practitioners identify specific sources of gender inequality in rural energy access and use. The index provides a systematic way to measure women's empowerment across multiple dimensions of energy access, enabling targeted interventions to close gender gaps. It has been field-tested in Nepal and India, with partial testing in Pakistan, demonstrating its practical application for informing policy and investment decisions that promote more equitable energy access for rural communities.

column16: Integrated solar irrigation solutions developed by IWMI and IFPRI to optimize water-energy-food outcomes in Africa and Asia
column17: Solar-powered irrigation is rapidly increasing in Africa and South Asia. This innovation addresses the urgent need for sustainable solar irrigation recognizing its intricate connections within the Water-Energy-Food-Environment (WEFE) nexus. It brings together a set of innovative solutions and approaches to the design, operation and implementation of solar irrigation that maximizes positive and minimizes negative outcomes. Components include (i) tools for optimal water pumping to prevent groundwater depletion, (ii) new approaches for evidence-based decision-making for assessing the financial feasibility of solar irrigation, (ii) capacity building programs for enhancing the understanding of the WEFE environment in which solar irrigation takes place, (iv) water-efficient irrigation practices (v) gender-responsive finance and business models; (vi) and evidence-based policy guidance promoting sustainable solar irrigation for multiple outcomes, including job creation, gender equality, climate action and improved nutrition.

column16: Basin digger under minimum soil disturbance for smallholder Conservation Agriculture (Pfumvudza) in Southern Africa
column17: Smallholder farmers in Zimbabwe, Zambia, and Malawi practice conservation agriculture by manually digging planting basins for crops like maize, sorghum, and legumes. This labor-intensive process, primarily performed by women and children, limits adoption to small plots despite proven yield benefits from precision input application. CIMMYT developed a low-cost mechanized basin digger that addresses this challenge by reducing manual labor requirements by 85% compared to traditional hand hoe methods. The tool enables farmers to expand conservation agriculture practices beyond small plots while maintaining the soil conservation and productivity benefits. This innovation specifically targets the drudgery barrier that has prevented wider adoption of the successful Pfumvudza conservation agriculture program, making the practice more accessible to women, youth, and elderly farmers across the region.

column16: Establishment of local seed production system in potato through Apical Rooted Cutting (ARC) for women farmers in Koraput and Puri (Odisha)
column17: Establish a local seed production system for potatoes using Apical Rooted Cutting (ARC) with women groups to promote self-sufficient seed systems in Odisha through identification, training on technical and economic viability and demonstrations. Apical cuttings are rooted transplants produced in a screen house from tissue culture plantlets. Rather than allowing tissue culture plantlets to mature and produce mini tubers, cuttings are produced from the plantlets. Once rooted, the cuttings are transplanted into the field to produce seed tubers.

column16: Development and deployment of digital climate advisory services through the Agvisely Livestock Application for cattle and poultry raisers in Bangladesh
column17: The Agvisely digital service for livestock integrates location-specific meteorological forecasts generated by the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) with species specific biological thresholds for weather variables (Temperature, rainfall, and temperature-humidity index (THI). When a biological threshold is to be breached in next five days' forecast, the system automatically generates location-specific management advice for livestock farmers. Advisories are based on a decision tree developed by the Bangladesh Livestock Research Institute (BLRI) and the International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center  (CIMMYT).; ; Agvisely is a smart phone app and web-based service developed by CIMMYT with the of the Securing the Food Systems of Asian Mega-; Deltas (AMD) for Climate and Livelihood Resilience and the Transforming Agrifood Systems in South Asia (TAFSSA) initiatives in collaboration with Bangladesh Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE) and Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) that can be used by extension agents and officers.

column16: Improving Product Advancement Meetings that advance varieties from idea to production within 7 CGIAR Center.
column17: This activity examines product advancement processes across seven CGIAR centers and their national partners. The study assessed how agricultural products progress from breeding to market launch through interviews, standardized questionnaires, and observations of product advancement meetings. The evaluation covered diverse crop programs: CIP's potato breeding, IITA's soybean development, rice improvement at both IRRI and AfricaRice, CIMMYT's sorghum program, ICRISAT's groundnut breeding, and common bean advancement at the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT.; ; Key findings revealed varying adoption levels of the One CGIAR stage-gate process, highlighting the importance of partnerships, market segmentation, and Target Product Profiles. Challenges in licensing, seed production, and commercialization planning were identified. Recommendations focus on defining core activities, clarifying partner roles, implementing market-segment-focused breeding, and formalizing product advancement meetings to enhance efficiency across the CGIAR system.

column16: Management of food legume pod borer and aphids through intercropping in Morocco
column17: In Morocco, faba bean and kabuli chickpea are the most important legume crops for their high protein content and incomes for farmers. Farmers practice different cropping systems but their ecological services like pest management are not investigated. In this study, we investigated the roles of coriander intercropping as alternative management of pod borers in chickpea and faba bean aphids.  Results showed that Coriander intercropping with chickpea reduced the mean number of pod damage (28%) as compared with sole cropping (49%). In faba bean, the mean number of aphids was decreased in faba bean intercropped with Coriander as opposed to sole cropping.  Intercropping increased the number and diversity of natural enemies that affect the two pests. This innovation will be further demonstrated under farmer field conditions in 2023/24 cropping season.;

column16: Development and evaluation of eco-friendly biopesticides against aphids and pod borer of food legumes in Morocco
column17: Pod borer and aphids are the most economically important insect pests in chickpea and faba bean respectively. Besides their economic damage, aphids play a role as virus vectors on food legumes. This study aimed to validate eco-friendly biopesticides (entomopathogenic fungi and essential oils) on pod borers and aphids selected in 2021/22. Laboratory results showed that two entomopathogenic fungi (Verticillium lecanii and Paecilomyces farinosus) were effective against second instar larvae of chickpea pod borer.  Similar results were found under field conditions where the two entomopathogenic fungi reduced larval population. The essential oils extracted from Ocimum basilicum and Origanum vulgare at 5000 ppm were the most effective against aphids under field conditions. Entomopathogenic fungi and essential oils can be integrated in the management of pod borers and aphids as eco-friendly alternative pest management options in Morocco. Efforts will be made to test different formulations in 2023/24 cropping season.;

column16: Demonstration and scaling of integrated management of parasitic weeds on faba bean in Northern Ethiopia and Morocco
column17: Parasitic weeds (Orobanache and Phelipanche spp) are food legume crops production constraints in Mediterranean region and East Africa highlands. Integrated management of parasitic weed management (IPWM) on faba bean was demonstrated and scaled in Morocco and Ethiopia in 2022/23 cropping season. Application of two sub-lethal sprays of glyphosate herbicide at flowering stages of faba bean was effective in managing the parasitic weed (O. crenata) in both countries. Based on 2021/22 results (two sprays of sub-lethal herbicide, fungicide seed treatment against faba bean gall and partially resistant cv. Hashengie in Ethiopia, IPWM options were adopted by many farmers in the intervention zones. Partial budget analyses showed high incomes for the innovations. Moreover, alternative non-host crops were identified to be included in the cropping system to reduce the seed bank of O. crenata. The IPWM innovations will be further scaled out in 2023/24 cropping season in both countries.;

column16: Standardized Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning (MEL) tools for tracking innovation reach and users with modules for all Sustainable Farming Program innovations
column17: This innovation is a beta version of integrated and standardized MEL tracing tools to support the use of common KPIs and generate more harmonized data across all Areas of Work (AoWs). This integrated tool strengthens consistency in tracking outputs and outcomes across W3 and bilateral projects, enabling easier aggregation, analysis, and program-level learning. The tools identify MEL evidence and tracking needs across all AoWs, covering CapSha capacity, innovation piloting and scaling and other crosscutting priorities. These needs are compared with a review of existing tools and innovation uptake instruments used across Sustainable Farming Program, Plant Health, Mixed Farming Systems. Common measurement themes and AoW-specific requirements such as innovation uptake, reach, inclusivity, and agronomic performance are integrated into a unified tool design. The tools are digitized and programmed in user-friendly formats such as ODK to support consistent deployment across countries and partners. The resulting integrated MELIA tools enables standardized collection of output-level data (e.g., CapSha activities, training coverage, innovation uptake) and supports outcome-level assessment for scaling and performance.

column16: Assessing Farmer Preferences for Silvopastoral Production System Sustainable Intensification Interventions: Preliminary Results from Northern. Laos
column17: In 2023, farmer preferences for silvopastoral sustainable intensification interventions involving both private and public good benefits assessed through mixed mode surveys based on Best-Worst Scaling (BWS) workshops, a Choice Experiment (CE) and a payments for ecosystem services conservation tender approach in two districts of Northern Laos. In 2024, the PES conservation tender approach was implemented and 534 farmer bid offers (involving ≈320 individual farmers) across 7 interventions in 17 communities in 2 Provinces were received. Of these xx bids were selected for implementation, considering cost-benefit ratio (e.g. cost per tree planted), conservation value (e.g. native species), and equity considerations (e.g. household's land size, gender, number of households that could be supported). Selected bids included (1) 135 households participating in forage trials, (2) 118 households establishing living fences with over 40 tree species, (3) 62 households protecting trees on pastures, and (4) 17 households producing tree seedlings for inclusion in silvopastures;

column16: Strengthening Scaling Capacity through Scaling Champions and Institutional Learning
column17: This outcome introduces a new approach to supporting the adoption and sustained use of agricultural and water innovations by strengthening the people and institutions that enable long term uptake. The Learning Alliance provided the space for experimentation and learning, while the Scaling Champions approach emerged from this process and can now be applied in other programmes and contexts.; ; The outcome provides practical guidance for strengthening institutional learning, training, and coordination, helping universities, extension services, and partner organisations embed responsible scaling within their regular programmes. This supports more consistent adoption, adaptation, and continuity of innovations after project funding end. ;

column16: Demand-driven assistance provision as part of agribusiness acceleration programs for high-impact sustainable agribusinesses to successfully start and thrive through a conducive policy and regulatory enabling environment
column17: A conducive enabling environment for agribusinesses is fundamental for African economies to grow rapidly. The unit for enabling environment technical assistance supports agribusinesses identified by agribusinesses acceleration programs to practice inclusive and sustainable agriculture, investment, value chain development, and trade, with a high impact potential: benefitting and creating employment for the disadvantaged and marginalized groups, including women, youth, and migrants, and fostering climate-resilient agriculture, climate adaptation, and sustainable natural resource management. This unit assists agribusinesses in three general clusters: (1) mapping, (2) networking, and (3) advocacy. The first two are “low-hanging fruits,” providing agribusinesses with research-based evidence on the policy, market, and regulatory environments to increase awareness and connect them with public and private actors for market expansion and overcoming bureaucratic bottlenecks. The advocacy cluster, a “high-hanging fruit,” seeks to drive regulatory change through collaboration with national governments, a long-term process, and links businesses with industry associations toward this goal. ;

column16: Identification of begomovirus resistant okra accessions for improved variety development
column17: Begomovirus is a genus of plant virus that can infect okra. It is transmitted primarily by whiteflies and can cause diseases such as okra leaf curl disease or okra yellow vein mosaic disease. This virus poses a significant problem for agriculture as it induces symptoms like leaf distortion, yellowing, and reduced yield, impacting the productivity and quality of infected crops. New genetic resources with resistance to key diseases are needed to strengthen seed systems. From 2023-2024, the National Horticultural Research Institute in Nigeria collected and shared 256 accessions of various Abelmoschus species (okra) with the World Vegetable Center. The accessions were tested as possible resistance sources against begomovirus diseases and preliminary experiments showed some resistant candidates.  In 2025, the World Vegetable Center finished evaluating 450 okra accessions from diverse origins (Benin, Ghana, Nigeria, Thailand, Niger, and Côte d’Ivoire) to identify resilient and resistant to begomovirus diseases. This research addresses critical productivity gaps caused by biotic and abiotic stresses in West Africa. The findings provide a strategic roadmap for okra improvement in West Africa. Identifying disease-resistant and drought-tolerant lines enables initiation of crossing blocks to develop climate-smart varieties. The wide diversity in pod morphology (length, diameter, and color) enables breeders to tailor new varieties to specific consumer preferences in regional markets. Accessions with desirable traits have been used as parental lines to develop advanced populations. Better Diets and Nutrition’s work on improved varieties is part of the end-to-end approach, an innovation which combines demand, food environment, and supply interventions to increase desirability, affordability, accessibility, and availability of fruits and vegetables and sustainable healthy diets more broadly. The supply interventions are designed to address known barriers faced by vegetable farmers. In this case, the provision of disease-resilient vegetable cultivars tackles the lack of quality inputs.

column16: The AADGG-Dairy mobile app for smallholder buffalo farmers to collect dairy data
column17: The AADGG-Dairy mobile app, co-designed by the Africa-Asia Dairy Genetic Gains (AADGG) program and the Digital Innovation (DI) Initiative, enhances real-time data capture and validation while ensuring functionality in low-connectivity areas. Developed in collaboration with the DI and SAPLING initiatives, the app provides rapid data summaries and feedback to support livestock extension personnel. The app features an intuitive interface, guiding extension agents through a series of prompts to collect farm and animal data efficiently. Its offline data capture ensures usability in remote areas, with automatic synchronization when online. Farmers and agents can track individual animals, maintaining comprehensive records on breeding, health, and productivity. This improves farm-level productivity, ultimately leading to higher incomes. In 2024, the app was rolled out in Kenya, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda, and Nepal, with training sessions conducted for users. The AADGG platform (https://portal.adgg.ilri.org/) continues to support multi-country genetic gains in smallholder livestock systems.

column16: Brachiaria grass hedgerows in maize-forage legume rotation systems for improved crop and livestock productivity in conservation agriculture systems
column17: Forage legumes such as velvet bean, lablab, and cowpea are usually of a vigorous growth habit and their integration as rotational crops in maize systems reduces the competition between the maize and the legumes. In such systems, more biomass is produced such that a part of it can be fed to livestock while another part is retained as mulch although in most cases it is not adequate. However, such diets are usually high in protein with the need to balance them off with high-energy grasses for a more balanced diet for animals. The introduction of Brachiaria grass (Brachiaria ruziziensis) as a hedgerow in the maize-forage legume rotation system is a possible solution. The maize and the legume are grown in two separate fields and rotated annually. In each phase of the rotation, Brachiaria is grown between the first two and the last two crop rows as hedgerows.

column16: Economics of Agricultural Resource Degradation and Ecosystem Service Losses (APEARD) to quantify and monetize ecosystem services lost due to inaction, gained/prevented through action, and returns on investments combating land degradation
column17: Economics of Agricultural Resource Degradation and Ecosystem Service Losses (APEARD) tool is an innovation that involves three separate but complementary modules each with specific function. The first module enables researchers and experts to estimate the quantities and monetary values of ecosystem services (ESS) lost due to inaction to combat land degradation (LD). If a package of suitable policy, institutional, and technological innovations for combating LD have been identified, the second module enables to estimate the benefits (in terms of the quantities and monetary values of ESS that can be prevented from being lost) due to the interventions. The third module estimates the cost of implementing the package of innovations,  total discounted benefits of action over the entire planning period, and ultimately provides estimates of the returns on investment that are provided in the form of benefit:cost ratios – i.e., the monetary values of the returns on every dollar invested in combating LD.

column16: Local Indicator Selection Process (LISP) for developing context-specific agroecological performance assessments
column17: To generate both locally relevant and global comparable evidence on the impact of agroecology, the AE-I has developed the Holistic Localized Performance Assessment or HOLPA Framework. The goal of the Local Indicator Selection Process (LISP) is to co-develop a set of performance indicators with stakeholders in each Agroecology Living Landscape (ALL) that are relevant for and customized to their farming systems and respond to the vision and interventions that will be implemented in the ALL. Indicators identified in the LISP will be combined with the global performance indicators common to all ALLs, as well as the farm context and agroecology characterization modules to form the Holistic Localized Performance Assessment Tool, which will be implemented in each ALL. ;

column16: Yellow Jacaranda (Schizolobium Parahybum) as a potential coffee and banana shade tree
column17: Most coffee and banana shade trees are slow growing – taking multiple years to provide needed shade levels. We are evaluating a novel tree – yellow jacaranda as a potential source of shade for coffee and possibly banana to improve the adaption to climate chnage. The tree is fast growing, nitrogen fixing and will thus improve nutrient recycling while offering shade for the crops. Its fast-growing nature [up to 5 meters in the first year] could allow for the needed shade levels for coffee to be obtained in a shorter time duration. The trees can produce branches at heights of over 10 meters if not pruned. Studies will also focus on their management [pruning and spacing] for attainment of the optimal branches and shade levels. As a global good, the tree will also improve carbon sequestration of the coffee-banana systems.

column16: Development of 100 days orange fleshed sweet potato variety/es to fit in yearly 3 crops cropping system of farmers in Bangladesh
column17: In Bangladesh, it is primarily cultivated by smallholder farmers, with a growing focus on biofortified and early bulking varieties to combat malnutrition and improve yields. This study evaluated the yield performance and adaptability of early bulking sweet potato genotypes across different environments in Bangladesh using advanced yield trials. The AMMI (Additive Main Effects and Multiplicative Interaction) and joint regression analyses were conducted to assess genotype-by-environment interactions. The results indicated that genotype and environment significantly influenced sweet potato performance, with check variety SP12 exhibiting the highest yield. However, the assessment of viral disease incidence revealed that all the studied genotypes were susceptible to significant viral infections, which could undermine their overall viability in production systems. Consequently, while genotypes P4-22 and P2-551 demonstrated adaptability across environments, their severe susceptibility to virus diseases highlights the need to replicate the trials with clean material in the next season for a definitive conclusion.

column16: Nano-culture technology developed at CIAT is now being used to safety duplicate the cassava collection at a partner institute
column17: National partner Agrosavia, La Selva branch, now hosts a partial safety duplicate of part of the cassava collection managed by CIAT. CIAT has purchased and maintains incubators at Agrosavia, which currently safeguards 4,280 accessions in nano culture, a technique developed at CIAT. In 2024, CIAT have been adjusting lightening conditions and long-distance monitoring of environmental conditions in the growth chamber with the in vitro nano cultures to optimize cultures longevity. CIAT will continue using this safety duplicate platform as part of routine operations going forward. In 2025, he method has been implemented and is in routine use; Nano-culture is a plant tissue culture technique in which cassava in vitro plantlets are cultivated under sterile, controlled conditions—regulated light, temperature, and photoperiod—within small containers (2 ml) at a slow growth rate. This technology enables the preservation of a large number of accessions in a minimal space. Additionally, it is a highly efficient method that requires less plant tissue as source material, reduces propagation time, and minimizes culture medium consumption due to the small container size.

column17: Agriculture in Bangladesh is dominated by rice-rice monocropping with rice covering 75% of the total cultivated area. column16: Spent waste of the edible mushroom Pleurotus ostreatus has potential as a bio-control agent to suppress Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense.
column17: Currently no single strategy has been successful in the control of Fusarium wilt of banana caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc). We observed spent waste of an edible mushroom species to suppress Foc in vitro and under screenhouse conditions. As a follow-up to this, trials to evaluate its potential to suppress Foc under field conditions were set up in 2023. Preliminary results show a single application of mushroom waste over a one-year period to be in adequate for lowering disease pressure on farm., while repeated close applications look to potentially reduce Foc on farm. More bio-active cultures need to still be explored with more regular applications following bio-priming at planting.

column16: Development of a Digital Twin for water resources management in the Limpopo River Basin in southern Africa
column17: Water resource management in any basin, like the Limpopo River Basin with its intermittent supplies, is complex due to factors like rainfall, water allocation, quality, ecosystems, and risk to citizens. Balancing these factors often exceeds most managers' capabilities, despite the existence of numerous data sets. ; This project aims to develop a Digital Twin, a real-time, data-backed digital replica of the ground situation. Enhanced with machine learning and AI, it will integrate available data and models, providing easy and intuitive access to information. Grounded in real data, its outputs will be of tangible value, making it indispensable to water resource managers once fully developed.

column16: Use of Doctor Vida device for virus testing in sweetpotato by Loop-mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) method
column17: Many virus detection methods are mostly performed in a laboratory but also are time-consuming, and expensive. The Loop-mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) method has been adapted and/ or adopted for using on site (i.e., greenhouse, field, etc.) and it is cheaper and rapid in detecting viruses. Doctor Vida is a portable device originally developed LAMP detection of SARS-CoV-2 during the COVID-19 pandemic and is now being adapted for testing plant pathogens as a cost-effective alternative for virus detection. Comparative tests using the same reagents and virus-infected samples showed 100% concordance and similar sensitivity between Doctor Vida and Genie (the gold standard) for detecting sweetpotato viruses (SPFMV, SPCSV, and begomoviruses). Besides, Doctor Vida operates with portable power sources like cell phone power banks, making it suitable for on-site virus detection. These findings confirm the reliability of LAMP tests on Doctor Vida device for detecting plant pathogens.

column16: Refinement of deep learning detection models to enhance a digital tool for pest and disease surveillance of banana pest and diseases
column17: The Tumaini app has undergone significant upgrades to improve banana disease detection. FasterRCNN models were replaced by more advanced YOLOv8 models, resulting in faster and more accurate detections. A step-by-step intelligent detection algorithm, developed with expert phytopathologists, guides users through symptom scanning, improving accuracy by identifying the most affected plant parts and comparing them to reference images. Region-specific AI models were also developed for different continents, increasing the total number of models from 7 to 35, further enhancing detection precision. New diseases, such as Moko in Latin America and Leaf Spot in India, were added to the detection system. Tumaini now requires user registration, ensuring data security and allowing plant detections to be linked to specific users. Additionally, users can map and georeference healthy or diseased banana plants, sharing this information in real-time through the online dashboard. Lastly, This new Tumaini version includes gender disaggregation to collect data on users.

column16: Circular Economy for Colombia
column17: The NATURE+ Initiative aims to establish circular economy innovation hubs in target countries to create an ecosystem for innovation and entrepreneurship in circular economy. In Colombia, partnering strategically with Servicio Nacional de Aprendizaje (SENA), which operates 118 training centers nationwide, a decision was made to form a collaborative network (Recicle +) instead of creating a new center. This network includes SENA, circular economy businesses, and other key players, forming a supportive ecosystem. With the involvement of universities, research centers, incubators, accelerators, and private sector entities, the network aims to broaden its impact. This diverse collaboration seeks to cultivate a supportive environment, encouraging knowledge exchange, training, coaching, and the promotion of circular economy entrepreneurship.; In 2024, a number of activities have been organized such as innovation challenges, student hackathons, hands-on workshops have strengthened capacities in students, farmers, and local communities, encouraging sustainable practices. While the Recicle+ Network is no longer operating under its original name, its core approach and objectives have evolved into the CircularEconomy4Colombia (CE4C) innovation challenge. Developed in collaboration with IWMI, CGIAR Accelerate for Impact Platform (A4IP), GIZ, SENA, Universidad EAN, and the Colombian Ministry of Environment, CE4C was launched in 2024 through a national bootcamp, followed by an accelerator programme and a Demo Day held in March 2025.; The challenge strengthened capacities of circular economy entrepreneurs, facilitated access to networks and institutional partners, and consolidated a collaborative ecosystem in which participating ventures continue to exchange opportunities and engage with public and private support organizations. Key institutions such as SENA and GIZ remain actively connected to the supported business models, indicating sustained relevance and uptake of the innovation.;

column16: Accurate detection of Banana Xanthomonas Wilt in complex african landscapes using high-resolution unmanned aerial vehicles and deep learning
column17: Bananas and plantains are crucial for food security and smallholder livelihoods in Africa. Diseases like Xanthomonas wilt of banana (BXW) threaten production. Traditional disease surveillance methods lack accuracy. We developed a deep-learning system to detect BXW-affected stems in mixed landscapes in Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo using Red, Green, Blue (RGB) and multispectral (MS) images from unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), improved through pansharpening algorithms. Two deep-learning models, Yolo-V8 and Faster R-CNN, were compared. Our system achieved precision, recall, and F1 scores between 75% and 99% for detecting healthy and BXW-infected stems. RGB and panchromatic (PAN) images performed well, while multispectral images struggled due to lower resolution, though certain vegetation indexes showed potential for larger-area detection. This research highlights the promise of UAV imagery and deep learning for crop health assessment, offering a novel approach to BXW detection, revolutionizing agricultural practices, and enhancing food security and early disease management in Africa.

column16: Selection of 65 days potato variety/es for the farmers of Bangladesh to catch up early market segment for higher income
column17: This study evaluated Participatory Adaptive Trials of early bulking potato varieties in two locations of Bangladeshi over two years. Among ten varieties assessed, BARI ALU 79 emerged as the highest yielder with superior tuber size, adaptability, and potential for improving food security and livelihoods. Gender-sensitive farmer preferences showed that male farmers prioritized yield, while female farmers valued color and culinary traits, emphasizing the need for integrating diverse farmer insights into variety selection. By capitalizing on the early bulking traits of BARI ALU 79, this variety has the potential to significantly improve farmers' livelihoods and boost food security in Bangladesh. Future collaboration with seed companies and ongoing farmers engagement is crucial for successful adoption and market alignment.

column17: Many released varieties are not adopted by farmers and other end users because of lack of important traits desired by end-users. End users including gender related traits were captured in the TPP that were developed for each market segment/breeding pipeline. These traits are considered during selection of genotypes for advancement at each breeding stage. Pesek-Baker and DISIRE programs are used to develop indices that are used for selection of genotypes that combine all desirable traits on TPPs. column16: AI Powered Realtime Banana Fusarium wilt detection using Unmanned Aerial Vehicles
column17: Using a custom-trained YOLO-v8 deep learning model, we expanded detection capabilities to include video analysis, enabling real-time disease identification. We successfully surveyed banana fields via drones, identifying healthy and Fusarium-infected plants. While further validation is needed, the most groundbreaking aspect is the establishment of a real-time disease detection pipeline using drones. Over 8,000 drone images from Fusarium-infected fields in Vietnam and Peru were analyzed. In 2024, we trained a YOLO-v9 model to differentiate between Banana Xanthomonas Wilt (BXW), Fusarium wilt, and healthy plants, using datasets from the Democratic Republic of Congo for Banana Xanthomonas Wilt and Vietnam for Fusarium wilt. The model achieved a mean average precision (mAP) between 68-80% across all categories foe YOLO-v9, with Faster R-CNN slightly outperforming YOLO-v9 for Fusarium detection.

column16: Reference Diet Deprivation (ReDD) index: a tool to measure diet quality and explore how policies are driving dietary change
column17: The Reference Diet Deprivation (ReDD) index is estimated from household consumption survey data and measures the incidence, breadth, and depth of diet deprivation (the voluntary or involuntary shortfall in consumption) across multiple food groups. It can be used to compare diet quality across households or populations or track changes in diet quality over time. The advantage of the ReDD index is that it can be integrated into an economic model to examine changes in diet quality under different food and agriculture policy scenarios or external shocks. More recently, the ReDD index has been used as part of the underlying data for the Food Security Simulator, a tool for assessing the potential short-term impacts of food price or household income shocks on food security and people’s diets. It is showing to be a useful tool for researchers and decisionmakers to assess diet quality and examine the drivers of dietary change.

column16: Establishment of national or regional networks for rice disease surveillance and monitoring
column17: The Global Biotic Stress Monitoring and Screening Network (Global BioNET) was established, aiming to enhance the surveillance and monitoring of rice diseases and pests, crucial for early detection and effective management. In 2023, substantial progress was made in setting up national and regional surveillance networks in Bangladesh, India, and Vietnam. BioNET-Bangladesh was launched after identifying major rice diseases and experts through a survey. In India, global BioNET was launched in agreement with the "All India Coordinated Research Project on Rice" (AICRPR), a well-established system for monitoring rice diseases and pests. In Vietnam, the BioNET-Vietnam network was marked by a scientific workshop that focused on enhancing cooperation among research institutions, improving the evaluation of rice varieties, and enhancing research on resistance genes. In 2024, BioNET was introduced to African rice pathologists. These activities represent major steps in addressing rice diseases and pests at both national and global levels.

column16: Penside rapid diagnostics for African swine fever for use by veterinarians and veterinary technicans in Low and Middle Income Countries.
column17: Diagnostic of African swine fever(ASF) includes from clinical diagnostics to identification of the agent to serological tests, according to the World Organisation of Animal Health. Clinical diagnostics is often challenging since ASF shares common clinical signs with other pig diseases in its acute form; and for the chronic forms subtle clinical signs can be overlook. Laboratory diagnostics are more accurate, including the identification of the viral particle or the presence of antibodies against the virus. However, all these laboratory test pose the same problem, they are difficult to implement in the field where infrastructures and human expertise is limited. A new generation of rapid lateral flow assays for the ASF diagnostic have been developed by various companies for both viral particle detection and anti-ASF Virus antibodies detection. We evaluated different LFA with interest for the African market. A report with the findings and a proposed way forward will be provided.

column16: A policy support toolkit for informing Agriculture Diversification in Eastern and Southern Africa
column17: This activity provides support for policy design, implementation and appraisal in the area of agriculture diversification in the Eastern and Southern African region with a specific focus on the Ukama Ustawi focus countries. The toolkit will have two components for a start namely; a) an up-to-date database of indicators relevant to diversification, and b) a policy oriented report. The policy support tool, thus, seeks to avail timely and comprehensive information on the key indicators of diversification, its benefits and challenges. These indicators will include inventories of key value chains in the region and for each country, highlighting the current and past levels of productivity, shares of intra-and extra-regional trade and opportunities enhancing, and challenges limiting sustainable diversification and value chain development. The  toolkit also tracks and highlights the status of socio-economic characteristics of the population in the Eastern and Southern Africa, and their interface with agriculture outcomes. The data generated will also be availed in interactive maps to permit quick analysis and presentation of information  for decision making. The report will present key recommendations for policy makers and practitioners to ensure regional and country resilience, and food security  for all, through sustainable agriculture diversification.

column16: PathoTracer 2.0: Advanced Rice Disease Management through Dynamic Data Visualization and Analysis
column17: PathoTracer, developed by IRRI, is a decision-support platform for rice disease and pathogen management. In 2023, it underwent a transformation from the PathoTracer RShiny to a more advanced QlikSense application, aiming to automate data management and improve visualization of rice pathogen data, especially for Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo). The updated PathoTracer2.0 dashboard, powered by QlikSense Enterprise and Amazon Web Services, offers dynamic visualization and analysis, enabling users to track global Xoo incidences and dominant AXoo strains. Incorporating data from 19 partner institutes, it also lists rice varieties with resistance genes, aiding informed decision-making in rice disease management. In 2024, PathoTracer was improved and reverted to using Rshiny and R visualization libraries for mapping Xoo isolate locations. The application currently houses data submitted from 22 partner institutes. List of varieties containing R-genes for specific Axoo populations was also enabled.

column16: Development of a high-throughput genotyping platform to monitor rice blast pathogens from field samples
column17: Leaf blast in rice, caused by Magnaporthe oryzae, is challenging to manage due to diverse avirulence (AVR) genes. Effective resistance deployment requires detecting AVR genes specific to M. oryzae strains. The pathogen has four populations based on genomic characteristics (genome-wide SNP data), each with distinct pathogenicity patterns. We developed and validated 8 SNP markers to distinguish these populations and 39 markers targeting AVR genes, including AVR-Pizt, AVR-Pii, AVR-Pia, AVR-Pik, AVR-Pib, AVR-Pi9, and AVR-Pita. Using PACE, 26 markers showed ≥80% sensitivity, 50% specificity, or 81% accuracy for monitoring. Additional markers are under development, with successful ones integrated into the PathoTracer platform and validated with isolates from other countries.

column16: Pathways towards improved economic resilience for women in agrifood systems
column17: The evidence synthesis collates evidence on how gender norms facilitate or hamper women’s abilities to achieve women's economic resilience in agrifood systems, specifically in the context of climate change.  In the synthesis, fifteen overarching gender norms which play out at individual, household and / or institutional levels that affect women’s economic resilience, are identified, and described. The synthesis covers the production domain of the agrifood system as well as the consumption domain.  Better understanding on how gender norms affect women’s ability to build economic resilience opens up opportunities for targeted gender-transformative development interventions. The evidence synthesis proposes an Economic Resilience Pathways Conceptual Framework that could be used to structure further research into women’s economic resilience in the face of climate change. As such this innovation might act as a guide for policymakers, practitioners, and stakeholders that are seeking to strengthen women's economic resilience in agrifood systems.

column16: Social behaviour change communication (SBCC) approach, through social media and other approaches, for gender-transformative change including more equitable engagement in, and benefit from, agribusiness for women and youth in Tanzania
column17: Gender norms in Tanzania discourage women from engaging in business, including livestock business, particularly when the business becomes lucrative. To address these discriminating norms, we team up with an award winning social media company for behavioural change (Shujaaz) and implemented various campaigns, targeting the youth in particular, through social media and a bundle of other communication approaches. The innovation has now been expanded to Vietnam which faces similar challenges. In Vietnam we are working with the Vietnam Women Academy to implement the approach for the gender transformative work through other communication approaches e.g WhatApp, Poems, Competitions on the best key messages, Women and Farmers unions, farmer WhatsApp groups.

column16: Supplemental irrigation of wheat to mitigate productivity loss when the soil moisture content drops to 60% during periods of drought in rainfed cropping systems in Morocco and across MENA
column17: Supplemental irrigation is the practice of providing additional water to crops to support their survival, especially during periods of drought. Wheat cropping systems in Morocco and across much of the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) are predominantly rainfed and vulnerable to poor crop yields or total failure with increasing rainfall variability and high-temperature extremes. Crop yield reduction or total loss can cause economic, social, agricultural, and food security challenges. In situations where supplemental irrigation is possible, irrigation scheduling is done through the in-situ measurement of soil moisture content at a depth of 90 cm. Irrigation water is applied through drippers when the available soil moisture content in the soil profile drops to 60 %. In drought years, the precise application of 28-166 mm supplemental irrigation (depending on drought severity) has been found to increase wheat productivity by 2-3 t ha-1 when compared to rainfed conditions.

column16: Artificial intelligence tool developed to identify rice accessions in genebanks
column17: IRRI genebank staff with private sector partners, have imaged thousands of rice seeds and panicles and generated data to train AI tool to discern seed morphological characteristics and identify rice accessions. The AI tool has been trained on 100,000 accessions and successfully identifying accessions with morphological distinctions. The tool is improving the efficiency in managing 130K rice collections and can also contribute to high-throughput phenotyping approaches. As a result of the AI tool development, the IRRI genebank won an award from Google in 2023 to refine the tool and use it to carry out a large-scale evaluation for tolerance to flooding, salinity and drought. Using the tool, over 60k IRG accessions were screened for abiotic stresses (drought, submergence, salinity).  Best accessions for these traits identified. ; In 2025, the digitization of seed images of the entire collection was completed.  Screening the entire collection has been completed for flood tolerance. Novel flood-tolerant donors have been identified. Initial screening the entire collection for drought is completed and data analysis is ongoing. Initial screening the entire collection for salinity is ongoing and data analysis is ongoing. The methodology to screen the entire collection for anaerobic germination is optimized and screening is ongoing. The methodology to screen for disease (blast) tolerance is ongoing.

column16: Decision support tools developed to manage Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN) during maize seed production
column17: One of the important components for the sustainable and efficient management of MLN is to implement a digital tool/app for efficient data management with several partners.  An App, which is known as Maize Clean Seed Production Tracker has been developed in collaboration with IITA. This App is ODK software-based and is enabled through a web-based toolbox to support data management and decision support for conducting MLN surveillance in a time series and to implement SOPs for MLN pathogen-free commercial seed production. The App is being piloted in Kenya in partnership with Kenya Plant Health Inspectorate Service (KEPHIS), and will be further scaled in sub-Saharan Africa in partnership with relevant regulatory agencies. During 2024, a total of 204 staff members (including 175 Male; 29 Female) of KEPHIS were trained at Kitale and Nakuru Counties in Kenya on the use of the App.;

column16: A cost-effective fungicide seed-dressing for the control of seed-borne bacterial pathogens
column17: Seed-borne bacteria impact plant health and yield, and bacterial-contaminated seed is a source for the transboundary spread of pathogens. Due to a lack of effective seed-dressing agents, eliminating seed-borne bacteria involves the hot-water treatment, which is laborious, sensitive to temperature settings, and known to affect seed viability. This study evaluated mancozeb and carbendazim for their bactericidal properties by testing against eight seed-borne bacterial species (Bacillus cereus, Bacillus subtilis, Ralstonia solanecearum, Xanthomonas manihotis, Pantoea stewartii, Xanthomonas glycinea, Xanthomonas oryzae and Xanthomonas vignicola) in three crops (cowpea, maize, and soybean). Seed dressing with mancozeb resulted in 100% suppression of seed-borne bacteria and serves as the broad-spectrum reagent for seed dressing to eliminate seed-borne bacterial infection. Mancozeb is widely available, and doubles as a reagent for preventing seed-borne and bacterial contamination. To our knowledge, this is the first study to validate the effectiveness of mancozeb to control seed-borne bacterial contamination.

column16: Marker-trait association identified, developed and deployed for key traits in yam breeding to mainstream best practices in breeding pipelines
column17: Developing improved yam varieties through classical breeding is slow and complex. In 2023–2024, IITA made major strides in modernizing yam breeding by deploying molecular tools. Focused on key tuber traits—dry matter content, flesh oxidation, and boiled/pounded yam quality—14 trait-associated markers were validated using 374 varieties. Eleven were converted into KASP-PCR and integrated into the breeding program. Marker-assisted selection (MAS) was applied at the seedling nursery stage, enabling early identification of favorable alleles. The middle-density SNP marker panel was also refined to boost selection accuracy.; In partnership with the Salk Institute, a pan-genome analysis of six yam varieties (2 D. alata, 4 D. rotundata) led to the development of a haplotype-based reference genome. This revealed key structural variations and novel genes, expanding the genetic pool for breeding. These advances strengthen the yam discovery pipeline and support precision breeding for resilient, high-quality varieties.;

column16: Genomic assisted population improvement strategy implementing genomic predicted cross performance for cross-selection in yam
column17: In yam breeding, selecting meritorious parents and optimizing their matings to maximize genetic gain are critical steps in developing improved varieties. To enhance this process, efforts were made to optimize parent selection and identify the best cross combinations by leveraging molecular tools and advanced genomic selection approaches.; A Genomic Prediction Cross-Performance (GPCP) pipeline was developed and integrated into YamBase analytical functions, enabling the identification of parental cross combinations with superior genetic merit for multiple traits. In 2024, the yam breeding program combined GPCP with Optimum Crossing Selection (OCS) to refine parent selection and crossing plan development.; This integrated approach was successfully applied to advance several progenies of white yam, ensuring that crosses were designed based on crossing merit and alignment with Target Product Profiles (TPP). By incorporating genomic predictions and optimized crossing strategies, the breeding program has strengthened its capacity to select and advance superior yam varieties with improved genetic potential;

column16: Carbon project in the Colombian Orinoquia: Transforming grasslands for emission reductions
column17: The project “Natural silvopastoral systems in the Colombian Orinoquia Region” is a grouped carbon project comprising a set of activities to improve grassland management in approximately 150,000 ha of Vichada and Meta, Colombia. The crediting period is 2020 to 2040 applying the Verra Methodology for Improved Agricultural Land Management VM0042 Version 2.0. The project primary objective is to achieve a reduction in overall emissions by focusing on carbon sequestration. This will be accomplished mainly by implementing adaptive multi-paddock grazing with improved deep-rooted grass cultivars, specifically Urochloa humidicola. An estimate of the annual average and total GHG emission reductions and removals are approximately 270,000 t CO2eq per year and 5,400,000 t CO2eq, respectively. Prior to the implementation of the project, livestock practices in the regions are characterized by annual burning of savannas and low-quality animal feed. The project was successfully listed in the pipeline of the Verra Registry in November 2023.;

column16: Pre-released sweetpotato genotypes selected for on-farm evaluation:  triadic comparison of technologies approach.
column17: Sweetpotato product development team uses the triadic comparison of technologies approach. In 2024, CIP Mozambique tested 11 pre-released clones under on-farm for multi-stakeholder validation across five provinces (Niassa, Nampula, Zambezia, Manica and Inhambane) ensuring representation of diverse environments and farmer conditions. In each province 5 districts were selected for on-farm trialing and a total of 170 farmers successfully established the trials. The TRICOT design was the experimental design of choice.  Most agricultural actors, including farmers, extension officers and other local government representatives were involved in the setting up of trials and their assessment. Farmer and other stakeholders feedback on performance clones will be utilized and incorporated into decisions of variety release and genetic gains in farmers’ fields will be calculated. The validation system strengthened the selection and adoption of new varieties, integrating farmer needs and gender considerations into breeding advancements.

column17: Nutritional traits are important in sweet potato breeding. Iron is important to prevent anemia in pregnant mothers and children. High levels of polyphenols inhibit iron absorption and its always important to strike a balance between the two. The list provided shows genotypes that were selected for advancement due to high levels of iron and zinc. After further analysis of nutritional content, eating quality traits and agronomic data, four clones in the orange fleshed pipeline and seven clones in the white fleshed pipeline were selected, handed over to the national agriculture research program for final testing and variety release of at least one clone from each pipeline. Released varieties have a wider reach to communities that suffer most from micronutrient deficiency problems. ;

column16: Rapid propagation techniques significantly increased the supply of sweetpotato vine cuttings of promising clones, enabling the establishment of advanced yield trials across breeding programs in Uganda, Mozambique, Tanzania, and Rwanda.
column17: Sufficient planting material is a major limitation in sweetpotato trialing. However, rapid clonal propagation methods now enable large-scale multiplication of planting materials within a few months. This approach was used to multiply breeding clones for advanced yield trials. In Uganda, the International Potato Center (CIP), in collaboration with the National Agricultural Research Organization (NARO), Rwanda Agriculture and Animal Resources Development Board (RAB), and Tanzania Agricultural Research Institute (TARI), generated 74,450 vine cuttings for advanced yield trials conducted at 20 locations. Each trial was replicated three times, with 45 plants per plot. Additionally, CIP Mozambique produced 2,050 kg of 20 breeding clones for testing in Target Population of Environments (TPE), Multi-Environment Trials (MET), and on-farm trials. In total, 170 on-farm trials, 10 replicated TPE trials, and 7 replicated METs were established. Variety release decisions are informed by data collected from METs and on-farm trials.;
