column17: Change in agri-food systems towards increased climate resilience requires the support of industries. Entrepreneurship also requires capacity building and support to flourish, so that it can affect the agri-food system positively. The start-up business eocsystem in Cambodia is a platform for young men and women to engage in agriculture and the food system.; ; The innovation is a business accelerator program that equips start-up groups with business and financial capacity, and links them with the appropriate technical support to enable them to have products and services that have value to their customers. This innovation specifically targets the involvement of women in business. The selection of start-up groups are linked to four universities in Cambodia, and target young people. column16: Integrated rice-fish aquaculture systems for climate resilient rice based communities taken further through other national and regional programs in Cambodia
column17: Integrated rice-fish aquaculture systems for climate resilient rice-based communities in the Cambodian Mekong Delta taken further through the ASEAN CGIAR Innovate for Food Program and the Promoting Climate Resilient Landscapes in the Tonle Sap.; Rice and fish are the main commodities produced and consumed in Cambodia. They provide the most contribution to caloric intake, but are affected by climate change. Aquaculture within rice fields is proposed as a climate-resilient practice to manage the production for both rice and fish. This innovation ensures rice management is suitable for integrating the fish, and also that selection of fish species and aquaculture management are suitable for rice-based systems. Integrated rice-fish culture entails growing the rice while fish is able to enter the fields at specific periods, maintaining fish shelter through small pond or canal, and integrated management suitable for both rice and fish.; ; The Initiative co-designed the climate-smart aspects of integrated rice-fish culture. It has completed one season of experiments in semi-controlled conditions and is now incorporating the lessons drawn to improve the design of the approach and test in the field again later.; ; In 2025, these efforts were sustained in partnership with the ASEAN program that is aiming to refine the technical package and identify pathways to scale.

column16: Protocol for the Inspection and Certification of Quality Declared Seed (QDS) to be used by QDS producers themselves to self-declare the quality of their seed
column17: Quality seed certification is often a bottleneck for smallholder seed producers, particularly for vegetatively propagated crops like cassava. The International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) developed this digital protocol to enable seed producers to self-assess and declare the quality of their cassava planting material. The methodology combines digital tools including Seed Tracker and PlantVillage Nuru applications, allowing producers to conduct quality assessments and transmit results electronically to Tanzania's Official Seed Certification Institute in real-time. This innovation addresses the challenge of expensive and time-consuming traditional certification processes. The protocol is being tested with 20 quality declared seed producers in Tanzania, with careful attention to gender balance in participant selection and analysis.

column16: Breakthrough discovery on plant odour sources to mimic attractant pheromones
column17: In Africa, food legumes like cowpeas and beans are vital protein sources but suffer yield losses of up to 80% due to insect pests. Smallholder farmers rely on insecticides, contributing to resistance and food safety concerns. This study explores a sustainable alternative using semiochemicals for pest management. Using coupled gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC–MS) and coupled GC-electroantennographic detection (EAD) analyses, this study identified 2-methylbutyl 2-methylbutanoate as the aggregation pheromone of Clavigralla elongata, a key legume pest. Field trials in East and West Africa showed this pheromone and its aanalog isopentyl butanoate, attracted multiple pests, including Maruca vitrata, Megalurothrips sjostedti, Bemisia tabaci, and the natural enemy Gryon fulviventris. Optimized pheromone traps significantly reduced pests and increased natural enemy density sixfold. Legume yields in pheromone-treated fields matched insecticide-treated ones, exceeding controls by 320–590%. These findings establish coreid bug pheromones as effective, sustainable tools for legume pest management without insecticides.

column16: Maize seed treatment protocol developed and validated for eliminating contamination of Maize Lethal Necrosis (MLN) causing viruses
column17: Clean seed movement (MCMV disease-free) from endemic countries is very critical for containing and preventing the spread of MLN.  A seed treatment protocol using TSP (10%) for removing MLN (especially MCMV) virus contamination from the seed is developed. A new seed treatment prototype with the capacity of 700 pouches (each with 200 kernels) has been designed. Over 7000 germplasm entries were decontaminated using the protocol, with less than 1% of treated samples showing positive for MCMV. The protocol was validated using a different set of MLN-contaminated grain samples. The protocol is being further refined in collaboration with KEPHIS, KALRO and Kenya Seed Company. A prototype with larger seed treatment capacity (0.5 ton) has been fabricated and will be further tested in 2025.

column16: Stem-cutting dipping in insecticides and entomopathogenic biopesticides control cassava whitefly (Bemisia tabaci)
column17: Cutting dipping in Mandiplus significantly reduced adult whitefly numbers by an average of 74% and nymphs by 63% compared to the control. Cassava brown streak disease (CBSD) incidence was 31% in Mandiplus, and 21% in Mandiplus + Lecatech compared 52% in the control at 6MAP. CMD was absent. Entomopathogenic biopesticide Lecatech combined with Mandiplus reduced CBSD but had no significant additional effect on whitefly numbers. Average root yield per plant increased significantly by 73% in Mandiplus, and 61% in Mandiplus + Lecatech treated plots compared to the control.

column16: Creation of the Salinity Forecasting System: A Framework for Advancing Water Resource Sustainability and Climate Resilience through Local-scale Hydrological Modeling in the Ganges Delta
column17: This innovation entails the development of a salinity forecasting system for the 34/2p Khulna polder in the Ganges Delta, utilizing machine learning and deep learning techniques. The system will leverage readily available historical temporal datasets, including information on rainfall, groundwater level, groundwater quality, river salinity, river discharge, tidal height, land use/catchment characteristics, and water extraction patterns within the polder. These data, along with other pertinent co-variates, will serve as proxies to predict salinity levels. This predictive model aims to provide valuable insights to farmers, guiding them on the optimal timing to initiate their agricultural activities.

column16: Comprehensive assessment of salt and water dynamics in polder systems through integrated water modelling approach for advancing water resource sustainability and climate resilience in the Ganges Delta
column17: This innovation aims to conduct an in-depth analysis of salt and water dynamics within the 34/2p polder system. The approach combines an integrated modeling approach on surface and groundwater interaction modeling with hydrochemical modeling to understand the factors influencing water and salinity dynamics. This comprehensive assessment will shed light on the area's unique environmental and hydrological conditions to gain insights into the factors that impact water and salinity dynamics within the specified polders. ; ; The model, which is now being adopted by CG researchers, will utilize available data on irrigation conditions, groundwater levels and quality to serve as the basis for model calibration and validation, and conducting further scenario analyses. It is designed to creating scenarios and implementing sustainable management strategies to evaluate the effect of different interventions aimed at enhancing agricultural productivity. Governments, local agriculture and water authorities, and researchers are expected to benefit from the results and recommended strategies.

column16: The Open Learning Portal: Centralized Education on Sustainable Agriculture Practices through Moodle-Based Platform featuring Microlearning Courses and Collaborative Tools

The platform's rich features include an extensive series of microlearning courses, interactive discussion forums, and timely announcements, all aimed at fostering a dynamic learning environment. It hosts a wealth of educational resources, complemented by engaging assessments and quizzes to enhance the learning experience. Progress tracking and user analytics are integral components, providing valuable insights for continuous improvement. Through the Open Learning Portal, the platform notably advances team capabilities. It offers a structured process for course development, starting from needs assessment, moving through content curation and storyline development, to comprehensive course review, user testing, and ultimately, the launch.  ;

column16: Comprehensive Agronomy Solutions (CASH) Hub: Streamlining Digital Data, Enhancing Research, Providing Crop Advisories, Standardizing Guides, Facilitating Mechanization, and Revolutionizing Agricultural Practices for Increased Productivity and Sustainability
column17: The Comprehensive Agronomy Solutions Hub serves as an innovative website, disseminating agricultural solutions across four main areas: digital data management, crop-specific advisories, standardized agronomy guides, and mechanization. This website streamlines the collection, management, and accessibility of digital data, significantly enhancing agronomic research and fostering innovation. It offers targeted advisories for annual crops, including recommendations on optimal fertilizer use, planting schedules, variety selection, and weather forecasts. In addition, the hub provides access to standardized agronomy guides and resources for prioritizing practices, thereby establishing best practices in the field.This approach revolutionizes agronomic practices by making them widely accessible, thus markedly improving agricultural productivity and sustainability. The website is catering to researchers, farmers, and other stakeholders, currently features 16 solutions developped under EiA. Moreover, the platform allows users to filter solutions by specific crops or regions, showcasing the global application of the Sustainable Farming Program’s diverse solutions.

column16: Sustainable Farming Program (SFP) Events: A Global Platform for Facilitating Agronomic Conversations on Sustainable Intensification and Climate Change Adaptation, Uniting Experts,Practitioners for Knowledge Dissemination, Innovation, and Strategy Development in Agriculture
column17: The "Sustainable Farming Program (SFP) Events" stand as a pioneering initiative, orchestrating pivotal conversations on vital agronomic themes like sustainable intensification and climate change adaptation. These events form a dynamic platform where a diverse mix of experts, practitioners, researchers, policymakers, and farmers worldwide converge to engage in in-depth discussions, exchange innovative ideas, and share best practices.; SFP's role in these gatherings is integral. It not only disseminates cutting-edge knowledge across the global agronomy community but also sparks innovation and drives actionable strategies in the realm of modern agriculture. The events are designed to cultivate a synergistic environment, encouraging stakeholders from various sectors to unite, learn collaboratively, and jointly pursue sustainable, climate-resilient agricultural methodologies. This holistic approach ensures that each event not only fosters dialogue but also equips participants with the tools and insights necessary to make a tangible impact in the field of agronomy.; ; The SFP Events analytics show strong, demand-driven engagement consistent with a public events and outreach platform. With approximately 2,600 active and new users, the platform achieved broad reach, primarily through direct access and organic search, indicating that users intentionally visit the site to access event information. The activity timeline displays sharp spikes rather than steady usage, reflecting traffic surges around specific events, announcements, or registration periods rather than continuous daily use. The short average engagement time of 13 seconds is therefore expected, as users typically visit briefly to view event details, speakers, or schedules. Wide geographic distribution, led by the United States, China, and several African and European countries, demonstrates strong international visibility and confirms the platform’s effectiveness in supporting global event promotion and dissemination.; ; In 2025, the main development was the update of the branding to fit with SFP.;

column16: Participatory variety selection and early generation seed production of cereals and legumes
column17: The highlands of North Shoa in Amhara region are dominated by cereals  followed by food legumes. The productivity of cereals and food legumes is low due to biotic and abiotic factors as well as insufficient input supplies like certified seed, inoculants and other inputs. Because of diseases and insect pests, acidity and water logging problems, farmers are reducing areas of food legumes and growing more cereals leading to low crop diversity, reduced soil fertility, incomes and food diversity. Several cereals, food legume and potato  varieties are released by many centers did not reach farmers due to limited demonstration to create awareness and demand and shortage of quality early generation seed. Moreover, popular varieties certified seed production is hampered due to shortage of breeder and pre-basic seeds of new and popular varieties from research centers. The poor access to quality seed contributes to low crop productivity and crop diversity.

column16: Empowering Tanzanian Farmers Through Farm to Market Alliance: Establishing Farmer Service Centers for Enhanced Productivity, Market Linkages, and Comprehensive Agricultural Services
column17: Farm to Market Alliance (FtMA) offers a platform to provide last mile service delivery to farmers in rural Tanzania via Farmer Service Centres. To realize this, the project seeks to establish a robust network of  farmer service centers scattered across six regions of Tanzania. Farmer service centers are grouped in three main categorizes; 1) Agricultural Marketing Cooperative Society (AMCOS), 2) Micro, Small and Medium Enterprize (MSME) led (comprising of agro-dealers, aggregators, processors etc.) and 3) Individual entrepreneurs (comprising of Village Based Agricultural Advisors/agents (VBAAs), lead farmers). Through the Farmer service centers and applying a demand led approach, farmer services that enhance smallholder productivity on farm can be accessed through facilitating linkages with input companies. These services include agricultural inputs, mechanization services, advisory, finance to mention but a few. The farmer service centers also double as aggregation hubs and link farmers to markets.

column16: Crop yield estimation using Artificial Intelligence for Rice Crop Manager (RCM) database in Odisha, India
column17: The Rice Crop Manager (RCM) database contains 283,346 recommendations across 31 districts in Odisha, eastern India. RCM's functionality can be extended beyond fertilizer recommendations to include comprehensive crop management decision-making and the development of support systems for various stakeholders. The methodology employs advanced technologies such as machine learning to create a model that selects optimal parameters for generating these recommendations. The target yield has also been estimated using a calibration and validation ratio of 70:30, with performance evaluation primarily based on R-square, Root Mean Square Error, and Mean Absolute Error calculations. The analysis indicates that the approach is suitable for the data collected and can be automated to generate more valuable information for farmers' benefit.

column16: Milk quality monitoring platform for collecting and analyzing quality and price data from Milk Collection Centers in Uganda
column17: This platform provides raw (anonymized) data of over 14,062 milk samples submitted by Milk Collection Centers (MCC) in Mbarabra, Kirihura, Kazoo,, and Ntungamo in Uganda. The data was recorded through 75 milk analyzers installed by the Ugandan Dairy Development Authority in randomly selected local MCC. The platform allows one to select a custom date range (e.g., the last 30 days) and obtain the average butter fat (%), average solids-not-fat (SNF), (%), average protein (%), and average added water (%) of samples taken for each MCC. The platform provides the average price paid (in UGX) and the average milk quantity (liters). The platform also reports the total number of samples submitted to each MCC during the selected period. In addition to averages by center, the platform also provides the evolution of overall averages over the chosen time frame (using moving averages). In 2025, researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition conducted follow-up research with 20 MCC to understand how price signals at different points in the value chain influence sourcing behavior, investment in quality, and overall market dynamics. Data generated by the platform is an important input into this ongoing study.

column16: Strategies for the management of seed yam reinfection and seed degeneration in seed yam production plots
column17: Yam mosaic virus (YMV) transmitted by aphid vectors is the most important production constraint to seed and ware yam production in West Africa. Due to the lack of host resistance, protecting clean seed yams from YMV reinfection by aphids is crucial to prevent yield losses and seed degeneration. Trials were organized to identify methods to avoid YMV infection using two Dioscorea rotundata varieties. Approaches used include: (i) use of tall growing cereal as a barrier to interfere with aphid movement, and (ii) 3% (v/v) mineral (paraffin) oil sprays to prevent aphid feeding. The second-year trials in 2024 continued this model but only using insect-proof net instead of tall growing cereal as a barrier as mineral oil sprays were ineffective. YMV incidence increased from the first month after planting, with the highest incidence of 70% in control after three months. There is a delay in infection in protected plots.

column16: Remote sensing and AI tools for mapping banana fields for banana bunchy top virus (BBTV) surveillance.
column17: Banana production faces a serious threat from the invasive banana bunchy top virus (BBTV). Surveillance is challenging due to the fragmented nature of banana farming. We developed remote sensing-based Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools to identify banana fields for targeted BBTV surveillance to address this. Using synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data from the Copernicus Sentinel-1 satellite and AI algorithms such as random forest (RF) and convolutional neural networks (CNN), we achieved over 85% accuracy in identifying banana fields in Nigeria, Benin, Togo, and Ghana. We used Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) RGB images and the GoPro action camera photos to train and validate the models. These tools improve efficiency in mapping BBTV spread, aiding data-driven decisions for containment strategies and supporting sustainable banana production in African smallholder systems.

column16: IRRI Area-based Yield Index Insurance for rice, based on satellite data in the Philippines
column17: An area-based yield (ARBY) index insurance for rice based on satellite data was developed and tested in the Philippines. ARBY provides coverage based on historical average yield of a specific geographic area, rather than individual farmers’ yields, to determine payouts in the event of crop losses. The current and historical yields are based on the Philippine Rice Information System (PRISM, https://prism.philrice.gov.ph/), an innovative satellite-based rice mapping and monitoring system. Operational since 2018, PRISM uses time series Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR), a smart detection system, and crop growth simulation modeling to map rice areas and provide timely yield forecasts and end-of-season rice yields. It is more efficient than the traditional indemnity-based crop insurance which involves manual visits and verifications for each claim. By leveraging modern technologies, better crop insurance products and services can be offered to farmers to help improve their resilience to climatic risks.

column16: National and provincial Indigenous foods platform for strengthening island food systems with Indigenous food and improving nutrition in Solomon Islands
column17: Solomon Islands remains a highly agricultural society with high rates of consumption of traditional subsistence garden produce and aquatic foods. Imported foods have a role to play, but only if they are viewed as complementary to the local foods produced from gardens and seas rather than being a major component of the diet. Imagining food futures based on strengths in Indigenous food systems is important to change the course of island food systems in transition. Strengthening Indigenous food systems in Solomon Islands has been a priority by WorldFish and KastomGaden Association. A tokStori (indigenous forum format) brought together rural actors and key stakeholders to talk about traditional farming and aquatic foods under a nutrition-sensitive approach and to listen to ideas about what the Solomon Islands food systems future could look like. It has created a social movement platform for strengthening island food systems with Indigenous foods. ; Still relevant in 2025, where we have expanded the scope in partnership with the Pacific Food Revolution and the Solomon Islands National University Centre for Islands to develop the Island Food Council in Solomon Islands. ;

column16: A scalable, multi-actor in vitro system for mass production and distribution of four released matooke hybrids, enabling timely access to improved planting material through public and private sector collaboration.
column17: This innovation introduces a decentralized, scalable system for the mass production and distribution of four released matooke hybrids—TARIBAN1 to TARIBAN4—in Tanzania. It combines the in vitro multiplication capacities of two public research labs (TARI Arusha and Dar es Salaam) and two SMEs (Crop Bioscience Solutions and Mauri Mazuri) to ensure a reliable supply of quality planting materials. By linking production to nurseries and distributing plantlets through both public and private channels, the innovation increases farmer access to improved banana varieties. column16: Defining harmonized indicators to understand and drive breeding modernization, improve organizational performance, and aid recognition of contributions to the germplasm development process by diverse research teams, individuals and partners

column16: Innovation in Economic Modeling for Growth, Poverty Reduction, and Food Security Insights
column17: The interrelationship between economic growth, poverty, and food security is highly complex, with relatively few studies conducted on this topic in recent years. To address this gap, the Growth, Poverty, and Undernutrition Monitoring Model (GPUMM), developed by IFPRI, serves as an economic modeling tool designed to better understand these connections holistically by employing a macro-micro modeling approach linking a macroeconomic model with micro-level household survey data. ; ; We have completed the model calibration, enabling us to provide a comprehensive and consistent view of how macroeconomic changes influence income distribution, which in turn drives poverty and hunger rates over time. ; ; Using this model, we developed projections of how economic growth will affect poverty and undernutrition rates through 2026. This projection results help countries in tracking their progress toward achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth).;

column16: Rice-Fish Suitability Decision Support System Modelling to inform the sustainable planning and management of rice-fish systems leading to improved food security, nutrition, incomes, and employment in Myanmar and Cambodia
column17: Known as the rice-fish decision support system (DSS), it is a bundle of digital and analytical tools used to inform the planning and management of rice-fish systems. Suitability maps derived from the DSS have shown the potential for the transformation of 15,700 km2 across the Ayeyarwady region, supporting improved local food security, nutritional security, incomes, and employment. As well as helping identify areas most suitable to the introduction of rice-fish polyculture, the tools help ensure that the needs of stakeholders are taken into consideration. A similar Decision Support System (DSS) for rice-fish suitability is now being developed for Cambodia, following the same approach and method as the one in place for Myanmar. In addition, the DSS for Myanmar has now been refined at a lower scale to support decisions at the local level.; ; 2024 and 2025 the innovation is still relevant and active, but no further development.

column16: Small-scale feed processing and marketing by youth and women groups in Ethiopia
column17: Feed resources are scarce and expensive in the Initiative intervention area of Bonga and Doyogena in Ethiopia. Two youth and women groups in these regions have been supported through research and development activities in the last number of years to improve their small ruminant production. The lack of nutritious and inexpensive suitable feed resources has now solved through the introduction of a complete feed processing unit composed of a grinder, conveyor belt and feed mixer. Each farmer group has received a feed processing unit which is produced by a local manufacturer. International Center for Agricultural Research in the Dry Areas and its partners have developed suitable feed ratios taking into account the availability of local ingredients. The co-designed business plans show the potential of this local feed production. This innovation will improve access to inexpensive quality feed and generate income for groups through feed commercialization and feed grinding services.

column17: Fertilizer scarcity and high price coupled with climate change impact have necessitated the need for alternative fertilizers that are developed from locally available raw materials with less or no impact on the environment. This innovation will therefore look at using of different organic waste materials to develop a fertilizer that would address the above challenges. In 2024, screening of organic materials and experiments were conducted to determine their suitability for fertilizer formulation—based on degradability, temperature resistance, and moisture retention.

column16: Measuring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) framework for monitoring deforestation emissions from Colombia
column17: In Colombia, the sector that contributes the most to national emissions is Agriculture, Forestry, and Other Land Use (AFOLU), where the loss of natural forests for conversion to other land uses has a significant impact. Monitoring non-deforestation associated with agricultural and livestock supply chains at the farm level is a challenge. Therefore, one of the main challenges faced by the public-private initiative of the Zero Deforestation Agreements is to develop agile, cost-effective, and transparent tools and protocols to monitor compliance with non-deforestation commitments in these supply chains. The protocol developed serves as an implementation tool for the Zero Deforestation Agreements (ZDA) and can serve as a reference for other sectors and stakeholders, including the financial sector. The document provides a guide for information collection and the processes of MRV (Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification) of non-deforestation resulting from agricultural activities, thus contributing activity data to national inventories.

column16: Cooperative Climate Cleverness Check: Improvement and testing of tool to assess current farming practice of cooperatives and opportunities for climate smart agriculture
column17: The Climate Clever Check (CCC) tool, developed by Agriterra and the Alliance, is designed to integrate climate considerations into cooperative assessments. It provides an accessible, user-friendly way to evaluate climate impacts without the need for specialized knowledge. Unlike more complex tools, the CCC allows for quick, objective assessments by users without special technical expertise. The tool covers the key areas of Food and Agriculture Organizations (FAO)'s climate smart agricultural practices and helps cooperatives prioritize climate issues, identify risks, and design effective response strategies to protect both production and income; ; Tested in four cooperatives in Mekong River Delta (MRD), the tool offers comprehensive climate assessments. While it works well for agricultural cooperatives, it needs improvements to be fully effective for fisheries and livestock cooperatives. Key upgrades include adding a universal climate risk index, adjusting the weighting of questions, and ensuring an even distribution of questions across categories to avoid bias.;

column16: Indicators to measure access to seed by women and other vulnerable socio-economic farmer groups that can be used by seed producing and distributing agencies and researchers
column17: Access to seed of improved varieties holds the potential to transform the lives of farmers who use them. Efforts such as The African Seed Access Index (TASAI) are dedicated to mapping bottlenecks in the seed industry value chain.  However, to date these efforts have paid limited attention capturing data on access to quality seed by women and other unreached farmers. To fill this evidence gap, we have developed a set of 20 indicators that may be used by private sector, public sector, research and extension agencies, community seed banks to capture data on access to quality seeds of improved seeds by women and other vulnerable farmers. Survey questionnaires have been developed to capture the data and have been piloted in Uganda. These can now be used by other actors in other places with context-specific adaptations.;

column16: Development of education and training materials for agricultural practices based on farmers' needs provided through digtal application (Zalo) for farmers in Vietnam
column17: In the context of AMD-WP1 and aligning with the ongoing work on Agro-climatic Bulletin (ACB) development under AMD-WP3 in Vietnam, the project team from the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT, in collaboration with the Dragon Institute at Can Tho University and the Department of Crop Production (now Plant Production and Protection Department-PPPD), developed online training materials for rice farmers in the Mekong River Delta. The goal is to provide high-quality, user-friendly e-learning materials. These will be disseminated through the Zalo messaging app, along with climate/practice advisory cards of the ACBs. To ensure the materials meet farmers' needs, six gender-segregated focus group discussions (FGDs) were conducted across three communes in Hau Giang and Soc Trang in 2024. These discussions identified the top ten agricultural practices that farmers find important yet challenging. The team reviewed existing training materials and created ten new technical resources, including blogs with images and videos, to offer practical guidance. The videos are validated through reviews by technical experts and farmers, and are shared directly by technical staff from sub-PPPDs and/or extension officers in MRD provinces via Zalo groups. In addition, these technical resources have been integrated into the ACBs as QR codes and are currently being tested in Can Tho Province (in areas formerly part of Hau Giang Province). Initial feedback is being collected to further refine and improve the videos linked to the ACBs.

column16: Development of a Participatory Guarantee System (PGS) by Seed Equal partners for Seed Quality Assurance in farmer producer organizations that are producing seed
column17: Participatory Guarantee System (PGS) is an integral component of a decentralized, farmer-led seed system that aims to empower farmer groups with the collective authority to validate the standards of truthfully labeled seeds (TLS). Mainstream seed certification procedures require a licensed seed officer to verify the quality in accordance with the Indian Minimum Seed Standards and provide certification. Smallholder and women seed producers might not be able to adhere to or afford the stringent requirements of formal certification procedures. PGS transfers the responsibility of quality assurance and certification from government to Seed Growers’ Associations, that  facilitate the procurement of seed and provide their members advice on processes and practices. They certify the seeds produced by member farmers based on assessment of seed sources and production processes through regular inspection and record keeping. While promoting equity and diversity within the seed chain, the PGS also ensures that seed quality is preserved.

column16: Digital platform to support agro-climatic bulletin (ACB) development and tracking in Vietnam
column17: The Alliance team are testing a digital platform (Agro-climatic Bulletin builder) that will further streamline the process of developing Agro Climatic Bulletins (ACB) and improve the systematic tracking of ACB advisories. The system is designed to provide an accessible and intuitive environment where technical teams can create dynamic templates, configure customized workflows, and produce tailored bulletins for farmers and other beneficiaries. It supports flexible template definition, allowing each region to structure content according to its specific needs, including climate conditions, crop status, hazard alerts, recommendations, or lunar phases. Templates can also include review and approval steps for technical validation.; A bulletin versioning mechanism ensures traceability, supports continuous improvement, and maintains adaptability for evolving use cases. The system follows a User-Centered Design approach, with both pre-designed templates and the platform interface evaluated through usability testing to ensure users can efficiently navigate and manage the full bulletin production workflow with minimal training. During bulletin composition, users can manually enter content or import information from external services via configurable API connectors, such as weather providers, agricultural advisory services, or communication channels. The system does not store or automatically generate external data, prioritizing transparency, flexibility, and user control in data handling. Bulletins can be exported in standard formats, including PDF, PNG, and JPG. The project scope covers the entire system development lifecycle: architecture and design, implementation, testing, deployment, and usability assessments, ensuring the platform effectively supports human-centered workflows and meets the diverse needs of its users.

column16: Crop Decision Tree (CDT) for development of seasonal Agro-Climatic Bulletin (ACBs) for rice farmers in Mekong River Delta (MRD), Vietnam.
column17: The Crop Decision Tree (CDT) is a supplementary tool designed to systematically support the development of seasonal Agro-Climatic Bulletins (ACBs), which are based on forecasted rainfall scenarios for the entire growing season.; Under the Asia-Mega Initiative (AMD), the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT collaborated with the Department of Crop Production (now the Plant Production and Protection Department – PPPD) and sub-PPPDs across seven former Mekong River Delta (MRD) provinces to develop rice-specific CDTs at both regional and provincial levels. The provinces involved were Tien Giang, Hau Giang, Kien Giang, An Giang, Can Tho, Tra Vinh, and Soc Trang.; Under S4I, provincial partners continue to use the CDT as part of the seasonal ACB development process.; Due to recent administrative restructuring, the original seven provinces have been consolidated into new provincial units:; Can Tho (including Hau Giang, Soc Trang, and Can Tho); An Giang (including Kien Giang and An Giang); Dong Thap (including Tien Giang and Dong Thap); Vinh Long (including Tra Vinh and Vinh Long); While the government is still finalizing the working mechanism for ACB development under the new structure, the provinces continue to maintain and apply the CDTs to cover the geographic areas of the former seven provinces.; The development of the CDTs was informed by historical seasonal ACBs and the technical expertise of national and provincial agricultural specialists. The CDTs consist of:; (1) A crop calendar detailing crop growth stages and associated climate risks.; (2) Farming recommendations aligned with crop growth stages under different seasonal rainfall scenarios (above normal, normal, or below normal).; (3) Farming advisories tailored to crop growth stages under extreme weather conditions.

column16: Improving the the Agro-Climatic Bulletin (ACB) provided to farmers using human-centered design methods in the Vietnam Mekong Delta
column17: The use of the Human-Centered Design (HCD) approach improved the Agro-Climatic Bulletin (ACB), providing better quality, and consistency of advisories, and accessibility to farmers. This process focused on farmers for their practical use, and the Technical Working Groups from the district and provincial government for their development and dissemination of the ACB. The improvements include (1) an enhanced ACB template, in which practice cards are based on historical data, with expert inputs replacing manual recommendations; (2) a user-friendly design featuring icons, pictures, and a more engaging design and color scheme; and (3) supplementary training materials with new videos and guides integrated as QR codes within the ACB practice cards. By using separate practice cards, advisories can be tracked over time and across different locations, providing opportunities for further analysis, and improvement, and as a step towards ACB digitalisation.

column17: Citizens' Juries (CJs) are a form of deliberative democracy fostering public participation in decision-making. column16: Climate Security Sensitivity Tool for practitioners and policymakers to assess the peace potential of climate adaptation interventions
column17: The Climate Security Sensitivity Tool is a 2-step user friendly tool to assess the peace potential of climate adaptation interventions. Peacekeeping and climate adaptation are rarely integrated in adaptation initiatives. The Climate Security Sensitivity Tool tries to close this gap by assessing whether climate action programs and their implementation are appropriate for the context in which they are carried out and recommending solutions to improve their appropriateness. It is aimed at practitioners, policymakers, and international organizations interested in diagnostic research for peace-responsive climate action in agricultural and rural development.

column16: Development of Version 1 of model to project water table using limited satellite data
column17: Mechanistic modeling of the water table using satellite data enhances traditional agricultural models by incorporating 2D/3D water movement, including lateral seepage, and optimizing parameters via satellite imagery. This is crucial for researchers and users needing accurate irrigation status information (e.g., irrigation frequency). Rice cultivation is a major source of non-CO₂ agricultural emissions due to methane release from flooded fields, yet it holds significant potential for emission reduction. However, investments in methane reduction primarily focus on waste management and livestock, with limited funding directed toward rice farming. A key challenge, particularly in the Mekong Delta, is the lack of atmospheric Earth observation (EO) data, which limits effective irrigation management and emission monitoring.

column16: AquaIndex: a framework of indicators for sustainable aquatic foods.
column17: Reliable qualitative and quantitative data on aquatic food systems are essential for ensuring sustainable food production and development. AquaIndex is a structured framework of indicators designed to assess the sustainability of aquatic food systems, covering environmental, social, and economic dimensions. AquaIndex provides a standardized approach for evaluating sustainability outcomes, enabling stakeholders—including researchers, policymakers, industry actors, and development agencies—to measure, compare, and track progress over time. The framework will help synthesize and benchmark the sustainability performance of aquatic food systems at local, national, and international levels. AquaIndex supports evidence-based decision-making to improve aquaculture governance, policy interventions, and investment strategies. It will help guide sustainable practices, ensuring that aquatic food systems contribute to food security, climate resilience, and economic stability while minimizing environmental impact.

column16: Spatial Production Allocation Model (SPAM) 2020 for country studies of crop production systems
column17: IFPRI’s global cropping system model – Spatial Production Allocation Model (SPAM) comprises the estimates of crop area, yield and production for 40+ major crops under four rainfed and irrigated production systems across a global 5 arc minute grid. This is done through a downscaling approach that accounts for spatial variation in the biophysical conditions influencing the productivity of individual crops within the cropland extent, and that uses crop prices to weigh the gross revenue potential of alternate crops when considering how to prioritize the allocation of specific crops to individual gridcells. Based on the SPAM global model, we further developed the SPAM country model, so it is more suitable for regional and country studies. The most recent global SPAM products are outdated (global: 2010, Sub-Saharan Africa: 2017). Under the ClimBeR initiative, we update the input data to 2020 to capture the recent changes of crop production to develop climate-risk profiles.

column16: Development and release of locally adapted, improved varieties of tomato in Tanzania
column17: Vegetable adaptation trials are crucial for evaluating different varieties under specific growing conditions, aiding farmers in identifying the most suitable options for their region. In Tanzania, where tomatoes are an important income generating crop, the World Vegetable Center through Better Diets and Nutrition, is conducting adaptation trials on locally adapted, improved tomato varieties. These varieties are selected based on traits like yield, perceived disease resistance, and physical characteristics that may impact marketability. Before release, all new vegetable varieties go through iterative workshops and consultations with key stakeholders as part of the World Vegetable Center's variety release process. In 2025, six top-performing tomato varieties were released (TARITOM1 through TARITOM6), contributing to the enhancement of crop productivity and quality in the region. Better Diets and Nutrition’s work on improved varieties is part of the end-to-end approach, an innovation which combines demand, food environment, and supply interventions to increase desirability, affordability, accessibility, and availability of fruit and vegetables and sustainable healthy diets more broadly. The supply interventions are designed to address known barriers faced by vegetable farmers. In this case, the provision of climate-resilient vegetable cultivars tackles the lack of quality inputs.

column16: Urban Infant Foodscape Intervention designed to improve food hygiene behaviours among caregivers of young children living in low-income areas of Nairobi, Kenya
column17: A cluster-randomised proof-of-concept trial  in Dagoretti, Nairobi to evaluate the potential for a locally designed intervention to improve the food hygiene behaviours of caregivers living in a peri-urban, low-income area of Nairobi, Kenya. Fifty community health volunteers (CHVs) were selected and assigned, randomly, to intervention or control arm (1:1). 101 households (one caregiver/household) under the CHV’s catchment (2-3 per CHV), with at least one child aged 6-24 months, were selected for participation. Caregivers in the intervention group (n=50) received a CHV-delivered food hygiene intervention and those in the control group (n-51) received no intervention. Blinding was not possible. Follow-up was four weeks post intervention delivery. Our primary outcome was the proportion of caregivers observed to practice five pre-specified food hygiene behaviours. Secondary outcomes assessed these five observed behaviours individually as well as a sixth behaviour - the proportion of caregivers who report always boiling the child’s drinking water.

column17: ; A randomised controlled trial assess the effectiveness of three packages (T1 = basic/low-cost technology with basic motivation; T2 = advanced/higher-cost technology with basic motivation; T3 = basic/low-cost technology + advanced motivation based only on “Scores on Doors/Cards”) of vendor-based interventions to improve food safety in the food sold by meat vendors in Addis Ababa, in a context of engaging with food safety authorities (and developing recommendations for current Government food inspection and scoring scheme). The intervention explores critical success factors for the interventions and potential for sustainability and scalability.; ; The interventions are based around the three-legged stool concept addressing 3 groups of stakeholders (enabling environment with authorities, training & technology with vendors, motivation with vendors and consumers). The advanced motivational intervention builds on the Ethiopian government’s existing annual food safety rating system, by providing more frequent food safety assessments, and providing vendors with a way to signal their rating to consumers. The advanced motivation has brought significant changes in the knowledge and practices of meat vendors, and also reduced E. coli contamination of meat and meat handling environments.;

column16: Responsible Digital Transformation Toolbox in Agri-Food Systems: Addressing challenges in technology design, access, and system complexity by guiding practiioners and decision-makers
column17: The digitalization of agri-food systems calls for an approach that ensures ethical and sustainable technology use. Current frameworks focus on fairness, privacy, and stakeholder involvement but face challenges like an overemphasis on technology and inadequate engagement. This work introduces the Responsible Digital Transformation Toolbox, designed for agri-food practitioners. It categorizes digital innovation challenges into cyber, social, and physical aspects and centers on technology design, accessibility, and system complexity. The toolbox aims to guide practitioners towards sustainable and equitable digital practices in the agri-food sector.

column16: DINA artificial intelligence chatbot developed by CIMMYT to guide researchers in digital innovation for agricultural development
column17: DINA (Digital Innovation Navigation Assistant) is an experimental artificial intelligence chatbot that helps agricultural researchers navigate digital innovation opportunities. Developed by CIMMYT through the Digital Transformation initiative, DINA uses advanced AI technology combined with a curated evidence database to answer user queries about digital solutions for agriculture. The system compares responses from multiple AI sources and learns from user interactions to improve its guidance over time. This tool addresses the challenge researchers face in identifying relevant digital innovations and evidence for their work. DINA supports the agricultural research community globally by making digital innovation knowledge more accessible and actionable for development impact.

column16: Layanan Konsultasi Padi (Rice Crop Manager Indonesia): A digital advisory service for rice farmers in Indonesia
column17: Layanan Konsultasi Padi (LKP) is a free-to-use digital advisory service that helps Indonesian rice farmers use fertilizer more efficiently by providing field-specific recommendations on the type, amount, and timing of application. Developed by IRRI with Indonesia’s Ministry of Agriculture and partners, LKP is delivered mainly through extension staff and other dissemination channels, enabling farmers to receive a simple guideline tailored to each plot.; In 2025, IRRI and BRMP documented farmers’ experiences and field results from using LKP across eight provinces representing irrigated, rainfed, and swampy rice ecosystems. Feedback from farmer respondents showed that LKP encouraged more timely and balanced fertilizer splitting, reduced inefficient nutrient use, and improved farm performance. Across agro-ecologies and seasons, yields under LKP were consistently higher than farmers’ usual practice, averaging about a 0.6 t/ha increase, with strong benefits in rainfed environments. Farmers also reported generally positive perceptions of the tool, with most indicating willingness to continue using LKP and recommend it to others.; These results strengthen the case for institutional transition and scaling of LKP 2.0 within Indonesia’s extension and fertilizer programs, supported by ongoing collaboration between IRRI and government partners.

column16: Nature-Positive Aggregated Permaculture Farms: Enhancing Ecosystem Services, Livelihoods, and Sustainable Farming Practices for Smallholder Farmers in Nyando and Vihiga, Kenya
column17: More than 165 farmers in Nyando in Kenya have aggregated their land to form two large farms. One farm is 32 hectares in Agoro East sub-location aggregated by 83 farmers and the other in Jimo East sub-location we have a 10 hectare farm aggregated by 80 farmers. Farms will be design to embody permaculture principles in which farmers jointly designed various aspects of the farm including cereal reduction, vegetable production, fish ponds, irrigation, agro-forestry, apiculture and a section for livestock production. farmers jointly share resources, participate in joint production and value addition activities with the aim of achieving economies of scales while at the same time contributing to eco-system services and livelihoods. In Vihiga, where special aggregation is not possible, we have aggregated production at landscapes level with 52 farmers. In 2025, we set up the farms in terms of infrastructure, the farm being now operational.

column16: Simulation modelling of leaf blast, neck blast, and bacterial blight epidemics to identify risk factors, develop management recommendations, and reduce yield losses under different climate change scenarios.
column17: Leaf blast, neck blast and bacterial blight are the most important rice diseases. Simulation modelling will facilitate the identification of  risk factors, develop  management recommendations, and reduce yield losses under different climate change scenarios. Simulation models for leaf blast and bacterial blight were improved and neck blast was developed based on EPIRICE, a generic model for rice diseases. Infection rates were mainly driven by relative humidity, temperature, rainfall, and crop age. The values of parameters were based on field experiments, pest surveys and published literature. The coupling point for the leaf blast and neck blast models was a linear regression on the effect of leaf blast severity on neck blast incidence. Simulated levels of leaf blast severity, neck blast incidence and bacterial blight incidence were generally higher in the wet season than in the dry season. Additional research activities are necessary to improve the performance of the models.

column17: The project multiplied clean sweet potato planting material in greenhouses and through Ukama Ustawi trained Decentralised vine multipliers (DVMs).  Farmers therefore accessed orange fleshed sweet potato (OFSP) seed from the research stations and from  DVMs. Public extension workers were responsible for beneficiary registration and provided short training to sweet potato seed beneficiaries.  This innovation is relevant  because it is high in beta carotene a precursor for vitamin A which  contributes to a reduction in Vitamin A deficiency and provides  income to smallholder farmers through its commercialization.  In addition, this innovation is drought tolerant, can be grown throughout the year, even in marginal soils  and hence can provide reasonable yield hance  contributing to food security under drought  conditions or in relatively poor soils .

column16: Community-designed One Health Units as a model for integrated human, animal and environment health service delivery to pastoralists in the Horn of Africa
column17: The One Health Unit (OHU) serves as a collaboration and coordination platform for frontline service providers and community-based actors to deliver integrated services to improve the health of humans, animals and the environment. In mobile OHUs, frontline service providers move along pastoralist/livestock routes, according to a monthly schedule, changing sites every day and responding to the needs of the population in a certain site/location. In static OHUs, frontline service providers work side by side in a common facility (e.g., human/animal health post, water point or other village gathering site). The OHU is generally staffed by government employees from different sectors who are released from their regular duties to deliver integrated services through the OHU. The services are targeted towards pastoralist and agropastoralist communities, their livestock, and the rangelands which they access, with a particular focus on vulnerable and hard-to-reach communities.

column16: Intensifying Homestead Gardens to Boost Food Security and Empower Women in Bangladesh
column17: Homestead gardening is the most complex multi-strata integrated production system that combines all farming components (crop, livestock, tree, and occasionally fish) and provides household food security, employment, and income generation opportunities. Homestead gardens are mainly managed by women. With this innovation, SI-MFS in collaboration with BARI, aims at intensifying and diversifying homestead gardens, benefitting households by increasing nutritional status and extra income. Ensuring small packages of good quality seeds and seedlings through local service providers or local seed companies will increase year-round vegetable and fruit production. The cowdung from livestock production are used to fertilize homestead gardens and the crop residues from homestead gardens are used as fodder to livestock. In addition, this innovation will also increase women's empowerment.

column16: Integrated Striga Management for Maize
column17: Using Striga tolerant maize hybrids and a popular benchmark Striga-susceptible variety, we tested three options for Striga management in western Kenya through on-farm trials. The options were maize sole crop, maize intercropped with soybean and maize intercropped with Desmodium. Farms with heavy Striga infestation were chosen to host the trials. Eight farms were selected in three counties in western Kenya to host the trials. The trials were farmer-managed with researchers only collecting data at the critical stages. Data were collected on the number of Striga plants that had germinated in the plots and harvested field weight.  The differences in performance between the Striga tolerant hybrids and the commercial hybrid were very clear for both grain yield and Striga germination. A farmer field day was hosted at one of the sites and a flyer on Striga management were distributed to farmers.

column16: Cassava peel as a nutritious animal feed for livestock feed suppliers and livestock-keepers
column17: Nigeria generates 15 million tons of cassava peels annually from food and industrial processing. These peels typically rot near processing centers, releasing methane and polluting water sources, or are burned, creating toxic smoke. The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) developed a technology that transforms this waste into high-quality cassava peel products for animal feed. This innovation addresses decades of failed attempts to commercially dry cassava peels at scale. The technology provides livestock feed suppliers and farmers with a nutritious, low-cost feed ingredient while solving a major environmental problem. ILRI has trained processors in Nigeria and documented successful performance, with potential for global application beyond Africa.

column16: Integrated Agriculture-Aquaculture (IAA) systems that produce aquatic and terrestrial foods on the same land using the resources from one to benefit the other
column17: Integrated Agriculture-Aquaculture (IAA) systems are diversified farming systems where aquatic and terrestrial foods are grown together on the same plot using the resources from one to benefit the other. In Egypt, for example, the production of fish such as Nile tilapia, mullet, and African catfish creates nutrient-rich water that can then be used to irrigate crops such as date palm, olives, figs, pomegranates, guava, onions, sugar beets, and tomato. IAA includes a range of technologies and methods that can be put together and adapted to each farming situation as needed. IAA is one of the most promising and fastest-growing food production systems in Egypt since it enhances production diversity, land productivity, water efficiency and nutrient cycling on farms.

column16: Production of saline tolerant potato variety under zero tillage using rice straws during the fallow winter season for farmers in rice-based ecosystems in West Bengal, India
column17: The potato production through zero-tillage using rice straw as mulch (PZTM) is an innovative technique to sustainably intensify agricultural production with potato uses few inputs and residues from the previous crop without disturbing the soil. It has the potential to address issues being exacerbated by climate change like excessive input use leading to detrimental environmental effects, water scarcity, and worsening air quality due to rice straw burning and, as such, significantly contribute to a sustainable agroecological transformation in India. Key to this practice is the efficiency principle, by increasing resource-use efficiencies of major inputs. It recycles straw as mulch, creating value for a residue that would have been burned otherwise. As this technique is associated with economic gains as well as women’s empowerment, it improves rural livelihoods and promotes gender equity, and as such adheres to the principle of human and social values.

column16: Contextualized better management practices (BMPs) for Genetically Improved Farmed Tilapia (GIFT) to support tilapia seed production in Timor-Leste
column17: Better Management Practices (BMPs) for monosex tilapia seed production were developed to support the development and scaling of tilapia farming in Timor-Leste. The objective was to present step-wise interventions – Genetically Improved Farmed Tilapia (GIFT) hatcheries establishment and monosex seed production and distribution; conduct of on-farm grow-out trials; training and capacity building; and extension, communication and marketing services - carried out, and demonstrate how availability, accessibility and consumption of fish could be increased sustainably in the subsistence farming systems of Timor-Leste.

column16: Reusable plastic crates to improve tomato transport and storage piloted in Benin and Tanzania
column17: Postharvest losses are a global challenge, and fragile fruits, such as tomatoes, often suffer significant losses. Starting with FRESH in the previous CGIAR portfolio (2022-2024), and continuing in Better Diets and Nutrition researchers are exploring a novel approach to packaging and transporting tomatoes across multiple contexts. Progress on this innovation was previously reported in the Philippines. In 2025, results from two pilots were published. In Tanzania, results suggested that reusable plastic crates outperformed traditional wooden crates in reducing postharvest losses and maintaining tomato quality throughout the supply chain. The reusable plastic crates minimized compression damage and overloading, leading to lower weight and quality losses compared to traditional wooden crates. Tomatoes transported in plastic crates achieved higher market value, as better quality resulted in improved prices. Results from Benin were inconclusive, making it difficult to state that reusable plastic crates perform better compared to traditional baskets. This study also highlighted adoption challenges related to cost and logistics. ;

column16: Enhancing PCR-based methods for bacteria detection on rice seeds. Validation and verification of detection procedures for seedborne bacteria
column17: PCR (polymerase chain reaction) based methods are proven to be faster, cheaper and still highly effective methods for the detection of presence of bacteria in seeds compared to the traditional methods. In spite of the cons, such as the need of highly specific equipment and technical competence or the higher rate of false-positive results, these methods provide reliable and fast results allowing  the streamlining of end-to-end transboundary movement of seeds, with a lead time of 3-5 days as compared to 10-12 weeks. To attain the validation and verification of these highly specific methods, protocols require thorough evaluation under strict standards. The implementation of such methods and their cross validation with the national plant protection organization, will allow the Seed Health laboratory at IRRI to offer this service to researchers, partners and  external customers in the Philippines to enhance their capacity to import and export rice seeds.

column16: Measuring aquatic food consumption in the first 1000 days of life: An approach to estimating portion sizes in Timor-Leste
column17: Dietary assessment provides crucial data for understanding dietary patterns as a key driver of nutritional status and associated health outcomes in individuals and populations. Currently, little is known about the consumption patterns of aquatic Foods (AF) in Timor-Leste, particularly during the first 1000 days of life. Accurate dietary assessment of AFs is particularly challenging given the high diversity of fish, seaweed and marine invertebrate species consumed throughout the country’s coastal areas.; Together, WorldFish and CSIRO, with the support of the Directorate General of Fisheries, Aquaculture and Marine Resources of the Timor-Leste government, have developed a quantitative food frequency questionnaire FFQ designed specifically to capture aquatic food consumption in Timor-Leste in the first 1000 days of life. The approach includes a survey module and two visual aids to help participants accurately recall both the type and quantity of AF consumed: (1) a species identification tool and (2) a portion size estimation tool.

column16: Development of a Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) method  for detection of seedborne diseases by Burkholderia glumae
column17: The  increasing  global  temperature  due  to  climate  change  causes  an  increase  in  new  or  previously  negligible  diseases.  The  incidence  of  Burkholderia  glumae  has  been  reported  to  increase  in  recent  years  in  many  rice  growing  regions.   Burholderia  glumae  is  a  seedborne  pathogen  causing  bacterial  panicle  blight  of  rice.  It  infects  rice  at  different  growth  stages  causing  grain  rot,  sheath  rot  and  seedling  rot  symptoms  depending  on  the  rice  growth  stages. Bacterial  panicle  blight  is  difficult  to  manage  in  the  absence  of  effective  chemical  control  measures. Rapid and early disease detection  is needed to avoid severe yield losses. The development of this diagnostic method and the scaling out through the National Seed Quality Service of the Philippines enables the fast and inexpensive early detection of the agent on rice seeds across the country preventing farmers losses due to panicle blight. As part of scaling out this method, IRRI-SHU introduced it to the Bureau of Plant Industry-National Seed Quality Control Services (BPI-NSQCS) through a Capacity Development Workshop on the Rapid Detection of Bacterial Panicle Blight of Rice to validate the method, enhance the seed health diagnostic skills of BPI seed analysts, and facilitate the adoption of LAMP technology to strengthen seed quality management and plant quarantine efforts.

column16: Research tools on the impact of gender norms on women's economic resilience to climate change in order to develop gender transformative approaches to improve women's resilience
column17: The project developed a toolbox to understand the impact of gender norms on women’s economic reliance to climate change impacts. The adapted qualitative tools are used to identify and map the key stakeholders in agricultural and fisheries value chains and ii) understand which norms constrain women and other groups from participating in and benefiting from work in the different nodes of the value chain iii) how women and other value chain players at the different nodes of agricultural value chains are coping with climate change impacts and also make use of Vignettes and attitudes and behaviour assessment plots to analyze whether or not gender norms that may affect value chain actors are weakening or shifting. This analysis will also allow us to see under what conditions actors can deviate from the norm and how that impacts their economic resilience to climate change impacts.

column16: Intelligent Agricultural Systems Advisory Tool-an AI Powered Platform for Scalable Contextual Agro-Advisories
column17: The Intelligent Agricultural Systems Advisory Tool is an AI–enabled digital platform developed by ICRISAT and its partners to deliver timely, location-specific agricultural advisories at scale. The innovation is designed as an end-to-end system that integrates data resources, analytical decision processes, digital delivery tools, and capacity strengthening to support informed decision-making by farmers and extension systems.; ; The platform initially operated through automated, rule-based advisory generation using expert-defined thresholds and crop-stage guidance. These rule-based advisories were piloted in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, demonstrating the value of timely, weather-informed guidance for farm management. Building on these learnings, the platform is now undergoing a major transformation into a fully AI-powered system and training a domain LLM model for this platform.; ; In its current phase, the platform brings together standardized climate, weather, crop, and field-level datasets into a structured and reusable data resource that supports consistent advisory generation across locations and seasons. Decision engines combine expert knowledge with data-driven methods to generate more adaptive and context-specific guidance, improving relevance and accuracy under variable climate conditions.; ; Advisories are delivered through digital communication tools that enable timely dissemination to farmers and extension personnel. These tools support local languages, capture user feedback, and allow monitoring of advisory reach and use. The system is designed to be adaptable across crops, regions, and institutional contexts. As part of its evolution, a small test case has also been undertaken in Ethiopia to assess data readiness and applicability beyond India.; ; In parallel, the innovation emphasizes capacity strengthening and inclusion by training extension staff and partner institutions, raising farmer awareness; ; The platform was piloted in Ananthapur district and subsequently scaled in Odisha, reaching more than 6,000 farmers.; ; Current development focuses on strengthening data ecosystems, decision engines reasoning for LLM model (personalised agri model),  delivery to support resilient and productive agricultural systems.

column16: Mobile application for digital extension and advisory services (IDEAS) to support smallholder chicken farmers in poultry production and management
column17: This is an interactive digital extension and advisory service app (IDEAS) to leverage various components of poultry production and provide inclusive support to smallholder poultry farmers. This App is primarily designed to support farmers in identification and access to chicken breeds available in each country, formulation and use of locally available feeds, disease prevention and treatment, market information, and linkages, creating a platform for discussion and knowledge sharing, and real-time advisory and support services. It is developed in various languages and comprises various visual, interactive, text, and video features that can deliver tailored services for smallholder poultry farmers.

column16: Multiplication and dissemination business model, for tropically-adapted and farmer-preferred improved chicken breeds, for value-chain actors, research and development partners in Lower and Middle Income Countries (LMIC)
column17: The scaling business model is proposed based on approaches as suggested by Lundy et al. (2012) that includes three major steps. First, mapping the existing business model using the nine caveats and identifying major challenges and opportunities. The existing business model was mapped using data from baseline and marketing assessment surveys focusing on inputs supply, production, marketing, institutional support, vertical and horizontal coordination along the value chain. Second, identifying business cases using lessons learned from previous tropical poultry genetics solution activities in Sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia. Third, developing the new business model considering the business cases identified above. The proposed scaling business model has six  major components: establishing partnership, organizing and building capacity, access to inputs and services (i.e . feed, heath, finance, breed, training and extension services), production and support, value addition and marketing (through aggregators, wholesalers, retailers and processors), monitoring and optimization.

column16: Integrated nutrition education package to smallholder chicken keepers for increased consumption of animal source food (ASF) and improved nutritional status in Ethiopia, Kenya and Tanzania
column17: The integrated nutrition education package is a nutrition-sensitive intervention that aims to enhance the consumption of chicken meat, eggs and other nutrient-dense foods and improve the nutritional status of smallholder farmers, most notably under-five children, lactating mothers and pregnant women. This activity will be embedded in the existing on-farm chicken performance testing program and it will be provided to smallholder farmers using digital and paper-based nutrition education tools. The package will have different contents suitable for smallholder farmers. Baseline and end-line data will be collected to explore the impact of the interventions.

column16: Animal identification and traceability system for livestock keepers and other stakeholders for selection of superior genetics based on livestock farmers' good animal husbandry practice in Nepal.
column17: The unique animal identification protocol is developed for tagging dairy buffaloes and other livestock species (cattle, goat, sheep, pig, dog etc.) which will be used to select superior genetics based on performance records. Animal Identification Tracking System (AITS) is a necessary component in livestock development to help in identifying and tracing animals. The identification of animals enables selection of those with superior performance, monitoring of their health status, managing and monitoring productivity in herds and tracking the movement and trade of animals and animal products. It will also help target beneficiaries with government schemes and health insurance companies to identify insured animals and reduce unwanted  compensation claims.

column16: Integration of multipurpose forages with improved agronomic practices, cereal-legume intercropping, for enhanced productivity and climate resilience in mixed crop livestock systems of Malawi
column17: Multipurpose forages, integrated with cereal-legume intercropping systems, offer opportunities for crop-livestock integration, diversification, and intensification, particularly in areas with limited land. Agronomic knowledge and practices can be shared on the same plot, delivering multiple benefits: diversified food production, improved biomass for livestock feed, and increased manure for soil fertility enhancement. Additionally, these systems reduce production costs and contribute to ecosystem services, such as soil erosion control through deep rooting, Biological Nitrification Inhibition (BNI), and carbon sequestration. Forage legumes also fix atmospheric nitrogen, enhancing soil fertility and supporting crop production, while promoting climate resilience.

column16: Robust management practice ('ram effect') for enhanced reproductive performance of sheep for farmers in dryland areas.
column17: The innovation describes how sheep use a unique amalgam of behavioral, physiological and genetic mechanisms to preserve fertility under a looming scenario of warmer climate. Management of reproduction that relies on naturally based solutions is extremely important to counter the negative perception around hormone-based interventions. In Mediterranean latitudes and wider regions of non-tropical drylands, sheep do not normally ovulate during spring but exposure to a ram can induce oestrus and ovulation. This innovation promotes the use of the response of maiden Barbarine ewes in drylands to the ‘ram effect’ during springtime for improved fertility.

column16: AgWise: A Modular Framework Delivering Tailored Agronomic Recommendations for Farmers
column17: AgWise is an innovation designed to provide tailored agronomic recommendations based on specific demands from partners to improve farmer productivity and/or profitability. This freely available, modular framework offers data-driven advice on fertilizer requirements, optimal planting dates, suitable cultivars, and other agricultural practices. column16: Participatory videomaking: a tool to improve understanding of adolescents' perceptions of their food environments and inform interventions for sustainable healthy diets in VIet Nam
column17: Participatory videomaking is a methodological tool that can be used to promote community engagement in research and develop critical awareness of an issue or topic. In Viet Nam, researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition and the National Institute of Nutrition used this methodology with 54 adolescents (15-17 years old) selected from public schools in three districts. The adolescents documented their perceptions of their food environments using cameras on their mobile phones. Analysis of the videos revealed challenges and opportunities adolescent face in accessing and consuming sustainable healthy diets. In 2025, researchers used the analysis and the videos themselves to co-design community action plans to enhance food environments for better diets, results of which were described in a published brief.

column16: Timely, accurate, and cost-effective means for high-frequency monitoring of both food affordability and security applied in Ethiopia, Myanmar, and Sri Lanka
column17: The affordability of sustainable nutritious food for all is an important dimension of food security. Timely, high-frequency indicators of food affordability are rarely collected in any systematic fashion despite the reality that food price volatility is a driver of food insecurity. Furthermore, even though development agencies have made investments in expanding food price monitoring, they have paid insufficient attention to monitoring wages and to measuring real food wages as a food security indicator. This innovation demonstrates how tracking wages of unskilled workers can be a timely, accurate, and cost-effective income proxy for monitoring food affordability for critical populations. The research team, including members of Sustainable Healthy Diets and Fruits and Vegetables for Sustainable Healthy Diets, apply the method using data from well-known food price crises in Ethiopia (2008, 2011 and 2022), Sri Lanka (2022) and Myanmar (2022).  ;

column16: Guidance for conducting better evaluations of food system interventions to improve planetary and human health published to inform effective actions for food systems transformation
column17: Global interest in the need to transform food systems to protect human and planetary health provides a major opportunity for improving nutrition in tandem with achieving other societal goals. Ensuring that food systems transformation truly leads to sustainable healthy diets for all requires a much stronger evidence base than what is currently available. Policymakers, funders, implementing partners, and researchers are looking for credible evidence about what works to guide food systems transformation in better directions. The guidance draws on six program evaluations from Africa and South Asia, experts, including one from the previous CGIAR portfolio (2022-2024), and provides six recommendations for designing better evaluations of food system interventions. Better evaluation methodologies for such complex studies can generate the evidence that is urgently needed to support the ambitious goals of food systems transformation. In 2025, researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition involved in developing these guidelines continued efforts to disseminate them and demonstrate how methodological challenges in evaluations of food environment interventions can be overcome using examples from CGIAR research.

column16: Retail Diversity Index: a tool to characterize the diversity of foods that retailers offer to consumers in urban and peri-urban food environments in Viet Nam
column17: Currently there is no feasible indicator that assesses the diversity of foods that retailers offer to consumers in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Researchers from Sustainable Healthy Diets have developed and validated a simple, cost-efficient, tool that can fill this methodological gap in food environment research. The Retail Diversity Index (RDI) measures the diversity of the retail food environments at two levels: at the food group level and at the outlet level. It also captures basic information regarding the level of processing of the food items available in these food outlets. To date, the tool has been validated across 374 food vendors in one urban and one peri-urban site in Viet Nam.
