column16: Holistic conceptual framework: a resource for decisionmakers to use in navigating the politics and processes of food systems transformation
column17: Decisionmakers lack guidance on how to transform food systems from their current unsustainable trajectories toward more desirable, healthy, sustainable, resilient, and equitable outcomes in a comprehensive and integrated way. This conceptual framework integrates multiple perspectives and practical experiences on transition, transformation and politics to propose a holistic diagnostic and prescriptive tool for decisionmakers to navigate the process. The two-dimension framework combines domains of politics with processes of transformation, which, together, outline how temporal configurations of political actions could be  leveraged to overcome persistent unsustainable regime trajectories and drive food systems toward more normative transformative goals. The framework can be applied as a diagnostic tool to understand past transformation processes and investigate why new ideas, institutions, innovations, and narratives failed to emerge or to be scaled up. It can also be leveraged by actors across various levels to assess the nature of diverse politics that hinder current transformation actions.

column16: Methodology for building participatory national food system monitoring dashboards tested with stakeholders in Bangladesh, Ethiopia, and Honduras
column17: The goal of food system dashboards is to offer users the opportunity to monitor or assess national food systems. One challenge is how to strike an acceptable balance between the complexity, specificity, and multi-sectoral nature of food systems while also ensuring that the information remains accessible and usable for decisionmakers. Rarely are these dashboards co-constructed with local stakeholders. This case study from Sustainable Healthy Diets describes how a replicable yet rigorous methodology for co-creating food system dashboards was applied in Bangladesh, Ethiopia, and Honduras. The three pilots demonstrate that it's feasible to integrate comprehensive and multi-sectoral inputs from national stakeholders into dashboards that are functional, evidence-based, and reflective of the country’s specific features. The methodology has the potential to progressively build capacities of decisionmakers to make more informed and evidence-based decisions to curb negative outcomes of food systems, like the triple burden of malnutrition.

column16: AI-driven system for common bean disease detection
column17: An AI-driven system for common bean disease detection was developed using advanced deep learning and object detection technologies. A comprehensive image dataset was collected from disease hotspots in Africa and Colombia, focusing on five major diseases: Angular Leaf Spot (ALS), Common Bacterial Blight (CBB), Common Bean Mosaic Virus (CBMV), Bean Rust, and Anthracnose. Pod images were available only for ALS. This innovation used data augmentation and both whole and micro-level annotations, training three YOLO architectures: YOLOv7, YOLOv8, and YOLO-NAS. YOLO-NAS achieved the highest mean average precision (mAP) of 97.9% and recall of 98.8% for whole leaf detection, while YOLOv7 and YOLOv8 performed better for pod detection. Micro annotations showed lower performance across all diseases. The YOLO-NAS models were deployed in an Android app, achieving 90% classification accuracy on unseen data. These models were integrated into the new Tumaini bean app for real-time disease detection.

column16: Development of a Machine Learning Model for Predicting Rice Blast Disease
column17: This early innovation presents a novel approach to assessing Rice Blast (Pyricularia oryzae) severity in rice plants through machine learning and remote sensing. Using a visual scale from 0 to 9 to gauge infection severity, the research collected data from nine trials conducted between 2022 and 2024 at CIAT in Palmira, Colombia. These trials included various rice genotypes and control varieties to benchmark resistance levels. Drones equipped with RGB and multispectral cameras gathered data, later processed with Agisoft Metashape and Phenoi software to extract vegetation indices. Machine learning models were then developed using PyCaret and Scikit-learn, with datasets balanced through oversampling and undersampling techniques. The Random Forest classifier performed best, achieving up to 0.98 accuracy for binary classification (resistant vs. susceptible) and 0.91 accuracy for multiclass classification. This innovation underscores the potential of integrating machine learning and remote sensing for accurate disease monitoring in agriculture focusing on rice diseases.;

column16: 70 high-value genes were deployed to an elite indica background as high-quality near-isogenic lines
column17: A major limitation in improving the efficiency of rice breeding through utilizing major genes is the availability of those genes in elite genetic backgrounds. To enable rice breeders to gain the value of these major genes without the penalties associated with the original landrace donors, deployment of selected genes has been initiated into an elite genetic background. The deployment includes rigorous Quality Control (QC) standards for introgression, including >95% recovery of the elite background and <2cM introgression size. To date, over 70 major genes have been deployed, mostly to the IRRI 154 background.  Many of these are now validated, and lines (single genes and pyramids) have been distributed to many partners.

column16: Sampling Frames Tool: Empowering Researchers in Data Collection, Validation Trials, and MVP Testing through Interactive Google Earth Engine-Based Web Application for enhanced Decision-Making
column17: The Sampling Frames tool is a public web tool providing support to design data collection strategies for validation trials, surveys, or testing Minimum Viable Products (MVPs). It guides users through a simple interface to choose the most relevant environmental clusters, reducing variance due to environmental factors and making trial results more representative in the target area.  ; ; The tool supports Use Cases in understanding agroecological heterogeneity and aids decision-making within their focus areas. It relies on Google Earth Engine and offers a simple, interactive, and adaptive web interface that requires minimal computing skills, making it more accessible than code-based systems. Users can easily ‘click through’ selections, such as focus area, variables, and cluster number, to generate outputs.

column16: Implementation of the CGIAR MFL SP Incubation and Acceleration  Program for Green Agribusiness
column17: In 2024, the Agroecology Initiative started implementing the following business incubation and acceleration programs, designed to encourage agribusinesses in embracing sustainable and eco-friendly agricultural practices:; ; 1.  The Agroecological Business Incubator/Accelerator, developed by the Agroecology Initiative, provided funding for testing new agroecological business model ideas in Burkina Faso, Peru, Tunisia and Senegal.; 2. The CGIAR Food Systems Accelerator (CFSA) 2024 cohort, a partnership with the Ukama Ustawi Initiative, boosted agroecological business models in Kenya and Zimbabwe. ; 3. The Neycha Accelerator and Fund Cohort 2 Bootcamp, in partnership with Biovision, provided a transformative platform for agroecological entrepreneurs from Kenya to gain practical skills, insights, and mentorship to drive sustainable business growth.; These programs aimed to foster new or redesigned agroecological business models, supporting the transition of food systems towards more sustainable and equitable production and consumption. ; ; Based on these experiences and building on additional learnings from the Nature Positive Initiative, in 2025 the Multifunctional Landscapes program launched the CGIAR MFL SP Incubation & Acceleration Program for Green Agribusiness as pilot, to provide technical and/or financial support for establishing, strengthening and escalating selected green business models located in the MFL SP’s sites. The Incubator/Accelerator is currently supporting three green agribusinesses in Kenya, Tunisia and Zimbabwe, in the transition towards becoming more agroecological, nature positive, restoration and conservation focused.

column16: Gene-edited cassava lines with enhanced resistance to bacterial blight developed using CRISPR technology by Alliance researchers
column17: Cassava bacterial blight is a devastating disease that significantly reduces cassava yields, threatening food security for millions who depend on this staple crop. Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT researchers developed new cassava lines by editing specific sweet genes using CRISPR/Cas9 technology to create resistance against the bacterial pathogen. The team modified the MeSweet 10a and 10e genes in cassava variety 60444, which was previously susceptible to the disease. column16: High-fidelity genome editing tool for banana using Cas-CLOVER
column17: The International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) has developed the highly versatile Cas-CLOVER system as an alternative to CRISPR-Cas9 for gene editing in banana. The Cas-CLOVER system operates through a dimeric mechanism, utilizing two guide Ribonucleic acid (RNA) and the Clo051 endonuclease, and has proven effective in inducing mutations across a variety of plant species, including banana. In light of intellectual property (IP) concerns and licensing challenges associated with CRISPR/Cas9, the Cas-CLOVER system offers a valuable alternative for gene editing in crops like banana. We are currently developing excision tools, such as the piggyBac system, to enable the creation of transgene-free bananas using Cas-CLOVER, ensuring that no foreign genetic material remains in the edited plants.

column16: Diversity for Restoration (D4R) India - A digital solution to enhance resilience of trees-based restoration in Western Ghats, India
column17: The digital tool supports India's strategy in land restoration through improving outcomes of tree-based restoration and planting activities. The tool was developed for the Western Ghats, a biodiversity hotspot region, to help with choosing appropriate tree species and seed sources for tree-based restoration or other tree planting activities. Using species distribution and suitability models, the tool can choose appropriate tree species that survive current and future climatic conditions for a specified location. The tool uses a trait-based approach (based on 110 functional traits) to identify appropriate species (from 246 species) from a suitable list of species for the region based on local site conditions and restoration objectives while also accounting for current and future climatic scenarios. A list of species with seed sources based on restoration objectives and species diversity is provided to the user as a guide to select appropriate species and seed sources for restoration of specified location.

column17: Bangladesh, an agriculture-based country, has over 70% of its population in rural areas, with nearly half of the workforce dependent on agriculture. These centers go beyond teaching modern techniques—they aim to strengthen agricultural systems, build resilient communities, and promote environmental sustainability. By fostering a culture of learning, collaboration, and innovation, agricultural learning centers help drive economic development and create lasting, positive changes for farmers and their communities.

column16: Genome-edited rice varieties with enhanced nitrogen use efficiency developed by IRRI for improved yields in the Philippines
column17: Rice production faces challenges from inefficient nitrogen use, leading to reduced yields and environmental concerns. The International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) developed genome-edited rice varieties that better accumulate and utilize nitrogen within the plant. Using targeted gene editing techniques, researchers modified genes involved in nitrogen metabolism to enhance the plant's ability to redistribute nitrogen from leaves to grains during development. This innovation was applied to both transplanted and direct-seeded rice varieties commonly grown by farmers. The enhanced nitrogen use efficiency aims to increase rice yields while maintaining grain quality, potentially reducing fertilizer requirements and supporting more sustainable rice production systems.

column16: Development of a protocol for the isolation of protoplasts from cassava (Manihot esculenta) from friable embryogenic callus
column17: The use of protoplasts in gene editing has revolutionized crop improvement, as these are plant cells lacking a cell wall, facilitating the direct manipulation of their genetic material. This approach is particularly relevant for crops like cassava (Manihot esculenta), a staple food in tropical and subtropical regions that faces significant challenges, including susceptibility to diseases and the presence of toxic compounds in its tissues. This protocol is drafted such that it does not only optimizes the conditions necessary for successful protoplast regeneration but also enhances the efficiency of the gene-editing process, enabling the faster and more reliable production of modified plants.

column16: Advance market commitments for climate-resilient traits in food crops for low-income countries: An expert convening
column17: Climate change requires a more urgent approach to innovation and scaling, especially in food systems that are vulnerable to extremes weather events. Much of the critical work required to address these extremes through crop improvement is associated with high costs and risks, especially for private sector innovators and investors. In situations like this – where commercial incentives for innovation trail behind social value – there is scope for novel "pull" mechanisms to spur innovation. One such instrument is an Advance Market Commitment (AMC) for crop improvement. This convening explores the application of AMCs to design, develop, and deliver new varieties to farmers' fields in low-income countries. The convening explores the economics of AMCs for climate-resilience traits, responses from breeding programs, and the enabling policy environment required for AMCs to succeed.;

column16: My Farm Trees: Digital platform with blockchain to incentivize farmer- and community-led tree-based restoration of degraded landscapes:  Laos country module
column17: My Farm Trees is a digital tool for the documentation, verification and quality control of tree seed supply networks for agroforestry and land restoration, and for connecting and rewarding network actors for ecosystem services. It uses blockchain to create a transparent link of information from seed collection to tree growth – to improve livelihoods, food security and climate change mitigation. A module of the tool was developed for Laos, including 188 local tree species with their scientific, Lao and local names. The tool allows farmers to document and report their efforts on integrating trees in silvopastoral and other mixed farming systems, to access payments for ecosystem services

column16: Improvement of genetic gains in the market segment for the TMeLS-I (Transplanted Medium Maturity Long Grain Soft Grain - Irrigated) breeding pipeline in rice with NARES partners engagement
column17: The IRRI TMeLS-I (Transplanted Medium Maturity Long Grain Soft Grain - Irrigated) market segment has been benefiting nearly 6M hectares in South Asia, with 6 NARES partners in India and 3 in Bangladesh. OneRice strategy has shortened breeding cycle length from 6 to 3 years. Breeding materials tested in the 2023 wet season were generated using marker assisted selection in Rapid Generation Advance. After field evaluation in the TPE (target population of environments) sites, genomic selection was used to generate multiple-location summaries with gBLUP (genomic best linear unbiased prediction) estimates. GEBV (genomically estimated breeding value) estimates were generated for both tested and untested lines. High performing lines were selected for stage 2 testing. Comparison of average yields of current year tested materials against previous years showed positive genetic gain trend. The 1.77% rate of genetic gain was achieved through NARES engagement, strict implantation of population improvement, and predictive breeding methods.

column16: Research Enabling and Oversight Unit to guide genome editing research

column16: Underground transfer of floods for irrigation: Strengthening Climate Resilience and Groundwater Management in India's Ganges Basin
column17: A novel form of managed aquifer recharge known as underground transfer of floods for irrigation (UTFI) has been piloted in the Ganges Basin, enabling extensive evidence gathering and stakeholder engagment. UTFI has since been recognized as an important part of the solution to two crises facing India: destructive floods and recurring water shortages. The CGIAR Initiative on NEXUS Gains is now supporting the Government of Uttar Pradesh to better implement a national water conservation program. As a result, UTFI ponds and recharge wells have been constructed in hundreds more villages, increasing groundwater availability by up to 8 percent to date and strengthening climate resilience.

column16: Prime editing technology developed by International Potato Center to create virus-resistant potato varieties for farmers
column17: Potato virus Y causes significant yield losses in potato crops worldwide, particularly affecting farmers who grow susceptible varieties like Shangi in Kenya. The International Potato Center developed prime editing constructs that target specific genes to create virus-resistant potato varieties while maintaining desirable traits farmers value. This genome editing approach uses naturally occurring resistance patterns as templates to introduce precise genetic modifications. The technology is currently being tested in potato cells to evaluate its effectiveness before advancing to field trials. This innovation could help farmers maintain their preferred potato varieties while gaining protection against devastating viral diseases that threaten food security and livelihoods.

column16: Prime editing technology for enhanced potato resilience developed and tested by International Potato Center in Kenya
column17: Prime editing is an advanced genome modification technique that enables precise genetic improvements in crops. The International Potato Center developed this technology to enhance potato resilience against environmental stresses and diseases. The innovation involves specially designed genetic constructs that have been successfully tested in potato cells under controlled laboratory conditions. The technology includes optimized methods for delivering genetic modifications into potato cells and regenerating whole plants from modified cells. This breakthrough enables targeted improvements to potato varieties without introducing foreign DNA, offering a promising approach for developing more resilient potato varieties. The technology has demonstrated successful genome modification at the molecular level and is progressing toward field applications to benefit potato farmers facing climate and disease challenges.

column16: Improved Forage for Livestock Nutrition, Soil Fertility, and Sustainable Crop-Livestock Integration for smallholder farmers in Malaw
column17: On farm- and on-station trials explore diverse forage types useful for strengthening crop livestock integration, diversification and intensification of smallholder farming systems in Malawi. Sensitization and improvement of quality roughages, can improve both biomass yield and quality, providing better nutrition for animals. Some forages, such as Brachiaria, are adapted to low rainfall and offer additional environmental benefits like  controlling soil erosion, reducing nitrogen loss, and sequestering carbon. Mucuna pruriens, another forage, serves as a cover crop but also has potential as livestock feed. Forage legumes, like Crotalaria, also fix nitrogen in the soil, enhancing soil fertility. Dual purpose maize and groundnut varieties can increase biomass yields and quality on croplands without compromising grain yield. Private sector interest in forages like Brachiaria and Crotalaria is growing, increasing seed availability. Mucuna pruriens is produced locally, further supporting sustainable livestock feed.

column16: Effective QTL for improving grain zinc in rice
column17: The qZn5 Quantitative Trail Locus (QTL) was previously reported as contributing to grain zinc in rice, however validation was lacking and no elite material appeared to contain the gene. Deployment of this QTL into an elite background was completed, to a purity of >99.3% recovery of the elite genomic background.  Evaluation of the near-isogenic elite deployment products showed that qZn5 indeed does produce about 4ppm increase in grain zinc, which represents approximately a 40% improvement over the baseline level in the elite recurrent parent. The increase in grain zinc was apparent in milled, polished grain, so this represents zinc that would be available in rice consumed. Evaluation of the elite lines also showed no further penalty for yield (which was seen in early-generation products), so there are no penalties for breeders to use this QTL. The QTL interval was reduced by 90% to just 300kb/1.5cM.

column16: Elite lines with multiple resistance genes effective against rice yellow mottle virus
column17: Rice yellow mottle virus is a major disease limiting rice productivity across Africa and Madagascar.  Several resistance genes and alleles have been identified in previous studies, but none were available in modern elite backgrounds.  Most of these were found in Oryza glaberrima, and hence extremely difficult to introduce into Oryza sativa (common cultivated rice).  Deployment of these genes has been achieved, including those from O. glaberrima, to very high quality standards.  Elite lines have been registered and shared with AfricaRice and various national partners in ESA.  Testing of lines in Mbe (west Africa) and several sites in ESA (Kenya, Tanzania, Mozambique) have shown the effectiveness of most of these genes, with the exception of rymv2.  A resistance strategy combining rymv1-5 + RYMV3 or rymv1-2 + RYMV3 has been developed.  Plans are being laid to increase the frequency of these alleles in elite material, with some populations already established.

column16: Open Data Cube repository developed by IWMI's Digital Innovation team to organize spatial datasets for environmental modeling in river basins
column17: The International Water Management Institute's Digital Innovation team created this data repository system to support environmental decision-making in river basin management. The system organizes satellite imagery, climate data, and other spatial information into a structured format that researchers and water managers can easily access and analyze. Built using open-source technology, it enables users to quickly retrieve and visualize environmental data for real-time monitoring and long-term planning. The repository was initially developed for the Limpopo River Basin but can be adapted for other regions. This innovation addresses the challenge of managing large volumes of scattered environmental data by providing a centralized, user-friendly platform that supports both immediate decision-making and comprehensive environmental analysis.

column16: Eolo Platform for Seasonal Forecasting in Honduras
column17: Eolo is a tool designed to support the development of climate bulletins, enabling the comparison of different forecasts and the generation of detailed reports at a seasonal scale. Developed under the AgriLAC project, Eolo aims to strengthen the resilience, sustainability, and competitiveness of agri-food systems in Latin America and the Caribbean. In Honduras, it has been implemented to support the meteorological service (COPECO-CENAOS- Comité Permanente de Contigencias  in Spanish), considering the diversity of forecasting methodologies used by each National Meteorological Service. Eolo enhances the ability to respond to climate variability by facilitating the analysis and comparison of seasonal forecasts, contributing to climate adaptation and strengthening the national framework for climate services. Its use allows for better planning and the development of adaptation and risk mitigation strategies, benefiting both farmers and policymakers.

column16: Incidence and distribution of seed-borne viruses of chickpea and faba bean seeds in Tunisia
column17: The study investigates the incidence and distribution of seed-borne viruses in faba bean and chickpea crops in Tunisia, focusing on their economic and agricultural significance. Seed samples from 20 locations across Tunisia were tested using tissue-blot immunoassay (TBIA) for six viruses: Broad Bean Mottle Virus (BBMV), Broad Bean Stain Virus (BBSV), Pea Seed-borne Mosaic Virus (PSbMV), Bean Yellow Mosaic Virus (BYMV), Alfalfa Mosaic Virus (AMV), and Cucumber Mosaic Virus (CMV). Among 4,587 faba bean seedlings, only BYMV was detected in two seed lots with a seed transmission rate of 1.7%. For 4,000 chickpea seedlings, AMV and PSbMV were identified in three and nine seed lots, respectively, with seed transmission rates of 1.0% and 3.2%. The highest PSbMV transmission rate (8.3%) was found in two chickpea lots. These findings underscore the need for regular monitoring, improved seed quality, and further research to mitigate virus transmission and enhance crop productivity in Tunisia.

column16: Detection of Four Legume Viruses (AMV, CMV, BYMV, PSbMV) in One Multiplex RT-PCR Test Applied at ICARDA’s Seed Health and Virology Laboratory
column17: Viruses such as Alfalfa mosaic virus (AMV), Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV), Bean yellow mosaic virus (BYMV), and Pea seed-borne mosaic virus (PSbMV) significantly impact legume crops in the WANA region. These RNA viruses are transmitted via aphids and seeds, threatening the productivity of crops like faba bean, lentil, and chickpea. Current detection methods, primarily ELISA and TBIA, are costly and labor-intensive, requiring separate tests for each virus. Additionally, obtaining specific antisera is challenging. To address these limitations, ICARDA’s Seed Health and Virology Laboratory developed a validated multiplex reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) assay. This molecular tool efficiently detects and differentiates the four viruses in a single, sensitive test, streamlining virus diagnostics and enabling high-throughput screening of samples. The approach enhances cost-effectiveness and precision in managing virus-related threats to legume crops in the region.

column16: Reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) assay for detection and characterization of Alfalfa mosaic virus (AMV) in legume crops applied by ICARDA’s Seed Health and Virology Laboratory
column17: Alfalfa mosaic virus (AMV) is a significant plant pathogen affecting a wide range of legume crops across various regions of the world including WANA countries. AMV is transmitted by aphids in a non-persistent manner and via seeds of several hosts (including faba bean, chickpea, and lentil). Seed transmission makes managing AMV more challenging, as infected seeds can introduce the virus into new areas and lead to infections in the next growing season, even before aphid vectors are active. Accordingly, seed testing and the use of certified seeds are key strategies to mitigate the spread of AMV as a seed-borne virus. Early detection and accurate diagnosis of viral diseases is critical for the application of appropriate control measures. However, the accuracy and reliability of molecular methods is a fact beyond dispute. This report describes a validated molecular tool for AMV detection and characterization applied by ICARDA’s Seed Health and Virology Laboratory.

column16: Field-based Assessment of the Effectiveness of Rust Resistance Genes Under Field Conditions in Lebanon, Morocco and Tunisia in 2024
column17: Trap nurseries comprising yellow, stem, and leaf rust resistance genes planted under natural infection in two locations in Lebanon and Morocco. Despite the availability of differential seeds, the trap nurseries were not planted in Tunisia. In Morocco, a high level of susceptibility to leaf rust was observed in several leaf rust genes, including Lr10, Lr11, Lr12, Lr13, and others across different locations. In contrast, resistance was noted in genes such as Lr2b, Lr3, Lr9, Lr19, Lr34, and others. In Lebanon, field observations indicated differences in yellow rust resistance across two locations, with various resistance genes (e.g., Yr1, Yr2+, Yr3, Yr5, Yr6+, Yr15, and others) remaining effective at Tel Amara and Kfarchakhna. In Marchouch, stem rust resistance genes like Sr21, Sr11, and Sr38 showed effectiveness, while others, including Sr5, Sr6, and Sr36, were ineffective. Details of effectiveness of Yr, Sr, and Lr genes in Morocco and Lebanon is provided.

column16: Surveillance and Monitoring the Cereal Rust Diseases in Lebanon, Morocco and Tunisia
column17: Achieving durable resistance to wheat rust disease and effectively managing it requires continuous monitoring of pathogen movement and analyzing their pathogenic variations. Despite the severe drought in wheat-growing areas across CWANA in 2024, the Regional Cereal Rust Research Center in Turkey, along with national rust surveillance teams, conducted rust monitoring in Morocco, and the rust surveys in Lebanon and Tunisia were conducted by the national rust survey teams, adhering to BGRI surveillance guidelines. Surveillance data were collected from 35, 64, and 27 locations in Lebanon, Morocco, and Tunisia, respectively. The ODK rust survey mobile application was use during the rust survey in Morocco, Lebanese and Tunisia that carried out rust surveys in wheat-producing regions. They recorded GPS coordinates, rust disease status, and crop phenology, then shared this data with the online Global Cereal Rust Surveillance and Monitoring System in accordance with BGRI's standard protocol

column16: Analysis of prevalent races of wheat rust pathogens in Lebanon, Morocco, and Tunisia for effective wheat rust management
column17: During the 2024 rust surveys, wheat rust samples were gathered from farmers' fields and research stations in CWANA including Lebanon, Morocco, and Tunisia using the RCRRC sampling kit. The Turkiye-ICARDA Regional Cereal Rust Research Center in Izmir received a total of 595 samples, with 88 from these three countries: 21 from Lebanon, 49 from Morocco, and 18 leaf rust samples from Tunisia. Severe drought prevented yellow rust observations in Morocco and Tunisia, but Lebanon's yellow rust samples were classified as PstS2+virYr27 and PstS17. Additionally, three stem rust races were identified: TKKTF in Lebanon, and TKTTF and TTTTF in Morocco. Leaf rust samples are currently undergoing race analysis following several purification steps. Understanding of the prevalent races of wheat rust will enable more effective management of this major disease in the CWANA.

column16: Building Resilience, Inclusive Growth & Holistic Transformation (BRIGHT) Integrated Household Survey, Sri Lanka 2024/25: Household Questionnaire.
column17: The BRIGHT survey contains several innovations that aim to uncover new insights into important survey methodology issues and shed light on intra-household resource allocation and gender and age differences in individuals’ perceptions on various household welfare dimensions. The two main innovations are:; 1) Randomization of the subjective household wellbeing module: Both female and male respondents randomly receive this module and at three different points during the interview. By randomizing the households' respondents, gender differences in the subjective assessment of household wellbeing can be examined. By randomizing the placement of the module, the sensitivity of reported wellbeing levels to topics surveyed prior to the assessment can be analyzed.; 2) Duplication of several modules in the male and female respondent parts, as well as in the parts to multiple respondents of the same gender. These include the employment module where the man responds for himself, and the female responds for herself and all of the other household members; the women’s empowerment module, where both respondents answer questions on empowerment; the debt and savings module, where both respondents answer questions on their own savings; and the food-away-from-home consumption module, where female and male respondents answer questions for their families and their spouses. This innovation allows researchers to analyze intra-household gender and age differences in perceptions on the surveyed topics.; Other innovations include two versions of a water security scale, as well as an energy security scale. This allows researchers to examine which version performs better in capturing access to and quality of water and energy, respectively.  The new modules incorporated in the survey allow for a more granular analysis of various poverty dimensions

column16: Fall armyworm (Spodoptera frugiperda) management using pheromone-based mass trapping data on summer maize at the PHI platform in Qob Elisa, Lebanon
column17: The fall armyworm (FAW), *Spodoptera frugiperda*, threatens irrigated summer maize production in Lebanon and the West Asia-North Africa region, jeopardizing food security and farmer incomes. A 2024 field study in Qob Elias, Bekaa Valley, evaluated an Integrated Pest Management (IPM) approach using pheromone traps and insecticides to manage FAW in imported maize cultivars. Monitoring with pheromone traps guided timely insecticide applications, targeting peak pest activity between September 10 and 29. Early planting and pre-peak interventions were crucial. The IPM strategy significantly reduced FAW infestation to negligible levels compared to traditional methods used by neighboring farmers. Knowledge-sharing sessions, supported by ICARDA and LARI scientists, encouraged local farmers to adopt these sustainable practices. This study emphasizes the effectiveness of pheromone traps in reducing pest populations and insecticide use, offering a practical solution for controlling FAW while promoting sustainable maize production in Lebanon.

column16: Management of food legume pod borer and aphids through intercropping in Morocco-24
column17: "In Morocco, faba bean, kabuli chickpea and lentil are key crops in the cereal-based cropping system and provide food and incomes for small holder farmers. Pod borers and green pea aphids are key pests contributing to high yield gaps in the two crops because of weather variability. Farmers practice different cropping systems, but their ecological services are not well investigated. In this study, we investigated the roles of coriander intercropping as alternative management of pod borers in chickpea and green pea aphids on lentil. column16: Demonstration and Scaling of Integrated Management of Parasitic Weeds on Faba bean in Ethiopia, Morocco and Tunisia
column17: "; Parasitic weeds (Orobanche spp.) severely hinder food legume production in the Mediterranean and East African highlands. To combat this issue, a multi-pronged approach was implemented in Ethiopia, Tunisia, and Morocco during the 2023/24 cropping season. This strategy involved integrating partially resistant faba bean varieties with sub-lethal herbicide application and mixed cropping techniques.; In Ethiopia, the combined application of sub-lethal herbicides and fungicide seed treatments significantly boosted faba bean productivity, with widespread adoption by both male and female farmers. In Tunisia and Morocco, Corum herbicide application effectively reduced parasitic weed infestation on faba bean crops.; To further drive innovation, the production of early-generation seeds of partially resistant varieties should be facilitated in Ethiopia and Tunisia. Additionally, exploring mixed cropping crops within the cropping system, as well as validating the use of Curum herbicide to control both parasitic and non-parasitic weeds in North Africa, are crucial steps for the 2024/25 cropping season.;

column16: A policy decision support tool for priority setting amidst competing interests of Water-Energy-Food-Environmental (WEFE) sector stakeholders
column17: In 2025 we advanced two workstreams: ; 1) We enhanced the WEFE DST developed in 2024 into becoming a full-fledged policy decision support tool called “Stakeholder WEFE Efficiency Evaluation Tool (SWEET)”. Governments can use SWEET to prioritize available budget for investment among the different WEFE sectors by maximizing the synergies and minimizing tradeoffs in the WEFE nexus amidst competing (and sometimes conflicting) stakeholder interests. The SWEET DST is an operational policy decision-support tool with structured multi-criteria analysis (MCA) design where stakeholders’ weighting is aided with not only technological options, but also with economic indicators (costs, and profits). The tool is now designed as one which can be freely made available for anyone to apply it to any country setting (with language translation options). Its analytical visualizations (weights, radar plots, trade-offs) are very informative for decision makers who aspire to optimize the WEFE nexus. ; 2)  We developed a manuscript applying the SWEET to the case of Uzbekistan to assess stakeholder priorities across the WEFE nexus and identify areas of convergence and divergence among water, energy, food, and ecosystem interest groups. The paper is now submitted to an ISI journal.

column16: Enhanced direct seeded rice breeding network expanded to over 50 sites across Asia and Africa by IRRI
column17: Rice farmers in Asia and Africa face challenges growing rice in diverse environments including drought-prone uplands and water-scarce areas where direct seeding is preferred over traditional transplanting. The International Rice Research Institute expanded its direct seeded rice breeding network by adding new research partners across South Asia and East and Southern Africa, creating a comprehensive testing system with over 50 screening sites. This expanded network better represents the diverse growing conditions where farmers cultivate rice, including the addition of a new breeding pipeline specifically targeting upland environments in South Asia. The enhanced network enables more effective development and testing of rice varieties suited to direct seeding methods across different climatic and soil conditions.

column16: Climate-resilient high night temperature tolerant rice from genetics to variety
column17: As a proof-of-concept, new technologies in the form of heat-tolerant potential rice varieties were successfully developed by identifying the key genes with at least 0.5 tonne of yield advantage under HNT under Aus and late Boro seasons with good grain quality. Through multi-location trials, we identified superior heat-tolerant rice lines, with some yielding between 3.0 to 5.6 tons per hectare under HNT conditions in Aus season. Notably, varieties like IRRI154 and IR18C1005 showcased resilience to high temperatures (HDT+HNT) for Boro season, to enhance rice production in heat-prone regions based on participatory varietal selection. An economic surplus analysis was done to estimate the projected net economic contributions of IRRI’s heat-tolerant rice varieties (IR18C1002, IR18C1004, IR18C1005, IR18C1009) in Bangladesh from 2025 to 2034. We estimate that net present value of IRRI  and its partners’ contributions to varietal yield changes in Bangladesh for the 2025 to 2034 period is approximately USD 84.81 million.

column16: Global updated rangeland ecosystem climate change projections through 2050 using evaluated parameters and up-to-date climate forecasts
column17: Climate change in rangelands creates uncertainty that hinders the long-term direction of research, land management and agricultural production, and policy. The updated rangeland ecosystem projections under climate change use the most recent global climate forecasts (CMIP6) with evaluated model parameters for the G-Range global rangeland simulation model to project how rangeland ecosystems may change through 2050. The spatial dataset produced includes fundamental ecosystem attributes such as net primary productivity (NPP), soil carbon, cover of grass, shrubs, trees, and bare soil, and root:shoot ratio, on a decadal basis. G-Range was driven by climate inputs produced using MarkSimGCM, specifically CMIP6 from 2001 to 2050, and historical data from 2001 to 2020. These outputs are used as inputs to other models and analyses, or for national to global scale estimates of rangeland ecosystem status, structure, and function under climate change, with significant implications for research, land management and agricultural production, and policy.

column16: Management of persistently aphid-transmitted faba bean viruses in Tunisia
column17: Faba bean, an essential cool-season legume in Tunisia, faces productivity challenges from viruses transmitted by aphids. A 2023/2024 study at Menzel Bourguiba and Mornag INRAT Station tested virus and aphid management strategies using two faba bean varieties (Najeh and Chourouk), two planting dates, and seed treatments with Cruiser® (Thiamethoxam) at two doses (1.00 and 1.2 cc/kg), compared to untreated seeds. Results showed no virus infection in early planting or Cruiser-treated plots during the second planting, while untreated plots during the second planting had low virus detection (0.4-0.7%). Both varieties produced significantly higher yields with Cruiser-treated seeds. Low rainfall and high temperatures reduced aphid activity, underscoring the effectiveness of adjusting planting dates and seed treatment in managing virus and aphid vectors.

column16: Restoration Co-Design (ReCoDe): fusing global with local knowledge for cost-effective, scalable, sustainable restoration
column17: Land restoration can increase agricultural and ecological productivity where restoration helps producers achieve their livelihood objectives cost-effectively and sustainably. Restoration Co-Design (ReCoDe) is a structured process for fitting restoration techniques based on global and/or local knowledge into the contexts of local management systems. Producers (pastoralists, farmers), practitioners (NGO, government) and researchers (ILRI and partners) co-design restoration protocols, producers test them, and the results are scaled up in producers' restoration plans. ReCoDe is an efficient approach for designing restoration of rangelands, drylands, pastoralist and other communal grazing lands, and other challenging environments for restoration.

column16: A new era in agricultural training: Bangladesh launches pioneering combine harvester simulator
column17: This innovative simulator is transforming operator training in Bangladesh by offering a safe, controlled environment for skill development prior to operating actual machinery. Through strategic collaboration with private sector partners Metal Agritech Ltd., Abedin Equipments Ltd., and CSISA-MEA the initiative aims to attract young entrepreneurs to the agricultural machinery sector while improving operational efficiency and safety nationwide. CSISA-MEA has progressed in operationalizing combine harvester simulators through partnerships with Metal Agritech Ltd. and Abedin Equipments Ltd. Simulators have been installed at company warehouse offices in Jhenaidah Sadar, Jhenaidah District, and Bhaluka, Mymensingh, where combine harvesters are stored and delivered to local service providers. Following installation, a total of 42 technical officials (over 30 from Abedin Equipments Ltd. and 12 from Metal Agritech Ltd.) were trained on simulator operation. The simulators are currently used for in-house after-sales service training and operator orientation. Although wider adoption remains limited due to reduced combine harvester sales following the postponement of the government subsidy program, the initiative has established a strong foundation for rapid scaling once market demand recovers.

column16: Toolkit for exploring yield growth to 2050: Updating exogenous yield growth parameters in impact
column17: This toolkit is composed by guidelines, a manual, and example Power Point slides to update exogenous yield growth. The toolkit is expected to be used during the preparation and implementation of the expert consultations for review and updating of exogenous yield growth parameters to 2050 in the International Model for Policy Analysis of Agricultural Commodities and Trade (IMPACT) of the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI). These exogenous yield growth parameters, commonly referred to as “Intrinsic Productivity growth Rates” (IPRs), represent a component of agricultural productivity that cannot be attributed to price effects, climate change and water shocks — elements which are explicitly captured by IMPACT. Yield growth from IPRs can represent, for example, new technologies, better management, improved input use efficiency, etc. Estimating IPRs to 2050 can be better understood as an exercise to derive future yield growth parameters from an informed extrapolation of observed past trends.

column16: Agroecological Business Model for the Dairy Value Chain of Bobo-Dioulasso (Burkina Faso)
column17: This AgroEcological Business Model (AE BM) integrates and articulates three agroecological business models of upstream actors of the Bobo-Dioulasso dairy value chain: AE BM of dairy farmers, AE BM of milk collectors and AE BM of dairy processors. Each BM integrates agroecological technologies into their value proposition such as: agriculture-livestock synergies and recycling among farmers; economic diversification of services provided to farmers and processors among collectors; economic diversification and the promotion of local food traditions among dairy processors. The overall AE BM integrates agroecological principles such as fair trade, connectivity, and participation. At the end of 2024, funding has been provided to dairy processors  by the Accelerator nechanism set up under AoW 3 of teh Agroecology Initaitive.  In 2025, we have evaluated the first effects of this financing mechanism through the Accelerator process.

column16: Agroecological Dairy Production in Burkina Faso: Sustainable Farming Innovations for Balanced Feed, Biodiverse Forage, and Efficient Resource Recycling
column17: Dairy farmers who are members of the Agroecological Living Landscape (ALL) of Burkina Faso (The ALL corresponds to the Dairy Innovations Platform of Bobo-Dioulasso) have established dairy production units on their farms that integrate several principles of agroecology such as the biodiversification of the fodder system, the strengthening of agriculture-livestock synergies, the recycling of crop and livestock co-products from the dairy production unit, the reduction of industrial inputs (feed concentrates), and therefore several agroecological technologies such as: fodder cultivation, forage seeds production, the recycling of crops and livestock co-products into fodder and manure, the balanced use of the farm's feed resources to feed dairy cows (spontaneous pastures, fodders, and limited use of concentrated livestock feed). column16: Cooperative forage seed production and sharing system among dairy farmers of Bobo-Dioulasso (Burkina Faso)
column17: In Bobo-Dioulasso (Burkina Faso), dairy farmers have a growing need for quality fodder. Faced with an inadequate local market for forage seeds, dairy industry stakeholders operating under a Dairy Innovation Platform (DIP) have been experimenting with a forage seed production and sharing system based on cooperation between dairy farmers. Mother dairy farmers set up a Fodder Demo-Plot on their farm consisting of 4 forage crops (maize, sorghum, cowpea and mucuna). For each crop, 2/3 of the FDP's area was dedicated to forage production and the remaining 1/3 to seed production. Seeds produced are divided into three equal parts between the 'mother farmer' and two 'babies farmers' with a view to introducing three FDPs in year n+1.

The majority of dairies make yogurts based on imported milk powder and flavor the yogurts with artificial flavors. The Bobo-Dioulasso dairies that are members of ALL and that process locally produced fresh milk have started to diversify their yogurt production by flavoring them with natural extracts of non-timber forest products and local agricultural products (pineapple, sweet banana (poyo), coconut, date, ginger, horchata (chufa), kinkéliba, mango, mint, moringa, nere, monkey bread (théodo), orange-fleshed sweet potato, tamarind, zeguene (balanites)). And it works. There is an outlet for these yogurts that we can qualify as ''agroecological yogurts'' because they are made from real milk and flavored with local natural flavors.

column16: ShareFair: An Interactive Knowledge-Sharing Event for Practitioners, Policymakers, and Researchers to Exchange Innovations and Best Practices
column17: A ShareFair is an interactive and collaborative event designed to facilitate the exchange of knowledge, innovations, and best practices among diverse stakeholders. Bringing together practitioners, policymakers, researchers, and community representatives, a ShareFair creates a dynamic space for learning, networking, and co-creation. The format includes thematic sessions, hands-on demonstrations, open discussions, and storytelling, offering participants an opportunity to explore tools and approaches in areas such as sustainable development, agriculture, and knowledge management.; ; Focused on inclusivity, ShareFairs emphasize local knowledge, cross-sectoral collaboration, and practical solutions. They often integrate both traditional methods and digital tools, creating a balance between face-to-face engagement and technology-mediated interaction. Participants leave equipped with actionable insights, new partnerships, and strategies for addressing pressing challenges in their respective fields. By fostering a culture of shared learning, ShareFairs promote the collective advancement of ideas and innovations for sustainable impact.

column16: Water champions to promote One Health in Ethiopia
column17: Until recently, water was notably absent from the national One Health planning and committees, where human, animal, and environmental health converge to address complex health challenges. Water management experts from relevant institutions are now identified and nominated to serve on national One Health committees. These experts participate in comprehensive training programs and are equipped with the necessary knowledge to inform committee deliberations on the role of water in pathogen transmission and on water management solutions to safeguard public health.

column16: Optimized biodiversity management of rice based ecosystem for improved ecosystem services and climate change resilience in Cambodian farming communities: progress and results
column17: Rice, a staple in Southeast Asia, is a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions, with climate change increasing insect pest risks. Sustainable solutions are crucial for enhancing rice the resilience of the rice sector. This study evaluates farmers’ preferred biodiversity management strategies to improve ecosystem services and profitability. Farmers identified mung bean as the preferred bund crop and watermelon as the preferred dry-season crop following wet-season rice. Between 2022 and 2024, replicated field experiments tested four treatments, varying pesticide application, bund crops, and dry-season planting. Key metrics assessed included arthropod diversity, pest damage, agronomic performance, costs, and greenhouse gas emissions. Results indicated that pesticide-free systems with diversified cropping experienced less thrips damage, maintained stable grain yields, achieved higher benefit-cost ratios, and produced lower emissions compared to conventional practices. Further analysis will focus on the role of biodiversity management in strengthening climate resilience.

column17: Livestock producers often struggle to optimize feed resources, limiting animal productivity and farm profitability. This mobile-friendly version makes feed assessment more accessible in field conditions, supporting evidence-based decisions to enhance livestock production efficiency. The application is available through Google Play Store and has demonstrated strong user demand during testing phases.

column16: Marker development and validation for high throughput monitoring of African bacterial blight populations
column17: African Xoo, a causative agent of leaf blight in many parts of Africa, has been found to be widely different from Asian Xoo in terms of genomic characteristics. They have diverged and formed four populations based on existing genomic data from NCBI. To understand how this affects the strategy of resistant variety deployment in Africa, there is a need to monitor the distribution of African Xoo populations and what resistance genes are effective against each population. Our objective is to select and validate SNP markers that can be able to distinguish each of the populations for high-throughput and inexpensive monitoring systems. Validation results showed that the selected markers have low accuracy due to too few numbers of samples available for validation. Hence, there is a need of redesigning the markers and increase number of samples for marker validation

column16: The innovation model for integrated decentralized food system governance at the district level in Cambodia
column17: WorldFish, in collaboration with the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) through Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) Initiative piloted the the innovation model for integrated decentralized food system governance at the district level in Cambodia in 2024. In 2025, the innovation supported food system decentralization by enhancing the connectivity between community fisheries (CFis), community fish refuges (CFRs), irrigation systems, and rice farming as components of an integrated food production system. It focuses on improving water governance and promoting collaboration among CFis, CFRs, farmer water user communities (FWUCs), community ecotourism groups, and other relevant stakeholders. Together, these groups work to manage fisheries, water resources, rice farming, and irrigation through collective approaches that enhance food production and support local livelihoods.To date, two district-level Technical Working Groups (TWGs) have been established and are operational.

column16: Integrated Agroecological Knowledge: Empowering Farmers in Zimbabwe Through Seed Fairs, Field Days, and Farmer Field Schools
column17: This innovation development integrates seed fairs, field days, and farmer field schools into a dynamic framework promoting sustainable agriculture. Seed fairs celebrate agricultural heritage, offering farmers access to diverse seeds while fostering community engagement and partnerships. Field days demonstrate agroecological practices, providing hands-on learning and exposure to tools, techniques, and technologies in real-world settings. Farmer field schools equip stakeholders with skills in soil health, ecosystem restoration, and climate adaptation, fostering collaboration for resilient landscapes. Together, these activities create interactive platforms for knowledge exchange, innovation, and sustainable farming, emphasizing agroecology's role in economic and social development. The bundle strengthens local seed systems, highlights sustainable practices, and encourages partnerships among farmers, agribusinesses, and organizations, driving agroecological transitions, enhancing food security, and building climate-resilient landscapes.

column16: Workflows for conducting spatial ex ante analysis of agronomic interventions
column17: This manual provides workflows for conducting spatial ex ante economic analysis of agronomic interventions. We especially leveraged the classic text by Alston et al (1995) that summarized all the methods for evaluating agricultural research and development innovations. Our task was simply to organize the different methods that spawned after Alston et al (1995) as standard operating procedures (SOPs) —i.e., analytical procedures that can be reproducible and replicated in other contexts.  In this manual, researchers will learn how to conduct spatially explicit (mostly gridded) economic evaluation of agronomic innovations with R and other programming software including Octave, and python. Our purpose for these SOPs is to standardize the spatial ex ante economic analysis process with the aim of reducing the amount of time researchers spend on coding the common building blocks of spatial ex ante workflows and improving their efficiency. ; In 2025, some workflows have been updated based on user's feedback.

column16: Improved protocol for the germination of pigeonpea wild species
column17: The study evaluated the impact of hydropriming on the germination of five pigeonpea wild species: Cajanus cajanifolius, C. scarabaeoides, C. reticulatus, C. sericeus, and C. acutifolius. Seeds were scarified and soaked in four treatments: no soaking (T1), 12 hours (T2), 16 hours (T3), and 24 hours (T4), then sown in a glasshouse using a Completely Randomized Design. ANOVA showed significant effects of species, treatments, and their interactions. Among the species, C. sericeus showed the highest reduction in days to emergence (60%), while C. acutifolius showed the lowest (26.66%). The 16-hour soaking treatment (T3) was the most effective for improving germination. These results offer valuable insights for optimizing germination and using wild pigeonpea species in improvement programs.

column16: Automatic monitoring of trees in silvopastoral systems
column17: A tool in the widely used QGIS was developed to monitor canopy height, counting trees and measure canopy area of sparse trees in pastures using RGB images. The tool can retrieve informaiton in images of different spatial resolutions (<3m/pixel). Such a tool is highly useful for Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) systems by enabling efficient and accurate tree monitoring within silvopastoral and other land-use systems. Key benefits include:; -Biomass and Carbon Estimation: AI-powered analysis of tree distribution and development supports precise carbon stock assessments, crucial for climate action reporting.; -Sustainability Metrics: Facilitates tracking of biodiversity and environmental impact.; -Scalable Monitoring: AI integration allows large-scale, cost-effective assessments, reducing manual labor for data collection and analysis.; -Adaptability: Models can be fine-tuned to diverse ecosystems, enhancing MRV accuracy globally.; ; These capabilities streamline environmental compliance and data-driven decision-making.

column16: Online, interactive tool to provide policymakers with easy access to the results of trade-off modelling from Bangladesh
column17: Sustainable Healthy Diets researchers from Wageningen University and Research designed an online interactive tool ("dashboard") for policymakers in Bangladesh. The online tool allows users to dive deeper into the results from a foresight study analyzing the trade-offs between environmental, health and socio-economic indicators of different food scenarios in Bangladesh up to 2040 and 2050. The researchers used MAGNET, a global economic model. They compared a business-as-usual (BAU) diet to a planetary health diet scenario, which aligns with the diet proposed by the EAT-Lancet Commission, ("the EAT-Lancet diet"), and the Bangladesh food-based dietary guidelines (FBDG). The online tool is part of this Initiative's work to promote the use of decision-support tools that stakeholders can use to navigate food system trade-offs in a fairer, more inclusive and more equitable way.

column16: Training of trainers (ToT) program designed to support actors working on steering food systems transformation towards sustainable healthy diets in Bangladesh
column17: After launching an e-course on Food Systems Governance in 2022, key government partners of the CGIAR Initiative on Sustainable Healthy Diets identified a need for follow-up trainings held face-to-face. A team from this Initiative and representatives from two government ministries agreed that the best way forward would be to jointly develop a new Training of Trainers (ToT) program on food systems. The ToT program will increase the pool of in-country experts that can facilitate learning processes on using food systems approaches. At the same time, the ToT program will complement the national policy processes for food systems transformation, like the first plan of action for food systems transformation, by filling identified gaps in awareness of how sustainable healthy diets can be achieved through food systems transformation and how to apply food systems approaches in these specific, and more general, policy processes.  In 2025, government ministries, led by the Food Planning and Monitoring Unit (FPMU) in the Ministry of Food and in coordination with the Bangladesh National Nutrition Council and members of Better Diets and Nutrition, trained its initial cohort of expert trainers. In 2026, experts from Better Diets and Nutrition will continue to provide support when requested, but the ToT program will transition into largely partner-led activity that will grow through additional support from a bilateral grant.

column16: Scale to assess food safety experiences and concerns of consumers in low- and middle-income countries in development to diagnose constraints to consumption of sustainable nutritious foods
column17: Unsafe food creates a cycle of disease and malnutrition, affecting infants, young children, elderly and the sick. Fresh foods, particularly, fruits, vegetables, and animal source foods, are both more nutritious and riskier from a food safety perspective. Researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition and Food Frontiers and Security are developing a scale to assess food safety experiences and concerns. The focus is not to objectively assess or quantify food safety risks or how nutritionally adequate diets are. Rather, this measure will capture the subjective food safety experiences and concerns of consumers and how consumers respond to these concerns in choosing their diets. The scale is being developed in two phases. In phase one, the team is identifying important constructs that constitute experiences of food safety that the scale should reflect. Three sets of activities are involved, one, analyzing transcripts from 17 focus group discussions and 343 interviews conducted in six African and Asian countries which were part of the Drivers of Food Choice projects. Two, conducting 165 in-depth interviews in three urban contexts (Dhaka, Bangladesh; Addis Ababa, Ethiopia; and Hanoi, Vietnam) to explore perspectives of food safety among household members responsible for purchasing and preparing foods. Three, conducing an extensive scoping review of qualitative and quantitative literature published between 2000-2023 on food safety experiences to identify constructs of food safety experiences. In 2025, the team completed qualitative thematic analysis of 165 in-depth interviews, a list of candidate items for the metric, and cognitive interviews. Part of this work was published and shared at scientific conferences. Phase two will start in 2026 and will focus on the development and validation of the scale.

column16: Toolkit to support actors facilitating subnational implementation of the national action plan for food systems transformation in two provinces in Viet Nam
column17: The Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development designated Dong Thap and Son La provinces as pioneering provinces for subnational implementation of Viet Nam's National Action Plan for Food Systems Transformation (NAP-FST). To start, the provincial governments needed to create implementation plans with prioritized activities for their provinces. Sustainable Healthy Diets was invited to provide technical and coordination support to the provinces to meet this goal. An engagement process, comprised of several activities including capacity building, prioritization, and multi-stakeholder consultations, was designed and implemented in 2024. Recognizing the benefits of documenting the process and developing resources for use in other provinces or even by other countries embarking on subnational implementation of their national action plans, Better Diets and Nutrition published three separate manuals in 2025. column16: IWMI and African Group of Negotiators Expert Support have developed an Nationally Determined Contributions Capacity Scorecard to meet countries' NDC targets and identify potential areas for capacity building
column17: International Water Management Institute (IWMI) and the Africa Group of Negotiators Expert Support (AGNES) identified that countries were not aligning their capacity for implementation with their response to the UNFCCC. In response, IWMI and AGNES have developed an NDC Capacity Scorecard to provide an objective measure for countries to ascertain whether they have the capability to meet their NDC targets and identify potential areas for capacity building in government and national institutions. It is important for countries to have this understanding of their capability to deliver, given that they  will be held to account for the targets that are set. The consequence of only focusing on ever increasing targets for emissions reduction is that most countries in the Global South don’t have the capacity to achieve the targets, which sets them up for failure. A critical consideration is how to achieve a “whole of government” approach that links the business and private sector to develop a collaborative, sustainable approach. In a session held at the recent COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan, this question was explored with inputs from South Africa, Kenya, Uganda and the National Business Initiative of South Africa.

column16: Biometrical Genetics Workflow (Bioflow): CGIAR-NARES breeding analytics and decision support tool designed to enable faster decisions, accelerate breeding cycles, and increase genetic gains
column17: To accelerate genetic gain in priority traits for preferred and climate-resilient crop varieties, breeders require timely, accurate, and data-driven decision-making. This depends on the ability to integrate and analyze large, diverse datasets that capture variation arising from breeding populations, environments, and management practices—collectively described as the genotype × environment × management (G×E×M) complex. Addressing this complexity is essential for identifying and advancing fit-for-purpose candidate varieties. To support this effort,  through the Breeding for Tomorrow science program, Breeding Resources, in collaboration with Accelerated Breeding developed the Biometrical genetics workflow – Bioflow – a breeding analytics and decision-support platform that enables CGIAR and National Agricultural Research and Extension Services (NARES) breeders to access, integrate, and rapidly analyze data from multiple sources. In 2025, significant progress was made in strengthening Bioflow. New and improved modules were deployed in response to breeders’ needs, including tools to support genomic selection in clonal crops and enhanced quality assurance and quality control workflows to ensure data integrity. In addition, existing modules were refined through targeted bug fixes and performance improvements. To support breeding pipeline monitoring and reporting, we collaborated with Scriptoria to enable direct extraction of standardized metrics from Bioflow outputs for use in the Harmonized Crop Report. As a result, Sections 10 and 11 of the report can now be generated directly from Bioflow outputs, allowing breeding teams to track pipeline efficiency and communicate progress effectively to stakeholders. Overall, these enhancements strengthen Bioflow’s role as a core platform for genetic evaluation, performance monitoring, and evidence-based breeding decisions, contributing to increased efficiency and precision in breeding programs.

column16: Vegetable Irrigation for Climate Resilience toolkit to support humanitarian interventions
column17: Access to nutritious, affordable food can be challenging in emergency contexts. Traditional crisis responses often focus on staple crops to meet immediate needs, overlooking the nutrition and income opportunities offered by vegetable production. This toolkit seeks to fill that gap by providing practitioners with a variety of resources and tools to develop resilient irrigated vegetable projects in crisis settings. Vegetable irrigation is vital for nutrition and resilience, particularly as climate change and crises disrupt food systems. Designing and implementing efficient irrigation technologies and climate-smart practices reduces crop stress, boosts productivity, and strengthens resilience in the face of climate change. Investing in local irrigation solutions and supporting vegetable production helps vulnerable populations cope with humanitarian crises, sustaining their food, livelihood and nutrition security. The online geospatial tool is available for governmental agencies, humanitarian agencies, their local partners and donor organizations to identify suitable irrigation technologies to support irrigation investments targeting vegetable production within sustainable water use limits.

column16: Biochar as charcoal and carbon-rich material produced by partial oxidation of carbonaceous organic sources such as olive branches, to improve water holding capacity and soil structure in semi-arid areas, Tunisia
column17: The biochar technology, whereby organic materiel like olive branches are carbonized through a slow burning process is a low cost technology for small scale farmers. Its major effects are the improvement of soil structure through crumb structure formation, increasing water holding capacity and reduction of need and improved efficiency of mineral fertilizers. It is therefore a well adapted technology in semi-arid areas were rainfall is scarce and improved efficiency of water use is important to increase yields of field crops and trees. The technology is well adapted for small-scale farmers in olive - cereal based production systems where you have abandoned olive tree branches after pruning for processing into biochar. Biochar can be used to increase wheat production as the major and most profitable cereal crop grown in North-West Tunisia; Trials showed that combining biochar with mineral fertilizers nearly doubled durum wheat grain yield compared to treatments without biochar, highlighting biochar’s role in optimizing fertilizer efficiency. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating biochar to enhance soil health, improve biomass, and maximize grain production, offering a sustainable approach to farming in semi-arid regions undergoing agroecological transition.; In 2025 ICARDA's national partner, the olive institute, has received a pyrolyzer for biochar production and further trials. This reduceds the depandancy of commercial biochar.

column16: Rhizobial inoculation of forage legume seeds in Tunisia to enhance symbiotic nitrogen fixation, increase biomass production and promote sustainable agroecological practices in forage systems
column17: Leguminous forage crops, including sulla, faba beans, and vetch, establish symbiotic relationships with specific Rhizobia bacteria in their root nodules, enabling biological nitrogen fixation. This innovation involves inoculating forage legume seeds with carefully selected rhizobia strains tailored to crop species and local environmental conditions. The specific Rhizobia bacteria enhanced nitrogen fixation, leading to improved biomass yield, superior forage quality ( higher protein content), and increased crop resilience. Post-harvest, residual fixed nitrogen enriches the soil, benefiting subsequent crops like cereals by reducing the need for synthetic nitrogen fertilizers. This reduces production costs for farmers, improves soil fertility, and minimizes the ecological impact of agriculture. By integrating rhizobial inoculation into forage crop systems,  this innovation promotes sustainable agricultural practices while supporting soil health, crop productivity, and long-term agroecological balance.

column16: Controlled designation of origin for olive oil in Ellès-Sers, El Kef, Tunisia
column17: The introduction of a Geographical Indication (GI) for local olive oil in Ellès-Sers is an innovative labeling approach to valorizing the diversity of local cultivars and highlighting the region's unique olive oil characteristics. This initiative empowers small farmers, who primarily use traditional agronomic practices, by protecting their local expertise rooted in sustainable practices.; Focusing on agro-ecological specialization offers significant advantages for the community, safeguarding the historical significance of this olive-growing site as part of Tunisia's heritage. With its multi-centenarian plantations of ancestral cultivars, Ellès-Sers can maintain its distinct identity while developing a competitive business model.; By forming farmer organizations, producers can collaborate to enhance the value of their olive oils and promote regional knowledge, positioning olive oil as a catalyst for rural development and economic growth while preserving cultural heritage.

column16: Public Private Partnership to Foster Availability of Forage Seed Mixtures in Tunisia
column17: In Tunisia, some of the major constraints in crop-livestock production systems are monoculture of cereals leading to poor soil health and lack of nutrient rich forages for the key small ruminant activity. Forage seeds were insufficient, and no national seed company had been engaged in forage seed production as this wasn't considered beneficial to them.; In 2019, ICARDA and the National Institute of Agronomic Research of Tunisia – INRAT started a facilitation process for a Public-private partnerships through cooperation and engaging with COTUGRAIN, a private seed production and commercialization company. The partnership is set around the commercialization of some forage crop seeds, in addition to some forage mixtures (Vetch-Oat, Vetch-Triticale, Vetch-Oat - Triticale), pre-defined and advised by the research team composed of INRAT. Different formula for forage seed mixture were tested, recommendations were provided to the private company COTUGRAIN, to tailor its seed mixtures products for commercialization. ; Recently, Cotugrain acknowledged the integration of the co-design methodology into their projects, which has made it possible to create seed solutions adapted to new agroecological conditions. Cooperation with partners such as ICARDA has made it possible to increase the area cultivated with vetch and mixture seeds (ID 26 it doubles each year for mixture seeds it has gone from 10T to 30T to 80T), particularly for adaptation to changing climatic conditions. The enterprise has also strengthened its interactions with research institutions (INRAT, ICARDA) and has set up a tripartite agreement for the dissemination of adapted seeds and the application of agroecological practices on a larger scale".; The forage mixture seeds contain legumes, like vetch seeds. To increase productivity of vetch seeds coating with Rhizobia bacteria is advisable. In collaboration with OEP coating of legume seeds is tested and the production of Rhizobia bacteria has started at the new Rhizobia unit in El Grine. COTUGRAIN will be  potential seed company to apply Rhizobia to the forage seed mixture.

column17: Although significant adoption of improved seed of sorghum in Africa has been reported, its overall use remains low. column16: Integrated Rice-Field pond system for enhancing climate resilience and farm productivity in Cambodia
column17: The Rice-Field Fisheries Pond system strengthens climate resilience and farm productivity by integrating climate-smart practices into traditional rice mono systems. Key innovations include inlets and outlets that improve water connection between ponds and rice fields, supporting fish migration and efficient water management. Aquatic plants covering 30–40% of pond areas enhance biodiversity, while fish shelters protect stocks and deter illegal fishing. The system is further enhanced through the integration of vegetables on pond dikes and poultry, promoting nutrient recycling and diversified food and income sources. Designed with low input costs, the approach builds on locally available materials and farmer knowledge, making it easy and fast for farmers to adopt. The system enables at multiple productions good for household nutrition, ensures fish availability during water stress, and has increased rice and fish yields by 57% and 67%, respectively, improving profitability, food security, and livelihood stability in rural communities. column16: Strengthening groundnut breeding networks in eastern, southern, central and west Africa to develop more productive, disease resistant varieties that meet market and consumer requirements and generate income opportunities for farmers
column17: Although significant adoption of improved seed of groundnuts in Africa has been reported, its overall use remains low. There is a growing interest in groundnuts, particularly because of demands by consumer markets and the processing industry. CIMMYT seeks to strengthen national partners in eastern, southern, central and west Africa to work synergistically across countries with common challenges and opportunities, and develop more productive, disease resistant varieties that meet market and consumer requirements and also have lower aflatoxin contamination. The collaboration co-designs and co-develops five pipelines for food and processing. 12 country-level product design teams involving processors, farmer organizations, seed companies and scientists have defined Target Product Profiles and thereby prioritized breeding goals. Founder parents were selected from among 1200 lines from NARS, Australia and the USA, using genomic analysis and trials conducted at 15-30 locations. The targeted breeding cycle time in 48 months.
