column16: Accelerating genetic gains to augment food, feed and bioethanol productivity of sorghum varieties to improve food security and incomes of farmers in Asia, Africa and Latin America
column17: ICRISAT aims to develop high-yielding, climate-resilient, and nutritionally enhanced sorghum varieties that cater to the specific needs of farmers and consumers in Asia and Africa, ensuring that sorghum remains a sustainable and dependable crop for the millions who rely on it for sustenance and livelihoods. Food yields, fodder value, and grain mold, Anthracnose and leaf blight resistance are being improved in three normal sorghum and one sweet sorghum pipelines. Current cycle times are at 48 months. Genomic selection is being established. High-throughput phenotyping approaches and breeding schemes are continuously being improved to access greater genetic variance, increase selection intensity and accelerate genetic gains. Multi-environment trials cover up to 44 environments per subregion. Between 2022 and 2024, partners in India released 13 varieties, four of them improved for post-flowering drought tolerance. Three others are sweet sorghums which can potentially be used as a raw material for bio-ethanol production.

column16: Accelerating genetic gains to augment the productivity and resilience of biofortified or dual-purpose pearl millet hybrids and varieties to benefit farmers in Africa and South Asia
column17: ICRISAT's pearl millet research and breeding is aimed at further enhancing the crop's resilience, productivity, and nutritional quality to help farmers overcome challenges posed by climate change and scarce resources, ultimately promoting food security and uplifting livelihoods in arid and semi-arid regions across the globe. Grain yield, biofortification with zinc and iron, Striga, mildew and blast resistance are being improved in nine pipelines differing in maturity, targeted ecologies (better endowed,  drought or heat affected), and purpose (forage, dual-use, food). Current cycle times are at 36 months. Genomic selection is being established. High-throughput phenotyping approaches and breeding schemes are continuously being improved to access greater genetic variance, increase selection intensity and accelerate genetic gains. Multi-environment trials cover up to 33 environments per subregion. On-farm trialing with 563 growers established 20% higher yields of candidate hybrids. Between 2022 and 2024, partners in India and NIgeria released 11 varieties, nine of them biofortified.

column16: Accelerating genetic gains to augment the productivity, disease-resistance and micronutrient content of finger millet varieties to benefit farmers in South Asia and Africa
column17: ICRISAT engages in research and breeding efforts to develop improved varieties with higher yields, increased resilience to climatic stresses, and further enriching its nutritional value. It collaborates with local stakeholders and partners to ensure that finger millet's potential is fully harnessed in combating malnutrition, supporting livelihoods, and enhancing traditional food systems. Current cycle time is 60 months with the intent to reduce to 48 months. Genomic selection is being established. column16: Forum theatre play “She Inherits, She Sells” uses 'Theatre of the Oppressed' format to help communities address challenges faced by rural women's cooperatives in Morocco, stemming from societal gender norms
column17: The forum theatre play titled "She Inherits, She Sells" was developed to engage entire communities in exploring, analysing, and solving the challenges faced by members of rural women's cooperatives in Morocco, rooted in societal gender norms. Using the 'Theatre of the Oppressed' format, the play begins with actors portraying  a scenario of oppression where the oppressed character(s) fail to overcome the challenges. The play then restarts, inviting audience members to participate as active 'spect-actors.' These participants can step into the roles of the oppressed character(s), attempting new strategies to overcome the oppression, and other characters met along the way whose responses may either support or resist these interventions. The format of the play brings to light the challenges individuals face due to societal norms and provides a platform for collective analysis, exploration, and practice of possible pathways towards liberation.

column16: Improved protocol for drying pearl millet seed for long-term conservation
column17: A drying curve for pearl millet under the ICRISAT drying room conditions (150C and 15% RH) was developed to understand the drying pattern of pearl millet seeds. The purpose was to determine the time required for the seeds to reach the optimal moisture content for storage in Medium Term Storage (MTS) and Long Term Storage (LTS). It was found that pearl millet seeds take approximately two weeks to reach the target moisture content of 6-8% for MTS conservation, and about three weeks to achieve the target moisture content of less than 6% for LTS. This data will be re-validated in 2025 before being incorporated into the final conservation Standard Operating Procedure.

column17: ICRISAT's commitment to chickpea breeding has led to significant breakthroughs, focusing on developing varieties that are high-yielding and resilient to environmental challenges, especially drought. Current cycle time is between 36 and 48 months with the intent to accelerate through speed-breeding. Genomic selection is being established for 100-seed weight, days to maturity, plant height, and pods per plant. High-throughput phenotyping approaches and breeding schemes are being improved to access greater genetic variance, increase selection intensity and accelerate genetic gains. Multi-environment trials cover up to 20 environments. Genetic resources are being explored for resistance to Ascochyta blight diseases and Fusarium wilt, and higher protein contents. Between 2022 and 2023, partners in India registered three chickpea varieties. ;

column16: Methodology to assess the effective contribution of multi-stakeholder processes to food systems transformation applied in Honduras
column17: Sustainable food systems transformation requires multi-stakeholder processes. The current resources for the actors involved focus more on what needs to be done rather than how it can be done effectively. This qualitative methodology fills that gap and provides practical recommendations for supporting effective multi-stakeholder processes. It builds upon published frameworks and the building blocks assessment guide developed by the United Nations (UN), starting with five best practice principles for multi-stakeholder processes. It then assesses the compliance of the particular process to the principles based on a set of identified indicators, relying on a combination of desk review and interviews. The research team from Sustainable Healthy Diets applied the methodology to three recent food systems transformation processes in Honduras - creation of a national food systems profile, the 2021 dialogues to prepare for the UN Food System Summit, and the development of the Tegucigalpa Urban Food Policy Pact. ; ;

column16: Local Technical Agroclimatic Committees: Co-innovation and scaling in Guatemala
column17: The innovation bundle integrates Local Technical Agroclimatic Committees (LTACs/MTAs) with strengthened agroclimatic bulletins, digital climate analytics (including AClimate and seasonal forecasting tools), Human-Centered Design (HCD), and multi-channel dissemination (WhatsApp, SMS, radio, and extension systems). In Guatemala, the model is now institutionalized and government-led under the Ministry of Agriculture (MAGA) and the National Meteorological Service (INSIVUMEH). By 2024–2025, 21 LTACs operate nationwide, engaging more than 90 institutions and directly advising approximately 55,000 farmers. Outcome harvesting assessments confirm measurable behavioral change: around 40% of farmers adopt climate-smart practices, including adjusted planting dates, crop diversification, and improved soil and water management. The LTACs function as trusted territorial platforms that bridge national climate forecasts with local realities, strengthen institutional coordination, and demonstrate sustained scalability and policy anchoring across Latin America.

column16: Participatory Climate Risks Management Approach in High Nutritional Value Chains: Dairy Case in Guatemala
column17: The participatory methodology for climate risk analysis in the dairy value chain is a strategic approach designed to identify and manage climate risks affecting this agro-food chain, with the goal of strengthening food security and nutrition in low- and middle-income countries. The guide provides tools for organizations, NGOs, and development agencies to develop participatory strategic plans, involving stakeholders in a process that includes chain prioritization, risk analysis, and the design of adaptation strategies. This methodology, which has been piloted in the dairy value chain in Guatemala, allows for the assessment of climate events' impacts on the production, processing, and distribution of food, ensuring a contextualized and sustainable approach to mitigate the effects of climate change on the availability and quality of dairy products.

column16: A Step-by-Step Plan to Integrate Knowledge Acquired from the Digital Agriculture Plot and Courses into Academic Programs
column17: The digital transformation of Latin America’s agricultural sector has driven innovation, yet small and medium-sized producers in Guatemala struggle to access and apply these technologies. To bridge this gap, the Bioversity-CIAT Alliance and CUNORI-USAC developed the Digital Plot, an experimental space for agricultural technologies, complemented by digital training diplomas for teachers. These initiatives aim to modernize agronomy curricula and strengthen capacity for integrating digital tools into education. However, achieving systemic change requires stronger collaboration among stakeholders to align education and research with producers' real needs. Using Human-Centered Design, this report analyzes CUNORI’s teacher training initiatives and digital curriculum integration, marking a pivotal step in transforming agricultural education and fostering networks that promote digital innovation adoption. This experience serves as a reference for institutions across the region, emphasizing the importance of co-creating localized solutions to address food system challenges effectively.

Therefore, in 2025 major development steps were completed, including sequencing, genome assembly, polishing, and chromosome-level scaffolding. column16: Agroecology business model for the reduction of imports: production of composite bread incorporating 30% millet as a substitute for wheat
column17: In Senegal, approximately 10,000,000 baguettes of bread are consumed every day. Almost all of this bread is produced from wheat, a cereal imported and subsidized by the State of Senegal. This generates expenses of several billion CFA francs per year, representing a considerable loss of income for local sectors and small producers. However, agri-food research has shown that it is possible to produce compound bread, incorporating a high percentage of local cereals, such as millet. Although naturally gluten-free, millet can be used effectively in bread making. The Senegalese Institute of Agricultural Research (ISRA) has developed short-cycle millet varieties, adapted to climate change and producing large grains, ideal for flour production, thus meeting the needs of millers and bakers. It is in this context that we are developing compound bread, with an incorporation rate of 30% millet, making it possible to reduce wheat imports by the same proportion. In the past, millet was mainly sold raw in markets, without adding value. Thanks to this innovation, millet is now processed locally, contributing to wealth creation, reducing imports and generating jobs in local communities. In 2025, we advanced in the consumer preference analysis related to this type of product which is helping to adjust market offer and demand.

column16: An in-house long read DNA sequencing established for rapid monitoring of pathogen populations
column17: To overcome the challenges of high costs, outsourcing delays, and technical demands in DNA sequencing, an in-house setup was established using the portable MinION device by Oxford Nanopore Technology. This long-read sequencing technology provides a more complete understanding of a pathogen's genome and captures complex regions, unlike short-read sequencing, which relies on sequence assembly and may lose important genomic information. For bacterial diseases in rice such as bacterial blight, long-read sequencing enables the recovery of intact genome sequences without needing a reference genome. Initial sequencing runs on Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae isolates generated 855,000 reads in 22 hours, reducing turnaround time to three days. The MinION’s portability, affordability, and fast sequencing capabilities allow rapid investigation of new pathogen strains and support resistance strategies for rice breeding programs.

column16: Self-paced online training modules on project level Women's Empowerment in Agriculture Index (pro-WEAI)
column17: In response to the growing demand for WEAI surveys, the CGIAR GENDER Impact Platform's Methods Module developed a distance learning course on pro-WEAI. This online course teaches specific skills related to using pro-WEAI to meet the needs of various users: quantitative analysts, monitoring & evaluation specialists, donors, and field supervisors. Participants will receive digital certification upon successful completion of the course. The Pro-WEAI Foundations Module is available in English, French, and Arabic. This module introduces researchers and practitioners to the pro-WEAI tool, covering its background and practical application within project contexts. This module provides conceptual frameworks, resources, and approaches to integrating the index tools into projects, based on real-world experiences from the team that developed it. Completion of the Foundations Module is a prerequisite for all subsequent modules. The subsequent modules build on the Foundations Module and include:; Survey Fieldwork: Learn how to administer pro-WEAI surveys, from planning enumerator training to pilot testing and data collection. This module covers survey questions, response options, and fieldwork strategies.; Qualitative Analysis: Explore the qualitative methods used in pro-WEAI, including the rationale behind including qualitative methods, detailed protocols for different types of respondents, best practices for planning qualitative studies, and guidance on conducting analysis and disseminating results from qualitative pro-WEAI protocols.; Calculating the Index: Learn how to calculate pro-WEAI indicators and the pro-WEAI score. This module covers how to use the Stata do- and ado-files, read output tables and figures, and apply the results to your projects.; Interpreting and Presenting Pro-WEAI Results: Learn how to interpret both the qualitative and quantitative findings from pro-WEAI surveys. This module focuses on deriving insights for future programming and project management, building on the previous modules.

column16: Optimization of the germination test protocol for viability monitoring of Cytisus proliferus seeds in genebank collections
column17: The research investigated methods to improve the germination of Cytisus proliferus seeds, a perennial legume with significant potential for livestock feed. Different scarification techniques were examined to effectively overcome seed dormancy. These methods included the use of sulfuric acid, to chemically break down the seed coat; boiling water, a thermal method to soften the outer layer; potassium nitrate solutions, to facilitate germination by penetrating the seed; and the excision of embryos, a physical approach to remove the embryo from the seed. Each of these techniques was assessed for its efficacy in promoting germination and improving seed viability.  Excised embryos and boiling water at 80 oC for 15-25 minutes were most effective at increasing germination percentages compared to other scarification methods. The study concludes by recommending optimized germination protocols for genebank viability monitoring of this species, prioritizing practical, less labor-intensive methods for broader application.

column16: Age-structured, temperature-dependent population growth model for brown rice hopper (BRH) validated  to predict historical level of BRH population growth in select provinces in the Mekong River Delta in Vietnam
column17: Brown rice hopper (BRH), a key insect pest to rice, is known can change its longevity and fecundity due to rising temperatures. Here we modeled the response of BRH population growth to temperature using an age-structured population growth model, based on reported responses of BRH development time, survival, and fecundity to temperature. We applied this model to predict the historical level of BRH population growth in the Mekong River Delta (MRD) and compared the predictions with historically observed percentages of rice fields infested by BRH. The model was able to capture the seasonal variation in BRH infestation and the optimal temperature for BRH activities (app. 26.5 degrees C). These results highlighted the importance of temperature in regulating BRH population growth. The model, with further improvements as discussed, could be used for projecting BRH activity under rising temperatures or predicting BRH outbreaks due to seasonal temperature anomalies

column16: Empowering small-medium enterprises (SMEs) and Communities through Precooked and Dehydrated Bean Products: Enhancing Nutrition, Gender Equality, and Climate-Smart Solutions for Sustainable Growth and Social Impact
column17: This innovation offers a sustainable solution to the energy and nutritional challenges of cooking beans. Traditional methods require up to 2.6 kg of firewood for 1 kg of dry beans, contributing to deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions (Kajumba et al., 2022). Beans also take 3-4 hours to cook, limiting their use (Munthali et al., 2022). By boiling beans and using steam or pressure cooking, this innovation preserves nutrients like protein, fiber, and essential micronutrients while reducing anti-nutritional factors. After cooking, beans are dehydrated to extend shelf life, reduce food waste, and improve food security. The precooked and dehydrated beans cut cooking time and energy use, benefiting households by saving time and reducing the burden on women and youth. This cost-effective solution supports SMEs, improves nutrition, saves resources, and mitigates environmental impacts, with potential for wide-scale adoption in urban areas, contributing to food security and sustainability.

column16: Drone-assisted agronomic diagnostic for small-scale farming in Guatemala
column17: his innovation, leverages drone photogrammetry to provide precise, timely, and actionable data on crop growth and health, particularly focusing on maize due to its prevalence in the region. By systematically capturing high-resolution images and using satellite imagery, both with multispectral data, aims to empower local farmers with the knowledge needed to optimize crop management and yield, thereby contributing to the overarching goals of resilience and sustainability in the agricultural sector. During 2024, drone images were captured in two departments of Guatemala (Zacapa and Totonicapán) and processed for this purpose. Two key farmers organizations have been part of the development of the innovation (CDRO in western Guatemala and ADIPAZ in eastern Guatemala) and seek to apply the learning with their beneficiary farmers.

column16: Homestead pond aquaculture innovation for food production in the context of climate change in the Mekong Delta, Cambodia
column17: Cambodia's aquaculture sector is rapidly growing and at a critical development stage. It has the potential to address future supply shortfalls of both high-value and low-cost species, generate employment for men and women, and increase export earnings. There is an opportunity to develop profitable and sustainable aquaculture while conserving fisheries resources and enhancing nutrition and poverty alleviation. On-farm experiments show that certain fish species grow better under semi-intensive polyculture than standard practices. Innovative technologies are needed to reduce production costs and increase income. Introducing this model into Cambodian aquaculture allows local farmers to participate in fish culture, contributing to local food security by providing more fish for their households and relatives.

column16: Global Agricultural Data Innovation and Acceleration Network (GARDIAN) - CGIAR platform to accelerate evidence-based innovation for global food systems
column17: GARDIAN is a sustainable public good that provides open access to increasingly FAIR data, digital assets, and analytical tools, enabling rapid, evidence-driven insights for greater impact. Its data holdings are comprehensive and diverse, spanning agricultural disciplines, organizations, topics, and geographies. Users can access global collections of open agricultural publications, underlying datasets, and standardized geospatial layers—covering soil, weather, and crop production data—which can be visually explored and downloaded for specific locations or regions.; ; GARDIAN’s search engine allows users to discover agri-food datasets, documents, and digital assets from CGIAR centers and partners using multiple, complex criteria. Integrated analytics help users understand the “where” and “what” dimensions of research outputs, improving transparency and enabling faster knowledge synthesis. By making large volumes of publications and data easy to find and retrieve, GARDIAN supports data scientists, researchers, and analysts in accelerating innovation.; ; In 2025, the GARDIAN User Interface has been redesigned to improve navigation and usability. The search engine has been updated to simplify queries and now includes filters for year, country, and access rights. GARDIAN also incorporates datasets standardized through the Carob project, enabling seamless discovery through refined filters and map-based visualizations.

column16: Charting agroecological pathways: Multicriteria priority mapping for India’s sustainable transition
column17: The innovation titled "Multicriteria-Based Priority Mapping: Charting Agroecological Pathways in India" addresses the dual challenge of food security and environmental sustainability. Using a multi-criteria decision-making framework, it integrates diverse datasets such as net primary productivity, fertilizer consumption, rainfall patterns, groundwater levels, the aridity index, and others. Two distinct agroecological priority maps were created to reflect different stakeholder perspectives. The first focuses on food security by prioritizing rainfed, low-productivity zones, while the second emphasizes environmental restoration in high-input, degraded areas. The limited overlap in the highest priority class indicates divergent stakeholder views. These maps, developed through the Analytical Hierarchy Process, guide targeted areas for priority resource allocation and sustainable farming practices while balancing yield improvements with environmental conservation. The innovation highlights the importance of participatory decision-making, including priority zonation, dynamic policy formulation, and periodic updates to address evolving challenges. This approach offers a replicable model for scaling agroecological practices globally.

column16: Intensified farming through rice-rice production systems by consumptive use of surface and groundwater in the coastal zones of Bangladesh
column17: The Initiative on Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) builds on the work of the Sustainable Intensification Innovation Lab (SIIL) Project in Bangladesh through the International Rice Research Institute. Their joint efforts aim to implement a transformative project in the polder zone, targeting the untapped agricultural production potential of the region. Currently, the rice-rice production system was introduced in the southcentral (SC) and southwest (SW) coastal zones to increase land productivity. Since river water remain non-saline in most rivers of SC region, the farmer pumped water from the polder canals that entered inside the polders during high tides. While the river water becomes saline in the dry season in SW region and the farmers utilized groundwater (where salinity permits) for rice irrigation in conjunction with non-saline river water conserved in polder canals.  The farmers cultivated climate-resilient, nutritious and salt-tolerant HYV rice in both wet and dry seasons and harvested 10-12 t/ha/yr that significantly contributed to their food security.

column16: Food Systems Profile as a knowledge tool to enhance the capacity for health and agriculture staff in the Mekong River Delta in the implementation process of food systems transformation
column17: The Food Systems Profile for the Mekong River Delta is a strategic knowledge tool offering a comprehensive analysis of the region's food systems, including key drivers, components, and outcomes. It establishes a baseline for assessing the current state and future progress, addressing challenges and opportunities for transformation. Designed to enhance capacity, the profile can be integrated into university curricula and professional training for health and agriculture staff in the Mekong River Delta. By equipping stakeholders with evidence-based insights and practical frameworks, it supports Vietnam's National Action Plan for Food Systems Transformation, fostering a transparent, responsible, and sustainable food system by 2030.

The materials target agricultural sector officials, health sector officials, laborers mass organizations, and others.

column17: The guideline offers comprehensive instructions for designing nutrition-sensitive agri-food (NSAF) system projects in the Mekong Delta. The document outlines the fundamentals of NSAF projects, steps for project development, and the formulation of monitoring and evaluation (M&E) plans. Co-developed by MARD and published in 2024, the guideline was distributed to agriculture and health personnel in provinces participating in the Poverty Reduction Program. The approval of the guideline was authorized by Decision No. 2048/QĐ-BNN-KTHT by MARD on 28 June 2024.

column16: Improved protocol for drying of soya bean seed germplasm
column17: The longevity of soya bean seed germplasm is improved if seeds are initially dried at 40C compared with immediate drying in the genebank drying room at 17C. Fumigation after initial drying was also better for seed longevity compared with fumigation before initial drying. These results indicate how the post-harvest process needs to be optimized to increase seed longevity and reduce the requirement for regeneration due to declining seed viability.

column16: Personalized soil report for farmers in the Kiambu and Makueni County Agroecological Living Landscapes (ALLs) in Kenya
column17: The Agroecology Initiative Kenya Work Package 1 team developed personalized soil data reports in an effort to provide actionable data feedback to the farmers who participated in the co-design cycle. Prior to establishing the first trials, the team took soil samples. Rather than only using the scientific insights to advise on appropriate soil health measures, the team developed a generic report format for each trial participant that allowed sharing the main information back with each farmer. The report is structured in four sections: (1) general introduction about the project, (2) farmers’ personal data including name, farmer group, ALL, trial focus area, and trial practice, (3) individual soil data report with individual results for 15 soil elements that are relevant for agricultural production, including pH, Soil Organic Carbon (%), Total Nitrogen (%), Phosphorus (P), and Potassium (K) – alongside interpretation guidance ranges, and related personalized interpretations (high; medium; low), and (4) a generic soil data interpretation and recommendations guidance section. The personalized reports were shared with each trial participant during a technical training and a general data feedback workshop session.

column16: Decision-support tool for identification of conservation and restoration hotspots for native Asian tree species
column17: This decision-support tool helps to identify priority areas for the conservation and restoration of native Asian tree species: ; a)	Areas where most natural habitats have been converted to other land uses, but which are predicted to remain suitable for the target tree species under future climate conditions. These areas are suitable for forest and landscape restoration with the target tree species.; b)	Areas where human threats to the target tree species remain limited and large and relatively undisturbed populations are predicted to occur. These areas are suitable for expanding in situ conservation through protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs), and as quality seed sources for restoration.; c)	Areas which are predicted to become unsuitable for the target species in a changing climate. These areas should be prioritized for germplasm collections, to conserve the species’ genetic diversity ex situ. ; The tool includes information of >200 tree species across South, East and Southeast Asia.;

column16: Drone solutions to map river bodies for environmental flow (e-flow) assessments
column17: Environmental flow (e-flow) assessments are crucial for understanding river health, flow dynamics, and ecosystem interactions. They guide water management decisions to balance ecological sustainability with human water needs, benefiting researchers and policymakers. To improve e-flow assessments, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) and GroundTruth, under the CGIAR Initiative on Digital Innovation, have developed an advanced, less labor-intensive approach using drones and tethered survey vessels equipped with LiDAR and SoNAR sensors. This system captures high-resolution, near real-time hydrological and habitat data over vast areas, surpassing traditional manual surveys. By integrating these data into a digital twin of the Limpopo River Basin, researchers can model river flow, sediment transport, and aquatic habitats with unprecedented accuracy. This innovation enhances decision-making for water resource management, enabling proactive responses to environmental changes and ensuring the sustainable stewardship of vital river ecosystems.

column16: Performance Evaluation of Commercial Grass Cultivars in Guatemala
column17: The methodology provides a framework for establishing field trials to assess the adaptability, productivity, and nutritional quality of commercial grasses under the climatic and soil conditions of Izabal, Guatemala. A pilot field trial was conducted in collaboration with a local livestock association and academia in the Izabal department, Guatemala. Experimental plots were established on both well-drained and poorly drained soils, testing eight commercial grasses, including hybrids of Urochloa and Megathyrsus maximus. Each treatment was replicated and included both technical and participatory evaluations by local livestock farmers. The results can provide key information for designing forage management strategies adapted to the climate and local conditions, to strengthen livestock productivity in the region.

column16: Payments for Ecosystem Services tender approach for Incentivizing nature-positive farming practices in Northern Vietnam
column17: We describe an approach for incentivizing nature-positive farming practices, comprising of: (1) Best-Worst Scaling workshops to identify farmers' preferred practices, (2) Collecting competitive group tender bids from interested farmer groups for implementing the practices. Groups quantify their targets for implementation, and determine the in-kind compensation they require in return of ecosystem service provision, (3) Technical guidance in implementing the practices, (4) Distribution of the agreed rewards upon successful completion.; We applied the approach with indigenous farmers from in four communes in Northern Vietnam. Most preferred practices were improving agrobiodiversity by integrating native trees in farming systems and restoring erosion-prone lands through tree planting. In total 11 bids involving 81 farmers from 9 villages were selected for implementation, based on e.g. cost per area restored, species choices, and equity considerations (e.g. gender balance). In total 52 hectares were restored, 18,270 trees planted, 3 smallholder nurseries established, and rewards worth US$11,578 paid out.

column16: Identification and validation of sex genomic markers in Catla and Silver Carp for improved aquaculture breeding
column17: This study aimed to identify and validate male-specific genomic markers for two economically important aquaculture species, catla (Labeo catla syn. Catla catla) and silver carp (Hypophthalmichthys molitrix). By leveraging conserved male-specific genomic regions from closely related species—rohu (Labeo rohita) and bighead carp (Hypophthalmichthys nobilis)—researchers identified putatively male-only oligonucleotide sequences. These findings provide a valuable foundation for sex-specific breeding programs, offering potential applications in selective breeding, stock management, and genetic improvement in aquaculture.

column16: ILRI optimized manure-fed biogas digesters for Kenyan Ethiopian smallholder farmers
column17: The optimized production and use of biogas (clean fuel) and organic fertilizer from livestock manure management improve energy efficiency and agricultural sustainability. This system processes animal waste and other organic materials to generate biogas and bio-slurry. It enables small-scale agricultural producers and livestock keepers, particularly those with minimal GHG emissions, to contribute to a low-carbon rural economy through improved agricultural practices. By promoting a circular economy on farms, it enhances productivity while supporting climate change mitigation in livestock farming. Additionally, it improves nutrition and agricultural output by using bio-slurry for food production and biogas for cooking and farm operations.

column16: Remote Sensing-based Information and Insurance for Crops in Emerging Economies (RIICE) - A decision support tool for monitoring area, yield, and climate change impacts on rice production in Cote d’Ivoire
column17: As part of the TAFS-WCA initiative, Work Package 2 (Digital Agriculture) is piloting the Remote Sensing-based Information and Insurance for Crops in Emerging Economies (RIICE) tool (www.riice.org) for Bouake region in Cote d'Ivoire. This tool aims to support the government's endeavors to achieve rice self-sufficiency, through monitoring rice production at national scale. The preliminary activities have been conducted during the wet season 2023 over Bouake region using RIICE technology, in collaboration with IRRI, sarmap, AfricaRice, the Alliance of Bioversity - CIAT, and local partners.  The pilot activities were conducted to generate rice areas, Start-of-Season, Leaf Area Index (LAI), and end-of-season yield maps for the wet season 2023. In 2024 the plot continued with objectives to (i) generate Rice Baseline and Ecosystem Map, (ii) Generate Rice area-yield estimates for the main rice wet season 2023, (iii) conduct fields experiment, and to (iv) Validate the rice area-yield estimations.

column16: Lean data innovation for rapid diet quality monitoring at scale
column17: Diet quality is a major component of food and nutrition security across agrifood systems. Current priorities for sustainable development include the need for nutrition-sensitive agrifood systems, linking production with consumption and health outcomes for evidence-based impact of interventions and investments. Therefore, it is important to consistently assess diet quality over time and at varying geographic levels. To respond to this need, IITA and The Alliance Bioversity & CIAT have conducted a pilot study in 2024 to implement an innovative lean data system for monitoring dietary diversity in Nigeria, providing insights that can inform policy actions to improve nutrition and health outcomes in Nasarawa State. Specifically, the study aims to: (i) Develop a rapid data collection system for diet quality monitoring by incorporating lessons learned from previous efforts and ensuring alignment with the national context and (ii) Analyze diet quality trends across Nasarawa State over the data collection period.

column16: Digital Twin Drought Monitoring Tool for the Limpopo River Basin
column17: The drought monitoring tool for the Limpopo River Basin integrates Earth Observation (EO) datasets, meteorological indices, and hydrological modeling to track drought conditions in near real-time. Developed under the IWMI Digital Twin platform, it leverages climate data, precipitation records, and vegetation health indicators such as the Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) and Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) to assess drought severity and trends. The system incorporates satellite-derived rainfall anomalies, evapotranspiration assessments, and water balance calculations, helping policymakers and researchers understand the impact of drought on water resources, agriculture, and food security. The tool identifies regions most affected by dry conditions, enabling proactive decision-making for drought mitigation and adaptation strategies. By visualizing changes in water availability and vegetation health, it supports long-term planning for irrigation, water allocation, and climate resilience efforts. This comprehensive approach enhances early warning capabilities, helping governments and stakeholders implement timely interventions to minimize the socio-economic impact of droughts.

column17: Despite breakthroughs in genetic innovation, there is limited rigorous causal empirical evidence of the impacts of new varieties on smallholders’ livelihoods to justify investments in genetic innovation. Most estimates of the returns on investments in breeding are either modeling-based or stem from correlational rather than causal evidence. To fill this gap, Genetic Innovation started a new approach to impact assessment: designing and implementing a series of coordinated impact evaluations across CGIAR centers. The focus on impacts, coordination across centers, and the rigorous nature of these evaluations offers a more comprehensive approach to understanding how new varieties affect smallholders. Four proposals for randomized evaluations with implementation in India, Kenya and Malawi (HarvestPlus) were selected through a competitive proposal and the portfolio of coordinated impact assessments was launched through a workshop on October 24-25 in Nairobi. The workshop was the first step in aligning methodologies to ensure consistency across these four studies.

column16: Climate information systems (CIS) for aquaculture: Development of a temperature-based, early warning alert system for fish farmers in Zambia
column17: A temperature-based early warning alert system for fish farmers in Zambia has been developed. The advisory tool utilizes an air-water temperature relationship algorithm to forecast pond water temperatures, which is integrated with the data hub of the Intelligent Agricultural Systems Advisory Tool (iSAT) and an early temperature warning decision tree matrix. It also features a dashboard that uses input data and water quality parameter thresholds for critical scenarios affecting tilapia and catfish (Clarias gariepinus). When predicted temperatures approach these thresholds, a color-coded alarm is activated, triggering a specific action protocol to regulate pond temperatures. The goal is to mitigate the impact of high-risk (24°C minimum and 32°C maximum) and emergency (12°C minimum and 40°C maximum) temperature scenarios on cultured stock.;

column16: Feasibility of using an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted dietary assessment mobile app to characterize the quality of school meals and their contribution to children’s diets validated in Viet Nam
column17: School feeding programs reach approximately 368 million children globally and serve as a multifaceted intervention benefiting education, health, and nutrition. Despite these investments, there is limited data on diets and nutritional status of school-age children, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). For many reasons, monitoring the quality of school meal programs in LMICs remains challenging. This innovation builds on a collaboration that began in 2020 with CGIAR and the listed national partners from Viet Nam. (Its application in Ghana has been reported by Resilient Cities.) The collaboration developed the PlantVillage Food Recognition Assistance and Nudging Insights (FRANI) app, which offers a cost-effective solution for recognizing foods, providing consumption statistics, and estimating nutrient intakes in children and youth with accuracy comparable to professional dieticians but at a lower cost. In 2024, Sustainable Healthy Diets began a feasibility study to test how this innovation works in primary schools.

column16: Enhancing Productivity and Profitability: The Agronomic and Economic Benefits of Integrated Rice-Fish Farming Systems
column17: The agronomic and economic performances of an integrated rice-fish system were evaluated using a 1200 m² block subdivided into six plots of 120 m² each: a. a fish pond in the middle of the rice plot, b. rice monoculture with no fertilizer application, c. cultivating rice in the middle of the plot and raising fish around the rice, d. rice monoculture with the application of the recommended doses of fertilizers (NKP and urea). The fifth and sixth plots were in symbiotic association i.e., rice and fish were grown in two separate plots, and the water from the fishpond was used to fertilize the rice plot. The association of fish with rice significantly reduced the production cost by approximately 30-67% and enhanced both the profit (by 3-164%) and the producer’s income over rice monoculture.

column16: Social-Cultural Innovation for Disseminating Climate-Smart Agriculture Technologies and Information in Local Contexts Using Shared Everyday Life Situations
column17: A social-cultural innovation for disseminating validated climate-smart agriculture (CSA) technologies and enhanced climate information has been developed. This approach includes translating validated climate information and aquaculture manuals into local languages, performing dramas at special events such as agricultural and commercial shows and roadshows, and recording radio broadcasts, ensuring relevance within community contexts by leveraging shared everyday life situations. The aim is to enhance greater community engagement and accessibility of technology and information and promote farmers' adoption of climate-resilient agricultural practices. The content is also digitized and shared on social media platforms like YouTube, WhatsApp, and Facebook.

column16: Water-Energy-Food Nexus Decision Support System: A Sustainability and Resilience tool for India
column17: During 2025, the Dashboard and integrated hydrological modelling framework for the Ganges Basin was substantially enhanced through the incorporation of four improved management scenarios: (1) increased irrigation efficiency, (2) enhanced groundwater recharge, (3) expansion of irrigated area, and (4) crop diversification. These scenarios were implemented across all districts to quantify impacts on water demand, crop productivity, groundwater sustainability, and system-wide water balance. Parallel to this, a comprehensive environmental flow (e-flow) assessment was carried out for each major stream within the Indian portion of the basin, comparing Business-as-Usual (BAU) conditions with each scenario. This produced a detailed understanding of how management interventions influence seasonal flow regimes and ecological thresholds. Furthermore, the modelling system was upgraded to compute district-level Water–Energy–Food–Ecosystem (WEF-E) indices and generate a composite WEF score for each district. This advancement enables cross-sectoral comparisons, identifies nexus hotspots, and highlights scenarios that improve system resilience while reducing trade-offs. These updates significantly strengthen the Digital Twin’s decision-support capability and provide a more robust evidence base for policy formulation and basin-scale planning.	;

column16: Enhancing nutritional security of small farmers though introduction of improved homestead production system with vegetable and aquaculture practices in India
column17: To explore the viability and formulate effective strategies to improve resilience, income sustainability and nutritional security of farmers in India, the improved homestead production system with vegetable and aquaculture practices was introduced. Study revealed that the culture of IMC was more profitable (B:C ratio 2.49) in comparison to the system in which 50% (B:C ration 1.68) and complete replacement (B:C ratio 1.62) of IMC with monosex tilapia.

column16: A Temperature-Dependent Phenology Model for the Sweetpotato Whitefly Bemisia tabaci MEAM1 (Hemiptera: Aleyrodidae)
column17: The sweetpotato whitefly, Bemisia tabaci (Gennadius) MEAM1, is a globally distributed pest with a significant economic impact due to its ability to transmit numerous plant viruses. Understanding the temperature-dependent population growth is crucial for managing this pest effectively. Studies were conducted on B. tabaci MEAM1's development, mortality, and reproduction across seven constant temperatures (12° to 35°C). The Insect Life Cycle Modeling (ILCYM) software was employed to create a phenology model, predicting life-table parameters based on temperature. The model successfully predicted population development between 13.9 °C and 33.4°C, with the highest finite rate of increase observed at 26.4°C. Validated with field data, this model provides valuable insights into the species' potential distribution based on temperature, aiding in the design of pest management strategies globally.

column16: Development of forecasting models for management of pod-borer (Helicoverpa armigera Hübner) in pigeonpea (Cajanus cajan L) and chickpea (Cicer arietinum L)
column17: Pod borer (Helicoverpa armigera) is still significant challenge in pulse cultivation in India. We aimed to develop regression model using weather indices for forecasting pod borer outbreaks in pigeonpea and chickpea. The historical adult trap catch data; eggs and larval data, and actual weather data of ICRISAT location from 1991 to 2023 was used.  Models predict crop stage at the first appearance of the pest (Y1), and maximum population of the pest at peak infestation time (Y2). Results showed that temperature, relative humidity, rainfall, and sunshine hours significantly influenced the population dynamics of pod borer. For pigeonpea, model accurately predicted maximum eggs population at 43rd SMW and maximum larval population at the 45th SMW. In chickpea, model predicted the maximum eggs population at 45th SMW and the maximum larval population at 46th SMW. The model's effectiveness validated in current season for pigeonpea at major growing regions of Karnataka and Telangana.

column16: Multilocational leguminous and grass forages adaptation research to enhance diversity and forage options at the farm and landscape scale
column17: Implementation of multi-locational forage adaptation trials across major highland agro-ecologies of Ethiopia, specifically in Jimma Zone of Oromia Region, Hadiya Zone of Central Ethiopia, and North Shewa Zone of Amhara Region. ; Over the past two years, a diverse range of leguminous and grass forage species have been systematically evaluated under farmer-relevant conditions to identify well-adapted, high-yielding, and resilient forage options suitable for integration into mixed crop–livestock farming systems. In Hadiya and North Shewa zones, the trials focused on cool-season forages, where fourteen nationally released oat varieties and six vetch varieties were evaluated for their agronomic performance, biomass yield, adaptability, and potential contribution to improving livestock feed availability. These species were selected due to their importance in highland production systems and their potential to address critical dry season feed shortages while enhancing soil fertility through legume integration. In Jimma Zone, which represents a relatively humid highland environment, the trials included both grass and legumes suited to perennial and short-season forage production. Grass species such as Napier and Brachiaria grass were evaluated alongside leguminous forages including cowpea, alfalfa, and forage soybean. These forages were assessed for establishment, biomass productivity, and compatibility with existing cropping systems. Overall, the multi-locational trials were embedded within a broader farming systems framework aimed at diversifying and intensifying mixed crop–livestock systems. The overarching objective was to strengthen the supply of quality livestock feed, improve system productivity and resilience, and contribute to the provision of multiple benefits, including food production, income generation, and essential ecosystem services

column16: Leveraging the drone and satellite imagery to identify crop stresses in the semi-arid regions
column17: Quantification of crop stresses for targeted intervention, drone data was collected weekly to capture high-resolution imagery for monitoring crop biotic stresses, including diseases and pest infestations. This imagery helped map spatial disease patterns and assess the progression of stresses across different crops. Various analytical approaches were tested to refine detection techniques and improve early warning systems. Additionally, drone-based observations were compared with satellite imagery to evaluate differences in spatial and temporal resolution, ensuring a comprehensive assessment of crop health. The integration of these data sources enhanced the accuracy of stress detection, enabling timely interventions. The findings contribute to developing advanced biotic stress monitoring frameworks, supporting precision agriculture through early stress diagnosis and targeted management strategies. This research will enable researchers to integrate Earth observation technologies into crop health monitoring, improving resource management and resilience in agricultural systems, particularly in semi-arid regions where timely stress detection is crucial for sustainable farming.

column16: Genomic tools for selecting and deploying best-bet forages for farmers use
column17: The ILRI Genebank houses a vast forage genetic pool that can be leveraged to address feed shortages and enhance farmers' resilience to climate change. However, traditional methods of forage characterization and screening have been expensive and time-consuming. To overcome this challenge, we have developed and applied genomic tools to accelerate the selection of optimal forage accessions and expedite the deployment of genebank materials for use by farmers. By utilizing DNA markers, we have identified core collections of forage species, including cowpea, lablab, Sesbania sesban, Rhodes grass, oats, Urochloa spp., buffel grass, and Napier grass. Consequently, candidate best-bet varieties were identified and prepared for national variety verification trials. The Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR) is evaluating the performance of the promising subsets to submit applications for the registration of new forage varieties in Ethiopia. This milestone provides livestock keepers with new forage options, improving feed supply, livestock productivity, and livelihoods.

column16: Breaking dormancy in Macroptilium and Clitoria species for routine viability monitoring of genebank collections
column17: Dormancy-breaking treatments play a crucial role in enhancing seed germination and promoting seedling growth in Macroptilium and Clitoria species. In the case of Macroptilium species, it was observed that applying dry heat for a duration of 15 to 20 minutes significantly improved the germination percentage of seeds. Conversely, treatments involving concentrated sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄) and hot water resulted in a notable increase in seed mortality. ; For Clitoria species, two effective scarification methods were identified: using sandpaper and soaking seeds in hot water for 4 minutes. These treatments helped to disrupt the seed coat, enhancing water penetration and promoting germination.;  In contrast, treating Clitoria seeds with H₂SO₄ for 10 minutes led to seed damage, even though it reduced the hardness of the seed coat. Untreated seeds in both species exhibited poor germination, remaining hard at the final evaluation highlighting the need to break dormancy for germination.

column16: Integrated Thermo-Chemical Protocol for Bacterial Elimination in Rice Seed
column17: A major concern in the exchange of rice germplasm is the potential contamination of seeds with bacterial species. This contamination could have an effect not just on rice crops but also on other crops that are economically important. The integration of heat treatment with the use of fungicide is a viable and economical option that potentially targets both bacterial and fungal pathogens. In 2024, we carried on with heat treatment experiments, exposing seeds to temperatures between 50 and 70˚C  over different durations ranging from 3 to 20 days. Our study demonstrated that heat treatment at 60°C for three days effectively eliminated between 80 and 90% of the bacteria, offering a viable alternative to the use of bactericides, particularly when paired with fungicide (Teams) treatment.

column16: Alternative chemical and biological seed treatments to inhibit bacterial and fungal pathogens
column17: Seed-borne diseases pose significant threats to crop establishment and yield, making effective seed treatment a critical component of integrated pest management strategies. Chemical treatments such as Aluminum Phosphide (57%) and a formulation known as Team (Carbendazim 12.5% and Mancozeb 63%) have been widely used for controlling insect pests and pathogenic fungi, respectively. However, with regulatory changes and the recent ban of Team’s active ingredients in Europe, there is an urgent need to identify and validate alternative seed treatment agents that are both effective and compliant with current phytosanitary standards. This study evaluates the comparative efficacy of several alternative chemical and biological seed treatments in inhibiting seed-borne bacterial and fungal pathogens, using Team as the control. Alternative chemical and biological seed treatments, particularly Taqat, Fludioxonil, and RB 99 TM, have demonstrated strong potential to replace banned or restricted formulations such as Team for the management of seed-borne pathogens. Final validation trials are scheduled for 2026; definitive recommendations for phytosanitary protocol updates will follow the completion of these studies. The study identifies effective, regulation-compliant alternatives to banned seed treatment chemicals, ensuring continued control of seed-borne pathogens. The findings guide evidence-based updates to seed treatment protocols following final validation trials.

column16: EPIRICE: Models for predicting rice pests and disease risks and shifts due to climate change and other factors
column17: Epidemiological models are essential for monitoring pest and disease outbreaks, aiding prevention and management. This study standardizes EPIRICE, a rice disease model predicting rice blast, a major threat in sub-Saharan Africa. Experiments using a randomized complete block design were conducted across five locations in Côte d'Ivoire and three in Uganda (2023/2024). Predictor variables were analyzed to assess infection risk. Data collection was disrupted in two locations due to brown spot infection. In Côte d’Ivoire, epidemics began between May and July annually. EPIRICE accurately predicted blast onset, with p-values above 5%, confirming reliability. Predicted versus observed field data showed strong similarities. Temperature (20-25°C) had the strongest correlation with blast risk, while wind speed had minimal impact. Ongoing analysis will determine optimal decision thresholds based on 2024 harvest data from Côte d’Ivoire and Uganda. These findings will enhance disease forecasting, supporting effective rice blast management in the region.

column16: Optimising AQUAculture Development and Market Connectivity (AQUADMC): A geospatial platform for sustainable site selection, resource management, and market integration in aquatic food systems.
column17: Aquaculture plays a vital role in food security and local economies, yet selecting sustainable and viable sites remains a challenge, particularly in developing countries. Traditional methods rely on limited ground data, often leading to inefficient resource use, environmental degradation, and logistical constraints. Without satellite-based insights, decision-making is often based on outdated or incomplete information, making it difficult to meet sustainability goals. ; Optimising AQUAculture Development and Market Connectivity (AQUADMC) leverages remote sensing technologies and geospatial datasets to provide a comprehensive decision-making platform for aquaculture site selection. By integrating environmental, socio-economic, and logistical factors, AQUADMC delivers actionable insights for policymakers, investors, and local authorities. This approach ensures ecologically responsible and economically viable aquaculture expansion, while addressing emerging challenges such as climate change and market growth. As the platform evolves, it offers a transformative solution for improving sustainable aquaculture development, guiding decision-making with data-driven precision.

column16: An in vitro protocol for the estimation of banana aphid (Pentalonia nigronervosa) life cycle on Musa genotypes
column17: Controlling banana aphids (Pentalonia nigronervosa) is key to mitigating the banana bunchy top virus (BBTV) spread, responsible for the lethal banana bunchy to disease of Musa spp. Assessing the aphid life cycle (nymphs to adult stage) on Musa cultivars helps determine genotype suitability and the influence of environmental conditions on the aphid life cycle, but studying this under field conditions is challenging. To address this, an in vitro protocol was developed using banana pseudostem and agar media in small plastic boxes under laboratory conditions. The protocol was validated for the aphid life cycle on four banana cultivars: Agbagba, Cavendish-Williams (CW), Grand-Naine (GN), and Bluggoe. Mean development times from nymph to adult were 8, 10.5, 12, and 13 days, respectively. Agbagba supported the highest aphid growth, while Bluggoe was the least suitable. This demonstrates the potential of the protocol to determine aphid life table under controlled conditions crucial for phenology modelling.

column16: Decentralizing GIFT seed supply system in Nigeria – Scaling model for species diversification​
column17: With fish consumption rising globally but per capita supply declining in sub-Saharan Africa, Nigeria’s reliance on single-species aquaculture limits sector growth. To address this, a decentralized GIFT (Genetically Improved Farmed Tilapia) seed supply system is being established to increase access, improve growth performance, and support species diversification. Following the successful transfer of GIFT to Premium Aquaculture Limited (PAL) in Ogun State, a breeding population was established, demonstrating a 20% higher growth rate over 60 days compared to older strains. Best management practices (BMPs) were developed, and training programs expanded to farmers. Satellite hatcheries were set up in Delta State and expanded to two more states, increasing farmer access.; This innovative scaling model for Nigeria not only improves the availability of high-performance tilapia seed, but also creates opportunities for expanding other species value chains, fostering a more diversified and sustainable aquaculture industry in Nigeria and beyond.

column16: Amending the CGIAR Climate Information Services for Ghana using a downstream service for predicting fall armyworm and Striga infestation areas
column17: The digital advisory is an online and SMS service system that effectively delivers early warning and real time information on production stressors and advises small-scale farmers accordingly. Spatially explicit and multi-scale satellite data and climate and pests/weeds data are uniquely combined in a digital platform, and accurate advisory information is then channeled to end users. For instance, farmers could be advised to plant less cereal crops this season because of anticipated Fall Armyworm infestation for a specific location. Reliable information about abiotic/biotic production constraints will prove critical in managing sustainable cropland productivity. In due time, cropping systems information such as fields are under mono- or mixed-cropping or if fields are irrigated/rainfed will be added in order to improve pest and climate risk forecasting. The production constraints information over time can also be used to guide the scale out of climate and pest-smart agriculture, such conservation agriculture or the “push-pull” system.

column16: Using eDNA to transform aquatic food systems
column17: Environmental DNA (eDNA) technology is an emerging tool that enables non-invasive, cost-effective, and highly sensitive monitoring of aquatic biodiversity and ecosystem health. By detecting genetic material shed by organisms, eDNA allows researchers to assess species presence, track ecosystem changes, and monitor aquaculture sustainability without traditional sampling methods. Currently in development, this eDNA-based innovation is being piloted to support the sustainable management of fisheries and aquaculture, ensuring evidence-based decision-making. As it scales, eDNA technology will contribute to improving productivity, biodiversity conservation, and climate resilience, making aquatic food systems more efficient, sustainable, and resilient.

column16: Entrepreneurship Ecosystem model for sheep and goat value chain in pastoral systems
column17: The Small Ruminant Tools for Rapid Assessment of Pastoral Systems (STRAPS) initiative supports sustainable sheep and goat production in pastoral systems by integrating traditional knowledge, modern breeding techniques and sustainable practices. Developed by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), RECONCILE and the Baringo County Livestock Department, STRAPS provides four e-tools to assess three groups of actors in the value chain: pastoral communities, individual producers, service providers and market agents. Using the Open Data Kit platform, STRAPS generates actionable data to improve productivity, strengthen market links and address systemic challenges. By fostering an entrepreneurial ecosystem, the initiative enhances pastoralist livelihoods, boosts climate resilience and supports sustainable livestock systems in semi-arid regions.

column16: Group certificates of customary rights of occupancy for securing shared grazing lands in Tanzania
column17: In Tanzania policy and legislation provides for the provision of certificates of customary rights of occupancy (CCROs). However commonly these are issued on an individual basis and challenges arise when trying to secure tenure for a group that shares resources. The Livestock and Climate Initiative has been working with the Government of Tanzania to pilot the provision of group CCROs to livestock keeper associations. In 2022 the first CCROs were issued to four villages in a shared grazing land cluster called OLENGAPA securing around 85,000 hectares of grazing land. In late 2024 another group CCRO was issued to the Amei village livestock keepers association to secure 50,588 hectares of shared grazing land benefiting 15,407 livestock keepers predominantly pastoralists. Amei is part of the four village cluster of villages making up the ALOLLE shared grazing land.

column17: Community rangeland health workers (CRHWs) are an innovation approach to improving rangelands health in pastoral areas. Co-developed as part of One Health local level service delivery CRHWs are part of a local One Health team that works together, amplifying the One Health approach. column16: KAZNET: Using digital innovation and social learning to collect and disseminate near-real-time information on markets performance, rangelands conditions, and household food and nutrition security in the drylands
column17: The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) has been implementing an open-source digital crowdsourcing tool known as KAZNET (which stands for "Kazi kwa net" translated in Swahili to mean "working within a network") to alleviate data collection constraints and monitor resilience indicators in the drylands of Kenya and Ethiopia. KAZNET includes a dissemination component, where information gathered through the platform is processed in real time and channeled back to communities, development practitioners, and governments. The KAZNET app has a dashboard through which different types of information can be visualized. The graphic presentation of the information allows for the visualization of trends while also eliminating the need for more than basic literacy to understand the information presented. The disseminated information contains indicators of markets and rangelands performance. In addition, KAZNET disseminates information about the types of food consumed by households, livestock mortality, and the strategies used for coping with drought.

column16: Farming with Alternative Pollinators (FAP) is a proven ecological intensification approach that uses marketable habitat enhancement plants to increase pollinators, crop yield, and quality, in low- and middle-income countries.
column17: Farming with Alternative Pollinators (FAP) is a proven ecological intensification approach that integrates marketable habitat enhancement plants (MHEP) – such as oil seeds, spices, food crops and medicinal plants - within fields. These plants provide diverse floral traits (e.g., shape, colour, flower type) and nesting support to support a high diversity and abundance of pollinators and natural enemies (e.g., Hymenoptera, Hemiptera, Aranaea). Farmers using FAP report higher fruit yields, improved quality, and increased income compared to monoculture fields. Developed as a scalable alternative to (paid) wildflower strips, FAP offers an affordable solution for low- and middle-income countries.

column16: Microsite (Krishi kund) for restoration of degraded land for improved production and ecosystem services
column17: Microsite (Krishi Kund) offers a resource-efficient alternative for restoring degraded lands by concentrating natural amendments within specific areas for improving agricultural diversity, soil health, and overall ecosystem services. It also helps alleviate the pressure of intensive farming on other lands. Moreover, this practice holds promise for reversing migration among tribal communities.; This practice focuses on improving micro-sites rather than entire parcels of land using organic amendments. In this method, small cylindrical pits (did: 60cm, depth 60cm) are excavated at 1.2m intervals, filled with locally available organic materials. This approach improves approximately 20% (6450 pits per hectare) of the land area, resulting in a similar yield of fully restored land.; Drought tolerant crops viz pigeon pea, caster for the poor water availability sites and other cash crops including vegetables at sites of water availability are being grown. A two-year recovery period was estimated for the cost incurred on land restoration.

column16: On-farm Genomic Selection (GS) approach using a sparse testing design for rainfed upland rice breeding pipeline in Africa
column17: On-farm Genomic Selection (GS) using a Sparse Testing design has been implemented  in rainfed upland rice breeding pipeline covering six countries in Africa. A total of 898 (896 tests and 2 checks) upland breeding lines evaluated in six diverse target population environments (TPE) in Côte d’Ivoire, Mali, Nigeria, DRC, Guinea Conakry, and Sierra Leone using a P-Rep design. Thirty percent of the test lines (282 genotypes) were tested twice and distributed across farms and remaining 616 test lines were identically distributed into six countries . Two checks: 1 regional check (NERICA 4) and 1 local check were used, and each check was replicated twice within a country. The trial is being conducted using a modified  tricot design. column16: Enhanced predictive accuracy and efficiency in genomic-assisted sweetpotato breeding using deregressed best linear unbiased prediction (BLUPs) from the animal model and optimized training populations
column17: This study addresses key challenges in integrating genomic-enabled prediction into sweetpotato breeding, particularly genotype-by-environment interactions and constructing effective training sets. Two hypotheses were tested : (i) using deregressed ABLUPs (dABLUPs-best linear unbiased prediction from the animal model) in two-stage modeling improves predictive accuracy in observational trials, and (ii) optimizing training sets can reduce experimental effort while maintaining accuracy. Evaluating 1185 genotypes across six trials in Uganda and comparing four modeling approaches, dABLUPs consistently provided the best predictions, improving predictive ability by up to 37% over other methods. Optimized training sets further enhanced performance, demonstrating the potential for more efficient genomic prediction in sweetpotato breeding.

column16: Cassava practical haplotype graph, a pan-genomic resource capturing complete DNA sequence variation across cultivated cassava, enabling breeders to utilize genetic variation causal to important crop traits for agricultural improvement.
column17: Cassava previously lacked genomic resources representing both copies of its heterozygous diploid genome and species-wide diversity. This limited variant discovery and accurate prediction of missing sequence (imputation) in breeders sequence data. Previous sequence data also had high error rates hampering detection of variants linked or causal to agronomic and end-use traits. ; ; The cassava practical haplotype graph was created using newly generated highly accurate sequence data for 52 taxa, yielding 104 assemblies representing both genome copies and phased along chromosomes. Taxa represent elite breeding parents, disease resistant materials, and diverse landraces from Latin America and Africa.; ; The practical haplotype graph provides the assemblies, alignments, and variant calls in a compact, shareable format and provides tools to impute and call variants from inexpensive sequence data. The resource is already being applied to new DNA language models to identify variants for improved yield and disease resistance and to further improve imputation accuracy.;

column16: Multi-stakeholder seed delivery network developed by IRRI and India's National Seed Research Centre accelerates rice variety adoption
column17: Rice farmers in India often lack timely access to improved varieties that could boost productivity and climate resilience. To address this challenge, the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) partnered with India's National Seed Research and Training Centre to establish a comprehensive seed delivery network. This network brings together five state seed corporations, 15 private seed agencies, and 10 community-led seed organizations to strengthen seed multiplication and enable faster distribution of new rice varieties. The collaboration was formalized through the Seed Accelerator Meet 2025, where public, private, and community seed sector participants co-developed an action plan for seed system improvement. The network integrates national agricultural research varieties with publicly bred varieties, creating a unified platform that accelerates varietal turnover and ensures farmers can access climate-resilient, high-yielding rice varieties more quickly.

column16: Rapid cycle augmentation scheme for trait development and deployment in rice
column17: To facilitate further and more efficient diversification of elite backgrounds, a new strategy for augmentation has been developed.  This turns the linear process of upgrading a particular line with up to 3 new genes into a cyclical recurrent selection process, intercrossing amongst elite progeny to accumulate target genes.  The benefits of this scheme are decoupling the number of input and output lines, and a greatly increased capacity to select for a much larger number of genes with modest/tractable population sizes.  Initial founding lines and crosses are underway to establish this pipeline, initially for the medium maturity program and from there to direct-seeded material as resources permit. The scheme prioritized traits for disease resistance, abiotic stress resistance (e.g. drought) and improving grain quality. These traits aimed to produced breeding lines that would help combat impacts of climate change and increasing consumption of healthier rice without penalizing yield.;

These efforts aim to enhance smallholder farmers’ water and food security while building resilience to climate shocks. ; It has not only improved their farming techniques but also significantly enhanced their livelihoods by empowering them with CSA technologies; strengthening their resilience through access to important weather information; and linked them to aquaculture markets to sustainably improve income. ; Over 15,700 farmers have adopted sustainable farming practices, gained access to millions of fingerlings, and secured fish output markets offering premium prices for farmed fish. The team has introduced practical solutions to mitigate the impacts of climate change, such as integrated farming systems. Furthermore, farmers have adopted the design of modern fishponds capable of withstanding flooding and drought, significantly reducing fish losses during climate shocks(AIICRAContributed).

column17: The Metrics Library is an online database that provides a comprehensive collection of metrics for evaluating the performance of food and agricultural systems. This user-friendly platform will act as a one-stop shop for users to explore, search, and select the most appropriate metrics and tools for their specific needs. The library is aimed at a wide range of users interested in agrifood systems assessment, from policymakers and donors to development actors and producers. While originally developed under the IFAD-EC TRANSITIONS Metrics Project, in 2025 the Metrics Project and the CGIAR Multifunctional Landscapes Program teamed up to co-develop the next phase of the Library. This collaboration will help the library grow further and continue as a living product for the benefit of all.

column16: Digital Twin of the Dolo Ado district in Somali Region of Ethiopia
column17: The Digital Twin (DT) for Dolo Ado district is designed to revolutionize flood preparedness and response by providing timely, accurate early warnings to all stakeholders. Traditional warning systems often fail due to data scarcity, but the DT overcomes this by integrating diverse data sources—real-time ground monitoring (rainfall, river flow, water depth), high-resolution elevation data, and catchment-wide flood forecasting models. This virtual replica enables dynamic, real-time flood risk modeling across the region. The DT acts as a convening tool, fostering collaboration among government agencies, humanitarian organizations, local authorities, and community leaders for coordinated flood analysis and resource allocation. It empowers agencies to plan anticipatory actions, enabling targeted interventions and rapid response to minimize damage. Additionally, the DT supports sustainable land use planning by analyzing flood risk patterns, guiding decisions on floodplain development, urban planning, and infrastructure design to enhance resilience and reduce future disaster risks.

column16: AgriLLM: An open-source large language model grounded in CGIAR knowledge to deliver accurate and contextualized responses to farmers and extension services.
column17: AgriLLM is an artificial intelligence model based on large language model technology that provides accurate, context-specific agricultural advice to smallholder farmers, extension agents, policymakers, and researchers. Developed through a global collaboration of over 15 organizations led by CGIAR, this open-source innovation addresses the need for accessible, reliable agricultural information in diverse farming contexts. The model was trained using CGIAR's extensive agricultural knowledge base and over 7,400 human-generated question-and-answer pairs created by CGIAR staff. By making advanced AI technology openly available, AgriLLM enables agricultural advisory services worldwide to deliver more relevant and engaging support to farming communities, particularly in regions where access to expert agricultural guidance is limited.

column16: Excel file configured as an Open Data Kit (OKD)-compliant form aligned with Terminag variables, facilitating the design of standards-compliant data collection forms
column17: Most field data collection is carried out using tools built on ODK (Open Data Kit). It is therefore essential to simplify the design of ODK forms and ensure compliance with standards that enable data reuse.; ; This Excel-based ODK form template is fully ODK-compliant and directly mapped to TerminAg variables. TerminAg is a controlled vocabulary developed by the Carob project and used to standardize CGIAR legacy datasets.; ; The template allows you to design data-collection forms that automatically follow ODK syntax while enforcing TerminAg variable names. For multiple-choice questions, the tool suggests standardized answer options whose labels and names also come from TerminAg.; ; The data collection forms designed with this tool are standards-compliant, interoperable forms ensuring reusability of final datasets.
