column16: Nutrient-rich feed pellets from composted organic waste developed by IWMI and WorldFish for small-scale fish and poultry farmers in Africa
column17: Small-scale fish and poultry farmers in Africa struggle with expensive imported feed ingredients like maize and fishmeal. IWMI and WorldFish developed an innovative solution that transforms human manure and organic waste into safe, nutrient-rich feed pellets through controlled composting. The process heats materials for weeks to eliminate harmful organisms, then dries and forms them into pellets suitable for storage and transport. Laboratory testing confirms the pellets provide valuable protein, carbohydrates, and essential minerals while maintaining safety standards. The pellets serve as partial feed replacement for common fish species like carp, catfish, and tilapia, as well as poultry. This innovation reduces feed costs, decreases import dependence, and recycles urban nutrients that would otherwise be wasted, addressing multiple challenges facing African farmers.

column16: Modular prefabricated water storage tank for easy transport and quick assembly in remote areas
column17: Water scarcity in hilly and remote regions persists despite moderate rainfall because of inadequate decentralized storage. The conventional masonry tanks are costly, slow to build, and unsuitable for rugged terrains. To address this, IWMI and ICAR under the CGIAR Multifunctional Landscapes Program developed a modular prefabricated water storage tank—a low-cost, flat-pack system that can be assembled within 20 minutes without tools or skilled labor. Made of galvanized-iron panels and a reinforced liner, the tank (≈11 kL) is portable, durable, and reusable, enabling rooftop rainwater harvesting, small-stream diversion, or solar-pump filling. Field demonstrations in Mandla, Madhya Pradesh, showed significant improvements in household water security, year-round vegetable production, and women’s time savings.  The tanks also support agroecological homesteads, nurseries, and small-scale aquaculture. Affordable and scalable, the innovation aligns with CGIAR and IWMI priorities on climate-resilient water solutions, offering a replicable model for decentralized water storage and management across the Global South.

column16: Designing carbonisation solutions for sustainable livelihoods
column17: Rural energy poverty persists across landscapes despite the abundance of underused agricultural and organic residues such as maize stalks, rice husks, coconut shells, sugarcane bagasse, cow dung, and invasive plant species. This innovation harnesses these locally available resources through low-emission carbonization technologies, specifically slow pyrolysis and torrefaction to produce briquettes and biochar for clean cooking and household energy use. The innovation designs and develops a context-appropriate, low-cost carbonization system that can be safely operated and scaled across rural and peri-urban communities. By improving process control and product consistency, the system reduces health and environmental risks commonly associated with informal charcoal production. The carbonization unit is guided by three core principles: affordability, adaptability, and operational simplicity. Its design has been shaped through direct engagement with end users, including small-scale producers, women-led cooperatives, and youth entrepreneurs, ensuring relevance to local needs and capacities.

column16: Digital tool developed by IRRI to predict crop yield changes from climate and environmental risks globally
column17: Climate change and environmental degradation pose increasing threats to global crop production, making it difficult for researchers and policymakers to predict future agricultural outcomes and plan investments. Traditional crop modeling approaches often have incomplete geographic coverage, lack modules for key stressors like soil salinity, and require extensive computing resources. To address these limitations, the International Rice Research Institute developed a Crop Production Risk Index that combines climate and environmental data with expert knowledge to generate scalable risk scores and yield-change projections. This digital tool uses artificial intelligence to quantify expected future yield changes across different regions, providing evidence to support priority setting and investment decisions for climate adaptation in agriculture.

column16: End-to-end approach for increasing fruit and vegetable consumption to improve diets, nutrition, and health outcomes; whilst improving livelihoods, empowering women and youth and mitigating negative environmental impacts in Sri Lanka
column17: The end-to-end approach describes a combination of interventions at various points of the food system, namely supply interventions, demand creation interventions, and food environment interventions. Through a participatory process of co-development, which started during FRESH in the previous CGIAR portfolio (2022-2024), CGIAR researchers and local partners conducted extensive research that informed the development of this innovation. Now continuing under Better Diets and Nutrition, a longitudinal evaluation will assess the impact of the end-to-end approach on household vegetable production and fruit and vegetable (F&V) intake among women of reproductive age in Sri Lanka. By the end of 2025, the evaluation was designed including the selection of study sites and target population. Implementation will begin in 2026. In 2025, the supply interventions continued to be implemented and recent progress and results can be found in this year's report. In Sri Lanka, the package  of supply-side activities aims to enhance agricultural production practices to support safe, sustainable, and diverse vegetable cultivation throughout the year. column16: Good Agronomic Practices (GAP) package for smallholder vegetable farmers in Sri Lanka
column17: The good agronomic practices (GAP) package in Sri Lanka is tailored to two farming systems: 1) Continuous vegetable farming system, where vegetable cultivation is established, and 2) Staple farming system, where rice is predominant. In both instances the GAP package includes integrated management of water, nutrients, fertilizers, pests, and diseases to improve resource-use efficiency and ensure food safety and supporting the integration or diversification of vegetables through intercropping, relay cropping, and crop rotation to boost year-round availability. The GAP package was developed by the International Water Management Institute, the World Vegetable Center, and partners as part of their work in Better Diets and Nutrition. In 2025, through a collaborative process with local partners, the team established four demonstration plots in Welimada and Balangoda Divisional Secretariats (DS) from Badulla District and Ratnapura District, respectively. These plots, located in separate Grama Niladharis (GNs – the smallest administrative unit in Sri Lanka) are managed jointly with local farmers. Serving as production hubs, these sites are piloting technologies for integrated pest management, improved irrigation, conservation agriculture, soil fertility enhancement, and post-harvest handling. At each hub, groups of farmers were trained in these technologies and will serve as peer trainers for other farmers in each cropping season.  Farmer field days were organized to disseminate knowledge on GAP, strengthen market linkages by connecting farmers with vendors, and engaging private sector stakeholders such as seed companies, traders, and processors. Four technical guides for vegetable farmers and extension workers on good practices for tomato, bean, cabbage and carrot cultivation were also published. The GAP packages are part of Better Diets and Nutrition’s end-to-end approach, an innovation which combines demand, food environment, and supply interventions to increase desirability, affordability, accessibility, and availability of vegetables and sustainable healthy diets more broadly.

column16: Development and release of locally adapted, improved varieties of African eggplant in Tanzania
column17: Vegetable adaptation trials are crucial for evaluating different varieties under specific growing conditions, aiding farmers in identifying the most suitable options for their region. In 2025, three top-performing African eggplant varieties were released (TARINGOWE1 through TARINGOWE3), contributing to the enhancement of crop productivity and quality in the region. Better Diets and Nutrition’s work on improved varieties is part of the end-to-end approach, an innovation which combines demand, food environment, and supply interventions to increase desirability, affordability, accessibility, and availability of fruit and vegetables and sustainable healthy diets more broadly. The supply interventions are designed to address known barriers faced by vegetable farmers. In this case, the provision of climate-resilient vegetable cultivars tackles the lack of quality inputs.

column16: Political pledge as part of Nutrition for Growth Summit that CGIAR will scale 25 high-impact evidence-based food system strategies for nutrition into various sectors and programs globally by 2030
column17: Nutrition for Growth (N4G) commitments are global pledges by governments, organizations, and businesses to fight malnutrition in all its forms through increased funding, policy changes, and scalable programs, focusing on areas like health, climate-smart food systems, gender, and crisis resilience, aiming for universal healthy diets and better development outcomes. These commitments, tracked by the Global Nutrition Report, aim to ensure continuous action and leverage innovative financing for impactful nutrition interventions. For the 2025 Nutrition for Growth Summit in Paris, CGIAR made a bold commitment, which was drafted by members of the Better Diets and Nutrition team on behalf of the CGIAR System Organization, to identify and release 25 evidence-based food system solutions – technologies, products, practices, processes, programs, and policies or a combination of these by 2030. The new Better Diets and Nutrition program itself was a core part of the commitment, focusing on systems-level solutions beyond food supply. The Nutrition Accountability Framework (NAF) is the world’s independent and comprehensive platform for registering and monitoring SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound) commitments to take action on nutrition, and serves as the official tracker for the Nutrition for Growth (N4G) commitments from 2021 and 2025. CGIAR's registration of a commitment in the NAF is an example of high-level, high-profile political innovation.

column16: Guidance for estimating the impact of interventions on dietary outcomes measured by 24-hour dietary recalls
column17: The National Cancer Institute (NCI) method for 24-hour dietary recalls (24HR) is a statistical approach to estimate a population's usual dietary intake from a few, potentially single, 24-hour recalls, overcoming the limitation of needing many recalls for accuracy. Developed by the NCI, it uses modeling to account for within-person variation (daily fluctuations) and between-person variation (individual differences) to estimate typical consumption patterns, helping research diet-health links without costly, repeated recalls for everyone. Key aspects include using multiple passes during the interview and software to improve data quality. Researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition are working with academic partners to develop guidance on how to use the NCI method to estimate the impact of interventions on dietary outcomes, adapting the original purpose of the method to be used by researchers, development partners, and funders in the evaluation of programs.

column16: Subnational Cost of a Healthy Diet dashboard, an online data source for both county governments and national agencies in Kenya to inform the design policies and programs for healthy diets
column17: The Cost of a Healthy Diet (CoHD) indicator measures the lowest-cost combination of locally available foods needed to meet daily dietary requirements, as defined by national food-based dietary guidelines. Using observed retail food prices from  the Kenya Agricultural Market Information System, the indicator provides a practical measure of both physical and economic access to nutritious foods. In the Kenyan context, this information supports county governments and national agencies to design policies, monitor food affordability, and guide interventions that strengthen food and nutrition security. The CoHD indicator also aligns with Sustainable Development Goal 2 and contributes to tracking progress toward nutrition-sensitive agriculture and food systems transformation. The CoHD framework is produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations in collaboration with the World Bank’s Food Prices for Nutrition project.

column16: Advanced water use mapping delivering irrigation insights for Southern Africa.
column17: The application is an online mapping tool that shows how much water crops are using at the level of individual fields. It takes widely available satellite water-use information, which is normally shown in very large blocks, and turns it into clear, detailed maps that better match real farming patterns on the ground.; This makes it easier to see differences between irrigated and non-irrigated fields, to track how water use changes from month to month, and to identify areas where water demand is high. The application is designed to support practical decision-making, such as planning water allocation, monitoring irrigation performance, and responding to dry periods, especially in regions where farms are small and landscapes are complex.

column16: Experiential Learning Games for Participatory Water Governance to Support Shared Water Management
column17: Experiential learning games for water governance - Facilitated and participatory experiential learning games played by water users and stakeholders (e.g., farmers, village water-users) to experience the dynamics of shared water resources (surface or groundwater) and governance dilemmas around them. The games simulate the management of shared water resources such as groundwater or irrigation systems. They aim to foster understanding, cooperation, and collective decision-making for sustainable water governance  through experiential learning or learning by doing. During the game, participants make decisions in repeated rounds  around crop choice or water extraction levels. The group’s combined actions influence a shared water table or resource level. A critical component is the facilitated community debriefing discussion part after the game, where the community reflects on what happened in the game, relates it to their real-life water situation, and discusses or develops rules or collective strategies to address challenges. The games are part of a package of tools to help trigger awareness, motivation, changed mental models and relational learning (trust, cooperation) which can lead to institutional or behavioral change.

column16: Framework for analyzing and rewarding the social benefits of small-scale farming
column17: Small-scale farmers are often encouraged to adopt innovations that generate significant social benefits, including improved nutrition, food safety, and environmental sustainability, yet market mechanisms frequently fail to reward these contributions. Adoption of such socially desirable practices remains below the social optimum due to unobservable attributes, high verification costs, limited production scale, and misaligned private incentives. The researchers propose a simple framework that highlights four key dimensions influencing adoption: returns to farmers (R), adoption costs (C), inspection costs (I), and transaction scale (Q). Interventions can target these dimensions individually or in combination, such as reducing verification costs, aggregating production, subsidizing adoption, or enhancing market premiums. The researchers illustrate this framework through three case studies: aflatoxin mitigation, biofortified crop adoption, and conservation agriculture, demonstrating how technology, policy, and market-based instruments can be coordinated to incentivize the adoption of socially beneficial innovations and practices. Their analysis emphasizes the importance of multidisciplinary approaches, integrated public and private actions, and dynamic interventions that account for both immediate and long-term social returns. By explicitly connecting adoption incentives with verification and market constraints, the framework guides research and policy toward more effective strategies to reward smallholders for their contributions to public goods and sustainable development.

column16: Utilizing Theater of the Oppressed method to challenge restrictive gender norms and promote inclusive governance in rural Morocco
column17: This approach uses participatory theatre to create safe, open spaces where community members can reflect on everyday situations that limit women’s rights and participation in decision-making. Local actors and community members perform short scenes based on real-life experiences, such as disputes over land inheritance, women’s mobility, or control over income. After each scene, audience members are invited to step into the story, suggest alternatives, and act out different ways the situation could unfold. By encouraging dialogue rather than lecturing, the method helps people recognize how social norms shape behavior and power relations. Women and men are able to express their views, listen to each other, and collectively explore fairer and more inclusive ways of resolving conflicts. In rural Morocco, this approach has proven especially effective in addressing sensitive topics, such as inheritance, violence and income control, building confidence among women to speak out, and fostering greater understanding of shared responsibility in community governance and family decision-making.

column16: Improved classification of conflict and violence to strengthen evidence-based humanitarian and development responses
column17: This innovation improves how conflict and violence are classified in research and policy analysis, enabling clearer distinctions between different forms of insecurity that affect people’s livelihoods, wellbeing, and development outcomes. Traditional approaches often treat conflict as a single category, making it difficult for researchers and decision-makers to understand how different types of violence shape economic behavior, social outcomes, and the effectiveness of humanitarian and development responses.; ; Led by CGIAR researchers at the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), the innovation develops and applies an improved framework for categorizing conflict and violence using existing data sources in new ways. By distinguishing between forms of violence—such as organized conflict, localized armed violence, and criminal or interpersonal violence—the approach allows users to generate more precise evidence on how insecurity affects households, communities, and markets, particularly in fragile and conflict-affected settings.; ; The innovation supports researchers, policy analysts, and development partners by providing clearer, more policy-relevant evidence that can inform the design, targeting, and evaluation of humanitarian assistance, recovery programs, and longer-term development interventions. It also strengthens the comparability of results across studies and contexts, helping users better assess where and how different responses are likely to be effective.; ; This work builds on CGIAR’s long-standing research on fragility, conflict, and livelihoods and contributes to global efforts to improve the evidence base used by governments, donors, and international organizations working in crisis-affected contexts. By improving how conflict and violence are classified and analyzed, the innovation enhances the usefulness of research for decision-making and supports more informed, context-sensitive responses that aim to stabilize livelihoods and promote recovery in settings affected by conflict and crisis.

column16: Intensification of wheat-based cropping systems in the Jizzakh region of Uzbekistan using an integrated bundle of wheat-mungbean rotation cropping and Good Agricultural Practices to close yield gaps.
column17: An integrated bundle of solutions was developed to intensify wheat cropping systems and close the yield gap in the Jizzakh region of Uzbekistan. The bundle is comprised of establishing a wheat-mungbean rotation cropping system by planting mungbean in the fallow period (Jun-Oct) after harvesting the wheat crop (Oct-Jun) using an improved mungbean variety ('Durdona'), and a series of Good Agricultural Practices that includes using an optimized seed rate of ~16 kg/ha (versus higher rates such as ~25 kg/ha under existing farmer practices), improved crop establishment (e.g., bed planting with defined row/plant spacing), and targeted crop nutrition/biostimulant support through BioVak Y24 seed treatment (a commercial product in Uzbekistan) and/or suspension applications often combined with low-dose urea, alongside timely crop care and pest management where needed.

column16: Salinity forecast and irrigation advisories dissemination in polders of Coastal Bangladesh
column17: At the core of this intervention is an innovative AI-driven salinity modeling system designed to predict salinity levels in rivers and thereby provide salinity forecasts for irrigation advisory services. Piloted across two coastal polders, this system leverages machine learning models, open-access datasets, and localized data collection to deliver short-term salinity forecasts. By providing timely and accurate salinity predictions, the system enables farmers and water management groups to make informed decisions about irrigation scheduling and sluice gate operations.

column16: MDII:  Online Assessment Platform (Multi-Panel Minimum Viable Product) -A web-based platform for conducting MDII assessments, featuring administrator coordination, expert evaluation panels, AI-assisted translation, automated notifications, and PDF reporting.
column17: The MDII (Multi dimensional Inclusiveness Index) Online Assessment Platform is a web-based tool designed to facilitate inclusive evaluation of digital innovations in food, land, and water systems. It features multiple panels, including a coordinator and administrator panel, expert evaluation panel, and AI-assisted translation panel, along with automated notifications and PDF reporting. This platform enables structured, participatory assessments of digital initiatives, allowing diverse stakeholders to score and review innovations according to the Multidimensional Digital Inclusiveness Index. By centralizing evaluation, improving accessibility, and automating reporting, the platform supports evidence-based decision-making and strengthens inclusive, socially responsible digital innovation processes.

column16: Integrated Monitoring for Informed Decision-Making in Large Irrigation Systems
column17: The National Irrigation Policy of 2023 emphasizes the importance of volumetric water allocation for enhancing agricultural productivity in Nepal. A key part of this is enhancing the availability and use of flow data from canals to fields. Currently, Nepal lacks a consistent system for monitoring and managing irrigation water, resulting in inefficiencies and inequities in water distribution. Many systems suffer from poor infrastructure and ad hoc management, leading to serious head–tail disparities, where tail-end farmers receive little or no water, particularly in dry periods. The absence of regular flow and soil moisture data makes it difficult for both irrigation managers and farmers to make informed decisions about water allocation and irrigation scheduling. To support the policy’s goals, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), in partnership with the Department of Water Resources and Irrigation (DWRI), initiated a pilot intervention in the Babai Irrigation Project in western Nepal. The project involves the installation of basic instruments that monitor real-time water flow, soil moisture, and weather conditions. These tools help irrigation managers to distribute water more efficiently. This approach is expected to reduce water-use conflicts, promote equity, and strengthen the role of Water User Associations in managing irrigation fairly and effectively.

column16: Hydro-economic Decision Support System developed to optimize Pakistan's water resource allocation based on Computable General Equilibrium for Water (CGE-W) Model
column17: The Hydro-Economic Decision Support System, based on the Computable General Equilibrium for Water (CGE-W) Model, is a sophisticated analytical framework developed by International Food Policy Research Institute and adapted by the International Water Management Institute (IWMI). It is designed to evaluate the economic impacts of water policies, management strategies, and climatic or hydrological changes across different sectors and regions of Pakistan. The CGE-W model integrates hydrological component and Social Accounting Matrix (SAM) within a unified analytical platform, allowing policymakers and researchers to simulate how variations in water availability, land allocation, and pricing influence the broader economy. Through scenario-based analysis, the model helps decision-makers to:; ; Assess trade-offs between competing water uses under different management or policy options.; Optimize resource allocation to achieve sustainable and equitable water distribution.; Quantify economic losses or gains resulting from climate change, or policy interventions.; Support evidence-based planning for long-term water security and resilience under climate change.; By linking water resource dynamics with macroeconomic variables, the CGE-W model provides a powerful decision-support tool that enhances understanding of the nexus between water, economy, and sustainability, enabling governments and development partners to design integrated and adaptive water policies that balance economic growth with environmental stewardship.

column16: A Pywr Water Resources Model: A Digital Decision-Support Tool for Integrated Water–Food–Energy Analysis in the Indus River Basin
column17: The world faces a deepening water crisis, making effective management critical. Digital tools are essential for handling complex water allocation in major shared river basins like the Indus River Basin. This basin supports over 238 million people and is a critical nexus of water, food, and energy security. It hosts the world's largest irrigation network, a colossal system that demands a sophisticated, data-driven approach.; Pywr water resources model, an open-source, Python-based tool. Its node-and-link architecture provides a detailed representation of the entire river system, from reservoirs to demand centers. Crucially, Pywr facilitates the analysis of trade-offs within the Water-Food-Energy connection, allowing for a more holistic and integrated approach to competing needs of agriculture and hydropower.; The development of the Indus Pywr model was a collaborative landmark achievement between the International Water Management Institute and the University of Manchester. It was designed through extensive engagement with national and provincial government agencies, including those managing river systems and power generation.; The model is built on a 30-year foundation of historical data (1991–2020) and incorporates all major structures of the irrigation system. It accurately simulates dam operations and integrates key nodes for hydropower generation at major dams. This capability is vital for assessing the energy implications of different water management strategies.; The initiative also established a Community of Practice (CoP), bringing together over 40 technical experts from federal and provincial departments. This collaborative, data-driven approach fosters confidence and consensus, empowering stakeholders to analyze scenarios and make informed policy decisions. The Indus Pywr model is more than a tool, it's a foundational element for a more resilient and sustainable future for the Indus Basin's resources

column16: A modern variation of eish baladi (al khobz al balady), Egypt's traditional, heavily subsidized flatbread, made by blending wheat flour with barley flour in ratios ranging from 90:10 to 70:30
column17: Eish baladi (al khobz al baladi) is a traditional Egyptian flatbread made with whole-wheat flour (87.5% extraction). It is a vital component of the national diet and a daily staple in Egyptian households, where a single piece can provide approximately 70% of an individual’s recommended daily carbohydrate and protein intake, 52% of their caloric needs, and essential micronutrients such as iron and zinc. Eish baladi is Egypt’s most heavily subsidized food, with EGP 22 billion allocated in 2022/2023, accounting for over 60% of food subsidies and benefiting more than 70 million people. To meet this demand for eish baladi, in 2022, Egypt produced 9.8 million tons of wheat and imported 11.8 million tons at a cost of USD 2.99 billion. This innovation is a modern variation of eish baladi that adds domestically produced barley flour alongside wheat flour, in experimental ratios ranging from 10:90 to 30:70, to produce a high-quality, nutritionally rich, consumer-accepted eish baladi product, along with a multitude of additional benefits and incentives such as creating a market for improved barley varieties which can be cultivated on marginal lands without displacing other crops. By increasing the share of domestically produced ingredients used in eish baladi, this approach reduces reliance on imported wheat, eases pressure on Egypt’s payments balance, and helps conserve foreign currency reserves, thereby contributing to greater food security and resilience to global markets shocks.

column16: Five new forage cultivars registered in Vietnam
column17: Registration of new forage cultivars matters because commercialization of seed and planting material requires an approved national variety list and reliable performance data. Registration triggers multi-location testing, so farmers and companies know which forages suit humid lowlands, upland hills, and seasonally dry zones. It also strengthens quarantine and traceability where many forages are introduced or imported, reducing risks of weeds, pests, and diseases. Once registered, cultivars can enter certified seed multiplication, receive extension support, and be included in dairy and beef development programs. This improves year-round fodder supply, lowers feed costs, and boosts animal productivity sustainably for smallholders.

column16: National Workshop in Dhaka on Salinity management for sustainable agriculture in Coastal Bangladesh
column17: Increasing river water salinity trends have been a growing concern in coastal Bangladesh in the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna Delta, with implications for agriculture, livelihoods, and drinking water availability. Shifts in precipitation and sea-level rise, and changes in upstream flow and siltation, together affect river salinity trends with implications for water and food security in the deltaic system.  Salinity trends in coastal Bangladesh vary from west to east, and several governmental and non-governmental research and development initiatives have been undertaken to assess and test solutions for salinity issues across the region. under the CGIAR Program on Scaling for Impact (building on the foundations laid by the Asian Mega Deltas (AMD) research initiative), the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) jointly with International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) and the Institute of Water Modelling (IWM), have been working to develop an innovative Artifical intelligence/Machine learning (AI/Ml)-driven salinity forecasting system designed to predict river salinity levels around polders and provide advisories to farmers regarding scheduling of sluice gates operations to support freshwater into the polders thereby reducing the risk of higher salinity within the polders.

column16: Digital toolkit developed by CGIAR to detect climate change disinformation in social media conversations
column17: Climate disinformation on social media platforms undermines public understanding and action on environmental issues. CGIAR's Climate Action initiative developed an integrated digital toolkit to identify and analyze false climate information, focusing on Amazon biome discussions in Telegram conversations. The toolkit includes TeleCatch for automated data collection, Telegram Analytics for message processing, and BERTopic for content analysis. These tools enable researchers and organizations to systematically detect misinformation patterns and understand how false climate narratives spread online. The innovation also features a Topic Explorer dashboard for visualizing results and comprehensive documentation through the Open Science Framework. This toolkit provides essential capabilities for combating climate disinformation globally.

column16: AClimate digital platform deployed by Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT to provide climate-informed agricultural decision support in Honduras
column17: Aclimate is a modular, data-driven climate information and decision-support platform that integrates historical climate data, real-time monitoring, seasonal forecasts, and crop-modelling components to assess climate risks and potential impacts on agricultural production. By combining geospatial analytics and crop modelling, Aclimate translates agro-climate data into actionable insights for governments, financial institutions, and development partners, supporting early warning, value-chain–specific risk analysis, and climate-informed planning and investment decisions. The platform is implemented and operational in Colombia, Guatemala, Honduras, Peru, Angola, Ethiopia, and Zambia, with adaptations tailored to national climate services, priority crops, and institutional needs.

column16: Methodology for examining the barriers to and opportunities for upgrading the groundnut value chain in Tanzania
column17: In Tanzania, groundnuts are consumed as snacks or processed into flour, often blended with maize flour for child feeding. Nutrient-dense and affordable, peanuts provide protein (capable of meeting up to 46% of the recommended daily allowance), healthy fats, and essential micronutrients such as potassium, sodium, calcium, manganese, iron, and zinc, making them vital for diets across all income levels. For low-income households, they offer a cost-effective way to improve nutrition, particularly for young children. The rise of micro-enterprises producing peanut butter is especially notable, providing employment and expanding market access for small-scale actors, a majority of whom are women. Groundnut value chains are expanding rapidly in Tanzania, driven in part by rising urban demand and the growth of peanut butter processing. However, supply chains remain fragmented and informal, with limited incentives or mechanisms to ensure quality and food safety, restricting the sector’s potential to improve nutrition, livelihoods, and public health. In 2025, researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition applied a qualitative methodology in two key locations, Dar es Salaam, a major hub for peanut butter processing driven by strong urban demand, and Dodoma, one of the country’s main groundnut-producing regions, to identify constraints to and opportunities for innovation. Five potential market failures were identified: (1) weak quality verification systems, (2) a lack of incentives for upstream quality investment, (3) coordination failures, (4) food safety externalities (e.g., lower-quality nuts with higher contamination risk entering other markets), and (5) incomplete markets for improved seeds. The results from the exercise informed a research agenda to test institutional and technological innovations to address market failures and strengthen quality incentives.

column16: Bundled intervention of training, equipment, monitoring, and incentives designed to improve hygiene and food safety in small- and medium-scale pork slaughterhouses
column17: Pork is major source of protein in diets in Kenya and in Viet Nam. Like all animal source foods, pork is susceptible to bacterial contamination throughout the production process. In both contexts, a significant number of live pigs are typically processed in small- and medium-scale slaughterhouses, which handle fewer than 30 pigs daily. Poor hygiene in slaughterhouses can create food safety risks. This innovation is a combined intervention of Training, Equipment, Monitoring (TEM) and incentives. Meat handlers are provided training on hygiene. In Kenya, they are provided with personal protection equipment, handwashing facilities, and cleaning equipment and in Viet Nam, a stainless-steel grid and posters. Meat inspectors are monitored for how well they monitor compliance with recommendations over a 2-12 week period. Each worker is given an economic incentive to apply the training and use the equipment. Researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition and Sustainable Animal and Aquatic Foods have been testing the innovation with local partners through randomized controlled trials to assess its impact on food safety (the presence of Salmonella in pork sold at traditional markets) among other outcomes.

column16: Interactive dashboard analyzes multilingual Amazon Biome discussions on Telegram for climate action research in Latin America
column17: This digital tool examines how Amazon Biome topics are discussed across public Telegram channels in English, Portuguese, and Spanish. Developed by the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT as part of climate action research, the dashboard uses advanced topic modeling to analyze message patterns and debate framing about the Amazon region. The tool addresses the need to understand public discourse around this critical ecosystem by processing data collected through TeleCatch and analyzed with BERTopic technology. Currently in exploratory phase, it provides separate analysis tabs for each language and serves researchers studying climate communication patterns. Future development will include refined comparative models across languages to better understand how Amazon-related climate discussions vary by linguistic communities.

column16: Adaptive and data-driven irrigation advisory services for managing salinity in polders towards resilient agriculture in Bangladesh
column17: Existing hydrological forecasts in the region primarily focus on climate extremes, floods and droughts, with limited operational tools for river salinity forecasting. To address this gap, an AI-based river salinity advisory system has been developed and piloted in two polders in the Khulna region. The system forecasts temporal windows during which river salinity remains within acceptable thresholds for agricultural water use, particularly at the start and end of the monsoon seasons.

column16: Sustainable rangeland management toolkit with a holistic and multidisciplinary approach for addressing the biophysical and sociocultural aspects under changing climate and land use leading towards more resilient pastoral systems
column17: The sustainable rangeland management (SRM) toolkit advocates for a holistic and participatory multi-stakeholder approach that emphasizes the important role played by governance of rangelands using bottom-up landscape restoration. It emphasizes the need to ensure that decisions are based on both indigenous knowledge and modern science to address site-specific challenges. The goal of the toolkit is to assist and prepare practitioners working closely with local communities perform proper diagnostic, plan, and implement specific interventions and continuously monitor and evaluate rehabilitation or restoration efforts. Users have access to a collection of validated SRM practices aimed at achieving a neutral level of degradation (LDN) and offering a strong potential to rehabilitate and restore degraded rangeland ecosystems. The case studies demonstrate step by step how the toolkit is used to identify practical solutions that are integrated and socially accepted leading towards more resilient livestock and pastoral systems.

column16: Crop Observatories: An open data platform for various stakeholders in the crop value chain
column17: The Crop Observatories  is a global open-data platform designed to centralize and streamline access to comprehensive agricultural information for key key CG crops (e.g., rice, beans, cassava, and other that continue to be added). Hosted by the Alliance of Bioversity International and the International Center for Tropical Agriculture (CIAT), the platform aggregates production, trade, consumption, price, quality, research, and policy data from multiple open-access sources into a unified, user-friendly interface. It serves stakeholders across the crop value chain—from researchers and policymakers to private sector analysts, extension services, and educators—by enabling easy exploration and analysis of crop-specific indicators that historically were scattered across disparate databases and reports.; ; At its core, the observatories aim to transform raw data into actionable insights that support more informed decision-making. By harmonizing and visualizing information such as production volumes, export and import statistics, price trends, and varietal characteristics, the platform equips users with a clearer understanding of the dynamics shaping global and regional crop markets. Features like country comparators and thematic dashboards allow users to identify patterns and trends, enhancing the capacity for evidence-based planning, forecasting, and investment decisions.; ; This integrated approach is particularly valuable for market intelligence, as it enables analysts to monitor supply and demand shifts, track competitive positioning, and assess the impact of policy or environmental changes on crop sectors. In a world where agricultural data are abundant but fragmented, the Crop Observatories provide a centralized, open-access resource that reduces information gaps, supports strategic planning, and fosters transparency in agricultural markets. Ultimately, this enhances competitiveness, supports value chain resilience, and contributes to greater food system understanding across public and private stakeholders.

column16: 3D model of the floodplain of the Dolo Ado district in Somali Region of Ethiopia
column17: Point cloud data were collected in Dolo Ado, Somali Region, Ethiopia, using UAV-based photogrammetry (SfM–MVS) from a DJI Mavic Pro 2 (RGB, geotagged imagery) and processed in DroneDeploy, to create a 3-dimensional (3D) model. Flights were conducted at ~100 m AGL (330 ft), producing a ground sampling distance (GSD) of ~1–5 cm, sufficient to resolve floodplain micro-topography, settlements, and linear infrastructure.; ; To maintain reconstruction quality and manage processing limits, data acquisition followed a block-based mission design. Approximately 22 mapping blocks were flown with high forward and side overlap to stabilise tie points and reduce occlusions in dense settlements and vegetated areas. In total, ~47,287 images (~460 GB) were acquired over >40 flight hours, covering ~16.4 km². Survey effort prioritised flood corridors, settlements, roads, embankments, and other vulnerable infrastructure to ensure decision-relevant outputs rather than exhaustive visual coverage.;  ; Processing was conducted iteratively by block within DroneDeploy, avoiding oversized single projects (≤10,000 images per run). DroneDeploy performed camera calibration, bundle adjustment, and dense reconstruction, producing dense point clouds, orthomosaics, and DSMs. The primary performance gains resulted from rigorous image quality control, including removal of blurred images, exposure outliers, and low-texture sequences.;  ; As expected, photogrammetric performance over open water was poor due to specular reflection and surface motion; analysis therefore focused on hydraulically meaningful edges and stable features. Additional artefacts arose from radiometric variability (dust, haze, harsh illumination) and vegetation motion, causing local noise and distortion.;  ; Given the use of a non-RTK platform without LiDAR, outputs were treated as having high relative accuracy but limited absolute vertical accuracy without supplementary ground control.

column16: Methodology for identifying opportunities to reduce nutrient loss in the bean value chain in Honduras
column17: Contamination and food loss and waste are some of the hazards in the value chain that can reduce the nutrient content of beans. Tools that identify the barriers and opportunities to prevent nutrient loss are needed by governments and market system actors so that appropriate solutions can be designed. This methodology was adapted by researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition from the Nutrition-Sensitive Value Chain methodology co-developed and piloted by CGIAR and the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) during the CGIAR Research Program on Agriculture for Nutrition and Health (A4NH), (2012-2021). This version starts the value chain mapping from low-income, rural consumers and includes diet, retail, and wholesale nodes. The methodology considers at each node how practices increase or decrease the nutritional value of end product available to consumers in Honduras. The overall application of the methodology includes a CGIAR-supervised MSc thesis and training of government staff from the Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (SAG) and the subunits on value chains and food and nutrition security on how to apply the methodology. In 2026, SAG intends to use the methodology to finish assessments of the bean value chain plus three more value chains for cacao, beef, and dairy in northern Honduras.

column16: Gender-transformative framework developed by CGIAR to guide equitable seed system design across crops, livestock and aquaculture globally
column17: Traditional seed systems often fail to meet the diverse needs of women and men equally, perpetuating gender inequalities in agriculture. CGIAR researchers from the International Food Policy Research Institute, International Potato Center, Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT, and International Livestock Research Institute developed this comprehensive framework to transform how seed systems operate. The framework provides practical guidance for designing seed systems that not only serve diverse users but actively promote gender equality through strategic use of information and communication technologies. It addresses seed systems across crops, livestock, and fish, offering pathways for more equitable access to quality seeds and breeding materials. This innovation enables development practitioners and policymakers to create seed systems that empower women and transform gender dynamics in agricultural communities.

column16: Innovation Portfolio  Management Game
column17: CGIAR's Scaling for Impact initiative developed this interactive card game to address the challenge of managing complex innovation portfolios effectively. Traditional training methods often fail to convey the nuanced decision-making required when selecting and scaling innovations across diverse contexts. The game transforms abstract concepts into hands-on learning experiences where participants assume decision-maker roles, selecting innovations and matching them to appropriate settings while managing limited resources like knowledge, trust, and investment. Players discover through gameplay that successful innovation scaling requires understanding context-specific needs, strategic resource allocation, and collaborative approaches rather than one-size-fits-all solutions. The game structure mirrors real-world processes through phases of idea selection, preparation, and testing, followed by reflection sessions that translate gaming experiences into practical insights. This learning tool helps development practitioners, researchers, and decision-makers better understand why context matters in innovation deployment and why collaboration is essential for achieving meaningful impact at scale.

column16: Subnational Food System Profiles, concise snapshots decisionmakers in Ethiopia, Honduras, and Viet Nam can use to assess food systems and prioritize interventions
column17: A Sustainable Food System Profile is a short document that synthesizes critical information necessary for public and private decisionmakers to obtain a holistic but synthetic overview of the components that are recognized to be critical for the sustainability of countries’ food systems. During Sustainable Healthy Diets in the previous CGIAR portfolio  (2022-2024), CGIAR researchers developed a methodology that would result in country profiles that are more than a simple compilation of national indicators. Instead, they were designed and constructed to identify hotspots of unsustainability in food systems and prioritize interventions at multiple scales to address these through targeted actions and investments. Researchers from Better Diets and Nutrition adapted this methodology so it could be used for the development of subnational profiles, applied so far in Ethiopia, Honduras, and Viet Nam. In all countries, the guidelines emphasize that  key public and private food system stakeholders need to be engaged in both identifying the data and validating results and emerging key messages. In 2024, guidelines based on the experience in two municipalities in Honduras were published, and in 2025, more training for government staff on how to use them were completed. In 2025, separate guidelines based on the experience with local and provincial authorities in Dong Thap and Son La in Viet Nam and in Amhara region in Ethiopia were published. The profiles have become a key activity that supports the subnational implementation of Viet Nam's National Action Plan on Food Systems Transformation towards Transparency, Responsibility, and Sustainability by 2030 (NAP-FST).

column16: Community socialization toolkit for anticipatory action programming
column17: This toolkit is being co-designed with the World Food Programme (WFP) and local leaders in Mali to support anticipatory action programming by strengthening understanding, buy-in, and strategic decision-making among local leaders and community members. Using locally grounded visuals—pictures and graphics that clearly illustrate why and how acting early can reduce the longer-term impacts of shocks—the toolkit translates anticipatory action concepts into accessible, practical guidance. While piloted in Mali, the toolkit is explicitly designed for adaptation and scaling across other WFP country operations and settings where anticipatory action is implemented by humanitarian actors.

column59: The innovation originated as a conceptual idea for a novel behavioral change tool designed to help communities and local leaders understand the value of anticipatory action programming—specifically its role in mitigating climate shocks, preventing long-term environmental degradation, and improving food security and poverty outcomes.; This idea was advanced through basic research aimed at understanding how community leaders interpret and respond to information about anticipatory action and aid governance. We developed an initial prototype of the tool and piloted it with more than 2,500 community leaders across six regions of Mali. Through this process, we experimentally tested alternative ways of presenting information on anticipatory action and aid design, generating new evidence on which framings were most salient and credible to local decision-makers. Findings from these experiments were documented in a discussion paper and complemented by structured feedback from potential scaling partners.; Building on this foundational research, we moved into the design and formulation phase by refining the intervention based on empirical results and user feedback. This included testing leaders’ preferences over key dimensions of aid programming—such as transparency versus other design attributes—and incorporating these insights directly into the tool’s content and structure.

column16: Electric or Tractor-Operated Silage Wrapping Technology to Improve Forage Conservation for Small and Large Ruminants and Enhance Smallholder Livelihoods
column17: The project aims to introduce an electric or tractor-operated silage wrapping machine to improve the conservation and quality of forage crops for feeding small and large ruminants. By enabling efficient ensiling, the technology reduces post-harvest losses, preserves nutritional value, and ensures year-round availability of high-quality feed. This contributes to improved animal health, productivity, and resilience to seasonal feed shortages. The machine is designed to be accessible to small-scale farmers through individual ownership or shared service models, promoting cost-effective adoption. Improved feed management will lead to higher milk and meat production, increased farm income, and enhanced food security. Overall, the intervention supports sustainable livestock production and strengthens the livelihoods of smallholder farmers.

The initiative is currently in its pilot stage at the Potato and Sweetpotato Genebank at the International Potato Center (CIP).

column16: AGX global community platform developed by CGIAR to accelerate inclusive digital transformation in agrifood systems
column17: AGX is a digital platform that connects diverse stakeholders including smallholder farmers, researchers, policymakers, technologists, and investors to collaborate on agricultural technology solutions. Developed by CGIAR's Digital Transformation initiative with IFPRI and ILRI, this community addresses the challenge of fragmented innovation efforts in agriculture across low- and middle-income countries. The platform facilitates knowledge sharing, partnership formation, and co-creation of digital tools that can reach farmers at the last mile. By bringing together agriculture and technology sectors, AGX aims to create interoperable, farmer-centric solutions that enhance agricultural livelihoods and build resilient digital ecosystems for sustainable food systems transformation.

column16: Soil health assessment and management framework
column17: Soil health is a critical enabler of food security, climate resilience, and sustainable livelihoods, especially for smallholder farmers in the Global South. By regulating water, nutrients, and biological activity, soils directly shape crop productivity and the capacity of farming systems to withstand stresses such as drought, erosion, and nutrient depletion. However, these functions are highly context dependent, varying with climate, soil type, land use, and management history. This diversity makes it insufficient to rely on isolated or generic indicators, underscoring the need for assessment protocols that are both standardized and locally meaningful.; This innovation advances soil health decision-making by developing a coherent and scalable assessment and monitoring approach tailored to the diversity of farming systems within SFP target regions. Its overarching objective is to harmonize the soil health assessment methods currently used by SFP-affiliated centres, with a particular focus on soil physical and chemical parameters that are widely measured but rarely comparable. Building on this foundation, the initiative delivers a unified soil health assessment and monitoring tool that can be consistently applied, adapted, and scaled across regions.; The innovation addresses this challenge through an outcome-oriented framework that integrates soil physical and chemical indicators within a modular, adaptable assessment system. The framework accommodates the differing objectives of researchers, advisory services, policymakers, and farmers, while enabling comparison, aggregation, and learning across spatial and temporal scales. Key outcomes include improved consistency and interoperability of soil health data across SFP regions, clearer links between soil condition and agronomic and environmental performance, and strengthened capacity to monitor change over time.; By translating complex soil processes into actionable information, the innovation supports evidence-based management and policy decisions, accelerating the use of soil health knowledge to drive resilient, inclusive, and sustainable agricultural transformation in the Global South.

column16: CGIAR Soil Health Explorer
column17: Soil health is the backbone of productive and resilient smallholder farming across the Global South. CGIAR has built an enormous body of soil research over the years, but a lot of that knowledge is difficult to find and use. The new Soil Health Explorer changes that. It opens up CGIAR’s evidence base on soil health so researchers, development partners, and investors can easily access what CGIAR already generated, and avoid repeating past work. It also supports smarter R&D, helps donors target their investments more effectively, and strengthens efforts to scale soil health innovations in the right places. And importantly, developing this tool shows how CGIAR’s Sustainable Farming Science Program (conceptualization) and Project Performance Unit (development) can work together to accelerate the spread of practical, science-based soil health information worldwide.

column16: AI-powered chatbot developed by ILRI provides livestock health advice for farmers across multiple developing regions
column17: Livestock farmers in developing countries often lack access to expert veterinary advice, leading to poor animal health outcomes and reduced productivity. To address this challenge, researchers at the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), working with a Kenyan consultant under CGIAR's Digital Transformation initiative, developed an artificial intelligence chatbot that provides expert answers on animal health questions. The chatbot covers various livestock species from poultry to large ruminants and uses advanced technology that searches through thousands of research articles to generate accurate responses. This digital tool makes veterinary expertise accessible to farmers who previously had limited access to professional animal health guidance, potentially improving livestock productivity and farmer livelihoods across multiple developing regions.

column16: Open Data Cube Manager App
column17: Managing large collections of environmental and agricultural data has been challenging for researchers and organizations working on climate, water, and land issues. CGIAR's Digital Transformation initiative developed this web-based application to address this problem by providing a comprehensive solution for organizing datasets within open data platforms. The tool enables users to create, update, index, and delete data products while ensuring datasets remain consistently structured and well-documented. It streamlines data management workflows and maintains reliable, accessible information that supports evidence-based analysis and decision-making. The application is particularly valuable for organizations managing complex environmental datasets that require systematic organization and regular updates to support ongoing research and policy development.

column16: Community Grazing Management (CGM): an innovative process designed to support the management and restoration of smaller community grasslands in mixed farming systems and agro-pastoralist areas
column17: CGM is a local producer-driven approach for improving management of grazing lands to benefit livelihoods and the environment. CGM proceeds through a structured set of steps, moving from context characterization, to prioritization of management objectives, and focusing at its core on management planning for grazing, land restoration, and the rules or bylaws needed to accomplish these plans successfully. Initial implementation of key management plan components enables action research testing of co-designed grazing and restoration techniques. These tests, managed by local producer institutions, demonstrate the benefits of the management plan and land restoration to producers,  while providing valuable data for quantitative evaluation of the impacts from changes in grazing and restoration.

column16: MDII Offline Desktop Assessment Application - A standalone, offline-capable desktop application enabling MDII assessments in low-bandwidth and connectivity-constrained environments.
column17: The MDII Offline-Friendly Desktop App is a user-centric digital tool that enables the application of the Multidimensional Digital Inclusiveness Index in low-connectivity contexts. Designed for policymakers, practitioners, and researchers working in food, land, and water systems, the app allows users to assess, score, and reflect on the ethical, social, and inclusiveness dimensions of digital innovations without requiring continuous internet access. By supporting offline data entry, local storage, and later synchronization, the app facilitates inclusive digital assessment processes in resource-constrained settings, strengthening evidence-based decision-making and responsible digital transformation.

column16: AgWise Forecast Workflow: Seasonal Forecast–Based Optimal Planting Date & Cultivar Advisory Generation
column17: AgWise delivers tangible impact from climate science investments, transforming ensemble forecasts and data innovations into actionable advisories that directly improve planting decisions, productivity, and resilience for smallholder farmers. It operationalizes the forecast-based action, bridging the gap between global climate intelligence and local agricultural services- enabling governments and partners to act early, plan better, and manage risk more efficiently. Tested across Ethiopia, Kenya, Zambia, and Rwanda, AgWise has demonstrated scalability, cost-effectiveness, and adaptability to diverse agro-ecological and data contexts, positioning it for national and regional integration under ongoing climate service initiatives. By converting climate information into livelihood decisions, AgWise strengthens food security systems, advances the CGIAR and AICCRA goals on digital innovation and resilience, and demonstrates clear value for money and long-term sustainability for donor investment. The current activity aims to shift climate forecasts from being passive information to becoming active decision inputs that directly drive agronomic optimization within the AgWise advisory engine. Building on lessons from WeRise, Climate+ and EDACaP-NextGen (Seid et al., 2023), the work follows a dual-timeframe approach: (i) strategic planning (3–6 months) using seasonal forecasts to inform variety selection, planting windows, and access to bundled services such as climate-linked finance (AFR-2419, 2024); and (ii) tactical execution (around 10 days) using higher-frequency forecasts to guide in-season actions such as timing fertilizer applications, managing supplementary irrigation, and optimizing harvest decisions (CGIAR, 2024).

column16: Innovative nutrition delivery through Community Health Workers (CHW)-led model to scale small fish consumption in vulnerable communities in Bangladesh
column17: This innovative delivery model addresses malnutrition in vulnerable Bangladeshi communities by integrating small indigenous species (SIS) fish nutrition knowledge into existing community health worker systems. Rather than creating parallel delivery systems, WorldFish developed this approach which integrates SIS-specific nutrition knowledge, practical counselling skills, and user-friendly learning aids into an existing, trusted community health worker (CHW) workforce. Leveraging CHWs’ routine household and community engagement, the model enables continuous, high-coverage delivery and reinforcement of fish-based nutrition messages, moving beyond one-off training approaches. The approach is highly cost-efficient, scalable, and aligned with existing health systems, while addressing critical gaps in SIS nutrition messaging and food-based indicators. By transforming CHWs into agents of dietary change using locally available aquatic foods, the model supports sustainable nutrition improvement and contributes to broader food system transformation goals.

column16: MI (Market Intelligence) Transfer: From Fragmented Evidence to Decision-Ready Market Intelligence
column17: MI (Market Intelligence) Transfer is a market intelligence innovation developed to support evidence-based product design within the CGIAR breeding network. Product design is a country-led process involving economists, agronomists, gender and nutrition specialists, and value-chain actors. The demand for high-quality MI has grown substantially. However, critical MI insights remain fragmented across publications, datasets, project reports, webinars, and tacit expert knowledge. This fragmentation makes it difficult for Product Design Teams (PDTs) to access credible, timely, and consistent evidence during key decision moments, often resulting in uneven inputs and reliance on who happens to be present in the room.; ; MI Transfer was developed in response to this challenge. Designed by the GloMIP team for PDTs, breeders, and national partners, MI Transfer provides a standardized, harmonized, and state-of-the-art MI foundation that is accessible regardless of users’ prior expertise in market analysis. Through the MI Transfer platform, diverse sources of MI evidence are consolidated and synthesized into validated, decision-ready outputs. Its flagship product, the MI Evidence Briefer, delivers concise snapshots of market segment, target product profile (TPP), essential improved traits mapped to value proposition, and synthesis of MI evidence at crop- and country-specific levels—exactly the information PDT members have identified as critical for trait prioritization and Target Product Profile refinement.; ; The innovation was iteratively shaped through key informant interviews, and workshops, including the Product Design Standard workshop in Nairobi, where stakeholders underscored the need to systematically embed market intelligence into product design decisions. A proof-of-concept MI Evidence Briefer for rice in Tanzania demonstrated how structured MI synthesis can support more consistent, transparent, and evidence-based decisions across CGIAR and its partners.; ; Ultimately, MI Transfer strengthens product design by making market intelligence actionable, reducing reliance on ad hoc expertise, aligning breeding decisions with value-chain and consumer demand, and increasing the likelihood of adoption and impact of future CGIAR products.

column16: Digital twin solution for tropical dairy cattle enables temperature stress evaluation
column17: Livestock systems are increasingly exposed to heat stress, posing significant risks to animal welfare, productivity, and long-term resilience, particularly in tropical and subtropical production environments. In response to these challenges, the Digital Twin for Livestock project at Kapiti Ranch, ILRI Nairobi, led jointly by the International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI), Scotland’s Rural College (SRUC), and technology partner Bodit, represents an innovative approach to livestock phenotyping and resilience research. The project focuses on developing near-real-time digital replicas of individual animals to enable deep phenotyping of heat tolerance in cattle.; ; The project integrates wearable and environmental sensors, GPS tracking, and CCTV video, streamed into a unified digital twin platform that supports comprehensive monitoring of animal behaviour, physiological responses, and thermoregulatory traits at the Kapiti Farm experimental site in Nairobi. By overlaying multiple data sources, the platform generates a cohesive and dynamic representation of each animal’s status, allowing researchers to monitor responses to heat stress, changes in movement patterns, and other welfare indicators under real-world grazing conditions.; ; This technical report in the evidence section describes the development of a digital twin representing the grazing behaviour, environment and heat stress of a group of crossbred dairy cattle. The digital representation revealed that feeding is significantly reduced during periods of high heat stress with some cattle being much more affected than others. This approach offers a scalable phenotype proxy for animal adaptation to environmental stressors. ; ; Building on these findings, a broader research and innovation agenda applies machine learning to interpret animal behaviour as proxies for fitness and adaptability. This AI-driven phenotyping framework constructs digital twins that capture holistic animal performance under real-world environmental pressures, offering a scalable and cost-effective measure for resource intensive traditional phenotyping.

column16: Regional digital innovation hub launched by CGIAR in Malaysia to accelerate agricultural technology adoption across Asia
column17: CGIAR established the Asia Digital Hub at WorldFish headquarters in Penang, Malaysia, creating the first regional center dedicated to digital agricultural innovation in Asia. The hub was developed to address fragmented digital transformation efforts across Asian agriculture by providing a coordinated platform where researchers, government partners, and practitioners collaborate on technology development and scaling. It functions as both a physical facility and digital platform offering training programs, technology experimentation spaces, and knowledge exchange networks. The hub accelerates adoption of CGIAR's digital innovations across Southern and South-Eastern Asia while facilitating reverse learning that brings Asian expertise and locally-developed solutions back to the global CGIAR network, strengthening collective capacity to deliver agricultural impact at scale.

This proof of concept demonstrates how AI-driven assistance can enhance inclusivity, engagement, and user-centered design in digital assessment tools.

column16: Ganges delta salinity: Bangladesh scaling pathway and roadmaps; Navigating Salinity Challenges in the Polders of Coastal Bangladesh: AI-Based Advisories for Farmers and Water Managers
column17: Increasing river water salinity trends have been a growing concern in coastal Bangladesh in the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna Delta, with implications for agriculture, livelihoods, and drinking water availability. Shifts in precipitation and sea-level rise, and changes in upstream flow and siltation, together affect river salinity trends with implications for water and food security in the deltaic system. Salinity trends in coastal Bangladesh vary from west to east, and several governmental and non-governmental research and development initiatives have been undertaken to assess and test solutions for salinity issues across the region. The Bangladesh Delta Plan (BDP) 2100 is designed to be a comprehensive techno-economic adaptive plan that deploys interventions across water, land, ecosystems, and the environment to ensure resilient futures for the Ganges Delta. Connecting these siloed interventions can help align them on a shared pathway towards coordinated salinity management efforts in Bangladesh.

column16: Bulletin Builder Platform - Modernizing agroclimatic information delivery through a user-centered, scalable, and traceable system
column17: Egypt faces compounding challenges of water scarcity, rising salinity, and declining agricultural productivity. To support more informed planning, NEXAR-Egypt is being developed as a prototype diagnostic tool that integrates water accounting, salinity conditions, and crop productivity into a single analytical system. Adapted from the co-designed system and validated NEXAR framework in Uzbekistan, the Egyptian version aims to identify hotspots, diagnose constraints, and highlight priority interventions. The prototype tool combines WA+ outputs, salinity data, crop yield statistics, soil characteristics, and climate information to generate clear, actionable insights for policymakers and technical teams. Its modular design enables users to explore indicators supported by local farmer practices and spatial analytics. Next steps include system validation, refinement, and institutional integration, followed by scaling to additional governorates. NEXAR-Egypt has the potential to become a national platform that strengthens water governance, improves resource efficiency, and enhances climate-resilient agricultural planning.

column16: Scaling Water Accounting Plus (WA+) dashboard innovation to support integrated water resources management and evidence-based decision-making in Morocco
column17: This activity applies the Water Accounting Plus (WA+) framework in the Tensift Watershed in Morocco and supports the development of an interactive dashboard to visualize and communicate WA+ results in an accessible and decision-oriented manner. Building on earlier implementation in the Souss Massa Basin, the WA+ dashboard innovation in Morocco has now scaled geographically to a second major basin, demonstrating its scalability and relevance across different hydrological and institutional contexts. The dashboard will integrate satellite-based water balance components, basin performance indicators, and spatial analyses to support evidence-based water planning, monitoring, and dialogue among stakeholders. By extending WA+ to the Tensift Watershed, the initiative strengthens national capacity for basin-level water accounting, promotes transparency in water management, and contributes to more informed and resilient water governance under increasing climate and water scarcity pressures.

column16: Development of a prototype of a next-generation water mentoring system (NEXAR) for the Kashkadarya region in Uzbekistan
column17: Water-scarce regions like Kashkadarya in Uzbekistan face increasing pressures from climate change, agricultural demand, and limited, fragmented data to support decision-making. In response, a prototype for a Water Monitoring System (NEXAR) has been co-designed with stakeholders to address these challenges by integrating satellite data, analytics, and user-friendly dashboards. Developed through a co-design process, NEXAR harnesses the power of remote sensing, big data, and predictive analytics to support evidence-based decisions and strengthen climate resilience.

column16: Building a Water Accounting Plus (WA+) dashboard for Egypt and linking with salinity and crop productivity
column17: Egypt faces compounding challenges of water scarcity, rising salinity, and declining agricultural productivity. To support more informed planning, NEXAR-Egypt is being developed as a prototype diagnostic tool that integrates water accounting, salinity conditions, and crop productivity into a single analytical system. Adapted from the co-designed system and validated NEXAR framework in Uzbekistan, the Egyptian version aims to identify hotspots, diagnose constraints, and highlight priority interventions. The prototype tool combines WA+ outputs, salinity data, crop yield statistics, soil characteristics, and climate information to generate clear, actionable insights for policymakers and technical teams. Its modular design enables users to explore indicators supported by local farmer practices and spatial analytics. Next steps include system validation, refinement, and institutional integration, followed by scaling to additional governorates. NEXAR-Egypt has the potential to become a national platform that strengthens water governance, improves resource efficiency, and enhances climate-resilient agricultural planning.

column16: Automated Large-Scale Mapping of Crop Planting Dates Using Multi-Temporal MODIS–VIIRS Vegetation Indices and Phenology Detection on the AgWISE Platform
column17: The innovation lies in combining long-term multi-sensor satellite data with an automated, scalable processing pipeline that ensures continuous crop monitoring despite sensor transitions, enabling consistent planting date estimation and crop mapping over more than two decades. This methodology uses long-term satellite vegetation index data to automatically estimate planting dates and crop phenology. It relies primarily on Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) sensor and Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) series (250 m, 8-day resolution) and transitions to Expedited Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (eVIIRS) data after 2023 to ensure continuity as MODIS is phased out. An automated processing workflow developed in AgWISE enables: (1) Preparation of the data environment, (2) Interactive downloading of MODIS (MOD13Q1, MYD13Q1) and VIIRS vegetation index data, (3) Reprojection, merging, renaming, and harmonization of satellite files, (4) Seasonal analysis to derive planting dates and crop development parameters. Administrative boundaries and crop-specific validation datasets are integrated to support spatial aggregation and improve accuracy.

column16: A seed treatment protocol developed for forage crops using fungicide, ensuring clean, disease-free seeds for both conservation and distribution.
column17: Seedborne fungal pathogens pose a significant threat to seed quality, germination, and crop establishment, and can spread through international germplasm exchange, creating serious biosecurity risks. This study evaluated the efficacy of selected fungicides as seed treatment for controlling seedborne fungi in forage germplasm. The seeds of five forage accessions with a history of fungal infections were treated with SAAF (Carbendazim 12% + Mancozeb 63% WP), Apron Star (Thiamethoxam 20% + Metalaxyl-M 20% + Difenoconazole 2% WS), Carbendazim (Carbendazim 50% WP), and untreated control. The fungicide-treated seeds were incubated on moist blotter paper and Potato Dextrose Agar (PDA) at 23 ± 1 °C for seven days and then examined for fungal infection. Treatment efficacy was assessed based on the incidence of infected seeds, diversity of fungal genera, and percentage reduction relative to untreated controls. Results showed that SAAF exhibited the highest efficacy, achieving a 96.60% reduction in seed infection, followed by Carbendazim (50%) and Apron Star (48%). The untreated seeds (control) recorded a 44.29% infection incidence, with multiple pathogens detected including Alternaria, Fusarium, Aspergillus, and Phoma. Overall, the results demonstrate the superior performance of SAAF, formulated with carbendazim and mancozeb, providing the most effective suppression of a broad range of seedborne fungi. Fungicide seed treatment, especially with SAAF, therefore, offers an effective strategy for improving seed health and reducing the risk of pathogen dissemination with seeds
