column16: Development of an ex vitro virus elimination protocol for yams using external sprays of ribavirin
column17: Yam (Dioscorea spp.) is frequently infected by viruses, creating major constraints for the safe conservation and international exchange of yam germplasm. Conventional in vitro virus elimination methods, particularly meristem culture, are time-consuming (12–24 months) due to the slow growth of yam tissues. To address this limitation, efforts are underway to develop faster ex vivo virus elimination approaches, combining treatments such as chemotherapy and thermotherapy to recover virus-free planting material that can serve as clean stock. An initial trial was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of external ribavirin sprays, a widely used antiviral chemotherapeutic agent. Four yam genotypes were selected to test the robustness of the protocol across diverse genetic backgrounds: Mecakusa (D. rotundata) and Wonder yam, Akuabata, and Vayam (D. alata). The experiment was laid out in a completely randomized design and conducted in an aphid-proof screenhouse at IITA, Ibadan, Nigeria. Virus indexing confirmed the presence of Yam mosaic virus (YMV) in Mecakusa and Yam mild mosaic virus (YMMV) in the three D. alata varieties. Vine survival following cutting, nutrient supplementation, and rooting hormone application was generally high across all genotypes. Of the 60 vines planted per variety, Wonder yam and Akuabata maintained 100% survival throughout the assessment period, while Mecakusa and Vayam showed slight reductions by six weeks. At termination, the number of successfully rooted vines ranged from 55 to 60 per genotype. Plant growth was monitored over 0–6 weeks in two trials using leaf area, vine length, and number of leaves as indicators. Ribavirin treatments substantially reduced virus symptom expression. Untreated plants exhibited mild to moderate symptoms, while 10 ppm ribavirin reduced symptom severity. Plants treated with 20–30 parts per million (ppm) consistently recorded a virus score of 1 (no symptoms) across genotypes, demonstrating the strong potential of ribavirin for ex vivo virus suppression.

column16: Development of a procedure for phytosanitary safe exchange of semi-autotrophic hydropoincs (SAH) cassava plantlets in sub-Saharan Africa
column17: Clonally propagated crops such as cassava, banana, and yams are traditionally exported as virus-free in vitro plantlets. However, many countries in sub-Saharan Africa lack sufficient capacity for post-flask management of in vitro plantlets. This is a major bottleneck for the adoption and use of clonal crop germplasm in the importing country. As an alternative, we have explored the export of clonal crops propagated using the Semi-Autotrophic Hydroponics (SAH). The SAH system involves multiplication of virus-free in vitro plantlets or shoots in sterile peat (Klassman TS3, steam-sterilized growth media) under insect-free screen house conditions. The SAH plantlets are virus-indexed, and health materials are shipped for export. The growing conditions are well-maintained to prevent other pests and pathogens (fungal, bacterial, etc.). The rooted plantlets in the SHA boxes are then sprayed with TEAM (mancozeb and carbendazim) to avoid any fungal infections during transit (usually 1 to 2 weeks). The procedure has been standardized for the export of cassava and yams from IITA, Ibadan, to several countries in sub-Saharan Africa (Angola, São Tomé and Príncipe, Madagascar, Cote d’Ivoire, Liberia, and the Central African Republic). This model of export has so far received positive appraisal from the quarantine agencies of the importing countries.

column16: Diagnostics protocol developed for the detection of Cowpea mosaic virus (CpMV)
column17: Cowpea mosaic virus (CpMV; genus Comovirus) is a major viral pathogen of cowpea and other legume crops worldwide. It is endemic in West African legume production systems and is transmitted both through seed and by beetle vectors. Seed transmission of CpMV poses a significant risk to germplasm regeneration and international exchange, necessitating routine screening of germplasm to detect and eliminate contaminated materials. Current diagnostics rely primarily on reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). While RT-PCR offers high sensitivity, ELISA remains the most economical and convenient option for high-throughput screening. However, ELISA-based detection of CpMV currently depends on commercially sourced polyclonal antibodies. This study aimed to generate CpMV-specific polyclonal antibodies and to standardize their use in a direct antigen-coating (DAC) ELISA format. A CpMV isolate collected from infected cowpea plants in IITA experimental fields in Ibadan, Nigeria, was characterized and maintained as a pure culture under screenhouse conditions. The virus was propagated in cowpea plants and purified using differential centrifugation. Purified virus preparations were used to raise polyclonal antibodies in rabbits. The resulting antibodies were evaluated for specificity and sensitivity against CpMV and several unrelated cowpea-infecting viruses, including cucumber mosaic virus, bean common mosaic virus, cowpea aphid-borne mosaic virus, and cowpea mild mottle virus. The antibodies showed high specificity to CpMV and reliably detected the virus at dilutions up to 1:5000. The DAC-ELISA protocol was optimized for CpMV detection in cowpea leaf sap extracts at a 1:10 dilution using antibodies at 1:5000. Further validation using field and screenhouse samples is ongoing. This development enhances diagnostic capacity by improving cost-effectiveness and reducing processing time for large-scale germplasm screening.

column16: Co-development of scaling pathways and roadmap for the Hinga Smart Platform (formerly DACA) in Ghana.
column17: CIAT, through the TAFS-WCA initiative, adapted the HingaSmart platform (formerly Digital AgroClimate Advisory) to support climate-informed decision-making among farmers in Ghana. HingaSmart provides location-specific agro-climatic and agronomic advisories to help farmers choose suitable crops, optimal planting dates, and appropriate input use. Following a 2022 workshop on platform customization, data collected in 2023 was used to tailor the advisories to Ghana’s context. A validation workshop in November 2024 confirmed the relevance and accuracy of the information for Ghanaian users. Building on these efforts, a scaling workshop was held from December 16–18, 2025, to develop scaling pathways and a national rollout roadmap. The workshop brought together stakeholders from NGOs, research institutions, the Ghana Meteorological Agency, and Farm Radio International.

column16: Projected Benefits and Strategic Foresight Tool for Market-Driven Breeding
column17: This innovation strengthens CGIAR’s capacity to anticipate future market needs and quantify the long-term benefits of breeding investments by embedding strategic foresight and projected benefits analysis within the Market Intelligence Area of Work (AoW) of the Breeding for Tomorrow  Science Program. Building on the Global Market Intelligence Platform (GloMIP), the approach integrates forward-looking indicators into the Impact Opportunities Portal to support more demand-driven, inclusive, and climate-resilient breeding decisions.; ; Currently, around 20% of GloMIP’s 245 indicators are forecasted, with a strong focus on nutrition and health outcomes, poverty and demographics, and greenhouse gas emissions. These indicators underpin projected benefits metrics that allow breeding teams to assess how innovations may contribute to CGIAR Impact Areas under future scenarios. As presented during the foresight sessions of the Market Intelligence AoW Annual Workshop and the Product Design Standard (PDS) workshop in Kenya, this work combines top-down global foresight data with bottom-up insights from local partners to generate future impact opportunities and market segments.; ; A key component of the innovation is the alignment of projected impact opportunities with future market segments. Through tools such as the Seed Product Market Segment Database (SPMS), the Intrinsic Productivity Growth (IPR) tool, and the IMPACT model, national- and crop-level projections for harvested area, yield, prices, and demand are downscaled to the market segment level and visualized through GloMIP. This enables Product Design Teams to explore how market size, constraints, and trait priorities may evolve over time.; ; Collaborative foresight workshops, including the IRRI and Alliance Bioversity-CIAT  hybrid workshop in June 2025, have further advanced this innovation by harmonizing methodologies, establishing a foresight working group, and linking GloMIP with Crop Observatories. Together, these efforts provide a coherent decision-support system that helps CGIAR breeding programs prioritize investments based not only on current needs, but on credible projections of future impact.

column16: ImpactSF Support to the Tropical Resilience Fund: Embedding CGIAR Climate and Resilience Analytics and a Resilience Monitoring Framework into a Global Innovation Lab-Endorsed Blended-Finance Fund Design
column17: ImpactSF operationalises CGIAR science within financial systems by embedding climate and environmental analytics into fund design and measurement systems. In 2025, the core deliverable was technical support to design the Tropical Resilience Fund (TREF), a targeted USD 100 million blended-finance debt vehicle deploying risk-tolerant capital to early- and growth-stage resilience and nature-based enterprises across tropical food systems. First closing and deployment expected in 2026. TREF was selected for the 2025 Global Innovation Lab for Climate Finance and endorsed by its network of public and private investors, and was also selected for the International Climate Finance Accelerator. CGIAR supported TREF soft launch at COP30. ImpactSF integrated CGIAR-derived resilience screening, climate-risk diagnostics, impact taxonomies and MRV logic into TREF’s architecture, and co-designed a resilience monitoring framework embedded in the fund’s MRV system. This work shows how CGIAR research can be translated into science-driven financial architectures that strengthen decision-making.

column16: Spatial analysis to support market segmentation by characterizing production environments
column17: The innovation centers on integrating spatial analysis into agricultural market segmentation to make breeding and seed development more evidence-driven and responsive to real demand. In 2025, CGIAR researchers and national partners identified approximately 690 Seed Product Market Segments (SPMS) using eight harmonized market segment criteria that ensure consistency across crops and regions. These criteria are now being applied not only to cereals but also to vegetables like tomato and pepper, with further expansion planned for other crop groups.; A key challenge in market segmentation is finding relevant data that accurately reflects the varied environments in which crops are grown. To tackle this, the innovation leverages spatial datasets—such as elevation and climate zone data—to characterize production environments, allowing segmentation to be grounded in geospatial reality. For example, the team adapted a framework originally developed for potato regions, combining FAO Global Agro-Ecological climate classifications with NASA elevation data to define distinct “mega-environments” such as tropical lowlands and subtropical uplands. This approach was illustrated through a maize production environment case study, revealing how spatial mapping helps distinguish production contexts that matter for product design.; ; Beyond mapping existing environments, the innovation is designed to evolve. CGIAR invites partners—including research institutions, national programs, and data specialists—to refine thermal climate classifications, validate elevation thresholds, and contribute additional spatial datasets to improve the precision of production environment delineations. This collaborative model enhances the relevance of segmentation, supporting more targeted breeding, seed development, and investment decisions.; ; By embedding spatial analysis in market segmentation, CGIAR is helping shift agricultural innovation from supply-driven to data-informed and context-specific, ultimately improving the alignment of genetic innovation with real user needs.

column16: Web-based tool to gather, in a gamified way, pairs of field-relevant Questions and Answers
column17: This innovation is a simple, one-file Shiny/R app to gather field-specific pairs of questions and answers in a gamified way. It is therefore perfectly suited to run datathons during which Q/A pairs are crowdsourced from the participants. Questions, answers and their source references are stored in a SQLite database on the host from which the app is running. This innovation was used at ILRI (Nairobi campus) on 09 June 2025, in the framework of the CGIAR-wide effort to contribute to the training of the upcoming AgriLLM large language model. Since the tools allows information gathering from differente categories of participants (personas/roles), it enhances inclusion while providing a fun way for a diverse array of participants to engage with asking and answering questions. Participants therefore effortlessly build a valuable dataset that can be used e.g. to train large language models.

column16: Red Meat Market Segmentation to Support Livestock Breeding Programs
column17: The Red Meat Market Segmentation innovation is a new, stand‑alone concept that introduces the first standardized, evidence‑based framework designed specifically for the global red meat value chain. Unlike existing segmentation approaches—which historically focused solely on crops—this innovation represents an entirely new domain of market intelligence for livestock.; By establishing a structured segmentation system tailored to sheep, goats, and cattle, it fills a long‑standing gap in an industry where producers have never adopted formal market segmentation. This new framework overcomes the fragmentation and inconsistent definitions that have hindered priority setting, product design, and coordinated action, enabling CGIAR and its partners to align investments and interventions more effectively across red meat systems.

column16: CircularIQ artificial intelligence assistant developed by IWMI transforms waste management knowledge for entrepreneurs and communities globally
column17: Waste management poses significant challenges for entrepreneurs, farmers, and communities who lack technical expertise to convert waste into valuable resources. IWMI developed CircularIQ, an early-stage digital innovation that bridges this knowledge gap by making circular bioeconomy concepts accessible through an interactive chat interface. The artificial intelligence assistant transforms complex research into practical guidance, helping users understand how household waste, agricultural residues, and wastewater can become useful products like compost, clean water, or energy. Users can explore sustainable business models, learn about successful reuse practices, and understand implementation options through simple conversations. Currently at Innovation Readiness Level 4, this prototype demonstrates how large language models can connect scientific research with practical application, supporting better decision-making for sustainable waste management and contributing to climate mitigation through reduced greenhouse gas emissions.

column16: The iKrishi Platform An ICARDA-MP Govt. Joint Venture to Support Small Holder farmers  to Foster Climate Smartness and Sustainable Intensification with Digital Augmentation
column17: Central India farmers face growing climate risks from erratic rainfall, droughts, and heat stress. Current climate information systems are often too technical, poorly localized, and disconnected from farmers' contexts, limiting their ability to make informed decisions on planting, irrigation, and risk management.;                          The iKrishi system, co-created with Madhya Pradesh Government and ICARDA under the CGIAR Science Programs (CASP, SFSP and DTA) along with recently concluded Precision Agriculture India project, has demonstrated how locally tailored climate services can transform smallholder decision-making. By translating complex climate data into actionable, farmer-friendly advisories, iKrishi empowers farmers to better manage climate risks. Its proven success and official government endorsement provide a strong foundation for broader application. The iKrishi system has enabled farmers to achieve notable gains despite climate and economic challenges. Beneficiaries increased cotton, soybean, and wheat yields by 8-15% through timely, locally tailored advice. Additionally, farmers reduced pesticide use by 15-20% saving 1-2 sprays per season and cut fertilizer use by a similar margin, especially for nitrogen and phosphorus. Improved irrigation scheduling saved 1-2 doses per crop cycle, resulting in a 25-30% boost in net farmer income. column16: Remote sensing algorithm for Tracking Rangeland Degradation from invasive species invasion
column17: The invasion of Prosopis juliflora poses a growing threat to dryland ecosystems and pastoral livelihoods across East Africa. This study presents an integrative approach that combines satellite remote sensing, machine learning, and participatory GIS (PGIS) to detect and map the spatial extent and socio-ecological impacts of Prosopis juliflora in Baringo County, Kenya. We evaluated the performance of three satellite platforms, Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and PlanetScope, using a Random Forest classifier trained on field-collected presence–absence data and vegetation indices. Sentinel-2 outperformed the other sensors, achieving a classification accuracy of 90.65%, with key variables including Visible Atmospherically Resistant Index (VARI), Ratio Vegetation Index (RVI) and red-edge bands emerging as the most important predictors. To enhance contextual understanding and validate remote sensing outputs, we conducted PGIS sessions with gender-disaggregated community groups, capturing local perceptions of invasion hotspots and blocked access to grazing routes and water sources. The comparison of satellite-derived maps and PGIS outputs revealed strong spatial congruence, particularly along water bodies, roads, and croplands. Our findings demonstrate the potential of combining Earth observation and citizen science to generate actionable knowledge for managing invasive species in data-scarce dryland environments. This hybrid framework supports inclusive and spatially targeted interventions for rangeland restoration and ecosystem resilience.

column16: Citizen science and machine learning technology developed by ILRI to map invasive Prosopis juliflora in Kenya's rangelands
column17: Prosopis juliflora, an aggressive invasive woody species, threatens pastoral livelihoods across Kenya's semi-arid rangelands by degrading fragile ecosystems. Traditional field surveys to monitor this invasion are costly and limited in coverage. The technology provides a cost-effective, scalable solution that strengthens evidence-based decision-making for adaptive and sustainable rangeland management in Eastern Africa.

column16: UAV-Based Biomass Assessment in Kenya’s Drylands
column17: This study develops and validates a UAV-based approach for estimating dry-season herbaceous biomass in semi-arid rangelands at Kapiti Research Station, Kenya. High-resolution RGB and multispectral imagery, combined with extensive field measurements, were used to characterize vegetation structure, differentiate herbaceous cover from shrubs and bare soil, and quantify spectral–biophysical relationships across diverse soil and vegetation types. Orthomosaics, vegetation indices (NDVI, NDRE, GNDVI, SAVI), and digital surface models were derived to assess fine-scale variations in forage conditions. Preliminary results indicate limited NDVI variability during the dry season and weak correlations with fresh biomass, highlighting the need to integrate additional indices and structural metrics. The dataset establishes a foundation for seasonal biomass modeling and will support wet-season analysis to capture vegetation response dynamics. Ultimately, this work contributes to developing high-resolution, spatially explicit forage monitoring tools to improve grazing management, drought preparedness, and decision-making for pastoral and agropastoral systems in East Africa.

column16: New high value red-rice variety for rural prosperity
column17: More than half of the world’s population relies on rice as a primary staple food, particularly in Asia, where rice has been domesticated for thousands of years. This initiative represents a significant step towards diversifying rice systems and increasing overall rice production.

column16: Three-legged stool approach developed by ILRI scaled out across Southeast Asia and Ethiopia to improve food safety in traditional pork markets
column17: Food safety risks in traditional pork value chains pose significant health threats in low- and middle-income countries, particularly affecting vulnerable populations who rely on informal markets. The International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI) developed and tested an ECM approach that combines regulatory environment improvements, training and technology for market actors, and behavioral change motivation - known as the 'three-legged stool approach.' This One Health intervention was implemented and evaluated across multiple countries including Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, Thailand, and Ethiopia to demonstrate its effectiveness in making traditional pork value chains safer. The approach addresses the complex challenges of food safety in informal markets where conventional regulatory approaches often fail, providing a scalable solution for improving public health outcomes in diverse cultural and economic contexts.

column16: TAAT soil health technology toolkit to address soil degradation
column17: Poor soil health threatens agricultural productivity worldwide, affecting millions of farmers and food security. The International Institute of Tropical Agriculture developed this comprehensive toolkit to address soil degradation by providing governments, private sector, and development organizations with proven, field-tested technologies. The toolkit includes conservation agriculture practices like minimum tillage and surface mulching, crop rotation systems combining maize and legumes, and innovative organic inputs such as biochar and products derived from Black Soldier Fly. It also features practical assessment tools that help users monitor soil health improvements over time, enabling data-driven decisions for soil restoration efforts. This resource supports large-scale implementation of soil health solutions that enhance water retention, improve nutrient cycling, increase carbon storage, and reduce pest and disease problems.

column16: Scaling resilient finance: a climate-linked credit risk tool for Guatemala’s livestock sector
column17: Scaling Resilient Finance is a digital credit risk scoring innovation that integrates real climate data with livestock producer profiles to improve lending decisions in Guatemala’s livestock sector. The tool enables microfinance institutions (MFIs) to assess exposure, vulnerability, and on-farm practices, generating a climate risk score and tailored recommendations at the point of credit appraisal. By embedding climate risk into credit assessments, it reduces portfolio risk while incentivizing producers to invest in climate-resilient practices. Co-designed with local financial actors and built on real field data, the platform is more accurate than traditional models that ignore climate variability. Already piloted with MFIs, it supports safer lending, expands access to climate-smart credit, and strengthens the resilience of smallholder livestock producers.

column16: Forager: a low-cost, off-grid hydroponic barley forage production system producing over 200 kg of fresh forage a week for smallholder livestock farmers
column17: The "Forager" innovation is a low-cost, off-grid hydroponic barley forage production system that, when used with elite barley genotypes selected for high forage productivity, can produce more than 200 kg of fresh and nutritious forage per week - enough to feed seven sheep for seven days. Hydroponic forage production is a viable option for providing farmers with a highly palatable, nutritious forage during periods when conventional sources are scarce, such as during prolonged droughts. Most existing hydroponic forage production systems are expensive to purchase and operate, are highly technical, and difficult to repair. They also typically require a reliable electricity supply, which limits where they can be installed. Forager overcomes these constraints by using a simple, low-tech, off-grid, do-it-yourself design that does not require external power sources. This makes it well-suited for use in rural and dryland communities in Morocco and across the drylands.

column16: Inclusive Food System Living Labs: Locally-led Innovation for Sustainable and Low-Emission Food Systems
column17: This Living Lab approach functions as a robust  innovation ecosystem that prioritizes the process of co-creation, and collaboration. Its success is anchored in inclusivity, long-term support, and adaptive governance, enabling strong collaboration among stakeholders. Through this collective approach, an inclusive advisory board was established to guide an innovation agenda focused on low emission development for food system transformation. A rigorous assessment framework is embedded in this approach, and it evaluates proposed innovations based on gender and social inclusion, sustainability, mitigation potential, viability, and scalability, with a clear focus on reducing GHG emissions. This approach demonstrates how innovation rooted in local realities and supported by flexible governance can drive low emission development. Embedding this innovative approach within local institution ensures shared power, ownership, and long-term impact in building resilient, locally driven transformation.

column16: Pioneer Positive Deviance in Pastoral Systems of Ethiopia: Community-Led Innovation in Animal Health and Feed/Forage for Resilient Livelihoods
column17: "The Pioneer Positive Deviance (P-PD) approach empowers pastoralist communities to identify and scale up their own successful practices in animal health and feed management that enhance resilience to changes. It builds on the principle that within every community, some households, adaptation pioneers, achieve better livestock outcomes under the same conditions as others. By studying and sharing these locally effective, low-cost, and sustainable practices, communities enhance herd health and productivity using their own knowledge systems. This innovation adapts the P-PD approach developed for mixed systems to pastoral systems. ; The process is community-driven and inclusive, involving herders, women, and youth in every step, from defining key challenges to identifying positive deviants, validating practices, and sharing results through peer learning. Gender equity is central, ensuring women’s often-unrecognized contributions to animal care and feed management are visible and valued.; By fostering local ownership, trust, and collaboration between pastoral innovators and animal health professionals, P-PD bridges traditional and formal systems. Through storytelling, demonstrations, and dialogues, communities spread proven practices, building adaptive, resilient livelihoods rooted in local strength. Their uncommon solutions will also inform alternative livelihoods in particular for youth and women. ";

column16: An integrated One Health approach for wildlife farming management and zoonotic disease prevention in Thai Nguyen Province, Vietnam
column17: Based on evidence from previous studies demonstrating zoonotic pathogen circulation and behavioral risk factors among wildlife farmers, this innovation applies an integrated One Health approach to improve wildlife farming management and reduce zoonotic disease risks in Thai Nguyen, Vietnam. It combines practical capacity building for local authorities (forestry, animal, and human health sectors) and wildlife farmers on current regulations, farm-level biosecurity, and hygiene. The approach integrates a gender lens by addressing differentiated roles and exposure risks of women and men along wildlife value chains. By reducing high-risk practices, strengthening compliance, and enhancing collaboration across sectors, the innovation supports safer wildlife farming while protecting public health and sustaining local livelihoods.

column16: Drone-mounted methane sensors developed by ILRI to measure livestock emissions in Kenya
column17: This innovation documents the first successful field application of drone-mounted methane sensors to measure enteric methane emissions from grazing livestock in African livestock systems. The approach represents a novel and emerging monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) method that complements conventional ground-based measurements by enabling flexible, spatially explicit methane monitoring under real production conditions. The field testing demonstrates the technical feasibility of drone-based methane measurement for livestock systems and provides a foundation for further development, validation, and potential scaling of this MRV approach to support low-emission livestock strategies and methane mitigation planning.;

column16: AgroTutor Model Marketplace: Integrating Weather, Soil and other Models into Location‑Specific, Digital Advisory Services for Smallholder Farmers
column17: AgroTutor is a digital platform developed by CIMMYT that provides farmers with practical agricultural advice through familiar mobile chat applications like WhatsApp. The platform combines location-specific weather forecasts with soil condition data to generate customized fertilizer recommendations and planting guidance, presented as simple images rather than complex technical information. This approach makes advanced agricultural modeling accessible to farmers without requiring technical expertise. The platform uses a modular architecture that allows different advisory services to be easily added, updated, or customized for local conditions while maintaining a consistent user experience. Currently deployed in Mexico, the platform addresses the challenge of delivering timely, location-specific agricultural information to smallholder farmers who may have limited access to extension services or technical resources.

column16: Scalable, low-cost livestock bodyweight estimation for Sub-Saharan African production systems using segmented heart-girth equations by ILRI
column17: This innovation presents a low-cost approach for estimating livestock bodyweight in Sub-Saharan African production systems using robust, segmented heart-girth equations. Drawing on a large, geographically and genetically diverse dataset covering cattle, sheep, and goats across multiple production systems, the method improves prediction accuracy—particularly at the upper and lower extremes of bodyweight where existing equations perform poorly. By segmenting heart-girth ranges and tailoring equations to species, breed group, and production system, the approach substantially reduces prediction error while remaining simple to apply using weigh tapes or charts. The innovation enables accurate bodyweight estimation without the need for weighing scales, supporting livestock management, veterinary dosing, productivity assessment, and greenhouse gas emission estimation in low-resource settings. The work represents an enabling methodological innovation and a tool, and provides a foundation for scalable application and future integration into monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) systems.;

column16: Interactive hands-on training method developed by ILRI improves food safety practices among pork vendors in Vietnamese traditional markets
column17: Traditional pork vendors in Vietnam's markets often lack proper food safety training, posing health risks to consumers. ILRI developed an innovative interactive training approach that replaces conventional classroom methods with hands-on practice using demonstration stalls that mirror vendors' actual working conditions. The method features five practical scenarios with simple illustrated materials covering common daily tasks and food safety risks. Designed to be gender-inclusive, the training encourages participation from both women and men in pork selling activities. Implemented across five Vietnamese provinces in 2024 through the CGIAR One Health Initiative, the approach generated strong vendor engagement and positive feedback. Its effectiveness led local authorities to adopt and expand the method to two additional provinces, demonstrating its potential for broader application in improving food safety practices in traditional market settings.

column16: Regional Southeast Asia Partnership for Accelerating Agricultural Solutions Scaling Mechanized Direct-Seeded Rice Through Public–Private Partnerships, Network Mapping, Bundled Agronomy Practices, and National Investment Pathways in Cambodia, Vietnam and Philippines
column17: Partnership for Accelerating Agricultural Solutions Scaling (PAASS) platforms in the region were operated in Cambodia and Vietnam through EiA. In 2025, a regional PAASS was envisioned, with mechanized direct-seeded rice scaled across Southeast Asia as the core innovation. The innovation was packaged alongside agronomic practices such as improved weed management, laser land leveling, and improved fertilizer and pest management. A DSR Conclave was held in India, convening an Asia-wide sharing of mDSR innovations and bringing together public-private partners of the Direct Seeded Rice Consortium. A Southeast Asia and India network assessment was conducted to discuss the vision and potential strategies for scaling. At another workshop, a more specific mapping of relevant stakeholders for the Philippines was implemented. These network mapping exercises provide insight into bringing in actors relevant at the country and regional levels into the PAASS. In Cambodia, the mDSR will be scaled through a large blended investment (240M USD) under the CAISAR Project, while in Vietnam the mDSR will be scaled through the 1 M Hectare national program.

column16: Conservation Agriculture combined with supplemental irrigation enhances resilience and food security in Morocco’s rainfed drylands
column17: Morocco’s rainfed drylands are highly vulnerable to recurrent drought and increasing rainfall variability, threatening wheat production and national food security. Conservation agriculture (CA) and strategic supplemental irrigation (SI) offer promising pathways to stabilize yields and improve water productivity in these fragile systems. This study evaluates the combined effects of CA and SI on grain yield, biomass production, and water productivity of wheat at ICARDA’s Merchouch research station during the 2021–2022 season under exceptionally dry growing season.

column16: AKILIMO Digital Advisory Tool for Cassava Site Specific Recommendation in Ghana, Nigeria and Tanzania
column17: AKILIMO is a digital advisory tool developed to address the challenge of blanket agricultural recommendations that often fail to match local conditions. The tool integrates soil characteristics, climate data, and farming practices to generate customized fertilizer and crop management advice for individual cassava farms. Developed through CGIAR research and partnerships, AKILIMO replaces generic advice with data-driven recommendations tailored to specific locations and farmer circumstances. The tool is delivered through mobile platforms and extension services, enabling smallholder farmers to improve nutrient use efficiency, increase yields, and achieve better economic returns. The system continuously learns from farmer feedback and performance data to refine its recommendations and support adaptive scaling across diverse farming contexts.; ; In 2024, AKILIMO Nigeria Platform agreed on a combined access to agronomic advice on fertilizer, optimum, safe planting window, and variety choice for cassava, maize and rice (AKILIMO Nigeria Sassakawa). This is currently beeing developped as a component of the AKILIMO chatbot.

column16: Chemical decontamination of meat in mass-markets of low and middle-income countries
column17: Microbial contamination of foods is responsible for the majority of over 420,000 annual deaths due to foodborne disease, with the greatest burden attributed to animal source foods.  CGIAR research under the One Health Initiative has shown that behavioral interventions targeting meat value chain actors from slaughter to retail are successful at improving food hygiene practices and the cleanliness of hands and surfaces. Reductions in microbial contamination of meat itself, however, are elusive.  ; This innovation adapts the use of low-cost, food-safe microbial decontamination technologies widely used in high-income countries and export value chains within low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) to mass-market contexts in these same countries. We are developing decontamination protocols appropriate to the level of contamination and storage conditions of meat in these contexts, and plan to pilot, and hopefully scale, these with national partners. ;

column16: Seed system strategies to accelerate delivery of improved Legume varieties in West Africa
column17: In 2025, several strategies were used to accelerate the delivery of quality seed for improved legume varieties to smallholder farmers and other stakeholders. The strategy focused on moving away from reliance solely on a formal, centralized seed supply system to a multifaceted approach that combines innovative partnerships, technical capacity building, a digital database platform for registration and monitoring of stakeholders, multi-stakeholder strengthening, supportive policies, and deliberate gender-inclusive interventions. These innovative models increased access to improved legume varieties and increased productivity in farmers’ fields. The strategies not only ensure quality and affordability but also improve accessibility and availability of seeds, thereby effectively bridging the gap between research and the farmer's field. Working with the NARS and private sectors, Nigeria produces 5111.7 tons of cowpea and soybean seed. The production comprised of 11.2 tons of cowpea breeder seeds, 164.6 tons of foundation seed, and 2142.4 tons of certified seeds, with varieties less than 10 years old accounting for 90% of the total production. In addition, for soybean, 12.3 tons of breeder seed, 189.2 tons of foundation seed, and 2786.5 tons of certified seed were produced. The production was accomplished through collaborative efforts involving IITA-CGIAR and public- and private-sector partners, including farmers’ groups and youth and women’s groups.  The enhanced seed production and delivery have increased farmers' access to improved crop varieties, increased farmers' field productivity, raised incomes, and improved livelihoods

column16: Accelerated wheat breeding network by CIMMYT delivers 40 climate-resilient, high-yielding varieties across Africa, Asia and Latin America
column17: Growing wheat demand in Africa, Middle East, and South Asia faces mounting challenges from climate stresses, pests, and diseases that threaten food security. CIMMYT and partners developed an innovative breeding network through CGIAR's Breeding for Tomorrow initiative that cuts breeding cycles from five to three years, achieving 40% faster variety development. The network operates five specialized breeding pipelines selecting for heat and drought tolerance, high yield potential, and disease resistance while maintaining grain quality standards. In 2025, partners successfully released 40 new wheat varieties across target regions, offering farmers improved stress tolerance and disease resistance. Current development includes zinc-enriched varieties and strengthened seed systems to ensure rapid farmer access to these climate-adapted innovations.

column16: CG Labs - Improved high-performance computation infrastructure for data scientists in low bandwidth environments
column17: The Collaborative GARDIAN (CG) Labs high-performance compute-and-store solution was improved to address user requirements for enhanced storage and computing. Specifically, these needs enabled computation for Large Language Modeling (LLM) and other Artificial Intelligence models and applications in agriculture to address user needs. This infrastructure works like a supercomputer cluster but is optimized for low bandwidth environments. An authenticated user (typically a data scientist) can choose a high, medium, or low computing environment based on their needs, and CG Labs will spin up a virtual machine for them/their teams to proceed with setting up particular large data sources, analytics jobs etc. CG Labs is used by data scientists across Programs and projects.  ; ; Enhancements in 2025 involved systematic collection and analysis of user needs to determine the appropriate upgrades necessary to support more demanding AI and other computational workflows and larger datasets. Based on the findings, the infrastructure was updated to provide significantly expanded resources, including 1472 GB of RAM, 80 additional CPU cores, 280 TB of NAS storage (upgraded from 80 TB), and 8 TB of SSD storage. These updates ensure that CGLabs can efficiently handle high-performance computing tasks, large-scale data processing, and storage-intensive applications, aligning the infrastructure with current and anticipated user requirements.

column16: Community Conversations to address One Health Hazards in Africa
column17: This participatory social innovation enables communities in low-resource settings to identify, analyze, and respond to health risks at the human-animal-environment interface,  including diseases transmitted from animals to people (zoonoses), antimicrobial resistance, and food safety concerns. The approach brings together male and female community members, local leaders, and frontline service providers through structured activities like storytelling, role-playing, and visual exercises led by trained facilitators. These inclusive sessions help participants understand how gender roles, local knowledge, beliefs and behaviours influence exposure to health threats while developing locally appropriate solutions. Along with partners, the International Livestock Research Institute developed this innovation with evidence showing improved community knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding One Health hazards. The approach includes a practical facilitator guide and is designed for integration into existing health and agricultural extension systems, making it simple, affordable, and scalable for widespread use.

column16: Training and regulatory oversight of hygiene practices in slaughterhouses
column17: Meat inspectors are present daily in all licensed slaughter facilities in Kenya, where their primary role is to ensure meat is free of visible abnormalities. This innovation leverages the presence of meat inspectors to conduct hygiene training and oversight of slaughter workers. Good hygiene practices prevent meat from becoming contaminated with invisible pathogens, which constitute a major threat to public health, whereas visible abnormalities are typically not of great importance to health, but are rather primarily cosmetic. The redirection of regulatory effort toward hygiene practices thus has the potential to improve the safety of meat and thus health outcomes.

column17: The study covered the entire Western Ghats mountain chain, across six states, extending 25 km beyond its formal boundaries to include surrounding ecological transitions. Using MaxEnt-based SDMs, each species’ current and future habitat suitability under three climate scenarios (SSP126, SSP370, SSP585) was mapped. Four threat layers representing land-use change, fire frequency, human pressure, and climate impacts were combined with 16 species traits, such as bark thickness and canopy height, to calculate overall vulnerability.

column16: IRRI develops Excel-based carbon footprint calculator for rice products (CF-Rice) enabling standardized carbon footprint assessment for rice production systems globally
column17: Rice production contributes significantly to greenhouse gas emissions, but measuring carbon footprints across different rice systems has been challenging due to lack of standardized tools. The International Rice Research Institute developed CF-Rice, an Excel-based calculator with a user-friendly interface that enables researchers, policymakers, food industry professionals, and consumers to easily calculate and compare carbon footprints of rice products. This tool standardizes carbon footprint assessment methods across different rice production systems globally, supporting greenhouse gas inventories, mitigation projects, and field experiment evaluations. By making carbon footprint calculations accessible and consistent, CF-Rice facilitates informed decision-making for climate-smart rice production and helps identify opportunities for reducing emissions in rice value chains worldwide.

column16: Excel-based Cost-Impact Analysis for Emission Reduction (COMPARE) tool developed by IRRI and UNIQUE forestry and land use GmbH for automated cost-benefit evaluation of mitigation projects in Vietnam
column17: The Cost-Impact Analysis for Emission Reduction (COMPARE) tool addresses the need for accessible greenhouse gas mitigation project evaluation in developing countries. This Microsoft Excel-based software features built-in formulas that automatically calculate cost-benefit indicators and greenhouse gas emissions based on user inputs. Developed through collaboration between the International Rice Research Institute and UNIQUE Forestry and Land Use, the tool enables project developers and policymakers to efficiently assess the economic and environmental impacts of mitigation initiatives. COMPARE simplifies complex calculations that previously required specialized expertise, making greenhouse gas project evaluation more accessible to local organizations and government agencies working on climate change mitigation in Vietnam and similar contexts.

column16: The Climate Security Observatory (CSO) for livestock production systems
column17: The Climate Security Observatory (CSO) is an online dashboard targeting policy and decision makers, development and humanitarian practitioners and advisors to help them with targeting, programming and prioritization of investments particularly in areas under climate stress. The CSO uses a mixed method approach to give answers to four lead questions: Where are the most vulnerable areas to climate-related insecurities and risks? Who are the groups vulnerable to climate and security risks that should be targeted? How does climate exacerbate the causes of conflict? What needs to be done to break the vicious cycle between climate and conflict? The CSO brings together robust, localized and contextualized and policy-relevant evidence on the climate-security nexus. It includes a dashboard on climate security programming for climate finance, the climate security sensitivity tool, climate security mapping and an interactive dashboard for climate security dialogues. ;

column16: Standardized breeding framework developed by CGIAR to align crop improvement with market needs across seven regions
column17: CGIAR's Breeding for Tomorrow program developed a comprehensive framework that standardizes how crop breeding programs align with market demands. The system catalogues 1,135 traits across all CGIAR crops, organized into 15 value propositions that deliver benefits to farmers, seed companies, and consumers. The framework includes Target Product Profiles that guide breeding decisions and a Breeding Portal that assesses whether breeding goals are both scientifically feasible and market-relevant. Currently, 295 breeding profiles meet feasibility criteria, targeting improvements in productivity, pest resistance, climate adaptation, nutrition, and end-use quality. The framework covers 359 million hectares across 105 countries, reaching areas where 47 million people live on less than $2.15 daily. Twenty national partners have adopted this approach, creating 291 additional breeding profiles, demonstrating successful knowledge transfer and organizational change in crop improvement practices.

column16: Framework developed by IFPRI to measure gender-sensitive climate adaptation in agrifood systems for climate finance
column17: Climate finance often fails to adequately address gender equality in agricultural adaptation strategies due to lack of clear measurement frameworks. The International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) developed this national-level framework to help governments and organizations measure how well their climate change adaptation strategies integrate gender considerations in agrifood systems. The framework provides practical guidance for directing climate financing toward projects that promote both climate resilience and gender equality. It includes key elements that can be applied across different contexts to ensure climate adaptation investments benefit women and men equitably in agricultural communities worldwide.

column16: Hyper-Localized Fertilizer Advisory System: Precision Nutrient Management for Ethiopian Smallholder Farmers
column17: The innovation is a personalized fertilizer recommendation that demonstrates and generates a two-stage optimal fertilizer rate. The first stage builds on legacy agronomic data-driven optimal fertilizer recommendations at 30 m resolution from a machine learning decision support system. The second stage is a refined farmer-reported context-based fertilizer adjustment from the data-driven baseline application. The farmer context input considers localized soil, terrain, moisture, and crop management factors. The system applies a percentage adjustment for hyperlocalization to the data-driven recommendations.

column16: Spent Pleurotus ostreatus Substrate Has Potential for Controlling the Plant-Parasitic Nematode, Radopholus similis in Bananas
column17: Spent mushroom substrate (SMS), a waste product from mushroom cultivation, in addition to being rich in essential nutrients for crop growth, contains actively growing mushroom mycelia and metabolites that suppress some plant pathogens and pests. SMS thus has potential for fostering the suppressiveness of soil-borne pathogens of farms. This study determined the potential of using the spent Pleurotus ostreatus substrate (SPoS) to suppress the plant-parasitic nematode Radopholus similis in bananas. R. similis is the most economically important nematode in bananas worldwide. The effect of SPoS on R. similis was assessed through two in vivo (potted plants) experiments between May 2023 and June 2024. Five-month-old East African highland banana (genome AAA) plantlets that are highly susceptible to R. similis were used. In the first experiment, the plantlets were established in 3 L pots containing (i) pre-sterilized soil, (ii) pre-sterilized soil inoculated with nematodes, (iii) pre-sterilized soil mixed with 30% (v/v) SPoS, (iv) pre-sterilized soil mixed with 30% (v/v) SPoS followed by nematode inoculation, (v) SPoS without soil, and (vi) SPoS without soil inoculated with nematodes. The SPoS was already decomposed; thus, it may or may not have contained active mycelia. The nematodes were introduced two weeks after the SPoS application. In the second experiment, SPoS was introduced two weeks after nematode inoculation. The SPoS treatments without soil were not evaluated in the second experiment. Both experiments were monitored over a three-month period. Each screenhouse treatment contained four plants and was replicated thrice. In the first experiment, data were collected on changes in soil nutrient content, below- and aboveground biomass, root deaths, root necrosis due to nematode damage, and R. similis population in root tissues and soil. In the second experiment, data were collected on root deaths and the number of nematodes in root tissues and the soil. The SPoS improved crop biomass yield, reduced root damage, and colonization by R. similis.

column16: Field evaluation of spent Pleurotus ostreatus substrate reveals limited suppression of Fusarium Wilt in banana
column17: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc), the causal agent of Fusarium wilt of banana, can persist in the soil for extended periods as chlamydospores or endophytes in weeds, complicating control measures. No single control strategy is effective. Biological agents present an increasingly important control option. This study explored the potential of the spent P. ostreatus substrates (SPoS) to suppress Foc R1 in a field with high Foc inoculum, following laboratory and greenhouse studies that highlighted the potential of P. ostreatus as a biocontrol agent against Foc. A susceptible cultivar ‘Sukali Ndizi’ and a resistant cultivar ‘Mpologoma’ were used for the study. SPoS was compared with farmyard manure (FYM), a combination of SPoS with FYM and a control without treatment. A one-time application of the treatments at planting did not consistently and significantly (p > 0.05) reduce the prevalence and severity of leaf symptoms, pseudostem splitting and corm damage in the mother and ratoon plants of the susceptible cultivar. No symptoms occurred in ‘Mpologoma’. SPoS applications at planting and after every two months over an 8-month period did not significantly reduce leaf symptoms and corm damage in ‘Sukali Ndizi’, while it increased pseudostem splitting. The marginal and irregular reductions in FW could be due to an observed high weevil damage in SPoS treatments and other confounding factors such as weather, SPoS quality, and pathogen load in the field. Further research on weevil–SPoS interactions, use of P. ostreatus mycelium-rich substrate, and other confounding factors is crucial for fine tuning P. ostreatus use.

column16: Screening for the Efficacy of Botanicals and Soaps in Controlling the Banana Aphid Pentalonia nigronervosa (Hemiptera: Aphididae) Under Laboratory and Screenhouse Conditions
column17: Controlling banana aphid (Pentalonia nigronervosa) vectors of banana bunchy-top disease is crucial for integrated disease management. Synthetic insecticides, though effective in aphid control, pose health and environmental risks. Biorational pesticides (including botanicals and soaps) are safer alternatives. This study screened four fresh and fermented aqueous plant extracts (chili pepper, garlic, neem, and peppermint) and three soaps (bathing, laundry bar, and liquid soap) singly or in mixtures against banana aphids through in vitro and in vivo experiments. Aphid-inoculated banana leaf-blade disks were used for the in vitro studies over 96 h. Potted plantlets were used for the in vivo studies over eight weeks. Applying these preparations resulted in significant (p ≤ 0.05) aphid mortality (28.6 to 100%) compared to the water control (3.3%) at 96 h post-spray (hps). In vitro, a single application of nimbecidine® (Azadirachtin 0.03%), garlic, chili-pepper botanicals, insecticidal, and bathing soap caused >50% mortality at 96 hps. Mixed applications of chili pepper, garlic-based, and neem botanicals with soap caused >70% mortality at 96 hps in vitro. Binary mixtures of neem oil, garlic, fermented garlic, or fermented peppermint with insecticidal soap, and neem oil with bar soap, were promising in vivo, reducing the aphid populations to <20/plant compared to the control, which had >200 aphids after week 8. However, these potential preparations incurred a higher cost (USD 1.30/banana mat) compared to the synthetic pesticide (USD 0.022/mat). Thus, biorational mixtures have a potential to effectively control banana aphids.

column16: Banana Fusarium wilt TR4 mitigation in Vietnam
column17: In Vietnam, bananas are a major crop cultivated widely throughout the country. Banana production is predominantly small-scale, commonly integrated into household gardens or small-holder farming systems. Fusarium wilt, caused by Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc), is one of the most destructive diseases affecting banana production in Viet Nam. In particular, Foc Tropical Race 4 (TR4) has spread rapidly and caused severe damage to Cavendish banana cultivars. To mitigate the impact of TR4, Formosana, a banana cultivar with tolerance to Fusarium wilt, was introduced in Viet Nam. The activity assessed TR4 incidence and agronomic performance of Formosana under field conditions in Viet Nam. In addition, a biological control trial using the SH-Lifu product was conducted to evaluate its effectiveness in reducing FW incidence. Field observations showed that the incidence of Fusarium wilt in Formosana was consistently lower than that in the local cultivar Pink Cavendish across all experimental sites, including Hanoi, Hai Phong, Vinh Phuc, and Hung Yen. The FW incidence in Formosana plantations ranged from a few percent to a maximum of 22%, with an average disease incidence of 8.5%. In contrast, Fusarium wilt incidence in Pink Cavendish ranged from 60% to 80%, with an average of 70%. These results clearly indicate that Formosana possesses a substantially higher level of tolerance to Fusarium wilt compared with Pink Cavendish. Results from the biological control trial demonstrated that SH-Lifu contributed to a reduction in FW incidence. In Formosana, disease incidence in the SH–Lifu–treated plots was 8%, compared with 15% in the untreated control. Similarly, in Pink Cavendish,FW incidence was 25% in treated plots, compared with 35% in the control. These preliminary results suggest that SH-Lifu has potential as a biological measure for reducing Fusarium wilt incidence in banana. Regarding growth and development, Formosana exhibited good vegetative vigor under field conditions

column16: CGIAR Centers adopting EBS and ensuring that their onboarded data is FAIR: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable.
column17: As a fully operational, open-source, and license-free breeding data management platform, the Enterprise Breeding System (EBS) has been designed from inception to comply with the FAIR data principles. FAIR compliance is not treated as a downstream add-on or post-processing activity; rather, the principles of Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability are structurally embedded into EBS across research workflows, data collection processes, and system architecture.; ; Consequently, when a CGIAR Center adopts EBS and onboards its breeding data, it inherently contributes to improving the FAIR maturity of its data assets:; ; - Findable: EBS provides structured metadata management and intuitive search capabilities through a user-friendly interface, enabling users to efficiently discover datasets across programs and experiments.; ; - Accessible: Once configured, EBS leverages CGIAR identity and access management mechanisms, allowing authenticated users to securely access data in accordance with defined authorization levels, ensuring appropriate access while maintaining data protection.; ; - Interoperable: EBS supports standardized API protocols, including BrAPI, enabling seamless data exchange with external systems and applications such as Fieldbook for data collection and BioFlow for advanced analytics.; ; - Reusable: Data onboarded into EBS can be reused across multiple experiments, breeding cycles, and analytical contexts. In addition, externally generated analytical outputs can be reintegrated into EBS, preserving data lineage and enabling longitudinal use.; ; As a result, the number of CGIAR Centers and Breeding Programs adopting EBS are also making EBS data APIs accessible which serves as a direct and meaningful proxy indicator for progress against the FAIR principles at the organizational level.

column16: Seed production system for iron-rich potato varieties developed by International Potato Center scaled in Peru to combat anemia
column17: The International Potato Center developed a comprehensive seed production system to scale iron-rich potato varieties that help address anemia in rural communities. The system involves producing laboratory plants of biofortified varieties and providing them to Peru's National Institute for Agricultural Innovation for multiplication in greenhouses to create foundation seed. Commercial producers then multiply this to generate certified seed for farmers. This approach produced 50,000 laboratory plants of two iron-rich varieties, with the system expected to generate 1,500 tons of certified seed for cultivation across 1,000 hectares, benefiting 32,000 farmers. Peru's Ministry of Agriculture supports this initiative as part of national nutrition improvement efforts through agriculture.

column16: Application delivering customized recommendation for Rice Crop Management
column17: RCM Vietnam enables farmers, extension workers, and crop advisors to generate customized recommendations through a user-friendly interface accessible via computer, tablet, or smartphone at https://webapps.irri.org/vn/rcm-rebuild/. The application collects essential field and management information through five modules comprising 12 questions, including farmer registration, field location, yield target, fertilizer rates, and timing and sources of application. Recommendations are delivered in a concise one-page format, facilitating timely and actionable decision-making. By integrating Site Specific Nutrient Management (SSNM) principles into a digital platform, Rice Crop Management (RCM) Vietnam supports improved rice productivity, profitability, and soil health while contributing to national and global efforts for sustainable agriculture. This report outlines the development, key features, and underlying SSNM-based calculations for nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) that form the foundation of RCM Vietnam. The recommended SSNM (fertilizer rate and application timing) for Mekong River delta (MRD) of Vietnam was verified through a field trial of 24 farmers in 03 districts for the most common aluvial soil type in this region.

column16: A scalable data infrastructure and analytical framework for characterizing small-scale aquaculture systems globally.
column17: This innovation consists of a scalable data infrastructure and analytical framework for the systematic characterization of small-scale aquaculture systems. It integrates modular household survey instruments, robust sampling and triangulation protocols, geospatial suitability analysis, and standardized indicators covering production practices, socioeconomic performance, food security, poverty, and environmental outcomes.; First implemented in Bangladesh for small-scale carp aquaculture, the infrastructure is designed to be transferable across species, production systems, and countries. It enables fine-grained, farm-level analysis that captures the heterogeneity of small-scale aquaculture systems, addressing a critical global data gap that constrains evidence-based policy design, intervention targeting, and impact assessment in aquatic food systems.

column17: Rice supports four billion people and 144 million jobs, yet smallholder yields are increasingly threatened by climate change, and cultivation accounts for one-third of agrifood emissions. column16: Antimicrobial resistance AquaShield: a participatory learning game to promote responsible antimicrobial use in aquaculture
column17: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global public health threat, often driven by the irrational and excessive use of antimicrobials. In aquaculture, inappropriate and excessive antimicrobial use (AMU), frequently linked to limited awareness and restricted access to veterinary advice, contributes to the spread of resistant bacteria, affecting the health of organisms across the food chain. To raise awareness and encourage responsible practices among fish farmers, aquatic animal health practitioners and agrovet medicine sellers, WorldFish in collaboration with Massey University, developed AMR AquaShield, Snakes and Ladders game for antimicrobial stewardship (AMS). The game was developed as part of the Practitioner Engagement Program (PEP), supported by the UK aid-funded Fleming Fund AMROH-SA project and CGIAR’s Sustainable Aquatic and Animal Foods (SAAF) science program.

column16: Eolo digital platform developed by Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT to enhance climate forecasting and advisory services for Honduras meteorological agencies
column17: Climate variability poses significant challenges for agricultural planning and disaster preparedness in Central America. The Eolo platform addresses this by providing meteorological services with advanced tools to compare multiple climate forecasts and generate comprehensive seasonal reports. Developed by the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT under the AgriLAC initiative, this digital innovation enables Honduras' national meteorological service (COPECO–CENAOS) to better analyze seasonal climate predictions using diverse forecasting methodologies. The platform strengthens climate adaptation capabilities by improving the accuracy and accessibility of climate information, ultimately supporting farmers and policymakers in making informed decisions for agricultural planning and risk management strategies.

column17: The AgroTutor GenAI infrastructure provides a configurable framework that lets local projects build their own GenAI/RAG advisory chatbots without rebuilding core components each time. It allows teams to plug in their own agronomic corpora (bulletins, guidelines, FAQs, research summaries), connect these to project-specific crops and contexts, and select or swap the underlying language model according to their requirements. The system supports iterative tuning and refinement of prompts and knowledge bases, and can automatically compile a compendium of question–answer pairs over time, making it progressively easier to maintain a high-quality, locally grounded advisory service. This turns GenAI advisory into a reusable capability that projects can adapt to different geographies and use cases, instead of a one-off, hard-coded chatbot per project

column16: Technical Agroclimatic Committees (MTAs) Dashboard: An interactive dashboard developed by CIAT to monitor participatory climate services across Latin America
column17: This interactive dashboard provides standardized monitoring evidence from 50 MTAs across Colombia, Guatemala, and Honduras, drawing on 668 survey responses collected between 2024 and 2025. Data were gathered through a monitoring survey administered to participants during in-person and virtual MTA sessions, in close coordination with national and subnational facilitating partners. The dataset reflects direct inputs from actors actively engaged in agroclimatic dialogue and decision-making processes. The dashboard synthesizes evidence on who participates, how information is disseminated, and how agroclimatic information is perceived and used. By making these patterns visible, the innovation supports data-driven learning, strengthens accountability, and informs targeted investments to improve the effectiveness, inclusiveness, and scalability of participatory climate services in smallholder agricultural systems.

column16: C limate services participatory assessment tool (CS-PAT) developed by the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT to strengthen climate services ecosystems for improved decision-making in Kenya
column17: Climate Services - Participatory Assessment Tool (CS-PAT) is a structured, participatory diagnostic and decision-support methodology designed to assess and strengthen national and subnational climate services ecosystems. CS-PAT addresses persistent challenges in climate services development—including institutional fragmentation, weak alignment between service providers and users, limited inclusion, and uneven capacity across the climate services value chain—by placing stakeholder engagement and co-production at the centre of the assessment process.; The tool combines ecosystem and institutional mapping, climate services inventories, provider capacity assessments (including national meteorological and hydrological services), and participatory user research grounded in human-centred design principles. Through iterative engagement with service providers, intermediaries, and end users, CS-PAT identifies bottlenecks and opportunities across the climate services cycle—from data generation and forecasting to translation, dissemination, use, and feedback. These insights are jointly interpreted with stakeholders to inform priority actions for improving accessibility, usability, and sustainability of climate services."

column16: MapAWD: Excel-based tool developed by International Rice Research Institute to assess suitability of water-saving rice farming techniques globally
column17: Rice production consumes large amounts of water and generates significant greenhouse gas emissions. The MapAWD tool addresses these challenges by helping researchers and practitioners identify where Alternate Wetting and Drying techniques can be most effectively implemented. This Microsoft Excel-based assessment tool uses a water balance model to map climatically favorable areas for water-saving rice cultivation methods. Developed by the International Rice Research Institute, the tool supports greenhouse gas mitigation projects and enables evaluation of field experiments measuring emission reductions. The tool is freely available and designed for use by agricultural researchers, project developers, and organizations working on sustainable rice production systems worldwide.

column16: Project Brief: A new water balance model leveraging satellite observations for effective water management decisions in data-scarce Paddy-dominated regions
column17: "PaddyWA+ Model is a new 30-m, daily water balance model designed for paddy systems, integrating satellite data to better capture ponding depth, soil water dynamics, and blue/green water use—addressing gaps in traditional WA+ and other water balance models.; Why It Matters: Rice cultivation is highly water-intensive (24–40% of global irrigation withdrawals) and a major methane emitter, yet existing models cannot simulate paddy-specific features like bunded fields, hardpan-limited percolation, or variable irrigation.; Improved Accuracy: Compared to conventional WA+, PaddyWA+ produces more realistic AET , irrigation demand, and percolation estimates, revealing dominant green water use and significant spatial variability in ponding and soil moisture across Bihar.; Decision and Policy Value: The model supports irrigation scheduling, water budgeting, climate-resilient agriculture planning, and crop diversification by offering actionable field- to district-scale indicators.; Future Applications: Can assess water management practices, identify intervention hotspots, support sustainable systems (e.g., rice–fish culture), evaluate climate impacts, and help estimate methane mitigation potential.; "

column16: Excel-based greenhouse gas calculator for cropland developed by International Rice Research Institute to support climate mitigation globally
column17: Climate change mitigation in agriculture requires accurate measurement of greenhouse gas emissions from cropland, particularly rice production which is a significant methane source. The International Rice Research Institute developed SECTOR (Source-selective and Emission-adjusted GHG CalculaTOR for Cropland), a comprehensive calculator based on IPCC Tier 2 methodology. Available in Excel and web formats, this tool enables users to input cropping area, yield, and management practices to calculate emissions. SECTOR supports national greenhouse gas inventories, mitigation project development, and evaluation of field experiments, providing essential data for evidence-based climate action in agricultural systems worldwide.

column16: Annotated source codes of a machine learning model that predicts the extent of tropical cyclone-induced inundation in rice production area for ungauged basins.
column17: Rice farmers in the Philippines face severe flooding from frequent typhoons, but many areas lack early warning systems to predict inundation extent. IRRI and the Alliance developed a machine learning model using historical flood data from the Philippine Rice Information System to predict typhoon-induced flooding in rice production areas. The model was specifically designed for the Bicol Region, one of the Philippines' most typhoon-prone areas, and can work in ungauged basins where traditional monitoring is unavailable. The annotated source code enables partners to adapt and implement the technology for flood prediction and early warning systems, helping rice farmers prepare for and respond to typhoon threats.

column16: Digital water monitoring system developed by Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT helps Ethiopian dryland farmers manage livestock during droughts
column17: Ethiopian dryland farmers struggle with water scarcity that threatens livestock survival and creates conflicts over limited water resources. To address this challenge, the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT developed an innovative digital early warning system that integrates satellite data, weather forecasts, and community knowledge to track water availability in real-time. The system delivers practical advisories to mixed crop-livestock farmers about nearby water sources, optimal grazing locations, and livestock movement strategies. By providing timely, actionable information, this technology enables farmers to make informed decisions that improve livestock survival rates during drought periods while reducing competition and conflicts over scarce water resources in challenging dryland environments.

column16: Nature-based solutions monitoring framework piloted by Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT
column17: The blog describes how Kenya is piloting a national Nature-based Solutions (NbS) Monitoring & Evaluation (M&E) framework in the Chyulu Hills landscape to strengthen consistent tracking, learning, and reporting on NbS outcomes. It explains the growing pressures on Kenya’s ecosystems—land degradation, deforestation, competing land uses, and climate change—and why NbS are increasingly central to national priorities and commitments (including NDC targets on restoration and forest cover). Using Chyulu Hills (spanning Makueni, Kajiado, and Taita Taveta) as a case study, the pilot tests whether proposed indicators are practical and relevant across a complex, multi-use dryland system that is vital for biodiversity, water resources, and livelihoods. Key lessons highlight that NbS practices are widespread but fragmented and poorly documented, and that effective monitoring must integrate ecological, socio-economic, and governance dimensions through strong collaboration with counties and communities.

column16: Establishing Ethiopia’s Multi-Stakeholder Platform to Strengthen Coordination, Bundle Agronomic Innovations, Align Policy and Digital Systems, and Accelerate Sustainable, Locally Owned Scaling Pathways for System-Wide Agricultural Transformation
column17: Agricultural systems across low- and middle-income countries continue to face a persistent “scaling gap,” where proven technologies, digital tools, and improved agronomic practices fail to reach smallholder farmers at meaningful scale. This challenge is less about the absence of solutions and more about fragmented actors, weak coordination, limited integration between research and implementation, and insufficient alignment with policy and delivery systems.; ; Partnerships for Accelerating Agronomic Solutions at Scale (PAASS) was developed to address these systemic constraints through a structured, multi-stakeholder platform approach. PAASS convenes researchers, government agencies, private sector actors, NGOs, farmer organizations, and donors within a shared governance framework that enables joint prioritization, co-creation, validation, and scaling of context-specific, demand-driven innovations. By bridging research with extension, markets, and policy processes, PAASS ensures that solutions are not only technically robust but operationally feasible.; ; A core feature of PAASS is innovation bundling—integrating technical, digital, and institutional solutions to address interconnected farmer challenges such as soil fertility, water management, climate risk, and market access. Embedded monitoring, evaluation, and learning systems enable continuous feedback, adaptive management, and evidence-informed decision-making. Digital enabling platforms further support coordinated delivery and knowledge exchange.; ; Ethiopia provides a strong case for PAASS due to its rich research ecosystem, digital extension ambitions, and policy commitment to agricultural transformation, alongside persistent coordination gaps. The Ethiopia PAASS platform has been established through an iterative, collaborative process focused on institutional anchoring, partner alignment, and national ownership. It supports harmonized advisory approaches, policy integration, and AI-enabled knowledge systems to accelerate sustainable, inclusive scaling of agronomic innovations beyond project cycles.

column16: A Scalable, African-Owned Climate Intelligence and Governance Platform Integrating Climate Hazards, Finance Flows, and Litigation Data
column17: Africa is widely recognized as a continent facing persistent data scarcity. The continent could achieve far greater outcomes if the quality, accessibility, and ownership of data-and the information derived from it-were improved. Beyond improving data quality, efforts in Africa should transform to data ownership. In the era of rapidly evolving, data-intensive artificial intelligence, Africa must becoming a continent of data ownership and ensure its digital sovereignty. This Innovation develops a scalable database for observed climate hazards and impacts, climate finance flows (and instruments), and climate litigation cases across Africa. The database will be enriched both retrospectively and proactively with rigorously verified information on observed climate hazards, their impacts, climate finance instruments, and the status and trends of climate-related litigation cases across the continent to inform climate adaptation, mitigation, Loss and Damage policies, support Africa’s climate negotiators, enhance Africa’s digital sovereignty and evidence-based climate governance.
