column16: Nutritious small indigenous fish cultivation system for low-income communities in East Kolkata Wetlands, India
column17: Small indigenous fish species in East Kolkata Wetlands have been overlooked despite their high nutritional value and importance for food security. These native fish enhance pond productivity and provide essential nutrients for wetland-dependent communities. CGIAR's International Water Management Institute developed an integrated cultivation system that combines policy support, capacity building, financial access mechanisms, and quality seed provision. This innovation enables small farmers to revitalize indigenous fish farming, addressing both ecological restoration and livelihood needs in India's threatened wetland ecosystems while improving household nutrition for vulnerable populations.

column16: Rust Surveillance under Drought Conditions Reveals Limited Stem Rust Incidence in Morocco and Minimal Infection in Lebanon in 2025
column17: Wheat rust diseases caused by Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici, Puccinia triticina, and Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici remain a major constraint to wheat production in the Central and West Asia and North Africa (CWANA) region. During the 2025 cropping season, severe and persistent drought affected major wheat-growing areas, including Morocco and Lebanon, substantially limiting crop development and rust disease expression. Nevertheless, systematic rust surveillance was conducted to support early detection and regional preparedness. Surveys were carried out in more than 70 wheat fields following standard Borlaug Global Rust Initiative (BGRI) protocols, with geo-referenced data collected using the ODK mobile application and integrated into the Wheat Toolbox platform. In Morocco, stem rust was detected at low incidence in 37 fileds of surveyed fields and at moderate incidence in 16 fields, with high incidence observed in only one field; the remaining fields showed no infection. Leaf rust and yellow rust were rare and highly localized. In Lebanon rust diseases were largely absent in 50 visted wheat fields duirng the rust surveys, with only a single trace stem rust infection detected during the survey period. No significant rust infection developed in rust trap nurseries established in either country. Although drought conditions limited disease pressure and resistance evaluation, the detection of stem rust under unfavorable environments confirms pathogen persistence in the CWANA region and underscores the importance of sustained surveillance and coordinated early warning systems.

column16: Develop accurate molecular detection tool for Poleroviruses affecting cool-season food legumes in Central and West Asia and North Africa to support breeding for resistance and crop management purposes
column17: Viral diseases causing yellowing, stunting and leaf roll, that transmitted by aphids in a persistent manner, are among the most devastating diseases affecting cool-season food legumes worldwide. Virus species of genus Polerovirus (family Solemoviridae) cannot be distinguished serologically using polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies due to their cross-reactivity with other non-target viruses, and the often-low viral concentration in plants. Furthermore, antibodies for many Polerovirus species are not readily available. To overcome these limitations and enable accurate virus identification for resistance breeding and crop management purposes, a molecular diagnostic toolbox for poleroviruses infecting legumes was developed using generic and species-specific reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) primers, followed by sequencing of the target coat protein gene. The developed tool clearly demonstrated the presence of several Polerovirus species, causing yellowing and stunting, that naturally infect a range of cool-season food legumes in Central and West Asia and North Africa (CWANA). These viruses are Beet western yellows virus (BWYV), Chickpea chlorotic stunt virus (CpCSV), Cucurbit aphid-borne yellows virus (CABYV), Cotton leafroll dwarf virus (CLRDV), Pepper vein yellows virus (PeVYV), Pepo aphid-borne yellows virus (PABYV) and Phasey bean mild yellows virus (PBMYV). The molecular tool was validated by testing food legumes samples collected from Ethiopia, Tunisia, Morocco, Nepal and Uzbekistan. It was also shared with partners participating in the diagnostic network to accurately identify Polerovirus species, their diversity, and their prevalence in the CWANA. The resulting diagnostic framework provides scientists and breeders with a clearer understanding of viruses that may pose a threat to legume crops, and a suitable tool for field surveillance, epidemiological studies, germplasm screening within resistance-breeding programs, and required crop management options.

column16: Identification of three wheat stem rust races TKKTF, TKTTF, and TTTTF in Morocco during the 2025 Season
column17: Monitoring wheat rust pathogen variability is critical for sustaining effective resistance breeding and disease management, particularly in resource-limited regions where new virulent races emerge frequently. Continuous surveillance enables early detection of population shifts and supports informed deployment of resistance genes. This study reports stem rust race composition identified through coordinated surveillance conducted during the 2025 cropping season in the CWANA region, with analyses performed at the Türkiye-ICARDA Regional Cereal Rust Research Center (RCRRC), Izmir. Wheat rust surveys were conducted in farmer fields and research stations in Morocco and Lebanon. Rust samples were collected using standardized protocols and processed under quarantine conditions. Viable Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici isolates were multiplied, purified through single-pustule isolation, and characterized using the 20 North American stem rust differential lines. Infection types were assessed using standard scoring and race nomenclature systems. A total of 41 rust samples were received, including 25 stem rust samples from Morocco. Severe drought conditions limited disease development and sample recovery, resulting in unsuccessful yellow rust isolation. Three stem rust races, TKKTF, TKTTF, and TTTTF, were identified, with TTTTF being the predominant race. Virulence analysis showed that resistance genes Sr24 and Sr31 remained effective against all isolates, indicating the absence of Ug99 lineage races during the 2025 season.

column16: Surveillance and risk assessment of lentil viruses in Nepal using accurate serological and RT-PCR diagnostic tools
column17: A field survey was conducted during 23–27 February 2025, in three regions of Nepal (Kathmandu, Lumbini and Gandaki) to assess the prevalence of viruses affecting lentil crops. A total of 2,041 random samples and 210 symptomatic samples were collected from 22 lentil fields and tested by tissue blot immunoassay (TBIA) using a battery of polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies. Further testing of selected TBIA-positive samples was performed using RT-PCR with generic and specific primers. The TBIA results showed that the most prevalent lentil viruses were Pea seed-borne mosaic virus (PSbMV) (overall infection rate in the random samples of 18.5%), Cucumber mosaic virus (15%) and number of polerovirus/luteovirus species. Molecular testing has confirmed for the first time the presence of the following viruses in Nepal: Beet western virus (BWYV), Cucurbit aphid-borne yellows virus (CABYV), Chickpea chlorotic stunt virus (CpCSV), Brassica yellows virus (BrYV) (genus Polerovirus, family Solemoviridae) and Soybean dwarf virus (SbDV) (genus Luteovirus, family Tombusviridae). The widespread presence of seed-borne viruses (PSbMV and CMV) highlights the need for seed testing within the lentil seed certification system. The presence of several aphid-transmitted poleroviruses also necessitates the development of diseases management strategies, as outbreaks in Nepal’s lentil crops can lead to significant yield losses. The findings of this study will contribute to the development of serological and molecular tools for virus monitoring and identification. Furthermore, this study provides essential information to support the Nepalese lentil breeding program for developing virus-resistant varieties and will guide the Nepalese Seed Certification Authority in implementing seed-borne virus testing in lentils.

column16: Integrated Agroecological Innovations for Sustainable Systems in Tunisia
column17: This innovation bundle combines four complementary agroecological technologies designed to strengthen the resilience and sustainability of cereal–forage–olive farming systems in Tunisia’s semi-arid regions. Together, they promote soil regeneration, efficient water and nutrient use, and improved crop–livestock productivity for smallholder farmers.; ; The first innovation (code: 16668) introduces biochar, produced from olive pruning residues through low-cost pyrolysis, to enhance soil structure, water-holding capacity, and fertilizer efficiency. Field trials show that biochar nearly doubles durum wheat yields when integrated with mineral fertilizers.; ; The second (code: 16681) focuses on forage mixtures combining vetch, oat, and triticale, which diversify cereal-based systems, increase biomass production, and improve feed quality for small ruminants. These mixtures are being co-developed with national research institutions (INRAT, OEP, ICARDA) and commercialized through private sector partners.; ; The third innovation (code: 16685) promotes Rhizobia inoculation of legume forage seeds (vetch, faba bean, sulla) to boost biological nitrogen fixation, reduce fertilizer dependence, and build long-term soil fertility while improving forage protein content and yield.; ; Finally (code: 7359), a public–private partnership with COTUGRAIN ensures the large-scale production and dissemination of adapted forage seed mixtures, including inoculated seeds from the new Rhizobia unit in El Grine. This collaboration has greatly expanded seed availability and adoption, linking research innovation to field-level impact.; By integrating these solutions—biochar for soil enhancement, legume–cereal forages for diversity, biological inoculants for fertility, and seed partnerships for scaling—this bundle offers a holistic pathway toward agroecological transition, increasing productivity, sustainability, and climate resilience across Tunisian farming systems.

column16: Registration of 6 new maize hybrids in Mexico
column17: CIMMYT has newly registered six maize hybrids at the Mexican Registration Office (SNICS), enabling scaling partners to produce and sell certified seed in Mexico. The newly registered, high-yielding, climate-resilient and multiple-stress-tolerant hybrids include: CSTHY18103, CIM20LAPP2B-2, CIM20LAPP1A-11, CIM20LAPP1A-12, CIM20LAPP1C-9 and CIM20LAPP1C-10. Mexican government programs require that the seed they purchase be officially certified (as opposed to quality-declared seed, which is also allowed under Mexican seed regulations). These varieties will therefore be attractive to seed companies targeting government clients. Many Mexican farmers also prefer to purchase certified seed for their own use. Because these varieties have been registered directly under CIMMYT's name, CIMMYT is able to issue non-exclusive licenses to scaling partners to produce certified seed. In the absence of this registration, CIMMYT would be obligated to issue only exclusive licenses (e.g., to a NARES partner or private-sector scaling partner) for certified seed production and commercialization, which would limit the potential for scaling the product through multiple partners.

column16: A Zero-Tillage Rice–Potato System with Rice Straw Mulch to Boost Yield, Save Water, Cut Emissions, and Increase Income for Smallholder Farmers in India and Bangladesh
column17: The primary focus is on enhancing agricultural productivity and sustainability. Specifically, the innovation aims to increase yield and marketable yield in zero tillage potato and rice straw mulch (PZTM) compared to conventional tillage (CT). It also seeks to reduce water use by 50%, doubling water productivity. Additionally, the innovation aims to reduce global warming potential and emission intensity, leading to significant economic returns for farmers due to savings in input costs and higher returns from increased yields.; The primary users of the innovation are smallholder farmers in India and Bangladesh. The project targets 2,000 smallholder farmers who have introduced zero tillage potato production using rice straw mulch. These farmers are expected to see an increase in gross margins by 15%. The innovation also involves training and empowering women farmers, with a target of 1,000 women confirming an improvement in their position as producers in the rice-potato zero tillage cultivation system.

column16: AI-powered digital platform to accelerate tropical forage breeding
column17: Tropical forage breeding faces challenges in efficiently analyzing large datasets from field research and remote sensing. The Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT developed a comprehensive digital infrastructure that enables the creation, management, and deployment of artificial intelligence tools for forage research. This infrastructure supports machine learning operations by providing the technical foundation needed to build datasets, develop predictive models, and create software applications for high-throughput plant analysis. The system facilitates iterative research workflows that help scientists accelerate trait discovery and improve breeding cycles for tropical forages. This innovation addresses the growing need for advanced digital tools in agricultural research, particularly for crops that are essential for livestock systems in tropical regions.

column16: ERA is A FAIR, harmonized dataset integrating 198,310 agronomic observations to accelerate modelling, AI analytics, and policy-ready insights for climate-resilient agricultural decision-making in Africa.
column17: vidence for Resilient Agriculture (ERA) v1.0.1 is a breakthrough FAIR data innovation that transforms fragmented agronomic knowledge into a structured, standardized, and machine-ready evidence ecosystem. ERA harmonizes 198,310 observations from 2,916 agricultural studies conducted across Africa between 1934 and 2018, covering 364 management practices and technologies and 87 agronomic, environmental, and socioeconomic outcomes. All observations are geolocated and temporally tagged, enabling the dataset to be linked with climate hazards, soils, infrastructure, and other contextual layers. This creates an unprecedented foundation for cross-scale modelling, climate-risk analysis, and AI-driven evidence synthesis.; ; ERA addresses a critical bottleneck for researchers, policy actors, donors, and advanced analytics teams: agronomic evidence has historically been scattered across thousands of inaccessible or incomparable studies, slowing decision cycles and limiting the ability to design scalable, context-specific interventions. ERA converts this complexity into a unified, comparable evidence platform that significantly reduces analysis time, lowers transaction costs, and increases confidence in identifying what works, where, and under which conditions.; ; ERA is now used across multiple CGIAR programs and partner institutions to support climate hazard mapping, modelling workflows, soil and nutrient management research, and policy-ready evidence briefs. It has been integrated into AI pipelines for automated evidence summarization and decision-support, enabling rapid translation of scientific data into practical insights for investment planning and agricultural adaptation strategies.; ; By establishing a high-quality, open, reproducible agronomic evidence base, ERA directly strengthens CGIAR’s capacity to generate targeted, climate-smart recommendations, enhances the rigor of multi-country analyses, and supports national and regional policy dialogues. As a foundational data innovation, ERA enables more informed, timely, and equitable decisions for building resilient farming systems across Africa.

column16: Framework for Embedding Nutrition into Breeding Pipelines and Processes (FENBPP), a tool for integrating, categorizing, and tracking nutrition objectives within CGIAR breeding pipelines
column17: In 2025, Better Diets and Nutrition lead the development of the Framework for Embedding Nutrition into Breeding Pipelines and Processes (FENBPP), a classification and design tool for integrating, categorizing, and tracking nutrition objectives within CGIAR breeding pipelines. The FENBPP is: (1) Consistent with CGIAR Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning, and Impact Assessment (MELIA) principles, (2) operationally realistic for breeding programs, and (3) actionable for nutritionists and scaling teams. The FENBPP enables transparent, consistent prioritization of nutrition across the breeding and innovation continuum, from discovery and product profile development through breeding, release, and scaling, while recognizing that yield, resilience, and agronomic performance remain the primary determinants of varietal adoption. The guidance note on the FENBPP explains how the framework is assigned using a decision tree; the description and application of the framework options; where and how the framework is applied across the innovation lifecycle; indicative governance and roles to support application of the framework; and relevant resources and a glossary of key terms. This innovation is a strategic part of Better Diets and Nutrition's goal to see nutrition embedded into breeding pipelines and processes. ;

column16: Iron and zinc-enriched pearl millet varieties PM-ND1 and PM-ND2 released by ICRISAT and partners in Zimbabwe
column17: ICRISAT collaborated with Zimbabwe's Crop Breeding Institute to develop and officially release two biofortified pearl millet varieties, PM-ND1 and PM-ND2, specifically adapted to local growing conditions. These varieties contain enhanced levels of iron and zinc, essential micronutrients often lacking in traditional diets. The varieties were selected for their superior agronomic performance, consumer acceptance, and nutritional content. Their release addresses widespread micronutrient deficiencies and food security challenges in Zimbabwe, providing farmers with climate-resilient crops that can improve household nutrition. The varieties have potential for broader adoption across the Eastern and Southern Africa region, where pearl millet is an important staple crop for smallholder farmers in semi-arid areas.

column16: ICRISAT develops speed breeding protocol enabling four to five finger millet generations per year for faster variety development
column17: Finger millet is a nutritious crop vital for food security in Asia and Africa, but traditional breeding takes years to develop improved varieties. ICRISAT created Rapid-Ragi, a speed breeding protocol that accelerates finger millet breeding cycles from the current one or two generations per year under field conditions to four or five generations annually. This breakthrough significantly reduces the time needed to develop new finger millet varieties with improved traits like drought tolerance and enhanced nutrition. The protocol enables breeders to deliver improved varieties faster to farmers, supporting food security and climate resilience in regions where finger millet is a staple crop.

During deployment in 2025 ~1500 experimental plots were measured using CT imaging.

column16: Two-step screening method developed by ICRISAT uses imaging technology and field testing to identify drought-tolerant groundnut varieties
column17: Groundnut crops need early vigour to survive drought conditions, but measuring this trait in the field is challenging and resource-intensive. ICRISAT developed an innovative two-step screening method that combines high-throughput imaging technology (Leasyscan) with managed stress environment testing. The method was optimized between 2021-2024 and deployed in 2024-25 to evaluate approximately 1,600 groundnut lines. The imaging platform rapidly measures early vigour, allowing researchers to select the most promising 20% of varieties for further field testing under controlled drought conditions. This approach dramatically reduces the resources needed for drought tolerance screening while maintaining accuracy in identifying resilient groundnut varieties for breeding programs worldwide.

column16: Digital platform developed by International Livestock Research Institute consolidates feed composition data for livestock stakeholders across Sub-Saharan Africa
column17: Livestock producers and researchers in Sub-Saharan Africa often lack access to reliable feed composition data, limiting their ability to make informed decisions about animal nutrition. The International Livestock Research Institute developed this centralized digital platform to address this challenge by consolidating feed information from multiple sources into a single, validated repository. The platform features a user-friendly interface that allows users to easily search, filter, and export feed data without technical expertise. A secure approval system ensures only validated data is published, maintaining reliability. The system uses modern technology including React frontend and Python backend for long-term scalability. Standardized data entry templates reduce inconsistencies, while dashboards provide insights into feed types and geographic coverage, supporting evidence-based livestock development across the region.

column16: Livestock Feed Quality Database: An Open-Access Platform for Feed and Forage Nutritional Data
column17: The Livestock Feed Quality Database is an open-access digital platform designed to collect, manage, and disseminate high-quality nutritional data on livestock feeds and forages. Developed as part of a broader effort to strengthen feed data management, accessibility, and consistency across livestock research and development initiatives. To ensure technical harmonization and enable future integration, the platform was built using an advanced technology stack comprising a React-based frontend, a Python backend, and a MySQL relational database. This standardized approach supports long-term scalability, easier maintenance, and improved synchronization across regional feed databases. It supports a role-based login system, structured data submission through standardized templates, and a defined approval workflow to ensure accuracy and reliability of published data. The platform provides intuitive search, filtering, visualization, and export features, enabling users to explore feed quality information efficiently. By combining robust data governance with user-friendly design improvements, the database enhances accessibility, comparability, and reuse of feed quality data, supporting research, ration formulation, and informed decision-making in livestock systems.

column16: Stepwise Calibration and Field Application of Our Sci Reflectometer for Soil Organic Carbon Monitoring and Advisory Services in Moroccan Drylands
column17: This report describes calibration and validation of affordable, fine-scale hand-held Our Sci-Reflectometer, a soil organic carbon monitoring device and generating actionable advisory for improving soil fertility in Dryland soil in Morocco. The device was calibrated  by using over 400 soil samples collected across different ecology in Central Morocco and analysed in the soi laboratory. This describes an end-to-end workflow for rapid, geo-referenced monitoring of soil organic carbon (SOC) in Moroccan dryland croplands using the Our Sci-Reflectometer integrated with the SurveyStack Kit mobile application. The workflow converts discrete-wavelength soil reflectance measurements (10 LEDs spanning 365–940 nm) and embedded environmental sensors (temperature, humidity, pressure) into (i) SOC predictions, (ii) SOC status classes, and (iii) field-level, actionable soil-fertility enhancement recommendations displayed immediately to farmers/extension staff.

column16: Plot-Specific Fertilizer Advisory Tool for Major Dryland Crops to Enhance Yield and Farm Profitability While Minimizing Nutrient Losses and Environmental Impacts
column17: This report presents the evidence based and scalable, plot-specific ‘Fertilizer Advisory’ Tool for major Dryland crops that enhances crop yield and farm profitability while minimizing nutrient losses and environmental impacts. ICARDA developed and validated Excel-based Fertilizer Advisor Tool, which integrates—soil properties, climate/weather data, and farmers provided management practices—to establish a realistic yield target, estimate indigenous nutrient supply, and generate nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K) recommendations aligned with 4R Nutrient Stewardship principles (right source, rate, time, and place). The tool has been validated against survey dataset of 2,042 wheat fields in Egypt demonstrates tool’s superior performance compared to farmers’ practices. Tool-generated rates show strong alignment with observed yields (R² = 0.89 for N; 0.69 for P₂O₅; and 0.39 for K₂O), while farmers’ rates exhibit near-zero correlation (R² = 0.009, 0.008, and 0.02, respectively). For wheat in Egypt, on average, the tool recommends 176 kg N/ha versus average farmers’ 246 kg N/ha, indicating potential to reduce N overuse by approximately 28% without yield penalty, alongside more targeted P and K applications that address both overuse and underuse. This tool directly supports enhanced productivity, resource efficiency, climate resilience, and reduced environmental footprints in intensified cropping systems.

column16: Aflasafe Biocontrol for Aflatoxin Prevention in Staple Crops: Field-Level Protection, Farmer Awareness, and Safer Food Systems to Safeguard Health, Trade, and Livelihoods in African Smallholder Farming Communities
column17: Aflasafe, a biocontrol technology developed by IITA to prevent aflatoxin contamination in staple crops such as maize, sorghum, and groundnut. Aflatoxins are toxic compounds produced by Aspergillus fungi that occur naturally in soils and crop residues. They are invisible, odorless, and tasteless, making contamination difficult to detect and awareness low among farmers, traders, and consumers. Yet aflatoxins pose severe risks to human and livestock health, contributing to liver cancer, stunting, weakened immunity, and reduced market access.; ; The work addresses aflatoxin contamination at its source in the field. Because infection begins during crop growth and can worsen through poor post-harvest handling, weather variability, and storage conditions, prevention at the farm level is critical. Aflasafe contains naturally occurring, non-toxin-producing strains of Aspergillus that competitively displace toxin-producing strains. Applied by simple broadcasting at low rates during crop growth, the product reduces aflatoxin contamination before harvest, aligning with the principle that prevention is more effective than remediation.; ; The program combines farmer awareness, training, and dissemination strategies to increase understanding of aflatoxin risks and promote safe crop management practices. By integrating Aflasafe into smallholder farming systems, the initiative supports safer food and feed supply chains while improving trade opportunities for farmers whose produce meets safety standards.; ; Aflasafe is environmentally friendly, affordable, and easy to use, and works across multiple crops at the same application rate. This multi-crop applicability enhances cost-effectiveness and accessibility, enabling broad uptake among smallholder households. Overall, the initiative contributes to improved public health, food safety, agricultural productivity, and livelihoods, while strengthening resilience in staple crop value chains across Africa.;

column16: The Global Biodiversity Digital Hub to connect researchers, practitioners and innovators across biodiversity conservation and digital innovation ecosystems
column17: The Global Biodiversity Digital Hub (GBDH), launched by CGIAR, serves as a community-owned digital gateway that connects researchers, practitioners, and innovators within the biodiversity conservation ecosystem. The hub addresses the fragmentation of biodiversity data, tools, and expertise across diverse platforms and institutions by providing intelligent linkages rather than duplicating resources. It comprises five interconnected spaces: The Exchange, which facilitates AI-enhanced dialogue; The Collection, which offers curated data portals and tools; The Lab, which supports emerging innovations; The Academy, which provides learning resources; and The Nexus, which fosters partnerships. These spaces promote discovery, collaboration, and knowledge sharing without geographic limitations. The hub's zero-storage, link-back architecture ensures that original data providers maintain ownership and gain visibility to a global audience. Coordinated by the International Potato Center (CIP), the hub is structured for community governance. By enhancing the discoverability of existing resources and facilitating professional connections, the GBDH advances biodiversity conservation and supports large-scale collective action.

column16: AquaSmart digital irrigation tool tested by smallholder farmers in Guatemala's Dry Corridor to optimize water use
column17: Water scarcity and unpredictable weather patterns in Guatemala's Dry Corridor threaten agricultural productivity for smallholder farmers. To address this challenge, the Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT, in collaboration with Centro Universitario de Oriente, developed AquaSmart, a digital irrigation tool that helps farmers make informed decisions about when and how much to water their crops. The user-friendly application features a simple interface accessible to farmers with varying digital literacy levels. In 2024, farmers pilot-tested the tool at the Digital Agroclimatic Plot under real field conditions, providing valuable feedback that guided its development. By enabling farmers to optimize irrigation timing and water quantities, AquaSmart helps reduce water waste and enhance crop resilience in climate-vulnerable agricultural systems.

column16: Pheno-i digital phenotyping system to detect rice diseases early using drone-based aerial imaging for breeders and farmers
column17: The Pheno-i Drone system supports early and reliable detection of major rice diseases by analyzing images collected from drones flying over farmers’ fields and breeding trials. It is currently used to monitor rice plants affected by hoja blanca disease and rice blast disease, two conditions that cause serious yield losses if not identified in time.; ; Using aerial images, the system observes changes in plant color, leaf damage patterns, and uneven crop growth that are difficult to detect from the ground. These visual signals are automatically translated into clear field maps showing healthy areas, moderately affected zones, and severely affected patches. This allows breeders, researchers, and field teams to quickly understand where disease pressure is highest and develop disease classification models.; ; For breeders, the system helps compare rice lines with traits such as disease tolerance, stable growth under infection pressure, and better recovery after stress. This supports faster selection of resilient rice types suited for disease-prone environments.; ; For farmers and extension teams, the drone-based view enables early warning and targeted field visits, reducing unnecessary spraying and helping protect yields. By combining wide field coverage with simple visual outputs, the Pheno-i Drone system turns field images into practical decisions for both crop improvement and disease management.

column16: Semi-autotrophic hydroponics system developed by IITA accelerates yam breeding and seed production in West Africa
column17: Yam breeding has traditionally been hampered by slow multiplication rates and long breeding cycles, limiting farmers' access to improved varieties. The International Institute of Tropical Agriculture developed a semi-autotrophic hydroponics system that transforms yam breeding by enabling rapid multiplication of early-generation planting material. This system achieves multiplication rates of 1:5 to 1:10 within eight weeks, reducing breeding cycles by 2-3 years and producing hundreds of thousands of minitubers annually. The technology has enabled distribution of six improved yam varieties to 47 locations across 15 Nigerian states, with expansion to Ghana, Benin, and Côte d'Ivoire. By addressing the critical bottleneck of seed availability, this innovation strengthens the entire yam improvement pipeline and enhances food security for millions of yam-dependent households in West Africa.

column16: Adaptive scaling approach to enable food system transformation in the Global South
column17: Adaptive scaling views scaling as a living process that evolves alongside people, technologies, markets, institutions, and local conditions. Recognizing that systems change over time, adaptive scaling must adapt to those changes. It emphasizes relationships, learning, and collaboration among different actors, helping them work together to navigate complexity and support lasting transformation in food systems. It acts as a guiding compass, enabling innovators, decision-makers, and businesses identify where change is possible, manage risks and trade-offs, and align collective action as conditions shift. Adaptability is central to scaling efforts must be responsive, reflective, inclusive, and flexible to remain effective. In practice, operationalizing adaptive scaling is through four interconnected functions: Creating protected spaces where new ideas can be tested and improved; Supporting wider use by tailoring innovations to local needs and contexts; Removing barriers by aligning policies, finance, skills, and infrastructure; and embedding scaling into broader systems, influencing rules, norms, and ways of working to enable system change.

column16: Global online marketplace connecting capacity development resources and providers with users in the CGIAR and in agricultural research organizations
column17: Agricultural research organizations worldwide often struggle to find relevant training programs, expertise, and capacity development resources, leading to fragmented and inefficient skill-building efforts. To address this challenge, CGIAR's Capacity Sharing (CapSha) Accelerator developed an innovative digital marketplace that serves as a comprehensive online platform. The CapSha Marketplace is a core component of CGIAR’s Capacity Sharing Accelerator, designed as a demand‑driven matching platform that connects the capacity needs of National Agricultural Research and Innovation Systems (NARIS), CGIAR centers, and other partners with the existing supply of expertise, training, tools, and capacity sharing services across the CGIAR system. This marketplace maps and connects capacity development resources, training programs, and service providers across the global agricultural research ecosystem. The platform enables individuals and institutions to easily discover, access, share, and collaboratively develop training opportunities and expertise. By functioning as a centralized hub, it reduces duplication of efforts, amplifies reach, and promotes equitable, demand-driven collaboration for knowledge and skills strengthening across diverse agricultural research and innovation communities worldwide.

column16: Enabling Environment Digital Toolbox for Scaling Innovations in Agrifood systems
column17: The Enabling Environment Digital Toolbox (EE Method toolbox) is designed to strengthen the systemic conditions for scaling inclusive agri-food and climate innovations, specifically curating interoperable, field-tested digital and analytical tools across eight enabling environment pillars to promote uptake and institutionalization by national governments, development partners, and local stakeholders through user-friendly interfaces, trainings, and guidance. The initiative is designed to address a long-standing challenge in agrifood systems where innovations are ready for scaling.  Promising solutions often fail to move beyond pilots because the policy, institutional, financial, social, and technological conditions required for large-scale adoption are not consistently in place.  The ultimate goal is to deliver a modular, AI-assisted toolbox that curates and connects methods aligned to CGIAR’s 8 enabling environment pillars and guides users through application and adaptation across countries and regions.

column16: Seed Production Hubs for building a sustainable hybrid maize seed market system in Nepal
column17: Nepal’s maize sector has historically relied heavily on imported hybrid seeds, constraining farmer profitability and weakening national seed system resilience. To address this challenge, CIMMYT, in collaboration with the Nepal Agricultural Research Council (NARC), private seed companies, and local governments, has supported the development of a sustainable hybrid seed market system through targeted local capacity development and market-oriented interventions. A central strategy has been the establishment of hybrid seed production hubs in key maize-growing districts, including Dang, Kapilvastu, and Kailali. These hubs promote coordinated seed production by clustering farmers, improving access to technical support, strengthening quality assurance, and reducing transaction costs for seed companies. Farmers received hands-on training on hybrid seed production protocols, quality control, and post-harvest handling, while private seed companies supplied parental lines, technical supervision, and buy-back guarantees. As part of this effort, six micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) operating in the seed sector were directly supported to enhance their technical, managerial, and market capacities. Support to these MSMEs included improved access to breeder and foundation seed, technical training on hybrid seed production and quality standards, and facilitation of linkages with producer groups, NARC and local governments. Strengthening MSMEs has been critical to anchoring local seed production and expanding commercial distribution networks. The results have been substantial. Domestic hybrid maize seed production increased significantly, production areas expanded, and farmer participation rose markedly. In Dang district alone, locally produced hybrid seed now covers thousands of hectares, and increasing farmer incomes. The intervention has also strengthened women’s participation, particularly in skilled seed production roles. By reinforcing linkages among farmers, MSMEs, research institutions, and the public sector, the initiative has laid a  foundation for an inclusive, resilient, and commercially viable hybrid seed system in Nepal.

column16: Introducing mechanized Mechanized Direct Rice Seeder: Supporting climate-resilient rice systems in Madagascar
column17: A 15-row direct seed rice (DSR) machine was introduced in two major rice cultivation hubs of Madagascar—Ambatondrazaka and Tsiroanomandidy—through a mechanization service provider. This activity responds to increasing climate-related constraints, notably highly variable rainfall patterns, including delayed or premature onset of the rainy season, which significantly affect the reliability of transplanting-based rice systems. Direct seeding represents a promising climate-resilient alternative; however, the lack of performant and locally adapted machinery has limited its adoption.; ; The initial phase of implementation prioritized familiarization of service providers and operators with the machinery under real field conditions. This learning-by-doing approach aimed to ensure proper handling, calibration, and maintenance of the equipment before performance optimization. In parallel, experimentation is ongoing to identify best operational conditions, including land preparation quality and seeding settings. The generated evidence will support informed decision-making on technical suitability and guide potential scaling pathways for DSR through service provision models adapted to local contexts.;

column16: Demand Intelligence Platform to improve coordination, prioritization, and investment decisions
column17: The Demand Intelligence Platform is a decision-support and data-integration innovation that consolidates fragmented demand information into a single, governed system to improve coordination, prioritization, and investment decisions. It harmonizes multiple sources of demand evidence (e.g., needs assessments, policy and learning reports, survey/workshop outputs) into a structured dataset with provenance, quality checks, and shared definitions (Need, Demand, and Effective Demand).; Using an AI/NLP pipeline (topic clustering and semantic modeling), the platform generates demand signals and demand clusters, and links these to innovation supply records (e.g., PRMS innovations) to surface coverage, gaps, and response readiness.; In the current development cycle, researchers are the primary user group for controlled PoC testing and internal validation, while extension, policy, and funding stakeholders are engaged to validate assumptions, interpretability, and decision-usefulness. Initial pilots focus on Bangladesh and Nigeria, with an emphasis on building reliable data refresh and governance workflows to support scale-out and sustained use beyond the pilot phase.

column16: KASP-based validation of markers for AVR gene detection and lineage identification in philippine rice blast isolates
column17: To support high-throughput monitoring of rice blast incidences globally, previously designed markers for AVR gene detection (n=22) and blast lineage identification (n=8) were validated for competitive allele-specific PCR technology (KASP) as implemented by Intertek. 376 rice blast isolates (Magnaporthe oryzae) from PPHPR collection were genotyped using the mentioned markers. Validation results for AVR gene markers showed high performance for Avr-Pi9, Avr-Pii, and Avr-Pia, in which all genes scores at least 80% in accuracy. Avr-Pizt and Avr-Pita markers resulted to lower accuracy and may benefit from marker redesign and validation. As for the blast lineage detection, majority of the philippine rice blast isolates from PPHPR collection were under lineage 3, with few isolates temporarily identified as lineage 1. Lineage structure for philippine blast reaffirms previous reports conducted using genomic analyses.

column16: Technical specification for multi-crop raised bed planter suitable for intensified small-holder farmers in Egypt
column17: Egypt’s irrigated agriculture is under intense pressure from water scarcity, land fragmentation, and rising input costs. Mechanized raised bed planting has already been demonstrated in Egypt to improve water-use efficiency, nitrogen-use efficiency, and wheat productivity compared with traditional flat planting and flood irrigation (Devkota et al., 2026). Studies from ICARDA and national partners show that raised beds can save ~20% irrigation water, reduce seed rates by ~30%, and increase yields and profitability in wheat and other crops in the Nile Delta and Valley. Yet, widespread adoption is still constrained by the lack of scale-appropriate mechanization for bed formation and planting. Most existing raised bed seed drills manufactured or imported for Egypt are heavy, designed for higher horsepower tractors, and often poorly matched to the small, fragmented holdings that dominate the old lands. Many smallholders operate tractors in the 45–60 hp range or rely on hired services with limited maneuverability in narrow plots, irregular field shapes, and soft soils. Oversized or overweight planters increase fuel use, cause excessive compaction, are difficult to transport between small fields, and are economically unattractive for service providers serving many small clients.

column16: Wholesale price discount system developed and tested to encourage agricultural retailers to promote improved maize varieties in Kenya
column17: Small agricultural retailers often avoid stocking newer, stress-tolerant maize varieties due to uncertain demand and financial risk. CIMMYT developed and validated an incentive system that offers temporary wholesale price discounts to agricultural retailers on selected improved maize hybrids. This reduces retailers' commercial risk while encouraging them to learn about and actively promote these products. Testing in Kenya demonstrated that the system effectively increases retailer willingness to stock newer varieties, shifts sales toward improved hybrids, and enhances advisory services to farmers. The intervention proved particularly effective with risk-averse dealers, improving their product knowledge and recommendations to farmers without requiring changes in retail prices.

column16: Stem rot resistant groundnut breeding lines developed by ICRISAT for enhanced disease tolerance in global breeding programs
column17: ICRISAT developed eight elite groundnut breeding lines with strong resistance to stem rot disease, showing less than 20% plant mortality under disease pressure. The lines serve as valuable parent materials for national agricultural research systems and breeding programs worldwide to develop improved groundnut varieties. Stem rot is a significant constraint to groundnut production, causing substantial yield losses in many growing regions. These resistant lines provide breeders with genetic resources to develop varieties that can better withstand this destructive disease while maintaining productivity and quality characteristics important to farmers and consumers.

column16: Sustainable Pest Management  for Reducing Pesticide Use in Rice-Based Systems: Diversification Strategies and Biological Control
column17: Climate change is increasing the risk of insect pest outbreaks in rice production, threatening the stability and sustainability of rice-based farming systems. Addressing this challenge requires sustainable pest management approaches that reduce reliance on chemical pesticides while enhancing ecological resilience. Crop diversification and biological control are effective strategies for strengthening natural pest regulation, improving productivity, and minimizing environmental impacts, yet their adoption in rice-based systems remains limited.; This material presents the background, concepts, and design principles of rice-based diversification, with a focus on rice–mungbean–watermelon systems. It explains how diversified cropping systems influence pest pressure, natural enemy populations, and pesticide use. Drawing on field trial results, the report highlights the impacts of diversification on insect pests, biodiversity, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and economic performance, showcasing climate-smart, low-pesticide practices that support resilient and environmentally sustainable rice-based farming systems.;

column16: Digitally Enabled Seed Information System (DESIS) to improve smallholder farmers’ access to quality seed
column17: To strengthen Nepal’s seed system and improve smallholder farmers’ access to quality seed, CIMMYT and the Seed Quality Control Center (SQCC) co-developed the Digitally Enabled Seed Information System (DESIS) – a digital platform that streamlines seed demand, supply, and quality information across the country’s seed value chain. DESIS replaces slow, paper-based processes that once took 6–8 months to aggregate early-generation seed (breeder and foundation) data with real-time digital management, accelerating planning and decision-making for seed multipliers, regulators, and farmers alike. The platform hosts a digital catalogue of more than 80 crops and 800 registered varieties, giving stakeholders access to detailed varietal information that supports informed choices for production and distribution. By enabling near-accurate demand–supply analysis, DESIS helps ensure timely delivery of seed to producers, improves transparency, and supports evidence-based planning and investment. The upgraded DESIS 2.0 integrates additional services, including online variety release and registration, digital seed inspection and certification via mobile apps, a blockchain-backed seed tracking system to control counterfeits, and digital management of seed import/export permits. These innovations reduce bureaucratic hurdles, lower transaction costs, and strengthen overall system efficiency. By connecting breeders, seed businesses, inspectors, policymakers, and farmers through a unified digital tool, DESIS is enhancing seed access, supporting quality assurance, and contributing to more responsive, inclusive, and resilient seed systems in Nepal.

column16: Eight climate-resilient and nutritious maize varieties developed by IITA released for farmers in Ethiopia and Sierra Leone
column17: National agricultural research partners in Ethiopia and Sierra Leone officially released eight improved maize varieties developed by the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) through the Breeding for Tomorrow initiative. The four Ethiopian varieties offer distinct benefits: fall armyworm tolerance, early maturation, drought tolerance with striga resistance, and enhanced vitamin A content. Sierra Leone received four hybrid varieties including one single-cross and three three-way cross hybrids, all featuring drought tolerance and striga resistance for better climate adaptation. These varieties address critical challenges facing smallholder farmers including pest damage, unpredictable rainfall, parasitic weeds, and malnutrition, providing farmers with improved options for sustainable maize production in changing climate conditions.

column16: Whole-Farm Bundling as a structured, system-level approach to scaling integrated innovations within existing agricultural delivery
column17: Whole-Farm Bundling as a Delivery Innovation for Responsible Scaling builds on evidence from the CGIAR Mixed Farming Systems Initiative in Malawi and aligned national investments in cropping systems, soil health, fertilizer management, digitization, and inclusive service delivery. It responds to consistent empirical findings that smallholder farmers face interlinked constraints across production, finance, markets, advisory services, land and water governance, and social norms, which limit the effectiveness of stand-alone innovations. The approach addresses a documented demand for integrated and differentiated design solutions by organizing technical, institutional, financial, and social innovations into coherent, system-embedded bundles aligned with farmer typologies and delivery platforms. Co-design processes and innovation readiness analysis validate that innovation systems are often technically more prepared than levels of farmer use, particularly for commercial and digital innovations, while uptake remains higher for accessible, socially embedded options. Whole-Farm Bundling therefore functions as a design and delivery innovation, explicitly linking system readiness with farmer realities to improve feasibility, coordination, and persistence of use. These insights inform a practical roadmap for scaling integrated innovations through existing agricultural delivery systems in Malawi.;

column16: Assessment protocol for biological control agents
column17: One of the biggest challenges that negatively impacts rice production is climate change. The Philippines has been facing stronger typhoons, longer drought periods, and flooding that destroy rice fields, thereby significantly increasing crop losses. Rising temperatures can help insects grow and reproduce faster, allowing it to complete life cycle for a shorter time, resulting to more generations per year, hence greater pest population which can cause more damage to rice crops and reduce yields. The increase in pest driven by climate change could make pests more difficult to manage and may intensify reliance on pesticides. Effective management under climate change necessitates integrated approaches such as good farming practices, use of resistant varieties, proper pest monitoring, judicious insecticide use and biological control. The use of biological control agents (BCAs) has been recognized to be a safer and more sustainable option to manage pests. Augmentative field releases of laboratory-reared BCAs enhance ecossystem service of pest regulation. The community-wide production and utilization of BCAs identifies gaps and provides solutions to improve BCA production systems in the regions of the Philippines. Before a BCA is deployed, its efficacy and effectiveness must be assessed using an appropriate and properly designed protocol.

column16: Leveraging Large Language Models for Remote Sensing–Driven Digital Agriculture
column17: This innovation development will design and test a “geospatial co-pilot” that uses large language models to turn satellite- and drone-based crop monitoring information into clear, actionable guidance for agriculture users. Many remote sensing outputs are difficult to interpret without specialist skills, which limits their usefulness for extension, planners, and smallholder-facing services.; The proposed approach combines existing geospatial analytics with a language model that can (i) retrieve supporting technical notes and local agronomic guidance, (ii) explain what observed patterns mean in simple language, (iii) answer user questions about crop condition and risks, and (iv) draft tailored advisories and early warnings that are easier to act on. To support responsible use, the system will be designed to reference source evidence, apply constraints (so it does not “invent” answers), and enable expert review before dissemination.; Expected outputs include a proof-of-concept workflow and prototype interface for interpreting geospatial indicators, plus initial testing with intended users to refine usefulness, clarity, and trust.

column16: An integrated bundle of agronomic innovation bundle to improve soybean productivity and water-use efficiency in wheat-based irrigated systems in Egypt
column17: The innovation bundle comprises an integrated package of agronomic practices designed to improve soybean productivity, water-use efficiency, and system sustainability within irrigated wheat-based cropping systems in Egypt. The bundle positions soybean as a high-value summer rotation crop that enhances both economic returns and agroecological performance while supporting national goals for crop diversification and reduced reliance on imported vegetable oils and protein feed. Core components of the bundle include minimum tillage to reduce soil disturbance, conserve soil moisture, and maintain soil organic matter, thereby improving soil health under intensive irrigated systems. Biofertilizer application is promoted to enhance biological nitrogen fixation, improve nutrient-use efficiency, and reduce dependence on synthetic nitrogen fertilizers. The bundle also emphasizes precise planting practices, including mechanized or hand-held roller planters, to achieve optimal plant population, uniform crop establishment, and improved crop vigour. Improved irrigation management is a central element of the package, focusing on optimizing irrigation timing and application rates to increase water productivity while avoiding moisture stress during critical growth stages. All demonstrations utilize the improved soybean variety Giza 111, selected for its high yield potential and adaptability to Egyptian growing conditions when combined with improved management practices. The bundle is implemented through a demonstration-based extension approach, with farmer-led demonstration fields established across diverse agroecological zones to enable direct comparison between improved and conventional practices. Complementary farmer field days and participatory learning activities strengthen knowledge exchange among farmers, extension agents, and researchers. Collectively, the bundle provides a practical, scalable pathway to integrate soybean into wheat-based irrigated systems, delivering higher yields, improved resource-use efficiency, and greater resilience to climate and market pressures.

column16: Evaluation of the efficacy and effectiveness of biological control agents (progress report)

column16: Turning Rice Decision Rules into Adaptive, Farmer-Friendly Advisories Using Large Language Models
column17: This innovation development will translate validated, rule-based rice knowledge into a scalable, context-specific advisory system powered by large language models. It will emphasize clear explanations, multilingual communication, and mechanisms to reduce unsafe outputs (e.g., rule-based checks and human review).; Expected outputs include a structured framework and prototype workflow that can generate context-aware recommendations, explain rationale to build trust, and support extension services with timely, farmer-relevant guidance. The work is positioned to improve productivity and resource-use efficiency while supporting climate-smart practices and responsible scaling.

column16: An integrated bundle of agronomic solutions to improve soybean productivity and water-use efficiency in wheat-based irrigated systems in Egypt
column17: The innovation bundle comprises an integrated package of agronomic practices designed to improve soybean productivity, water-use efficiency, and system sustainability within irrigated wheat-based cropping systems in Egypt. The bundle positions soybean as a high-value summer rotation crop that enhances both economic returns and agroecological performance while supporting national goals for crop diversification and reduced reliance on imported vegetable oils and protein feed. Core components of the bundle include minimum tillage to reduce soil disturbance, conserve soil moisture, and maintain soil organic matter, thereby improving soil health under intensive irrigated systems. Biofertilizer application is promoted to enhance biological nitrogen fixation, improve nutrient-use efficiency, and reduce dependence on synthetic nitrogen fertilizers. The bundle also emphasizes precise planting practices, including mechanized or hand-held roller planters, to achieve optimal plant population, uniform crop establishment, and improved crop vigour. Improved irrigation management is a central element of the package, focusing on optimizing irrigation timing and application rates to increase water productivity while avoiding moisture stress during critical growth stages. All demonstrations utilize the improved soybean variety Giza 111, selected for its high yield potential and adaptability to Egyptian growing conditions when combined with improved management practices. The bundle is implemented through a demonstration-based extension approach, with farmer-led demonstration fields established across diverse agroecological zones to enable direct comparison between improved and conventional practices. Complementary farmer field days and participatory learning activities strengthen knowledge exchange among farmers, extension agents, and researchers. Collectively, the bundle provides a practical, scalable pathway to integrate soybean into wheat-based irrigated systems, delivering higher yields, improved resource-use efficiency, and greater resilience to climate and market pressures.

column16: New method for in vitro viability monitoring for regeneration
column17: Within CIP’s Hackathon Initiative, the Genebank led Challenge 6 to develop an Artificial Intelligence (AI) tool to improve monitoring of the in vitro potato collection (approx. 6,570 accessions). Three multidisciplinary external teams competed to design a solution. Traditionally, in vitro viability assessment is being conducted manually, an expertise-intensive, repetitive process that carries some risk of variability in regeneration decisions and depends on a small number of highly skilled technicians.; The innovation consists of a genebank-specific image recognition model trained on CIP’s own data and genebank images to automatically assess plant viability and predict regeneration needs. This tool improves accuracy, standardizes monitoring, reduces human error, and helps prevent loss of accessions. In 2025, the best prototype was selected, and the code is now with CIP for further refinement and future implementation.

column16: Validation and application of a multiplex PCR Protocol fordetecting Pantoea subspecies in rice seeds
column17: Rice seeds are vulnerable to contamination by various bacterial pathogens, among which Pantoea species have recently been recognized as important seed-borne threats. These bacteria can cause considerable economic loss by reducing crop yield and quality, as well as by limiting trade due to quarantine regulations. Detecting relevant Pantoea subspecies during seed screening is thus essential for crop protection and compliance with phytosanitary regulations. Traditional culturing and singleplex molecular assays, while effective in certain contexts, are often not suitable for high-throughput diagnostics, especially when multiple pathogens or subspecies must be detected concurrently. The multiplex PCR approach described in the study enables simultaneous detection and differentiation of P. ananatis, P. stewartii, and P. agglomerans, as well as general Pantoea spp., using one assay improving efficiency and reliability. The study aimed to optimize a sensitive and specific multiplex PCR protocol for the detection of Pantoea spp. and key subspecies (P. ananatis, P. stewartii, P. agglomerans) in rice seeds, to validate this protocol under laboratory conditions using positive controls and a range of seed samples, to provide a user-friendly and scalable diagnostic tool for seed health laboratories and phytosanitary agencies.

column16: Diagnostic protocol developed for the detection of cowpea aphid-borne mosaic virus (CABMV)
column17: Cowpea aphid-borne mosaic virus (CAbMV) and Bean common mosaic virus (BCMV), both members of the genus Potyvirus, are endemic in West Africa and many tropical regions, where they pose serious constraints to cowpea and other legume production. With broad host ranges that include cultivated and weed species, both viruses are efficiently seed-transmitted, posing a major risk to germplasm regeneration and international exchange. Routine virus indexing is therefore essential to prevent the distribution of contaminated seed lots. Although reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) is widely used for virus detection, running separate assays for CAbMV and BCMV is costly and time-consuming, particularly when co-infections are common. This study focused on developing a reliable multiplex RT-PCR assay for the simultaneous detection of CAbMV and BCMV. Initial evaluation revealed that previously used in-house CAbMV primers showed inconsistent amplification of known positive samples. New primer sets were therefore designed to improve sensitivity and enable multiplexing with BCMV. While these primers enhanced detection, cross-amplification was observed under some primer combinations, compromising diagnostic reliability. To overcome this limitation, a second CAbMV-specific primer set targeting the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRP) gene was designed and optimized. In silico analyses confirmed high specificity and compatibility with BCMV primers. Experimental validation demonstrated consistent amplification of the expected 246 bp CAbMV product across a range of template concentrations, with no cross-reactivity. The optimized multiplex RT-PCR assay provides a sensitive, accurate, and cost-effective diagnostic tool for the simultaneous detection of these economically important potyviruses, strengthening germplasm health management and seed certification efforts.

column16: GALS4GTR: A Gender-Transformative Framework for Inclusive Food Systems
column17: The GALS Toolkit is a household and community-led tran,sformative tool that offers researchers and practitioners a guide to drive inclusive transformation across food systems. It promotes income growth, food security, and the adoption of climate-smart innovations such as ; conservation agriculture by creating safe spaces for inclusive decision-making. The approach helps stakeholders analyze current realities, track gender-transformative change, and co-develop gender-equitable visions. GALS was not originally designed with a research mandate and so lacked a research component, which includes designing research questions, prioritizing household issues, analyzing them through conceptual and analytical frameworks, and co-developing indicators with the communities. This is a critical gap that GALS4GTR aims to close. The development of the tool provides steps for how to operationalize GALS as a transformative research methodology that supports inclusive and transformative outcomes for innovations.

column16: Regional Agronomy Community of Practice and Farmer-Centric Co-Design for Scaling No-Till under Generation Green
column17: The Regional Agronomy Community of Practice (RACoP) and Farmer-Centric Co-Design Lab were established to accelerate large-scale adoption of no-till conservation agriculture under Morocco’s Generation Green strategy, targeting one million hectares. The initiative convenes researchers, extension services, farmer organizations, service providers, financial institutions, and policymakers to exchange regional experiences, strengthen technical capacity, and co-design locally adapted solutions. Activities combined technical training, demonstration trials, machinery calibration, residue management, crop rotation planning, and use of digital tools for crop monitoring and advisory support. Over 200 participants from public and private institutions engaged in structured dialogues, field demonstrations, and mentoring sessions to address barriers to adoption, including equipment access, service delivery quality, and knowledge gaps. The platform promotes coordinated governance, action research in real farm conditions, and strengthened professional networks to sustain learning beyond the workshop. By improving soil cover, reducing erosion, enhancing water retention, and optimizing input use, no-till supports climate resilience and environmental restoration. Increased productivity, reduced fuel and labor costs, and better resource efficiency contribute to farm profitability and poverty reduction. Inclusive participation of farmer groups and local organizations strengthens knowledge access and shared decision-making. The RACoP model links evidence, partnerships, and practical innovation, creating a scalable pathway for sustainable intensification, institutional alignment, and long-term agricultural transformation in Morocco.

column16: New generations of faster growing genetically improved rohu
column17: The WorldFish genetically improved rohu strain is under continual genetic improvement (i.e. selection for rapid growth).  A generation interval of 2 years is targeted, however activities are undertaken every year.  The genetic improvement program is family based (i.e. all fish are tagged and the pedigree of all fish is known back to the founding population).  The breeding cycle consists of spawning full sib families, nursing in hapas (one family per hapa), tagging once fish are of sufficient size, pooling of families after tagging and grow out in a common environment, harvest age measurement, genetic analysis to generate estimated breeding values (a measure of the genetic merit of individual fish), parent selection using optimal contribution methods to maximise genetic gain while controlling long-term inbreeding, the development of a mating plan to ensure closely related parents are not mated.

column16: Gender and Social Norms Research Tools
column17: These research tools address the challenge that gender norms often limit women's and girls' participation, resource access, and decision-making in aquatic and agri-food systems. WorldFish developed participatory methods that systematically identify and analyze gender norms, youth aspirations, and power dynamics within communities. The tools generate evidence-based insights that organizations, including CGIAR centers, can use to design gender-transformative interventions, policies, and programs. By providing structured approaches to understand how social norms operate, these tools enable more effective targeting of initiatives aimed at promoting gender equity and empowering marginalized groups in food systems across diverse contexts.

column16: Development of small-scale maize combine harverster to improve harvest efficiency in smallholder systems
column17: A two-wheel-tractor-powered maize harvesting system was developed through an iterative innovation process that combined design, fabrication, field testing, diagnosis of failures, and redesign. The work began with an integrated concept to carry out multiple harvest steps in a single pass (crop intake, ear detachment, dehusking/shelling, cleaning, and residue handling) using a low-horsepower power source suited to small farms. Early trials revealed recurring operational problems—especially crop feeding interruptions, blockages, and unstable performance on uneven terrain—so the team moved into a targeted improvement phase. Key modifications were introduced to address specific bottlenecks: the crop-feeding mechanism was redesigned to reduce jams and improve continuity of material flow; the conveying system was extended and repositioned to capture ears more effectively; the cleaning approach was adjusted to better separate grain from light materials; and the support and mobility elements were strengthened to improve handling in the field. Subsequent tests generated performance evidence (work rate, turning losses, and grain losses) that helped pinpoint where losses originated—such as poor capture of ears, lateral ejection, and difficulties feeding lodged plants. The process concluded with a strategic design lesson: fully integrating all harvest functions with a small two-wheel tractor is technically demanding, and a modular or sequential configuration may deliver more reliable results.

column16: Pesira digital platform integrated into common bean multi-stakeholder platforms by Alliance researchers to enhance value chain coordination in East Africa
column17: Smallholder bean farmers in East Africa struggle with poor market access and low incomes due to fragmented value chains and limited coordination between farmers, suppliers, processors, and traders. The Alliance of Bioversity and CIAT developed and integrated the Pesira digital platform into existing multi-stakeholder networks across Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Rwanda. This platform features specialized digital modules that connect agrisuppliers, processors, cooperatives, and aggregators, enabling streamlined operations and improved information sharing. The integration facilitates better market linkages, reduces transaction costs, and enhances transparency throughout the bean value chain. Early results demonstrate improved coordination and data-driven decision-making among stakeholders, creating a more efficient ecosystem that benefits smallholder farmers through enhanced market opportunities and income potential.

column16: Limpopo Basin Water Accounting Dashboard: An Interactive Decision-Support Platform for Basin-Scale Water Availability, Use, and Balance Analysis - To be integrated with Water copilot
column17: The Limpopo Basin Water Accounting Dashboard is a comprehensive digital decision-support tool developed using Tableau to support evidence-based water resources planning and management in the Limpopo River Basin. The dashboard integrates hydrological model outputs, Earth Observation data, and population statistics to provide a basin-wide view of water availability, utilization, and balance. It is organized into multiple interactive tabs, including basin overview, water yield distribution, water balance, water availability, monthly water balance, and water accounting indicators. Together, these components enable users to explore spatial and temporal patterns of rainfall, evapotranspiration, water yield, consumption, and per capita water availability from 2003 to 2024. Visual tools such as maps, sunburst charts, heatmaps, and anomaly analyses help identify seasonal variability, long-term trends, and water stress conditions. By translating complex datasets into intuitive visual insights, the dashboard supports policymakers, water managers, and researchers in assessing basin closure, prioritizing interventions, and improving sustainable and equitable water allocation across transboundary contexts.

column16: Emerging Livestock-Feed Business Models and Value-Chain Constraints in Laikipia County
column17: The report examines livestock-feed business opportunities in Laikipia County, Kenya, where livestock production remains central to rural livelihoods but is constrained by feed shortages, climate variability, and market challenges. Using three focus group discussions (FGDs) with feed producers, livestock fatteners, and key stakeholders, alongside key informant interviews (KIIs) with producers and community grazing committee members, the study explores constraints, opportunities, and synergies within the livestock-feed and beef value chain. Conducted in February 2025 across Laikipia East and North sub-counties, the participatory appraisal identified barriers such as limited access to quality feed, weak linkages between producers and markets, and inadequate institutional support. Insights highlight potential feed business models that build on existing producer cooperatives, self-help groups, and grazing management structures to strengthen feed supply, enhance value addition, and improve market access. The analysis also underscores the need for an enabling environment, through policy support, coordinated extension services, and collaboration among government, research, and community actors, to catalyse sustainable, locally anchored livestock-feed enterprises that boost productivity and resilience.

column16: Virtual reality digital twin system developed by IWMI to enhance flood risk management in river basins
column17: The Somali region of Ethiopia, particularly Dolo Ado, faces unpredictable weather and severe flood risks driving displacement and humanitarian crises. Traditional 2D mapping often fails to convey the urgency needed for decision-making. This study introduces an immersive Digital Twin leveraging Virtual Reality (VR) to support Anticipatory Action (AA) in flood risk management. High-fidelity UAV photogrammetry captured a 16.4 km² floodplain with a DJI Mavic Pro 2, producing data optimized via Blender for real-time performance in Unreal Engine 5.5.4, using the Cesium plugin for dynamic terrain streaming. The system models two flood events (November 2019 and April 2023), visualizing hydrological, socio-economic, and displacement impacts. Dual-mode accessibility allows both PC VR immersion and desktop access. The study shows consumer-grade photogrammetry can produce high-accuracy Digital Twins in resource-limited contexts, while future integration of Generative AI and real-time hydrological APIs could enable predictive flood monitoring.

column16: Developing a Digital Platform for  Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification  of Carbon Claims in Agricultural  Practices
column17: The presentation, titled "Advancing Carbon Farming through Technology and Investment," details the development of a digital Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) platform by Dr. Mukund Patil and his team at ICRISAT. The primary objective is to validate carbon sequestration claims and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in agricultural practices, specifically within the Hirakud command area in Odisha, India. The project focuses on shifting from a "Baseline" scenario, characterized by puddled transplanted rice, continuous flooding, and high nitrogen use, to a "Project" scenario involving direct-seeded rice (DSR), alternate wetting and drying (AWD), and optimized nitrogen management. Field trials demonstrate that these regenerative practices significantly reduce methane emissions compared to traditional methods. Technologically, the MRV platform integrates mobile and web applications with remote sensing data from Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellites, processed via Google Earth Engine. This allows for real-time tracking of field operations and monitoring of vegetation indices. Key reflections emphasize the need to refine carbon protocols by recognizing nitrogen fertilizer's role in methane emissions and enhancing digital MRV using Generative AI to address data gaps caused by cloud cover.

column16: AI-powered image analysis tool developed by ICRISAT quantifies crop residue retention in rice fields for carbon monitoring
column17: Rice farming practices that retain crop residues help store carbon in soil, but accurately measuring residue coverage has been challenging for carbon monitoring systems. ICRISAT developed an artificial intelligence tool that analyzes field photographs to automatically detect and measure the percentage of crop residues left on rice fields. The tool uses advanced image recognition technology to classify different residue management practices and calculate precise coverage percentages. This innovation enables farmers and organizations to accurately track carbon storage for environmental reporting and climate programs, supporting better decision-making for sustainable rice production practices.
