column16: An integrated bundle of agronomic solutions to improve barley production in irrigated and rainfed systems in Uzbekistan
column17: This innovation is a field-tested, integrated barley production bundle designed for two contrasting agro-ecological zones in Uzbekistan: the irrigated and partially saline southern oases (Karshi–Kashkadarya, Samarkand) and the low-input, rainfed foothills (Jizzakh–Syrdarya). The bundle combines agronomic practices, input recommendations, and risk-reduction measures into a coherent package that can be applied as a whole or adapted to local conditions. It includes location-specific varietal choices, pairing high-yielding, salinity-tolerant varieties for irrigated areas with early-maturing, drought-tolerant types for rainfed zones. Sowing windows, seed rates, row spacing, and planting depth are defined to ensure uniform emergence and improve cold tolerance, establishment, and yield stability. Balanced nutrient management is a core component, including banded phosphorus at sowing, reduced and better-timed nitrogen, systematic potassium application, and the use of organic amendments to improve soil fertility and structure. Soil and water management practices address local constraints: in irrigated and saline environments, the bundle provides guidance on land preparation, drainage, salinity control, and irrigation scheduling; in rainfed fields, it emphasizes moisture conservation through minimal tillage, residue retention, and timely planting to maximize stored soil water. Risk-reduction measures include seed treatment, integrated pest, disease, and weed management, and targeted control of early foliar diseases such as Rhynchosporium. Priority “must-do” practices are highlighted to help farmers focus resources on the highest-impact interventions. Together, these components form a harmonized barley production bundle that raises yield ceilings in irrigated systems, closes yield gaps in rainfed areas, and improves input-use efficiency and resilience across Uzbekistan’s diverse barley-growing environments.

column16: An integrated bundle of agronomic solutions to improve mungbean production in irrigated and rainfed systems in Uzbekistan
column17: This innovation is an integrated mungbean production bundle designed for irrigated and rainfed systems in Uzbekistan, where mungbean is increasingly used as a short-season pulse after wheat or between irrigations. The bundle addresses common yield constraints, including late sowing, poor seed quality, lack of inoculation, early weed competition, missed irrigations, heat and drought stress, and susceptibility to Ascochyta blight and sucking insects. The package combines agronomic, nutrient, water, and pest-management practices into a coherent set of interventions. It includes the use of short-duration, heat-tolerant, released varieties such as Durdona, Baraka, Zilola, and Marjon, sown at the appropriate regional windows on moist, well-prepared, levelled seedbeds. Seed treatment and inoculation with Rhizobium or locally available bio-products (Uzgummi, Gummimaks, BioVak 24, Bioazot) are promoted to ensure uniform emergence and effective nitrogen fixation. Field preparation and conservation practices include light tillage, residue retention, and ridge/furrow formation in saline patches to improve infiltration, conserve moisture, and protect the shallow-rooted crop. Balanced nutrient management combines modest starter nitrogen (20–30 kg/ha) with phosphorus and potassium, supplemented with compost or FYM where available, and 2–3 foliar/biofertilizer sprays to stabilize growth under heat or moisture stress. Irrigation management emphasizes 2–3 light irrigations at critical stages (emergence, flowering, and pod filling), or a single lifesaving irrigation in rainfed areas, keeping water use efficient and avoiding waterlogging. Weed management prioritizes early control using pre-emergence herbicides and one hand/mechanical weeding before canopy closure. Disease and insect management relies on scouting and timely application of locally recommended fungicides and insecticides. Together, these components form a practical and adaptable mungbean production bundle that improves early establishment, stabilizes yield under hot, dry, or saline conditions, enhances nitrogen fixation, and supports short-season pulse intensification in both irrigated and rainfed systems across Uzbekistan.

column16: An integrated bundle of agronomic solutions to improve chickpea production in irrigated and rainfed systems in Uzbekistan
column17: This innovation is an integrated chickpea production bundle designed for both irrigated oases (Karshi, Samarkand) and rainfed regions (Jizzakh–Syrdarya–Samarkand), where chickpea is a strategic legume that can follow wheat or cotton and supply biological nitrogen to rotations. The bundle addresses common yield constraints, including late sowing, poor soil preparation, low or missing phosphorus and potassium, pest and disease pressure (Ascochyta blight, Helicoverpa pod borer, cutworm, aphids), and missed or poorly timed irrigation. The package combines agronomic, nutrient, water, pest, and biostimulant management into a coherent set of interventions. It includes the use of adapted, short-to-medium duration chickpea varieties, such as Yulduz, Guliston, and Iftixor, sown in the optimal regional windows: mid-February to early March for irrigated systems and late February to early March (or November when moisture allows) for rainfed systems. Seed treatment and inoculation with Rhizobium secure nitrogen fixation and protect against seed- and soil-borne diseases. Field preparation and establishment include well-drained, levelled seedbeds for irrigated areas and moisture-conserving seedbeds for rainfed zones, with light tillage, residue retention, and row sowing at 30–45 cm spacing to ensure uniform emergence and facilitate weed control. Balanced fertilization applies basal phosphorus (40–60 kg P₂O₅/ha irrigated, 30–40 kg rainfed) with a small starter nitrogen dose (20–30 kg N/ha), avoiding high nitrogen that suppresses nodulation. Irrigation is applied at high-payoff stages, especially flowering and pod set, with additional water only if available, while weed, disease, and insect management focuses on early interventions and threshold-based sprays. Foliar biostimulants are applied 1–2 times on actively growing crops to buffer heat or drought stress. Timely harvesting ensures pod maturity and prevents shattering under hot conditions. Together, these practices form a science-based, adaptable chickpea bundle that improves establishment, supports nodulation, protects yield from biotic and abiotic stress, and maximizes productivity across both irrigated and rainfed systems in Uzbekistan.

column16: An integrated bundle of agronomic solutions to improve wheat production in irrigated systems in Uzbekistan
column17: This innovation is an integrated wheat production bundle designed to close yield gaps in Uzbekistan’s irrigated systems, where wheat is grown on over one million hectares, mostly in rotation with cotton, maize, and short-season legumes. Long-term research and on-farm assessments indicate a 42% yield gap, primarily caused by late sowing, soil salinity, spring heat, erratic rainfall, and imbalanced fertilizer use. The bundle combines agronomic practices, input optimization, and risk-management measures into a coherent package, tailored to the specific challenges of irrigated and partly saline environments. It includes high-yielding, rust-resistant winter wheat varieties adapted to heat and episodic salinity, such as Yuksalish, Turon, Gozgon, and Krasnodar-99. Proper field preparation and soil management, including leveling, drainage, clod reduction, summer ploughing, and incorporation of organic matter, improve infiltration, reduce salt stress, and enhance fertilizer efficiency. Timely sowing and optimized crop establishment are central to the bundle, with recommended regional sowing windows, seed rates, row spacing, sowing depth, and use of seed drills to ensure uniform stands. Seed treatment protects against seed-borne diseases and early foliar infections, supporting strong early growth. Balanced nutrient management combines organic amendments with a full mineral fertilizer program, applying nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium at appropriate rates and timings. Irrigation is managed around critical crop stages, including crown-root initiation, booting, and grain filling, to optimize water use and prevent salt accumulation. Integrated pest, disease, and weed control measures protect plant stands and yield potential, while conservation practices such as reduced tillage, residue retention, and drill seeding improve soil health and resilience in marginal or saline fields. Together, these components form a practical and adaptable wheat production bundle that increases productivity, improves input-use efficiency, enhances resilience to climate and water stress, and supports progress toward wheat self-sufficiency in Uzbekistan’s irrigated systems.

column16: Crops-to-Go: An AI-powered system for recommending and matching germplasm to accelerate access to genebank collections for researchers, breeding programs and other users
column17: Crops-to-Go is an AI-powered germplasm recommendation system designed for CGIAR genebanks, with initial implementation focused on CIP's potato and sweet potato collections. The system addresses a significant bottleneck in germplasm distribution, namely the manual matching process, which previously required 60 to 90 days and numerous email exchanges per request. By reducing this timeline from months to days, Crops-to-Go expedites access to genetic resources for researchers, farmers, and breeding programs globally.; At its core, a classification engine employs large language models to interpret complex multi-trait queries across more than 17,000 CIP accessions, generating ranked recommendations accompanied by confidence scores and natural-language explanations. The system evaluates all accessions based on trait-match quality rather than curator familiarity, thereby reducing historical bias toward well-documented varieties and promoting the use of underexplored genetic diversity essential for climate adaptation and food security.; Key technical features include a customizable configuration system for managing traits, which Genebank staff can modify without programming expertise. The system also provides tools to identify missing or low-quality data and incorporates a process in which human experts review AI-generated suggestions to ensure expert judgment is enhanced rather than replaced. The AI-powered classification and ranking engine is designed to operate independently of the user-facing interface to support future accommodation of multiple user interaction modes, including guided forms, conversational chatbots, and direct programmatic access. This flexibility facilitates application across diverse operational contexts.; Developed in partnership with the AWS GenAI Innovation Center, Crops-to-Go targets an 80% reduction in email exchanges and high curator acceptance rates, unlocking curator capacity for strategic activities while democratizing access to genetic resources. The system embeds responsible AI principles, including transparency about data limitations, algorithmic bias mitigation, and mandatory human oversight.

column16: Improving Product Quality, Nutritional Value, and Shelf Stability through Mild Hydrothermal Stabilization of Parboiled Unpolished Rice
column17: Mild Hydrothermal Stabilization (MHS) is an optimized parboiling approach designed to produce high-quality parboiled unpolished (whole-grain) rice while preserving nutrients and improving shelf life. Developed by AfricaRice in collaboration with the Fortified Whole Grain Alliance, the method uses short-duration atmospheric steaming (about 10–15 minutes), combined with surface wetting and low-temperature drying (~40 °C). This controlled, milder treatment effectively inactivates lipase and peroxidase enzymes responsible for lipid rancidity, achieving shelf-life stability comparable to conventional parboiling but without excessive browning, hard texture, or long cooking times. Because the rice remains unpolished, key minerals concentrated in the bran (iron, zinc, calcium, magnesium) are retained. Overall, MHS enables the industrial production of nutritionally superior, visually appealing, and shelf-stable whole-grain parboiled rice, offering a practical and scalable upgrade to rice processing in West Africa.

column16: An integrated bundle of agronomic solutions to improve wheat production in rainfed systems in Uzbekistan
column17: This innovation is an integrated production bundle for rainfed wheat grown on 280,000–300,000 ha in Jizzakh, Syrdarya, and parts of Samarkand and Tashkent, where rainfall is low and variable. Average farmer yields are around 1.5 t/ha, while well-managed fields can reach 2.5–5.0 t/ha. Yield limitations are mainly due to late sowing, poor soil preparation, drought, heat and cold stress, yellow rust, weed pressure, and unbalanced fertilization. The bundle emphasizes moisture-first agronomy, combining conservation agriculture, timely sowing, drought- and rust-tolerant varieties, modest but balanced fertilizer application, targeted irrigation, and integrated pest, disease, and weed management. Varieties include Tezpishar, Surkhak-5688, Oq bugdoy, Istiqlol-6, and Sanzar-6, with seed renewed every 3–4 years. Sowing is done on moist soil between October and early November, using line sowing at 15–20 cm rows and 4–5 cm depth for uniform emergence. Field preparation follows conservation agriculture principles: minimal tillage, residue retention, leveling, and contouring or tied ridges where needed. Fertilizer is applied basally (20–25 kg N/ha and 15–20 kg P₂O₅/ha), supplemented with FYM or compost if available. Seed treatment protects against early-season pathogens, while early weed control (20–25 DAS) and threshold-based pest and disease management safeguard the crop. Where irrigation is available, a single light application at crown-root initiation or booting maximizes efficiency. Biostimulants such as BioVak 24, epin extra, and gumifild are applied 1–2 times to buffer stress. Together, these practices form a science-based, integrated rainfed wheat bundle that conserves soil moisture, stabilizes yields under erratic rainfall, and improves productivity and resilience across Uzbekistan’s low-rainfall wheat systems.

column16: Farmer information and price incentives for accelerated varietal turnover
column17: This output develops and validates a combined point-of-sale information and price-promotion intervention designed to stimulate farmer experimentation with newer maize hybrids and accelerate varietal turnover. The innovation integrates a general, product-agnostic informational campaign that encourages farmers to consider newer hybrids, alongside temporary retail price discounts that lower the financial cost of trial at the moment of purchase. Rather than promoting specific brands, the information component highlights the potential advantages of newer varieties and presents farmers with an overview of recently introduced products available in the market. By jointly addressing uncertainty about the value of newer hybrids and the perceived cost of experimentation, the intervention increases both the likelihood and intensity of initial adoption. Experimental evidence shows that information alone shifts farmer choices toward newer products, while the addition of a price promotion further increases purchase quantities and induces experimentation that persists into subsequent seasons, even after prices return to normal levels.

column16: GenebankAI: Accelerating Stress-Resilient Crop Discovery using Artificial Intelligence
column17: GenebankAI is an artificial intelligence–enabled approach that turns genebank information into practical recommendations for crop improvement. It brings together existing and newly generated data (such as passport information, genetic profiles, observed plant traits, and environment data) and uses machine learning to identify and rank promising accessions for specific needs (for example tolerance to drought, heat, salinity, and priority diseases). This helps breeders, researchers, and genebank teams move from “what is stored” to “what is most useful,” reducing manual screening and accelerating discovery of stress-resilient donor lines.; The work builds on IRRI’s International Rice Genebank and the wider CGIAR genebank network, responding to the persistent problem that many conserved accessions remain underused because trait information is incomplete, fragmented, or hard to search. It is designed to support a more user-friendly, faster selection and request process and to strengthen feedback loops so genebanks learn which materials perform well after distribution. The initiative also supports scaling across crops and partners by aligning tools, data standards, and capacity building for broader adoption.

column16: Deploying improved cassava varieties to support climate resilience and household food security in Sub saharan Africa
column17: This innovation introduces 14 new cassava varieties to help farming communities in Tanzania, Sierra Leone, and the Democratic Republic of Congo. These varieties offer high fresh root yields, strong nutritional value, and resilience to drought, heat, and irregular rainfall, safeguarding production under harsh conditions. Using advanced breeding and farmer-centred evaluations, the program identified varieties that perform well in the field and meet market and household needs. These include options for fresh consumption, processing, and biofortified uses, all developed entirely by IITA and national partners. Together, they expand farmers’ access to climate-resilient planting materials, strengthen food security, and support national efforts to build more resilient cassava value chains.

column16: Pal.ai: AI-powered rice advisory service using a tailored language model and curated rice knowledge library
column17: Pal.ai is an artificial intelligence–powered rice advisory service that provides timely, localized guidance to support farmers’ day-to-day decisions and help extension workers deliver consistent, high-quality digital advisories. The service is being developed with national partners and is informed by real farmer needs across multiple rice-growing provinces.; In 2025, the team built a training-ready dataset of more than 300 question-and-answer pairs based on actual farmer questions to improve the accuracy and usefulness of responses. User needs assessments with rice farmers in Isabela, Laguna, Iloilo, and South Cotabato captured local production contexts, dialect and communication preferences, and access constraints to guide product design and localization. The project also consolidated key rice knowledge resources into a curated knowledge library and designed a source architecture so responses can be grounded in referenced, trusted materials. In parallel, an extension training design and rollout approach was drafted for partner review to support wider deployment through extension systems.; Early farmer consultations highlighted priorities such as weather-related risks, diagnosis and timing of operations, trust and onboarding needs, and usability barriers driven by low digital confidence. These insights are being used to simplify the user experience and strengthen decision-support features. Overall, this work directly contributes to developing an agriculture-focused, AI-enabled advisory product that improves relevance and user engagement for rice advisory services.

column16: Agroclimatic Bulletin Builder: a platform designed to support the creation and dissemination of agroclimatic bulletins
column17: The innovation provides an intuitive environment for technical teams to design dynamic templates, configure customized workflows, and generate tailored bulletins for farmers and other beneficiaries. It allows flexible template definition so that each region can structure content according to its specific needs, including climate conditions, crop status, hazard alerts, recommendations, or lunar phases. Templates can incorporate review and approval steps for technical validation, while a built-in versioning mechanism ensures traceability, supports continuous improvement, and maintains adaptability across evolving use cases.; Built on a User-Centered Design approach, the platform and pre-designed templates undergo usability testing to ensure users can efficiently navigate and manage the full bulletin production workflow with minimal training. During composition, content can be entered manually or imported from external services via configurable API connectors, such as weather providers, agricultural advisory services, or communication channels. The system does not store or automatically generate external data, prioritizing transparency, flexibility, and user control.; Bulletins can be exported in standard dissemination formats, including PDF, PNG, and JPG. The project scope covers the full system development lifecycle, including architecture and design, implementation, testing, deployment, and usability assessments, ensuring the platform effectively supports human-centered workflows and meets the diverse needs of its users.

column16: Low Trophic Aquaculture Screening Framework: a digital analytical framework to assess low trophic aquatic species for sustainable aquaculture decision-making
column17: Reliable decisions on aquaculture development are often constrained by limited and uneven information on many fish species, particularly those feeding low in the food chain and with potential for sustainable production. The Low Trophic Aquaculture Screening Framework is designed to structure and interpret available evidence on locally occurring fish species in a transparent and systematic way. The framework organizes existing biological, nutritional, and production-related information into a small set of comparative indicators that allow species to be screened and compared, even when detailed data are not available. It draws on widely used global information sources, such as FishBase, and complements them with insights from published research and practitioner experience, explicitly documenting uncertainties and data gaps rather than masking them.  As an initial test, the framework was applied to freshwater and brackish water species that are native or commonly present in specific regions, using a limited number of parameters to explore relationships between feeding level, growth characteristics, nutritional value, and current use in aquaculture. The exploratory analysis demonstrated that meaningful patterns can be identified using partial data, while also highlighting where additional information is needed to improve confidence and relevance. By providing a structured way to compare locally relevant species under data-limited conditions, the Low Trophic Aquaculture Screening Framework supports research prioritization, helps identify low trophic species with potential for sustainable aquaculture development, and guides future data collection efforts. It lays the groundwork for more advanced analytical and decision-support tools and contributes to data-driven approaches that can inform aquaculture planning, policy discussions, and investment choices as evidence and capacity grow.

column16: Aquatic Food Systems Data and Digital Needs Framework: a participatory framework to Identify and Standardize Digital Data Needs for Aquatic Food Systems
column17: Reliable decisions in aquatic food systems depend on the availability of consistent, well-documented, and reusable data. In practice, data are often collected using different approaches, formats, and standards across countries and projects, making it difficult to compare results, identify gaps, or coordinate digital investments. This innovation is a participatory diagnostic framework designed to systematically characterize data and digital needs at country level for aquatic food systems. Its novelty lies in providing a standardized approach to assess what data exist, what are missing, how data are generated, and how digital tools are currently used, in a way that can be applied consistently across contexts. The Aquatic Food Systems Data and Digital Needs Framework brings together researchers, practitioners, and institutions to clarify priority data needs, document existing data flows, and identify gaps and constraints in data collection, management, and use. By applying the same framework across countries, it enables comparability, helps identify shared challenges and opportunities, and supports the identification of common pathways and synergies for data and digital development.  By making data and digital needs explicit and comparable, the innovation informs the design of standardized data protocols, ethical data practices, and coordinated digital solutions. It provides a practical foundation for improving data quality and interoperability, strengthening institutional practices, and guiding evidence-based planning, research, and policy processes in aquatic food systems.

column16: Evaluate mDSR field trials under One-million-hectare program
column17: Dry mDSR was designed to address labor, uneven emergence, and inefficient input use common in traditional dry seeding. The noticeable benefits of dry mDSR compared with wet direct seeding and farmer practices including substantially lower water use (up to 50%), lower greenhouse-gas emissions (up to 30%), reduced seed rates (<60 kg/ha), and reduced nitrogen needs (up to 20%) via deeper, more efficient fertilizer placement (about 50–60 mm). This crop establishment method also aligns with Vietnam’s low-emission rice initiatives, noting claims of 20–30% pesticide reductions and >5% yield gains. The prototype seeder was developed in an collaboration with Tu Sang company, with the configuration of tractor requirements (≥25 hp), and field capacity of ~0.5–1.0 ha/hour. Farmer also showed interest in adapting the technology for rotation crops with minor modifications.

column16: AI-powered data exploration tool developed by International Potato Center enables researchers to analyze agricultural datasets through natural language queries
column17: Agricultural researchers often struggle to analyze complex datasets due to technical barriers and lack of programming expertise. The International Potato Center developed Ask-the-Data, an artificial intelligence-powered web application that allows researchers to explore and analyze agricultural data using simple, conversational language instead of complex coding. The tool connects directly to research datasets and automatically generates statistical analyses, visualizations, and reports based on user questions. Deployed as a publicly accessible platform, this innovation transforms static data repositories into interactive research environments where scientists can quickly extract insights without technical programming skills. The tool demonstrates how AI can democratize data analysis in agricultural research and can be adapted for use across other research institutions, supporting evidence-based decision-making and advancing digital transformation in agricultural science.

column16: Co-design of a Gender Scorecard: A tool for scaling and monitoring gender mainstreaming guidelines within the Ministry of Agriculture - Ethiopia
column17: The Gender Scorecard aims to provide actionable insights, support accountability, and ensure that gender equality efforts are both measurable and contextually relevant within the Ethiopian agricultural sector. The Gender Scorecard is a comprehensive tool developed collaboratively by the Ministry of Agriculture (MoA) in Ethiopia, CARE-Ethiopia, and the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) to monitor and scale the implementation of gender mainstreaming guidelines of the MoA. The current version comprises of indicator-based questions, organised across two main assessment stages: system level (internal analysis of institutional structures, resources, capacity, and partnerships) and operational level (external analysis focusing on empowerment, resource access, decision-making, norms, and monitoring at the community and project levels). Each indicator is to be evaluated using a five-point Likert scale, using both quantitative and qualitative data collection methods, such as interviews, surveys, and focus group discussions.

column16: Hybrid school meals model to improve child nutrition in crisis-affected communities
column17: The International Food Policy Research Institute designed and tested a hybrid school meals model that combines milk with fortified cereal products to improve dietary quality for primary-school children living in conflict-affected areas of Yemen. The work responds to long-standing challenges faced by school feeding programs in humanitarian contexts, where food insecurity, micronutrient deficiencies, and disruptions to school attendance limit the effectiveness and expansion of conventional meal delivery approaches.; The model was assessed through a large-scale field experiment conducted in operational school settings, allowing researchers and implementing partners to examine feasibility, safety, and early nutrition outcomes under real-world crisis conditions. The intervention incorporated locally appropriate food-safety measures, supplier arrangements, and delivery procedures to ensure continuity during insecurity and supply interruptions.; The result provides governments, humanitarian organizations, and donors with evidence on a hybrid school feeding option that may strengthen resilience and nutritional impact incrementally while keeping operational and financial costs down. IFPRI led the study design, analysis, and dissemination of findings to global nutrition and education audiences, helping inform future program design and investment decisions for school meals in fragile and conflict-affected settings.

column16: Digital platform developed by AfricaRice uses satellite data to monitor rice production and climate impacts in Mali
column17: Rice production in Mali faces increasing threats from climate change, including unpredictable rainfall, droughts, and floods that affect crop yields and food security. To address this challenge, AfricaRice and the International Rice Research Institute developed an innovative digital monitoring system that combines satellite imagery with climate data and agricultural models. The platform tracks rice growth stages, water usage, and yield patterns across farming landscapes, providing real-time information about planting schedules, weather-related risks, and productivity trends. This technology enables early warning systems and helps policymakers, researchers, and development organizations make informed decisions about rice farming interventions. By monitoring climate risks and evaluating adaptation strategies, the platform supports the development of climate-resilient rice systems and strengthens food security planning in West Africa.

column16: An adaptable, modular, lean version of agrifood systems assessment survey
column17: This output documents IFPRI-led work to address a key constraint facing nutrition and food policy in India: the lack of integrated, locally relevant data linking agriculture, markets, diets, gender, and environmental risks. Building on earlier survey work under the Transforming Agrifood Systems in South Asia initiative, IFPRI researchers engaged with national and state-level policymakers and research institutions to assess how integrated agrifood systems surveys could better support state planning and program design. The work highlighted that existing data systems are often fragmented or too resource-intensive for routine government use. In response, and within limited available funding, IFPRI developed a streamlined nutrition survey module that can be adapted and embedded within existing survey platforms. This module offers a practical entry point for states seeking to strengthen evidence-informed decision-making and can be expanded or taken forward through future work if additional funding becomes available.

column16: Digital financial service for improving smallholder farmer resilience
column17: The innovation is a bundled credit-insurance solution, co-developed by IFPRI and scaling partners as part of the CGIAR Research Programs on Policies, Institutions and Markets (PIM) and Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security (CCAFS), and later Ukama Ustawi, S4I, and the Gender Accelerator. The solution determines a farmer’s creditworthiness by combining plot-level climate and soil health data with remote sensing and machine learning, developed using CGIAR data for ground-truthing. This is linked with picture-based insurance, pioneered by IFPRI to compensate farmers for visible crop damage from natural causes that could hamper loan repayment, protecting financial institutions from production risks that could lead to defaults. IFPRI-led randomized trials with approximately 5,000 farmers in two states in India, and seven counties in Kenya, validated the solution, proving its maturity and suitability for scaling. These trials demonstrated strong impacts on end-users’ financial inclusion, agricultural incomes, empowerment, and mental health, particularly among women.

column16: AgDataHub digital platform deployed by AfricaRice to enhance climate advisory services for farmers and decisionmakers in Mali
column17: AgDataHub Deployment to Improve Agrometeorological Bulletins and Advisory Services focuses on strengthening climate information delivery for agriculture through an integrated, data-driven digital platform. AgDataHub consolidates weather forecasts, historical climate data, satellite observations, and agro-climatic indicators into a single system that supports the production of timely, localized, and user-relevant agrometeorological bulletins. By enabling automated data processing, visualization, and dissemination, the platform improves the accuracy, consistency, and usability of advisories on rainfall, temperature, drought, floods, and crop management. The deployment emphasizes co-design with national meteorological services, agricultural extension systems, and end users to ensure institutional fit and operational sustainability. AgDataHub enhances early warning, seasonal planning, and risk management for farmers, extension agents, and decision-makers, while supporting climate adaptation strategies in agriculture. Ultimately, it strengthens climate services value chains, improves farmer decision-making, and contributes to resilient agricultural production under increasing climate variability and change.

column16: Web-based mapping tool developed by International Water Management Institute guides sustainable solar irrigation placement in Pakistan
column17: Solar Suitability Mapping is a web-based spatial decision-support tool, IWMI with funding from the SDC-SoLAR program and later completed and strengthened under the Climate Action Program and Policy Innovations Science Program (Area of Work 4). The main purpose of this innovation is to guide governments and development programs in identifying suitable and unsuitable locations for solar irrigation, while protecting groundwater resources. The tool was initially developed using data and conditions from Punjab, Pakistan and is now being upscaled in other provinces of pakistan intended for use by provincial departments, planners, policymakers, and solar irrigation programs to support sustainable adoption and upscaling of solar irrigation. This digital mapping tool helps decision-makers understand where solar-powered irrigation can be safely introduced and where it should be avoided. It brings together information about water availability, land conditions, climate, and groundwater stress to show which areas are suitable for solar irrigation and which areas are at risk of water depletion. By using this tool, government agencies and development programs can better target investments and subsidies to locations where solar irrigation can support farming without damaging water resources. It also helps protect sensitive groundwater areas by clearly identifying zones where pumping should be limited. Overall, the tool supports smarter planning and reduces the risk of uncontrolled water use.;

column16: Web-based mapping tool developed by AfricaRice helps farmers and planners identify suitable crop zones under climate change in Mali
column17: The Climate Suitability for Crop Maproom is an interactive, web-based decision-support tool that integrates climate data, crop requirements, and geospatial analysis to assess where and when crops can be sustainably grown under current and future climate conditions. It translates complex climate variables—such as rainfall, temperature, length of growing period, and climate variability—into clear, location-specific suitability maps. The Maproom enables users to explore seasonal, interannual, and long-term climate scenarios, supporting crop selection, spatial planning, and climate risk management. By combining historical climate records, satellite observations, and climate projections, it helps identify climate-resilient cropping zones and anticipate shifts in suitability due to climate change. Designed for policymakers, researchers, extension services, and development practitioners, the Climate Suitability for Crop Maproom strengthens evidence-based decision-making, supports climate-smart agriculture planning, and enhances adaptive capacity in agricultural systems facing increasing climate variability and change.

column16: Interactive web platform developed by AfricaRice to support disaster risk management and climate resilience planning in Mali
column17: The Mali Disaster Risk Management (DRM) Maproom is an interactive, web-based platform designed to support disaster preparedness, risk assessment, and decision-making in Mali. It integrates geospatial data, historical records, and real-time information on hazards such as floods, droughts, and extreme weather events, alongside socio-economic and agricultural vulnerability indicators. The Maproom enables users to visualize, analyze, and monitor disaster risks at national and local scales, providing actionable insights for early warning, emergency planning, and resource allocation. By combining satellite imagery, climate data, and local knowledge, the platform helps identify high-risk areas, anticipate impacts, and support targeted interventions to protect communities, infrastructure, and livelihoods. Designed for government agencies, NGOs, development partners, and researchers, the Mali DRM Maproom strengthens institutional capacity for disaster risk management, promotes data-driven decision-making, and fosters resilience in the face of climate variability and increasing environmental hazards.

column16: Web-based solar pump sizing tool developed by IWMI helps Pakistani farmers optimize irrigation systems and prevent groundwater overuse
column17: The Solar Irrigation Pump Sizing Tool (SIP-ST) is a web-based technical planning and design tool, developed by IWMI, initially supported through SDC-SoLAR funding and finalized under the Climate Action Program and Policy Innovations Science Program (Area of Work 4). The purpose of this tool is to help users select the right size of solar pump and solar panels based on farm conditions, crop water needs, and groundwater depth in order to improve efficiency and avoid over-pumping. The tool was developed using Punjab’s agricultural and irrigation context and is designed for use by farmers, service providers, government programs, and irrigation planners supporting solar irrigation deployment. This web-based planning tool helps farmers and service providers choose the right size of solar-powered pumping system for their fields. Users enter basic information such as crop type, field area, and water source depth. The tool then calculates how much water is needed for irrigation. Based on this, it suggests an appropriate pump and solar panel size. By promoting properly sized systems, the tool improves irrigation efficiency, lowers installation costs, and reduces the risk of excessive groundwater extraction.;

column16: Mobile decision-support tool developed by AfricaRice provides climate-smart rice farming recommendations for smallholder farmers in Mali
column17: RiceAdvice Lite is a mobile and web-based decision-support tool that provides farmers with location-specific, climate-smart agronomic recommendations for rice cultivation. By integrating local weather data, soil conditions, crop growth models, and management practices, the platform delivers tailored guidance on planting dates, fertilizer application, water management, pest and disease control, and harvesting. Designed for smallholder farmers, extension agents, and local agricultural advisors, RiceAdvice Lite helps optimize yields, reduce input costs, and minimize environmental impacts. The tool emphasizes simplicity, accessibility, and real-time updates, enabling farmers to make informed decisions under changing climatic and field conditions. By combining scientific knowledge with local context, RiceAdvice Lite enhances productivity, resilience, and profitability in rice systems, supports sustainable farming practices, and strengthens the capacity of communities to adapt to climate variability while promoting efficient resource use and improved food security.

column16: Ultra Low Glycemic index ORYLUX 6 parboiled rice
column17: This innovation produces rice that causes a much slower and lower rise in blood sugar after consumption, making it suitable for people seeking to prevent or manage diabetes and other diet-related conditions. It is achieved through a carefully controlled pre-cooking process, rather than through genetic modification or chemical additives.; ; The process involves soaking, steaming, drying, and milling rice grains under specific conditions. These steps modify the natural structure of the starch inside the grain so that part of it becomes harder for the human body to digest. As a result, glucose is released more gradually into the bloodstream after eating. At the same time, the process helps move and retain essential vitamins and minerals inside the grain that are normally lost during conventional processing.; ; The innovation combines appropriate processing conditions with rice types that naturally respond well to this treatment. The outcome is rice with an exceptionally low effect on blood sugar while maintaining desirable qualities such as good taste, acceptable texture, and familiar appearance. The rice cooks and is consumed in the same way as commonly eaten rice, allowing it to fit easily into everyday meals without requiring changes in food habits.; ; By improving how the body digests rice through processing alone, this innovation offers a practical, food-based response to the growing burden of diabetes and related health problems. It can be produced using existing rice value-chain infrastructure, making it suitable for large-scale adoption while supporting healthier diets and stronger local rice markets

column16: Adaptive scaling approach to enable food system transformation in the Global South
column17: Adaptive scaling views scaling as a living process that evolves alongside people, technologies, markets, institutions, and local conditions. Recognizing that systems change over time, adaptive scaling must adapt to those changes. It emphasizes relationships, learning, and collaboration among different actors, helping them work together to navigate complexity and support lasting transformation in food systems. It acts as a guiding compass, enabling innovators, decision-makers, and businesses identify where change is possible, manage risks and trade-offs, and align collective action as conditions shift. Adaptability is central to scaling efforts must be responsive, reflective, inclusive, and flexible to remain effective. In practice, operationalizing adaptive scaling is through four interconnected functions: Creating protected spaces where new ideas can be tested and improved; Supporting wider use by tailoring innovations to local needs and contexts; Removing barriers by aligning policies, finance, skills, and infrastructure; and embedding scaling into broader systems, influencing rules, norms, and ways of working to enable system change.;

column17: Agricultural innovations often struggle to scale effectively due to inadequate strategic planning and investment readiness. CGIAR's Scaling for Impact initiative developed a conceptual framework for an artificial intelligence-enabled web application that would help project teams create structured scaling strategies for mature agricultural innovations. The framework defines how AI tools could assist teams in assessing investment readiness, aligning technical solutions with financing needs, and connecting with appropriate partners. While still in early design phase, this groundwork establishes a systematic approach that could eventually support responsible scaling of impactful agricultural innovations globally. The conceptualization began in November 2025 and continues development through 2026 as a pilot initiative.

column16: Dashboard for Hot-spots and Land Suitability to inform investment, research, and scaling of climate-smart agronomic solutions in Middle East and North Africa
column17: This report describes a Web-GIS decision-support dashboard (INNOVATION) designed to map land suitability, agricultural hot-spots, and yield gaps across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region in a user-friendly way. The dashboard aims to reduce the barrier to using geospatial evidence by integrating interactive maps, data layers, charts, filters, and query tools so users can explore and compare spatial patterns without specialized GIS skills.; ; The tool targets major crops including wheat, barley, chickpea, lentil, faba bean, rice, maize, and cotton, and provides both visualization and derived indicators to support evidence-based targeting of interventions (e.g., where suitability is high but yields are low). The architecture is explicitly open-source and scalable, built around GeoServer as the spatial data server and Leaflet as the web-mapping client, supporting interoperability and maintainability. The geographic scope listed includes: Algeria, Egypt, Iran, Iraq, Israel, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Morocco, Malta, Oman, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Syria, Tunisia, Uzbekistan, and Yemen.; Overall, the report positions the dashboard as a practical platform for farmers, extensionists, researchers, and students to identify priority zones for investment, research, and scaling of climate-smart agronomic solutions, with the longer-term intent of integrating additional layers and analytics as new datasets become available.;

column16: Cropping Systems Design under Different Climate Change Scenarios in Non-Tropical Drylands in Morocco
column17: This report develops a decision-ready framework (INNOVATION) for redesigning cropping systems in non-tropical drylands under increasing heat, drought, and rainfall variability. It combines harmonized data inputs (climate, soils, management and constraints), standardized indicators, process-based simulation using APSIM, and a decision layer to identify robust system options across current and future climates.; The Morocco case study contrasts Settat (more climate-variable) and Merchouch and evaluates factorial combinations of (i) rotation design (cereal-dominant vs diversified rotations), (ii) tillage (conventional vs zero tillage with residue retention), and (iii) water management (rainfed vs targeted supplementary irrigation). Future climate risk is explored using CMIP6-aligned pathways (including low to high forcing scenarios).; The report’s main message is that resilience comes from bundled redesign rather than single changes. Simulations indicate that diversified rotations increase biomass inputs and improve soil organic carbon trajectories while raising median wheat yields. Zero tillage improves soil water conservation and stabilizes yields, with the largest benefits in dry seasons. Supplementary irrigation reduces interannual yield variability—especially in Settat—and interacts positively with soil-improving practices that reduce water demand. The recommended “resilience bundle” for Moroccan drylands is diversified rotations + zero tillage/residue retention + targeted supplementary irrigation at critical growth stages, supported by validation and scaling pathways.";

column16: Economic modeling tool developed by IRRI to measure how agricultural productivity improvements affect farm income in Mexico
column17: Agricultural productivity gains don't always translate directly into higher farm incomes due to complex market interactions and price effects. IRRI developed an equilibrium displacement model that analyzes these relationships by examining how productivity changes in specific crops affect overall farm value-added income. The model uses a two-commodity, multi-output, three-factor framework to capture the interconnected nature of agricultural markets. Applied to Mexico's agricultural sector, this tool helps policymakers and researchers understand the economic impacts of productivity interventions before implementation. The modeling approach provides crucial insights for designing more effective agricultural policies that maximize income benefits for farmers, particularly important for poverty reduction strategies in developing countries.

column16: Pathways for scaling the use of TV-disseminated technologies
column17: Disseminating agricultural information through edutainment - which translates scientific weather and agronomic information into actionable advice for smallholder farmers and disseminates this through national television and complementary digital channels - may not be sufficient to foster the use of recommended practices and technologies. Farmers may lack access to TV and recommended inputs might not be available, especially in remote areas. For instance, in Zambia, where CGIAR has supported the production of Munda Makeover, modeled after Kenya's popular TV show Shamba Shape Up, TV access is limited in rural areas, and farmers are required to travel long distances to obtain their inputs, increasing transaction costs. The International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) therefore evaluated impacts of two scaling pathways to strengthen the use of TV-disseminated technologies: (i) organizing screenings of Munda Makeover in villages, and (ii) organizing roadshows, or input fairs, closer to farmers' homes, where they can purchase recommended inputs. The interventions are being evaluated by means of rigorous impact evaluation and learning components, including a cluster-randomized trial assessing exposure, knowledge gains, and adoption pathways. IFPRI’s analytical work generates causal evidence on how to strengthen the impacts of mass media–based climate services on farmer decision-making, and identifies constraints to uptake, informing iterative improvement of the model. By combining media-led delivery and roadshows with embedded learning and evaluation, Munda Makeover represents a scalable, evidence-informed approach to climate information services that strengthens resilience and productivity among smallholder farmers.

column16: Assessing Agricultural Water Insecurity Experiences (AgWISE)
column17: Women’s water needs are traditionally understood as relating to water accessed and used for drinking, cooking, and other domestic tasks, including caregiving. The Agriculture Water InSecurity (AgWISE) module is an adaptation of the Water Insecurity Experiences (WISE) Scales. Co-designed with Northwestern University and in a participatory manner with local communities in southern coastal Bangladesh, AgWISE was applied in Bangladesh to generate evidence of women’s experiences of water insecurity in relation to agrifood systems. The AgWISE is a methodological innovation—a set of simple, context-specific questions that helps translate women’s everyday agricultural water insecurity experiences into actionable evidence and insight for water policy and governance interventions. The AgWISE tool allows for quantifying the material, as well as the rarely assessed relational and psychosocial experiences of water insecurity. In Bangladesh, our focus was on assessing intersectional gender disparities in agrifood systems focusing on class, religion, age and ethnicity. Designed to ensure flexibility and adaptability to the local context, the tool generates reliable data and evidence to enable more inclusive climate adaptation, food security, and gender-equity interventions. Evidence from the AgWISE module is presented across multiple forums and policy platforms to inform potential revisions to the National Women Development Policy and to guide the planning and implementation of Gender Responsive Budgeting initiatives.

column16: Detection of Alternaria padwickii (Ganguly) M.B. Ellis in Rice Seeds Using Hyperspectral Imaging to Enhance Seed Health Assessment in Germplasm Exchange
column17: The international exchange of rice germplasm is fundamental for crop improvement and production but poses risks of spreading seed-borne pathogens like Alternaria padwickii. Conventional detection methods, such as the blotter test, are effective but destructive and time-consuming. This study was conducted to investigate hyperspectral imaging (HSI) in the 400-1000 nm range as a rapid, non-destructive alternative method in detecting A. padwickii in rice seeds. Analyzing over 600 seeds from diverse rice accessions across 299 spectral bands, the research showed that the spectra related to the targeted biological regions of interest, such as the apiculus and sterile lemma, resulted to higher specificity, sensitivity and overall accuracy compared to the whole seed spectra. Dimensionality reduction using Partial Least Squares -Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA) and Variable Importance in Projection (VIP)-based wavelength selection identified the most informative features that resulted to perfect classification performance and predictive powers  that were exhibited by all machine learning models used.; ; This work demonstrates how HSI can strengthen seed health monitoring when sharing across borders. By offering faster, safer, and scalable pathogen detection, HSI helps ensure that genebanks maintain high-quality collections, supports disease-free germplasm exchange, and protects the integrity of breeding materials ensuring compliance with international regulations. Ultimately, this innovation contributes to more resilient conservation systems and healthier rice crops for farmers and future generations.

column17: Here is the description: Agent Bi is a platform that is being developed as a software backbone for last-mile delivery in Agricultural markets but could also be adapted for other sectors like health. The platform aims at turning fragmented, informal field agent networks into credentialed, and data rich eco-systems with visibility on their performance.; Agent Bi will elevate agents from informal workers to verified professionals by providing verifiable professional identity, performance tracking and recognition, career growth opportunities and operational utilities including tools for record-keeping and farmer registration.; For Agribuinesses, it will serve as a decision-making tool that transforms data into actionable oversight. It will provide structured agent screening and recruitment (which has been a persistent challenge faced by Agribusinesses), predictive heatmaps that integrate agent activity and behaviour to spot rollout failures before they occur and integrated modules for A/B testing of discounts, incentives, bundles and repayment patterns to determine which strategies drive the most adoption.; In order to analyze the Agribusinesses’, return on investments when engaging agents, the platform will have a Cost Benefit Analysis plug-in that has already been validated by selected Agribusinesses, together with the platform wireframes. column16: CGIAR AI hub: Transforming Agri research to AI Innovations
column17: Agricultural research faces increasing pressure to deliver faster, more effective solutions to global food security challenges. To address this need, CGIAR established an artificial intelligence hub in Abu Dhabi that connects the organization's scientific expertise with the United Arab Emirates' advanced AI ecosystem. The hub transforms CGIAR research into practical AI-powered tools for real-world agricultural decisions. Working with CGIAR Centers, Science Programs, and the Digital Transformation Accelerator, the hub develops products spanning agricultural advisory services, genetic resource management, water management, policy analysis, and livestock systems. Each product combines CGIAR's extensive data and scientific knowledge with external AI capabilities to accelerate development and adoption, ultimately increasing the real-world impact of agricultural research.

column16: Rapid Cycle Recurrent Selection (RCRS) in rice
column17: RCRS approach reduces the breeding cycle time from three years to one year. This approach was specifically designed to accelerate genetic gains for traits underpinning aerobic and DSR (direct-seeded rice) adaptation. The introduction of RCRS has resulted in a step change in breeding efficiency, enabling rapid recycling of superior parents and significantly shortening the time required to respond to emerging DSR constraints. This accelerated cycling has increased selection intensity and improved the probability of fixing favorable alleles for aerobic adaptation, early vigor, and establishment stability. Shortened breeding cycles and higher genetic gain per unit time directly support faster varietal replacement, enabling farmers to access improved germplasm more rapidly.

column15: Accelerated varietal improvement and seed delivery of legumes and dryland cereals in Africa (AVISA).: 0
column16: Regional on-farm verification trials through TRICOT to generate high-quality, representative, and actionable data on the performance of new cowpea varieties under real-world conditions to speed up variety adoption and release.
column17: The ITA breeding program successfully implemented a regional on-farm trial following the triadic comparisons of technology options (tricot) method. The main aim of the trial was to obtain high-quality farmer feedback on the performance of cowpea varieties and new breeding lines under real-world conditions to speed up variety adoption and release. The trial covered six countries across West and Central Africa, including Nigeria, Niger, Ghana, Mali, Burkina Faso, and Cameroon. The trial targeted 630 cowpea farmers across the region, both men and women. A total of twenty-one cowpea varieties were tested, out of which 2 were checks (a local variety and a commercial variety). The final number of registered farmers was 615, who contributed to this trial. Each participant assessed 3 different varieties and provided rankings for 14 trait(s). Trait preference analysis revealed that cowpea Grain size was the most preferred trait among farmers in the region, followed closely by marketability, grain color, early maturity, and Striga resistance. Six varieties outperformed both local and commercial varieties based on farmers’ overall rankings. These varieties will be recommended for further testing for specific adaptation and release to the farmers in the region.

column16: Women's Leadership in Agrifood Systems Conceptual Framework and Fieldwork Toolkit
column17: This innovation develops a shared conceptual framework and accompanying fieldwork guides to advance understanding, measurement, and support of women’s leadership in agrifood systems across diverse contexts. Recognizing leadership as multifaceted—spanning formal, informal, collective, relational, and organizational forms—the initiative integrates insights from CGIAR research, practitioner experience, and multi-country qualitative and quantitative studies to articulate how women exercise influence, what enables leadership to emerge, and how leadership translates into downstream agrifood outcomes. Through a collaborative process involving researchers, civil society, and policy stakeholders, the innovation synthesizes existing evidence into a unified framework organized around three pillars: understanding leadership, supporting leadership, and assessing leadership impacts. This framework is paired with adaptable fieldwork guides designed to help partners and researchers systematically document leadership pathways, enabling environments, and trade-offs in real-world settings. Together, these tools provide a practical foundation for generating comparable evidence across countries and organizational types, strengthening learning, and informing more effective, gender-responsive interventions in agrifood systems.

column16: Integrated delivery model for biofortified crops developed by CGIAR and partners tested in India for scaling nutrition programs
column17: This comprehensive delivery model tackles widespread micronutrient deficiencies by coordinating production, distribution, and consumption of nutrient-enhanced crops including high-zinc rice and wheat, and high-iron pearl millet. The model creates an ecosystem connecting research institutions, farmers, government programs, and private companies to deliver nutritious foods at scale. CGIAR and India's agricultural research council provide scientific expertise and crop varieties, while HarvestPlus Solutions builds implementation partnerships. The National Rural Livelihood Mission mobilizes women's self-help groups to expand production and create supply chains. Quality assurance through testing and certification builds market confidence. The model operates through government school feeding programs integrating biofortified grains into tribal nutrition initiatives, and commercial markets via the NEWTRII brand using online distribution. Testing in India demonstrates significant health improvements, including reduced iron deficiency in women and children.

column16: IFPRI Welfare-Assessment Method Integrating Learning, Lifetime Earnings, and Equity to Guide School Feeding Investments in Fragile Settings
column17: This innovation is a replicable analytical method developed by the International Food Policy Research Institute to evaluate school feeding and similar programs that build human capital.; The approach combines evidence from randomized trials on learning and nutrition outcomes with projections of lifetime earnings and models distributional effects across population groups, allowing decision-makers to assess overall social returns in a single, transparent benefit–cost framework.; Previously, economic evaluations of school feeding often considered short-term outcomes or financial returns alone. This method addresses that gap by explicitly valuing education gains, long-term income impacts, and equity benefits for disadvantaged children, making it suitable for humanitarian and development contexts where trade-offs across objectives are acute.; The innovation was developed through IFPRI-led research synthesized in a global review of school-meal evidence and formalized through a peer-reviewed application demonstrating the method for national school feeding programs. It is designed for adaptation by governments, donors, and humanitarian agencies seeking to prioritize investments that improve nutrition, learning, and resilience in fragile environments

column17: The Pakistan Drought Monitoring System (PakDMS) is an online portal that brings together weather, rainfall, and water-related information to help identify emerging drought risks at an early stage. By improving access to timely and reliable information, PakDMS supports earlier planning and response in agriculture and water management, benefiting farmers and institutions responsible for managing water resources in drought-prone areas.

column16: Allele mining pre-breeding initiative to introgress validated novel genes from CGIAR genebank sources into elite cowpea lines to enhance breeding heat and drought tolerant cowpea varieties
column17: IITA in partnership with the University of Clifornia Riverside (UCR) implimented an inititive to mine the climate adaptive genes from IITA genetic resource center (GRC). Molecur data from over 2000 cowpea genebank accessions were used in combination with climate data obtained based on the geographical passport data of each accession to conduct environmental genome-wide association studies (EnvGWAS). The EnvGWAS conducted by the UCR team, identified sources of heat and drought tolerance from the genebak. Ten Introgression populations were developed by IITA team using the genebank sources. The populations are at F1 generation stage and the plan is to conduct up to 3 backcrosses while tracking the drought and heat alleles using the top EnvGWAS SNPs once these are made available to the breeding team. For effective introgression, EnvGWAS favorable alleles will be incorporated into the existing cowpea mid-density DArTag panel to create an effective platform for tracking the favorable alleles in the backcross progenies..

column16: Development and standardization of a Standard Operating Procedure for the detection of Ceratobasidium sp. by PCR in in vitro cassava.
column17: This result corresponds to the design, validation, and formalization of a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for the phytosanitary detection of Ceratobasidium sp. in in vitro maintained cassava material using end-point PCR, developed as part of the germplasm health activities of the GHU-CIAT laboratory.; The diagnostic methodology was registered with the Instituto Colombiano Agropecuario -ICA (NPPO), the national phytosanitary authority, in compliance with the regulations applicable to fungal pathogen diagnostics and processes associated with the safe movement of germplasm. In parallel, the method was validated under the operational conditions of GHU-CIAT, considering key parameters such as analytical specificity against fungi commonly associated with in vitro crops, repeatability, robustness, and consistency of assay performance in cassava plant matrices.; To ensure the reliability of the method, characterized positive controls, as well as negative and reaction controls, were established, enabling continuous monitoring of analytical performance, implementation of quality control measures, and objective interpretation of results. Subsequently, the procedure was standardized through the definition of amplification conditions, critical technical parameters, acceptance criteria, quality control requirements, and associated records.; The process concluded with the preparation of the final SOP documentation, integrating technical, regulatory, and quality assurance requirements, and ensuring alignment with the principles of ISO/IEC 17025 and the current ICA regulations. This SOP significantly contributes to strengthening the laboratory’s diagnostic capacity for the early detection of Ceratobasidium sp. and supports phytosanitary management and the safe distribution of cassava germplasm conserved and disseminated by CIAT.

column16: Development of an innovative framework for carbon - neutral multifunctional landscape using advanced data driven tools enabled real-time runoff measuring device
column17: This pioneering research introduces an Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled real-time runoff measuring device designed to transform how we measure, monitor and manage surface runoff in streams. Traditional runoff measurement methods are often manual, costly, and limited in scope—especially in remote or inaccessible terrains. Our device bridges this gap by integrating advanced sensors, automated data logging, and real-time transmission, enabling high-resolution runoff monitoring across diverse watershed conditions.; The device is engineered for precision, resilience, and scalability:; •	Advanced Sensors: Capture surface runoff with high accuracy.; •	IoT Connectivity: Enables seamless remote monitoring and real-time data access.; •	Terrain Adaptability: Operates reliably in inaccessible or power-deficient regions.; •	Multi-Watershed Calibration: Ensures consistent performance across varied landscapes.; •	Automated Analysis: Supports continuous data acquisition for hydrological modelling.; Surface runoff is a key driver of soil erosion, sediment analysis, and water resources research and planning. Excessive runoff leads to land degradation, nutrient loss, and reduced groundwater recharge—threatening agricultural productivity and ecosystem health. Reliable runoff data is the backbone of predictive watershed model simulations. Our device empowers researchers and planners to:; •	Calibrate and validate models with real-time data.; •	Simulate rainfall-runoff dynamics with greater precision.; •	Assess land-use change impacts on hydrology.; •	Advance precision agriculture by linking runoff with soil moisture and crop water needs.; This innovation marks a significant step toward data-driven, climate-smart watershed management. It offers:; •	A cost-effective, scalable solution for hydrological research.; •	A technological bridge between conventional monitoring and modern analytics.; •	A tool for sustainable resource planning in the face of climate variability.; By empowering stakeholders with actionable runoff data, this device strengthens the foundation for resilient agriculture, improved water governance, and long-term environmental sustainability.

column16: Artificial intelligence tools for automated cowpea trait measurement piloted by CGIAR researchers and partners in Africa
column17: In 2025, the cowpea breeding program in colaboration with University of Clifornia Davis, Quantitative Engineering Design (QED.ai) and the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT (ABC) made a breakthrough by introducing Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled phenotyping tools into cowpea research. Using robotics and mobile devices equipped with deep-sensing cameras, thousands of high-resolution images were collected from cowpea experimental plots. These datasets are being used to train AI models for automated scoring of key phenotypic traits, including stand count, canopy coverage, flowering time, pod maturity time, and pod load. A Trait data extraction pipeline and an application named GxExMINI Phenotyping App was successfully developed that utilizes the trained models to predict the traits and output it for breeding selection decisions. The entire pipeline  include i) Sensors and hardware (Camera, weather, GPS, Ground and aerial plotform, and integrated phone snsing system) , ii) Data upload and storage (data storage, app upload, and data management), iii) Data processing (cordless image stitching, link to field design,  and AI model creation), iv) Trait output (Stand count, plant height, flower traits etc, export and visualize traits). This innovation represents a paradigm shift from manual data collection to high-throughput, objective, and time-efficient phenotyping. The integration of AI complements genomic selection efforts and enhances precision in trait evaluation. The success of this pilot demonstrates the potential of digital technologies to improvenhance data quality, acceleraexpedite breeding cycles, and ultimately deliver superior cowpea varieties faster to farmers more quickly.

column16: A holistic framework for valuing ecosystem services in livestock farming
column17: Analysis of socio-ecological systems is anchored on the humans-in-nature concept. Natural systems produce ecosystem services for humans, while social systems interfere in natural systems with positive and negative externalities. Livestock production takes place in a natural ecosystem with various human interventions leading to the production of both ecosystem services and disservices, and hence environmental benefits and costs. Our objective is to identify the main ecosystem services and environmental benefits present in livestock farming and propose a valuation strategy that is potent to provide credible estimates. To this effect, we established an expert working group which: 1) conducted an extensive literature review and identified and prioritized seven ecosystem services and three environmental benefits to value namely, food and feed production, carbon storage and sequestration, microclimatic regulation, soil fertility, habitat for species, aesthetic appreciation, generation/prevention of methane emissions, reduction/aggravation of water footprint, and degradation/preservation of landscapes, and 2) implemented a selection of integral valuation methods (social, economic, and ecological) in several case studies, specifically, evaluation of the reduction of methane emissions in silvopastoral systems with improved forages in beef and dairy production systems in Colombia and Kenya. Further refinement of the integral valuation method will be fundamental for the economic and environmental assessment of different interventions in livestock farming and will close the gaps and improve on some of the limitations of traditional cost-benefit analyses. We observed positive outcomes, where the environmental value prevented from being lost or newly generated due to interventions, outweighed the associated implementation costs – leading to high returns on investment. The integral value of ecosystem services and environmental benefits will provide invaluable support for informed decision-making on livestock production options, specific land and ecosystem restoration initiatives, and the potential return on investment for controlling ecosystem degradation or for enhancing ecosystem services.

column16: A novel approach to agricultural policy analysis applied to crop diversification in Bangladesh
column17: Traditional approaches to policy analysis often provide only a partial understanding of the complexities of agricultural policies and their outcomes. This study addresses the important problem of how to evaluate such policies in a manner that captures their effects across historical, political, socio- economics and environmental dimensions and operational challenges. To do so, the paper develops and applies a new analytical framework that combines elements of policy and program analysis with validation through the views of experts and intended beneficiaries. The framework integrates multiple dimensions into a cohesive structure and specifically applied to the case of crop diversification policies in Bangladesh (1971–2023), combining a PRISMA-guided systematic review of 1223 projects, trend analysis of crop production and qualitative insights from 12 key informants. The findings show that the framework uncovers critical gaps in policy design, highlights institutional and operational constraints, and brings out the perspectives of diverse stakeholders, thereby providing a more grounded account of agricultural policy outcomes of Bangladesh. The study contributes by offering a practical and adaptable method that improves transparency, deepens understanding of institutional dynamics, and supports the formulation of context-specific and effective interventions. The insights from Bangladesh demonstrate the broader relevance of the approach for low- and middle-income countries seeking to strengthen agricultural policy and promote sustainable development.

column16: Tool for Monitoring Agrobiodiversity, Gender and Social Inclusion in School Meal Programs
column17: This survey-based tool has been developed to support schools, program teams, and local governance actors in systematically reflecting on how school meal systems engage with two closely interconnected priorities: the use of agrobiodiversity in school meals and the inclusion of gender and socially marginalized groups in planning, implementation, and decision-making processes. The tool is intended as a structured reflection and learning instrument rather than a compliance or evaluation checklist. Its primary purpose is to help users understand current practices, identify gaps, and recognize opportunities to strengthen school meal programs in ways that are more nutritious, inclusive, and environmentally sustainable. Through a structured set of questions, the tool supports the characterization of how locally available and diverse crops are currently used in school meals, as well as how decisions related to menus, sourcing, procurement, and monitoring are made. At the same time, it encourages reflection on whose voices are included in these processes, with particular attention to gender dynamics and the participation of socially marginalized groups, including women, youth, and small-scale producers. By bringing these dimensions together, the tool helps make visible the linkages between food diversity, governance practices, and social inclusion within school meal systems. The tool was developed by the Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT and is supported by the Food Planet Prize and the Curt Bergfors Foundation and the CGIAR research for development network. It builds on ongoing research and practice at the intersection of agrobiodiversity, nutrition, and gender and social inclusion. At this stage, the tool is being piloted with a small number of schools in India. This piloting phase is intentionally participatory and iterative. Schools and program actors are invited not only to use the tool but also to actively provide feedback on its content, structure, and usability, with the aim of improving and refining it for wider use by school meal planners and implementers. The tool offers several potential benefits. The information generated can help schools and program teams design school meals that are more nutritious and environmentally friendly, while also strengthening linkages with local farming systems and supporting local farmers. It can also support more inclusive planning and decision-making by highlighting who participates, who is excluded, and where greater inclusion may be possible. In parallel, the information collected will contribute to the project team’s understanding of how to improve the monitoring of agrobiodiversity and gender and social inclusion within school meal programs.

column16: Targeted Climate-Smart Irrigation Advisory (T-CSIA)
column17: The Targeted Climate-Smart Irrigation Advisory (T-CSIA) is a location-specific decision-support tool that integrates remote-sensing–based drought and climate indicators with seasonal climate forecasts (temperature and rainfall seasonal probabilities) to deliver targeted irrigation forward looking seasonal advisories to farmers. The forward looking advisories can be generated up to one month in advance. Therefore, using georeferenced farmer locations, the innovation provides timely advance guidance of irrigation demand thereby giving farmers time to prepare relevant infrastructure and investments needed for upcoming season. The objective is to improve water-use efficiency, lower labour and production costs, and reduce yield variability amid increasing climate variability. The innovation focuses on improving farmer decision-making to optimize production using target irrigation or drought resistant crops rather than expanding irrigated area.
